2 DENNIS APTHORP - I heard the news of the death in October of Dennis Apthorp, owner of 'Bella' in the Cruiser Fleet, I am sure the sympathy of all Club Members go out to his wife Joyce at this time. COMMODORE 'S NOTES With the end of the Sailing Season, we have held the Laying Up Supper at the Heybridge which was an ex tremely pleasant evening. On behalf of us all I would like to thank Peter Bloomfield and the Social Committee for organising the event. Our thoughts now turn to the Winter activity to carry out a number of tasks at the Club ready for next year. These are being organised on a Fleet basis similar to last year and I would ask everyone to support their Fleet Captains so that the work is complete in time. If you can, please contact them rather than waiting for them to contact you. Elsewhere in this issue (see Page 11) the list for OOD duty is published. Please check the list carefully for your duty date and make re-arrangements well in advance if you cannot attend, Without an OOD on site, no Club racing can take place, I would like to wish you all e happy Christmas and a successful season next year. N.T. Pembleton Ed's note: Commodore's AGM report is deferred until next issue due to lack of space. AMENDMENTS TO BYE LAWS The Main Committee have approved the following Bye Law amendments and additions as indicated by the passages underlined. These amendments become effective from 15th October 1989 6. CAMPING Camping shall be restricted to members and their Guests except that it shall be open to members of R.Y.A clubs attending open race meetings at the Club. Camping shall only be permitted at times decided by the Committee, Before establishing camp, members shall report to the camping marshall or the 0.0.D., to pay the appropriate fee and receive any instructions on siting. No tent or caraven is to be on the site prior to 0830 hrs on the first day of camping and all tents and caravens must be removed before 2100 hrs on the last day of camping. 9. Winter Storage. Only those boats for which a Winter Storage fee has been paid may be left on the site between lst December and Ist March, All such boats are to be visibly marked with the Class of boat, Name and Telephone number of the Owner, The owner of any boat left on the site between the above dates for which a Storage Fee has not been paid will be subject to a fine not exceeding twice the Storage Fee which would have been payable. CHRISTMAS WORKING PARTY = FRIDAY 29TH DECEMBER Lots of helpers with rakes, spades and various other gardening-type tools would be a most welcome sight. Racebox flagpole to be taken down; work on Tender Rack; clearing of Ditch; cutting back of Hedge; clearing sea wall of any debris to allow future mowing; repair of a fence; clearing shingle fran hard, etc. Particularly welcome to Dave Fletcher would be any members who could came along with their Metal Detectors in order to seek out and retrieve any underground stakes in the dinghy park. Sunday 31st December OSEA ICICLE Race Round Osea Island for Dinghies, Sailboards & Catamarans Starting at lpm (HW 2, 39pm) Prizes for each class and the overall Handicap Winner Entrance fee £1, including soup and a roll after racing Offers of help with Rescue Boasts, Galley, Race Organisation Most Welcome Interested? Contact Ian Crumpen [redacted] or Nigel James 0245 [redacted] OSEA ICICLE: As OOD at this event, I would remind potential sailors that personal buoyancy will be required to be worn by helms and crews to qualify for the race. The Club also requires that wet or dry suits must be worn by competitors. The water will be extremely cold whatever the air temperature on the day, and these rules will be enforced, It should also be said that the Club rules are the minimum requirements for personal safety, but as always it is the individual's own responsibility to decide if he/she is adequately experienced and kitted out for the conditions on the day. Let's hope for a fine day and some good sailing. Ray Ball, [redacted]

SOLO FLEET NEWS You will all know by now that John Salmon has stepped down after a very successful 3 years as your Fleet Captain, Appointing me as Solo Fleet Captain is a bit like giving the job to the Goalkeeper but I've got Janet Keeble, the Lady World Champion, to look after the front of the fleet. Most of you will now be keeping your Solo's off the water until the start of the 1990 season. Now is the time to start on all those go-fast mods, but don't forget the simple things like renewing all those little bits and bobs that wear aut. Drinks are on the Solo Fleet Captain for all Solos on the water for Spring Points No.1 on Sunday 25th March, but anyone suffering gear failure buys me a drink, December/January Solo events are: 1, Working Party - Friday 29th December The Solo Fleet special job is to remove the evergreens from around the old cess pits so that the dinghy park can be extended. Bring gardening tools, bush saws, gloves etc, 2. Maldon Rowing Race - Saturday 30th December Start time 1300hrs from Maldon Little Ship Club, Hythe Quay. Come and support the Marconi Fisherman, We have two Solo ravers - myself and Roger Smith; and a couple of galley slaves - Ray Ball and Mike Hellewell, Mike is almost a Solo sailor, he has an old hull at home and keeps threatening to rig it up. Come and support us and get your Cherry Brandy tot from the prize we won last year, 3. Solo Dinner Party - Friday 19th January Venue as last year - the Cross Keys, Roxwell = 1930hrs - good food, good company = don't miss it. Please phone Pat Stuart to say how many are coming. Work: 0245 25820: Home: 0245 [redacted] Malcolm Stuart, Solo Fleet Captain Sa ed CRUISER FLEET NEWS Cruiser Fleet AGM: Wednesday 31st January 1990, 8pm, Conference Room, MASC, Beehive Lane, Mooring Buoys It breaks my heart to see so many defunct and deflated Mooring Buoys coming up at the end of each season, (Especially as one of them was mine.) I have approached Hippo Marine who manufacture buoys for the trade - the Visitors Buoy is one of theirs and has proved successful for a season, with no boat on it for most of the time, Although the initial cost of a buoy is high, they should last for many years, (They have been making them for eleven years.) Anyone who wants one, or who wants more information, should contact me before Christmas and a block order can be placed before the Boat Show. If we get a large enough order, we should be able to get a 10% discount. The cost for the S83 buoy will be in the region of £108 and the SB2 £139, less any discount I can get. Derek Hall, Billericay (0277) [redacted]. MIRROR FLEET NEWS At the recent Mirror Fleet AGM the competition for the post of Mirror Fleet Captain was intense but was finally won by David Ball age 13 and eleven-twelfths. Thank you to the Boreham family for hosting the meeting, - a pity that it turned out to be such a foggy night. David can be contacted at the same address and telephone number as Navigans Editor and will, I am sure, put pen to paper for Navigans on a few occasions in the future, Please do support the Fleet by getting your Mirror out on the water early and late season, and not just during Cadet Week! And please also see Page > for dates of Cadet Winter meetings - all ages welcomed by Mike while he is teaching the Cadets, Ed ### RNLI SPONSORED ROW - David was hoping to use a hard tender this year as a change from our inflatable which he used last year; and also he has had a recent offer from another of our cadets to join him if a suitable boat for rowing by two people can be found. If any of our Cruiser owners can lend either a one-man or two-man tender complete with oars, capable of being carried on a Mirror road trailer so that we can transport it ourselves, the Ball family (0245 [redacted]) would like to hear from you.

WINTER CADET PROGRAMME FOR 1990 Theme: Enjoy and Achieve DATES: 1) Sat 10th February; 2) Sat 24th February; 3) Sat 10th March; 4) Sat 24th March; 5) Sat 7th April. TIMES: 14,30 = 16.30 pm A full programme for each day will be arranged. There will be practical work, interesting discussion on At 1 specialist subjects as well as films, fun and games. We hope to see many of the younger cadets come along - however there is no age limit, Mike Turner, Cadet Fleet Captain HANDICAP NEWS Having been asked to represent the Handicap Fleet for next year, the first thing I must do is get to know its members, Being a relatively new member of the Club, there are many of you whose faces I cannot put a name to, although I may well have spoken to you during the course of 1989, So let's have a Handicap Fleet Meet ing/New Year's Drink/or even an AGM! We are going to hold this at the Crown Pub at Sandon, on Thursday llth January 1990 at 8pm. Potentially the Handicap Fleet is the largest at the Club with some 70-odd craft in the Dinghy park. Unfortunately only a handful of these have participated in the Club's racing programme during the past season and those of us who do race regularly on Sundays share the disappointment of the small turnout from the Handicap Fleet. There is no doubt that racing will improve your sailing skills and help you to tune your boat for a better performance. The Club provided a full sailing programme from March through to November, together with a most efficient race organisation team and competent rescue cover for participants. Last year Mike Duckmanton ran a race training day which was of tremendous help to those who attended. I think that Mike was a little disappointed that so few attended and I am hopeful that we can persuade him to repeat the programme at the beginning of next season (but hopefully to a larger class!) For those taking part in Handicap racing it is important to have a large fleet to race against, so that both the faster and the slower boats have some similar handicaps to race against. So step forward all you dinghy sailors, we would like to meet you on the water on Sundays. The sailing committee has assured me that the Race Officers will not be setting such testing courses as seen recently in the Whitbread Round the World! I would be delighted to hear from anyone who has any ideas or suggestions directed towards encouraging members to join in the Club's racing programme, I look forward to meeting you on Thursday 11 January in The Crown at Sandon - please try to attend. PEMBLETON COMMODORE 'S NOTES At the Christmas Working Party a lot of ground work was completed for some of the major projects over the Winter. In future the Club will be paying for every litre of water used instead of a water rate. We must exercise great care in our water usage, otherwise we will be faced with an immense increase in the water bill. AN EXPERIENCE NOT TO BE MISSED 4, The transition from one hull to two wasn't as smooth as I expected (or hoped!) All through the Summer and Autumn Series I had threatened to join the Cat Fleet with some late starts in my Enterprise and my chance arrived to try it officially in Autumn Points 11, On arriving at the Club I learned that the Boreham Dart was looking for a 'heavier crew'!, Well, “I'm game if you are,” making my first bad decision of the day. I eased myself into a borrowed trapeze harness and, walking on tiptoe, made my way to the hard, Up with the mainsail, adjustment to the jib and into the water. A few beats up and down the Blackwater to find my sea legs so to speak, and into the race, “Don't hang on to the shroud, just lie back on the wire," Right. Away we went wondering where the two Mercurys were hidden, "Abandon Ship,” or was it "Oh Sh... I heard, Anyway I was ahead of the game seeing the leeward hull dipping into the water and the windward hull rear high above me, I had somehow become detached from my wire as if the automatic ejector button had been pressed, "If I enter the water head first, the hull can only come down on my feet,” I thought. If I could only remember the technique and tidy up my entry, I think I'd stand a good chance in the World Springboard Championship, Now with the capsized Dart being blown towards Bradwell, I found myself all alone in the Blackwater, Ship Ahoy! two Darts heading for me; are they coming to finish me off? No, one of them tacked away leaving me firmly in Dave Onyon's sights. Up I climbed, feeling relieved at last to be pulled from the water, While all this was going on Damian had managed to right the Dart and made ready to sail again. "Right, there's your boat - jump." Back I was in the water, to be quickly hauled aboard and ordered to return to my station, Unfortunately with three sail battens broken we couldn't join the race so it was back to the club and an ‘early bath', The wind eased a little after lunch and I thought let's get back to sanity and take the Enterprise out, Tr proved to be my second bad decision of the day. The Hellewells joined us and we had a Handicap Fleet for the afternoon race, All rigged up, away from the hard and away we went in plenty of time to get a good start, I looked back and, yes, 'Paranoid' was in the water with the wind starting to blow up a bit, Did I say "back to sanity?” Once again the cry of “Oh sh...” rang out as the boom and gooseneck fitting was torn away from the mast, Nowhere to sail but the way I was pointing and beach the boat on Osea Island. What would we do without that last straw to grasp? Lose half the fleet, no doubt, Where did all that wind suddenly come from? and the waves! Still, at least we were upright and relatively sate holding onto the Enterprise just off Osea beach, While I took down the sails, Baddow Star was launched to our rescue and we were towed back to the Club for another early bath, Thankfully, only minor damage, but ales the end of an enjoyable season for E 4021, After a few Eskimo Rolls 'Paranoid' came in under tow from Jack B end racing was abandoned. One by one the stricken Solos returned from No.2 buoy and some unusual sailing techniques were observed, Well, I'm looking forward to next year and taking on the rest of the Handicap Fleet with my Enterprise 4021 after a winter lick of paint and varnish, Thanks, Damian for the brief taste of Catamaran sailing, tut I think I'll resist the temptation to change fleets. I prefer less contact with the water! lan Caruth BARN DANCE Saturday 17th February, 8.00pm - 12,30am, at the Marconi Athletic & Social Club, Beehive Lane, Chelmsford. IT'S A GREAT IDEA (shame about the planning) The MSC's Main Committee is always Willing to encourage new ideas and new approaches to the club's activities but, at the same time, the Main Committee has the duty to exercise a sensible control over what is happening in the name of the club - that is why you, the MSC membership as a whole, elect a main Committee to run the club on your behalf. There is no doubt that over recent years the club has become more adventurous and ‘high profile’ in its activities and public awareness. The revival of the Regatta, the introduction of the East Coast Piers Race and the embryo Osea Icicle, the various requests we receive to run special events for non-member groups (eg. Gull nationals in 1989 and Dart Travellers Trophy races in 1990) and the gradual extention of the club's own sailing season towards the 31 December each year all point towards a club which is changing, ever so gradually, in its basic character. These changes and new activities bring with them problems and implications which are not always appreciated by those who are suddenly blessed by a flash of brilliance . Things like insurance, safety, licencing laws, availability of equipment and services, the willingness of ‘people’ to do the less glamourous jobs that go with the ‘new idea’, even questions of tax, etc., have to be taken into account before embarking on a new venture. All these ‘problems’ are capped by the greatest ‘problem’ of al] - how much will it cost and who will pay ? As a matter of policy, the main Committee wish to make it known that:- (a) all proposals to extend the activities of the MSC should, in the first instance, be put to the appropriate sub-committee. This does not only cover the obvious new ideas such as the introduction of new sailing events but also applies to ideas to extend the ‘official’ sailing programme outside the 'normal' period, introduce new social events, new equipments, new services, etc. The appropriate sub committees will usually be the following:- - sailing sub-committee - Social sub-Committee - clubhouse sub-committee (b) Since each sub-committee has one member serving on it who is a Flag Officer, the Main Committee will automatically be made aware of the proposals being considered. Where the matter is purely ‘internal’ to the club, it will usually be considered sufficient for the sub-committee itself to make a final decision on the new proposals. However, where the proposals involve matters ‘external' to the club, particularly matters which could affect its public relations/public awareness image, then the Main Committee might wish not only to be consulted but also to take the final decision on the acceptance or rejection of the proposals. Liaison between the main Committee and the sub-committees is always maintained by the appropriate Flag Officer or an appointed deputy. Similarly, where the proposals involve/imply non-budgeted expenditures or the collection of non-budgeted income in the name/on behalf of the MSC, the main Committee might exercise its prerogative to make the final decisions. (c) No member of the MSC is permitted to issue press releases or make public statements in the name of the club except with the prior approval of the appointed club Press Officer (in the case of established activities such as Regatta, ECPR, etc) or, in the absence of an appointed Press officer, with the prior approval of thé Main Committee or a Flag Officer. If your reaction to this article is one of despair (ie. more ****** bureaucracy), just stop to think ‘who js responsible for the proper conduct of the club’ ? Nobody wants to unnecessarily curtail activity at the club and past and current main Committees have invariably encouraged and supported sensible new ideasy but some control has to be exercised otherwise you might find a keen member has organised a camping convention for his/her favourite charity - right in the middle of Regatta, E.C.P.R or the middle of winter when we ain't got no water supply ! FINAL COMMENT - NO MEMBER SHOULD ENTER DISCUSSIONS ON 'SPONSORSHIPS' FOR THE CLUB WITHOUT THE AGREEMENT OF THE MAIN COMMITTEE.

COMMODORE 'S ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING REPORT - NOV '89 The Club has this year seen a level of activity both on and off the water which exceeds that of the recent past and we must aim to nurture and carry forward this growth into the future, The weather this year has been exceptionally kind to us, The Regatta was extremely successful, and I must thank Malcolm Stuart and all the teams of helpers for the very smooth running of the event. Camping Fortnight was a success notwithstanding the problems of the water supply. The only really disastrous weekend for weather, coincided with the East Coast Piers Race, Tasks Carried Out: During last Winter each Fleet undertook a specific task which resulted in a very much smarter appearance to the Clubhouse and Site, Early in the summer the Water Board carried out a4 major rebuilding of the seawall immediately in front of the Clubhouse and we took the opportunity to have the Hard resealed between the blocks, This was much cheaper than it would have been if carried out as a separate exercise, Social Events: The Barn Dance and Laying Up Supper of last Winter were both very well supported, But support for the Fitting Out and the Mid-Summer Parties was disappointing and I am sure that the Social Committee would welcome suggestions and help on ways of improving the popularity of these two events. Future Tasks: This Winter we have a number of tasks to complete and the Fleet Captains have already agreed on the work to be carried out by each Fleet, Following changes in legislation relating to the use of Channel M2 by Clubs, we are having to replace sll the Club radios over the winter, as those in both the Race Box an Clubhouse are illegal; and the radio on Jack B cannot be modified to use Channel M2, This will involve an expenditure of approximately £2,000, We should, however, end up with a communications system with many years of operational life, We also have the task of replacing the water main fraa the Gate to the Clubhouse, which will cost about £1500 and which the Main Club has agreed to fund. Purchase of Field: We are currently negotiating with Cambridge University to buy the field beyond the Race Box which is an extension of the Cruiser Park, and again the Main Club has agreed to provide the money for this, Whilst this will allow us to utilise the existing space differently in the future, next Season the Cruiser trailers will be parked up there during the Summer so that a start can be made on improving the drainage of the Cruiser Park. The Main Committee has accepted the recommendation of the Sailing Sub Committee that a second Rescue Boat should be purchased, It is anticipated that the cost will be in the region of £6000 - £7000 and we have approached the Main Club for their assistance and until a reply is received from them, no date can be given for its purchase, As you are aware there have been problems with the Gate Lock this season, These have not been due to the lock mechanism itself but were caused by both pillars rising out of the ground and leaning apart. Our resident blacksmith/engineer Pete Clayton will be solving the problem for the future, Clubhouse Extension: A further problem that the Main Committee has been examining is the size of the mai: lounge area of the Clubhouse, because we are reaching the capacity of the Lounge on many occasions during the year, Also we have a permanent problem on Sundays after lunch with the state of the Lounge, which is normally wet underfoot and unpleasant for non-sailors to sit in. One solution would be to ban the wearing of wetsuits or wet clothes in the Lounge, which is impractical, Plans have been drawn up to extend the Lounge to the South, making it approximately twice the size, and providing a large workshop/storage area below, The first hurdle to overcome is that of planning permission which is now being pursued. However, the major problem will be the financing of the estimated cost of £60,000. We have approached the Main Club, but it is unlikely that this level of funding will be available, It will therefore be necessary for us to find a source of funds and to undertake to service the interest and repay the debt, Let's not back away because of the problems of funding, but tackle it, and provide the basis for the next twenty years of the continuing growth of the Club, I would like to thank all who have helped me during this year. When so many are involved, it is hard to single out particular people, but Malcolm Stuart and George Robinson both retire fram the Committee this year, Whilst Malcolm has been involved on the sailing side, the stature of the Club and its events have reached a peak due to his unflagging efforts, George has been involved with the Clubhouse and grounds and again has brought about some remarkable changes, In addition to them I would like to thank all those who have served on the Committees of the Club; those who have turned out at working parties; those who have had that marvellous idea, and when asked to carry it through have done so, and not left it "to the Committee"; those who have done the odd job for the Club of which none of us is aware, Without their support the Club would not function,

Lastly, I must thank a group without whom there would be no Club. I refer here to the wives and families of us all; they tolerate our absence whether we are sailing or serving on Committees, they support us by coming down to the site in all weathers and doing many tasks around the site which we take for granted, I believe that all of us who sail owe a major vote of thanks to them, N.T. Pembleton, Commodore SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT = AGM NOV '89 Mike (Hellewell) reported that it had been a very successful year with another increase in sailing activity due to an increase in membership, and very good summer weather, The Spring Season was very competitive with some exciting sailing. The highlight of the season was the very successful Regatts, and the Rescue Boat Competition was entertaining and enlightening, Also during the Spring the Club had hosted its first Sailboard Open meeting - for the over-40s which excluded almost all of our Club members. It was well attended and so successful that it is hoped to repeat the event at the Club next year. The Camping Fortnight had enjoyed two weeks of good weather during which time both Cadets and Adults were able to receive sailing training. The East Coast Piers Race had unfortunately fallen on the windiest day of the whole summer, which may have accounted for the lower than expected entries, The excellent organisation and superb rescue facilities made the event enjoyable to those who did take part, The event had also been a success in that it had raised £1400 the two charities, Two special achievements by members had been Robin Smith becoming the Hurricane European Champion, and Janet Keeble becoming World Ladies Solo Champion. It had been an enjoyable season, and on behalf of all the Helms, thanks were expressed to all those people who helped to make it all happen - wives/girlfiends; Race Officers; and especially Rescue Boat Drivers and Assistants, THE BLACKWATER AND COLNE SAILING PROTECTION ASSOCIATION = — BACSPA Representing the yacht clubs of the Blackwater and Colne Rivers Most of the boats have gone from our creeks and estuaries, leaving them to the Brent Geese, the ducks and the waders, A few hardy souls are still sailing, but I suspect that the majority are, like myself, sitting by the fire looking forward to the New Year and remembering a long sunny sailing season, The year started quietly enough but, as often happens, some clouds have begun to gather. Most of the potential problems seem to relate to money-making schemes of one sort or another, usually at the expense of sailing man or woman, Light Dues, for example, have surfaced again as a proposal, and of course some well-known marks have disappeared in the name of economy. A new idea involves charges for laying racing marks, and I have no doubt that somewhere lurks a confidential file marked ‘Licensing of Yachtsmen' waiting to be dusted off at an appropriate timel 'Development' too gives us problems, The Colne Barrier Project bodes very badly for Wyvenhoe Sailing Club, that fine old Colne family club who have been put in a potentially difficult position by the loss of their traditional sailing water and moorings, On the Blackwater, the Saltcote Marina Scheme has reappeared as an outline plan, It is to be hoped that common sense will prevail here also since no regard seems to have been paid to the manifest disadvantages of a large (150-boat) marina in the crowded, shallow, upper Blackwater. Despite protests, six swinging moorings have been allowed in a favourite anchorage and stopping-place at Osea Island, to go with a development on the Island. The precedent established here is extremely worrying. Above ell we cherish the freedom of our East Coast rivers, but, as ever, the price of freedom is vigilance. BACSPA frequently finds itself in the thick of things and our voice is heard. Please don't hesitate to contact John Chandler, Colin Lambert, Tony Williamson or myself if you hear of anything to the detriment of our river community. Whatever, wherever or indeed however you sail (or motor) may I wish you all good luck for 1990, { rd 7B

'S NOTES COMMODORE There are two important dates approaching for all Club members, The first is the 28th February by which time all renewals of membership should be received by Sen Bingley, Anyone who has not renewed by this date will not receive future issues of Navigans and will find that their key will NOT work the Gate or Clubhouse locks, If you are not renewing, will you please return your key to Ben, otherwise you may be charged for it. The second is the 18th March for the Working Party. Following all the activity over the winter to re-instate the gate, the water main and the tractor shed, there is considerable work required to re-instate the grounds. In addition the rest of the seawall needs clearing, the areas which are gravelled need making up and the entire club needs to be made ready for the season, It is essential that we have as many people as possible to help so that all the jobs are done, If anyone can bring a trailer to help move gravel or earth, this would be most welcamne, Meanwhile the gate lock is now fully serviceable, and if you have any problem using your key, please contact Membership Secretary Ben Bingley. The water has now been re-connected and all the stop cocks are in the Mens Changing Room, The one at floor level is the MAIN which turns off the Supply to all areas, During the winter this should be turned off when no one is at the Club, In addition there are separate stop cocks for the Hard Scrubbing Posts, Outside Tap, and main Clubhouse, all of which will be labelled in the near future. Indoors we clean windows and re-hang curtains taken home by various members for laundering. Traditionally this is the Working Party when the Galley cupboards are cleaned out and all the crockery washed. The bar may be a candidate for a spring clean too, as would any other part of the Club that is considered to need it. It would be helpful if you brought along your Marigolds and a bowl, tut cloths and cleaning liquids will be provided, Please come in large numbers and give your club your support, Ed. INFORMATION CIRCULATED BY MALDON DISTRICT COUNCIL HAZARDOUS CHEMICALS - There have been a few incidents recently of containers of HAZARDOUS CHEMICALS being washed up along the Essex Coast. Because of recent weather conditions, the shipping agents have been worried that more containers could be washed up over the next few weeks. The canisters have come fran the M.V. Murree which sank off the South Coast a couple of months ago. Over the past two or three weeks a small number of the containers have arrived in our area. Same gave off cyanide fumes; the contents of a drum washed ashore at Foulness becomes inflammable on contact with the air; and yet another turms to sulphuric acid on contact with water. The majority of the hazardous chemicals were in small brown bottles varying in size fram 100ml (about 25 teaspoonfuls) to 2.5 litres. They could be loose or packed in white polystyrene, possibly with marks giving chemical name and manufacturer - either M & B (May and Baker) or BDH. In addition to those already described, extreme care should be taken if any form of containers are discovered. Same of the chemicals involved are very nasty indeed and NO ATTEMPT SHOULD BE MADE TO INVESTIGATE THEM, T£ any suspicious containers are found, please contact Maldon Police, Tel. Maldon 852255, and they will alert the relevant response agency. MALCOLM STUART, CHELMSFORD [redacted], THE EAST COAST PIERS RACE AND THE RYA_SEANANSHIP FOUNDATION IN 1988 THE CLUB PUT ON THE FIRST EAST COAST PIERS RACE, A LONG DISTANCE EVENT FOR CATAMARANS UP TO WALTON-ON-THE*NAZE AND BACK; THAT YEAR IT SUPPORTED CANCER RELIEF AND ESTABLISHED AN EXCITING RACE FOR THE COMPETITIORS. IN 1989 IT WAS DECIDED TO SUPPORT TWO CAUSES OF DIRECT INTEREST TO US AS SAILORS, THE RNLI AND SAILING FOR THE DISABLED (ACTUALLY THE RYA SEAMANSHIP FOUNDATION); IN 1990 ALL THE PROCEEDS WILL BE GIVEN TO THE RYA SF, THE RYA SF IS A REGISTERED CHARITY FOUNDED BY THE RYA IN 1973 AND HAS THREE SPECIFIC AIMS. TO PROVIDE OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUNG PEOPLE, PARTICULARLY FROM DEPRIVED BACKGROUNDS, TO TAKE PART IN SAILING-RELATED ACTIVITIES, TO ENABLE HANDICAPPED PEOPLE TO LEARN TO SAIL ON EQUAL TERMS WITH THE ABLE-BODIED, TO IMPROVE THE LEVEL OF SEAMANSHIP IN THE PLEASURE=BOAT COMMUNITY. TO THESE ENDS THE RYA SF HAS BEEN INVOLVED IN THE PROVISION OF NEARLY 200 BOATS OF MANY CLASSES, OVER ONE HUNDRED OF WHICH ARE 15' CHALLENGER TRIMARANS DESIGNED FOR USE BY ABLE-BODIED OR DISABLED PEOPLE. IT IS THE ASPECTS OF THE WORK OF THE RYA SF THAT INVOLVE HELPING HANDICAPPED PEOPLE TO HAVE THE OPPORTUNITY TO SAIL THAT THE PIERS RACE IS SPECIFICALLY ADDRESSING, AND IT IS OUR HOPE THAT, GIVEN GOOD SUPPORT THIS YEAR, WE SHOULD BE ABLE TO PURCHASE A CHALLENGER FOR PLACEMENT BY THE SEAMANSHIP FOUNDATION WHERE IT CAN BEST BE USED. IF WE FALL SHORT OF THIS TARGET THEN THE MONEY RAISED WILL SUPPORT SAILING FOR THE DISABLED IN A MORE GENERAL WAY BY ASSISTING THE RYA SFWITH SOME OF THEIR MANY PROJECTS, IN 1989 THE PIERS RACE RAISED A TOTAL OF £1,600 FOR THE RNLI AND THE RYA SF; THIS YEAR WE INTEND TO BEAT THAT! WE WERE HELPED IMMENSELY IN 1989 BY ‘INDUSTRIAL AND COMMERCIAL ENGINEERING SERVICES' AND ‘BRAMHAM BROTHERS', TWO ENGINEERING FIRMS WHO PROVIDED THE CASH NEEDED TO RUN THE EVENT, AND ALSO BY A NUMBER OF PEOPLE AND ORGANISATIONS WHO PROVIDED HELP IN KIND. WE NOW FIND OURSELVES IN THE POSITION OF NEEDING SIMILAR SPONSORSHIP FOR 1990, £2,000 IS NEEDED TO ENABLE US TO PUT THE RACE ON IN A FASHION THAT WILL BE SAFE, ENJOYABLE AND PROFITABLE....FOR CHARITY 42,000 IS A LOT OF MONEY, BUT THE RACE HAS SHOWN OVER THE LAST TWO YEARS, EVEN WITH THE FOUL WEATHER EXPERIENCED LAST YEAR, THAT MORE THAN THE TOTAL SPONSORSHIP WILL BE GIVEN TO CHARITY, WE HAVE TRIED VERY HARD TO FIND SPONSORSHIP AT THIS LEVEL FOR 1990 BUT WITH NO SUCCESS SO FAR; IF ANYONE IN THE CLUB FEELS HE OR SHE HAS ANY IDEAS THAT MAY BE OF HELP, OR FEELS THAT HE OR SHE IS ABLE TO APPROACH HIS OR HER OWN EMPLOYERS FOR SUCH A GOOD CAUSE, THEN I'D BE VERY PLEASED TO HEAR FROM THEM.

HANDICAP FLEET NEWS I HOPE YOU HAVE ALL BEEN PAINTING AND VARNISHING DURING THE WINTER, AS I'M LOOKING FORWARD TO SEEING A SPLASH OF COLOUR FROM ALL YOU EARLY SEASON SAILORS. 3s SAFETY NOTE A recent incident highlighted the need for care and preparation when sailing from the Club, especially during the early part of the season when the water is cold. Accidents can happen to anyone, and by definition are unexpected. We can, however, prepare ourselves for an unexpected event by considering what could go wrong and then planning to minimise the effects of such a misfortune. The following may be worth considering SITUATION 1: Gear failure resulting in the boat drifting at the mercy of wind and tide. Contingency Plan. Is there an anchor on board? Is the boat provided with a second means of propulsion e.g. oars/paddle? SITUATION 2: Capsize or Swamping. Contingency Plan. Has the boat sufficient built-in buoyancy to support itself and crew? Is there a means of bailing the boat dry? Have you practised capsize drill amd recovered the boat once it has inverted? Are you protected from the debilitating effects of immersion in cold water? Are you wearing a buoyancy aid and will it support you? SITUATION 3: Boat Inverted and Cannot be Righted Contingency Plan Are you able to climb onto the upturmed hull? Are there lines or handles rigged to prevent your being separated from the boat? Finally, in the event of an accident, stay with the boat. Sail in Company, there is safety in numbers. Remember, we are each responsible for our own safety, do not rely on being rescued by someone else. Pat Black FOR SALE 6 Weeled Yard Trolley, built on Transit Axles + 2 x 13' RSJ's. 6. Summer is a'cumin in_-_ but not quite yet. Chapter 1 - Boater Beware At the time of writing, the sunis shining through my office window (actually it is snowing but we'll pretend it never happened) and itis altogethera most pleasant day (well is was until the snow came). With not too much wind apparent, it doesn't take too much effort to day-dream of going for a sail (remember, we're still pretending it isn't snowing) and I make a mental note to look for a suite of offices in Steeple. Judging from the rapid growth of plants in our garden, we've quite genuinely had a number of ‘very pleasant days' recently and it is tempting to assume that summer is, indeed, ‘a'cumin in' and has virtually arrived. However, as you will read elsewhere in this Navigans, although it might be a ‘very pleasant day' in the warm sunshine above the water level, it is still a very cold regime below the surface of the river Blackwater. Our unfortunate member who found him/herself with a problem, and in drastic need of outside assistance, can be forgivenfdr doing what he/she did onthe grounds of inexperience. However, I am sometimes surprized at the apparent inclination of some members to ‘strip off' the wet or dry suits at the first hint of the sun's warm rays. Perhaps I've got it wrong, but I thought the purpose of a wet or dry suit was not so much to keep me warm above the water, but to give me a fighting chance of survival when literally up to my neck in bee cold water - not to mention being up the creek without a paddle. As one who tends to wear the 'full wet-suit gear' even at the height of summer, it might be that I subscribe to the ancient chinese proverb which states "better to be a boiled lobster than a cold fish’. Chapter 2 - Remember, Remember, who's not a member. At a recent Main Committee meeting, someone asked if a member invited visitors to the club (without the visitors using the clubhouse or club facilities) then is it necessary to sign them in? The answer is YES, all visitors should be signed in even if they do not enter the clubhouse; it is sufficient that they are on the club site that they be signed in. The discussion then turned to consider ‘regular visitors' to the club i.e. those who are ‘regularly invited' to sail at the club. To be fair to those who pay both their MASC and Sailing Section subscriptions (and that is, of course, all fee-paying members) those who are ‘regular visitors' ought to be 'regular' members - '‘regular' in this sense meaning proper or correct paid-up members of the club in accordance with its rules. It is worth noting that one privilege of ordinary membership is that one's husband/wife and (their) children under the age of 18 are ‘permanent guests'. Presumably, once the kids are over 18 - they're on their own. Chapter 3. - SOSOTTI (is this a new kind of sausage ?) To those members both bushy of beard and somewhat long in the tooth, the meaning of the word SOSOTTI should be clear enough. No, it's not sausage; it is the annual war cry of the Results Secretary or, to be more accurate, the annual impassioned plea to helms and crew to help get the race results reasonably near correct. Just to remind you :- SO = SIGN ON ( forename and surname of both helm and crew - preferably printed rather than the 'signature') so = SIGN OFF (If you don't, you are automatically disqualified. Also please sign off in the right column. ie. If you are RETIRED then sign off under the RET column but, if you have FINISHED (in accordance with the racing rules etc) then sign off under the FIN column, Simple and straightforward ? You must be joking ! TTI = TIME THEM IN (This is aimed at the Race Officer. Please ‘Time In' all boats, even those in the single-class races. We need the info. for the end-of-season PYN Return to the RYA). Chapter 4 - Thine vehicle is inconveniently parked. Please be careful where you park. The gaps in the fence which divide the dinghy park from the car park have been especially left for pedestrian access - and left sufficiently wide to get boat trailers through. Several people have already managed to block these access points thi$ year, so please don't park so as to inconvenience others. Mike Boreham (Rear Commodore) \

COMMODORES NOTES The Regatta is nearly here and I would like to ask for people to help with the running. If you can assist with any of the Sailing activity please contact either Mike Helliwell (Chelmsford [redacted]) or Mike Boreham ([redacted]49). If you can help with the 'land' activity, particularly by doing half an hour or an hour behind the bar, please contact Bob Godbold (Chelmsford 2[redacted]) or Chris Davies (Chelmsford [redacted]). I would ask everyone to remember that all the organising and help at the event is voluntary and that if you are not prepared to help for an hour or so, that you do not complain about the organisation etc. I will remind all members that Anglian Water insist that tenders etc. MUST NOT BE STORED on the SEAWALL. Any dinghy found on the seawall is liable to be removed to the far end of the site by the gate, you have been warned. On the subject of tenders, a number of people have donated trolleys to the Club for the tender rack. These have been painted yellow and may be used by anyone but should be returned to the tender rack immediately after use. If you see a yellow trolley lying around on the hard or site, please take it back to the rack so they are not "lost'. The Club would be grateful for any further donations to help build the basis for the future. Would those people with cruisers around the concrete block as far as the row including Malcolm Yeomans, Conrad Barnard etc. please park their trailers tidily at the far end of the cat field but leave them so that we can move them later. This will allow us to layout the area for the tenders for 'E' and 'F' rows. Once sufficient boats have launched, we will retrieve the trailers from the 'cat' field and park them in the middle row of the cruiser field. As many of you are aware, we have been looking at the possibility of a second support boat. The current situation is that the Sailing Sub Committee have put a proposal to the Main Committee which has an estimated cost of £9,500.00 to £10,000.00. This has unfortunately coincided with the M.A.S.C. experiencing some significant financial problems as it has been running at a loss for the last two years. They obviously have to reverse this and at least reach a 'break-even' situation this year and profit in subsequent years. As a result, it will be at least two years before any spend of this scale can occur. In the meantime, we will continue to investigate other possible solutions. The M.A.S.C. financial position also means that the road repairs, which we urgently need to and legally must carry out, will have to be funded from our own resources. The current cost of these will be £2,500.00 approx. We are approaching the Water Board for assistance with this task as some of the damage may have been caused by their use. If we are successful in this and even taking account of the contribution that Cambridge University and others will make, we will still have a sizeable bill. It is therefore essential that we reduce our expenditure as much as possible so that we do not run a loss ourselves this year. Party time for the solo sailor - No, this is not the MSC Dateline service; nor is it an expose of high jinks by the solo 'Round-the-World' sailors who so recently finished their self-imposed exile. This is, in fact, an introduction to a ‘Thank You' to the Solo Fleet for inviting Maggie and me to their annual Solo Fleet Dinner held at the clubhouse on 21st April. It was a really super evening and we enjoyed it very much indeed. They're a social lot are the Solo Fleet, what with their BBQ and ‘get togethers' at various times of the year both in-season as well as out. The solo sailors (both male and female) cooked the meal and served it at table together with liberal amounts of wine (for those who were not driving). Dinner was followed by the 'social' programme organised by Len and Wendy Graves. The programme was organised on the basis of “Jeux sans Frontieres" so you can imagine it approached the anti-social now and again (well, most of the time to be honest). With much nudging, shoving, shouldering and assorted sculduddery (look it up in the dictionary), not to mention ooching, pumping and rocking, the two teams ‘battled it out' - if. not to the death then at least to the stiff back and creaking knees. Thanks everyone, it was great. Not only that, but we didn't have to drive because John and Margaret Salmon took us there and back again - thank you.John. How a hurricane helped repair a roof. It makes a nice change not to report some hurricane or tornado blowing over trees, fences or stripping tiles from roofs but, on this occasion, the hurricane (and others) took positive actions to repair roofs. I refer to the £10 raised for the Steeple Village Church Roof Repair Fund which was collected at the Easter Handicap Series. Not only did our visiting Hurricane 4.9 sailors contribute donations but so did our Own Club members who were sailing, sitting out or just watching the events of the day. Many thanks to you all. Steeple village is a lovely little village and the church is a delight. Hopefully, our club's donation will go some way to preserve it. It was a report of part of the ‘Safety at Sea' Conference held recently in London. The most interesting things in the report for me were the suggestions that:- (a) a dry suit was the best means of protection against ‘cold shock' on entering the water when 'man overboard’, as well as against hypothermia (b) 'man overboard’ can be more quickly recovered by adopting the ‘quick stop' (ie. yacht going head-to-wind) method of controlling the yacht so as to quickly locate and pick up the overboard crew - as opposed to the more usually taught method of ‘'reach-tack-reach' operation. It will be interesting to see what the yachting press has to say about these suggestions, and what will happen about the various ‘teaching methods' currently in voque. Admittedly, the discussion probably tended to be conducted within the context of offshore yacht racing, but nevertheless, it offers some food for thought for us creek dwellers. Treasurer Ed's note: Although the author of the next article would, no doubt, not mind being identified, I have deliberately amitted the name. The object of publishing this story and last month's warnings about the river being cold is not to embarrass any individual ('there, but for the grace of God, goes any of us') but to focus our minds at the beginning of the season to the potential hazards of our sport. We are at our most vulnerable when the water is so cold and we, and our gear, have perhaps not fully emerged from the winter's hibermation:

THAT INCIDENT In the May Navigans there were same notes dealing with an incident in March. I was the 'principal character' involved and had intended to give an account in that issue but was too late to meet the deadline, hence its belated appearance now. Having joined the Club in mid-summer last year it galls me samewhat to think I have gained same dubious prominence, if not notoriety! However, what's done is done. Let me say right away I fully subscribe to the constructive comments made, particularly about adequate and sensible preparation before setting sail. On the whole, I think my boat met those requirements and, certainly, the paddles were secure and at hand if I had decided to paddle up the creek! Nevertheless, I have learned that, particularly when sailing solo there are extra points to consider. The 'safety in numbers' suggestion is, I suppose, self-evident but I have a preference for solo sailing. In any case my present boat is a little cramped to accommodate a crew. There is also the difficulty of saneone willing to crew when you decide to sail, although I myself would welcame more opportunity to crew for experienced helmsmen. Undoubtedly I must give more thought to wearing clothing appropriate to the time and conditions of the season, but the wearing of the ‘full regalia’ in warm sunny weather I would find decidedly uncomfortable. There aught to be same concession to individual preference. As to what happened. I had a leeward capsize because, in a sudden strong gust of wind, although releasing the mainsheet in time, I was unable to do likewise with the jib sheet as it had got out of reach. The taut jib alone caused a complete heel over, ejecting me headlong into the grey water. Emerging, I unwisely delayed giving priority to righting the boat, squandering time and energy trying to recover items which drifted out of the storage locker (I had not secured the cover properly). One of my boots also came off during my exertions and pranptly disappeared! Eventually, having righted the boat, I caused it to capsize again by trying to make a quick entry over the side instead of the stem. Attempting another righting became more difficult as the jib sheet had sanehow fouled up underneath the boat, preventing me gaining enough purchase to throw it over the hull.....but before this account begins

6. to sound like Gerard Hoffnung's sketch of the descending barrel of bricks, suffice it to say I became quite suddenly aware of an overall chilling with numbing in the hands and, at the cost of extreme annoyance in having to do so, decided to signal for outside help. If I could just make my main point, I learned to sail last year on the adult course run by Mike Boreham and Malcolm Stuart. I found the relaxed nature, but steady tempo, of the course just right to enable me to fairly quickly venture out to sail solo which, apart fram once or twice when I crewed, I did up to the end of October. What I didn't do was re-inforce the capsize and recovery drill using my own boat, and without assistance. I think my neglect to achieve a higher proficiency was the main cause of an otherwise manageable situation deteriorating into a much more serious one. I need hardly say, therefore, that a high priority for me is more practice as soon as is practicable. Looking back, perhaps I can at least take same encouragement from the not-so-old English proverb; "if you don't make mistakes, you don't make anything" - but I hasten to add I acknowledge my mistakes also cost the efforts of other people. It follows that, although I have already done so, I would like here to record my appreciation for the efforts of Lee Tridini and Barry Marke in recovering my boat, and of Pat Black the OOD on 'that day'. In spite of everything my enthusiasm remains undanpened..... and I look forward to warmer days afloat. As Mike has said “Summer is a'cumin' in." Indeed, looking out of my window, I think it is a'cam! I should think most of us who sail could think of a few Gerard Hoffnung-type tales of our own activities over the years - and now for another OMe....-eeeee TROLLEY SAILING IN THE BLACKWATER I firmly believe that it can only be healthy for any sport or acitivity to embrace new developments and innovations. It is therefore with same sense of pride, if not a little humility, that I introduce this latest offshoot of sailing to the Club, namely, Trolley Sailing. The beauty of this activity is its simplicity. The objective is merely to sail a full blown Cruiser Trolley out into the river as far as you can. The Rules are extremely simple. The Trolley should be a substantial affair capable of carrying at least a medium-sized cruiser. Mickey Mouse affairs with pram wheels are not eligible, and the Trolley should not possess any additional buoyancy aids such as oversize tyres etc. Spinnakers are not allowed. contd....

Ti. As the only person, to my knowledge, to have engaged in this activity at Marconi to date, I can with some confidence claim to be the current Club Champion, with a sailing distance achieved of sane thirty feet (yet to be ratified). I can for those yet to be initiated in the sport, only attempt to convey the sheer excitement and intense adrenalin flow that the activity produces, especially if, like me, you inadvertently dismount the Trolley just before lift-off. My only concern in introducing this sport is that in time it will, like so many others, lose sight of its homespun roots and became over-sophisticated and over tuned. Will we eventually see an array of Pete Clayton Specials in racing black and gold livery, complete with balloon tyres, high aspect uprights and low wetted surfaces, sporting hard racing antifoulings and go-faster stripes, their crews resplendent in multi-coloured wetsuits? To get back to the present, however, the sport has the further attraction of opening up access to a number of spin-off activities such as Trapping the Stump (in which you aim to sink the trolley after its distance sailing attempt so that it straddles strategically placed stumps in the river bed - only for the particularly skilful, this one!) This leads naturally to Tractor Bouncing, in which you attempt to make a tractor airborne by pulling the trolley hard against the aforementioned stump. Then there is Trolley Jumping whereby the trolley has to be assisted in leaping the Stump. The attraction of this particular activity can be measured by the number of. people still involved at dusk on a Saturday night. There must be endless variations of this sport just waiting to be discovered. A whole Regatta could surely be organised around these and other associated activities such as Mast Tossing. On the other hand I might just go back to Sailing. It hasn't got anywhere like the same appeal as a spectator sport, but it's generally a lot more peaceful and I'm not sure that the limelight is all it's cracked up to be. 9. WE CAL THELED AMBULANCE Yet another water-skiing accident off Stansgate brought a bleeding and unconscious casualty to our hard at lunchtime on Bank Holiday Monday 7th May. The Club rose to the occasion and dealt very competently with the incident. It was particularly comforting to observe that we have a number of Club Members interested in First Aid and prepared to cane forward and do sanething constructive. The incident was almost an exact rerun of last year's Rescue Boat Campetition with the mangled eye and unconscious body, plus another member of the boat crew in deep shock. The extra factors in our real case were that the skier had taken in a lot of water and that he was already blind on one eye. The drowning bit solved itself simply by putting the casualty in the Recovery Position - he emptied himself although remaining unconscious. All we could do with the eye problem was to ensure a note was taken to hospital. The 999 call raised same interesting points. The ambulance cames from either Burmhan or Maldon and may take about 20 minutes to arrive. However, the G.P.s on the Dengie run a paramedic response which receives the same '999' call and invariably beat the ambulance to the scene, as in our case with the G.P. fran Althorne. Mike Boreham who initiated the 999 call very wisely went down to the main road to direct both the Paramedic car and the Ambulance up the Stansgate road. It is not unknown for new ambulance crews to get Stansgate confused with Stone and our G.P.fram Althorme hadn't known there was a Sailing Club at Stansgate. This incident will have focussed attention on the need for a high level of First Aid campetence in the Club. For those interested, who don't receive training elsewhere, Our own St John Ambulance team of David & Ione will be giving First Aid talks and demonstrations during Cadet Week. One thing they will be explaining is the latest thinking on resuscitation and hopefully we will have a copy of the British Heart Foundation video "Don't Just Stand There" which, amongst other things, points aut that the old 4 rapid inflations can actually do more harm than good. They now recammend, after clearing the airway, if breathing cannot be detected, two slow inflations making sure that the chest rises in response. A_STORM_IN AN EASTER EGG CUP (Through the Eye of the Hurricane) EASTER SUNDAY DAWNED CLEAR AND BRIGHT AND EXTREMELY WINDY, DESPITE A FORECAST OF WESTERLY FORCE 3, COMPETITORS TO THE EASTER SERIES WERE GREETED AT STANSGATE BY NORTH-WESTERLY FORCE 5 GUSTING 7! OUR VISITORS WERE IMPRESSED. WITH PERMISSION OF THE MAIN COMMITTEE, A NUMBER OF HURRICANE 4,9s HAD COME TO THE CLUB TO PARTICIPATE IN THE EASTER SERIES, THE HURRICANE 4,9 FLEET (FORMERLY THE CONDOR, BUT WITH AN UPDATED RIG) WILL BE HOLDING THEIR NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS DURING REGATTA, AND ASKED PERMISSION TO TRY THE WATERS IN ADVANCE, ABOUT 5 HURRICANES ARRIVED, AND ALTHOUGH SMALLIN NUMBERS THEY PROCEEDED TO EAT THE GALLEY CLEAN. JEAN FLOOK REPORTED THAT ONE INDIVIDUAL HAD 4 HAMBURGERS TO HIMSELF AT LUNCHTIME, RACE ONE CONSISTED OF R2B3, NO, NOT A DROID FROM STAR WARS, BUT A COURSE CONSISTING OF 3 LAPS OF As,1p,Cs,Bs & Ds, FOLLOWED BY 2 LAPS OF As,1s,Bs,Ds. THIS COURSE GAVE AN INTERESTING REACH BETWEEN C AND B AND WITH WIND AGAINST TIDE THE INFAMOUS BLACKWATER CHOP WAS THE ORDER OF THE DAY. WITH THE WIND GUSTING UP TO FORCE 7, ONLY 5 BOATS TOOK TO THE WATER, THE FLEET CONSISTED OF JOHN NICKALLS & CAROLINE HOLLINGS IN THE TORNADO, TWO VISITING HURRICANE 4,9s, ONE WINDSURFER AND A MIRROR, THE TORNADO LED, FOLLOWED BY THE HURRICANES AND THE WINDSURFER, THE RACE OFFICER WISELY DECIDED TO SHORTEN COURSE AND PLANNED A MAXIMUM OF TWO LAPS OF COURSE R, HOWEVER, THE COMPETITORS DECIDED DIFFERENTLY AND THEY ALL CHOSE TO RETIRE AFTER THE FIRST LAP. JOHN CLAIMS THAT IF HE HAD SPENT MUCH MORE TIME UNDERWATER HE WOULD HAVE QUALIFIED FOR A COURSE AT HMS PERISHER (THE SUBMARINE TRAINING SCHOOL.) ONE OF THE VISITORS PITCHPOLED, BUT INSTEAD OF GOING END OVER END, THEY PIROUETTED NEATLY ON THE LEEWARD BOW AND ACTUALLY CAME DOWN ON THE SIDE OF THE HULL. BEFORE THE CREW COULD BALE OUT, THE BOAT RETURNED TO THE UPRIGHT. HOWEVER, ALL WAS NOT WELL! THE FORCE OF THE "EVENT" SHEARED OFF ONE OF THE BOLTS HOLDING THE REAR BEAM, AND THEY DESCRIBED THE BOAT AS BEING AS STIFF AS A BOWL OF JELLY! THEY SAILED SLOWLY (7?) BACK TO THE CLUB. AFTER DEPLETING THE GALLEY OF FOOD, AND REALISING THAT THE WIND HAD DROPPED TO A MER® FORCE 4, 12 CREWS VENTURED ONTO THE WATER FOR THE SECOND RACE. THE RACE OFFICER AGAIN SET R2B3, AND AGAIN JOHN AND CAROLINE SPED INTO THE LEAD, HOWEVER, DAVID BEECH SAILING A HURRICANE 4.9 CHARGED AROUND THE COURSE AFTER JOHN, NEVER LETTING HIM GET TOO FAR IN FRONT, AND AT THE END DAVID TOOK HONOURS AND HANDICAP FROM JOHN, FURTHER DOWN THE FLEET, THE OTHER TWO 4,9s WERE RACING AROUND TOGETHER, FOLLOWED BY A GAGGLE OF CLUB DART 18s, IT WAS NOTICEABLE THAT THE 4,9s SEEMED TO POINT HIGHER THAN THE DARTS, WHICH GAVE THEM AN ADVANTAGE ON THE BEAT. MONDAY AGAIN DAWNED CLEAR AND BRIGHT, BUT THE WIND WAS ONLY A MERE FORCE 5 GUSTING 6, SO A GOOD FLEET ASSEMBLED TO START RACE 3, BECAUSE OF THE DIFFERENCE IN THE SPEED OF THE BOATS, THE RACE OFFICER SET A COURSE OF R3, WHICH STILL FAVOURED THE FASTER BOATS, BUT DID ALLOW THE MIRROR FLEET A LONG SPINNAKER LEG, IF THEY WERE BRAVE ENOUGH TO FLY ONE, ON SUNDAY THE STARTS HAD BEEN POSTPONED TO GIVE EVERYBODY SUFFICIENT TIME TO GET ON THE WATER, BUT THE RACE OFFICER CORRECTLY STUCK TO THE PUBLISHED TIMES ON MONDAY AND, ACCORDINGLY, BOATS WERE GOING IN ALL DIRECTIONS AT THE START OF RACE 3! IT DIDN'T HELP THAT THE RACE BOX CLOCK IS RUNNING ABOUT 2 MINUTES FAST (FROM GMT), THUS THE COMPETITORS WERE ALL EXPECTING THE SIGNALS AT DIFFERENT TIMES! JOHN AND CAROLINE MADE THEIR CUSTOMARY GOOD START AND SPED OFF IN FRONT. DAVID BEECH AND PETER GOLDING, 80TH IN HURRICANE 4,9s LED THE CHASE, FOLLOWED BY YOURS TRULY WHO, AS USUAL WAS POINTING IN THE WRONG DIRECTION WHEN THE GUN WENT, I MEAN IT WHEN I SAY GUN, AS THE CANNONS WERE IN USE AND THEY COULD BE HEARD ABOVE THE WIND, WHEREAS THE HOOTER WAS A BIT PATCHY. WITH A LOW-WATER SHORT-LINE START, THE BEAT TO 'A' MARK WAS FULL OF CRIES FOR WATER, AND WE ALMOST SHORTENED A 4.9 WHEN WE TRIED TO BEAR AWAY ACROSS HIS STERN (WE WERE ON PORT) JUST AS HE BORE AWAY (ON STARBOARD) TO AVOID THE MOORING BARGE. DAVE WAS YELLING FOR ME TO BEAR AWAY AND AS I PULLED ON THE TILLER IT JUST DECIDED TO EXTEND RATHER THAN OPERATE THE RUDDERS. THE 4.9, WHO HADN'T SEEN US TACK BY THE SHORE, COULD DO ABSOLUTELY NOTHING AS HE WAS SANDWICHED BETWEEN US AND THE MOORING BARGE. HOW WE MISSED EACH OTHER I DO NOT KNOW, BUT WE DID! HAD I TRIED TO TACK TO AVOID A COLLISION, WE WOULD HAVE UNDOUBTEDLY COLLIDED AS I WOULD HAVE ENDED UP DIRECTLY IN FRONT OF THE 4,9, THIS WAS JUST A CASE OF OBSTRUCTIONS BLOCKING BOTH HELMS' VIEW AND THE WIND BLOWING OUT CRIES FOR WATER, MEANWHILE JOHN WAS WELL AWAY, FOLLOWED BY THE TWO 4.9s, JOHN LAID 'C' MARK IN ONE TACK, WHILST EVERYBODY ELSE HAD TO TACK AT LEAST ONCE. ON THE LEG TO 'B' MARK WE PASSED THE SECOND 4,9 AND SET ABOUT OVERHAULING THE LEADING 4.9, WE SEEMED TO BE MUCH FASTER DOWNWIND THAN EITHER OF THE BOATS IN FRONT, AND WERE ABLE TO SAIL MUCH LOWER, THUS WHEN WE REACHED 'B' MARK WE WERE CLOSE TO THE LEADING 4.9 AND CLOSING ON JOHN. DAVID BEECH SEEMED TO BE POINTING AT LEAST 10 DEGREES HIGHER THAN US, BUT OUR SUPERIOR SPEED ALLOWED US TO PASS HIM AS WE CROSSED THE LINE FOR THE END OF THE FIRST LAP, MEANWHILE, JOHN AND CAROLINE WERE PULLING AWAY AGAIN. JOHN

3 12. LAID 'C' MARK IN ONE TACK AGAIN, WHILST WE HAD TO TACK, THE 4,9s WERE POINTING VERY HIGH BUT LOSING GROUND. DOWN TO 'B' MARK AND AGAIN WE WERE SAILING FASTER AND LOWER THAN ANYBODY ELSE. AT 'B' MARK WE WERE WITHIN A HUNDRED YARDS OF JOHN, BUT AGAIN HE PULLED AWAY ON THE BEAT, UP TO THIS POINT I HAD NOT ATTEMPTED TO TWIN WIRE, BUT IN AN EFFORT TO CARRY MORE POWER I LUMBERED OUT, THE TROUBLE WAS THAT WITH MY LACK OF WINTER EXERCISE (AND THUS BEING FAT!) AS WELL AS THE THERMALS ETC, UNDER A DRY SUIT, I FELT AND PERFORMED A BIT LIKE THE MICHELIN MAN, JOHN HELD HIS DISTANCE TO WIN THE RACE, BUT WE WERE BEATEN ON HANDICAP BY BOTH THE 4,9s THE ONLY CONSOLATION WAS TAKING THE MICKEY OUT OF THE FLEET WHO WERE BEATEN ON HANDICAP BY THE TWO YOUNG LADS IN THE MIRROR! THE ONLY MISHAP WAS THE MAST FALLING DOWN ON ONE HURRICANE 4,9, EVIDENTLY A STAINLESS STEEL RING BROKE AT THE BOTTOM OF THE FORESTAY, BUT APART FROM PRIDE NOTHING SEEMED TO BE DAMAGED. OUR THANKS MUST GO TO STONE SAILING CLUB WHOSE INFLATABLE (HINT, HINT!!!) RESCUE BOAT WAS ABLE TO GO ALONGSIDE THE CAT AND RETURN IT SAFELY CLOSE TO THE CLUB. THE WIND SEEMED TO EASE DURING THE LUNCH BREAK, ENOUGH FOR DAMIEN AND LUCY TO RIG THE BOREHAM DART 18 FOR THE AFTERNOON RACE, ROB STAHL SPENT A LARGE PORTION OF THE LUNCH HOUR PLAYING WITH HIS RIG (I THOUGHT HER NAME WAS ANNETTE!), AND FINALLY SETTLED FOR MORE MAST RAKE AND GREATER RIG TENSION. ON SATURDAY HE HAD ABOUT 4" OF PREBEND ON THE MAST, BUT AFTER QUESTIONS FROM THE CUSTOMS PEOPLE ABOUT HIS RIG BEING USED AS A_ LAUNCHING VEHICLE FOR MISSILES FOR IMPOVERISHED NATIONS (ALIAS A BOW AND ARROW), HE WISELY DECIDED TO REDUCE THE BEND, DAVE WANTED TO REDUCE OUR PREBEND FROM THE 2" WE HAD SET, BUT AS I DIDN'T THINK THAT WE WERE UNDER-POWERED, I PERSUADED HIM TO LEAVE IT ALONE. THANK GOOONESS I DID! RACE 4 FEATURED THE SAME COURSE AS RACE 3, THE WIND WAS A NICE FORCE 5, BUT AS THE 10-MINUTE GUN WENT, THE WIND INCREASED TO ABOUT A 6. HAVING REDUCED THE PREBEND, ROB AND ANNETTE DECIDED TO GO SWIMMING. BELIEVE IT OR NOT, THIS WAS ROB'S FIRST CAPSIZE IN HIS HURRICANE, AND HE HAS ONLY HAD THE BOAT 6 MONTHS! A MORE ORDERLY START TOOK PLACE, BUT AGAIN THE FIRST LEG WAS PUNCTUATED WITH CRIES FOR WATER. THE WIND WAS DEFINITELY STRONGER, WITH BIG WAVES ADDING TO THE DEGREE OF DIFFICULTY. JOHN NICKALLS AGAIN ESTABLISHED A BIG LEAD, FOLLOWED BY DAVID BEECH & PETER GOLDING, DAVE AND I WERE SERIOUSLY OVER-POWEREDI ON THE FETCH FROM '‘1' TO 'C' I HAD THE TRAVELLER RIGHT OUT TO THE END OF THE TRACK AND WAS STILL HAVING TO DUMP THE MAIN IN THE GUSTS, THE TOP 5 PANELS ON THE MAIN WERE ALMOST CONTINUALLY BACKWINDED, WE PASSED PETER GOLDING ON THE FIRST REACH TO 'B', BUT WERE IN CONSTANT DANGER OF PITCHPOLING AS WE RAN INTO THE BACKS OF WAVES, BOTH OF US WERE SITTING AS FAR BACK AS POSSIBLE. DAVE TRIED TRAPEZING BUT THE BRAKING MOTION OF THE WAVES MADE IT DIFFICULT TO KEEP HIS FOOTING. PETER GOLDING STUCK TENACIOUSLY TO OUR STERN (I NEVER DID FIND THE TOW ROPE!) WE COULD NEITHER GET AWAY FROM HIM, NOR CATCH THE BOAT IN FRONT. WHAT LITTLE WE GAINED ON THE REACHES, WE LOST GOING UPWIND AS THE 4,9 TEAM POINTED HIGHER AND TACKED MORE CLEANLY. DURING THE SECOND LAP, THE DARTS HAD BEEN ALMOST THE LENGTH OF 'C' TO 'B' BEHIND, BUT ON THE FINAL LAP THEY BEGAN TO CLOSE THE GAP QUITE DRAMATICALLY. COMING UP TO THE FINISH ON THE FINAL LAP, WE WERE HIT BY AN ALMIGHTY SQUALL. IT MUST HAVE BEEN AT LEAST FORCE 9, AS WE DUMPED BOTH THE MAIN AND THE JIB, YET CONTINED TO FLY A HULL. AT THIS POINT WE WERE ABOUT 25 YARDS FROM THE FINISH LINE AND 30 YARDS FROM THE SHORE, SO WE WERE FORCED TO TACK IN THE SQUALL. SURPRISINGLY ° WAS QUITE EASY, AS THE SEA WAS ALMOST FLAT! WHERE HAD ALL THE WAVES GONE? BLOWN TO NOTHING! PETER GOLDING TACKED BEHIND US AND CROSSED ABOUT 10 SECONDS AFTER US, IT WAS AN EXCITING IF HAIRY RACE, VERA DUCKWORTH (AKA MIKE DUCKMANTON) LED THE DART FLEET HOME, AND JUST PIPPED US ON HANDICAP, FOLLWED BY PETER FLOOK AND TOM DUCKMANTON, JOHN AND CAROLINE WON THE SERIES AND SOME ZIT GENERATING EASTER EGGS! DAVID BEECH WAS SECOND, WITH JOINT THIRD GOING TO PETER GOLDING AND PETER FLOOK, LEE HARRISON WAS THE FIRST CADET. OVERALL AN EGGCELLENT SERIES (SORRY, BUT I COULDN'T RESIST IT.) IT IS A PITY THAT SO FEW OF THE OTHER FLEETS PUT IN AN APPEARANCE, BUT IT WAS CERTAINLY BOAT-BREAKING WEATHER, THANKS ONCE AGAIN TO ALL WHO PARTICIPATED IN ORGANISING THE EVENT, AND OUR VISITORS CERTAINLY ENJOYED THEMSELVES. A view from the rear. > Who's a lucky boy then ? - I was much amused to read in one of the daily papers a snippet about Argentinian polo players being in great demand in this country; apparently they can get up to £10,000 per month for a 5-month season. It wasn't that which amused me (rather it made me lament my mis-spent youth not learning to ride a horse) but what followed in the article. I quote:- "| ....-£10,000 a month for a five-month season paid on top of accommodation, cars, expenses, ponies, equipment and a posse of female fans. One polo wife explained: "They eat with us, they train with us, they sleep with us. We own them for three months" ". As I was saying, who's a lucky boy then ? Say chaps, anyone for polo ? From little shrimps, mighty (h)elms will grow - I doubt that this saying will be familiar to many of you, although you will probably recall its better known partner which links ‘acorns' to 'oaks'. Never mind, we can't all be familiar with the rather fishy literature of 17th century Mersea oystermen, but it does serve as a rather lengthy way of reminding all you parents that there is a Cadet Series of races. The Cadet Series (for the Payne Cup) is a handicap series in any measured dinghy for helms aged 18 years and under on lst January (of the year in question). It is a well-known fact that sailing parents tend to use their offspring as forced labour at the sharp end of the boat. The Cadet Series gives said offspring a chance to shine as helms (and get their own back on the parents). However, not many parents would be willing to allow their ‘pride and joy' (ie. their boat) to be sailed off into the wild Blackwater river with little Jane or Johnnie at the helm - the risks would be too great (ie. risk of scratching the paintwork) . Thus, it is widely accepted that provided the Cadet does the helming, an adult can act as crew. My own children started helming in the Cadet races from the age of 8 and | can honestly say that I never touched the tiller from the 5-minute gun to the end of the race - but I did shout a lot. Now they teach me. "No Rules' Rules OK ? - we'd all like to think others see us as ruggedly independent, vigorously championing the rights of the individual against bureaucracy and standing aloof from the sheep-like obeisance of the rest of mankind. This image can be easily established by loudly proclaiming that rules are made to be broken, bad rules lead to bad government and rules should be applied with discretion. All very true but who judges when a rule is ‘bad', or should be broken ‘with discretion’ ? What carnage on the roads if someone wasn't prepared to apply the rules; what a worry if we really believed the majority would not, in fact, ‘obey the rules'. Even worse is a rule which cannot be enforced - or which ‘the authorities’ are unwilling to enforce. I heard the other day that a law (ie. rule) still exists which forbids Welshmen to be inside the walls of Chester upon pain of death ; now there's a case for discretion if ever there was one. A rule exists in the club's Sailing Instructions which is rarely (if ever) enforced and might just possibly be unenforceable. It is S.1.Rule 5. which says , amongst other things, that ‘for all sailing after October and sailing before the end of May, Wet or Dry suits must be worn by all competitors. Failure to do so in a race will result in disqualification’. A quite clear breach of this rule by several competitors in'a recent race (before end-May) resulted in neither automatic disqualification or subsequent protest. Let's be honest, who at our club level sailing would WISH to make such a protest; mone I would think. The day in question was gloriously sunny and warm at surface level and there was little wind; there was little danger of someone falling into the still cold waters of the Blackwater. Anyway, who is to say what is a ‘wet suit' or ‘dry suit' or whether such aq item should be worn ‘complete’ or in part, done up or open, or even be adequate for its normal purpose ? S.1.Rule 5 is unenforceable if those concerned are not willing to accept it as being enforceable; therefore the Rule should be changed to be a recommendation and not an edict. A 'bad' rule might be annoying but an unenforceable rule is a waste of everybody's time. Five Wise Men - a recent Sailing Sub-Committee meeting discussed at some length what was perceived to be a 'Race Officering' problem, ie. the general standard of Race Officering was not as high as it should, or could, be and that some sailing members of the club might leave unless the standard was improved. I'm not sure that many would actually leave, or that we should be worried if they did, but nevertheless it is very annoying for those who race if too many R.O. mistakes are occurring week in and week out. Since those who race are also those who perform R.O. duties, it follows that most of us are guilty. Therefore, it has been decided to find 'Five Wise Men' who will take it in turns to be available each week to give advice to the R.0. if requested. They will not dictate to the Race Officer, but merely introduce themselves and offer their advice if the R.0. feels he/she needs it. Another Five Wise Men - arising from the 'Five Wise Men' discussion, it was also suggested that each week, the Race Officer, the Officer-of-the-day, the Duty Coxswain, the Wise Man (for that week) and at least one Fleet captain should meet at 09.30 on the sea wall to assess and discuss the conditions of wind, tide, sea state and support boat status before the Race Officer decides and sets the courses for the day's events. (Mike Boreham)

TROLLEY SAILING IN THE BLACKWATER To put the records straight, Malcolm Shaft cannot claim to be the only person to indulge in this sport at M.S.C. In October 1988 I successfully floated an all-metal trailer. I therefore claim to be the inventor of 'Trolley Sailing', unless (to quote Esther Rantzen) "You know better". I will not dispute Malcolm's claim for the distance record, I only sailed 29'11" before being winched ashore, together with a suitable weight (sailing cruiser). On the same day I also invented (patent applied for) an automatic rudder dismounting process using the 'cruiser tipping' procedure. This involved positioning a 22' cruiser on a two-wheeled road trailer in such a manner that the centre of gravity of the unit is behind the axle, and then removing the support under the vessel's stem. The rudder is autamatically lifted from its pintles when the ster of the vessel strikes the ground. There are three disadvantages which I have yet to overcame - suggestions please: 1) Having to manhandle the boat back on the trailer. 2) Having to repair the stern of the boat where it struck the ground 3) Being reminded of the incident at frequent intervals by the rest of the family. Any member of M.S.C. can feel free to use this invention and I shall be grateful for any comments for improvements and on its effectiveness as a labour-saving process. Phil Shepherd

SAILING & RUNNING RACE > Now that the 1990 sailing season is under way, I thought that the readers of Navigans might enjoy a description of an unusual sailing event that two club members, Mike Turner and Jack Hardie, took part in last year. "I know where we can get a yacht" Memos fran the boss always induce something of a sinking feeling, and that's how I approached the one that landed on my desk in May 1989. Closer inspection proved that this one was at least different. It had the usual wad of typescript with the obligatory yellow-peril sticky note, but the note simply said "I know where we can get a yacht" and the typescript told of a new Five Hundred Mile, non stop sailing and running race. Start at Southampton; 100 miles sailing to Salcombe; 20 miles running to Dartmouth; sail to Exmouth; Royal Marines endurance course; 75 mile sail to Alderey, 10 miles run round the island, 100 miles sail back to Fowey in Cornwall; 30 mile run; 120 miles to Yarmouth; ten mile run to the Needles and sail back to finish in the Hamble. I thought he'd gone mad. Well, we did it. We came sixth in our class out of fifteen boats, gained a special prize for entering into the spirit of the race, and raised £700 for charity. The boat was a Dufour 39 donated by our sponsor, Lamerair Yacht Charter, who certainly did us proud. If you ever want to charter or buy a boat in the Solent area then I strongly recommend you give David Square a ring at Lamerair (04895-83601), he deserves the advert. We were a crew of six on the boat, of wham two were dedicated runners, with a backup tee ashore. Four of the team worked for our other sponsor - Ashridge Management College, so at least we had same theoretical expertise on teamworking! Apart from Mike Turmmer and ne, the rest of the team had fairly limited sailing experience so they had to learm as they went along. We certainly learned a lot; particularly about our own endurance and capabilities under stress. The two runners covered the equivalent of three marathons, over rough hilly coastal paths, in six days. Between runs they slept on the yacht and ate whatever food we could manage to provide them with, ranging from chicken casserole and rice at best to cold cooked pasta and Mars bars at worst. The four sailors worked the boat almost continuously for six days, sleeping in four-hour watches when conditions and landfalls allowed any sleep at all. Despite the stress, there was also a lot of fun and humour and not a sign of anger or irritation. Perhaps we were all too tired to disagree! Six days is too long to tell in full, and anyway it sticks in my mind as a series of snapshots, sane of them observed personally, same of them related by others. The first night with a strong headwind and a rough confused sea. The skipper/cook couldn't understand why the crew attributed the subsequent malaise to his Commish Pasties but pleaded that he wasn't prepared to invest in any more expensive fo considering the element of risk. The second night: winding the yacht up the muddy estuary of the River Exe in pitch darkness until we were finally stopped by shallow water, then the farce of dragging the rubber dinghy over partially covered mudbanks. We were trying to conserve the strength of our runner by sitting him in the dinghy while two sailors dragged him along. It worked well until, with the timing of a circus performer, he decided to stand up just when one of the sailors gave a mighty heave. Result: general collapse into the mud. The farce continued with the theft of our dinghy at one o'clock in the morning in a tiny Devon village. Sadly, I didn't witness the sight of two respectable citizens planning a temporary dinghy hi-jack to get them back to the yacht (how else do you acquire waterborne transport at one in the morning?), while a younger crew member looked on and pretended he wasn't with them. They returned at about 3 am, paddling a thing that looked like the smallest trawler in the world, and covered in mud from head to toe. One of our runners reporting to the Royal Marine Barracks after midnight, with balaclava helmet, track suit and two-day stubble, to be told at the gate to pop into the camp and find sameone to ask. I'm still not sure if they thought he was an honest citizen or such a pathetic terrorist that he deserved same help. All the times after that (having safely returmed our hi-jacked tender) we used the forty-foot yacht where we would normally use a dinghy, nosing it gingerly up to harbour walls, fishing boats, freighters and any other piece of terra firma where we could put our runners ashore with speed and safety.

7. -..-The frustration of my tactical error which left us within yards of the harbour at Aldermey but unable to cheat the tide to make the entrance. ...Our shore support team, filling up rabbit holes on Alderney where the runners would be in danger in twisting an ankle at night. Then the lights of the runners bobbing along in the dark while the runners themselves were invisible. ...-Becalmed in the shipping lanes off Alderney and poking my head up on deck, to see Mike Turner waving cheerfully at a towering wall of floating steel which had just altered course to avoid us. .«».The small town seen at night but not shown on the chart, and the subsequent confusion of the watch on deck until the 'town' detached itself from the shore and became an ocean liner. ...The sail change which should have taken a few minutes and took three quarters of an hour, because the crew were crippled by tiredness, seasickness, wave motion and an unlikely attack of the giggles. .-..The conversation overheard on the VHF between a becalmed yachtsman and a motor vessel skipper who was threatening to run him down if he didn't get out of the way - then the calm intervention of the British Coastguard who sorted the whole thing out with a few well-chosen words. ...The wild run from Plymouth to Yarmouth under full sail at night in a _ phosphorescent sea, with waves that needed bold and well-timed swings of the wheel to keep in control. After a four-hour watch in big waves, you really know the meaning of the phrase "shoulder to the wheel'. We averaged seven knots over 120 miles and missed the prize for the fastest passage by nine minutes. There are lots of 1esagne for sailing and racing. The secret of winning was not occasional brilliance, by constant campetence. Among the monohull boats, the differences in passage times were often less than an hour, and overall we beat our nearest rival by only forty minutes. When we lost time, we often lost it during the easy passages where we were too relaxed, and not so much when conditions were testing us to the limit. When we made mistakes there was often sameone who spotted it, but it wasn't always the person in nominal authority. We discovered that the cook was at least as important as the skipper and that sleep is more important than heroism. Would I do it, or samething like it, again? Funnily enough - yes! There was considerable disconfort and maybe a small element of real danger, but the experience of working towards a single clear objective, with a good team, over a significant period of time is - believe it or not - a luxury.
