REGATTA 1990 Congratulations to Marconi Sailing Club members :- Howard Knott and Stuart Knott Gull National Champions 1990 Howard and Stuart won the Gull National Championship at our Regatta over the week-end 26-28 May and we are very proud of having a national championship team which we can truly claim as being ‘home grown’. Howard was planning to sell his Gull and change to another boat, perhaps a 420. If he does sell, then he goes out on a ‘high’ but, if he doesn't sell, then he has set himself a high mountain to climb for the 1991 Gull Championships. Whatever he does, we are very pleased for Howard and his son Stuart. Of the Regatta itself, more than 120 boats attended the event. Of the 13 classes competing, two classes (the Hurricane 4.9/Condor and the Gull) were using the Regatta for their national championships. Strictly, speaking there were 3 classes doing so because the Condor championship was also awarded but there were only two entries. Saturday morning was devoted to the Rescue Boat Competition, an annual Marconi event designed to increase the awareness of rescue boat drivers and crew to various aspects of ‘the role of rescue'. Although the event was open to any BURC club, only three Marconi club teams took part and, to be honest, they were really scratch teams. Nevertheless, the competition was held and was judged by representatives from the Marine Division of the Essex Police, HM Coast Guard and St.John Ambulance and our thanks is extended to them for their help. Perhaps next year........se00? Saturday afternoon provided winds of around Force 3 for the practice race, enough to send the catamaran fleets up to the baffle and back down to number 4 and 2 channel markers. The purpose of the Practice Race is to allow visitors to get to know where the buoys are, and it is perhaps unfortunate that the Hurricane 4.9 fleet decided to include it in their championship race series - unfortunate because some of them couldn't find the marks. Presumably, none of the locals got lost and the Marconi Dinghy Challenge Cup race was extracted from the result. The small fee charged for the Practice Race was donated to the Steeple Church Roof Appeal and about £30 was raised. Both Sunday and Monday morning races (races 1 and 3) saw very little wind and competitors spent a long time on the water achieving very little. Some retired but some made it round the course and there was much moaning from some competitors. On Sunday, the sea breeze filled in during the middle afternoon and the race was started at 16.45 and at least gave the competitors a bit of a reasonable sail. On Monday, the race organisers feared that the Regatta Race 4 would have to be cancelled if the wind conditions were a repeat of Monday but, fortunately, by 13.45 it had increased in strength sufficiently for a 15.00 start and all fleets finished off Regatta with another reasonable sail, even if it was only a relatively short one. Although the Regatta race 4 might have been cancelled due to fast running out of time, the race organisers promised the Hurricane 4.9 and Gull fleets a 4th race to complete their championships for as long as the competitors were prepared to wait - even to running the race on Tuesday if necessary. COMMODORE'S NOTES 3 At some time between Sunday 17th June and Tuesday 19th June, Number One garage was broken into and the green Hayter mower was stolen. This mower cost the Club approximately sg99 when purchased in 1985, and it is unlikely that we will receive this amount from the insurance. It is essential that we all take more care of our, afid the Club's, property. A Sumber of members have complained to me that they have found the gate left open when they arrived at the Club. Short of asking Pete to weld it shut, I cannot ensure that it is always kept closed. Only you can, by always shutting the gate even if you see someone else just about to enter or leave the site. When you arrive ALWAYS SHUT THE GATE BEHIND YOU. If there is another car immediately behind you, check that he is a club member, do not just assume that he is. Remember that Club property is generally more securely locked away than your own; it may be your mast, tender, or dinghy that goes missing next time. You may remember that I wrote earlier this year about the comments that “the Club should revive the Winter Lecture series” and asked for two volunteers to come forward to organise them. Well, believe it or not, there has been no response whatsoever from the Club which comprises nearly 500 Members, of which You are One, Therefore, unless you come forward by the middle of September, only the Cruiser Fleet will be having a Winter Lecture Series, On the same theme, it is three months since I wrote to all Ordinary Members asking for a volunteer to replace Pat Black in the post of Hon Secretary, and a month since I wrote about Mike Boreham standing down from the position of Rear Commodore. To date there has been no response. I do not believe that strong arm tactics by the "Committee" is the right way to fill these positions and I hope that some of the "Club" - again, You Are The Club - will come forward to fill these posts. I am pleased to say that there has been some interest shown in a replacement for the Membership Secretary. Turning to the more immediate future. The East Coast Piers Race is being run on Sunday 16th September, to raise money for the RYA Seamanship Foundation who help the disabled to sail. John Nickalls and his Committee have done a tremendous job in organising this year's Race, The Race will be started by the Minister for the Disabled, Nicholas Scott, from the deck of HMS Puncher. Last year, more than £1,600 was raised by the event. I know that John and the ECPR Committee would like to try to double this. If you can, please come to the Club that day and support the event, even if only to see the tremendous sight of the start. AN IMMEDIATE ADDITION TO THE SAILING INSTRUCTIONS. At its meeting on 2nd July, the Main Committee unanimously agreed the following immediate additions to the Sailing Instructions:- Any boat which, whilst sailing under the MSC Sailing Instructions and associated Racing Rules, touches any part of a craft which is attached to an MSC mooring shall be automatically disqualified. For the purposes of this additional Sailing Instruction, the term ‘any part of a craft' shall be deemed to include the mooring, equipment and tackle to which it is attached, together with any temporary extensions to the moored craft and any part of a dinghy, tender or craft which is secured to the mooredcraft or its associated mooring, equipment and tackle. Any boat which, whilst sailing under the MSC Sailing Instructions and associated Racing Rules, touches an MSC mooring and associated equipment and tackle and to which no craft is attached, shall not be disqualified under the provisions of this additional Sailing Instruction. The technical reasons for the additional Sailing Instruction. There is no reason, other than lack of seamanship, why a boat (which is racing) should 'touch'sto a greater or lesser degree (eg. collide with; scrape past ),an obstruction such as a mooring, its equipment and tackle and/or any boat which is secured thereto. A boat which is racing should be sufficiently aware of the impending lack of room to clear the obstruction in a seamanlike manner. Where room to clear the obstruction is baulked by another boat which is sailing, then the boat which is impeded should ‘call for water' in order to pass to leeward, to windward, to tack or gybe in order to avoid the obstructing moored boat. Where 'water' is not given, the impeded boat should take seamanlike action to avoid or minimise touching/colliding with the moored boat and its...etc.etc. If the boat failing to 'give water' is racing, then a Protest can be raised but, if it is not racing, then a senior club member should be asked to ‘have a quiet word’ with the offending helm (who might not be aware of his/her obligations). The human reasons for the additional Sailing Instruction If you were to find scrape marks, dents or occassionally actual damage had occurred to your car whilst it was parked in the car park, you would naturally feel somewhat vexed. If you were to be told it was all part of the risks of modern-day driving and such things must be expected to happen, you might politely express a wish that the person responsible would (a) learn to drive with a little more care and consideration and (b) at least report the mishap.with an apology. If you were to be told that you can ‘always get it repaired on your insurance so what are you worrying about', you might get very cross indeed. So - why should your fellow boat-owners be expected to feel any different ? An appeal for mutual co-operation. Our club brings together a relatively few number of people who share a common interest in sailing but fulfill their interest in different ways. Thus we have sailboarders doing wonderful gyrations in wind conditions which keeps me firmly in the club-house. The satisfied joy of our cruiser members as they spend half the season painting, varnishing and anti-fouling their pride and joy, whilst our dinghy racers spend week-in and week-out chasing each other around the same local buoys - usually well within sight of the clubhouse (andequally usually with the same result) is another example of different people achieving the same degree of satisfaction in different ways. We implicitly trust our fellow members to act in a ‘reasonable way' both on and off the water and we are fortunate that the various interest groups within the club co-operate with considerable success. REGATTA '91 The Regatta Format - what should it be ? What should the club be aiming at in its promotion of Regatta - apart from promoting sailing ? Theoretically, one could say it depends upon what the club membership as a whole wished to achieve; in reality it depends upon what individual members are willing to do - or not to do - in order to run the Regatta. Whether Regatta is a high profile event, attracting lots of top class sailors, and providing side shows of discos, BBQs, meals-on-wheels, cabaret and crowded bars 100' long depends solely upon the willingness of individual members to provide all these things, either via money or effort, rather than by any resolutions of a committee. Whether this is what the membership ‘as a whole’ wants is questionable, but certainly in the past there has been a sufficient number of very keen individual members willing to put in the effort to provide these things. [redacted] DOGS ON THE SITE I recently received a letter from a Member expressing concern about unrestrained dogs at the Site. This was after an incident with a dog which, by being a little too friendly and too interested in their food, was really making itself something of a misance as the family tried to eat their lunch, In the end the family felt obliged to move their position in order to finish their meal in peace. Over the years in Navigans the Committee has often expressed disquiet about dogs roaming free on the site, especially in the summer when there are so many children about - which is an obvious reason for concern, There might also be occasions when trouble could arise simply by one circumstance leading to another - such as when an owner is walking his dog on a lead, or has secured his dog outside the family car on a hot day - when am encounter with a roaming dog could lead to friction between dogs and owners alike. CONtd. 26

If someone is busily engrossed in a particular task, the silent approach of a dog close to them can take them unawares afd cause a startled reaction, as happened to me some time ago when I had an unexpected eficounter with a large black shape in the gloom of the corridor by the Ladies Changing Room. Being startled just for a secorid I jumped, and the dog (which happened to be on a lead) bristled im reaction, perhaps thinking he was being challenged. We both relaxed immediately but I've always felt it could have easily led to an incident if he had been a less good-tempered animal than he obviously was. I was so shaken that I forgot to remind the owner, as I usually do on these very rare occasions, that dogs weren't allowed in the Clubhouse! Please remember that it is a Club Rule that dogs must be kept on a lead while on the Site, and that they don't enter the Clubhouse. Even without these rules, it should in any case be s matter of simple courtesy fot to allow one's dog to pay persistent and unwelcome attentions to other people in his vicinity. Ed. 8, This is an account of Rodnigon's 1990 Summer Cruise to North Brittanny and back, It followed on our last year's cruise to the same area which quite took our fancy, for those of you who do not know her, Rodnigon is a fin keeled Varne 27, sloop rigged, with a LOA of 8,5 metres and powered by a Volvo MD6A twin cylinder diesel. In the five seasons of our ownership we have cruised her to Holland and Belgium, down to Normandy, the Channel Islands and North Brittanny, Boulogne and N. France, as well as local sailing on the East Coast and one foray to Dartmouth, Cpermy S 7 oy, Peer ot. tok airy Rat 6 oJ MorlecTre M.S.C, - DOVER There are a number of routes which can be taken to cross the Thames Estuary, all of them dependent on the tide time and state. My own particular favourite is to go cut via the Spitway on the ebb and to cross the Sunk Sand just north of the Sunk beacon by the Black Deep No.5 buoy. Timed correctly, this allows you to take the new flood through Fisherman's Gat and down to Ramsgate or Dover, Not so good for the return trip unless you have an accurate fixing aid because Fisherman's Gat is not buoyed. In this instance we chose to take the inside route, as the wind was N/E giving us a downwind leg to S.\ Barrow, a broad reach acrossthe Kentish Flats to Margate roads and a short beat along to the North Foreland, Dover is more hospitable than one might think for a busy port, but contrary to advice in pilot books, the Port Control don't mind which entrance you use as long as you call them 2 or 3 minutes from the entrance to request entry permission, just stay well clear of the mumerous ferries and hovercraft, You have the choice of anchoring in the small craft area or of locking into the Wellington Dock, The anchorage can get quite rough in easterly winds but is handy if you do not wish to be tied down to dock opening times, (2 hours either side of Hw) DOVER - NEWHAVEN There is no reel refuge for deep keel yachts between Dover and Newhaven - Rye and Folkestone are both drying harbours, Eastbound this leg can be completed with the tide assuming that a yacht can make 44 = 5 knots and can reach the tidal gate at Dungeness as the tide turns, This tactic gives about 10 hours of favourable tide to cover the 50 miles, Westbound this is not possible so we anchored in Pevensey Bay to await the westbound tide to take us round Beachy Head and into Newhaven, past the Seven Sisters, Newhaven Marina is suffering badly from silting up so we found ourselves aground for an hour or so at low spring tide, this was so even in an outside berth and despite Rodnigon's modest 1.3m draught, The Yacht Club is very hospitable and comfortable and provides very reasonably priced meals as well as good showers. NEWHAVEN - CHERBOURG This is a long Channel transit of some 95 rm, There is nothing much to see excepting the heavy traffic and ferries. The main trick is to avoid being downtide when approaching Cherbourg as the tides are very strong on the approach, However, Cherbourg is a big target with its 2 entrances, a good ROF and the visual assistance given by the frequent exits and entrances of the cross channel ferries. Once inside the outer harbour you still have well over a mile to sail before reaching the yacht harbour. All facilities including showers, chandlers and duty free shops are available nearby,

9. CHERBOURG - ALDERNEY Only a short leg of some 20 miles but one which has to be planned carefully so as to cross the Alderney race before the southbound tide sets hard, We failed last year and arrived in Guernsey instead of Alderney after being set into the race, The approved ploy is to make use of the westbound inshore eddy toward Cap de la Hague, This allows you to arrive off Cap de la Hague at slack water ready to transit the eight miles to Braye, This transit must be made so as to position well north of the island and then to allow the tide to take you into Braye harbour, There are two main points to watch during the transit, firstly the overfalls cause really rough seas, even in calm weather and the underwater noise which transmits through the hull is definitely frightening - I was convinced that Rodnigon had sprung a leak! The second point is that Alderney lies in a N/E - S/W direction, this has the visual effect of fooling oe into thinking that you are further north of the island than is actually the case, The answer is to keep a really careful check on bearings from identified landmarks, On this occasion we positioned ourselves nicely for the harbour entrance, got to within 2 miles, when Alderney disappeared in fog, a common trick I am told. We crept in on Decca and when we finally got frightened by the rocks which appeared out of the murk, dropped anchor to find that we were actually in the harbour, We then motored very, very slowly in the general direction of the breakwater until some mooring buoys and a solitary yacht appeared with it's crew genially welcoming us to Guernsey! Alderney itself is a delightful little island although the harbour is subject to a lot of swell under certain conditions, There are showers available near the harbour and a number of shops including the Braye Chippie. We pedalled round the island on our bikes before returning to Rodnigon to take the tide through the Swinge and on to Beaucette Marina in Guernsey, ALDERNEY - BEAUCETTE A really downhill leg this one, we had the spinnaker up until an enormous broach rolled Sarah off the bunk, We went into Beaucette Marina for the night after a short wait on the buoy outside to allow sufficient water over the sill, Beaucette is formed from an old quarry which was allowed to flood and an entrance was then blasted through the cliff, It is really pretty although quite a long way from St Peter Port and its shops. The Solent sailors who crowd St Peter Port Marina at weekends do not seem to like Beaucette, perhaps the rock strewn entry frightens them, although it is well marked for both day and night entry. Macmillans Almanac contains a table which allows calculation of the sill depth at any particular time and there is a tide gauge at the entrance. GUERNSEY _- BRITTANY (TREGUIER) Off again down the Little Russell channel with good views of Herm and Sark as we left the Channel Islands behind. Another long leg with very little commercial traffic but lots of fishing buoys to look out for, A glance at the tidal chart will show that careful tide planning can carry you most of the way on a favourable, or at worst, a cross tide, The huge lighthouse on Les Roches Couvres shows up from a long way out as does Les Heaux lighthouse when approaching the Treguier River, Time now to hoist both the Tricoleur and the Breton Ensign and get out the French charts and the pilot for entrance to the Treguier River, There are three entrances of varying difficulty, all of them demanding careful attention to the marks and transits so as to avoid the many hazards, Once into the river proper, it's all straightforward although the Marina berths at Breguier are in the mainstream which flows very strongly through the pontoons, The Treguier river is very wooded and there is a very comfortable sheltered anchorage half a mile downstream of the town for those who do not wish to utilise the marina facilities, The chandlery is worth a visit, it's quite large and very traditional with all sorts of nice goodies. It is situated just over the bridge upstream of the marina, TREGUIER - PLOUMANAC'H While in Treguier we met a retired army RSM who was making a leisurely trip to the Far East via the Med. He came with us for the ride to Ploumanac'h which turned out to be a beat all the way. We had a good view of Les Sept Iles as we approached Ploumanac'h. This port of Brittanny is the Pink Granite Coast and this is literally true when the sun shines on the rocks because they show a pink hue. Ploumanac'h is easily picked out by the Chateau Costolaeves which dominates the entrance and looks rather like something out of a fairy tale film set, The pilot books claim a difficult entrance, but we found it fairly straightforward, although we had to anchor in the entry channel to wait for water over the sill into the very sheltered harbour, It is a nice place to spend a few visits and perhaps to sail over to the nearby Sept Iles which are well worth a visit. PLOUMANAC'H - PRIMEL Primel is another place with a dramatic rock strewn entrance so we kept very strictly on the approved line and moored on the visitor's buoys. A touch bouncy in the harbour so we stayed only the one night. PRIMEL - ROSCOFF The harbour at Roscoff dries out, although it is possible for keel boats to dry out against the harbour wall, We went in to have a look at the harbour, but elected to go around the corner to the Bloscon ferry port, where we found a nice little anchorage with some unoccupied buoys, Roscoff is literally surrounded by rocks and requires great navigational care when on the approach, The Chenal de Batz provides a good high water shortcut between the mainland and the Ile de Batz for yachts em route to L'Abervrach or further south, The weed in this area is very prolific and I had to don snorkel and wetsuit to clear

10, Rodnigon's propeller which was well fouled. Roscoff itself is a pretty little place and well worth a visit, especially so for the restaurants which sell an enormous variety of different crepes, ROSCOFF - MORLAIX Roscoff was the furthest west point of the holiday, an intention to go o~m the L'abervrach was frustrated by the wind and a lack of time, We sailed along the north side of the Ile de Batz before turning back and down towards the Morlaix estuary and its river. Initial perusal of the pilot book was somewhat twitch-inducing, but in fact the entry channels and transits are very clearly marked and give no problem in reasonable visibility, Again a dramatic rock strewn entrance to the wide Morlaix river which is navigable only on the tide. Morlaix is at the head of navigation and the marina is accessed by a lock which opens at HW - 1% hours, HW and HW + 1 hour. The town is dominated by a tall viaduct across the valley and is well worth a visit. We spent two days there making full use of our bikes to inspect the countryside, OUR RETURN was by a very similar route via Ploumanac'h, Guernsey (St Peter Port this time,) Alderney, Dover, Ramsgate to MSC with no major occurences other than a chance encounter with a fishing buoy, Hopefully this account will encourage more forays of the MSC Kamikaze Seagull into foreign parts. We certainly recommend North Brittanny as a cruising ground, but you do need three weeks' holiday, If you do intend a trip to this area it would be worth considering leaving your boat on the South Coast ready for the transit to Cherbourg or the Channel Islands. With this in mind, I have composed a list of these items, Perhaps other Navigans readers might like to add their own contributions: * Plastic Cable Ties - mousing shackles and numerous securing jobs, * Bag of Elastic Bands - quick release of Dan buoys and lifebelts, numerous securing jobs, closures of opened food containers, Micro-Minilights - you cannot have too many torches, these are small, powerful, watertight and focusable, z*¢- Pip Clips - provide secure housing for boathooks, torches etc, Bottle Closures - Handy if you don't really want to finish the whole wine bottle at one go. Post-Its - Sticky labels for noting courses, tidal heights etc. to which the navigator needs instant reference, They can be temporarily stuck on the chart. * Plastic Beer Bottles (Empty) - Cut the neck off, and slide the bottle upside down over your deck brush handle to give a flow of water over the brush head. KkKKKKKKKEE SPEED BOAT INCIDENTS Every class of water sports attracts its small minority of ‘idiots' - the sailboat category included. However, the ‘mechanised sea-horses' (ie. speedboats, jet-skis, etc) are, by their nature, rather likely to be more lethal than the average dinghy sailor ‘idiot' and therefore a great deal of trust and responsibility is placed in the hands of those who drive them. The Sailing Sub-Committee have been alarmed by what is perceived to be an increase in ‘incidents’ involving the speed boats and jet-skis . Without wishing anyone to get neurotic or paranoid about it, the Sailing Sub feel that if anyone experiences a genuinely dangerous incident then they should report it to the 0.0.D. with a view to reporting the matter to the police. You will need to note the number/name of the boats involved and, of course, have some independent witnesses. That is not to say that you report every time a speed boat's wash rocks your sailboat when you're trying to get across to Goldhanger with little wind and an adverse tide; the speed boats have as much right to use the river as we sailors and, like us, are normally considerate and responsible but occassionally make a mistake. Let's keep an eye on it - but not go overboard (literally). THE ABOVE NOTICE PUT IN AT THE REQUEST OF THE SAILING SUB-COMMITTEE Mike Boreham Rear Commodore

—e 'S NOTES COMMODORE What a Camping Fortnight. Although I was unable to attend, I believe the sun shone, it was warm (even hot) and dry for the whole time. I would like to thank all concemed who helped throughout the fortnight during which I understand there were fifty five Cadets attending. I am sure that everyone would join me in thanking Mike Turner for his efforts in arranging the Cadet Week tuition. Our next major event is the East Coast Piers Race which will be on Sunday 16th September and I am sure that John and his team will be hoping for similar conditions. Some concern has been expressed to me regarding the new rule in the Sailing Instructions. The potential risks of the increased number, size and speed of dinghies racing in the moorings was first brought up at the April Main Cammittee Meeting and was referred to the Sailing Sub Cammittee with a request that they put forward sane proposal. The matter was left with them, but they could not agree a suitable formla. At the July Main Cammittee Meeting it was decided to adopt the rule which is similar to that used by most of the Burmham Clubs. The intention is not to prevent sailing in the moorings, but to try to ensure that we do not end up with damage to racing Dinghies or Cruisers. While I am not conversant with the racing rules, I presume that any 'innocent' party who was disqualified as a result of the rule, would be able to protest any 'guilty' party. It is my intention that during the closed winter season, the whole question of the start line, the courses we sail and the support boat facilities is fully examined to formulate a way forward into the future. I will close by expressing my thanks once again to all who helped during the Camping Fortnight. While sailing on the Blackwater one sunny summer Sunday and passing north of the picturesque Bradwell Power Station, I noticed lots of yachts, same of them belonging to MSC alas, which appeared at first sight to be at anchor. Well they were all lying to the tide, sails neatly furled and with bits of rope or chain attaching bows to water. Then suddenly I realised my mistake, silly me, of course they were not at anchor. Quickly checking my 1937 Manual of Seamanship, I confirmed that ships at anchor in daylight must exhibit a round shape in the forward rigging. There was not a round shape to be seen on any of these yachts. It must be a new game to replace the now passe launching trailer sailing. I was daft enough to ask the Cruiser Captain the rules, but he just muttered something about Dutch motor sailing triangle, hit me with his scran bag and shambled off. (Saint) Dave Beane Unctuous Cottage Self Righteous Lake Verging on Sebacious Extracts from HMSO Manual of Seamanship Vol. 1 - 1937 To Sling a Hammock up, and secure the Lanyards 'The bight of the lanyard is placed over the hammock hook and the end rove through the ring, the hammock is then triced up to the height required and the end secured with a double or single sheet bend.' - Got it? Entering or Leaving a Boat ‘When entering or leaving a boat, the seniors enter last and leave first, unless permission to the contrary is given by the senior.' - Shall we see this on the MSC Hard? Must speak to the Commodore. Rules for Instructors Rule 1. - Do not lose your temper. Rule 9. - Insist on eyes being kept in the boat. Washing Clothes ‘When doing this care should be taken to rinse them out thoroughly; in the case of duck clothing, salt water might be used. It is not advisable to wash flannels in hot water or to rinse them in salt water. In all cases, clothes stops should be put in before washing the clothes. Clothes are stopped onto the clothes lines by passing the stops round the line and then reef knotting, care being taken that each piece is locked inside the piece on either side.' - No automatic washing machines or even clothes pegs for these guys! Dave Beane.

A view from the rear. Camping Fortnight - no doubt a more comprehensive account will appear elsewhere in Navigans but, once again, Camping Fortnight can be claimed to have been a great success. This year, all records appear to have been broken; the weather was brilliant, the two fields were full of campers, almost 60 cadets attended the Cadet Training Week - and Ione and David Saunders treated something like 100 ‘cases' in their St.John's ambulance unit. One 'tradition' also appears to have fallen by the wayside; for the first time in many years we didn't have a thunderstorm (not even a little one). Keyholders - thanks to the following who volunteered to act as 'keyholder' (ie 0.0.D) for a weekday during Camping Fortnight:- Peter Flook Linda Chaplin Chris Harrison Derek Holroyd Malcolm Stuart Andy Greenhalgh Dave Fletcher Bob Anderson Doug Eyles Dart 15 Demonstration Boats - the two Dart 15 Demo boats were also a great success although we could only use one of them due to a shortage of serviceable rudders. At least 58 people were '‘logged' as having used the single Dart 15, many of them experiencing catamaran sailing for the first time. In addition, I believe some 30-40 cadets from 8 years upwards also ‘had a ride’ on one of the five cats used to act as 'ferries' between the Club and Osea island during the Cadet Treasure Hunt. Several people have expressed real interest in buying a Dart 15. Laser 13 and Laser Fun Demos - thanks to Leone and Gordon Golding for arranging the demo Laser 13 and aser Fun boats. Despite my good intentions, I didn't find time to 'have a go' but I believe the boats were well used by others on site. Camping Bar Duties - nobody wanted a lunchtime drink (I'm glad to say) but we just about managed to get enough volunteers to open the bar each evening. Thanks to the following:- David & Marie Greenhalgh Dave and Zora Jibb Mark & Laura Strong Rory & Grant Strong and Jo Andy Greenhalgh and Paul Peter & Lesley Spittle David & Ione Saunders Dave Franklin & Tony Craighill Richard Willmott & friend. In case your wondering, Maggie and | also performed bar duties - several times - so we clearly needed additional volunteers. Camping Numbers - I calculate some 60 ‘units’ of varying sizes camped during camping fortnight, including about 16 Caravan and Camping Club units. A ‘unit' varied in size from a single (smallish) tent to caravans with awning and two small tents for 'the offspring and friends’. It proved very difficult to keep up with the comings and goings of those who camped for only a night or two and no doubt a few managed to escape the call from 'the rent collector’. The informal approach we have previously been able to adopt towards club Campers in past years might have to be reviewed if this year's numbers are to be repeated in the future. Cadet training - the ‘two Mikes' (Turner and Battle) again worked hard to produced an excellent training srogramme for almost 60 cadets of all ages. The two Mikes were given full time assistance by a number of elpers and part-time help from many others. Each 'era' of cadet training brings with it a group of ‘parent helpers! and, although enjoyable, is jolly hard work for the week - I know, I've had. my turn in the past. Each year the numbers attending cadet training seems to get bigger and bigger - where will it all end 1 ask myself ? Adult training - in contrast, the adult training is rather more informal and low key. After all, most of the adults are, in fact, the Mums of the cadets and consequently are busy organising children, preparing packed lunches and wondering what to have for dinner tomorrow (sexist but true). This year, I cut out the coffee Morning and theory and concentrated on getting the adults actually sailing, particularly with helming the boats. Fortunately, the winds and weather were just right to make this approach possible, Many thanks to Ian Caruth, David Ball, Lucy Boreham, Stuart Golding - and Maggie Boreham - for helping with the adult instruction, Incidents and mechanical sea-horses - the very week after the Autumn Navigans came out, we had occasion to report to the river police two rather serious ‘incidents’ concerning club sailors and speed boats. Fortunately, nobody was hurt - thanks to the quick reactions of club sailors involved. The worrying thing is that 'the incidents' appeared to have occurred out of basic ignorance of seamanship rather than of any evil intent. As I said before, the majority of power boat users are responsible people - it is the few irresponsible people you have to watch out for as you share, with them, the pleasures of the Blackwater. Watchfulness and tolerance should be the guiding principles; only report genuinely dangerous incidents (as with the two incidents mentioned). Mike Boreham Rear Commodore

SUNDAY 24TH JUNE 1990 - A DAY'S RESCUE What can be more pleasant than a day on rescue boat duty. No bruises, no getting wet, no trapeze belt cutting into you, or that's what I thought. Take a camera, you never know, might get some shots for the photo competition. Take a snack, won't be a lot to do except: - Bring back three sailboarders and two dinghies. - Look for two lost racing marks. - Put up with faulty radios. - Try to assist two cats. in trouble on lee shores. - Slip over on hard. Let's go back to the start of the list: Two sailboarders taken fran the water, neither wearing buoyancy aids, one transferred from a yacht with a damaged board, again no buoyancy aid, and yet Flag B was being flown. Ome young lady sailboarder when asked where her buoyancy aid was replied "In the club locker roam", She was informed in no uncertain termns of my views. Sailboarders must be exempt fram personal buoyancy, maybe they can't drown, only they know that perhaps they can walk on water. Still on the subject of personal buoyancy [an occupant of] one of the dinghies given assistance sported a new way to wear his buoyancy aid, almost round his neck. This was because it had ridden up, he must have been using it to keep his ears warm. Two lost racing marks, they still haven't been found [at the time of writing], so if anyone sees C mark and a red buoy with a flag on top, please return. Perhaps sameone can shed same light on the faults on the new radios, the one in the race box could not transmit and the hand-held one could not receive. Surely these problems, if only on safety grounds, should have been ironed out at the start of the season. I am fully aware of the lack of finances within the club, but I would suggest that those responsible for purchasing the OOD's boat try using the Jack B to get into a lee shore and assist boats in trouble. Perhaps if we had kept the old radios and not purchased an unsuitable runabout for the OOD the money could have gone same way towards the proposed new rescue boat. What happened to the repairs to the hard? I seem to remember raising at the last AGY about the cost of repairs and also the standard of repairs and reclaiming same of the costs fran the Contractors. Perhaps we will have to wait until sameone breaks something. If these Comments seem like moans - they are. What do others think? DAVE PAYNE Ed. would just like to chip in here and say that she, at least, was pleased to see the new Orkney arrive at the Club. Son David suffered a knee injury while out with his Dad on Baddow Star to help sameone on a rough day. Baddow Star - which is just not suitable for rough water and that's when her services were most often required - hit a steep wave off Osea and David was thrown fram his seat on to his knees. The injury made itself felt for many months afterwards before it cleared up. I'm told the Orkney is much better behaved on the water, and the extra work involved in pulling her up the hard is the price to be paid for a better OOD boat.

LETTERS TO THE EDITOR FROM SOME MEMBERS OF THE CAT FLEET: Dear Madame Editor, I feel that I must respond to a number of issueS raised in the last issue of Navigans! The introduction of a new rule which disqualifies dinghies which touch an obstruction (Cruiser or Mooring) is, in my opinion, a disgrace! This rule degrades the club dinghy sailors and implies that we are all Kamikaze helmspeople, who deliberately aim to hit these moored monoliths! This is blatantly not true! Let us use the same analogy as used in the explanation. Yes, I would be aggrieved if somebody deliberately damaged my car when it was parked. Accidents happen, and few people own up every time. I am sure that the people wanting this rule have given and received in this type of incident without either identifying/challenging the culprit, or owning up themselves, (Don't do as I do, do as I say!) However we are not talking about the car being parked in the local shopping park, we are talking of the equivalent of parking on the start and finish straight at Brands Hatch. I would not want to park my car anywhere on the track at Brands Hatch, let alone on the start and finish line as are same of our cruiser fleet! Would you expect any racing driver to deliberately ram another car? If not, why do the cammittee imply that dinghy sailors will? Marconi Club is in grave danger of becoming an US and THEM club, with the dinghy fleet eventually leaving to go to more suitable pastures. I an not joking, I have seen it happen at another club. The Club must make up its mind about dinghy racing. If it wishes to maintain a dinghy fleet, then it must either move the cruisers or the course! If you move the course, you may have difficulty running races in light winds, but moving the moorings may be even less feasible. The cruisers on the start line and close to the hard, and close to 'A' and 'F' marks are all in danger, so why leave them there? This new rule is contemptuous and should be treated that way until it is rescinded as being unnecessary. If the cruiser people are worried about their boats they can either surround them with a giant rubber tube, or remove them fram the water when not in use, (no, neither of these are serious suggestions, but they make a point. My second comment refers to the OOD's boat and the Comment by our Bosun on the difficulty of retrieval on the hard. This boat is already a sore point with a number of dinghy sailors. Why, when we had clearly identifed the need for an inflatable auxiliary rescue boat, did the club squander precious financial resource on a boat which is unsuitable to act as a rescue boat? Ray Ball makes this very point when he highlights the need for three crew. The new boat is undoubtedly better than the Baddow Star, but having used that boat for a number of years, what was wrong with waiting a little longer to get the boat we really needed? However, I heed the request for help, but don't expect me not to moan when I assist in retrieval. My third point is the comment about the dogs on site. With the exception of one or two thoughtless individuals, the owners of dogs almost always obey the club mules. However, the dogs which wander unrestrained around the site are often fran the farm and house by the club gates, and we seem unable to prevent them fran gaining access. The occupants of these properties seem reluctant to control their animals, so other than camplaining to the council, or putting a better fence around the Club what more can we do? COntdis.<0

8. It seems to me that the club is becaming a club of camplainers (isn't that just what I'm doing as well?) and unless this attitude is reversed the atmosphere will go fran bad to worse. People must be encouraged (cajoled?) to be open and honest and say what they feel to the people who are upsetting them, not to moan at everybody in general via Navigans or to introduce petty rules. Regards, Steve Keeble Dear Maureen, The August issue of Navigans has pranpted me to write to you concerming various aspects of Marconi Sailing Club which are giving me cause for concern, and I hope you will be able to print this letter in the next issue. I cannot claim to be a member who makes heavy demands on the Club's facilities. My involvement with Catamaran racing at International level, together with various duties as an RYA coach and an enthusiastic member of the Hurricane Class Association leaves few spare weekends for Club activities. However as a founder member of the Catamaran Fleet same nine years ago, I have always remained intensely loyal to Marconi Sailing Club, as witnessed by various reports appearing in both the Yachting Press and National newspapers from time to tire, despite being a member of Grafham Water Sailing Club as well. Over the last couple of years I have became increasingly concerned over the number of new rules and regulations which are being imposed on us, the Members. Whilst I an aware that as the Club grows there is a need to control certain aspects, I am sure that the petty bureaucracy we are now being subjected to is unnecessary in any form in a club such as ours, and contrasts strongly with the freedan normally associated with the sport of sailing. I must admit that the 1990 Club Handbook brought a smile to my face when I read Rule 3 - Clubhouse and Precincts: "Parking on the hard, adjacent to the Clubhouse and the Dinghy and CAR* Park is forbidden." Someone must have bumed the midnight oil working on that one! The August issue of Navigans was the final straw for me. Having read 'Catmodore's Notes' I felt that I had just been rebuked by a bad-tempered Headmaster. I am sure that if members felt a need for Winter lectures they would organise them without coercion, and presumably if any members have evenings to spare they could attend the well-organised Cruiser Fleet Lectures? Or does a closed shop operate? The nail in the coffin is the "new" Sailing Instruction. I would guess that a cruiser has’ sustained same sort of minor damage fram an unknown source, speedboat, jetski, fishing boat, log, another cruiser or whatever - the possibilities are endless. Hence we have the illogical solution to introduce yet another rule, with various references to 'lack of seamanship' being the 'technical' reason for a racing boat hitting an obstruction. CONT. sss

9. Members of this club have spent hours on Exhibition stands trying to attract new members to the Club. I do not recall that, because of the congested moorings in the start and finish area, it was a pre-requisite that same sort of qualification in boat-handling must be held by prospective members? I do however expect an announcement on the subject in the next issue of Navigans. I object very strongly to the assumption that new sailors should have no learning curve. he However, I am pleased to report that such is the inexperience of those responsible te” drafting the new Sailing Instruction, that it is invalid in its present form, and anyone so disqualified should appeal to the R.Y.A. I will be pleased to give guidance to anyone affected. Dear Maureen, When I saw the notice in the Club House amending Sailing Instructions to disqualify race competitors should they touch a Cruiser and/or its associated mooring, I became angry, fruastrated, and could not see the value of the rule when none of us sail to hit other boats. After my initial reaction I started to try and find out why the Main Cammittee had suddenly introduced the rule, and the following is based on information gleaned fran conversations with Cammittee Members. It would appear that the main concern is possible damage by Cats. travelling at high peed. No doubt introduction of a long line start for Cats as outlined in the Yearbook recognised that with a growing Cat Fleet, stationary Cruisers and a large number of Cats preparing to race do not mix, and the risk of damage increases. But throughout this year, Race Officers have not set long line starts. The Sailing Sub Cammittee is aware of this but has not made any efforts to change the situation, why not? The Main Cammittee, understandably concerned at possible serious damage, i.e. a sunken Cruiser, urged the Sailing Sub Cammittee to come up with a solution which the Sailing Sub Cammittee failed to do. What has the Sailing Sub Committee done about the position of moorings which are too close to the start line and the increase in moorings opposite the Clubhouse, another high risk area? What training have they introduced for new, inexperienced, members or Race Officers? I have came to the conclusion that the Main Carmmittee reacted to a situation which the Sailing Sub Committee should have dealt with earlier in the season. Why didn't they? They must now accept the blame for a lot of bad feeling being generated. Good communication between the interested parties is essential. Conta s...

10. I could go on, as there are other issues which this has raised - - Do we want racing craft at the Club? - Do we want inexperienced members? - Do we shun Members who are never going to achieve great seamanship? - What training is needed for Members? - How can cammunication between Members be improved? - How can the conflict of interest between Rescue and Mooring work be resolved? Marconi Sailing Club is a very good Club with a good reputation, but lack of direction and cammunication will lead to further misunderstandings and anger, which fosters bad feeling. To ensure the Club remains alive; the interests of various groups are catered for; and that sailing remains a pleasure for everyone; these issues must be tackled. Yours sincerely, Mike Duckmnanton Dear Maureen, CATAMARANS AT MARCONI During the course of the 1990 season a number of occurrences have led to the impression that the interests of the Catamaran Fleet are not being served as well as might be hoped. Recently letters to Navigans have indicated the level of dissatisfaction in same parts of the Fleet. I think it is important that all of us who sail Catamarans at the Club and who are not happy with recent events - particularly the imposition of the new Sailing Instruction - should understand the situation and take positive steps to ensure the Club continues to be (or becomes) the sort of Club to which we want to belong. My own personal feelings are: 1. The Club offers an excellent site, with good facilities, for Catamaran sailing. It would be hard to beat elsewhere for the variety it offers. 2. The Club caters for a wide variety of interests, and each group of members benefits fron the presence of the others: for instance a considerable number of Cruising members have very kindly offered their services in support of the Piers Race. The variety of interests necessarily implies a variety of facilities needed. 3. At any one time a large number of Cruisers are to be found unused on moorings. At any one time an equally large number of Catamarans can be seen in the Cat Field. 4. By their nature Cruisers have to be kept on moorings, and as such will inevitably became an obstacle to other river users. 5. Races imply a concentration of fast-moving craft, and as such will inevitably became a risk to other river users. 6. The moorings used by the Club are allocated by Maldon District Council; their positions may or may not be negotiable. The start line used for racing is in our owm hands, but is limited by the strong tide. 7. The wish to avoid severe damage to a Cruiser on a mooring is obvious. The need to take urgent steps to improve the present situation is debatable. The need to invoke CONTA sss

Fe a new Sailing Instruction aimed at outlawing samething which doesn't happen anyway (i.e. helms deliberately hitting and damaging Cruisers) is obscure to say the least. The method of introducing the new measure seems to have raised in same the emotions which might be associated with returning hame and finding the bailiffs have posted a notice re-possessing one's house. 8. Why do collisions occur? - [he start area is congested and control can be lost by the inexperienced in a melee of manoevering boats. - Tactical actions by same boats may lead to those less tactically aware into Situations where a collision ensues. - Leaving the Hard under certain wind conditions can be difficult. None of these will be affected by the new Sailing Instruction. 9. How can we reduce the risk of collisions? - Start in an area free of moored boats. - Clear the area in front of the Hard of moored Cruisers. 10. In light winds, collisions may occur but damage is unlikely. In strong enough winds the tidal flow beyond the moorings does not preclude a sensible start on a long line. 11. I propose: We keep the start line clear of moorings (and, no, this isn't done already). - In strong enough winds we start the Cats on a long line (i.e. beyond D mark and inside the orange flagged outer distance mark, using a transit of the racebox and D mark, not the mete.) - We find an effective means of signalling the starts and (metaphorically) bur the miniscule flags which are often unidentifiable. This may involve lights or shapes, and certainly much more noise. - We put a new mark off the south-east end of Osea Island. This would give an alternative first mark in westerly winds. - The risk involved in mooring Cruisers off the Hard should be recognised; we should also positively encourage those with, as yet, underdeveloped seamanship skills to sail amongst them. Where else can first steps in sailing be taken? - The new Sailing Instruction should be revoked with as much speed and vigour as those with which it was implemented. - Anyone who feels storage/mooring fees are inequitable should provide written evidence and generate a review based thereupon. I'm sure we'd all be in favour of a system which charged people campetitively for the facilities the site offers them. - Anyone who camplains about grass-roots representation on Club cammittees_ should stand themselves for election (and there's not a great deal of competition,) or should persuade a like-minded colleague to stand. The role of Catamaran Fleet Captain will be vacant. So much for my views. The Cat Fleet AGM will be held shortly after the Piers Race; I'll let you know the date when fixed. Judging by the heated emotions, the discussions should be lively. Please came along and let us have your ideas and your feelings. John Nickalls, Cat. Fleet Captain

13. LADIES CUP 1990. The winner of the 1990 Ladies Cup series was:- MAGGIE BOREHAM Congratulations to Maggie on repeating her 1989 success by again winning all three races of the 3-race series and thus retaining the Ladies Cup. Certainly, the series continues to attract a good entry; this year 15 ladies entered the series which consisted of 3 races, all held on the same day, 29 July, which was the middle Sunday of the camping fortnight. Sadly few, if any, of the ladies had done much in the way of helming since the same event last year, and several could be seen ‘brushing up' their boat-helming techniques the day before the event. The wind strength varied from SW F2-3 (Race 1) to SW F4-5 (Race 3) and was reflected in the entry numbers of 15 (Race 1), 11 (Race 2) and 5 (Race 3). The lighter winds of Race 1 (course AsXsB, 0; AsX- Fs) seemed to favour the monohulls but Race-2 (AyX>FsDs x 3) and Race 3 (ByRr) were much more attractive to the catamarans as was reflected in their finishing positions. Race Officer, Malcolm Stuart, arranged for the customary drinks after Race 2 and which were served with great aplomb by Ian Caruth. One could claim the event as ‘international’ with Vicki Bigden (OSC) and Charlotte Burck (Canada) adding the 'international' flavour to the event. Race 1 - the light wind and last of the ebb tide was clearly to the liking of the monohulls but the catamarans made a fine sight as they raced three abreast from A to No.1, looking for all the world like three Thames Barges in the 'old time' photographs. Mel Keeble sailed well to finish 4th, as did Sue Fletcher who, although apparently trailing the fleet because she was in the slowest boat, nevertheless actually finished 7th in this race. The four cats effectively had their own private race which was ‘won! by Anna Spittle, whilst Debbie Yorston and Lucy Boreham were separated by only one second at the finish. Race 2 - An increasing wind (Force 3-4) and 3 laps found more favour with the catamarans, with Anna Spittle and Lucy Boreham having a private duel but were 'split' on handicap by Pat Stuart (Mirror). Race 3 - Still more wind (Force 4-5) and a longer course attracted 5 entries but only two finishers (one of whom was disqualified). Charlotte Burck missed out on a 2nd place in this race by rounding the wrong mark at Goldhanger and subsequently retiring. Jenny Ball was ‘over the line' at the start but failed to return and was disqualified; this cost her a possible win in this race. Anna Spittle retired as did Sue Fletcher. 4. M.S.C./M.A.S.C. FINANCIAL RELATIONSHIP (and its effect on Club policy.) The Sailing Club operates as a section of the Marconi Athletic and Social Ci and as such is bound by its constitution. Under this the section is run by i committee(s) who have to discharge a responsibility to ensure the finacial wei being of the section; basically 'break even', not run at a loss. Whilst the section is not allowed to hold a bank account nor to enter into any loan agreement and it must have M.A.S.C. agreement for any major capital purchase, its finances are run in a seperate account within the MASC (this is the same for all sections). Such profit as is made by the section is held in a Reserve Fund, which bears interest, and used for two purposes. Firstly it can be used to "smooth' out a small loss in any one year, however the Main Committee policy is to avoid a loss in the first place. Secondly it is used to help with the cost of major equipment replacement such as replacement rescue craft, tractors etc.. The section has over the years managed its affairs in a professional manner and by following this policy operates free of interference from the MASC, unlike some other sections. Since the club moved to the Stansgate site, the MASC has invested £90,000.00 approx of their money by buying the site (i.e. it is owned by the M.A.S.C. not the Sailing Section, as are all the assets), building of the clubhouse, installation of the sewage plant and help with the Jack B purchase for example, in the site. For this and to offset the costs incurred by us at the MASC, accountant help etc., we pay an annual contribution; this year £7375.00. By this investment, they have demonstrated their willingness to help the section grow over the years. Turning to the events of the last couple of years, at the time that I first approached them for assistance with the second rescue boat and extension, this coincided with a downturn in their own finacial situation. As those who attended the MASC Annual General Meeting on the 26th September will know, they have operated with a loss of £23,000.00 in 1988/1989 and a loss of £30,000.00 in 1998/1990. This has obviously reduced their own reserves considerably. In part the situation has not been helped by the decrease in the Marconi working population as the level of Associate membership is limited to 12.5% by the Magistrates. Looking to the future the MASC has been involved in a cost reduction exercise which is starting to bear fruit this year. In addition it wants to amend its constitution to make all members 'Ordinary' not associate, this will remove the current restriction and allow a larger number of non GEC members. This resolution was put to a Special Meeting on the 26th September but had to be withdrawn because of some technical inaccuracies. These have now been resolved and a new meeting will be called on 17th October. Drawing some parallels with our own section, we found ourselves in the same situation in 1983/1985 when we had exhausted the Marconi companies for members. We wanted to improve and expand the facilities, costs were rising on the existing facilities, and there was a 'market value' above which subscription increases would lead to reduced membership. We therefore set out to increase the level of associate membership with all the heartache of 'the club will not be the same'/'the passing of an era' that the MASC is now experiencing. It is true that the club has changed but I believe that the foresight at that time was right and the club is the better for it today. We may have a new set of problems but we still have a club we all can afford. I am sure that the changes proposed by the MASC will have the same effect and would ask ALL Ordinary members to watch out for the notice of the meeting and come along to support the motion. Obviously these problems and the restrictions on the section by the constitution have affected the Section's Main Committee's plans for the future. E| Another view from the rear. NAVIGANS PAST - How many members actually read Navigans I wonder ? I guess we will never know ‘cos only those who read it could possibly reply to a questionnaire. Certainly in our household there's a fair old scramble to be first to read it. “What's your favourite feature?” I ask the rest of the family; "Through the eye of a hurricane" they reply . Thank's a lot family, nothing like loyalty to your nearest and dearest to cheer me up through the eye of the storm, let alone that hurricane. Although we've been MSC members from about 1972/73, I can't actually remember reading or seeing Navigans from the '70s. The earliest Navigans we kept was December'79 and shows a youthful Dave Lawson in very close proximity - and obvious enjoyment - to a belly-dancer at the Laying Up Supper. This might have been the same Laying Up Supper that the then Mirror Fleet were ‘well into their cups' - and resulted in a letter of complaint saying how dreadful it all was, speaking of which......seeceee NAVIGANS PRESENT - My suspicions were aroused at the late-August Bank Holiday Camping Weekend when a stream of gleeful members kept sidling up to the Fletcher's caravan for a peek at what was obviosly a pretty hot publication. Curiosity aroused, I casually wandered over to 'pass the time of day' and was met by Dave F with a grin well worthy of the cat (pussy-type) from Cheshire; “Collector's item this, Mike" he said “it's burnt brown and crisp around the edges". Well, I must say, it made good reading and, whether one agrees with ‘the letters' or no, it makes a change from the usual round of race reports and lists of winners, and even overshadows 'My trip up the Orinoco in Bathtub IV'. The September Navigans was somehow different. Handing back the crisped publication, the thunder growled, the lighting flashed and - down came the rain from the hosepipe inthe sky. Val F. advanced upon me accusingly, waving said crisped publication menacingly. "It's all your fault” she said quietly - but firmly. I nipped around the other side of the table, just to be on the safe side; “But they're entitled to their opinion" I cried , "and in any case, I was merely reporting the unanimous decision of the Main Committee - I was merely the winged messenger" (literally ready to take flight). "In any case, there were other 'dinghy' people at the meeting to voice opposition if they wished - it was a unanimous decision*®. I moved a chair nonchalantly soas toblock the nearest approach between Val and me; perhaps it was time to leave. "No", says Val "I'm not talking about ‘the Rule', I'm talking about the traditional thunder storm during camping fortnight. If you hadn't mentioned it had not come on time, this storm wouldn't have happened; It's all your fault". "Oh", says I, mightily relieved 4I suppose it is: Sorry" - and made off for the safety of my own caravan. At that moment the heavenly lights fused, the Thunder God belched and all hosepipes were clearly aimed at the MSC. SCHOOL MEALS UGH! - I'm not sure I agree with Robin Smith that Neil's comments in the August Navigans showed any marked bad tempered traits, but, if they were a little tetchy, then I'm not surprised. With a ratio of almost 500 members : 1 Commodore, the steady rain of complaints, gripes and moans covering all things under the (MSC) sun must get a bit wearing, even for a fairly mild-mannered chap like Neil. Still, if one allows oneself to be put up for ‘high office’ I suppose one must expect to be shied at now and again. As the saying goes:- ‘If you can't stand the heat, then get out of the kitchen' But how's this for a matching maxim:- ‘If you don't like the meals we serve, come into the kitchen and cook them yourself’ SPEECH DAY - There is no truth in the rumour that the AGM is to be re-named Speech Day, nor that the Laying Up Supper is to become known as the Master's Dinner Party. Mind you, the prospect of Neil appearing in mortar board and gown might bring in a bigger attendance at the AGM than usual, not that he need get up to such antics this year to attract an audience; I suspect this year it might have to be an open-air meeting and should provide lots of fun for all concerned. Let's hope the Thunder God has forgiven me and the Sunshine Girls look kindly upon me 'cos I'll be there. BEANE SAUCE - I enjoyed Dave Beane's little snippets evenifl didn't understand all the words (I couldn't find Sebacious in my dictionary but I think it's something to do with a border in the garden). The image of Derek Hall 'shambling off' scran bag over his shoulder, muttering about Dutch elm disease, or something, was worth contemplating. PS. What's a scran bag? # THOUGHT FOR THE DAY - it's not what you read, it's the way that you read it. ** joking apart, I rather like to read the cruiser articles. At least it covers a different type of sailing than I am used to and I remember Derek Hall's article with particular pleasure. Mike Boreham *scran = food; provisions. I know - it was Derek's ice box! (Ed.) Rear Commodore

THE EXPERIENCES OF THE THORNE FAMILY CAMPING For years Chris and I have told ourselves that we would stay at the Club for the Camping Fortnight. Most years we have only thought about it when reading the adventures of other people in Navigans. Every Blue Moon we have actually intended staying and once even hired a caravan only to be rained off almost as soon as we arrived. This year was going to be different. Our children, Stephen aged 12, and Michael aged 8, were going to do the Cadet Course and we bought a new tent to make certain it would not rain again. Full of hope we set off - I must admit I had already arranged an escape route of returning home during the fortnight for essential supplies and a comfortable night's sleep, — As everyone knows the weather was superb and our first week passed gently by. We even got our Cruiser in the water for the first time in two years, We still, as yet, haven't been anywhere in her - that highlight is still to core, Chris took our boys out in the Mirror and in true "Captain Bligh" spirit managed to upset them in a very short time. The usual helming skills of shouting continuously at your Crew with instructions they don't understand, being hit with the boom because your head isn't low enough or moving quick enough, and the tiller being rammed into your side because you haven't moved sufficiently aut of the way. Anyway Cadet Week started with Michael announcing that he wasn't going to do the capsize drill, and if that meant not doing the course then he wasn't going to do it, After a bit of "you are going to do it" persuasion, he agreed to do it, Neither boy had any real experience of sailing despite Stephen's assurance that sailing a Topper for half an hour at Center Parcs on a lake only 3ft deep throughout, was sailing single-handed, The boys entered into the spirit of the week and thoroughly enjoyed everything. Once Michael had done sis capsize drill he enjoyed falling into the water at every opportunity, By the time the boys were able to helm they too seemed to have caught the "Captain Bligh" spirit (is this something one catches sailing on the Blackwater???) Our funniest moment was listening to Stephen telling us about his first outing helming. there he was, helming and all his crew were interested in was looking at the other boats and not doing as he told them - even shouting didn't produce the right responses. I am sure other people will explain in greater detail the things the Cadets did in their week, but for us the pleasure of seeing our children sailing on their own in our dinghy was something we won't ever forget. We would like to take this opportunity to thank the two Mikes for all their efforts and the hard work they put in CONTD.....

7 to make the week so successful, The boys are already talking about next year and looking forward to the Winter Series, As to whether they will be so keen when normal sailing weather returns only remains to be seen, The only drawback to the fortnight was Chris and the boys sailing in the Cats, I can see this adventure might prove very expensive, Stephen's comment was "If we had one of those, Dad, we could core sailing every weekend." I have my suspicions that as time goes on I shall be outnumbered by the Sailors in my family and will pass some very contented weekends sitting on the sea wall, reading my book and getting sun tanned, or weather-beaten as the case may be, Still isn't that what family sailing is all about! An alternative venture is to take a trip by dinghy in the opposite direction with a view to exploring St Osyth creek, the village and priory. The creek is very twisty but deep enough for a dinghy at all states of the tide except for extreme low water. A row or motor of about two miles will bring you to the boatyard at the head of the creek, the site of a long-extinct tide mill. Here you can disembark and quench your thirst at the nearby pub just a few yards along the road to your left, Having satisfied this priority you can then walk further along the road towards the east and pay a visit to the remains of the 12th century priory before going back to your dinghy for tke return voyage, St Osyth creek joins Brightlingsea creek to the east of Cindery Island so it is possible to return to the trots by a slightly different route round the north of Cindery Island, Dave Beane IT COULD ONLY HAPPEN AT SEA - (Through the Eye of the Hurricane) As the newly-elected Chairman of the Hurricane Class Association I felt it to be my duty to accept as many free meals as was on offer at the recent Hurricane National Championships, Accordingly, Bank Holiday Monday morning found me filling my stomach with a generous helping of Eggs and Bacon thanks to the generosity of Chris and Trevor Milton, Duly satisfied, I left the two of them to proceed out onto the water for day 3 of the event, whilst I found myself a comfortable chair in the Race Box at Pentewan Sands Sailing Club to watch the 53 entrants chase the wind around the bay, My eyes felt like doorstops against which my brain was endlessly swinging, which will teach me to stay away from the booze which flowed after the Class AGM. CONTDO.....

Suddenly I was awoken fror my doze by the urgent calling of my mame! There before me stood Chris. "Help!" she cried, with e pleading look in mer eye, "I don't feel well, so will you crew for Trevor?" How could 1 refuse the woman who had filled my stomach that morning? My brain urgently sougkt an excuse! "I haven't got any sailing gear!" I replied with relief. "No worry, we'll find you some," came the reply. So with mo more ado I trotted, in time to the pounding in my head, around to the camper to kit up. As well as providing the sailing gear, Chris also provided the headache pills to see me on my way. Now you have to use your imagination! The wet suit belonged to Trevor, so it only fitted where it touched, If it bad been in green I could have done a very good impersonation of a Mutant Ninja Turtle. On me, the suit had more spare tyres than the Michelin Man, the legs looked like Nora Batty's stockings, and I had the only double breasted buoyancy sid available in the country! The trapeze belt felt like a loose-fitting pammock despite my attempts to pull it tighter as I waddled down the beach like a hippo, with Trevor only just managing to stifle bis laughter, "Whose gear ere you wearing?" asked Trevor, “Yours!" I replied, "No wonder it's big," smiled Trevor, "That's my spare suit and it's six inches too big for me!" “Ak well, I was always the wrong skape to model wet suits anyway!" We pushed the boat off and then came the difficult part. With all the spare tyres, and the double breasted buoyancy aid, I couldn't get on the boat, so I was dragged alongside for about tke first 50 yards, whilst Trevor made comments like "stop mucking about, and pull the jib in!" I finally struggled aboard and we headed for the start. "Hello Christine, where are your curls?" The comments care thick and fast from the rest of the fleet. Sore people kad difficulty getting their eyeballs back in their heads, after the shock of seeing me in all this gear, Well, whilst Trevor had been collecting me there had been a general recall,end accordingly the start sequence was only 5 minutes, and wren the gun went, we were 100 yards behind the line, facing the wrong way, whilst waiting to check the signal. We hadn't seen the preparatory signal amongst the melee of boats, so we were second from last across tke line, and with me clad in trainers we proceeded to bump together all the way around the course, To Trevor's credit he managed, despite my slippery antics, to get us back to the lower middle of the fleet by the end of the race, At tris point we decided that a comfort break was in order before the next race, so we headed for tke shore, The wind was onshore so as we headed for the shallows, I decided to slide along tke bows to step smartly off when Trevor rounded up to stop. Step off I certainly did! Unfortunately we were still 50 yards from tke shore, The boat dipped on a wave, and I said goodbye, fell between the hulls, and the boat sailed over me, 1 kept my head down to avoid the dolphin striker, so the water poured down the neck of the wet suit, giving me a good soaking inside. Meanwhile Trevor wko had been watching me to ensure that I was alright, proceeded to sail straight up the beach without stopping! The boat ended up about 10 feet clear of the water, but because the beach is sand and very shallow, no damage occurred, Whilst Trevor was driving up the beach, I was atterpting to swim for shore, Have you ever tried swimming in an oversize wetsuit, where with every stroke water pours in the front? After about ten strokes I stopped for a rest, and decided to let my legs dangle below me, It was then that I discovered the water was only six inches deep! Was I embarrassed! I struggled to my feet, floundered my way ashore, and explained to an anxious Trevor tkat I was alright and what had happened, After a comfort break, althougrt why I bothered I do not know, we went afloat again for the second race, With @ falling wind (it never did get above Force 2 during the whole weekend,) our combined weight, plus the water still resident in the suit meant that we gradually drifted slowly backwards through the fleet, to end up second from last - but maybe next time! Where was Christine when all this was happening? Sleeping her headache away and missing all the fun, My thanks go to Trevor and Christine for the breakfast and the loan of the gear, but next time I'll take my own boat and leave the falling off to Dave Steeve Keeble

9 CADET SERIES 1990. Once more, the Cadet Series turned out to be a cliff-hanger with any one of three competitors able to win the series as they went into the last race. The difference this year is that the winner of the Cadet Series was a young lady, so it is ‘Congratulations' to:- LUCY BOREHAM on winning the 1990 Cadet Series and becoming the first young lady to do so since Alix Richards in 1972. Before that it was Susan Tillotson (1969) and Anne Palmer (1968); 1 wonder what they are doing now ? Did they keep up their sailing ? Are they still members of the MSC under a different name ? Perhaps someone who knows could drop a line to Navigans. The winds this year were decidedly fickle, a typical pattern for the Cadet races being that the R.0. would set a course in a steady F2 (maybe Fl+), the wind would die at the start, causing the fleet to stay bunched together for the first lap, and then come up for the last lap (the race inevitably being shortened). Very frustrating for the competitors to say the least. Only the first (F2) and last races (F2/3) presented anything like asteady wind throughout. Debbie Yorston scored well in the fickle winds, scoring two lsts and a 2nd - plus a retired in the 4th race when the wind died. Going into the last race, Debbie needed to finish within two places of Lucy in order to win the series; in the event she finished 6th to Lucy's lst. Lee Harrison had an outside chance of winning on going into the last race; if he won and both Lucy and Debbie finished well down the list, he might just have got the series. Alas, he decided to round two buoys the opposite way to everyone else (and to R.O. Colin Willsmore's course instructions) and so scored a retired, although it would be fair to say that it would have probably made no difference to the overall result as the course tended to favour the monos rather than the cats. Another competitor to round the buoy the wrong way (in race 2, R.O.Phil May) was Chris Caruth in the Laser Fun. He decided to round F to port and chase off towards Breezy, instead of rounding to starboard and making for D mark. Claire Davies rounded the marks OK and always seems to enjoy her sailing. Mel Keeble had a good series in her Topper and actually won the last race by 21 seconds over Lucy (420). Ben Holroyd clearly enjoys his sailing in his Laser, which is not the easiest of boats to race in light winds. Stephen Caruth sailed well in the Enterprise and scored over his brother by ensuring he knew which way to go ! Paul Harrison sailed his Dart 15 consistently and it's nice to seem him out pretty regularly in the Cat races; keep going Paul, it's coming along nicely. David Ball's pare love for sailing is well known, as is his seamanship and boat-handling ability. By his own admission, he doesn't take racing too seriously - he just likes to sail. Tom Ashley sailed both Mirror and Marauder (but not at the same time) and finished 5th overall. Stuart Golding helmed his Mirror in the lst race but elected to crew for some of the remaining races. Mike Fletcher is always competitive, completed all the races and got some good results; next year...who knows? Finally, Ian Chaplin (aged 9 or thereabouts) took part in his first race, crewed by sister Rachel. The difficult light-wind conditions precluded him from finishing the course, but it was a good try. Ian's Mum, Linda Chaplin, once won the Ladies Cup so it's obviously ‘in the family’ and, again, in a year or twos time... who knows ?
