4, M.S.C./M.A.S.C. FINANCIAL RELATIONSHIP (and its effect on Club policy.) The Sailing Club operates as a section of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club and as such is bound by its constitution. Under this the section is run by its committee(s) who have to discharge a responsibility to ensure the finacial well being of the section; basically 'break even', not run at a loss. Whilst the section is not allowed to hold a bank account nor to enter into any loan agreement and it must have M.A.S.C. agreement for any major capital purchase, its finances are run in a separate account within the MASC (this is the same for all sections). Such profit as is made by the section is held in a Reserve Fund, which bears interest, and used for two purposes. Firstly it can be used to "smooth' out a small loss in any one year, however the Main Committee policy is to avoid a loss in the first place. Secondly it is used to help with the cost of major equipment replacement such as replacement rescue craft, tractors etc.. The section has over the years managed its affairs in a professional manner and by following this policy operates free of interference from the MASC, unlike some other sections. Since the club moved to the Stansgate site, the MASC has invested £90,000.00 approx of their money by buying the site (i.e. it is owned by the M.A.S.C. not the Sailing Section, as are all the assets), building of the clubhouse, installation of the sewage plant and help with the Jack B purchase for example, in the site. For this and to offset the costs incurred by us at the MASC, accountant help etc., we pay an annual contribution; this year £7375.00. By this investment, they have demonstrated their willingness to help the section grow over the years. Turning to the events of the last couple of years, at the time that I first approached them for assistance with the second rescue boat and extension, this coincided with a downturn in their own finacial situation. As those who attended the MASC Annual General Meeting on the 26th September will know, they have operated with a loss of £23,000.00 in 1988/1989 and a loss of £30,000.00 in 1998/1990. This has obviously reduced their own reserves considerably. In part the situation has not been helped by the decrease in the Marconi working population as the level of Associate membership is limited to 12.52% by the Magistrates. Looking to the future the MASC has been involved in a cost reduction exercise which is starting to bear fruit this year. In addition it wants to amend its constitution to make all members 'Ordinary' not associate, this will remove the current restriction and allow a larger number of non GEC members. This resolution was put to a Special Meeting on the 26th September but had to be withdrawn because of some technical inaccuracies. These have now been resolved and a new meeting will be called on 17th October. Drawing some parallels with our own section, we found ourselves in the same situation in 1983/1985 when we had exhausted the Marconi companies for members. We wanted to improve and expand the facilities, costs were rising on the existing facilities, and there was a 'market value' above which subscription increases would lead to reduced membership. We therefore set out to increase the level of associate membership with all the heartache of 'the club will not be the same'/'the passing of an era' that the MASC is now experiencing. It is true that the club has changed but I believe that the foresight at that time was right and the club is the better for it today. We may have a new set of problems but we still have a club we all can afford. I am sure that the changes proposed by the MASC will have the same effect and would ask ALL Ordinary members to watch out for the notice of the meeting and come along to support the motion. Obviously these problems and the restrictions on the section by the constitution have affected the Section's Main Committee's plans for the future. The cost of the second rescue boat is in the order of £10,000.00 and the extension

£60,000.00. These alone would represent an investment of £70.000.00. However it does not stop here as the annual running costs would increase and to maximise 5. the return will probably need a full time steward, both being an annual cost to be funded. In addition it would probably be necessary to provide some accomodation; another capital investment. All of this at a time when our backers have a major financial problem themselves. Under these changed circumstances the the planning of such large scale investment and ENSURING THE FUTURE WELLBEING (even survival) of the Sailing Club requires considerable research, time and effort. We all want to move forward into the future but the main committee does have to recognise the risks involved. I hope that this somewhat lengthy item will give you an indication of the background to, and the current situation. I would like to thank also all the members of all the committees who contribute freely their time and effort in running the club on the day to day AND planning its future. YARMOUTH & BREYDON WATER DEFINITELY OUR LAST LONG EXPEDITION FOR 1990, SARAH AND I DECIDED TO TAKE A WEEK OFF IN SEPTEMBER WITH A VIEW TO VISITING GT YARMOUTH AND BREYDON WATER, PLUS THOSE PARTS OF THE NORFOLK BROADS ACCESSIBLE TO YACHTS WITH FIXED MASTS, OUR DEPARTURE WAS SLIGHTLY DELAYED BY THE GREAT TOw-IN OF THE MAJORITY OF THE ‘TWO PIERS' CAT FLEET. NONETHELESS WE SET OFF ON MONDAY WITH A FAVOURABLE WIND AND TIDE, PASSED UP THE DEBEN ENTRANCE IN FAVOUR OF THE ORE AND ARRIVED OFF THE ORFORD HAVEN BUOY ONE HOUR AFTER LOW WATER, HAVING INITIALLY MIS-IDENTIFIED THE BEACON AND LINED UP AN ORANGE HOUSEWALL WITH THE GREY AND BLACK CHIMNEY, WE RECTIFIED OUR ERROR AND GOT ROONIGON ON TO THE CORRECT TRANSIT, AT THIS POINT THE ECHO SOUNDER FAILED AND A FISHING BOAT ARRIVED, SO WE FOLLOWED HIM IN, NOTING THAT HE DEVIATED WELL TO THE SOUTH OF THE TRANSIT LINE TO AVOID THE SHOALS EXTENDING FROM NORTH WEIR POINT. LATER CHAT WITH A FISHING BOAT SKIPPER INDICATED THAT THE ENTRANCE HAD MOVED WITHIN THE LAST 2 WEEKS BUT HE CLAIMED TO BE ABLE TO ENTER AT LOW WATER WITH HIS 5-FOOT DRAUGHT, WE PICKED UP A BUOY AT ORFORD AND PASSED A QUIET NIGHT AFTER A VISIT TO THE ‘JOLLY SAILORS', NEXT DAY SAW US DEPARTING ORFORD HAVEN AT HIGH WATER FOR A NICE BEAM REACH UP TO LOWESTOFT, THERE ARE NO REAL HAZARDS ON THIS RUN AND PLENTY OF GOOO LANDMARKS; ORFORDNESS LIGHT, SIZEWELL B, SOUTHWOLD HARBOUR, AND FINALLY, LOWESTOFT WITH A LARGE GASHOLDER JUST BEHIND THE HARBOUR ENTRANCE, IT WAS JUST A MATTER OF PICKING UP THE E. BARNARD BUO* AND FOLLOWING THE BUOYED PASSAGE INSIDE THE NEWCOMBE SANDS, THE HARBOUR ENTRANCE, WITH ITS TWIN WHITE PAINTED CUPOLAS EITHER SIDE, IS EASY TO SEE. THE EBB TIDE HAS A STRONG SET ACROSS THE HARBOUR MOUTH SO IT PAYS TO STAY CLOSE TO THE SOUTH SIDE ON ENTRY. ONCE INSIDE, THE YACHT HARBOUR AND THE ROYAL NORFOLK AND SUFFOLK YACHT CLUB ARE AHEAD AND SLIGHTLY TO PORT, LOWESTOFT PORT CONTROL OPERATES ON CHANNEL 12 AND SHOULD BE CALLED PRIOR TO ENTRY, IF YOU WISH TO VISIT THE LOWESTOFT CRUISING CLUB ON LAKE LOTHING, THEN YOU WILL NEED TO PASS THROUGH THE ROAD BRIDGE. THE BRIDGE CONTROL IS ALSO ON CHANNEL 12 AND WILL ADVISE YOU OF THE NEXT OPENING AS THEY PREFER TO CO-ORDINATE YACHT MOVEMENTS WITH COMMERCIAL TRAFFIC, THE YACHT HARBOUR IS FAIRLY BASIC, THE RN & SYC LOOKS PRETENTIOUS BUT IS VERY FRIENDLY, SERVES A NICE MEAL AND SELLS ADNAMS BITTER AT £1 A PINT, IT COST US £8 PER NIGHT STAY FOR RODNIGON'S 28 FEET, WE SPENT TwO NIGHTS IN LOWESTOFT, THEN DEPARTED ON THE TIDE FOR THE SHORT HOP UP TO YARMOUTH, THIS IS AN INSHORE PASSAGE INSIDE THE SANDS WHICH RUN PARALLEL TO THE COAST FROM LOWESTOFT TO YARMOUTH. IT WAS A FAST SMOOTH TRIP WITH JUST A SLIGHT POBBLE OFF THE NESS POINT (THE MOST EASTERLY POINT OF ENGLAND.) IN FACT WE ARRIVED TOO EARLY. HAVING OBTAINED ENTRY PERMISSION FROM YARMOUTH PORT CONTROL (CHANNEL 12) WE HAD QUITE A STRUGGLE AGAINST THE STRONG EBB OUT OF THE RIVER AND TOOK NEARLY AN HOUR TO COVER THE 2 MILES TO THE HAVEN BRIDGE. WE THEN COMPLETELY FAILED TO GET THROUGH THE BRIDGE, AS THE TIDE RUNNING THROUGH THE BRIDGE PIERS PROVED TOO STRONG FOR OUR 10 HP DIESEL. WE THEREFORE SPENT THE NIGHT MOORED ALONGSIDE AN OLD DRIFTER WHICH IS A FLOATING FISHING MUSEUM, THE RIVER WALL IS DEFINITELY NOT SUITABLE FOR YACHTS AS IT IS VERY ROUGH AND UNEVEN, DOWNRIVER FROM THE BRIDGE, YARMOUTH IS DEFINITELY A COMMERCIAL PORT FOR THE OFFSHORE OIL AND GAS INDUSTRY, BEING PACKED WITH SUPPORT AND SUPPLY VESSELS OF ALL KINDS OF NATIONALITIES. WE FELT VERY SMALL AND VULNERABLE IN SUCH COMPANY, THE NEXT DAY WE TRANSITED THE HAVEN AND BREYDON BRIDGES ON THE FLOOD TIDE IN COMPANY WITH A 35 FOOT YACHT WHICH HAD TRAVELLED UP FROM GIBRALTAR, WE WERE A LITTLE DISCONCERTED TO SEE HIM GOING THROUGH STERN FIRST, BUT APPARENTLY THE ENGINE HAD FAILED, SO WE GAVE HIM A TOW TO THE NEAREST MARINA, THERE HAD BEEN A SEVERE GALE DURING THE NIGHT AND WITH WIND AGAINST TIDE, THE WAVES ON BREYDON WATER WERE SURPRISINGLY SHORT AND STEEP, ONCE IN THE RIVER WAVENEY IT ALL CALMED DOWN AND WE MOTORED AS FAR AS ST OLAVES, WHERE FURTHER PROGRESS WAS BARRED BY A FIXED ROAD BRIDGE. IT AMUSED US TO NOTICE THAT THE BROADS HIRE CRUISERS INVARIABLY MOTORED ALONG WITH ALL FENDERS HANGING, WE THOUGHT THAT PERHAPS THE BOAT HIRERS MADE THIS A RULE TO MINIMISE DAMAGE! HAVING TURNED AT ST OLAVES, WE THEN SAILED UNDER JIB ALONE TO THE JUNCTION WITH THE RIVER YARE AND POTTERED ALONG TO REEDHAM FOR LUNCH AT A PUB NEAR REEDHAM RAILWAY SWING BRIDGE. THIS BRIDGE WILL OPEN ON REQUEST TO ALLOW ACCESS TO NORWICH, BUT WE HAD TO BE BACK AT YARMOUTH FOR OUR ARRANGED 15.30 OPENING OF THE TWO BRIDGES. THESE BRIDGES ONLY OPEN FOR COMMERCIAL TRAFFIC, OR BY PRIOR ARRANGEMENT USING R/T ON CHANNEL 12, OR BY PHONE, HAVING SUCCESSFULLY TRANSITED THE BRIDGES WE TRAVELLED ALONG PAST YARMOUTH AND GORLESTON AND OUT OF THE HARBOUR FOR OUR RETURN TO LOWESTOFT AND THENCE BACK DOWN TO MSC VIA PIN MILL. WE WERE VERY GRATIFIED TO FIND THE CRUISER CAPTAIN LURKING ON THE MERSEA FLATS TO WELCOME US BACK, BUT LESS PLEASED TO FIND OUR DINGHY MAKING LIKE A SUBMARINE. NONETHELESS IT WAS QUITE AN INTERESTING LITTLE VOYAGE, PERHAPS NEXT TIME WE WILL GO RIGHT UP TO NORWICH AND MAYBE SEE IF IT IS POSSIBLE TO GET UNDER THE NeW CUT BRIDGE FOR A VISIT TO OULTON BROAD OR BECCLES, DAVE BEANE, RODNIGON

9. THE 1990 EAST COAST PIERS RACE - (Through the Eye of the Hurricane) WHAT A WEEKEND! COLOURFUL, CROWDED, EXCITING AND,,.. WHO TOOK THE WIND? THE EAST COAST PIERS RACE WEEKEND STARTED ON FRIDAY WITH MANY OF THE MEMBERS OF MARCONI CLUB ARRIVING ON SITE TO ENSURE THAT ANY LAST MINUTE HITCHES WERE IRONED OUT BEFORE THAT GREAT MASS OF CAT SAILORS DESCENDED ON US LIKE A SWARM OF LOCUSTS, SATURDAY DAWNED! I ROLLED OVER AND RAISED MY HEAD TO LOOK OUT OF THE WINDOW AND MADE OUT THE SHAPES OF MANY COLOURFUL PRINDLE SAILS - THERE OUGHT TO BE A LAW AGAINST ASSAULTING PEOPLE'S EYEBALLS SO EARLY IN THE MORNING! I LOOK AGAIN AND REALISE THAT I CAN SEE RIGHT THROUGH ONE SAIL TO THE BOATS BEYOND. HOW CAN WE BE EXPECTED TO FIND OUR WAY ROUND THE COURSE WHEN WE DON'T KNOW FROM ONE WEEK TO THE NEXT THE SIZE, COLOUR OR POSITION OF THE MARKS? I HEAR THAT A BODY HAS BEEN APPOINTED TO LOOK INTO THE PROBLEMS OF START-LINE AND RACE-BOX LOCATION IN THE COMING SEASON, I DON'T ENVY THEM THEIR JO8, LET US HOPE THAT THEY REACH A SITUATION AMENABLE TO ALL, SO IF ANY OF YOU HAVE STRONG THOUGHTS, I AM SURE THEY WOULD BE GLAD TO HEAR THEM,** NO, DON'T WRITE TO ME, YOUR CATAMARAN CORRE SPONDENT PETER FLOOK ** NEIL INVITED MEMBERS TO LET HIM HAVE ANY IDEAS ON THIS SUBJECT IN LAST MONTH'S NAVIGANS, THERE WAS A DEADLINE OF 30TH SEPTEMBER AS THE WORKING PARTY WAS INTENDED TO MAKE ITS REPORT BY THE ENO OF OCTOBER, BUT IT MIGHT BE WORTH SUBMITTING ANY HELPFUL THOUGHTS TO NEIL EVEN AT THIS LATE DATE, ED, EAST COAST PIERS RACE AFTER SOME EXCELLENT PRELIMINARY RACING THE DAY BEFORE, SUNDAY 16TH SEPTEMBER FINALLY: DAWNED - GREY AND WINDLESS, HOWEVER, THE FORECAST WAS FOR A FORCE 2-3 AND IT WAS STILL EARLY YET, VERY EARLY IN FACT. AFTER SOME RUNNING AROUND TRYING TO SCROUNGE MORE TINS OF BEANS, WE ALL TOOK OUR RUBBER BANDS AND HEADED FOR THE WATER, WAS ALL THAT FILLING AND SANDING OF RUDDER BLADES GOING TO MAKE ANY DIFFERENCE, I ASKED MYSELF? UNFORTUNATELY HMS PUNCHER WAS ASKED TO MOVE DOWNSTREAM TO RECEIVE NICHOLAS SCOTT MP, SO FEW PEOPLE SAW HIM LOWERED FROM THE HELICOPTER, 1 PRESUMED THAT THIS WAS A SECURITY MEASURE, AS A MINISTER (ESPECIALLY ONE THAT HAS SERVED IN THE NORTHERN IRELAND OFFICE) HANGING ON A WIRE IN A PRE-ARRANGED SPOT WOULD MAKE A SITTING TARGET. HMS PUNCHER WAS SOON BACK ON STATION AS THE COMMITTEE BOAT, AND ROGER SMITH WAS ABLE TO SET A COMMENDABLY LONG START LINE. IT CAN'T HAVE HAD MUCH BIAS EITHER AS THERE SEEMED TO BE A FAIRLY EVEN SPREAD OF BOATS ALONG IT AS THE GUN WENT. I'M NOT SURE WHAT THEY FIRED, BUT I WISH WE HAD ONE AT THE RACE BOX. MY LIST SAYS THAT 118 BOATS STARTED, AND THAT THEY CAME FROM 24 DIFFERENT CLASSES, NOT BAD FOR ONLY THE THIRD EAST COAST PIERS RACE, WE THOUGHT THAT THE STARBOARD END OF THE LINE (SOUTH SHORE) WAS THE PLACE TO START SO THAT WE COULD KEEP CLOSE TO THE POINT JUST WEST OF THE CLUB IN AN EFFORT TO KEEP OUT OF THE TIDE, HAVING GOT AROUND THE CORNER, THE CONTD....

14, NORTH SHORE SEEMED THE BEST ROUTE FOR THE REST OF THE ESTUARY AND WE MADE OUR WAY ACROSS VIA GOLDHANGER SPIT ANO THIRSLET SPIT, APART FROM AVOIDING SOME TIGHT TACKING AMONGST THE CRUISERS (ENOUGH SAID!) I FOUND OUT LATER THAT WE HAD ALSO AVOIDED THE ATTENTIONS OF MALCOLM STUART ON THE P,A, HE WAS BUSY PUTTING OFF SOME OF THE OTHER DARTS IN FRONT OF THE CLUB - THANKS MALCOLM, THE CHEQUE WOULD HAVE BEEN IN THE POST IF WE HAD FINISHED, I'VE NO IDEA WHAT WAS HAPPENING AT THE FRONT, BUT THERE WAS SOME CLOSE RACING IN THE DARTS, AS THERE HAD BEEN ON THE SATURDAY. WE SEEMED TO SPEND MOST OF OUR TIME SAILING WITH A_ SINGLE-HANDED TORNADO, AFTER THE BRADWELL GATE, THE WIND PICKED UP A BIT AND JOHN EVEN TRAPEZED FOR A WHILE BEFORE A BIG WIND SHIFT CAUGHT US OUT AND WE LOST A LOT OF PLACES ROUNDING THE COLNE POINT GATE, I'M NOT SURE WHY THE WHOLE FLEET REACHED S/W BACK ACROSS THE ESTUARY WHEN IT WAS POSSIBLE TO LAY THE POWER STATION AT BRADWELL - I GUESS IT WAS JUST A CASE OF ‘FOLLOW MY LEADER', AS IT WAS ‘TWIST OR BUST' TIME FOR US WE BORE AWAY AND HEADED STRAIGHT FOR THE NEXT GATE = ONLY 'AIRWAVES' FOLLOWED US AND WE COULDN'T BELIEVE OUR LUCK, IF THE WIND HAD KEPT UP WE BOTH WOULD PROBABLY HAVE ACHIEVED A GOOD PLACE, BUT AS WE ALL KNOW, IT DIDN'T AND THE ONLY DECISION LEFT TO MAKE WAS WHEN TO GIVE UP AND ACCEPT A TOW, I HELD OUT FOR A WHILE BUT IN THE END I WAS GRATEFUL TO ACCEPT A TOW FROM *JOAJO', ONE OF THE MARCONI CRUISERS, CHRIS HARRISON CAME ON BEHIND US AND WE WERE AMONGST THE LAST TO ARRIVE BACK AT THE CLUB, AT THE TIME 1 DION'T GET A CHANCE TO THANK THE SKIPPER OF ‘JOAJO' (JULIAN ROYLE I BELIEVE), AS WE JUST CAST OFF FROM THE BACK OF THE LINE AND PADDLED ASHORE, AND I'M SURE MANY OTHER BOATS DID THE SAME THING, SO ON BEHALF OF THE OTHER COMPETITORS, I WOULD LIKE TO THANK ALL THE PEOPLE WHO CAME TO RESCUE US - WHETHER THEY WERE THE NOMINATED RESCUE CRAFT (27 IN ALL, I'M TOLD) OR JUST PEOPLE WHO STEPPED IN AT THE LAST MINUTE, ON THE SUBJECT OF ‘THANK YOUs' A QUICK COUNT UP OF THE PEOPLE WE ARE WRITING TO, TO THANK FOR THEIR HELP WITH THE RACE, CAME TO 70 PEOPLE, IN MANY CASES THIS DOES NOT INCLUDE PARTNERS, FAMILY OR CREWS OF THOSE PEOPLE, SO THE ACTUAL NUMBER OF PEOPLE WHO HELPED IN SOME WAY WITH THE EAST COAST PIERS RACE MAY WELL BE MORE THAN TWICE THAT NUMBER, IT'S GREAT TO SEE SO MANY PEOPLE FROM DIFFERENT FLEETS WORKING TOGETHER FOR SOMETHING THAT BENEFITS BOTH THE CLUB AND THE RYA SEAMANSHIP FOUNDATION, SO FAR OVER £2,000 HAS BEEN RAISED AND THE MONEY IS STILL COMING IN, WELL DONE, EVERYONE, AND FINAL THANKS TO MCNICHOLAS CONSTRUCTION WHO MADE IT ALL POSSIBLE. PAUL METCALFE ee DEAR ALL, JUST A LITTLE NOTE TO CONGRATULATE ALL THE ORGANISERS AND THE PEOPLE WHO HELPED TO RUN THE EAST COAST PIERS RACE, ON A GREAT SUCCESS, IT WAS A BRILLIANT WEEKEND, FORGETTING THE WEATHER, I WOULD LIKE TO THANK THE MEMBERS OF THE CRUISER FLEET WHO HELPED TO PROVIDE EXCELLENT RESCUE COVER, IT WAS COMFORTING TO KNOW THAT SOMEONE WAS NEARBY WHEN WE WERE DRIFTING IN THE DIRECTION OF HOLLAND, SPECIAL THANKS TO THE OWNERS OF 'MERLIN' WHO SAVED US FROM OUR PLIGHT AND .... BOREDOM, AND RETURNED US TO THE CLUB, ALSO TO THE BATTLES WHO LIFTED MY SPIRITS AND HELPED TUG THE BOAT UP THAT 'EVER SO LONG' HARD, BASICALLY, I WOULD LIKE TO THANK ALL THE MEMBERS OF M,S.C, FOR PUTTING UP WITH BOTH THE SWARMS OF PEOPLE AND ANY INCONVENIENCE CAUSED, WITHOUT YOUR SUPPORT THIS CHARITY AND FUN EVENT WOULD NOT BE POSSIBLE. THANKS EVERYONE ! ROSIE DUCKMANTON, DART 2626

Mike Duckmanton Dave Fletcher Frank Bennett (Hon.Treasurer) Maggie Boreham Barry Newboult Val Fletcher Mike Hellewell (Sailing Sec) Larry Botheras Malcolm Stuart John Weedon The aim of the meeting was to seek volunteers to undertake the task of reviewing and defining the detailed requirements and actions needed to run Regatta'91. The ‘Basic Task List' for Regatta'91 (as published in Navigans, August'90) was taken as the minimum starting point for the review and definition. The volunteers were requested to complete their review and definition in time for January, 1991 (say, by 15 January) so as to present their findings to the January'91 meeting of the Sailing Sub-Committee. It is not intended that the volunteers conduct their review and definition in isolation of each other, or of others members of the club. It is intended that those who attended the meeting be regarded as a Regatta Working Group (reporting to the Sailing Sub-Committee via the (new) Rear Commodore and/or Sailing Secretary) and that they should meet before Christmas (say November and December) to liaise with each other and ensure they are moving in the same general direction for Regatta '91 (or reveal any glaring problems if they are not 'in tune' with each other). By consulting with other members of the club, it is hoped our volunteers will gainfrom both 'old' and 'new' ideas and experiences for Regatta. Commodores Notes By the time that you read this issue of Navigans, the season will be nearly over, probably with just the "Last Fling" to sail on 18th November. Looking back over the season, the Regatta, East Coast Piers and Open Meetings were all very successful and the normal club racing has been well supported. This does not mean however that we have not had some problems from which we have to learn. The tide and wind conditions were one at the Regatta and, whilst we cannot control them, we do need to recognise that they could re-occur and be better organised to cope with them. I previously reported that the Main and Sailing committees would jointly setup a working group to look at the start line and their full report appears elsewhere in this issue. With two minor changes made by the Main Committee, both indicated in the report, it has been accepted by both Committees for use from the start of next season. As with many such situations the outcome always represents a compromise between many different views and I would ask all fleets, groups and members of the Club to give the recommendation a fair trial and to recognise that those involved in making the decisions believe that they are acting in the best interests of all in the Club. There is also a report from the Main Committee looking forward to the next five years of the Club and its development. Again I must thank all those who have been involved in a difficult situation reviewing the future in the light of the financial restrictions of the MASC. It is a compromise between doing nothing and our original plans for expanding the facilities but at least we have a plan which we believe we can achieve with your support. Finally may I remind everyone that the AGM is at 1300 hours on Sunday 18th November followed by Prize Giving and that we also have a Working Party on Sunday 25th November. I hope to see you many of you on these occassions. Neil T. Pembleton November Working Party on Sunday 25th November The tasks to be undertaken will include those listed below. 3. A ..eeeee. View from the rear My Word - if last month's 'View from the rear' was the penultimate one, then I suppose this ought to be entitled 'The ultimate view from the rear', but that would sound rather too boastful. An alternative title might be 'A final view from the rear' - but that sounds altogether too foreboding. 1 did give some thought to 'A last view from......etc', but felt it sounded too much like a last Will and Testament. Oh! dear; problems, problems. Still stuck foratitle (but starting from the basis of ‘ultimate') I decided to consult Roget's Thesaurus in search of a suitable expression to convey the sense of this particular ‘View from....' and came up with all sorts of possible words. How about, for example:- "An end view from the rear' - perhaps not; too open to misinterpretation "An extreme view from the rear' - could be politically controversial. Is he too far left or too far right ? ‘A distant view from the rear' - the further the distance the better ? "An aloof view....++.+..-etc ' = SNOOLY vices tases anced "A terminal VieW..ceseevevese' - too suggestive of unpleasant consequences "A cessational VieW....ceeeeee' - sounds like something from a US Congress debate ‘A last gasp view from.......' - could be appropriate; I get out of breath walking to the Race Bo In the end, I settled for 'A retiring view from the rear'; I'd like to think it offers some peace and quiet after a 'Year in Office’. In addition, it leads me neatly into......... Taking Early Retirement - someone remarked to me recently that they were surprized I was retiring after only one year as Rear Commodore. By way of explanation, I said that when I was first asked to be R.C. I said ‘NO' - and suggested a couple of other ‘names’. Clearly, they also said 'NO' because, with only one week to go to the 1989 AGM, I was again asked (but this time along the lines ‘We're desperate; scrapping the bottom of th barrel; you're our last hope). Always one to succumb to flattery, I said 'YES' but with the proviso it would only be for one year initially and, during that year, I would decide if I could continue for the more normal 2nd and 3rd year. In the event, I decided I could not give the time and effort to the job in the same manner as my predecessor; consequently, I advised the Main Committee at its June meeting that I would not continue as Rear Commodore. So there you have it. What's my (start) line ? - ‘What's my line ?' used to be the title of a very popular quiz programme on both radio and TV. The most famous 'line' (ie occupation) was that of 'A Sagger-makers Bottom Knocker' which, whatever the 'innocent' intentions of those who put it forward for the quiz, caused much hilarity and was the subject of much mis-interpretation. Something else likely to be subject to much mis-interpretation, but precious little humour, is the report of the Start-Line Working Group. The report was accepted by the Sailing Sub-Committee at its meeting on 23/10/90 but not without some considerable debate and soul-searching. It is true it was accepted by a majority decision, the voting being 5 'for', 1 ‘against’ and 1 ‘abstention’. By the time you read this, the Report will also have been considered by the Main Committee. Whatever the final outcome, I hope all members will show a willingness to abide by the majority decision of those whom you elect to conduct the business of the club. There might not be too many Sagger-makers Bottom Knockers left in the Potteries area - I wonder how many knockers we have in the MSC ? Naughty, naughty - the action of one of our fleets to arbitrarily alter a course without telling the Race Officer was, to say the least, a mite arrogant, particularly as the race officer had been guided in setting the original course by an expert member of the fleet in the first place. Admittedly, the alteration in itself was not unreasonable - only the manner of its execution leaves doubts as to whether it's worth individuals offering their services merely to be treated with disdain. The Race Officer didn't know of the change until after the race - but it did serve to explain why ‘the winner! didn't sail the correct course. Let's hope the habit of 'doing your own thing' doesn't get out of hand. After explanations, the Race Officer accepted the result as it stood but was none too pleased. Keeping it in the family - Steve Keeble suggested that the Cadet Series winner should be invited to take part in the helm of the Year final. I pointed out that, in which case, the Ladies Trophy winner should also be invited to compete but, on the whole, I didn't think it a good idea. I must confess to having a selfish motive in opposing the suggestion for 1990; to finish well behind my son was bad enough but the prospect of finishing last of the whole of the Boreham family would have been too much to ask of me - is it time for me to join the Bowls Section ? Mind you, it was a tempting suggestion - think what a unique record that would have set for Helm of the Year. Mike Boreham Retiring Rear Commodore

MARCONI SAILING CLUB - THE NEXT FIVE YEARS - From the Main Committee In his 'View from the rear' last month, Mike Boreham commented on the future &wv direction of the Club. Under Rule 2 the objects of the Club are:- "SHALL BE THE PROMOTION OF AMATEUR SAILING, THE ENCOURAGEMENT OF SOCIAL FELLOWSHIP, AMONGST ALL THOSE INTERESTED IN THE SEA AND THE PROVISION OF ALL POSSIBLE FACILITIES TO THIS END" The Main Committees interpretation of this rule is that we should be providing facilities for dinghies/cruisers, Racers/Non Racers, and "those who want to mess about in boats", and believe that this is the essence of the Club. Picking up from the article in last months Navigans on the financial relationship between the MASC and ourselves, the reason for the drive to increase membership to 500 was to enable the Club to meet its financial obligation and maintain the fabric without any major change in subscription level (except for inflation). This was based on a judgement made by the Main Committee in 1985 that this level would generate sufficient income to carry through some development to the overall facilities. It also recognised that to increase significantly above that number would require major capital developments such as extensions, safety cover etc. Generally the judgement has proved correct as witnessed by the total redecoration of the Club, rebuilding of the gate, filling of the ditch, new water main, new radios, repairs to the road, retiling of the Galley, building of the tender rack over the last two years. These have been achieved both by the additional funds from the increased membership and the effort of the members. Whilst this membership drive was in progress, the Main Committee have been looking further into the future to satisfy the likely needs. We clearly recognise the need for more accommodation and the question of safety cover. These plans had been developed sufficiently for us to approach the MASC for the necessary funding for an extension and second rescue boat. However the present financial situation within the MASC has come at the wrong time and we have had to carry out a major review of the situation within a number of significant constraints. These contraints include the facts that we as a section cannot enter into any loan agreement, we cannot spend any of the reserve account without MASC approval, that any surplus income over expenditure that we generate each year must be paid into the reserve account, that any major capital spend must have MASC approval, and that the MASC does not have the available funds to assist us at present. It is also our opinion that such assistance will not be available for the next 4-5 years. An obvious solution appears to be to purchase the site and sever the link with the MASC. Even if we assume that the MASC and the trustees would be agreeable to such a proposal, it will take a significant time to finalise the details. It will also be essential to ensure that the Club does not end up with a loan of such a size to finance the purchase that the capital and interest payments cripple the Club immediately. It is our opinion that such investigation, negotiation, raising of the finance and re-constitution of the Club will take at least 3-5 years even if we decided that this was an appropriate course. For all the above reasons we have recognised that any prospect of large capital spend in the next five years is very remote. It has therefore been necessary to plan our way through this time period to improve the facilities and minimise the costs involved. As part of the planned extension provision was being made for a comfortable lounge, a verandah, increased storage/changing area etc. These needs still exist and we are planning to take a number of actions to resolve them. The initial key is to find a

low cost method of releasing the garages from acting as storage areas and we need as soon as possible three or four portakabins at no cost (except possibly the transport); these will then be used for storage until the Dutch Barn becomes available from MCSL and is erected. During this winter approximately a quarter of the lounge at the West end will be converted into a comfortable area. At the same time the downstairs bar will be re-arranged to serve direct into No. 3 garage instead of under the awning and No. 3 garage will be improved. The comfortable area will be available for use by any members, guests or visitors in dry clothes; the majority of the lounge for those in wet clothes with an overspill available downstairs. Additionally we are finding out whether the roof over the changing rooms is strong enough to act as a verandah without strengthening. If this is the case we intend to erect a railing and staircase to allow access. If we are able to find sufficient storage to release garages 4 and 5 as well, this will open up the possibility of expanding the changing facilities. It would also be very desirable to provide tables and benches on the grass to the West of the Club. In order to achieve these plans we need your help and co-operation to find the materials and provide the labour. By doing this we can still continue to provide additional equipment etc. HERE WE URGENTLY NEED YOUR HELP TO FIND THREE OR FOUR PORTAKABINS OR SIMILAR BUILDINGS WHICH WE CAN USE TO HOUSE THE ITEMS CURRENTLY IN THE GARAGES. Regarding the second support boat, the answer is not so easy. Based on a number of proposals that have been considered, the likely cost is in the order of £6,000.00 to £10,000.00 and we would have to have MASC agreement to the spend. The Sailing Sub Committee have asked for, and the Main Committee approved, the use of the Orkney as a second support boat next season. This will help by demonstrating that we can run two boats and highlighting any problems. In the meantime we are actively investigating methods of funding a second boat which satisfies the relationship between the MASC and ourselves. These steps will allow us to meet the problems and improve conditions during the next five years. In the meantime the Committee will continue to examine the longer term implications of the MASC current financial problems to enable us to further develop the Club. KNOW YOUR LOCAL AREA - ST PETER'S CHAPEL Dave Beane, 'Rodnigon' The River Blackwater is reckoned to be one of the saltiest rivers in England, hardly surprising when you consider its lack of tributaries and how little fresh water flows into the river from the land. However, it is a river steeped in Essex history and it is interesting to reflect on this history while enjoying the pleasures of sailing its waters. Long before the bulk of Bradwell nuclear power station was built to daminate the eastern end of the Blackwater, St Peter's Chapel on Sales Point provided a conspicuous landmark for seafarers approaching the Colne and Blackwater Rivers from seaward. This chapel was built on the site of a Roman fortress and consecrated in AD 654 by Bishop Cedd. It subsequently was used by his followers to spread their gospel across southern England. In the ensuing centuries it was desecrated, used as a barm and allowed to fall into disrepair before being restored and reconsecrated in the 1920s. It is a very simple building which forms a fine example of a Saxon church. It is used for occasional services and is the destination for an annual pilgrimage which starts from the parish church in Bradwell, wends its way round the sea wall, and terminates with a gathering and service in the chapel. Near to the chapel, almost hidden in a small copse right on the sea wall, you can see the small weatherboard cottage where Walter Linnet, last of the Essex wildfowlers, spent what must have been a rather lonely existence shooting and trapping wild fowl to earn his living. The cottage is now used by the Essex Wildlife Trust as a base fram which to watch the prolific local bird life on the nearby marshes. This area is easily reached by the lane which is signposted from Bradwell village. There is a car park within easy walking distance (about half a mile) from the chapel, and for the more energetic there are the options of walking further south along the sea wall bordering the Dengie Hundred and overlooking St Peter's Flats or of turning left along the south shore of the Blackwater towards the power station and Bradwell village. Osea Island follows.......

9. KNOW YOUR LOCAL AREA - OSEA ISLAND Dave Beane With Osea Island right on our doostep, MSC dinghy and cruiser sailors alike will be fairly familiar with this little bit of Essex. Most of us will have completed the circumavigation across the Stumble at high tide and will know a bit about this island which can only be reached at low tide by wheeled vehicles using a narrow track which starts on the mainland at a point between Goldhanger Creek and Decoy Point and links across to the north west corner of Osea. The Island, normally and currently a peaceful island farm, was the scene of much warlike activity at the end of the First World War and up to 1926 when it was a naval base for a range of high speed Coastal Motor Boats. These were all of Thormeycroft design and were hydroplanes powered by petrol engines. They were variously anned with with torpedoes, depth charges and mines, and were capable of speeds of up to 55 knots. If you think you have problems with wet bikes and speed boats, just imagine being confronted with a 70' motor boat approaching at 50 knots! All that now remains of all this naval activity are same of the sheds which have now been converted for use to house farm implements. The large house on Osea was at one time a drying out haven for alcoholics but local legend has it that the return to sobriety of the inmates was samewhat hampered by the activities of the Fisherman who ran a profitable sideline by smuggling in bottles for the inebriates, doubtless at a healthy premium, It is possible, except at high tide, to land on the easter end of the island and to walk right round the island without trespassing. This walk takes you past the old wharf on the north shore where the Thames barges used to load the produce grown on the island. Once past the island end of the Causeway it is necessary to walk along the beach on the tideline past the fast-disappearing remains of Osea Pier and alongside the deep pool which provides a popular anchorage to the east of the pier. If you do decide to follow this route, please remember that Osea is privately owned and take care not to trespass on the main part of the Island. This stroll will take about an hour to complete assuming a fairly leisurely pace. 1990 RACING DUTIES Some of you may remember that I took on the task of organising Race Officers and Rescue Boat Crews for the Club racing this year. As anticipated it has proved to be an interesting and diverting activity, and one which I can thoroughly recommend to anyone with a thick skin and a tendency toward masochism. So to the many people who took on duties this season, and did their best with them, I would like to say on behalf of the Club, a very sincere Thank You. I do feel particularly grateful to those of you who changed their personal plans and stepped into the breach at short notice after my original intentions had tumed to dross (yes, it happened all too often!) and I must make particular mention in this respect to Mike Hellewell, the Keebles, the Duckmantons, and the Borehamns, for service beyond the call of duty. All of us who take part in racing at the Club always do so by courtesy of other members who are devoting their time and energy to fulfilling the racing duties, so there is really no better way of making your contribution to the fabric and wellbeing of the Club, whether you are helm or crew, than to take your share once a year at fulfilling those duties yourself. 11, HELM OF TYF YEAR, 1990. Orice again, the final of the Helm of the Year provided a close and exciting competition with the ultimate result held in the balance until the last race was completed. The eventual winner of the Helm of the Year Trophy for 1990 was:- DAMIAN BOREHAM This year, five finalists took part in the competition; they were:- Ron Greygoose (Solo Fleet) Steve Glynn (Catamaran Handicap Fleet) Mike Boreham (Monohul] Handicap Fleet) Damian Boreham (Dart 18 Fleet) Tom Ashley (MIrror Fleet) There should have been a sixth finalist but neither the qualif nor ier, runner-up, from the Sailboard Fleet could take part due to other commitments. As usual, a catalogue of mini-disasters accompanied the competitors as they battled it out on the water. Ron managed to hit a mark (Race 3) and run aground (race 4); Damian found his outhaul disintegrating before his eyes (Race 4) and also managed the only capsizes (twice) before the start of the 5th race. Mike probably collected most mini-disasters; his outhau] also came apart completely (Race 1), his self-bailer refused to shut (Race 3) and he managed to clonk poor, innocent, Steve on the head with his boom (race 5). The said Steve did nothing particularly wrong - except to leave his head in the path of Mike's boom and, the most disasterous of all, to vote at the Catamaran AGM to use Toppers for this final rather than Dart 15s before he knew that he would be taking part in the final. Ah, if only we had the gift of foresight. Tom alone seems to have avoided any major mini-disasters - wise chap. The Sailing Sub-Committee had decided to approach the Catamaran Fleet for the loan of Dart 15s in which to sail the final. However the Cat AGM felt it would be better (fairer) to use Toppers; after all, it was pointed out, Toppers were used for the 'Top Dog' competion of the various national dinghy champions. This arguement, coupled with Steve Keeble's offer of 6 Toppers from the International Topper/Hurricane Association, was something the Rear Commodore couldn't refuse. Amongst other things, it had the advantage of providing six boats of more or less even performance for the competition:- The race results were as follows:- Final Total Points Overall (based on 4 out Position. Helm Race 1 Race 2 Race 3 Race 4 Race 5 of 5 races counted) 1 Damian Boreham (Dart 18 Fleet) 3 1 1 2 1 4,25 2 Ron Greygoose (Solo Fleet) 1 2 4 1 2 5.50 3 Tom Ashley (Mirror Fleet) 4 3 2 3 3 11.00 =4 Steve Glynn (Catamaran Fleet) 2 5 5 5 4 16.00 =4 Mike Boreham (Handicap Fleet) 5 4 3 4 5 16.00 Wind: S (F3) S (F3) SE (F3) SE (F3-4) SE (F3-4) Race 1 saw an apparent good start at the windward end of the line by Mike, Damian and Tom - but Ron and Steve were wiser to start at the leeward end in stronger wind, reached the first mark with a handy lead and were never troubled. Mike's problems with his outhaul excited the hearts of the rescue boat who thought they had a customer - but ‘twas not to be, even Mike managed to stay upright in the Southerly Force 3 wind. Race 3 saw Ron hit a mark at a crucial point in the race as he contested the lead with Tom and Damian, with Mike not far behind. The subsequent 360 put him well behind and he just failed to snatch 3rd place from Mike, who had a boat half-filled with water due to the faulty bailer. If Race 3 was vital to Ron, then Race 4 was vital to Damian. He had only to win this race to secure the trophy and seemed all set to do so as he led the fleet. Unfortunately, his outhaul started to ‘fall apart’ and, as he tried to repair it 'on the move', he sagged off to leeward and allowed Ron and Tom to overtake him. He managed to claw back one place from Tom but failed to catch Ron, even though Ron did sportingly run aground as he approached the finish. Fortunately, Ron managed to extricate himself from the mud and won both this race and a chance to gain the trophy in the Sth race. In race 5, Ron and Damian merely needed to finish ahead of each other in order to win the trophy. Ron had the better start and looked all set to win as he led the fleet around the buoys. However, nothing is ever certain and Damian overhauled Ron on the close-hauled legs to win the race - and the Helm of the Year Trophy.

12, Commiserations to Ron who came close to adding a 2nd Helm of the Year win to his previous win in 1983. His demonstration of sailing technique and tactics on the water was well worth watching - particularly for those who found themselves following behind him for most of the time. Congratulations to Damian who finally won the Helm of the Year Trophy in this, his 7th successive attempt, having previously scored a 'Did Not Comnete', a 4th (ie. last), two thirds and two seconds. Tom Ashley sailed consistently well to take third place. Sometimes he led the fleet and was never far behind Ron and Damian. We'll certainly be seeing more of Tom's winning ways in the seasons to come. Mike and Steve sailed contentedly, but ruefully, at the back (but Steve had a good 2nd place in Race 1). In race 5 they sailed quietly side-by-side onthe run when Mike's boom, guided in a downward arc as he came offa wave, clonked Steve on the head. "Ouch" said a surpized Steve; "Sorry" said an embarrassed Mike. A 720 followed, thus ending Mike's race for all practical purposes. Before the event, the competitors agreed that one discard should be allowed, just to guard against catastrophic gear failure on what would be strange, non-club, boats. In the event, nothing went too seriously wrong (apart from the outhauls and self-bailer) and a good competition was enjoyed by all. The use of Toppers for this year's competition seemed to work well. Ron, Tom and Damian were of comparable weight, whilst although Steve and Mike might be described as ‘a little heavier’ they were nevertheless ‘in contention’ for most of the time - until an error put paid to their chances on the short courses. “What boat shall we use ?"isaquestion asked each year when considering Helm of the Year, and it is a difficul one to answer. Club boats, be they Mirrors, Lasers, Dart 15s or whatever, tend to vary greatly in performance due to various factors. It js also difficult to choose a boat which does not favour at least one of the finalists. Whatever is used is a compromise’ - and this year, the Toppers seemed to be a reasonably fair compromise bearing in mind that none of the finalists were ‘Topper sailors’. wm COMMODORES NOTES First, I would like to thank all those who attended the Annual General Meeting and took part in the debates on the motions. These debates were very useful and have given the Main Committee much information on the views of members about the current state of the Club and the direction in which we should be developing. Following the interest expressed by you, we will be arranging a meeting in March/April for the Main Committee to present the plans for the future. Even while we have been discussing them since the A.G.M., some have started to come to fruitition. Robin Smith has been able to obtain two 40 x 10 ft. containers at a very reasonable price which should be delivered to the Club by the middle of December. One will be positioned where the Mast Rack was and used by the cruiser fleet for mast storage. The other will go between the tractor shed and the seawall and be used by the Sailing Sub Committee for the race equipment/Rescue boat gear etc. In addition I have obtained 30 ft. of metal racking from M.C.S.L. to be installed in this second container. The plans to provide the comfortable area and convert Garage 3 as the overspill bar are virtually complete and it is our intention to finish this project by the start of the next sailing season. Also many thanks to those who helped at the Working Party when a considerable amount of tidying up was done. I would like to thank Dave for his efforts with the JCB which allowed us to uncover the rotten gas pipe, which we have to replace, and excavate the trench for the power to the tractor shed. When this is installed, we will be providing a couple of waterproof sockets on the shed for use by people in the dinghy park. All of the above have helped immensely towards the realisation of our long term aims. Finally, hot off the press, we learned on Saturday lst December that the RYA have for sale a 4 metre rigid inflatable with Yamaha outboard for £3,300.00. Following urgent discussions with the MASC and within the Main Committee on Monday 3rd December, it was agreed that we will send some members to Southampton and, if it is good value for money, attempt to purchase it. On behalf of all members, I would like to thank those concerned in the speedy action that was needed. All that is left to do this year, is to wish all of you a Merry Christmas and a New Year, and a successful 1991 Sailing season (and finish this winter projects, organise next year, plan the future, ..., ..., etc. with your help). Neil T. Pembleton ANNUAL RNLI SPONSORED ROW IN MALDON This is being organised once again at the Maldon Little Ship Club on Tuesday lst January 1991 commencing at 11.30am from MLSC Clubhouse, Hythe Quay, Maldon. Distance to be covered - 5kn. The Marconi Men's Team entering this year consists of Malcolm Stuart, Ray Ball, Roger Smith and Mike Hellewell. David Ball a Cadet entry; a young Ladies' Team (as last year); and a young Men's Team. And there may be others I haven't heard about. I can recommend this event as an excellent one for spectators and participants alike and Hot Refreshments are promised to be available. Do come along and support the Teams. If you would care to sponsor any of them, the proceeds, of course, all go to the Royal National Lifeboat Institution, and the West Mersea Atlantic 21 has put in an appearance on occasions in the past. Ed.

4. SANTA'S CHRISTMAS LETTER FROM A CAT SAILOR Dear Santa, You may not have heard from me recently because I'm meant to have grown up. However, I've been seeing my analyst lately, who tells me that, because I've taken up Catamaran sailing this year, I'm regressing to childhood. So if I'm back to those days I'd better write. After all, I do really believe in Father Christmas. I've been very good this year. I haven't hit any cruisers, and that Fireball that capsized was windward boat. 6. SO, YOU WOULD LIKE TO TAKE PART IN THE ADMIRAL'S CUP? At the start of last season, six Sigma 36 cruisers, each with an experienced skipper, were chartered for a weekend by members from this Club. We then held an informal mini regatta of three races over the two days, and, to give a bit of an edge to the racing, each boat was manned by a different Fleet, including ome manned by ladies. I will not go into the details of exactly what happened over the weekend but sufficient bar stories were generated to keep those who took part in pints of beer for most of this year. It seems, however, that despite the strong winds; the start line collisions (by S... you know who); the sinkings; the strandings; the gear failures; the tows; the boat modifications (conversion of wheel to tiller steering); the engine failures (many); and the excess of alcohol..... people want to try it again. Sail to a far distant island and moor alongside a pub; booze, eat, booze away the evening, then sleep on the boat. SUNDAY - breakfast for those who can face it followed by a race in the moming. Lunch, with a wee drink no doubt, then race back to the Solent in the afternoon, Stagger home Sunday evening. the cost will probably be around £70, excluding drink, and the date sometime around late February/early March. FOOD FOR THOUGHT At the 1990 A.G.M., during the discussion on increasing membership fees etc., there appeared to be a marked resentment from some quarters that the M.S.C. were not permitted to build up a capital reserve fund to be spent for the benefit of the M.S.C. alone : but had to abide by the rules of the M.A.S.C. whereby any M.S.C. funds are retained by the M.A.S.C. in a general account and any request for capital expenditure has to be approved by the M.A.S.C. and if approved, money is made available. The objection to this procedure seems to be centred around the fact that, like so many organisations today the M.A.S.C. is itself undergoing a financial crisis and therefore is unable to finance our current needs, which, if I read the mood of the meeting right, the first priority was for a replacement rescue boat. As I listened to the arguments both for and against 1 took stock of our surroundings and my mind went back to our first clubhouse on the river, the barge MAMGU, where we were restricted to sailing 2 hours either side of high water. It was only after intense negotiations plus the support and purchasing power of the M.A.S.C. that Stansgate became the new site for the Marconi Sailing Club. I say site because we did not have a clubhouse, but we did have a site from where we could sail at all states of the tide, which was a bonus. A clubhouse was soon forthcoming in the form of a wooden hut, obtained from 1 know not where, a working party added to the existing foundations leit over from WWe and erected the first M.S.C. Stansgate clubhouse, the facilities were few, but it was a beginning. Today we have a brick built Clubhouse and although the facilities may be overstretched at present, with a little give and take on all sides we can probably manage, changes may be desirable but are they essential 7? What we have has been obtained under the present rules and from before MAMGU to present day has been a big step - don’t knock it. To replace the Jack-B may be more essential, I leave it to the better informed to cecide, but do we have to purchase outright ? Is it possible to lease a suitable boat ? after all most companies lease all or part of their capital equipment, are boats available to lease 7 Alternatively is it possible for MSC members to become shareholders ina financial arrangement independant of the MSC with the objective of purchasing capital equipment (rescue boat 7?) that can be leased to the club, assets being retained by shareholders for the benefit of the club as a whole. If in time profits are accrued these could be paid back to the shareholders as dividends. It may take a financial genius to work out the pros and cons but I think it is worth looking into. Food for thought if nothing else Fred Partlett Ed's note to clarify one point: The desired new support boat is intended to be used in addition to, and not as a replacement for, Jack B.

THE CREW IMMEDIATELY DESERTED THE COCKPIT FOR THE» FOREDECK, SHOWING LITTLE INTEREST IN CONSTANTLY TRIMMING THE SAIL IN THE LIGHT, FICKLE BREEZE. THEY VERY © QUICKLY SHIFTED BELOW WHEN WE WERE INVADED BY A PLAGUE OF GREENFLY. WILLIAMSTEAD, ONCE A FORTIFIED TOWN, LOOKED DELIGHTFUL AS WE MOORED UP IN THE CENTRE, CLOSE TO THE WINDMILL. IT PROVED TO BE WORTH THE EFFORT OF ALL THE LOCKS, WATERWAYS, BRIDGES AND THE LIKE, THAT WE HAD PASSED THROUGH TO REACH SUCH A PLEASANT TOWN. BUT AT 2 IN THE MORNING THE CONTINUAL NOISE OF MOTORBIKES BEGINS TO DAMPEN ONE'S ENTHUSIASM FOR THE PLACE. RETURNING HOME WAS NOW VERY MUCH QN OUR MINDS. WITH TWO WEEKS OF OUR HOLIDAY GONE, WE DID NOT WISH TO RUSH BACK. HAVING SAID THAT, IT SEEMED A VERY FAST PASSAGE BACK DOWN TO ZIERIKZEE WITH JUST ONE NAIL BITING MOMENT AS YOU PASS UNDER THE ZEELAND BRIDGE. A LITTLE LESS TENSION THE FOLLOWING DAY AS WE GO UNDER THE BRIDGE AGAIN QN OUR WAY TO THE VEERSEMEER AND TO ONE OF THE SMALLER ISLANDS WHERE WE ALL ENJOYED A BARBECUE AND MADE ENOUGH NOISE, (SORRY, SINGING) WELL INTO THE NIGHT. THE NEXT DESTINATION WAS BRESKENS VIA FLUSHING. THIS WAS NO EFFORT, MADE EASIER DUE TO THE CHILDREN TAKING THE INFLATABLE AND MOTORING THE ENTIRE WAY - WELL, AT LEAST TO FLUSHING. WE HAD MISSED THE LOCK THAT 'FREYA' HAD TAKEN WHILE WE WERE STOWING THE DINGHY ON BOARD, SO WE HAD A SHORT WAIT UNTIL THE NEXT LOCK, THE TRIP ACROSS THE WESTERSCHELDE TOOK MORE TIME THAN EXPECTED, DUE TO THE STRONG TIDE, BUT THIS ACOOMPLISHED, WE TIED UP BOWS~TO THE PONTOON AND THE STERN TO A BUOY. I HAVE NEVER LIKED THIS METHOD OF MOORING AND THE FOLLOWING MORNING I DEMONSTRATED WHY. WITH MOORING LINE FIRMLY CAUGHT BETWEEN THE FIN AND THE SKEG THE WIND BLOWING ON TO THE PONTOON, AND THE REALISATION THAT TO ENGAGE GEAR ON THE ENGINE IS TO WIND MORE ROPE ROUND THE PROP QUICKER THAN WINDING CANDYFLOSS QN A STICK. BY A PROCESS OF SHOUTING, KICKING AND SCREAMING WE MANOBUVRE OURSELVES OUT OF THE MARINA AND INTO THE WESTERSCHELDE ONCE MORE, THIS TIME BACK TO OCOSTEND. THE WIND IS ON THE NOSE AGAIN, AND WITH A FRESH BREEZE AND A THREATENING SKY, WE PUT ON THE WORKING JIB AND PUT ONE REEF IN THE MAIN. COSTEND SEFMS TO TAKE FOREVER TO REACH, AND WHEN WE DO FINALLY REACH THE BREAKWATER WE HAVE TO WAIT FOR A FERRY BEFORE ENTERING THE HARBOUR AND TYING UP BY THE NORTH SEA YACHT CLUB. DURING THE NIGHT THE WEATHER TAKES A DISTINCT TURN FOR THE WORSE AND WITH THE SWELL NOW REACHING THE INNER HARBOUR, LIFE QV BOARD BECAME MORE THAN UNCOMFORTABLE. WITH EACH SUCCESSIVE WAVE THE BOAT SNATCHED VIOLENTLY AT THE MOORING WARPS AND NO AMOUNT OF BRACING WITH SPRINGS, ETC. LESSENED THE VESSEL'S MOVEMENT. FORCE 7, GUSTING 8, AND NORTHWEST, WOULD PUT MOST PEOPLE OFF GOING TO SEA. THE WALK DOWN TO THE END OF THE PIER CONVINCED US THAT THE DECISION TO LEAVE THE BOAT AT COSTEND AND RETURN THE FOLLOWING WEEK WOULD BE FOR THE BEST. SO ALONG WITH 'FREYA' WE LOCKED INTO THE MERCATOR YACHT HARBOUR AND MADE OUR PLANS TO RETURN BY FERRY. THE FOLLOWING WEEK WE WERE BACK TO SAIL 'LADY VERL' HOME - BUT THAT'S A STORY IN ITSELF. CONRAD BARNARD MOORING ACCIDENT ARTICLE FROM MARCH 1985 The question has arisen as to the liability of a mooring owner who allows another member of the Sailing Club to use his mooring without charge, on the basis that the User is responsible for checking and maintaining the mooring, In such a situation the mooring Owner is unlikely to be able to rely upon insurance, as the normal policy covers only damamge caused by the insured craft, and not damage resulting from an alleged defect in the mooring. The first point to be made is that for a third party, (i.e. the owner of another boat whose craft is damaged by the moored craft breaking free) to successfully sue the mooring Owner, same breach of duty to such third party must be established. In the present case there is a reference to "the negligent failure of your mooring" which presumable means it is alleged by the insurers' solicitors that the Owner was negligent either in the laying or maintaining of the mooring. At this stage, however, the solicitors provide no details of how the negligence is supposed to have occurred. The evidence from the mooring Owner suggests that the accident was caused by a manufacturing defect in the shackle pin. If this is the case, there is no negligence on the part of the mooring Owner, who could not reasonably be expected to carry aut metallurgical testing on the pin, which was presumably bought from a reputable chandler. Contd... 's

ll. It must be stressed that it is for the plaintiff to establish negligence, not for the defendent to establish that he acted with all due care. There are circumstances where it is presumed that no accident would have occurred without negligence, reversing the onus of proof; however, a yacht breaking its moorings would not fall into this category. It would seem well established practice that a member of a club using another member's mooring without payment, accepts all risks of accident, howsoever arising. Indeed even where moorings are hired out by a commercial boatyard, it is normally m the basis that the boatyard disclaims all liability. the point of custamn and practice it would, no doubt, be useful to obtain the written opinion of a body such as the RYA. In the present case, the mooring owner's position is further improved since it was agreed specifically that it was the User's responsibility to periodically check the mooring. On the facts as presently known, there would seem to be no liability on the part of the mooring Owner, and the next step would seem to be simply to repudiate the insurers' claim without going into details. If the insurers wish to pursue the matter, it will then be for them to establish how the alleged negligence occurred. P.R. DAVIS, 21-3-85

13. NAVIGANS PAST The Year is 1957 - a hesitant beginning, and there's trouble with the troops This is what will, I hope, be the first of a series of articles taking a look at Navigans Past. The aim of the articles is to try to get some flavour of the development of the MSC - and to see if the apparent problems of today are no more than replays of those of Yesteryear. I hope that those involved in the club's development all those years ago will not take offence at any ‘tongue in cheek' remarks I may make; I can assure you I am full of admiration for the efforts you put in and which gave rise to the club we have today. Perhaps those involved ‘in the past' will be able to 'fill-in' the detail; I'm merely looking at Navigans which doesn't reveal the ‘goings on' behind the scenes ! Vol. 1 No.1 - January, 1957 - The very first Navigans, a single typed sheet on one side of foolscap , and edited by the Hon.Sec., W.J.Hodge. The first thing I notice is that it is the “Monthly Bulletin of the MASC Sailing Section"; clearly no thoughts of UDI here. The inevitable invitation for news and views and a deadline of the lst Wednesday in each month. The 1956 AGM was held in November '56 and apparently decided the annual subscriptions really ought to have been paid before the AGM, otherwise membership would "be deemed terminated". I should say so; the smart operators presumably could sail all season and then ‘be terminated’ without spending a bean. Plans to hold an EGM to hear reports on the possibilities of alternative club accommodation - sounds exciting. Members of the club were serving on the Fleetwind Stand at the Olympia Boat show in 1957 and, oh, yes, they need someone to look after Avril. Now who is Avril I wonder ? Vol.1 No2. - February 1957 - The Editor hopes all members will subscribe to its contents; if they took that literally he'd be somewhat overwhelmed but we know what he means. He reminds everyone the 1957 subs are due and good news for Avril - someone offered to look after her. However, no romances in the air ‘cos Avril turns out to be the club boat - shame. A note that catamarans are not eligible for handicap races puts them firmly in their place and quite right too (oops, I'ma Cat owner so I'l] take that back). Vol.1 No.3 - March, 1957 - Oh! dear, the Editor reports "your committee deplores the lack of support shown by the Section to this bulletin" - ‘twas ever so I fear. He goes on to say “an aptitude for journalism is unnecessary for your Committee promises that any material submitted will be re-written if the writer so desires". Of course, the development of our modern comprehensive educational system makes this statement unnecessary - nowadays we'd just miss out “if the writer so desires". A meeting to hear Mr & Mrs Eric Hiscock ° lecture on their world voyage costs 2/6 (124 p in new money); I must say I like addressing the ‘Mrs' half as Mrs Eric Hiscock - must try it on Maggie sometime. The Fitting-Out Supper at the Jolly Sailor, Heybridge, is 4/- per person plus 2/6 return journey on the charabanc - assuming you want to return to-thetmsford:——By-the way, the annual subs for 1957 are still overdue. Vol.1 No.4 - April, 1957. - The annual subs are now considerably overdue and the Editor hopes to be over- whelmed by contributions. At last, a real contribution to navigans entitled ‘Going Foreign' by Charlotte Cottam which, being marked Chapter 1, promises more to come. Vol.1 No.5 - May 1957 - A note of exasperation from the Editor:- ‘To make the bulletin a permanent feature, it is essential that the support of all members of the Section be forthcoming" That will get ‘em going - provided they read the bulletin in the first place. Part II of 'Going Foreign’ was published. Guess what, annual subs are now long ovedue. Vol.1 No.6 June, 1957 - Great news ! An implied improvement wher’ the Editor writes "In spite of repeated requests, annual subscriptions are only trickling in”. Well, at least they are now trickling, the flood will come later. Chapter III concluded ‘Going Foreign' and, even at this distance in time, Charlotte must be congratulated as being the trail-blazer for all future articles in Navigans. You can buy a newly built Enterprise for £110 with racing sails an additional £26.10.0 Vol.1 No.7 - July, 1957 - Has the Editor's message finally got through ? Not a murmur about late subs. A second article entitled 'East Coast Delivery by 'Goose' - Step' (the humour was as bad then as it is now). Vol.1 No.8 - August, 1957 - Sorry, f got it wrong; many members remain on the books as unpaid. Surely they shouldn't be on the books if they haven't paid ? Vol.1 No.9 - September, 1957 - Laying-Up Supper at the Palm Court (don't get excited - its the Marconi Luncheon Club) costs 9/- per person. GP boat cover at £8.8.0 and Hornet cover at £ 9.7.6. Nowt about late subs, surely now all must be well ? Vol.1 No.10 - October, 1957 - Alas, we still have transgressors re. late subs but now the Committee is getting tough. Unless they're paid up in 3 weeks, their continued membership will be considered by the Committee in session. I guess 10 months credit ain't bad - were they charged interest ?

14. — Vol.1, No.1] - November, 1957 - Eric Cottam won the Fleetwind Points Series and the President's Cup in 'Muggs'. Now where have I heard that name before ? Eric scored 178 points (how many ?) and the 2nd helm, Terry Hallam, scored 162 points. Ah! they clearly had a different scoring system unless the results Secretary got it al] wrong (not entirely unknown occurence !). Vol.1 No.12 - December, 1957 - The editor has clearly given up on subs - either that or the Committee's threat to “ex-terminate, ex-terminate" has had the desired effect. The Editor again begs for contributions including suggestions and grievances (he should have jumped into a time machine and transported himself to 1990 before he wrote that ). He goes on to say "all that's required is for a rough outline to be submitted to the Editor who will write up the details in the form of an article” Desperate situations require desperate remedies but it wasn't a bad service to offer was it ? How about it Maureen ? So ends the first, uncertain, year of Navigans. Not much has really changed but the success of our club pioneers is here for all to read. Next month - 1958, ah! a good year was 1958! Mr and Mrs Mise Boreham \ TI II I tee tee Harare . Looks familiar. No doubt many of you, like Maggie and I, like to ‘browse around' the Battlesbridge 'Antiques Centre’ occasionally - just to see what's there. Much to Maggie's disgust I bought a few copies of old Essex Countryside magazines at 10p per copy - much better than the cheese dish that Maggie was eyeing at £36 (we didn't buy it). One of the magazines had a photograph which seemed familiar, and it turned out to be a photo taken from Stansgate looking towards Osea. It was taken by Mr.N.J.James and submitted for the magazine's competition for Essex yachting and boating scenes. Looking through the old copies of Navigans, I assume that the photographer was club member ‘Jimmy' James. Apart from the barge in the background taking my interest, it was the Enterprise dinghy in the foreground which drew my attention; undoubtedly a Marconi SC racing dinghy which, from the old Navigans, seems to have belonged to the Bigden family, but I don't know if if was Jack, Julian or Tim adoin' the sailing. The Enterprise sail number was £1563. I'd like to think that Mr.James won the competition but, even if he didn't, I got a great deal of pleasure in seeing the photograph for its own sake - and an additional pleasure knowing a little bit about its source, I forgot to mention the date of the magazine - it was December , 1967. CLUB NOTICE BOARD - BACSPA NEWSLETTER Speed Limit on the Hiver Blackwater There is 8 growing concern of all River users with the increasing menace of uncontrolled jet-skis and high speed power-craft now beginning to wreak havoc on our waters since the re-opening of the Public Slipway at Stone. The Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection Association BACSPA who pursue 6 policy of active participation with the 31 Watersport Organisation Members, believe that the Maldon District Council should exercise strict control of the Public launching site at Stone, to defuse a potentially lethal situation. At a recent BACSPA meeting it was agreed to pursue a policy with the MOC to set up zones for specific water sports such that the main Fairways would be left relatively free of unnecessary traffic. The Council has responded in this latter case by moving speed limit bouys from Stansgate southern shore to Osea Island thereby protecting the time-honoured anchoring area West of the Pier. Many of you will already be aware of a new organisation, The Blackwater Users Action Group BUAG, who have set themselves up to consider the interests of River users, including wildfowlers, bird watchers, ramblers, Osea Island, etc. They are proposing oan overall speed limit of 8 knots inland from a North/South line taken from a point near Stone Sailing Club. This policy has an immediate attraction and deserves carefull consideration before any decision is made, one way or the other. SPECIFICALLY, it must be realised that such control cannot be made for any particular type of craft and would have to include all River users. It would change the way of the River and how we use it, at this moment in time. It would become illegal to sail any performance dinghy when planing conditions prevailed (F3-4) as planing starts at 8 knots plus! Likewise, catamarans would have to be excluded from the Blackwater. Rescue Boats, of the planing variety, would be outlawed when everyone knows that speed in the time of an emergancy is of paramount importance. Sailing surf-boards could be a thing of the past. BACSPA believes that the Aiver Blackwater is one of the most beautiful settings that any water user will find on the whole of the East Coast and should therefore be carefully preserved for the benefit of ALL users. This will necessarily mean constraint in certain areas and perhaps relaxation in others to strike a balance that will allow us to live together with nature and with due respect and consideration of others. The River Blackwater is your River and BACSPA believes that each Member Club or Association should address the current situation with its own Membership to guide BACSPA along that path considered to be the most equitable to its Membership and to provide the next step towards our childrens’ heritage. Colin Lambert. Secretary, BACSPA. - 14th November 1990

FROM THE REAR..... Although by the time you read this the New Year will be well under way, I would like to wish you all a Happy New Year, and hope you all enjoy this season's sailing. My first comments in this feature must be to thank Mike Boreham for the help and assistance he gave me before I started on the task of Rear Commodore. For approximately 3 to 4 weeks he fed me with data and information, I'm not sure if he was trying to put me off at first, ....THANKS, Mike. In another article Neil Pembleton has referred to the second Safety Boat which we have now purchased from the RYA. At present this is sitting safely in a member's garage and his boat's on the lawn, but on 20th January, the safety boat will be transported to the Club. To make space for it, No.4 Garage is being emptied of Race Marks etc. and these are all being sorted for the season and stored in one of our containers. The containers will be sprayed a dark green to protect them fran the elements and make them less obtrusive, ....THANKS, Steve Glynn and Mike Richardson, One of the main items discussed by the Sailing Sub Camittee is Safety, and I have been asked to express their concern at the number of Cruiser tenders being heavily loaded when transporting crew and equipment from the shore to Cruiser. One additional trip would reduce the risk of a capsize and the resultant danger, Particularly as most Cruiser crews don't dress to withstand a long soaking in very cold water. The River can be a killer. Preparation and selection of Race Officers and support teams is well under way and a full list will be published in next month's Navigans. To ensure you know what to do and that you are scheduled for a duty, you will be contacted in the future. Each member who participates in races, can expect at least 2 duties during the year, excluding Regatta and ECPR, both of which will require all hands. There will be no excuses, all will be asked to help. For some time the Club start line has been the subject of controversy. A special Working Party was set up to identify ways of resolving the problem of starting races amongst moored Cruisers. A number of recammandations were put forward and accepted by the Main Committee. (See Navigans December 1990 Pages 6, 7 & 8). Practicalities of introducing the policy have been explored and same problems have been identified. The Main Committee have agreed the traditional start line (Mete to "D" for Monohull craft; and an extended line from "D" to an outer distance mark for Catamarans) can be used for the 1991 Points Series. Other events will make use of a Cammittee Boat start which will ensure all members obtain the best facilities - those racing the freedan of not being restricted by moored Cruisers, and Cruiser Members not having the worry of their boat being seriously damaged by a start line accident. The Easter Egg, May Bank Holiday events, and Regatta might make use of a line from the Racebox. The start line will still be reviewed to ensure the best facilities are provided for all our members. Mike Duckmanton, Rear Canmodore.

Chairman BACSPA - Firstly a word about our Organisation! BACSPA is run by the Clubs for the Clubs. We have no commercial or private interests and, although fram time to time we may find common cause with other River users, e.g. conservation bodies, the National Rivers Authority, Maldon District Council, contd.

4. BACSPA.... Fisherman, local owners etc., we represent only the Clubs, and Sailing. BACSPA is in fact a member of the RYA in its own right, and we are very grateful for their steady support in these difficult times. BACSPA's policy is set democratically by the Clubs at Spring and Autumn General Meetings each year, and is carried forward by its small Executive Cammittee in between. The work usually includes representation of the Clubs at the River Blackwater Consultative Committee (where we have established excellent relations with Maldon District Council), calling meetings of interested parties where co-operation is needed or where disputes have arisen, and very importantly, lobbying influential parties such as local MPs to make sure that the interests of sailing people are properly represented. An election for the executive is held each Autumn. COWBOYS AND ROGUE SPEEDBOATS. These have been causing continuing concern for a number of years but the problems are now more serious with the advent of jet-skis and wet bikes in our estuaries. At our Spring meeting we decided to submit to Maldon District Council, to all Clubs and to BACUAG (the new BLACKWATER USERS ACTION GROUP) our draft report on the very real problems identified by our members. The great majority of planing boat operators do act responsibly with consideration for other river users. Stone Watersports, who are members of BACSPA, set an admirable standard. The problems are _ twofold. 1. The Cowboys and the ill-informed (as ever); 2. Existing speed limits are largely ignored. BACSPA's policy was against any sort of blanket ban since this could be a_ two-edged sword in unsympathetic hands. We strongly recommended stronger policing of the existing limits; this would, in our opinion remove 90% plus of the problem. Education of newcomers is desperately needed, as is control at the launching sites of the offenders. BACSPA has had a generally favourable response to the report and MDC have picked up the suggestion of a temporary trial area at Steeple Creek dedicated to skibikes, as has been also done at West Mersea. Obviously we have to be extremely careful with such schemes, bearing in mind all the canpeting interests, but our last meeting confirmed the general view that there is room on the Blackwater for all current watersports with the present pattern of use. Clearly an explosion in ski-bike numbers (or anything else) would pose a new situation. On the Colne we now have a highly regulated situation, with 8 knots speed limit over most of the river, an area dedicated to waterskiing, and 4 knots speed limit in Brightlingsea harbour. The limits apply to all craft (including yachts etc.) and formal permission is required before holding any water events. We understand that there are major difficulties in policing the limits, which of course is the real problem. LIGHT DUES. The British Ports Federation report has recommended: a) canpulsory registration for all seagoing pleasure craft above 21' with a view to b)extracting an annual fee of £100 to support the cost of lights and navaids. The RYA has pointed out sO many inaccuracies and incorrect implications in the BPF report, that it is pretty well discredited. We are nevertheless writing to our local MP to point out that among the maritime nations, Britain is almost unique in trying to fund its aids in this crazy and ineffective way. It is also cheeky to bring in this idea when so many useful marks have recently been abolished or reduced. SALTCOTE MILL. The Maldon Plan envisages a “yacht harbour". This’ has been interpreted by developers in terms of a new marina and associated housing development. BACSPA, along with Blackwater SC and Saltcote SC have consistently opposed successive planning applications along these lines: We feel that a further increase in the number of deep draught yachts in the Upper Blackwater is totally inappropriate but that if the Plan policy is that it has to be, then numbers must be strictly limited. Moreover the implications of dredging, salt marsh disturbance and changed current flow are such that a major environmental study is essential before any work begins. We should also lose 12-30 swinging moorings, to be replaced by Marina berths at, perhaps, 30 times the cost. THE UNIFORM BUSINESS RATE. Fron April 1990 all Clubs have been seeing severe increases in their rates. One has no less than 300%, the norm seems to be around 200%. This means that a considerble proportion of Club income will have to go on Business rates from effectively non-profit making sports clubs, paid by the members

< BACSPA ... who already have paid their poll tax. It is manifestly unfair and illogical and same small Clubs may well close. The Ministry's view is that discretionary relief should be available, but that this must be negotiated at a local level. Of 21 Clubs in East Anglia who responded to a recent RYA questionnaire, one had had 100% relief from its Local Authority, 4 had 50% and the rest Zero. In Scotland all Clubs receive relief! BACSPA is not aware of any such relief locally; one Club to our knowledge has been turned down. Same have made progress on revaluation - a different issue. We need a consistent sympathetic understanding of Club problems fram our Local Authorities, and BACSPA is raising the matter vigorously. Meantime, as suggested in the RYA's excellent guide, Clubs must keep hammering on the door - don't take no for an answer. TAILPIECE. These are sane of this year's threats to us. Remember that BACSPA is set up to defend the Sailing Clubs, and no other organisation whatever, however high its motives! Good Sailing! CATATONIC SHOCK SETS IN...... LOOKS FAMILIAR - more information With regard to Mike Borehan's "Looks Familiar" in last month's Navigans, I thought I would write with my now sanewhat hazy recollections of Enterprise Sail No. E1563. The first Club owner of 1563 was Nomnan Palmer, who named the boat “Sue Ann" after his two daughters. He then raced the boat successfully for the Club's first one, two or three seasons at Stansgate. My brother Julian bought the boat, probably around 1966 or 1967 after samehow failing to emigrate to Barbados. Shortly after Julian acquired 1563 fran Norman, the boat's name was changed to Argus II (or III) and the colour changed fran white to black with a white stripe - the sort yachties call a boot top. In 1968 Julian tried another foreign jaunt; this time he DID leave the UK but went the wrong way and ended up installing Marconi's radar in Germany. While sitting out the sailing season in Germany, Julian did have the sense to lend the boat and crew (his future wife, Jill) to brother Tim (me) for a_ season's unremarkable racing. My recollection of the boat now becomes extremely hazy, but I can say that Julian raced her with reasonable success both at Club level and in the East Coast Nimbus Series. She gained new decks and a very stiff Proctor mast compared with its bendy (laterally 2-piece) collar predecessor; new Musto sails to replace the excellent but ‘past it' Windward ones. As for Julian, two Enterprises later he made another, third attempt at Barbados, this time missing by a mere few thousand miles and ended up in the States, and is yet to find his way back for a fourth attempt. I do know he recently got to Hawaii (warmer but not closer.) I hope this is of same interest, no doubt others will have other recollections.
