With the lack of suitable marks being available, the course was set around the few remaining moored boats in the river. Dami@én and Lucy were first to go, and were well into the first lap when the Prindle 18-2s started. Ian and Paul were obviously confident as they chose to start with or slightly after the rest of the fleet. That is, with the exception of Rob and Annette, who decided to give everybody a start! It was as if Damian had never been away! I understand that Damian is in the University 'B' team, so what must the 'A' team be like? (Who said four guys with a van and one all covered with metal work!) The faster boats were struggling to gain distance, whilst Steve Keeble and Lee Harrison were engaged in a two boat race which was probably slowing both of them up. Lee was definitely faster, but Steve was pointing much higher on the beat and gradually opened up a gap. With a lap lasting around 10 minutes, the fast boats had six laps to catch Damian, and on the 5th lap Steve Glynn & Tam overtook and passed Damien at the end of the beat to take an unassailable lead. Damian claimed second spot, with Steve Keeble & Dave Payne in third. What of the rest? Lee & Jenny were fourth. The two Micks were seen to be Sailing up to Goldhanger at one point, and this put them out of contention. Paul and Ian had given everybody too much of a start to be close, but Rob & Annette seemed to be flying as they closed the gap on the leading boats. If only they had started at the right time. So, a most deserved win in both the Osea Icicle and the Winter Series to Steve Glyn & Ton Duckmanton. Was the Winter Series a success? With an average entry of 5 boats, 13 different crews and no problems, the answer must be yes. Let's hope that we can try again next year and that more crews will take part. It is not often that we get to sail on an empty river. Thanks must go to all those who participated and helped run the Series, especially to Larry for acting as Race Officer/Rescue Coxswain/Butt of Some Jokes/Teller of Many. Now if only he would buy a real boat!

COMMODORE’ S NOTES The closed season work to mairitain and improve the facilities cortinues apace. The dignhy-equipment container is now being occupied, ard Garage 4 has been turned over to the new Rescue Boat. I am assured that the planned improvements to the dawnstairs bar arid the creation of the comfortable area upstairs will be complete by the end of March, ready for the season. Some of you may have read in the local paper of a planning application to exterd the Clubhouse. This is the one which involves extending the main lounge to the South, i.e. the dinghy park side, that we drew up about a year ago. Whilst this was being processed, we also looked at the possibility of extending over the Changing Areas. We deliberately left the original plan to complete the planning process so that we can incorporate any comments into the alternative design. Both plans have advantages and disadvantages from the functionality point of view, and one or the other may have a significant cost benefit. At the present time we have made no firm decision about which we will finally adopt. This leads conveniently on to the subject of the Discussion Meeting. At the AGM I made, on behalf of the Committee, the offer of a General Discussion Meeting in March or April. The date of this meeting has now been fixed for Friday 1éth April at 7.30 for Bpm, in the Conference Lounge at the M.A.S.C., Beehive Lane, Chelmsford. The purpose of the Meeting will be for the Committee to describe its thoughts and plans for the future of the Club. I hope that you will attend and partake in the discussion so that we can obtain a fair cross section of the views of the Membership. Obviously, as this is a discussion Meeting, there cannot be any formal motions, but your views are important to the Committee in planning the future. I would also ask that we restrict the discussion to the future, and not get bogged down in any of yesterday’s/today’s problems. If you have any points that you would like to see raised for discussion, I would be grateful if you would send me a note befare 30th March 1991 to the address below. Finally, I would urge you to support your Social Committee’s planned quiz right which is replacing the Fitting Out Party. As you are aware, this has been less well supported in recent years and your Committee has decided to try the Quiz Night format at the MTM.A.S.C. on 27th April, so form your teams of 4-6, buy your tickets, come along and test your knowledge. If you carmnot form a team beforehand, come along anyway and link up with others. CAT NEWS - A SHORT SHARP SHOCK TO THE SYSTEM That’s wot your Cat Fleet Captain gets when our horoured editor rings to say that the article for March (good grief, that’s the month we start sailing again!) 15 due on Friday, today being Wedresday. Fortunately (or unfortunately) I’m not ai Hurricare Sailor and so not blessed with the written equivalent of verbal diarrhoea (does he talk that much on the boat, Dave? Perhaps it wasn’t a dowrndraught....) This wan't be a long article. In the dead season, what’s happened? Well, there was the mass exodus ta the Hoat Show the day after Neil’s bit (he wouldn’t really have wanted the cruder element - that’s most of them - barracking in front of HRH would he?) It did seem as if most of Marconi was there (it must your after-shave, Neil.) My team was late, (what did I expect) but it did give me the opportunity of seeing our revered Cat Park Organiser making his first mistake of 1991. Hasn’t anybody told Fete that the sharp = pointy side of a Cat hull points downwards and the flat bit is on top? Perhaps he’s pre- empting several inversions next (this?) season? Sorry, Fete, I couldn’t resist that dig! Seriously, though, the Hurricane 500 locks an interesting piece of kit, dunno what it’1ll do in a good old Blackwater wind-against-tide chop. I reckon he only did it because all the people on the starid were wearing pink sweat shirts. Mind you, there was this guy in a jacket and tie with his hair slicked down whe bore ai remarkable resemblance to someone in our Hurricane Fleet ....No, it can’t have been Steve Keeble, can it? Next door on the more select stand were loads of phatas of Marconi. Mick Warr'’s efforts in the Winter Series preserved for posterity on the Prindle stand. I believe he’s thinking of changing his name to Beken of Cowes.... What a good day though, especially the Chinese afterwards.... A quick point of a serious nature. We've campaigned long and hard to get the second Rescue Boat - LET’S MAKE SURE THAT IT TURNS OUT EVERY WEEK. I.E. IF 17°S YOUR DUTY, TURN UP. DINGHY FIARK With Easter upon us it is time to think of opening the dinghy park for the new season. The layout for this year will be similar to last year, but with a few minor charges to ensure that we make the best use of available space. Last year at the peak of the summer (Aug/Sept) about 168 boats were stored in the park. These were made up of: Mirror 48 Eriterprise 8 Solo 20 GF14 6 Laser 15 Club 4 420 10 Others 47 Wayfarer 10 Of the "Others", no class was represented by more than 5 boats ard most were ones or twos. The Park was very full at the peak, but with good co-operation from members, all the boats were fitted in. This year the plan is for a total of about 180 boats. With so many different classes it would be very extravagant to allacate standard spaces of the same size for all boats. It is clear from previous years that the best use of space is made when boats of the same or similar classes are placed together, ard placed facirg the same way. Examples of this are the Solo and Mirror fleets. This year there will be dedicated blocks in the park for: Solo 20 Mirrars 45 420/GF/Ent. 26 Large H/Cap over 15ft 21 Other H/Cap 32 Club 4 Plus new areas for the narrower boats: Laser/Topper 13 Fireball/Hornet 2 The park will be available for accupation after the pre-season Working Party (Sunday 3rd March). Boats can be placed in any empty it space is in the correct block, but lagical and efficient that spaces are taken from the Clubhouse end first. Spaces will be pegged cut as a guide; hawever boats should be placed with a maximum gap of eft. hull-to-hull. If you want to site your beat on a road trailer in the dinghy park, don’t expect extra space. Road trailers belong in the area beyond the Cat. Park, and should be marked for easy identification of awnership. Ground Anchors are in short supply. A few are available on a first come first served basis. Mark your equipment /boat/cover/trolley/trailer. No road trailers in the Dinghy Park. Put the Hard Fee stickers on your boat where they can be easily seen. ia TRANSATLANTIC SUMMER CRUISE - GOSPORT TO NEWFORT AT LAST YEAR'S AGM/PRIZEGIVING, NEIL PEMBLETON SAID THAT IN THE PAST THERE HAD BEEN OCCASIONAL APPEARANCES IN NAVIGANS OF LOGS WRITTEN BY DINGHY SAILORS, AND THAT SOME OF THESE HAD BEEN WELL RECEIVED. THEREFORE, I THOUGHT I MIGHT WRITE UP MY EXPERIENCE OF THE LAST CRUISE THAT I DID BEFORE BECOMING A MEMBER OF THE CLUB’S CAT FLEET. THE ROUTE WAS FROM GOSPORT TO NEWPORT, RHODE ISLAND, ALTHOUGH THE EXACT DESTINATION WAS NOT DECIDED UNTIL WE WERE MOST OF THE WAY THERE. THE BOAT WAS CALLED *NORVANTES', A 47’ SLOOF AND ONE OF THE LAST WOODEN BOATS BUILT BY CAMPER & NICHOLSON. SHE WAS BUILT AS AN ADMIRAL’S CUP BOAT AND HAD SOME SUCCESS UNDER THE NAME OF ‘CERVANTES’, BUT IS NOW ONLY USED FOR CRUISING. THE CREW OF SIX WERE A COMPLETE MIXTURE OF NATIONALITIES AND OCCUPATIONS - PETER JAY (THE SKIPPER) AND JIM FORMED ONE WATCH; MICHELE AND NELSON (HONESTLY!) WERE ANOTHER, LEAVING JOHN AND MYSELF. OUR SAILING EXPERIENCE WAS EQUALLY VARIED, WITH MY TWO TALL SHIPS RACES AND 20-ODD CHANNEL CROSSINGS BEING ABOUT AVERAGE. ABOUT THE ONLY THING WE HAD IN COMMON WAS THAT WE HADN’T DONE THE TRIP BEFORE. I SHOULD SAY THAT WE HAD DONE A SHAKEDOWN TRIP TO IRELAND AT EASTER TO GET USED TO THE BOAT AND EACH OTHER. SO WE SET OFF AT NOON ON DAY 1, A FINE JUNE DAY. WE WERE LESS APPREHENSIVE THAN THE PEOPLE WHO WAVED US OFF, JUDGING BY THEIR FACES. WE HAD A GREAT SAIL OUT TO THE NEEDLES - FORCE 4, LOTS OF SPRAY AND SUN. THE BOAT FELT VERY SAFE AND STEADY, IT MUST HAVE BEEN ALL THOSE TINS. IF IT'S ALL LIKE THIS IT WILL BE A DODDLE. BUT, BY THE EVENING, THE WIND HAD DROPPED AND WE WERE IN FOG. I SPENT SOME TIME LISTENING TO TELEPHONE CALLS BEING MADE FROM THE GE2 AS SHE RETURNED TO SOUTHAMPTON, HIGHLY AMUSING BUT FROBABLY ILLEGAL. DAY 2. WE STARTED WATCHES AT MIDNIGHT AND JOHN AND I WERE FIRST ON, (WE KEPT UF 3- HOUR WATCHES FOR THE WHOLE TRIF, (UNLESS IT WAS A NEW TIME ZONE WHEN THE UNFORTUNATE FAIR HAD TO DO 4 HOURS). STILL FOGSY, PASSED CLOSE TO A SHIP THAT WE DIDN’T SEE OR HEAR, BUT ITS WAKE WAS ALL TOO OBVIOUS. FIRST WASH IN SEAWATER - CONCLUDED THAT *SEAWATER SOAF? WORKS NO BETTER THAN ORDINARY SOAF. WE HAD FITTED 2 EXTRA FLASTIC WATER TANKS FOR THE TRIF, BUT FRESH WATER WAS ONLY USED FOR COOKING AND DRINKING. DAY 3. SPOTTED THE FIRST SHARK A LOT EARLIER THAN EXPECTED, AND HAD QUR LAST SIGHT OF LAND. NAVIGATION WAS TO BE BY DEAD RECKONING AND SEXTANT - PETER COULD DO SUN SIGHTS AND STAR SIGHTS AND I WAS THE BACKUP WITH NOON SIGHTS ONLY. DAY 4. A VERY ORDINARY DAY, EVERYONE NOW SETTLED INTO THE WATCH ROUTINE, (I.E. PERMANENTLY TIRED). I STARTED BAKING BREAD WHEN THE OVEN WAS IN USE FOR SOMETHING ELSE, AND STARTED READING *SURVIVE THE SAVAGE SEA’ (TRUE STORY OF A FAMILY’S SURVIVAL FOR 38 DAYS IN A LIFERAFT) MUCH TO EVERYONE'S AMUSEMENT, DAY 5. THE WIND GRADUALLY INCREASED TO 20 KNOTS DURING THE MIDNIGHT TO 3am WATCH, BUT WE HELD ON UNTIL PETER AND JIM CAME ON SO THAT WE COULD CHANGE THE GENOA WITH 4 PEOPLE ON DECK. SAILED THROUGH A FLEET OF RUSSIAN STERN TRAWLERS LATER ON IN THE MORNING. ONE CALLED US ON THE RADIO, IN VERY GOOD ENGLISH, AND GAVE US OUR LAST POSITION CHECK. THEY ARE AT SEA FOR 6&6 MONTHS AND WERE VERY JEALOUS OF US. LATER ON WE WERE ALL STARTLED RY A LOUD HANG, THE SORT OF *CRUMP’ NOISE THAT BIG GUNS MAKE. IT WASN’T THE RIGHT NOISE FOR SOMETHING ON THE MAST BREAKING, BUT WE ALL WORRIED ABOUT IT UNTIL SOMEONE REALISED THAT IT WAS PROBABLY JUST THE SONIC BOOM FROM CONCORDE. WE WERE CERTAINLY UNDER AN AIR CORRIDOR, JUDGING BY THE VAFOUR TRAILS. DAY 6. 3-6am WATCH. QUITE A BIT OF WIND NOW, WE PUT 3 ROLLS IN THE MAINSAIL AND CHANGED TO THE STORM JIB AFTER A SMALL TEAR DEVELOFED IN THE NO.3 GENOA. I GOT VERY WET DOING THIS INCLUDING A BOOTFUL OF WATER (WHICH STAYED WET FOR THE NEXT 3 DAYS). BY THE MORNING THERE WAS A FAIR BIT OF CHADS RELOW WITH SAILING GEAR AND MASTERMIND PEGS ALL OVER THE FLOOR, AND THE HEADS DOOR FLAPFING ON ONE HINGE. A COUFLE OF PEOPLE WERE FEELING SICK FOR THE FIRST TIME, SO WE MOVED THE HAM AND THE FISH (SALT COD) TO AN OUTSIDE LOCKER. I DID THE 12 - 3 WATCH ON MY OWN WHILE JOHN MENDED THE TEAR IN THE NO.3. I THINK I HAD THE BEST OF THE DEAL BUT 3 HOURS WAS THE MOST I COULD HAVE MANAGED AT THE WHEEL IN THAT SEA WITH THE WIND ON THE NOSE, DAY 7. MORE OF THE SAME, WIND NOW 28 KNOTS. MICHELE RIGGED UP A LINE WHICH ENABLED US TO FULL DOWN THE FORESAIL FROM THE FOOT OF THE MAST, AND HENCE SFEND LESS TIME GETTINS SOAKED ON THE FOREDECK. WE HAVE ALL NOW GOT USED TO CHANGING SAILS WITH JUST & PEOPLE. HIGHLIGHT OF THE DAY WAS SEEING A STORMY PETREL, A TINY BIRD THAT FLIES A BIT LIKE A BAT AND OCCASIONALLY FPATTERS ITS FEET ON THE WAVES WHILE FLYING. i ARS SUPPOSEDLY AN INDICATION OF STORMS - A BIT LATE INA THIS CASE.

8, DAY 8. WIND GRADUALLY LESSENED THROUGHOUT THE DAY. ENOUGH SUN FOR A SUNSIGHT, BUT NOT ENOUGH TO DRY OUR GEAR. ENOUGH WATER UNDER US TO COVER MT. BLANC. LOTS OF PETRELS AND POSSIBLY SHEARWATERS FLYING ABOUT. DAY 9. THE LONGEST DAY OF THE YEAR, STARTING TO GET LIGHT AT 3am. GOOD DRYING AND SAILING WEATHER AT LAST. SAW TWO RAINBOWS IN THE SKY, NOT INSIDE EACH OTHER, BUT SEPARATE, AND WITH RED ON THE INSIDE OF ONE AND ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE OTHER - OR WAS I SEEING THINGS? A S’ TEAR APPEARED IN THE NO.1 GENOA AND A REPAIR WOULD HAVE USED UF THE BULK OF THE HEAVY SAILCLOTH, SO WE SWAPPED IT WITH THE SPARE NO.1 AT THE BOTTOM OF THE SAIL LOCKER. AT THE SAME TIME WE ALSO NOTICED THAT TWO STANCHIONS HAD BEEN BENT OUTWARDS. THE REASON FOR THIS, AND THE CAUSE OF THE SAIL DAMAGE, WAS THAT ALL THE HEADSAILS WERE CUT FOR RACING IN THE CHANNEL AND NOT PASSAGE-MAKING IN ATLANTIC STORMS. THEY ALL NEEDED A COUPLE OF FEET TAKEN OFF THE FOOT SO THAT THE BULK OF THE WAVES COMING OVER THE FOREDECK WOULD PASS UNDERNEATH WITHOUT HITTING THE SAILCLOTH. DAY 10. MORE WIND AND WAVES. WE HAVE NOW GOT INTO A ROUTINE OF ONLY EATING TWO MEA LS A DAY - A LARGE BREAKFAST AROUND 10-11am AND THEN DINNER AROUND 6-7pm. THIS SAVED GAS AND SLEEFING TIME FOR THOSE OFF-WATCH, AND WE KEFT IT UF FOR MOST OF THE TRIF. AROUND THIS TIME I DISCOVERED THAT SOMEONE WAS EATING MOST OF THE CHOCOLAGTE - ME! I WAS AVERAGING ABOUT 3 MARS BARS A DAY, AND A BIG BAR OF FRUIT AND NUT MOST NIGHTS. (THE TALE ABOUT CHOCOLATE GIVING YOU SPOTS IS OBVIOUSLY UNTRUE AS I KEPT THIS UP FOR ABOUT 3 WEEKS WITH NO SIGN OF ANY). NORODY ELSE SEEMED TO MIND, AS LONG AS I PROMISED TO KEEP ON MAKING THE BREAD. DAY 11. WIND GUSTING TQ 35 KNOTS AND THE WAVES ARE ABOUT HALF THE HEIGHT OF THE MAST FROM TROUGH TO PEAK. THAT SOUNDS A LOT, BUT THEY WERE WIDELY SPACED AND NOT TOO STEEP. ALSO THE HELM WAS MUCH EASIER NOW AS WE WERE ON A REACH WITH THE NO.4 Genoa UF. DAY 12. NOW DOING S-HOUR WATCHES TO COVER FOR MICHELE WHO IS VERY SEA-SICK AND STAYS IN HIS BUNK. EVERYONE WAS FEELING COLD, EVEN JIM, WHO HAD STARTED TO WEAR HIS SKY-DIVING SUIT. DAY 13. STORM JIB AND S ROLLS IN THE MAIN. THE ONLY GOOD NEWS WAS PETER ANNOUNCING THAT WE HAD CROSSED THE 30°W PARALLEL - 40° TO GO. DAY 14. AT LAST THE WIND HAD DROFFED AND WE WERE BACK TO NORMAL SIZED SAILS. IT WAS RAINING HEAVILY THOUGH, AND I DID MOST OF MY WATCH FACING THE STERN AND HOLDING THE WHEEL FROM THE WRONG SIDE TO KEEF THE RAIN OUT OF MY FACE, BUT BY THE AFTERNOON THE SUN WAS OUT AND WE ALL SPREAD OUT OUR CLOTHES TO DRY. DAY 15. ANOTHER FAST CHANGE IN WEATHER CONDITIONS - THE WIND PICKED UF QUICKLY AND WE WERE MAKING 7 KNOTS WITH NO MAINSAIL AND JUST THE NQ.3 GENOA. JOHN AND I HAD A BAD WATCH; HE DROPPED A WINCH HANDLE OVER THE SIDE AND I BLEW THE CLEW RIGHT OUT OF THE GENOA. BY THE TIME WE HAD STRUGGLED TO GET IT DOWN AND THE STORM JIB UP, THE WIND WAS A CONSTANT 38 KNOTS WITH GUSTS OF UF TO 45, (IT’S TRUE WHAT THE BOOKS SAY - THE TOPS OF THE WAVES REALLY DO START TO FOAM AT THIS STAGE). DAY 16. A BETTER MORNING AT LAST, BRIGHT SKY AND GETTING WARMER, THE MAINSAIL NOW MENDED AND HOISTED. HAD A HUGE BREAKFAST (AS NOBODY HAD EATEN MUCH THE DAY BEFORE), WASHED DOWN WITH A COUPLE OF BOTTLES OF CHAMPAGNE TO CELEBRATE THE END OF ANOTHER STORM AND BEING PAST THE HALFWAY MARK. I REALLY ENJOYED JUST SITTING IN THE SUN AND DRYING MY FEET OUT. LATER WE MOTORED FOR THE FIRST TIME AS THE BATTERIES NEEDED CHARGING AND THERE WAS ALMOST NO WIND. WHILE WE WERE DOING THIS, NELSON SPOTTED A WHALE, WE ONLY SAW A SFOUT OF WATER AND THEN ITS TAIL, THEN IT WAS GONE. THAT EVENING WE USED THE AUTOPILOT FOR THE FIRST TIME SO THAT WE COULD ALL EAT TOGETHER FOR A CHANGE. THE BEST DAY OF THE TRIP SO FAR. DAY 17. A QUIET DAY DRIFTING ALONG WITH THE SPINNAKER UF FOR THE FIRST TIME. THE ONLY EXCITEMENT OF THE DAY WAS SEEING A SHIF ON THE HORIZON, CALLING HER UF, AND FINDING OUT IT WAS THE GEe. THEY ALTERED COURSE SO THAT WE COULD TALK TQ THEM FOR LONGER - THIS SOUNDED ODD UNTIL THEY EXPLAINED THAT THEY WERE DOING 28 KNOTS. THE RADIO OPERATOR WAS VERY CHATTY (BORED, I THINK) AND HELFED US WITH A WEATHER FORECAST, TIME CHECK AND FOSITION, DAYS 18-20. FIRST SUNBATHING WEATHER. LOTS OF DOLPHINS IN THE WATER, BUT DIDN'T JOIN THEM. STEADY PROGRESS IN 15 KNOT WIND, AND A FEW MORE SHIFS ON THE HORIZON.

9. DAY ei. AS WE APPROACHED THE GRAND BANKS OFF NEWFOUNDLAND IT SLOWLY GOT MORE AND MORE FOGGY. A 25,000 TON FREIGHTER CAME WITHIN A MILE OF US BUT HE SAID THAT HE'D SEEN US ON RADAR S MILES AWAY. HE TOLD US WE WERE JUST INSIDE THE MAXIMUM LIMIT FOR ICEBERGS. BECAUSE OF THIS AND THE DENSE FOG, WE STARTED FOUR AND A HALF HOUR WATCHES OF THREE PEOPLE IN ORDER TO KEEF A GOOD LOOKOUT. WE WERE ALL VERY COLD. I HAD ICE FORMING IN MY BEARD AND THE PAIR OF NEOPRENE MITTENS HAD BECOME THE MOST PRECIOUS ITEM ON BOARD. DAY 22. A DUTCH CONTAINER SHIP REPLIED TO ONE OF OUR REGULAR FOSITION BROADCASTS SAYING THAT HE HAD BEEN ON A CONVERGING COURSE BUT HAD SEEN US ON RADAR. WE ALSO HAD ANOTHER QUICK TALK WITH THE GE2 AS THEY CAME FAST US AGAIN. THEY SAID THAT WE WOULD BE OUT OF THE FOG IN 60 MILES AND THE ICE LIMIT IN 100 MILES. DAY 23. THE SEA WAS NOW GREEN INSTEAD OF BLUE AND ABOUT 20 DOLPHINS WERE FLAYING AROUND THE BOW. IN JIM’S HONOUR WE CELEBRATE YESTERDAY BEING THE 4TH OF JULY. DAY 24-25. SUN AT LAST, AND WITH THE SPINNAKER UP, THE BOAT WAS FAIRLY STABLE, SO I WENT UF THE MAST TO CHANGE A HALYARD AND TAKE SOME PICTURES. DAY 26. NOW ABQUT 100 MILES SOUTH OF SABLE ISLAND - THE MOST INFAMOUS WRECKING PLACE IN THE NORTHERN HEMISPHERE ACCORDING TO THE PILOT. A LOOK AT THE CHART CONFIRMED THIS; THE ISLAND 1S SURROUNDED KY A DENSE LINE OF WRECKS AND A NOTE SAYING THAT THERE ARE TOO MANY TO POSITION ACCURATELY! DAY 27. AFTER ANOTHER RAF ID WEATHER CHANGE IT WAS NOW VERY WARM AND WE WERE ALL SLEEPING OUTSIDE OQUR SLEEPING BAGS. A PLEASANT DAY COASTING SOUTH AT 7 KNOTS UNTIL WE CALLED COASTGUARD RADIO HALIFAX (NOVA SCOTIA), WHO ADVISED US THAT WE WOULD SOON GET MORE FOG, THEN VERY STRONG WIND FROM A LOW THAT WE SHOULD AVOID IF FOSSIBLE. DAY 28-29. THEY WERE RIGHT OF COURSE, THE FOG ARIVED. THE WIND DROFFED AND WE STOPFED MOVING COMPLETELY FOR A FEW HOURS. SAW A PLASTIC CUF AND SOME MATCHES, THE FIRST SUCH DEBRIS FOR 3 WEEKS. WE MOTORED OUT OF THE CALM IN THE END, DAY 30. ONLY A COUPLE OF HUNDRED MILES TO GO BUT IT WASN'T ALL OVER YET. THE FIRST SURPRISE WAS A ROGUE WAVE. NELSON WAS AT THE WHEEL WITHOUT OILSKINS AS THERE WAS ONLY ABOUT 10 KNOTS OF WIND, WHEN HE SUDDENLY YELLED SOMETHING, SPUN THE WHEEL, AND GOT FLATTENED BY A WAVE WHICH COVERED THE BOAT FROM THE BOW TO THE COCKFIT. NONE OF US HAD EVER EXPERIENCED ANYTHING LIKE IT. SOON AFTER THAT THE SEA STARTED TO GET LUMFY, THE BAROMETER FELL, AND THE SKY WENT BLACK, WITH THE ODD FLASH OF LIGHTNING. WE REDUCED SAIL AS FAST AS THE WIND CAME UF, STOPPING ONLY TO WATCH A BUTTERFLY GO PAST AND SOON WE WERE BEING THROWN AROUND AGAIN. DAY 31. SHAKEN EARLY TO HEAR THAT 3 PEOPLE ARE SICK AND A JUMPER STAY HAS FARTED IN THE NIGHT. THE LOW MUST HAVE PASSED RIGHT OVER US, AS WITHIN A COUPLE OF HOURS THE WIND WAS BLOWING EQUALLY STRONGLY BUT FROM THE OTHER DIRECTION. THIS WAS VERY DISCONCERTING BECAUSE, WITH NO SUN OR LAND AS A REFERENCE IT SEEMED AS IF WE HAD TURNED ROUND AND WERE SAILING THE WRONG WAY. OF COURSE THE COMPASS WAS THE THING TO CONCENTRATE ON. EQUALLY STRANGE WAS A FISHING BOQAT THAT WALLOWED ACROSS OUR BOWS - THERE WAS NOBODY ON DECK OR IN THE WHEELHOUSE, AND IT HAD A SMALL HELICOPTER LASHED TO THE CARIN ROOF. IT'S ONE OF MY LASTING MEMORIES OF THE WHOLE TRIP. DAY 32. WOKEN BY CRIES OF LAND AHEAD, AND SURE ENOUGH, AFTER 3600 MILES, THERE IT WAS. ALMOST AS APPEALING WAS THE SIGHT OF JIM USING ALL THE REMAINING EGGS THAT HADN’T GONE BAD TO MAKE TWO HUGE OMELETTES. WE SEEMED TO BE IN IN NO TIME, THE ONLY PROBLEM WAS DECIDING WHICH TO HAVE FIRST - A SHOWER OR A STEAK. AFTER SAVOURING BOTH, WE HAD ONE LAST SURPRISE - NONE OF US COULD RUN ON DRY LAND - IT WAS NO PROBLEM ON THE FOREDECK, EVEN IF IT SEEMED MOTIONLESS, BUT ON SOLID EARTH IT WAS JUST IMPOSSIBLE. AFTER A DAY SORTING THE BOAT OUT WE ALL WENT OUR SEPARATE WAYS. I WAS SAD TO LEAVE THE OTHERS (AND THE BOAT, AS IT WAS DESTINED FOR THE CARRIBEAN) BUT TIME WAS RUNNING OUT AND I HADN’T SEEN ANYTHING OF AMERICA YET. FAUL METCALFE

NAVIGANS PAST 10, 1959 - cursethe cat, stub your toes, and throw themover the side. January - not a lot in this January issue. The Editor (W.J.Hodge), who also happens to be the Hon. Secretary, asks that one and all should at least aim to keep one new year's resolution and send their subscriptions to the Hon.Treasurer as soon as possible. And who is the Hon.Treasurer ?... yes, you've guessed it.... poor Mr.W.J.Hodge. No wonder he gets a bit fed up with those members who keep their wallets well and truly glued down. February - the report on the National Boat Show states "a Cat craze had swept the industry" - and to think I thought it had all happened within the last year or two. It seems that Sheerwaters and Swifts are the ‘in thing’ Cat-wise . The Financial Accounts record that the hiring out of Avril brought in £11. 8s. Od for the year and, of course, Mr. Hodge again complains of the members' tardy response to the call to 'pay your subs pronto' (or words to that effect). It seems that Subscriptions brought in £25 during the year compared to £75. Os. 6d for the Laying Up Supper. It is clear the ‘members’ interests lie very firmly within their stomaches rather than within their conscience. ‘Potential Membership ' is, we are told, now 110 (ie. if they all paid up). March - an article giving advice to those contemplating buying their first boat. The new ‘Enterprise’ is recommended for those who want to trail their racing dinghy on holiday (clearly the age of the semi- professional ‘circuit goer' has not yet arrived) whilst the Silhouette or Ballerina is recommended for the would-be cruiser owner of limited means (presumably meaning ‘financially limited' but, bearing in mind the oft-quoted image of owners standing under icy cold showers tearing up £50 notes**, the writer might have had something else in mind). The poor old Catamaran comes in for a bit of stick. "These are very fast (on certain points of sailing) and expensive. Thiswinter there seems to be more Sheerwaters on the second- hand market thanany other 0.0. and they are all fairly cheap." Well, that's not too bad surely...but now comes the cruncher....."they do not seem a very good buy". I bet that was written by a cruiser man. April - A list of "Officers of the Day" and “Time Keepers" is published for the year and, would you believe it, our Editor/Hon.Sec/Hon.Treas Mr.W.J.Hodge has been landed with not one, not two but THREE such duties. They really do put upon him but, as they say, one willing volunteer is better than 10 pressed MEN..e An article 'The art of Sailing' states " bare feet will usually provide the surest grip on deck and floor- boards". He must be joking ! That might have been OK in Nelson's day but, in my brief experiment with "bare-foot boating', it usually provided stubbed toes, foul language and a distinct lack of concentration. May - apparently the Fitting Out Supper held on board MAMGU during April was judged very successful both financially and socially but, there is a sting in the tail (or should it be tale ?). I quote "Mamgu is now well established as a centre for week-end activity - the general disorder and unhygenic conditions prove the point". I think someone's trying to tell us something but I suspect the message was about as successful as the Keep Britain Tidy campaign. The first of many articles by 'Barnacle' appears in Navigans. No doubt Barnacle, like Alistair Cook and his Letter from America, only expected to write a half-dozen (NB. this is the pre-metric age) articles but went on to produce a monthly article for many years. Now, I wonder who ‘Barnacle’ was ? dune - the Editor (Hon.Sec/Hon.Treas/0,0./Time Keeper) again draws attention to the disorder and lack of cleanliness on board Mamgu. It seems that if things don't improve, they might have to identify the culprits and withdraw their keys - now that sounds very painful and that only for the lst offence. At least with Mamgu, a whole host of possible sanctions could be applied. How about keel-hauling, walking the gangplank (with parasoles) or, when all patience and temper has been exhausted, pitch the untidy so- and-soes over the side (without parasoles). July - clearly things are not satisfactory as far as OOD and Time Keeping duties are concerned and}I now quote "Surely it's not much to ask members that they devote just a few hours of their time once during the course of the season in return for all the benefits provided by the club." Alas, not all members see it that way, either then or now but thankfully the present-day MSC has a pretty good bunch of enthusiasts able and willing to get things done. Come to think of it, they must have had a pretty good bunch of enthusiasts in 1959 as well - after all, our present-day club is evidence of it. A notice requests "..all members must identify and remove old clothing,etc....". OK for dinghy sailors who usually change for sailing - but those cruiser chappies, why they seem to wear their old clothes the whole time. Watch this space for further startling revelations. Actually, the notice asked that the clothing be removed "from Mamgu" and not bodies ** at one time it was £5 notes. Then is was £10 notes. Alas, the effects of inflation are felt everywhere. even in the metaphorical shower.

WwW. August - sound advice for the cruiser man - but equally appropriate to the dinghy helmsman. The advice suggests that whilst rowing out to a mooring, the passenger should "press their hands together, as if in prayer, and point the best direction to go". I know the feeling - and don't we all ? It is usually accompanied by “for ---'s sake get that spinnaker up" or " quick, get out on the wire", or "“quick,come in off the wire", or "set the -------------- jib" or "...........". Yes, there are times when the power of prayer might seemingly be more effective. So don't forget you cruiser folks, in 1991 I shall be watching to see how many of your passengers are seemingly praying - and pointing back to the clubhouse as the best direction to go. September - a familiar lament. A notice asks "The last year has seen a big increase in the number of larger boats and the family-type boat. Are we doing all we can to introduce youngsters to the pleasures of racing dinghy sailing ?". October - the announcement of the forthcoming 1959 AGM makes it plain that Mr.Hodge will not be standing for re-election as Hon.Sec/Hon.Treasurer - but will he continue as Editor ? A charge of 5/- was made for use of the dinghy park during the year (they're a trusting lot, collecting the fees after the event) and, for those members who have obviously complained about exorbitant charges,‘it is pointed out this is approximately ld (one old penny) per week, and that it costs 10/- to moor on the river. Ah ! The golden age when the air was pure and free - and the water very nearly so. The season's sailing results reveal (1) that the sailing program was considerably less than it is now and (2) P.Harris seemed to win most of the races. I also wondered why the Ladies Trophy didn't have a winning name inscibed on it for 1959, its' second year of competition. I feared it had been due to lack of interest but it appears that it was cancelled due to bad weather. November - my conclusions from the sailing results werecorrect. This month's leader comments on the Laying Up Dinner/Dance and associated prize giving and states "If there was any boredom at all, it arose from the monotonous recital of events won by Peter Harris. Surely there is someone in the club capable of offering him competition ?". Barnacle offers some advice on buying a cruiser ".......take the owner's judgement (on the excellence of his craft) with a pinch of salt. It may be well to remember............they don't realise their boat is just about everything that a cruiser should not be". Well, what would you expect ? If the average cruiser owner spends 80% of his leisure time scraping the bottom of his favourite possession, he's not likely to see anything but perfection. December - W.J.Hodge took his farewell, not only from the duties of Hon.Secretary and Hon.Treasurer but also those of Editor. At this distance in time, I say "Well done Mr.Hddge and thank you. If you'd given up the struggle to establish Navigans, our club today would be the worse for it". In his report to the 1959 AGM » Mr.Hodgewas able to list improvements achieved for Mamgu in 1959, such as electricity and water supply, furniture and "following a rather unfortunate mishap when one member, attempting to board Mamgu froma temporary structure, was unceremoniously ducked into the water, a permanent access gangway was hastily erected". What I want to know is ‘was the member drunk or was he not ?! Anyway, they'd still better watch their step in 1960 'cos 'a hastily erected' gangway still sounds a bit risky to me. Finally, Mr.Hodge returns to his favourite ssubject - who ain't a-payin' of their subs ? He reports "Payment of subscriptions is still far from complete and quite frankly, we are worried". Money, money, money - always worrying about money. Nothing changes. Happy retirement Mr.Hodge. EXTRACTS FROM THE CONSTITUTION AND BY-LAWS. GENERAL. i. Officer of the Day. An Officer of the Day shall be appointed on all appropiate occasions, and will act as the executive officer of the committee in all matters relating to the conduct and welfare of members and the club during his period of office. In the absence of an appointed Officer of the Day, any committee member at the club may assume the responsibility. 2. Insurance. ALL boats brought to or sailed from the club shall be adequately insured against third party risks. All vehicles driven on club premises shall be adequately insured against third party risks. The M.S.C. and M.A.S.C. will not be Liable for any form of claim. (Rule 21). 3s Losses. The club shall not be held responsible for any loss or damage sustained by a member or his visitor. (Rule 15). 4. Visitors. ALl members except Temporary members shall have the privilege of introducing not more than three adult guests to the club at any one time. The name(s) of the guest(s) and that of the introducing member shall be written in the Visitors Book. SAILING. I Identif ication. All boats and covers must be named or numbered for easy identification. 2. Berths. (a) No boat shall be brought to the club before registration and payment of the appropiate fees. (b) Boats should only be left in their allocated boat park space as shown on the club notice board, or as notified by a club officer. (c) Any member contemplating acquiring a cruiser and wanting a mooring et Stansgate must first apply to the Moor ings Secretary to determine if a mooring is available. Moorings will only be allocated to boats for which all relevant fees have been paid. Purchase of a cruiser on an existing mooring does not entitle the new member to a mooring. (d) Any member with a mooring at the club, contemplating changing his cruiser, must apply in writing to the Moorings Secretary for approval before bringing the new cruiser to the club. (e) Moorings shall be accurately positioned and laid down as directed by the Moorings Secretary, or Mooring Team Leader. (f) ALL maldon District Council mooring fees shall be paid via the club. SF Buoyancy and Sefety. (e) ALL dinghies used from the club shall be fittef with bouyancy to Class Rules, or eas the Committee May reasonably require. (Rule 25.1). At all other, times personal bouyancy should be carried aboard all boats and wearing of this bouyancy shall be the personal decision of the individual. (Rule 25.2).

(ec) In addition to (b), under 18 year olds using dinghies from the club shall at ell times wear personal bouyancy, except with the permission of the parent or guardian who shall be responsible for any consequences. Advice given by any official of the club is of an advisory narure only. (Rule 24). Outside these hours, Parents and Guardians have the sole responsibility for their children and wards end must appreciate that the club cannot be expected to exercise control and supervision. Even during club racing the club cannot accept responsibility for any person. Doesn’t Time Fly When You’re Enjoying Yourself....... Hello, playmates! Here we are (well, we will be by the time you read this) under full steam again with the New Season. First, may I apologise if I repeat anything from the April issue. Having just moved house, that one has yet to catch up with me. I must admit that this is the first year in my sailing career that I’ve only had a lay off from 31 December to 10 March - yes, a number of nutters from the Cat Fleet couldn’t wait (i.e. Dave & Anna; Steve & Tom; The Two Micks; Mick Jones & Don; Tan & Steve Caruth; and Yours Truly - ably assisted by the redoubtable Chris Caruth) and

8. had a Very Nice Sail on 10th. On 17th the numbers were bolstered by Steve Keeble & Dave Payne: Paul Ellis & Crew; and Bob Anderson trying out Cat Balou. Another good day was had by all, despite the lack of wind. The first points races were extremely well supported with (I am told) fourteen in the Fast Fleet and three in the Slow. Racing amongst the twin trapezers was highly competitive despite it being a comedy of errors, i.e. Steve Glynn & Tom deciding to invert, me trying to plough furrows across the banks in Goldhanger (have you ever tried to bear away into deep water with your rudders up?), Dave Payne testing the temperature of the water with his head, and my noble crew trying to waterski off the trapeze astern of the boat - and they're only the ones that I saw! (Yes, Chris, I know I fell off as well!!) None of it mattered anyway because we’d all remembered that it was Rear Commodore’s benefit (you have to let him win sometimes). The afternoon race was even better than the morning with that man Dave Allan & Anna proving that the practice over the last two weekends was well worth it. Just watch out Dave, those two 19’s are after you!! Steve Glynn & Tom managed to redress the balance following their a.m. swan dives. Mind you, they did only manage to pass Chris and me after we tried to nick G Mark tightly, and hit it. Everyone’s comment on the day was that it was the best day’s racing we’ve had for a very long time, and it bodes well for the rest of the season. On a personal note I should like to add how pleased I was tao see rule infringers doing their 720s. I reckon if this close racing continues we’1ll all be experts on them by the end of the season.... Easter Egg went quite well with (according to the Race Officer on Sunday) 22 Cats. I was sorry to miss it but the pleasures of driving the RIB almost made up for it! It’s amazing trying to keep up with Cats going upwind even in light airs - we were probably doing 5-6 knots, and we weren't tacking! Monday was a hooligan, and being April Fool’s Day we had a Keeble Special course. Well done, Steve Glynn & Tom for finishing in such style, and congrats on winning the series. As a sailor, I’d like to express my appreciation for the way in which the shore based organisation has improved through the closed season. It certainly shows on the water. Well done Mike D and the Sailing Sub. It appears that we have the prospects of VLFs (Very Large Fleets) this year with a Significant number of Dart 15s and (much to my relief) a good number of new members with Dart 185 - some of whom are recruits from other Clubs with others newcomers to the sport. We could see around 10-12 twin trapeze boats with around the same in Dart 18s in the "“Quick" Fleet and at least 7-8 Dart 15s in the "Slow" Fleet. What a prospect, 25+ Cats in the Blackwater! PLACING OF CATS IN CAT FARK - One correction to a previous announcement, Pete Flook is no longer IC Cat Park. He has taken responsibility for the RIB, so parking issues are down to me. We don’t want to get too involved in moving boats around, but please try to leave no more than 2’6" between boats. That way we can fit more in without encroaching on the Car Fark. Also make sure that your boat, trolley arid/or trailer are marked with Your Name, Class and Sail Number; (otherwise they could end up being moved anywhere - within the Cat field that is....) For those sculs who wish to contact yours truly outside sailing times, please note that my new Phone No. is [redacted] If I’m not in, my answerpnone is quite friendly. NAVIGANS PAST i. 1960 - a quiet revolution and the need for new heads, ++eeeeand those damned dinghy sailors !!! KkKK KE January - the new Editor/Hon.Sec/Hon.Treas. is F.W.Garrett. One thing that has struck me when reading these old Navigans is the steadfast adherence to formality. 'Mr.W.J.Hodge' or 'Mrs S Harris' It is - and articles are signed merely by initials, almost as though it would be pretentious or undignified to sign the author's full name. How very different from our 1990s Navigans where all are addressed by their first name as though they were long-lost friends - and the trading of 'insults' (well, perhaps only "getting at' each other with a gentle niggle) occurs fairly regularly. Anyway, the change of Editor brings with it a slip in the mask of apparent inscrutable correctness as I discover that W.J.Hodge is known to his friends as ‘Wally! as Fred Garrett (for Fred is his name) pays tribute to his predecessor. February - Fred asks 'Wes you bin and gone ?' but not quite inthatiway. What he actually writes is "....it would greatly facilitate the keeping of records......if members would advise the Secretary of any changes of location." Yep, I guess it would ; it would also help to catch up with the ‘subs demand’. The accounts for 1959 show an improved Subscription income of £45 5s Od and a reduced Laying-Up Supper income of £60 15s Od. Obviously, the membership not only shows a commendable pang of conscience but also a determ- ination to diet. The Fitting-Out Supper brought in £16 4s 2d (why 2d ?) with catering expenses of £3 (how much ? What did they eat - dry bread and jam ?) and ‘other' expenses of £9 8s 9d. Now for the exam question: Without taking more than five seconds, calculate the profit for the Fitting Up Supper ? NB. the answer is at the end of this article and, be honest, how many got it right within the time allowed ? March - a revolution might well have been declared between February and March, 1960, or maybe even a coup d'etat has been attempted - but I doubt if many people noticed. Until now, Navigans has always been described as the "Monthly Bulletin of the Sailing Section, M.A.S.C". However, in the historic month of March, 1960, Navigans become the “Monthly Bulletin of the Marconi Sailing Club, M.A.S.C." Was this a deliberate decision of the Sailing Section's Main Committee - or merely a unilateral whim of the Editor to declare UDI ? With regard to the forthcoming sailing season, mention is made of team races with at least four visiting clubs. The Portsmouth Standard Handicap for the Enterprise is 98 (Terylene sails) or 103 (Cotton dails), whilst the International Cadet races to 129 compared to the club's rating of 130 for ‘Avril’. Presumably, Avril falls into the category of 'slow but steady’. April - a new Editor, but the same old problem '".....many subscriptions remain outstanding". Formality has been restored with "A considerable amount of work has been undertaken on our clubhouse under the direction of Mr.Bigden", These days, even those of us who did not know him would, I am sure, unhesitatingly refer to him as Jack Bigden and he subsequently did an awful lot more work for the club. The memory of Jack Bigden is . deservedly preserved by our main support boat ‘Jack B'. The club dance is to be held at the Odeon (cinema ?) and tickets are 5/- each. "Barnacie' writes an article "On learning to Sail" and recommends Peter Heaton's book "Sailing". At this time I hadn't even thought about sailing but when I did, sometime in 1961, the first book I bought was, in fact, Peter Heaton's book. I still have it and feel it is one of the nicest books to read on learning to sail - I should know, I've read an awful lot of them ! May - instructions concerning the club 'flattie' (I first read this as 'fattie') and readers are instructed "When mooring her, tie to the rope mooring line..... «-with a hitch that will not ride up the mooring line." Now come on you dinghy sailors, how many of you could do that first time without having to think about it ? Come to that, how many cruiser sailors could do it ? Hang about whilst I take time off to read up on "Knots to tie and Knots not to tie ". P.S. What's a 'flattie' ? An article on 0.0.D.duties ‘reveals that the 0.0.0. is also the Race Officer - now, what a good idea ! Apart from the ‘usual' duties, he has also to collect 2/- from each helm entering the race, except not from those who have paid a ‘block payment' for the season. Some years ago at an AGM, someone suggested that the club dispense with a hard fee and charge each time a member launched their dinghy. The heat generated by that one scortched the ceiling. Anote about the America's Cup, reporting the NYYC's acceptance of a challenge from Australia for 1962. Now I wonder what Alan Bond was doing at that time - and what chance a challenge by the MSC in 2001 ? Who knows to what extent the MSC will develop; maybe we can take Dennis Connor's last 'defence' as a precedent and make a «challenge in a catamaran ? Finally, a note about a visit by Dabchicks Sailing Club members - but a somewhat unusual arrival. tt seems they came in a sailing smack - and abandoned the boat completely ‘some distance' downstream due to lack of water, coming ashore in their dinghy. The smack itself was left to come in on its own with wind and tide

12. alone to guide it. Apparently, it berthed itself very neatly alongside Mamgu. I must say, that's what I'd call a well trained boat. Of course, in recent years some of our catamaran members have had a go at training their cats to manoeuvre unattended on the river. Alas, although the cats glided off under their own guidance system very impressively, they failed to answer to their master's 'return' whistle and we had to send out the cat-catchers to retrieve them. June - at last, another small crack in the armour of formality appears; Jack Bigden is referred to as Jack Bigden whilst mention is also made of Stan Allerton, Pete Harris and Brian Partridge. I think Maylandsea Bay Sailing Club won the team race held on lst May; at least the results show MBYC = 73.50 and M.S.C. = 46.0. As far as I can tell, the main sailing programme seems to have consisted of a single handicap fleet series - and not too many entries in the two races to date. July - a reprimand to members, "Too many members are sailing without personal buoyancy in conditions that demand more discretion". A visit to Ariel S.C. (BBC) at Teddington for "the return team races" is reported. Alas, the MSC team '".....was hopelessly outclassed by the BBC who knew all the dodges on their home waters". Well, they would, wouldn't they ! A report of a letter of thanks to Blackwater SC's rescue boat for rescuing a number of MSC capsized dinghies. Did we have a rescue boat then? From what I read, I get the impression we did not have a rescue boat, at least not one that went out as duty boat during races. August - the Editor again chides members for lack of cleanliness, tidiness and hygiene on board Mamgu, and is particularly concerned about the toilets. He states, " These (ie. the toilets) should only be used as a last resort and then only in a minor way" (72777) What, I ask myself, do you do whilst you await the blessed state of 'last resort’ so that you can legitimately use 'the heads’ aboard Mamgu ? By the time you do get to the 'last resort’ stage, what was presumably relatively 'minor' will more than likely have become 'major', and you're still banned ! No wonder they don't get many ladies with parasols on board Mamgu - not for long anyway. First mention of a club rescue launch - a vessel is being acquired and is to be commissioned shortly. The prime function of the launch is to be for rescue purposes and assisting members in distress. Another duty for the 0.0.0. Apparently, when Mamgu was flying the Red Ensign, club yachts were suppose to dip their own ensign in salute - and the OOD was supposed to acknowledge in like manner. What with acting as Race Officer, unblocking the loos (sorry, heads) and generally looking after the clubhouse, the poor 00D doesn't get much time to relax does he ? No chance for him to put a coat of anti-fouling on his boat..in those days. By the way, is the saluting etiquette still required to be observed ? Certainly, I've never done it when acting as 00D - there's never been time to look at passing cruisers and, anyway, I'm not sure I'd recognise the salute if I saw it. Fings definitely ain't wot they used ter be. September - a Fleetwind team race against MBYC took place in bright and sunny conditions - but not for the MSCteam. MBYC took lst, 2nd and 3rd places and MSC occupied 4th-6th. An article by ‘Barnacle’ entitled "Helmsmanship and Seamanship" no doubt caused some considerable comment amongst the members - especially the dinghy sailers. Maybe Barnacle had had a bad day at the office or, more likely, a particularly harrowing experience the previous week-end but he certainly gives the dinghy sailers a roasting. He states, "The last few years has seen the rapid growth of an entirely new breed of 'sailor' - the ‘dinghy boys'. Many.......are absolutely first rate seamen but.......many others cannot be called seamen at all" He continues, "Having won a race or two they consider themselves fine helmsmen, as maybe they are, but they also consider themselves fine seamen, and that theymost certainly are not". Barnacle then goes on to blast the dinghymen with examples of lack of seamanship which, I must confess, I recognise myself as being a guilty party. However, some respite is granted the dinghymen when he re-directs his attack towards what he calls “marine motorists" (Ah! says our modern-day dinghyman, NOW we can relate to him !) and, perhaps surprizingly, he soundly belabours the ‘large racing cruisers’. Rather more in hope than expectation, he ends the article by saying he sincerely hopes no one will take offence ! Ah, well! He's a nice chap really and just felt like ‘blowing his top' - but I think I'd have kept out of his way for a bit, just in case. October - a winter meeting entitled 'Blackwater Mud' - now there's a subject to get stuck into. Barnacle is still with us and presumably still acceptable. His article on ‘Laying Up' no doubt pricked the conscience of those cruisermen who read of those things they ought to have done - and of those things they ought not to have done - as winter approached. At least the dinghyman can hide his folly in the garage. flovember -- the AGM reveals a paid-up membership of about 150, including 21 associate members. December - a winter meeting not to be missed; an illustrated lecture by Hervey Benham. I love reading his books and would dearly liked to have heard him speak. Sadly, 'The Sailing Barge Preservation Society’ is to be wound up, and, even sadder, 'they' plan to break up ‘Black Eagle', a sailing barge which had served as the home of a former Commodore of the Maldon Little Ship Club. What a shame. Is Mamgu safe I wonder ? Exam Question Answer: £3 15s 5d (I think!) M.P.B./Mr.M.P.Boreham/Mike Boreham (take your choice)

COMMODORE’S NOTES af Firstly, many thanks to Frank and Bob for their efforts in re-arranging the downstairs bar and to the members of the Cruiser Fleet for the redecoration and painting of the floor. It certainly appears that the Club riow has a more sheltered and useful area. Now can we, between us all, manage to open both bars regularly on Sundays, particularly on those hot bright sunny days which I am sure will come this summer. Secondly, many thanks to the Social Committee for organising the Quiz evening. The numbers present certainly justified the change of format and all who took part seemed to enjoy the evering even if the brain cells suffered from overload. The Discussion Evening regarding possible future directions for the Club was very informative. There was general support for the Executive’s view that we should aim to keep the membership level around 500; the number of Permanent Guests this year is approximately 1300, and the potential number of people on site is 2000 therefore. The Executive’s plans for an extension to the South of the Clubhouse were rot well received and it was felt that we should examine the possibility of building over the Changing Rooms. The main areas that members appeared to want to see improved were the changing and lounge facilities with improvement also shought for the storage anid working facilities on the Club Boats over the winter. We will be examining the possible options during the next few months. I would like to thank all who attended, and recommend to future Executives that the exercise is repeated on an Annual basis. Our two main Open Everts of the year are rapidly approaching - Regatta and East Coast Fiers Race - and as always, their success deperids very much on the degree of help received from you all. At the risk of being accused of being Headmasterly, may I remind you all that the Club’s, Regatta, and East Coast Piers Committees do spend a lot of time thoughout the year planning and running the Club. Please can you show your support by giving a couple of hours’ help at these events. Confucious said "Many hands make light work", I will add "No hands make for tired, disillusioned ard frustrated Committee Members". OFFICER OF THE DAY ae As you are all aware, we are a self-help Club and it was decided by the Main Committee that any person who had been a member of the Club for at least three years would be allocated an OOD duty. Following the successful start last year, the system has been continued for this year. Obviously, when allocating the duties we do not know people’s availability, and therefore have to rely on you either arranging a swop with another person, or, in the last resort, informing Steve Hill [redacted] at least FOURTEEN DAYS BEFOREHAND. The task of 0.0.D. has been considerably simplified this year, now that the activities associated with the Racing and Rescue are more directly under the control of the Race Officer and Duty Coxswain. It is now mainly being responsible for unlocking the Club, etc; ensuring that the boiler is lit etc; organising that the bar is open at lunchtime; finally, ensuring that all above are locked up before leaving the site. You should receive a reminder and set of duty instructions about twenty one days beforehand; if you have not received these by then, please contact Steve Hill. In the event that you fail ta perform your duty you will be asked to explain your reasons to the Executive Committee arid be giver a chance ta perform the duty at a later date. In the event that your reasons are considered unsatisfactory, and/or you are unwilling to carry the duty cut at a later date, the Executive will recommend a course of action which may include withdrawal of your membership. ADDERS ON THE SEA WALL ADDERS HAVE BEEN SEEN IN THE LONG GRASS ON THE SEA WALL ALONG THE CRUISER FARK RECENTLY SO WOULD MEMBERS, AND PARTICULARLY CHILDREN, AVOID WALKING THROUGH THERE, BECAUSE THOUGH AN ADDER WILL NOT APFROACH HUMANS, IT WILL BITE IF TRODDEN ON, I UNDERSTAND THAT THE PREGNANT FEMALE ADDER LIKES TO BASK IN THE SUN AND IS RELUCTANT TO MOVE ON SOMEONE*S APPROACH -— WHICH IS THE REASON THEY ARE SEEN MORE OFTEN BY PEOPLE AT THIS TIME OF YEAR. (THE YOUNG ARE BORN IN SEFTEMBER, ) BITES ARE VERY RARELY FATAL, BUT DO REQUIRE IMMEDIATE MEDICAL ATTENTION IF THEY OCCUR. 8. "THE DENGIE CHRONICLE" Salmon sighted on the Blackwater Such is the stuff of 'headlines'; it doesn't have to mean what it says, merely make you want to read what it implies it is saying. The Essex Chronicle has recently introduced a weekly ‘Sailing Report’ and the MSC was asked to submit a weekly report which I waS be pleased to supply. Unfortunately, the lst report submitted was for the week 'they' didn't print a Report in the Chronicle. However, undaunted, I submitted a 2nd report and SUCCESS, 'they' printed a report in the Chronicle issue of 3 May - albeit they got one or two bits twisted around somehow. Never mind, its good to see an attempt to give sailing some publicity in the local press and even better when it features the MSC. However, for the record, here are the two reports I submitted (more or less). Spring points 7 & 8 (21 April) Marconi SC members enjoyed magnificent sailing on Sunday in SW force 3-6 winds, with a total of 8 Solos and 19 Catamarans turning out for Spring points 7 & 8. Marconi's Solo Fleet is always competitive, so new member Simon Liddington's two wins were particularly noteworthy. John Salmon scored two second places in his new boat, whilst 3rd place was taken by local helm Ron Greygoose in the morning and by Roger Smith in the afternoon. In Marconi's ever growing Catamaran Fleet, David Allan and Anna Spittle (-Uurricane 5.9) showed exceptional downwind speed to get lst in the morning and 3rd in the afternoon in the Fast Catamaran Handicap race. The club's lady helm, Lucy Boreham (Dart 18), crewed by Tom Ashley, took 2nd place in the morning, whilst Fleet captain, Larry Botheras (Prindle 19), crewed by Chris Caruth, placed 2nd in the afternoon. The Slow Catamaran handicap race produced a win for local helm, Dave Payne (Dart 15). The club's youngest regular catamaran helm, 12-years old Paul Harrison (Dart 15), crewed by Stuart Golding, took second place. Spring Points 9 & 10 (28 April). Forecast winds of NE force 3-4 turned out to be a very variable Fl and a bit. Unfortunately, this meant a number of competitors found themselves “out of time" in the morning races. Out of an entry of 16 Fast Catamarans (less than PYN 90), only John Nickalls/Caroline Hollings (Hurricane 5.9), Steve Glynn/Tom Duckmanton (Prindle 19) and Steve and Janet Keeble (Hurricane 5.9) finished the course in lst, 2nd and 3rd places. Three others finished “out of time" and 10 retired, having been caught on the wrong side of the river with little or no wind and a strong adverse tide between them and the next mark. The afternoon race attracted 17 entries in Force 1 - 2 and this time 14 finished and 3 retired. This race was won by Paul Ellis (Dart 18), John Nickalls/Caroline Hollings (Hurricane 5.9) wnd and Lucy Boreham/Tom Ashley (Dart 18) 3rd, The Solo Fleet attracted 8 entries for race 9 and 6 for race 10 and generally coped much better with the fickle, swinging wind than the ‘catamarans. At one time, boats only yards apart and heading in exactly the same direction on a beat to windward were actually on opposite tacks. John Salmon, sailing his new boat, won both races with new member Simon Liddington 2nd each time, the afternoon race being a particularly close battle between them. Third place was taken by Roger Smith (race 9) and Peter Collis (race 10). None of the Slow Catamaran Fleet(PYN 90 and above) finished in the morning and only Colin Kidner (Dart 15) completed the course in the afternoon. In the monohull] Handicap Fleet, race leader, Mike and Maggie Boreham (420) finished a minute ‘out of time’ in race 9, whilst Howard Rogers/Paul Wilkinson (Fireball) won race 10. NB. If John Salmon had kindly capsized, the ‘headline’ could have read ‘SALMON SIGHTED IN THE BLACKWATER’. PS. The 'headline' in the Essex Chronicle was nothing to do with me; ‘twas all their own inspiration. 10. NAVIGANS PAST 1961 - signs of dissent, and a very sad loss plus plans to make the ladies flush with delight. January - the Editor's Comments state "There appears to be many misconceptions about the true aspect of club working days during the off season..........Bearing in mind our prime function is as a sailing club we can, nevertheless, attend to our creative comforts as well. The club provides the material and the money (on a very slender budget) and a disservice is done to those individuals who give of their time and skill in this work by taking it for granted, or that the job is someone else's ‘pigeon', or we keep a permanent ‘cinderella'........ cracks about ‘dirty old barge', or ropey dinghy park facilities do not help. Those who think this way should ask themselves the obvious question." February/March - two issues in one due to the recent indisposition of the Editor, Fred Garrett, who is also Secretary/Treasurer, He seeks a volunteer to take over both the Editorship and the whole of the production of Navigans (ie. 200 copies). This means collecting,editing and preparing copy followed by arranging for stencilling & checking before printing, and the final chores of stapling and distribution. Stan Allerton questions if it is fair for, say, two parents, two children and two friends to all sail on the basis of a single subscription ? Although he recognises that family sailing is a fundmental part of the club's activities, he feels that once the children become ‘earners' they should become members in their own right. To this end he proposes a Junior Membership (16-21) be established - and he deliberately avoids the term 'cadet' to avoid confusion (identification ?) with the Cadet dinghy class (and presumably its implications of a younger age group, 15 and under). He also feels the need to encourage Associate Members under the age 21, and suggests a subscription well below the normal Associate Subscription of 34/-. In this way he hopes toguide the ‘youngsters' into the club's adopted fleets of Fleetwind and Enterprises, thus maintaining these fleets and avoiding the introduction of other classes which, he feels, the club could not sustain. The coming season offers fleet racing for trophies in Enterprise and Fleetwind (12 races, 6 to count), and handicap racing for two Menagerie classes (103 and under; over 103), with a small prize for the winners of each of the 12 races scheduled. Three starters are necessary for each race. The BJRC agree various adjustments to the ‘Portsmouth harbour speed figures' and our favourite club boat 'Avril' is rated 130, putting her between the Cadet (Terylene sails) at 128 and Cadet (Cotton sails) at 132. April - Fred (now writing under ‘Secretary's comments) announces that responsibility for editing and publication of Navigans has been taken over by Nick Tovey and his Wife Daphne as Editor. I can't help feeling that he really ought to have said that the new Editor was Daphne Tovey assisted in the publication by Husband, Nick - but it was in the good old days when it was a man's life at sea and the ladies were presumably not too bothered either way. Fibre-matting was fitted to the launching ramp to give a more secure foothold - anda stiff broom provided to clean it down. Was the fibre-matting successful - and did the new broom sweep clean ? Bad weather on Easter Sunday forced postponement of the 'Tuning-up race' until Easter Monday but even worse weather resulted in only a scratch race of two boats. Turnout for the first four Points races was 4,5, 3 and 3, with Peter Harris in his Fleetwind 'Muggs' winning all but the 3rd race in which, of the 3 entries, one sailed the wrong course, one capsized and one hit a mark ! The block racing fee for the season will be él. Socially, it rained, but didn't it rain, for the Fitting Out Supper. About 70 people enjoyed a programme of colour films including some about the English Electric Valve Company, surf boatmen of Ghana and Canadian sailing. This reminds me that when I was a very young lad, I used to go around to the local village hall for the once-a-week film show; some of them were silent movies and the local baker's wife used to play the accompanying piano enthusiastically - but very badly. The Supper finished with, I quote, 'A gay accompaniment .....provided by the 'Remo's' a local skiffle group at Heybridge’. How about a gay group for the 1991 Laying Up Supper ? Oh! I forgot to mention; the Supper was held on board Mamgu. May - a call for volunteers to operate the new rescue launch and training will be given. It will operate under the control of the 00D (who is also Race Officer). A team race against Ariel SC, Teddington (ie. the BBC) but, alas, it seems we learned nothing from the 1960 defeat. Once again the MSC ‘was hopelessly outsailed by the BBC who were up to all the dodges of the river and knew where to expect the gusts’. Even more alas - we were beaten by MBYC in a team race and didn't do too well in the Enterprise Open Team race competition, «lso held at Maylandsea. The lst Picnic Cruise to Osea was not too well supported - only one boat made the trip and had to be towed back to Heybridge due to steering trouble. However, a 2nd Picnic Cruise to Osea on Whit Sunday was more successful with 16 boats and 50 people making the trip to Osea. The youngest to attend was 8-month old Kerry Sims.

ji. June - an evening working party resulted in the successful stepping of Mamgu's mizzen mast, plus removal, and replacement, of the rescue launch engine to effect repairs. Peter Harris came 2nd in the Fleetwind East Coast Area Championships and Maldon Little Ship Club beat us in a team race. A Maldon Little Ship Club boat also won the Marconi Cruiser Cup whilst a Hornet from Maldon Yacht Club won the Marconi Challenge Cup. It would appear that Maldon sailors rule the river; I wonder if it has anything to do with the aftermath of the Vikings' victory at Northey some 1,000 years ago - you know, all that rape and pillage they seemed to go in for in those days. Robbie Sims organised a successful camping/cruising weekend with 17 people travelling to East Mersey, some going by road and some in one of the 5 boats that made the trip . July/August - a sad day for the family and friends of Fred Garrett and a sad loss for the club. Fred died on 18 August, 1961 after a short illness. There can be few members in our modern-day club who knew or can personally remember him - but the name of Fred Garrett must be one of the most well-known to club members through the Garrett Memorial Trophy which is awarded annually to the most outstanding cadet member of the club. In the tribute to Fred Garrett, we are reminded that he took a leading role in the conversion of Mamgu from a dilapidated old barge yacht intoaviable floating club house, and that he also provided a valuable link between the MSC and its parent organisation, the Marconi Athletic and Social Club. As a result of the passing of Fred, Robbie Sims took over as. the MSC Secretary. Robbie has clearly issued a set of ‘House Rules' for the club, although it it is not clear how they were circulated and advised to members since they don't appear to have been printed in previous issues of Navigans. Whatever 'the rules', he has caused John Scarlett (also a member of Maldon Little Ship Club) to write a letter of comment (some supportive, some critical) to Navigans. One of the rules presumably required each member to perform an OOD duty because Mr.Scarlett writes " I cannot see the inactive majority liking the idea of paying 10/- a year and being expected to spend one day every other year at Heybridge staying there until everyone else has departed, possibly in the small hours of the morning. Some of these members might not bother to remain in the club......... Objections to the duty of SOD can be expected from ** the more responsible of the ‘inactive’ members but there is a risk of others just not bothering to turn up". This has a very familiar ring about it; the current OOD duty roster is drawn from all members of more than 3 years standing and results in a duty roughly every 2 years but, from recent experience, not all members seem keen to 'do their bit’. Strange isn't it, even after 30 years, the same old problems and same old arguements rule the day. September - a committee has been formed to organise a collection to purchase a permanent memorial to Fred Garrett, initial thought being possibly a piece of furniture, a barometer or some other article for Mamgu. At last, team wins for the MSC, this time against Osea SC and MBYC - but don't celebrate too loudly 'cos the return match (on our home waters) against Ariel SC (BBC) resulted in the BBC winning handily. In the Points racing, race 9 is considered to have attracted a large turn-out with 8 entries - most races seem to attract 3 - 5 entries. The Ladies Race, I suspect, attracted 3 entries and was won by Miss J. Fairbains October - MSC was beaten by Maldon Little Ship Club in a team race ! The Childrens’ Party held on board Mamgu attracted 30 children and ‘Uncle’ Peter Makins reputedly brought along his Performing Flea . This gives a whole knew meaning to ‘scratch race’. Inflation is catching up; tickets for the Laying Up Supper are 15/- this year. November - the new Secretary, Robbie Sims, asks for a good turn out for the 1961 AGM since "...(it) will be very important for the future of the club; indeed, as a result of increased membership we have reached a turning point." Thirty years later in 1991, have we again reached a turning point ? Some believe so. The last page of Navigans is a questionaire about possible club activities covering Sailing Activity, Summer Evenings (ie, apres sailing), Winter Evening and the member's attitude towards the use of Mamgu - plus space for ‘constructive suggestions’ (but not ‘destructive criticism’). December - Arthur Adam (Commodore) writes a Christmas Message, dispells the gloom and doom expressed by some members at the AGM, and mentions that some want to buy a shore-based site - but no available site is known. Now, I wonder what was happening down river around the Stansgate area at that time ? The AGM attacted 90 people - not bad for a total membership of about 200. The number of dinghies has "increased considerably to 46", Robbie Sims is elected Vice-Commodore and good news for ladies - consideration is being given to installing a flushing ‘Ladies' aboard Mamgu. Who knows, we may yet see a host of waving parasoles on board Mamgu in the summer of 1942, “* Now this is a serious question; Path. : - F in the context of the i Mike Boreham h Sailing Club, what does SON stand for ?

Use of Hard e&.1 Access to the hard through the gap in the seawall anda 3.6 metre (le ft) strip from this gap to the low water mark should be kept free of parked dinghies and launching trolleys at all times. Dinghies can be launched or landed on any part of the hard except during launching of cruisers. The east side of the hard MUST not be used for launching or landing of dinghies when cruisers are being launched or recovered. TO THE CRUISER FRATERNITY Having perused the latest issue of Navigans, it was very abvious that the Cat and Dinghy members are the erudite cones with hyperactive biras and lots ta Say. This prompted me into immediate production af another of the *Local Area’ articles as a means of leading by example to try and coax more Cruiser folks into contributing. So come on you lot, write something about something, handy hints, trips, techrical bits, news or whatever. Make Maureen happy with a flow of material for Navigans. Dave Beane Know Your Local Area wt WEST MERSEA West Mersea is famous in the annals of Essex Maritime tradition. Many of the skippers and paid hands for the well-to-do owners of racing yachts were recruited from the area in the 20s and 30s. Most of these men were Fisherman in the winter ard paid yacht hands in the summer. Their exploits are recorded in many books dealing with this area. Mersea Island itself is joined ta the mainland by a causeway which flocds at high spring tides. As yet there are no marina-type develcepments on the island nor are any plarmed. The facilities there are within easy reach for MSC yachtsmen, and the moorings in Mersea Fleet or Quarters give access to the sailing Clubs, pubs, shops and restaurants to be found on the island. For the MSC yachtsman arriving from Stansgate there 1s normally enough water to allow a short cut acrass the Nass Shoal into the channel leading into Mersea Quarters. This charmel starts at the Nass beacon and is marked by port and starboard buoys until the first of the moorings is reached. Shortly after this the channel divides intca three branches; the Strood, the Ray and Salestt Channels, all three beirg heavily populated with moorings and navigable, depending or draught, for a reasonable distance. It is normally possible ta pick up one of these moorings, especially when local boats are absent. The West Mersea Yacht Club boatman will give advice as to the availability of moorings. The best charnel with regard to proximity ta the landing stage is the first ta starboard as the Channels divide. It is fairly narrow, ard shallow at the edge, sa stay reasonably close to the line of moorings until you find a vacant ome. This route takes you clase to starboard of the old Oyster shed, a square shed with a corrugated iron roof. Having found a mooring you will have ta ga ashore by dirighy, or by halling the boatman for a ride ashore. If intending to return after dark it 1s preferable to rig a riding light and to make careful note of the nearby boats as the crowded moorings can prove quite confusing especially in the dark ard with a different tidal state and alcohol level thar when you ventured forth. Orice safely ashore you carn explore Mersea City with its picturesque clapboard cattages, have a drink in the Yacht Club or walk to one of the pubs. The alternative ways to access the island are te sail across the Mersea Flats ard inta the Colne opposite Brightlingsea and to anchor in the Fyefleet pool or ta pick up a mooring in the Pyefleet. Beware, though, the landing area in the Pyefleet is extremely East Coast muddy at low water. The landing from the Pyefleet pool is v ery much firmer. Both landings involve a mile or sco walk te the nearest pub, just ercugh to work up a thirst. As with all the East Coast voyages in our local area, the East Coast Rivers handbook is a strongly recommended, indeed irivaluable, guide to pilotage. It is alsa very interesting if you carry books about this area on board with you. "The Salty Share” and "Last Days of Sail" are twa examples which concentrate particularly om the Essex area, as also do several of Hervey Berham’s books about sailing barges. Dave Heane, Readnigen, April 1991
