STILL, THE MARK ROUNDING PRACTICE WAS GOOD, BUT THE WIND GOT UP WHEN THE SLEET FELL. DID WE ALL GET ASHORE FAIRLY RAPIDLY (MOST OF US VIA Osea TO DROP THE MAIN.) PARTICULARLY FRUSTRATING WAS THE VISION AFTER WE'D SHOWERED AND CHANGED OF A NICE GENTLE 3/4... CURSE OUR WEATHER! MONDAY DAWNED WITH A SINGULAR LACK OF ENTHUSIASM (DUE TO OVERINDULGENCE ON THE FRISBEE FIELD?) AND A GREAT DEAL OF RELIEF WAS FELT WHEN DEAR OLD MICK JONES POSTPONED FOR HALF AN HOUR. WE AGAIN HAD THE SHORT COURSE, AND THE BY NOW DE RIGEUR STAMPEDE AT THE FIRST MARK. IT WAS STILL 5/6 AND INTERESTING. I MUST ADMIT THAT CHRIS AND I FIND THOSE CONDITIONS WEIGHTED TOO MUCH TOWARDS SURVIVAL AS YET AND SO MY ENJOYMENT TENDED TO BE COLOURED BY THE NUMBER OF CHANGES OF UNDERWEAR REQUIRED DOWNWIND. (WHO TOLD THAT DIPSTICK TO MOOR THAT CRUISER 30 FEET FROM F?) THE ONE EXCITING MOMENT FOR ME WAS THE FEEL OF PAUL ELLIS’S LEEWARD BOW TRYING TO PENETRATE MY NETHER REGIONS IN A MOST UNSEEMLY MANNER! AND THAT GAVE ME THE OPPORTUNITY TO UNFURL THE PROTEST FLAG!!! (THANKS FOR DOING THE 720, PAUL.) THE PLAN FOR THE AFTERNOON WAS TO SAIL THE REMAINING @ RACES BACK-TO-BACK. THE WIND WAS BY NOW A MERE 4 - 5 ZEPHYR AND THERE AS TALK OF MORE POWER. 22 CATS QUEUED UP FOR....NO, A DIFFERENT COURSE. A1C X F THREE TIMES, MIND YOU, ‘A’ MARK THE FIRST TIME ROUND WAS SOMETHING ELSE. POOR OLD DAVE ONYONS & DEN TRIED TO TACK ONTO PORT STRAIGHT AROUND 'A’ TO BE CAUGHT IN A STREAM OF 21 STARBOARD BOATS'! AS WE MORTALS APFROACHED 'C’ - WHAT'S THIS? BIG JOHN & CAROLINE AHEAD OF ROBIN & LISA” THAT DIDN’T LAST FOR LONG THOUGH' BEFORE SETTING OFF WE'D BEEN TOLD THAT THE SECOND START WOULD BE 15 MINUTES AFTER THE LAST BOAT FINISHED, SO WE ALL WENT OVER TO OSEA AND BEACHED FOR A VERY PLEASANT FEW MINUTES’ CHAT. WHAT A NICE FLEET WE'RE IN AND WHAT AN AWE-INSPIRING SIGHT OF 20 PLUS CATS SIDE BY SIDE ON OSEA. THE FINAL RACE WAS TWO LAPS OF THE SAME COURSE AND IF (AGAIN) YOU DIDN’T GET AN INSIDE BERTH, IT MEANT ROUNDING ‘AY SOMEWHERE SOUTH OF THE CLUBHOUSE. DEFINITELY BACK TO MORE CIVILISED CONDITIONS AND BACK TO ’°JACK-THE-FOWER-ON-CHAPS’. DESPITE THE SHORT COURSE, I THINK YOU CAN SAFELY SAY THAT THE RACING WAS (AGAIN) MARVELOUS. I KNEW CHRIS AND I HAD A GREAT TUSSLE WITH TIM WALLACE DOWNWIND WHILST CLAWING QUR WAY BACK FROM A STUFFED (WHAT'S THAT? - ED) TACK. SORRY YOU WERE OVER AT THE START, ROBIN & LISA, BUT CONGRATS TO JOHN & CAROLINE (1ST) AND STEVE & TOM (2ND). MY ONE REGRET? ONLY TWO MONOHULLS OUT ALL WEEKEND, AND ONE OF THOSE SAILED BY A CAT MAN, WE'LL BE STAGING A TAKEOVER BID NEXT! THE FOLLOWING WEEKEND WAS A BIT MORE LIKE IT. AWAY WENT THE STEAMER, OUT CAME THE LONG JOHN - AND THAT WAS PROBABLY TOO HOT! THIS IS WHAT I REMEMBER ABOUT SAILING, BOILING HOT DAYS WITH THE SHADES AND HAT ON TO STOP SUNSTROKE. UNFORTUNATELY, SOMEQNE FORGOT TO TELL THE WIND TO GET OUT OF BED ON SUNDAY MORNING. BOB ANDERSON DREW THE SHORT STRAW AS RACE OFFICER, WITH THE UNENVIABLE JOB OF DECIDING WHEN AND IF TO START US. WHAT WAS THAT? A PUFF OF WIND, AND OFF WE WENT HARING ALONG WITH THE TIDE TOWARDS 'A’. THEM WOT CHOSE TO STAY OUT IN THE RIVER (I.E. CHRIS CARUTH & I, PAUL METCALFE & CREW) FOUND OURSELVES PROGRESSIVELY BEARING AWAY TO LAY THE MARK UNTIL... DAMMIT, MISSED! THE NEXT THREE QUARTERS OF AN HOUR WAS SPENT POINTING AT °A® AND WATCHING IT RECEDE INTO THE DISTANCE UNTIL THE TIDE CHANGED. LOADS OF PEOPLE APPEARED TO BE RETIRING (UNUSUAL, CAT SAILORS ARE NOT WHAT YOU WOULD REALLY CALL RETIRING PEOPLE...) AND THEN - A GUST! WE ROCKETED ROUND A’ AND NO. 1 AND BREEZY, PAUSED FOR A LULL AND THEN TWIN-WIRED TOWARDS THE FINISH,...ONLY TO DISCOVER THAT BOB HAD, WISELY, ABANDONED. UNFORTUNATELY MY PEN HAD OBVIOUSLY CAUGHT ME OUT BECAUSE THE TWO MICKS WERE ON RESCUE DUTY AND WE WERE THE ONLY CAT NOT TOLD OF THE ABANDONMENT.... THANKS, GUYS, JUST YOU WAIT! BOB WAS VERY KEEN, WE GOT ASHORE AT 1 O'CLOCK, POURED DOWN A PINT AND STUFFED DOWN A HOT DOG, TO BE TOLD THE AFTERNOON START WOULD BE 1.30. | THE FAITHFUL CHRIS NEARLY WENT ON STRIKE AT THAT POINT. WE LINED UP FOR THE START AND WERE POWERING UP BEHIND ALL THE PEOPLE WHO'D DECIDED TO STOP CLOSE TO THE LINE TO CRIES OF "UP, UP" AND "YOU CAN’T BARGE IN”. UNFORTUNATELY THERE WASN'T AN 86" PRINDLE 19 SIZED GAP FOR US SO CHRIS AND I HAD NO CHOICE BUT TO EXECUTE A 360. FOR SOME REASON ON COMPLETION THIS GLUT OF SLOW MOVING BOATS WERE STILL MOVING VERY SLOWLY TOWARDS 'A’. WE, FORTUNATELY, WERE ABLE 10 GENERATE SOME SPEED AND BREAK THROUGH. JUST GOES TO SHOW HE WHO LAUGHS LAST, ETC. WE MANAGED TO GET THREE LAPS IN WITH THAT MAN DAVE ALLEN & THE LOVELY ANNA SHOWING US ALL A CLEAN PAIR OF HEELS, MIND YOU, DAVE & ANNE, STEVE & TOM AND CHRIS & I WERE ALL VERY SURPRISED TO NEARLY LAP A FEW BOATS. AS PEOPLE FINISHED, IT BECAME OBVIOUS THAT THE SAILING SUB’S EFFORTS AND PUBLICATION IN NAVIGANS WAS WASTED SINCE HALF THE FLEET AND ALL THE SLOW CATS NEGLECTED TO USE THE CORRECT FINISH LINE. READ YOUR SAILING INSTRUCTIONS CHAPS. STILL, WHAT A CHANGE FROM SLEET, SNOW AND GALES,

6. AND SO TO THE FINAL BRACE OF THE SPRING SERIES RACES. IT BEING THE LAST WEEKEND BEFORE REGATTA, THERE WERE ALL SORTS OF SLJs (SILLY LITTLE JOBS) TO DO AND WITH RESET TO NO WIND, OUR REVERED COMMODORE OF THE REAR SUGGESTED A POSTPONEMENT 10 CARRY QUT THE WORK PARTY BEFORE RACING. I CAN TELL YOU THAT THOSE OF US ALREADY CHANGED DID CALL HIS PARENTAGE INTO QUESTION! SQ THE CAT FLEET DISAPPEARED ONTO THE ROOF TO GET THE AWNING BITS DOWN AND ERECT SAME. AS WE SUSPECTED THOUGH, WITHIN MINUTES, THE WIND PICKED UP AND SO WE DASHED OFF FOR AN 11.30 START. UNFORTUNATELY THAT WAS PROBABLY A BIT OPTIMISTIC AS A NUMBER OF US ONLY JUST MANAGED TO GET TO THE LINE IN TIME FOR THE GUN. THERE WAS AN ' INTERESTING’ FIRST BEAT TO 'A’ WITH SEVERAL SHALLOWS-HOPPERS TESTING THE DEPTH OF THE HARD AND THEN GETTING TANGLED WITH THE STARBOARD TACKERS WHO'D GONE OUT FIRST. THE USUAL TRIUMVIRATE HAD GOT AWAY SMARTLY (NOTE: I MUST GET ON THE LINE AT THE START SOMETIME) WITH, INITIALLY, BIG JOHN AND CAROLINE LEADING, STEVE & TOM AND DAVE & ANNA. WE MORTALS WATCHED THEM SHOOT OFF INTO THE DISTANCE, AND I (CREWED FOR VARIOUS LONG-WINDED REASONS BY JOE Adam, A NEW DART 15 SAILOR) SPENT THE REST OF MY TIME TRYING TO CLAW MY WAY PAST DART 18s. SECOND TIME AROUND WE GOT TANGLED UP WITH THE SOLO FLEET TOWARDS YE MARK AND UNFORTUNATELY COLLIDED WITH DAVE ONYONS & BEN. OUT CAME THE PROTEST FLAG, PLUS MUCH SWEARING AND GNASHING OF TEETH - AIMED MAINLY AT MALCOLM STUART (BUT HE'S USED TO IT). LET US THEN DRAW A VEIL RAPIDLY OVER THE INCIDENT. THE RECORD WILL SHOW NO CONCLUSION REACHED BY THE PROTEST COMMITTEE FOR VERY GOOD REASONS, AS 1’VE SAID BEFORE, PROTESTING IS NOT 'UNSPORTSMANLIKE’, IT IS THE ONLY WAY TO GET A JUDGEMENT(!) IN A SPORT WHERE THERE IS NO REFEREE AND IT HELPS ALL OF US LEARN MORE ABOUT THE RULES. BELIEVE ME, THAT IS NOW AN ESSENTIAL IN THE CAT FLEET, WITH THE LEVEL OF COMPETITION WERE EXPERIENCING THIS YEAR. AT THE FRONT OF THE FLEET STEVE & TOM EVENTUALLY TOOK LINE HONOURS FROM BIG JOHN & CAROLINE, AND THAT MAN DAVE ALLEN & ANNA. THE WIND GOT UP A LITTLE FOR THE AFTERNOON EXCEPT FOR THE FEW MOMENTS AROUND THE GUN, AND SO SEVERAL PEOPLE WERE VERY SHY OF THE LINE. 1 MADE MY USUAL ABYSMAL START, BUT DID ACTUALLY MANAGE TO POWER THROUGH A BIT. THE FRONT OF THE DART FLEET SEEMED TO BE HIGHLY COMPETITIVE WITH JOHN TUCKWELL & CREW, TIM DE B & CREW, LUCY BOREHAM & TOM ASHLEY, DAVE ONYONS & BEN , PAUL ELLIS (SINGLE OR DOUBLE HANDED), CHRIS PATMORE & JULIE MILLS, AND EVEN OUR VENERABLE COMMODORE OF THE REAR BASHING IT OUT TOE-TO-TOE AT THE FRONT. WATCH IT THOUGH, GUYS (& GAL), BECAUSE THOSE CHAPS BEHIND YOU ARE CLOSING FAST... IT ALSO MAKES, CONTRARY TO MALCOLM’S THOUGHTS, THE DART 18 THE BIGGEST RACING FLEET IN THE CLUB. STEVE GLYNN & TOM CLINCHED THE SERIES FROM BIG JOHN & CAROLINE AND THAT MAN DAVE & ANNA, DESPITE THE LATTER'S WIN IN THE PM, $0 THAT'S 17. ONE THIRD OF THE RACING SEASON OVER. AN OVERALL ENTRY OF 21 AND AN AVERAGE TURNOUT OF, IF MEMORY SERVES, 14+ BOATS (AND THAT INCLUDES THE RACES WHEN ONLY 2 OR 3 NUTTERS WENT OUT') LET'S LOOK FORWARD TO EVEN MORE CROWDED START LINES FOR THE SUMMER SERIES, THAT LEADS US NEATLY ON TO REGATTA. MANY TRUSTY CAT FLEET MEMBERS TURNED UP FOR THE FRIDAY WORK PARTY IN DRIZZLE AND COLD, BUT FORTUNATELY THE WEATHER (NOT THE WIND) IMPROVED OVER THE WEEKEND. MARKS WERE CHANGED, WHITE LINES PAINTED AND WE WAITED FOR THE ARRIVALS, SATURDAY DAWNED BREATHLESSLY, AND WE HAD THE THE COMPANY OF A VISIT OF A HNURRICANE 5,3 FROM THE ARMY AND A CONDOR (WELCOME TO THE CLUB, MATTHEW HERBERT). MANY OF OUR REGULARS WERE CONSPICUOUS BY THEIR ABSENCE, WITH STEVE GLYNN CAVORTING ON A KEELBOAT IN SCOTLAND AND THE TWO MICKS LEARNING TO SAIL (SOME WOULD SAY NOT BEFORE TIME!) WITH DON FINDLAY AT ABERSOCH. THE MARCONI DINGHY CHALLENGE ON SATURDAY AFTERNOON 1S BEST FORGOTTEN BY THE CAT FLEET, MOST OF WHOM, EXCEPT LEE HARRISON & TOM ASHLEY WHO WERE FLYING THEIR KITE, WERE ACTUALLY LED AROUND THE COURSE BY A SELECTION OF MONOHULLS. WE SHALL GLOSS OVER QUICKLY, BUT SAVE FOR LEE, THE LAST PLACES WERE FILLED BY... THE 6 CATS RACING. (SOLIDARITY, 1 CALL THAT.) SUNDAY DAWNED WITH A ROBBIE SIMS SPECIAL COURSE - THIRSLET, GOLDHANGER, DOCTOR AND BACK. WE ALL DUCKED THE TIDE ONCE WE'D MANAGED, FINALLY, TO CROSS THE START LINE AND SPLIT INTO TWO FACTIONS; THOSE THAT STUCK TO THE SOUTH SHORE AND THOSE WHO WENT NORTH, I.E. ME' I SOON DISCOVERED AT THIRSLET (REACHED IN AN HOUR) THAT NORTH WAS WRONG - ESPECIALLY AS I WAS EMBARASSED TO SEE PETER FLOOK & MIKE STEELE ON THE 18-2 BREATHING DOWN MY TRANSOMS! WE THEN HAD A VERY INTERESTING TACK DOWNWIND TO °C’ AND ALL ENDED UP FINALLY IN A HEAP AT 'S', THE REPLACEMENT FOR NO.1, STILL GYEING MERRILY UP-RIVER IN A GAGGLE OF MONOHULLS. FORTUNATELY, I'D PAID MY DEBTS (OR SOMETHING) AND GOT MY OWN PRIVATE BREEZE ALL THE WAY TO THE FINISH AND MANAGED TO MAKE MY HANDICAP ON ALL THE BOATS WE'D BEEN AMONGST TO GET 4TH BEHIND. DUCKMANTON, NICKALLS, AND DAVE & ANNA - NOT NECESSARILY IN THAT ORDER, WE PROVED HOW KEEN WE WERE IN THE AFTERNOON BY HAVING A GENERAL RECALL WHICH PUT OUR START BACK TO 3,50 ALBEIT ON A MUCH SHORTENED COURSE (B, C, E, A, HOME) AND ALL TOOK OFF FOR BREEZY ON THE FALLING TIDE. HAVING HAD OUR OBLIGATORY RUBBISH START, CHRIS & I ROUNDED 'B’ ABOUT 9TH AND SAW A GAGGLE OF BOATS MID RIVER STOPPED, AND DRIFTING OUT, WE POINTED TO MY FAVOURITE NORTH SHORE AND SPED OFF AT HALF A KNOT. WAS IT THE BEER? WAS IT SUNSTROKE? WAS IT THE PROSPECT OF LISTENING TO THE CRICKET? FOR SOME REASON PEOPLE STARTED TO RETIRE. (MAYBE IT WAS THE NUMB BUM SYNDROME INDUCED BY SITTING THERE FOR AN HOUR AND GETTING NOWHERE.) WE EVENTUALLY TRICKLED UP THE NORTH SHORE DODGING MUD AND GRAVEL BANKS (UNLIKE SEVERAL MONOHULLS WHO GOT THEMSELVES LANDLOCKED) AND GOT ROUND ‘A’ AT ABOUT 6.15 IN A SMALL PUFF - WILL WE MAKE THE TIME LIMIT? AROUND ‘A’ TO THE DULCET TONES OF DUCKMANTON ON THE PA COMMENTATING ON OUR PROGRESS. REMINDED ME OF MY ROWING DAYS WITH THE "CHEERS" FROM THE BANK. THE WIND DROPPED, WE DRIFTED BACK, COMING TETE A TETE WITH ‘RASPUTIN’ - HOW EMBARASSING IN THE SIGHT OF THE COMMODORE - WE TACKED TO MISS IT, AND THE WIND CAME! NICKALLS TRIED TO PUT US OFF BY COUNTING DOWN 1 MINUTE EARLY, BUT I SHOULD THINK WE MADE IT BY 50 SECONDS. THAT SET THE CLOCK TICKING ON THE ONLY TWO REMAINING IDIOTS, MIKE STYLES AND OUR ARMY VISITORS, AND THEY ALSO MADE 17. WITH THE PROBLEMS OF SUNDAY'S RECALL, AND AGAIN NO WIND, THE DECISIONM CAME TO PUT THE CAT START LAST SO THAT THE MONOS WOULD BE CLEAR. THE IDEA WAS A SMALL COURSE WITH SEVERAL ROUNDS, SO WE WERE OFF TO BREEZY, S, A, E, A AND HOME ON A RIPPING INCOMING TIDE, STARTING INSIDE ‘D’, MOST OF US WALKED UP THE SHORE AND HELD THE BOATS WRITING FOR THE START. EVERYBODY 1S WATCHING LIKE HAWKS INSIDE THE S-MINUTE FOR THE FERSON WHO PUSHES FORWARD RATHER THAN GETTING ON.... AND WE'RE OFF!

Ve DECISION TIME AGAIN, LOADS OF MONOS AND DISTURBED AIR FROM ALL THOSE ROLL TACKS INSHORE, SO WE SET OFF ON OUR NOW OBLIGATORY NORTH SIDE FLYER, FOLLOWED BY TIM WALLACE WITH THE REST OF THE PACK INSHORE. WE GOT SOME SUPERE BREEZE AND OVERSTOOD THE MARK TO ALLOW FOR THE TIDE, BUT THE WIND DROPPED AND WE WHISTLED BACK UPRIVER JUST IN TIME TO SEE BIG JOHN & CAROLINE JUST NICK ROUND THE MARK. CHRIS & I EVENTUALLY ROUNDED BY WHICH TIME BIG JOHN & CAROLINE WERE OFF OSEA, SO WE RESIGNED OURSELVES TO A POOR SECOND. BUT AT 'A’ WE WERE AMAZED TO SEE BIG JOHN TRYING TO CLAW HIS WAY AROUND THE SPIT OFF ALONG WITH SEVERAL MONOS. WE HAD CARRIED OUR OWN PRIVATE BREEZE AND SNUCK AROUND IN FRONT! OK, I ADMIT IT WAS ALL LUCK,THE FUNNIEST BIT WAS CATCHING AN OSPREY ON PORT, AND SEEING HIS FACE AS HE REALISED HOW LONG WE WERE. THE AFTERNOON RACE WAS THE DECIDER, BIG JOHN & CAROLINE NEEDED TO BEAT US TO WIN THE EVENT. UNFORTUNATELY IN THE MASSIVE TIDE AND INCREASED WIND OUR CHALLENGE BECAME SOMETHING OF A BUSTED FLUSH WHEN WE CLOBBERED °E’ MARK AND HAD TO DO A 720, STILL, A GOOD WEEKEND DESPITE THE COMPUTER HITCHES WITH THE RESULTS; CONGRATS TO EQUIPE NICKALLS, WELL, FOLKS, THAT’S ENOUGH FROM NR FOR MAUREEN TO TYPE, SEE YOU NEXT MONTH.... ll. NAVIGANS PAST 1962 (January - June) - with official clots up-river and sinister plots down-river. KKK KKK January - a note about the club's President, Mr.£.Eastwood, receiving the CBE in the New Year's Honours list. Also, a note drawing attention to Barnacle's article about mooring; apparently several boats went ‘drift about' during the 1961 season. Then, of course, the inevitable note about the need to pay the annual subscriptions on time - some hopes ! A number of ‘temporary’ sub-committees have been formed to help the (main) committee to run the club. These sub-committees are (a) the Sailing Sub-Committee (b) the Social Sub-Committee and (c) the Clubhouse Sub- Committee. I don't know about you, but I don't think they'll last very long, do you ? The Commodore is A.M.Adams, the Vice Commodore is R.F.Sims, the Rear Commodore is 8.W.Partridge and the Sailing Secretary is A.Pratt. The Sailing Sub-Committee plan to offer sailing instruction to novice members, the training to be organised via the official club C.L.0.T. (Central Liaison Officer of Training). By popular request, the former Menageries Fleet is, henceforth, to be known as the Handicap Class. Information has been received about plans for a holiday camp downriver. Guess where ? Yes, you've guessed it - on land adjoining the river near Stansgate Abbey. Also plans for an oi] refinery or store at Tollesbury. Both this and 'the holiday camp' are to be kept under scrutiny through the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee. Finally, the results of the 'Club Activities’ questionaire are published and, as far as the ‘Sailing Activities' part is concerned, the results were:- Day Picnics 50 Longer Cruises 27 Cruiser Racing 12 Weekend Cruises 30 Learning to Sail 24 and the least favourite sailing activity ? I hardly dare reveal it:- Dinghy Racing 3 votes (Oh! dear. Oh! dear. Oh! dear) It looks more like the results of the European Song Contest. February - the name of the Editor is missing from the title page of Navigans ! Is this merely a typing error or has the club enforced a state of purdah on poor Daphne ? The new Hon.Sec. (G.Edwards) shows he means business by issuing an ultimatum, effectingly saying 'pay your subs,...this is the final public warning !' What, I ask myself, are the private warnings - and will retribution meted out to the transgressers be public or private ? Mind you, I've no sympathy; they really ought to have paid up by now. The dinghy parking fee is still 10/- per year; park ona first come, first served basis. A letter from Ken Beavins asking members to object to the proposed Tollesbury oi] refinery project by writing to various authorities and to the M.P. for Maldon. A note from the Hon.Treasurer (J.H.Hind) noting, amongst other things, that the MASC own the capital assets (eg. Mamgu, Avril, ramp, etc) and that the sailing club owes the MASC £75 for the purchase of the rescue launch, and which will be repaid at £25 per year commencing 31 December, 1962. After that, the rescue launch will presumably belong to the MSC but, since the MASC owns the capital assets of the club, the launch will presumably belong to the MASC - once we've paid for it. In the mean-time, whilst we pay our installments, the launch belongs to the MASC. Are you confused ? So am I but I get the feeling I'm in a ‘heads you win, tails I lose! situation, but I'm sure it's all very logical to the accountants. March - the Editor's name is restored to its rightful place - at the top of the lst page of Navigans. A call to attend the MASC AGM in April "...to back, or oppose, as the case may be, motions tabled that may affect the organisation of the sailing section." Now, I wonder what was going on ? The dinghy park layout is published ( 4 rows of dinghies) with spaces allocated to the 32 members who have paid their fees to date. Those who haven't paid are out of luck - the dinghy park is full ! However, it is hoped to negotiate an extension of the dinghy park with the owner of adjoining land. Cars are banned from the dinghy park and cannot be taken in even to deliver (or remove) dinghies. THAT rule applies today. A list of BURC handicaps shows the Solo as 102 (Terelyne sails) and 103 (cotton sails); now that's what I'd call a sensible handicap for the Solo. The sailing programme starts on 7 April with Novice Instruction (sounds like a convent), followed by the Fitting Out Supper on board Mamgu. Sailing proper starts on 8th April with a Tune-Up race (start 15.30) and lst Points races on 15 April (start at 11.30) - don't forget, they're tide-bound at Heybridge. The Enterprise have an Open Series (all Blackwater club boats) of 6 (4 to count) and a club Closed Series for the Knight Cup (4 out of 6). The Fleetwind fight for the President's Cup with a series of 12 races (8 to count), whilst the Handicap Fleet sail individual races ( a small prize for each winner).

Foo Re The correct title is probably spelt 'Mugg's', but our 'modern-day' spelling is probably more apt; after all, how else can you describe anyone who (voluntarily ?) sits at the wet end of a boat, takes al] the spray full in the face, gets shouted at, blamed for all that goes wrong - and then has to stand second-in-line as "the hero' receives the prize (assuming there is one). A VERY LATE ENTRY FOR NAVIGANS - Typed by yours truely (so do not blame the Editor) Saturday, June 8th 1991 At dawn there was no wind and rumour had it that an event "Try Sailing" would take place at the Club. Foolishly I decided that I would attend and explain that I had come to try these 'Two Hulled Things', that was safe enough as no one would want to go out with no wind. Shortly after arriving I was standing around in an old wetsuit looking the part and very keen, when the Rear Commodore descended on me and, passing me a life jacket and harness, informed me that Lee was going to take me out. After realising that my plans as usual were going drastically wrong, I climbed on board with Lee and we set off. Lee obviously realised that Coomodores need treating with respect and took me for a gentle tour of the river, No - He didn't put up the Reacher, No - He didn't force me onto the trapeze. However we still seemed to cover an immense distance in no time at all. On being safely returned to the Hard, I discovered that Pete Bloomfield was also acting the school boy and pretending to enjoy all this crazy activity - I was thankful for the support on at least one other person from the cruising fraternity. At this point I was accosted by a glamorous blonde and asked if I wanted to try a Laser. I thought that I struck quite a good bargain; I would try the Laser if she would try a Sailboard. So off I went in the Laser and much to my surprise failed to tip it over but this business of hanging over the side to keep it upright is not so good for the old stomach muscles. By the time that I returned Julie had also joined in the fun and been for a ride on a Cat. She and Pete decided to to try the Laser as a two person boat and I believe gave an excellent demonstration of the technique for righting such a boat. I was now collared by John to try his Hurricane and who was I to argue with him. After looking at the river he decided that we should go towards Bradwell to find enough wind so that I could try the trapeze. All went well until we tacked to come back up river and mixing my legs, arms, and various bits of rope, found myself ‘skiing' beside the boat at the end of the trapeze wire. Once John had hauled me aboard and considerably shortened the trapeze wire (by golly his crew must be tall) we came up the river with both of us on the wire. I thought about suggesting that we return to the Hard but was too late, we had already passed the Club and were up beyond Osea Pier. I was able to have a breather while John 'Hove To' after Lee had the misfortune to capise, before we returned to the Hard. At this point Pete now went for another ride. On behalf of all the others, Pete and Julie, and myself, who had a go on the boats available, may I thank all those who took the time to produce such an enjoyable day, and if you ever repeat it, I for one will definitely be there. (If I can do it, how about the rest of the cruising fraternity). Finally I am looking forward to seeing the blonde on the sailboard sometime during the rest of the season when I am there, how about a special demonstration event by her at the Fun Day. (Mr Rear Commodore can arrange that I am sure). Very many thaks to you all for a throughly enjoyable day.

EAST COAST PIERS RACE - THANK YOU ALL Quite often after a major event at the Club, my thoughts as I drive heme run along the lines of "Was it worth it? Never again," and it takes a week or sa ta decide that it was worth it. However as I drove home on Sunday night after the East Coast Piers Race, I felt elated and had no hesitation in deciding that it was worth it and that I believe we should continue with the race. My reasons for the feeling of elation started on Friday evening wher John and Sheila King with their children and Marconi Challenger arrived. It was so obvious talking to them and other Challenger sailors the gratitude that they felt for our efforts ta help them to enjoy the sport that we love. COVE ES: s.6 tasers.

Or, the Saturday, apart from the successful Challenger racing ard the two catamaran races, a mnumber af visitors came looking for me to express their thanks for being invited to the Club. They all told me that we have a super site, and a_ very welcoming, helpful and relaxed atmosphere provided by everyone present. Sunday made me realise how lucky I have been to be Commodore of the Club. Throughout the day wherever I looked there were pecple giving their time and effort to help with the event. In some cases the members had asked friends to come and help as well. During the weekend there was support on the water provided by many types of boats ard people, there was help with the site organisation, with providing B.B.Q.s and other food, with marming the bar and numerous other activities. There were willing offers of assistance ard numerous people, when asked, leapt to help. Additionally, there had been a fantastic amount of effort beforehand, much of it behind the scenes carried out quietly and efficiently. This included many cases where members had seught the help of friends, and other organisations to support the event at no or minimal cast. The Fiers Race has always posed a major worry to me as it is an immerse event toa organise, which could peterntially give very great problems. I thank all of you very much fer the help and support that you gave. The expression of thanks from the Challenger sailors, the visitors the support of visiting organisations, ard, mast of all, your help and support, make me feel very honoured ta be Commodore of such a friendly, willing and supportive Club. I hope that we will have been able ta sail the full course and would like tao thank all these who helped, beth on the water and at the Club. 3. A continuation of the reports to "The Marcon Guessitte" (also submitted to the Essex Chronicle reporter who sounded enthusiastic - but will his Editor) give us pride of place over Goochie ? Unlikely folks! Fun Day, Sunday, 23rd June - The rain did not dampen MarconI's enthusiasm for its Fun day entertainments for its members. Having recently held a very successful ‘try sailing’ Open Day, it was a the turn of the members to enjoy the amenities of the large club site and some fun and games on both water and land. The highlight was the catamaran 'fly a hull' competition which provided keen rivalry on the water and considerable mirth and admiration off the water. The practice sessions provided many capsizes, but gradually the competitors got the hang of it, the best technique seeming to be to place the the crew on the leeward side (also the wettest side!), haul in the.sails to lift the windward hull and to sail as slowly as possible, the helm keeping the boat balanced as best he/she could. The first competition was sailed in westerly F4 wind and was for who could 'fly a hull' for the longest time. Steve Glynn (Prindle 19) won with a time of 3 mins. 23 secs, with David Allan (Hurricane 5.9) 2nd with 2 mins. 55 secs. So much fun was had by all that they demanded a second competition, this time who could ‘fly a hull' for the longest distance. Once again Steve Glynn was the winner with just over 1 mile at his first attempt, and again David Allan was 2nd with a similar distance - but at his second attempt. However, of more significance was the time they took; each sailed on the single hull for well over 10 minutes and one unofficial time-keeper believed it was nearer 15 minutes of slow motion, slow progress sailing. Whilst team of Steve Glynn/Tom Duckmanton undoubtedly won both events on Technical Merit, by popular acclaim the team of David Allan/Anna Spittle won the award for Artistic Interpretation. And don't forget all the others; by the end of the day, many were ‘flying a hull' well over 3 minutes at some time or other, and David Ball in his single-handed Unicorn was not far off rivalling David and Steve for longevity in both time and distance. 7. " THE MARCONI GUESSITTE" A genuine imitation news-sheet to record the sailing reports submitted to the Essex Chronicle. Sunday, 9th June - Marconi's Cadet Members are those who are 18 years and under on lst January. Apart from organising Cadet winter lectures and a very enjoyable and comprehensiv e sailing instruction during the club's camping fortnight each year, a Cadet Members Handicap Series is also held, consisting of 6 races held at various dates during the summer months. Cadets Race 1 was held in westerly winds force 4/5 plus and an ebbing tide. Three laps of the relatively short triangular course of Al F D_ provided the opportunity for an equitable race for all entries ranging from the Mirror dinghy to the AuFricane 5.9 catamaran. However, the more experienced helms were sailing the catamarans and dominated the top places The winner was Lucy Boreham (Dart 18) followed by Lee Harrison (Hurricane 5.9), Ben Holroyd (Dart 18) and David Ball (Topper). The less experienced helms found the wind and tide difficult to cope with but Alison Battle (Mirror) sailed particularly well to finish in 5th place. Both Rebecca Fowler (Mirror) and Clare Davies (Mirror) found the tide too much of a problem and retired, as did Stephen Caruth (Gull). Paul Harrison (Dart 15) retired after hitting a mark and three other entries decided not to start in the rising wind conditions. For the main Marconi Summer Points Series, Race 3 started in westerly winds force 4/5.. later rising 6/7,the Fast Catamaran Fleet found the going particularly difficult on their long course. With a number of capsized craft on the river, the Race Officer decided to abandon all races. Although this was unfortunate for the Monohull Handicap and Solo Fleets who appeared to be coping with the conditions without problems at the time, the wind continued to increase in intensity as the afternoon wore on and gusts of force 7/8 were observed on the windspeed indicator. Marconi's race support vessels performed very well and were pleased to be able to offer assistance to a‘ neighbouring club. Sunday, 16th June - Marconi's 5th Summer Points race was sailed in very light winds. The Fast Catamaran Handicap was won by Steve Glynn/Tom Duckmanton (prindle 19), Larry Botheras/Chris Caruth (Prindle 19) 2nd and Tim Wallace/ (hurricane 5.9) 3rd. First Dart 18 home in 4th place was the team of John Tuckwell and Lynda Chilton. In the Slow Catamaran Handicap, Willie Pitcairn/Joyce Allen (Dart 15) were lst, Colin Kidner (Dart 15) 2nd and Paul harrison/Stuart Golding (Dart 15) 3rd. John Salmon continued his run of successes by winning the Solo race, followed by Simon Liddington and John Rutherford. The Monohull Handicap saw a good win by Evan and Luke Davies (Mirror) with Mike and Maggie Boreham (420) 2nd. When the time came for the 6th race of the series, the wind had virtually failed completely. As competitors walked their boats to the start-line, several continued to walk after the 5-minute gun and brought forth a bevy of protest flags. Having started the fast and Slow catamaran Handicap and the Monohull Handicap fleets, the Race Officer found himself with fleets spread out on the water with no wind to drive them. As thunder roared and lightening flashed over Maldon and threatened to make its way to Stansgate, the Race Officer decided to abandon all races, not having started the Solo fleet at all. Some disappointed competitors decided to go for a pleasure sail, but most had to be towed back eventually. Sunday, 23rd June - the 2nd Cadet Members handicap race was held in winds SW F 4-5 over a course consisting of A(F1AD x 6), the small triangle giving the Race Officer the option of shortening the course, which he did after two laps. Lucy Boreham (Dart 18) scored a 2nd win in the series, followed by Lee Harrison (Hurricane 5.9) 2nd and Chris Caruth (Prindle 19) 3rd. Paul harrison (Dart 15) took 4th place whilst David Ball, having secured 4th place in race 1 in a Topper, took 5th place in his Unicorn cat. The monohulls again showed their inexperience in handling the tide, the temptation to ‘strike out' for A-mark in an adverse tide immediately after rounding No.1 caused them to be swept down stream and left struggling to make their way upstream against the strongest tide stream just outside the cruiser lines. Mike Fletcher (420) took 6th place and Richard Battle (Mirror) finished in 7th place. Kerry Styles (Dart 18) unfortunately went the wrong side of D-mark and was disqualified and the remaining entrants retired. Saturday, 22nd June - the Mud race over a ‘shallow water’ course, took place in very windy conditions WSW F5-6. and was run as a pursuit race. The event attracted only 4 entries, possibly because it was run on a rather dull and dismal Saturday - despite it being designated a 'Fun event and Midsummer Night Revels'. Only Malcolm Stuart (Solo) survived the course. Steve Glynn (Prindle 19) and Tom Ashley (Mirror) capsized and retired, whilst Lucy Boreham (420) attacked the boom of her boat =- and lost the contest on a ‘retired hurt’ decision. Malcolm, having survived 4 laps and seeing no one else in sight, beached himself on Osea Island to ‘wait out the time limit', launching himself in time to take the winning 'hoot' from the support boat. Malcolm's Solo victory could well have been a devine sign and could possibly be interpreted as justifying the ancient saying which goes as follows:- "You might well call a Solo for ‘water’, but you can't always make it stick" NB. only selected parts of the above reports were actually submitted over the telephone to the Chronicle

NAVIGANS ‘PAST 1962 (July - December) - kitchen sink drama, and "was there a link with the right man"? eee eee wee eee e ee July/August - this issue of Navigans has 15 pages, but it does cover two months news. Mr.'Darby' Stebbens has been appointed the part-time club steward, presumably a paid post. Was he the first paid employee of the MSC ? John Tillotson won the 2nd Cadet race with Julian Bigden 2nd; there were four entries. A report by Miss S.P.Maxwell and Mr C.B.Hansford (both cadets ?) on the very successful camping weekend at Mersea Stone, whilst the MASC organised a Gala Day and Robbie Sims organised the impressive display of boats as the MSC contribution. In addition, an MSC Open Day attracted about 200 guests. A letter from Peter Darney questions the amount being spent ‘on the few' at the expense of ‘the many’. He points out that only about 8 or 9 members take part in racing out of a membership of 200. That shows an interesting shift in the activities of the club; after almost 30 years, by 1991 the club membership has increased by about 250% but those taking part in racing has (probably) increased by about 1900%. Peter questions the need to spend more money on improving the facilities on board Mamgu, etc., in view of the possibility of moving the club to a new location. He suggests improving the facilities forordinary (presumably non-racing) members, particularly the appointment of an 00D during the ‘non-racing/non-programmed' days. He also wants such activities as picnics, cruises and camping weekends actually recognised as part of the ‘sailing programme'. Finally, he suggests that if it is felt that financial stringency does not allow extension of facilities, an increase of subscriptions would not be amiss (since) "...ten shillings a year is such a small sum..... - little more than two packets of cigarettes..... Ne Readers are invited to respond to his ‘controversial letter’. September - Daphne Tovey has had to give up the post of Editor and Phil Luke is the new Editor with his name at the top of this issue of Navigans. A ‘set of rules' is published covering the use of the rescue launch. Amongst other things, on race days it is to be ready and tested 30 minutes before the race, but is to remain on its mooring until required by the 00D. Also, it is not to be used as a fishing boat, or for joy rides and “,..is out of bounds to members not on rescue duty." Following Peter Darney's letter, the Committee have decided to appoint OODs for all Saturdays and Sundays (during the season) - not just on ‘programme' days. Some of the ‘jobs needing doing', as highlighted in the unquoted part of Peter's letter, have been taken up by ‘volunteers’ - and Peter has taken on some of the jobs himself. Great news - MSC have at last beaten the Ariel S.C. (BBC) in a team race event. The Mona's cup attracted 9 entries, of which 7 capsized - and Peter Darney, no doubt weighed down by all the jobs he's talked himself into, managed to miss out a mark. Pity the poor old Race Officer; he intended to shorten course, but got it wrong and, as a consequence, there was a ‘protest against the race committee’ which was upheld. By golly, I bet they didn't 'alf moan; with a little bit of imagination, you could almost hear their outraged voices floating down the river on the wind - the ghosts of yesteryear come to haunt us. That's one area of the club activities that certainly hasn't diminished ! The points races attracted 3 - 5 entries whilst the Ladies Cup attracted 4 entries and was won by Sarah Darney with .sister/mother/daughter(?) Rosine 2nd and a certain Eleanor Eldridge 3rd. Now I'm sure I should know who Eleanor Eldridge was, but I can't quite place her - or can I ? An article by 'The Commodore's lady' about the delights of helping in the galley; I quote "It is a well-known principle that any sink is preferred, by wives of otherwise impeccable devotion, to that provided by her indulgent spouse, especially if a bit of gossip about the ways of said spouses be thrown in". Oh! Lord ! I hope Maggie doesn't ‘tell all' about me (signed ‘Worried, Billericay'). Finally, a ‘thank you' to the Cadets, especially the girls for helping in the galley (the boys, I suppose, had all the fun of splashing paint over themselves and each other, as well as over the club boats they were supposed to be painting). October - Philip Luke re-introduces the ‘Editor's Comments'. Although recognising that the Main Committee must expect to be on the receiving end of complaints, nevertheless he does wonder if some (members) regard the committee members as nurse-maids ? MSC apparently beat the Osea S.C. in a team race event for the Beatty Challenge Trophy, but lost to Maldon Little Ship Club in another team race event. No matter, MSC helmsmen (yes, helmsmen, things were quite well ordered inthose days) took the first 5 places in a Blackwater (Sailing Club) event. Alas, it appears that Darby Stebbens is no longer club steward - members will have to clear up after themselves from now on.

10. November - 200 people attended the Laying-Up Supper. Guests included the Mayor and Mayoress of Maldon (after all, the Maldon sailors do seem to be winning everything), all the Commodores and their ladies from other Blackwater sailing clubs, plus those of the Ariel S.C. (BBC). Arthur Adam announces he will not be standing as Commodore for the coming year - principally because he wants to start sailing again ! A certain Peter Wright, replying on behalf of the guests to Arthur's toast, reminded the assembly that his Father, G.M.Wright, (late Engineer-in-Chief, Marconi) had tried to buy Osea Island for the Marconi Company for £4,000. I've heard of that before and believe it might have been in the 1920's or 30's. Finally, Mrs. Lancaster (wife of the Commodore of the Maldon Y.C.),replying to the MSC President's toast to the ladies, said " Man was God's first thought; Woman was only his second - but second thoughts are always best". December - at the AGM, Mr. T.W.(Terry) Hallam is elected Commodore, A.S.Bigden Vice Commodore, Peter Darney as Rear Commodore (he must have done his particular jobs very well) and Nick Tovey is the new Sailing Secretary. Clearly there has been some considerable ‘action’ regarding the possibility of moving to another site. Detailed reports ("based upon the report circulated to members") were given on the rival Stansgate and Maldon sites. A vote was taken to give guidance of the feeling of the membership (but will not commit the club to any particular action) as follows:- "In the event of the club having to vacate the present site and position on the river, which of the two sites mentioned beforehand do the members consider best to move to ?" Voting was : for Stansgate: 41 votes. Maldon: 8 votes. Still, I can't really think anything will come of it. After all, who wants to commute to the far reaches of the river in order to sail ? No, I reckon they'll stay at Maldon, even if the tide does have a habit of leaving you high and dry at the most inconvenient times. The last thing for December, and 1962, is an article about BACSPA (the Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection Association). The idea for the Association developed at the beginning of 1962 when a number of planning applications, and rumours of applications, appeared to be threatening the whole future of the Blackwater Estuary as a plesant sailing area. Amongst the (then) applications and rumoured applications were:- - a holiday camp at Stansgate - an oil storage depot at Tollesbury The alarm engendered amongst the sailing fraternity by the ad hoc and disparate "voice for sailing” at the Public enquiry re. "the holiday camp" so shocked everyone that, arising from an initial suggestion by the Marconi Sailing Club, the BACSPA was formed. It had its inaugural meeting at the Blackwater S$.C. on 15 April, 1962. Arthur Adam, who wrote the article, ends by saying "This club played an important part in the formation of BACSPA; we should continue to support it to the full in the future." I know from my own brief experience on the Main Committee that the club has maintained that support by sending a representative to BACSPA meetings and getting reports of what is going on in our sailing area. I also get the impression that we might well be in need of BACSPA over the next few years, Reading the 1962 Navigans, one gets the feeling that things are 'on the move' in more ways than one. If the size of Navigans is anything to go by, then the MSC is really getting going; most of the monthly Navigans must have had at least 10 pages and it seemed to contain a whole load of interesting bits and pieces about racing and sailing, socialising , boat and seamanship knowledge and, of course, ‘the club’. Mike Boreham KKKKKK KKK

The name of the club shall be "Marconi Sailing Club" (hereinafter referred to in these rules as "the club"). 26 The object for which the club is formed is to promote and facilitate the sport of yachting and also to provide social and other facilities for members as may be determined from time to time. CTION - Officers. 3 The Officers of the club shall be Full or Family members of the club and shall consist of a Club President, a number of Vice Presidents, a Commodore, a Vice-Commodore, a Rear-Commodore, an Honorary Secretary and an Honorary Treasurer. Officers shall be elected at the Annual General Meeting in each year and shall hold office for one year, retiring at the termination of the Annual General Meeting in each year. All Officers shall be eligible for re-election except that the Commodore, Vice Commodore, and Rear-Commodore shall not serve more than three consecutive years in any one post. 4. The Honorary Secretary shall: - (a) With the Registrar keep a register of club members names, addresses, boats and fees paid; (b) Conduct the correspondence of the club; (c) Keep custody of club documents; (d) Keep full minutes of all meetings of the club, the committee (as defined in Section 4) and, with the sub-committee secretaries, all sub-committees which shall be confirmed and signed by the appropriate chairman upon the agreement of the club, the committee or sub-committee at the following meeting of the club, committee or sub-committee; (e) Administer such insurance policy or policies as may be needed fully to protect the interests of the club, its officers, its members and its property; (£) Maintain contact with the club's legal adviser to ensure that the club's affairs are managed in accordance with the current law. 5. The Honorary Treasurer shall: (a) Cause such books of accounts to be kept as are necessary to give a true and fair view of the state of the finances of the club. (b) Cause all returns as may be required by law in relation to such accounts to be rendered at the due time. (c) Prepare an Annual Balance Sheet as at 3lst December in each year and cause such Balance Sheet (and accounts as necessary) to be audited at least once annually and shall thereafter cause the same to be exhibited in the club premises at least fourteen days before the Annual Ceneral Meeting. 2. COMMODORE’S NOTES Once again August has crept up on us and it seems as if there are only a few weeks left of the season. Camping fortnight has finished for another year. I am told that we now have another sixty Cadets ready to do battle on the water during racing. Let’s keep hoping that the weather af the last few weeks keeps going until the end of the season. N.T. Pembletorn D.I.Y. Whisker Pole When running downwind, there is often a need to pole out the genoa or cruising chute. This is particularly so when running goose-winged as the foresail tends to be blanked by the main as the wind shifts. Having investigated the prices of whisker poles, I decided to make my own. I bought a second-hand sailboard mast. This is made of fibre glass, is very light yet strong, and can easily be cut to length to suit. This mast is tapered and I fitted a dinghy spinnaker fitting to the small diameter end with a release cord leading to an eye fitted to the middle the pole. The thick end of the pole has a large diameter dog clip which attaches to the spinnaker pole attachment on the mast. Finally, I fitted an eye to the middle of the pole to which the spinnaker pole uphaul clips. A downhaul could be fitted if required but in practice does not seem to be necessary. The whisker pole, complete with fittings, cost less than twenty pounds, a considerable saving on the cost of a commercial pole. I bought the mast from Jaguar yachts on Carvey Island but any sailboard dealer may be able to supply a suitable mast. NAVIGANS PAST 1963 - farewell Mamgu, au revoir Heybridge, goodbye Avril, we've had to leave you now. - welcome to Stansgate, the original ‘back of beyond'; the nearest bar's two miles away! January - the Editor writes "This year...... may be more than ‘just another year' in the history of the club; it may well be the year in which we move our headquarters to one of the sites mentioned at the AGM, it doesn't need a crystal ball to foresee the upheaval that will cause". Barnacle's regular technical article is devoted to "leaks" - most appropriate for a club whose Headquarters is a sailing barge ! February - the MASC Finance Committee has granted the Sailing Section £303 towards the expenses for 1963. Michael Eyre has been elected Cadet Captain. Was he the same M.Eyre who took part in the 1962 Cadet races ? If so, the Cadet Captain is, truly, a Cadet. Also an appeal for help in repairing and renovating Avril; the man-in-charge is John Scarlett. All members are reminded of the rules passed at the 1962 AGM including the requirement to have 3rd party insurance. Finally, Barnacle continues with his theme of January; in other words he's gone for another leak. March - members are warned that sailing may be cancelled in April - and that the current dinghy park at emTMHeybridge is only available up until May. April - another sad loss through the death on llth April of Eric Cottam who was both a founder-member and a past-Commodore . In the tribute to Eric, he was rated as a natural and very skilled helmsman, despite a handicap due the effects of polio at the age of 18. Our present-day link to Eric is through ‘The Mug's Mug! which , perhaps, should be more properly called 'The Mugg's Mug'. It was Eric who built the Fleetwind 'Muags' which has featured so prominently in the club's sailing results and history. A Special General Meeting held on 10 April attracted 58 people. The Commodore (Terry Hallam) reviewed the history of the search for a shore-based site and advised that a draft lease for the Stansgate site was being considered by the Committee and (Marconi) company solicitors. The main features of the lease were:- (a) 3-year lease with no option for an extension (e) (granted) exclusive use of the foreshore; (the club) (b) sole use of the site restricted to MSC members to regulate its use (c) "the club" (MSC or MASC ?) would support any (f) no boats to be placed on the sea wall development scheme in keeping with sailing as (g) keep the site tidy, clear and circumspect with the put forward by the Landlord use of the road (d) No high speed motor boats to be launched from (h) byelaws, when available, to be rather stringent the site and no water-skiing to take place (i) the rent to be £ 150 per year for 3 years, with near the shore no road charges. Not unnaturally, considerable debate ensued and it was revealed that there was no possibility of buying the eTMsite at the moment. Also, that Mamgu had been sold for £450 (subject to a surveyor's report), that all dinghies had to be removed from the Heybridge site by May, but could he moved to the new(ie. Stansgate) site from the conclusion of the meeting (dinghy parking fees now £1 summer, 10/- winter; cruiser fees had still to be settled with the river bailiff). It was proposed by Mr.Alan Pratt and seconded by Mr.D.Bedwell "This club changes its Headquarters from Heybridge to the Stansgate area of the river Blackwater". It was reported "there was no opposition. There were, however, two abstentions". This sounds very much like Hobson's Choice to me; what with (Mamgu's) floorboards being sold from beneath their feet, and their dinghies likely to be cast over the sea-wall, what else could the 56 members do but not offer any opposition ? I wonder why two people 'abstained' ? Faced with the choice of ‘owt or nowt', I'd have thought the real choice was really 'no choice at all'. Maybe faced with the reality of the move they couldn't face committing themselves to the ‘short-term known" - and long term unknown. I'm willing to bet there were many who had begun to wish they'd opted for the Maldon site instead. Having presumably obtained the support of the club members for the move, the Commodore now reveals he has some work for them to do. He reveals that 2,000 bricks have been purchased, a lorry, complete with driver and mate, has been provided by a member and, hopefully, cement, sand,ballast and other building materials will be delivered to site. Coupled with the knowledge that the club had already secured a temporary wooden building at a cost of £250 (and which was in store awaiting planning permission) what, I wonder ,;would have happened to all this stuff if the meeting had decided not to support the move ? =| suppose ‘they’ would have had to keep calling Special General Meetings until the proposal was 'successful'. After all the excitement of the meeting and imminent move, spare some sympathy for Avril. It seems our Avril has bad leaks, split planks, broken ribs, needs re-caulking, re-filling, re-rigging and, surprise, surprise, she also need re-painting. Apart from that there's not a lot wrong with her; sounds like a candidate for a used-car mart. However, rejoice, rejoice, for the honour of being the winner of the lst race from the Stansgate site goes to the official club-CLOT , Brian Partirdge, who won the inaugural pennant race on Easter Monday, 1963.

6. It is worth noting that racing was severely restricted due to the need to hold working parties to complete the tremendous amount of work necessary at Stansgate. Whilst working parties were in operation, there was to be only one race per week-end, starting at 15.30 - and even this would be cancelled if it was rough weather due to the rescue boat not yet being in commission. Another intersting snippet is that the Sailing Instructions require all boats entering ‘internal club races' to carry a 41b.(minimum) anchor and minimum 6 fathoms of warp (unless stated otherwise in class rules) since “We think this is essential, to prevent boats being washed out to sea". May - a very good 'fillip' to the MSC since I believe they again beat the Ariel (BBC) S.C. in a team race, the victory being all the more sweet since the event was held at Teddington. A planned picnic on Osea was not undertaken due to "brisk, cold winds" - sothey " sheltered in tent or car and drank their tea in comfort". I don't blame them; our present day monohull handicap fleet had planned to have a cruise to Maldon on Saturday 15 June (1991) but it also suffered from “brisk, cold winds" and they didn't go. I personally "sheltered in my front room and had my coffee and eccles cake in comfort" ! The first Points races from the new club site were not held until 26th May. June - Associate Members of the MSC can now make full use of the MASC - jolly good ! On the sailing scene, the Ladies Race was postponed due to lack of entries, the Mona's Cup was won by Brian Partridge. However, I was more interested to read that Ian Shaw and a certain Linda Partlett "capsized off Osea and were towed back" Now, I happen to know that Linda Partlett is still a member of MSC - but under a different name as is the wont of ladies who get married (at least is was the "wont" in those dim and distant days, but I find it all too _ confusing these days). Anyway Linda, what were you thinking about, letting the boat capsize ? The Maylandsea Bay Challenge Cup was "rather dismal....". Apparently, 55 started but only 2 finished due to Jack of wind. Also, the Mamgu Trophy was presented to the MSC by Mr and Mrs A.M.Adams. August - there doesn't appear to have been a July issue, but John Tillotson won the cadet race on 20 July, all other races being cancelled due to lack of entries. John also won the Pilot's Cup, raced from Stansgate to Maldon Promenade as a pursuit race so that the entrants would be in time for Maldon Regatta. A note about the ‘anchor and warp' rule (sounds like a good name for a pub; perhaps we should call the MSC the Anchor and Warp ?); | a reminder that the anchor ought, for best effect, be tied to the warp and, silly me, the warp really ought to be tied to the boat for maximum efficiency during use ! Finally, what I believe might be the first 'lost' notice in Navigans, which was for a large V-necked pullover, with long sleeves in green/brown wool. Now, I'm certain I've seen that in the boiler-room recently. September - alas, Avril is beyond it. Since the members didn't come forward in sufficient numbers, or with sufficient help, to undertake the necessary repairs, Avril is to be sold since the cost of professional repair was more than her value. A much happier report that helmsman and crew, David Farthing and Rosaleen Littlewood, had changed status to "captain and mate" after the vicar had checked that no protests had been raised. A party of Marconi Cadets visited MBYC Cadet Week in August and also the Blackwater S.C. "but couldn't compete with the easier handicapped Sprites". A few years ago, our Cadets visited the Blackwater S.C. to take part in One of their cadet races, but a sudden storm blew up, caused many capsizes and virtually obliterated the view of the scene to a few feet due to the intensity of the rain. Not one of our cadets capsized however, and all handled the situation in very seamanship-like manner, a tribute to the teaching of then-Cadet Captain, Derek Hall. The Ladies Cup was won by Mrs Houlding (GP14) in Force 3-5, with 5 helms taking part. The Mud Trophy was won by Nick Tovey, MSC won the "Twin Flag" trophy by beating Ariel SC in a team race, and Eric Payne, in 'Rainbow', won the Stone Cruiser Trophy. Clearly, Stansgate is proving 'a lucky place' for the MSC. October - Ian Shaw won the Cadet trophy, there being a total of 4 entries over the series. November/December - Approximately 65 people attended the AGM. The sale price of Mamgu, at £450, was apparently a 50% profit over its purchase price (presumably £300). We are told that the lease for the Stansgate site had been signed on 31 March, 1963, and the Commodore paid particular tribute to Alan Pratt and Jack Bigden for their efforts in getting the site fit for use. As a result of the move to Stansgate, club membership now stands at 282 (the reports says this is an increase of 82%, so I suppose many ‘original' members left the club when it was decided to move to Stansgate). One disadvantage of the new site is clearly the two mile journey to Steeple village, for we are told that the meeting, after much discussion, overwhelmingly voted for the club to apply for a bar licence. Presumably “the much discussion" concerned what beer to stock ? Eric Payne, past-Commodore and donator of the Cadet Trophy, was voted a Life Honorary Member. Thus ended Marconi's first year at Stansgate; a great deal of work has been achieved but a lot more remains. In those days, did they envisage a brick-built clubhouse, 120 cruisers, some 160 dinghies and more than 60 catamarans? Of course they didn't, ; after all, they only had the site with certainty for 3 years. There must have been many who wondered if they'd done the right thing and, with all the inevitable hassle and arquement which goes with development and growth, must have looked back with nostalgia to the days of ‘the hut on the wall' - and Mamgu. Mike Boreham

vi THF 'LADIES TROPHY' - 1991 Congratulations to:- MAGGIE BOREHAM who won the Ladies Trophy on Saturday, 27 July, 1991 - but only just; commiserations to Jane Williams who, in her first year with the club, came close to taking the trophy from Maggie in the 3-race series which saw three different winners for the races. With a total of 11 entries in the series, the formula for the Ladies Trophy would appear to be successful but the scheduled 4 races in one day was, to say the least, a little ambitious, and the race officer sensibly reduced it to a more manageable 3-race series which produced some good racing and close finishes. Race Officer Robin Smith, assisted by Lisa Gatton, adopted the ‘equal time' handicap racing formula designed to ensure, as far as is reasonably possible, that all boats sailed in more or less the same conditions of wind and tide. The system is certainly worth looking at for all the club's handicap series events but needs to be 'studied' for its 'smags' as well as its declared advantages. As so often happens, attempts to ameliorate one perceived inequality might well introduce other inequalities. Race 1- (South-easterly F 0 - 1); alas, little wind and an adverse tide saw all 5 Mirrors and one of the Dart 18s retire, the Mirrors failing even to reach the first mark despite valient efforts. The race was kept to a straight-forward 1-lap event and Jane Williams (Laser) crossed the line some 24 minutes ahead of Maggie Boreham (420) with Pat Stuart a further 10°°4 minutes behind. Race 2 - (Southerly F 2); by the time race 2 was ready to start, the wind had shifted to the south and the tide had turned - but was still against the competitors because the R.O. had reversed the direction of the course in anticipation of a further shift to the south-west. Alas, the wind did not co-operate and the R.O was left with a reaching start whichever way he sent them. Unfortunately, the four Mirrors stood out into the adverse tide as they tried to round 'A' mark and had a bit of a struggle to make it. Incredibly, Maggie's spinnaker pole broke (in force 2 ?) but she still managed to win the race from Jane, with Pat again in third place. In fact, all boats actually finished within a 12-minute time slot, but the Dart 18s completed 4 laps to the 2 laps of the Mirrors. Race 3. - (Wind SW 3+) ; With each having one win and one second place, both Jane and Maggie had to finish ahead of the other in order to win the trophy. A close-reach start with spinnaker flying gave Maggie a handy initial lead around 'A‘ and No.1 but this suddenly turned into 3rd place behind Jane and Pat. Fighting back, Maggie again contested the lead with Jane and, barring a capsize, looked set to take the lead and the trophy. So what happened ? Yes - Maggie capsized (at which point shore-based husband Mike also '‘capsized' and went off to make a much-needed 'cuppa'). In the meantime, the two Dart 18 helms (Debbie Yorston and Lucy Boreham) found the wind much more to their liking and were busy gobbling up as many laps as possible. Mike, having found the effort of putting the kettle on with shaking hands too much of an ordeal, returned to witness the finish of the race - and was much surprized to see Maggie once more ahead of Jane. Who actually won the race ? Why, ‘twas Lucy (Dart 18) with 6 laps, Debbie (Dart 18) 2nd with 5 laps, followed by Maggie in 3rd place and Jane in 4th place. All boats finished within an approx. 14-minute time slot. Caroline Hollings again decided to sail the Laser (as in 1990) and gained two creditabk® 4ths but allowed conscience to get the better of her and she stayed ashore to entertain her guests for the 3rd race; pity, because the stronger wind would probably have been more to her Jiking in the 3rd race. Jenny Ball entertained her french ‘exchange visitor’ Claire Bourgeteau, with the joys (and frustrations) of sailing the Mirror, whilst Clare gavies decided to 'go it alone’ by sailing single-handed. Keri Styles was even more adventurous; she took her brother David as crew. Well then,. Keri - did you and David argue ? I don't suppose you did any more than wife and husband team of Denise and Evan Davies did in their Mirror. Finally, Linda Chaplin is a past winner of the ladies Cup; Linda took along her daughter Rachael as crew and, hopefully, Rachael's name will also appear as a winner on the Ladies Trophy in the years to come. With many thanks to Robin and Lisa and the support boat crews, we look forward to the 1992 Ladies trophy event. NB. Please see next page for the ‘list of results’. The ‘Equal Time' Handicap Race Formula. Formula C = —E x M x_ 100 N x A Where C = Corrected Time; M = Number of laps completed by the yacht sailing furthest —E = Elapsed Time; A = fctual number of laps sailed by the particular yacht N = Portsmouth Yardstick Number Each yachts' finishing time is adjusted in inverse proportion to the number of laps sailed, so that the adjusted time represents the time each boat should have taken to sail the same number of laps as the fastest boat. The PYN is then applied to these ‘adjusted times' to give corrected times.

The 'Rumtub & Bung' - 21 July, 1991 The Rumtub and Bung is one of the oldest sailing events on the Blackwater, having been originated by the Mulde7 Yacht Club in the 1950s and open to all members of the BURC clubs. For the last few years it has been run on behalf of the Maldon Yacht Club by the MSC and the race is traditionally to the Bench Head and back. Unfortunately, for the 1991 race, the lack of wind forced the Race Officer (John Salmon) to restrict the race to the Nass Beacon and back, the wind being approx easterly Force 0-1. Of the 23 starters, 7 were from Osea SC, 5 from Steeple Bay SC and MSC, and 2 each from Maldon YC, MBYC and Blackwater SC. With an easterly windward start and favourable tide, it initially appeared that those who started in the middle of the river had made the right choice, but soon lack of wind reduced everybody to being tide-borne only. Those close by the northern shore then whistled up their own private wind and pulled well ahead, leaving the rest struggling and frustrated. Eventually, the wind picked up enough to enable the majority of boats to make the Nass Beacon before the tide turned and helped us back to the finish in a lightish wind. A VIEW FROM THE PIER The 1991 East Coast Piers Race, Sunday 7th July. The sheep wert *BAA’, the cows went ’MOO’ and the hens went *CLUCK CLUCK’ - but cmnly the sheep were genuine. The cows and hers were passable imitations provided by Marconi S.C.s resident announcer Charles Anderson in his ’wakey wakey’ call ta the mary overseas ard UK visitors, and home-club members, whe had eritered for the 4th East Coast Piers Race held by the Marconi Sailing Club based at its extensive site on the River Blackwater in Essex. Amongst the averseas visitors were a team from the OSC and three from Holland. With camping on site and breakfast provided, the entrants had no excuse for missing the 8 am race briefing ready for the 9.30 am start of the premier east coast catamaran race from Osea Island pier to Walton pier and back again. With so many other major catamaran everits upset by either tac much or too little wind in recent weeks, the ECPR had a particular attraction as one of the UK’s major racing catamaran events. From an entry not far short of 100, some 84 starters covering 23 different classes of catamaran actually crossed the start line in an easterly force 2-3 wind, a little less than the predicted force 3-4. The initial lead was taken by the Nacra 6.0 of Glyn Ruth and Martin Young, followed by Graham and Lyrm Eeles (Hurricane 5.9) and the host Club’s world class team of Robin Smith and Lisa Gatton (Hurricane 5.9). Former Olympic Champion Reg White and Stepher Olle, sailing the formidable-locking Hurricane 6.5, had to work hard to catch the leading bunch, but nevertheless had taken the lead by the time they rounded the mark at Walton Pier and started the return journey. At about 3.50 pm Reg had reached the final turning Buoy just off Bradwell, some 23 minutes ahead of the Hurricane of Robin Smith who was followed at one minute intervals by the teams of Mark Barnes/Francis Ball (Hurricane 5.9), Thorn DeVries/Remco Kenbeek (Tornade), Glyn Ruth/Martin Young (Nacra 6.0) ard Eric Van Der Plas/deYorg Henh (Nacra 6.0). The actual line honours were taken at about 4.15pm by Reg White/Stephern Ollie (Hurricane 6.5) followed by very tight bunches of Hurricanes, Tornados, Nacras and Prindles. However, on handicap, the race was wor by Rebin Smith/Lisa Gaton (Hurricane 5.9); end - Mark Barnes/Francis Ball (Hurricane 5.9); 3rd - Brian Figgott/Terry Beech (Hurricane 4.9). The light wind unfortunately meant that most of the smaller catamarans such as the Dart 18 were officially ‘out of time’ at the limit of 6pm, but many still arrived before 6.30pm ard the Race Officer timed them all in. A particularly noteworthy performance was that of Tim Swinburn/Susie Pepper (Dart 18) who were the only Dart 18 ta finish inside the time limit and achieved 7th place on handicap, just behind the Hobie 18 of Paul Pascoe/Guy Warr. Just over 20 support craft covered the whole course. Of the 84 starters, only 3 retired and @2 others requested a tow back. The rest enjoyed a slight increase in wird as they approached Bradwell and had the immense satisfaction of completing the course, if not under their own steam, then under their owr sail. contd. <<:

5. OF CATS AND CREWS In response to requests from our revered editor, I am not going to report all the sordid details race by race (thank God, they all cry) in order to save space. The Cat Fleet continues to go from strength to strength with Sunday 11th August having a turnout of 26 boats in superb Force 4-5 Westerly conditions. That is actually more than the Hurricane 4.9 Nationals, and as marly as several Open Meetings. Entries for the Summer Series have reached the unbelievable level of 36 boats!! Racing continues to be as keen as ever, no longer is it good enough to turn up regularly to guarantee success, you now have to win or come second to have a sniff at the overall prizes. Congratulations to Steve Glynn and Tom Duckmanton on their win in the Series and to Dave and Anna for the close second. Obviously, this sort of success brings its own problems, with much closer proximity between boats and the resultant increase in "incidents". I’m delighted to say that Sportsmanship (the capital letter is deliberate) has been almost without question. Having sailed in various big club fleets in the 70s I can tell you that it is very refreshing to see the level of responsibility adapted by the Cat Fleet. Well done, you guys! Fortunately most contacts have resulted in nothing more serious than a 720 or possibly a protest meeting. Just beware though as you improve in standard through the fleet, increasing demands and expectations will be placed upon you rounding marks etc. - that’s all part of learning to sail faster!! In previous articles I've mentioned that you could catch up rapidly in a Cat if you dropped a clanger, that’s no longer the case. If you’re not somewhere clase to the box seat at the start, it’s goodnight! The problem is now to decide where we want to go as a Fleet in the medium term. Several points need ta be considered and probably aired at the Cat Fleet Meeting (which will be held late October/early November - watch this space) ard I'd like to ask for you to think about items you'd like discussed and let me know. It is your Cat Fleet, and up to you to make of it what you want. I obviously include, in my plea for comments, those people who don’t race. I have come to recognize over the past year that the very strength of Marconi is based on its breadth of types of sailors all with very different priorities for their requirements from the facilities, so if I don’t see you down at the Club on a Sunday (or Saturday) please do your best ta let me know your thoughts. Away from the serious for a moment, 80% of the Prindle Fleet spent August Bank Holiday in Sunny Weymouth at the National Regatta and I am delighted to be able toa report that the Club reputation was more than upheld. In fact I think we had the biggest single attendance from any Club. The weather was immaculate except that the wird was rarely above Force 2 (no real drifters though) and with all due modesty I have to say that Steve and Tom, Chris and I spent the whole time mixing it with the leaders. Corigrats ta the aforementioned pair for their fourth place overall (I'11 get you next year Glynn). It was an education ta sail at that end of a very competitive fleet where, although sailed very fairly, no quarter was given or asked for, and I’m sure all Club crews learnt a lot. Just watch out in the Autumn Points!! Larry Botheras MARCONI SAILING CLUB LAYING UP SUPPER SATURDAY 9TH NOVEMBER 1991 at The Heybridge Moat House Hotel Roman Road, Ingatestone. FUTURE OF UK MARINE RADIO-NAVIGATION (Press Notice No. 174 from the Department of Transport, 21 June 1991) The Decca Navigator marine radio-navigation system is to be retained in United Kingdom waters, Malcolm Rifkind, Secretary of State for Transport announced today. Mr Rifkind’s decision follows a review of the position reached in the International negotiations on the alternative proposal to replace Decca with Loran C, together with consideration of revised proaposals from the Racal Electronics Company for automating the UK Decca chains at lower cost. Answering a Parliamentary question from Dr Charles Goodson-Wickes MP (Wimbledon), Mr Rifkind said: "The United Kirigdom has been negotiating over a period of time with eight other countries on the possible adoption of Loran C as part of a joint regional system of marine radio-navigation in north west Eurcepe and the North Atlantic. My right honourable Friend, the then Secretary of State told the House in April 1990 the conditions on which the United Kingdom would in principle have been prepared to eriter into an international agreement if it could be achieved by mid-1991. Some but not all of those conditions have been met. But a new factor has been a revised proposal recently put to me by the Racal Electronics Company to modernise and cperate the existing Decca chains in the UK at a lower cast than in their 1988 proposal. "IT have examined the proposal carefully and Racal have made further improvements to it. I now have decided to accept the Racal proposal and to withdraw fram the Loran C discussions. Two main factors have led to this conclusion. First, it is now very doubtful whether an international agreement could be concluded and brought into effect which would both ensure a three-year transitional period before the closure of the UK Decca system (under the existing contract by early 1997) and avoid a price increase in the Loran C investment. Second, the revised Racal proposal means that the case has changed significantly in favour of retaining the Decca system, bath in the overall economic appraisal and in the effect on light dues. After taking account also of the casts of a change for users, I have concluded that, despite some factors which point towards Loran C, it would no longer be reasonable to impose this change of system on the UK user community. In reaching this caornclusion, I have had Particular regard to the representations made to me by the fishing and electronics engineering industries against a charge to Loran C, ard to the fact that the Decca system cantinues to serve the mariners’ needs satisfactorily within the overall requirements of marine safety. Our partners in the international negotiations on the Loran C proposal are being informed of my decision. I now intend to invite the General Lighthouse Authorities to give effect to my decision by entering intca formal negotiations with the Racal company on a new contract for operating the Decca system."
