Li NAVIGANS PAST - 1964 This chapter of 'Navigans Past’ is dedicated to the memory of Gordon Golding whose sudden and unexpected death on 14 August has caused his.family and many friends so much sadness and sorrow. Gordon's links with the club go back to its very beginnings and I know he enjoyed reading this Navigans Past series of articles. Equally, I very much enjoyed our conversations as he told me of his personal reminiscences of 25-35 years ago when he was a very successful racing helm. His name is on many a trophy throughout the length of the river from the Blackwater S.C. to Tollesbury. Part of the aim of the Navigans Past series is to remind us of how much we owe our present-day successful club to the efforts of the past members; Gordon was very active in the club long before I joined it and I am grateful not only for knowing him, but also for his part in the making of the club all those years ago. January - an announcement of the names of the members of the six sub-committees of Finance, Clubhouse, Sailing, Social, publicity - and Bar ! The Editor, Phil Luke, explains the recent deterioration in the readability and quality of recent Navigans issues. Poor ‘readability’ is due to ".....a senile typewriter which has gradually got worse and worse" and "...the poor way in which the copies have been run off the stencil." Poor ‘quality’ is due to ".....the almost complete lack of material; if it wasn't for Barnacle, Navigans would be almost non- existent." Actually, I thought the content was pretty good but I guess he's complaining that not enough people submit material; as usual it is all down to 'the few'. Phil goes on to complain he has received no write-up on the Laying-Up Supper, Christmas Eve dance, talks by Charles Stocks and Kit Hobday or the Norfolk Broads film evening. However, he had received a separately circulated social news letter which obviously didn't please Phil for he says "...this would seem to be the answer - let each sub-committee send out its own news sheet and to the devil with Navigans". I get the impression all is not well in the hierarchy of the club ! Anyway, the exasperated Phil has my sympathy. By the way, the good Barnacle wrote an article entitled "Steaming the ribs"; well, that makes a change from our modern-day predilection to barbeque the spare ribs. However, Barnacle was, of course, talking about boat building in the pre-GRP era. February - The Hon.Sec (G.Edwards) writes that club pin badges are now for sale. Also, the club's Sailing Rules are published.but the best announcement is that " the brewers have initiated the new bar - and it's now ready for opening time." Three cheers everyone Hic! Hic! Hooray. Rear Commodore, Peter Darney, writes " in thecase of good sailing manners and consideration for others, our club is noticeably at least as good as other clubs on the river..." He also comments on the racing rules and (the raising of) protests; "...if you have a good reason to protest against a competitor, then do so, as it will encourage others (and yourself) to stick to the racing rules...". March - a "thank you" letter from Eric Payne for the retirement present of life-jackets from MSC members upon his retirement from the Marconi Company; he is, of course, also a Life Honorary Member of the MSC A successful children's party, masterminded by Jack Bigden but assisted by many others, was held at the clubhouse at Stansgate for 25 children (4 - 10 years). If that was the old wooden clubhouse at Stansgate, it must have been mightily crowded. I bet there'sa few late 30s /early 40s 'kids' who will remember uncle Jack dressed as a clown, surrounded by pirates and such. In the late 1970s, I can remember Damian and Lucy gojoying the club's Christmas parties at the MASC. Thiswissue contajns ‘the MSC Racing Rules’ (as distinct from the Sailing Rules). A new points system is to be used ie. Ist = “4, 2nd = 2, etc, llth and over earns 11 points, non-starter/retired earn 11 points, and disqualified/non-entry earns 15 points. Races cancelled due lack of entries or bad weather, each entrant earns 7 points (why ?) and abandoned races = 7 points (again why ?) I don't know whether a loose-leaf notice belongs to the March or April Navigans, but it announces the Marconi Regatta Day Cruiser Event, 2lst June, 1964, with an entry fee of 2/6. The event will be in the nature of a seamanship or obstacle race, the object being to have a pleasant day out. Was this the birth of the club's Regatta - or merely an event of the same name ? April. - Mr Sawyer of Steeple Post Office has kindly agreed to hold 3 sets of clubhouse keys - but no unsocial hours please ! The club has bought a brand new 14ft dinghy for use as an inshore rescue boat at a price of £114.5s.0d with a 5 h.p. Seagull at £38. The MASC paid £75 towards the cost (of the boat only) and the MSC has to find the remainder - plus the cost of the engine. Commodore Terry Hallam hints that 4/- from each of the approx. 300 members could meet the sum - ona voluntary basis ! Clubhouse Rules include:- (a) no children under 10 allowed in the clubhouse unless accompanied by an adult (b) no dogs allowed in the clubhouse or to roam free on the site (c) no gambling on club premises.

8. Barnacle continues with his series of articles, the latest being entitled "Any fool can screw". Sometimes our friend Barnacle surprizes me; 1 wonder who he (or she) was ? May - John Perrin is the new Editor for Navigans. John, being full of enthusiasm and hope, says he wants more articles and club news from members, a possible (new) front cover for Navigans - and he hopes to be able to maintain the magazinets tiigh standard. Hang about, I thought Phil Luke had been complaining about the poor quality, etc ? June - Terry Hallam's appeal for donations toward the new rescue boat engine has raised £15.17s.0d towards the £60 target sum. On the sailing side, the club obviously hosted the Graduate Southern Championships since a "thank you" letter from the Graduate Association is published. The Ladies Cup race scheduled for 20 June has been postponed to 4 July due to only two entries being received. July - John Perrin's wish to adopt a new front cover has been swiftly fulfilled. The new design incorporates the capital letter 'N' of 'Navigans' with the outline of a sailing boat - but I feel the effect is not quite right. I keep seeing the left-hand side of 'N' as a pot-plant, whilst the rest spells ‘lavigans'. However, we should not decry the good efforts of our predecessors. With the benefit of hindsight, it is interesting to see , little-by-little, the departure of the club from being merely the ‘sailing section of the MASC' to becoming the Marconi Sailing Club with its unique and recognisably separate identity. How long, I wonder, before full independence is achieved ? Mrs Sutherland (whose husband was Managing Director and Deputy Chairman of Marconi Co.) has presented a new boa to the club; it is called 'Brazil'. We still have Brazil asa club boat, along with Idlevice and the two mini- sails - plus presumably the sailboard. A total of £28.17s.0d. has been raised towards the target of £65 to pay for the new outboard engine. On the sailing side, 10 entries for the Ladies Race which was won by Jane Cottam. Ian Shaw (Fleetwind) and a Mr.Whiffin (Kestrel) did well in the Blackwater & Colne Dinghy Championships (200 entries, plus alarm spread by a fleet of 'Hell Cats'). Some of our cruisers took part in the Blackwater Cup, whilst non-racing types took themselves Off to Osea for a picnic, some 9 people crowding into Jack Bigden' causing Jack some consternation apparently. Finally, "beware of venemous snakes" by the gun emplacement ! August - Stan and Margery Allerton held their Silver Wedding Anniversary at Stansgate, the event being celebrated "more uproarously than usual" - and ending in midnight sailing and swimming. Marconi cadet members took part in the MBYC Cadet Week, and won the team race against the MBYC cadets. Also, an obviously very sincere ‘thank you' to the club's cadet members for their hard work and assistance with club events, both sailing and social. Arthur Adam and crew came 6th in class and 7th overall in an East Anglian 0.R.A. race from Harwich - Ostend, with 45 starters. The Marconi Challenge Cup attracted 46 entries with best MSC result being Nick Tovey (Enterprise) in 5th place. Now {1 saw Nick and friends/family paddling his own canoe recently; it's rather a unique tender for a cruiser don't you think ? Also a list of Members Boats :- 31 Enterprises; 8 Fleetwinds; 65 Handicap; 5 Catamarans (ie 2 Cheetahs, something called a Supercat 17 Cruisers; and two of unknown parentage). Considering that in April, we appeared to have approx. 300 members, the number of boats registered appears to be surprizingly low; I wonder why ? September - 'The Committee' (main or Sailing ?) have discussed the adoption of a 3rd racing dinghy class and Commodore Terry Hallam writes an article on the subject. The club's original adopted class (Fleetwind) "seems to have developed into a class for Cadets", whilst the 2nd adopted class (Enterprise) appears to be relatively expensive (£200 + £30 for sails) and ",..requires a certain amount of agility to keep it upright, and to race Properly the average person would have to be on the right side of 40". (NR. Now you modern-day Enterprise sailors, read that as you will; I'm saying 'nowt !). Terry's article quite clearly favours the Snipe class, on the basis of growing fleets at nearby Stone, Maldon, Maylandsea and Burnham - and that one local helm was apparently National Champion at 69 and, at 70, is still going strong. Well, that's encouraging; move over, Lucy, I can't wait to get at that Dart 18. Peter Darney follows up with a letter to the Editor on the same theme but seems to favour two new classes. He leans towards the Snipe for the “older member" and another (less expensive ? more exciting?) class for "the younger and probably impecunious racing tyro". Mind you, there are no Snipes in the club at present but the Commodore can/will arrange some demo-Snipes at Stansgate for 4th October. On the Social side, the Laying Up Supper is to be held on 13 November at the Marconi Research Laboratory Dining Room (sounds very exotic - "whatcher wan’ deaarh ? am an' chips or plaice an’ chips?"). However, it's good value for money with dancing to the Blue Ramblers Orchestra and tickets at 18/6 inclusive (but they don't say inclusive of what ?). A notice draws attention to the fact that, under the terms of the lease, we are not permitted to use the east side of the hard. It's just as well we only had 5 catamarans in those days.

9. We finish with a note on the successful Cadet Weekend (22/23 August) in which we were joined by Cadets from Maylandsea and Stone clubs. I quote "....the cadets on the river all know each other well both on and off the water, and this produces some very keen racing". Clearly the local sailing scene was very different from that of today and I wonder what 'state of development' the Stone SC had reached to still find time to send its Cadet members down to their near neightours; would it work today ? October - A correction to last month's notice re.use of hard; we can use the east side. It appears it is the west side we can't use. Ah ! A very easy mistake to make by the informant but let's hope he (or she ?) is not navigator on your boat for a time. Re. the laying-Up Supper, someone else must have asked ‘inclusive of what?' because we are told the 18/6 includes dinner, wine, free buffet and dancing. Terry Hallam's 'Buy a Snipe ‘cos it's a snip’ article has, I fancy, touched a few raw nerves amongst some members in the club. Ken Beavins (signing himself very formally as Kenneth S.Beavins) takes Terence Hallam to task for his obvious bias towards the Snipe. Ken states "To my mind it would be about as reasonable for him to advocate the adoption of the Blandford Twelve Footer - we do at least have one of these boats in the club already". I get the impression there's a bit of heat being generated around the club. On the actual sailing side, the Mud Trophy is to be held on 25 October. Apparently the Sailing Committee had a problem since the 'traditional course' around Northey is rather a long way off now. It has been suggested that the mud banks between the MSC and Mersea be used. You can buy a 2nd-hand Enterprise (Terylene sails) for £120, or buy Eric Payne's GP14 (cotton sails) for £130. November/December - two issues in one. Dinghy Park fees for the 1965 season are to be £1 (1 March'95 - 30 April'66) or 10/- (1 September'65 - 30 April'66). The mooring fees (paid to the club thence to Maldon Borough) are to have an additional 10/- to the club itself for dinghy space for tenders, previously, cruiser Owners managed to get away with it free of charge. Commodore Terry Hallam's ‘Christmas Greetings' state "...this has been the best season for many years...." but I think he means 'weather-wise' rather than 'sailing-wise'. In his Commodore's report, we read we have a total of 513 subscription-paying members made up of:- 237 Marconi Employees; 78 Associate Members; 46 Cadet Members 101 Marconi family Members; 51 Associate Family Members; This shows a remarkably rapid growth since the club moved to Stansgate, and particularly since April'64 when we apparently had approx. 300 members. However, Terry points out that out of the 100-odd dinghies in the dinghy park, only a few supported the racing. In fact, the results sheets show 32 different dinghy helms took part in the Points and Handicap Series, whilst there were no cruiser entries except 4 in the Cruiser Cup. The race results show that 'the younger elements' (ie Cadets) were as big a 'pain' to their ‘elders and betters’ in those days (in that they would keep winning the non-cadet races) as they are today. I sometimes think the term 'Cadet' gives the wrong impression i.e. that of young children ‘mucking about’ in boats to the superior amusement of the 'real' (ie.adult) sailors. Our Cadet Members are, by definition, aged up to and including 18 years of age, effectively covering a range from guininely ‘very young children' to ‘young adults'. In fact, as I recall the exploits of ‘Cadet Members' such as Colin Harper, Chris and Robert Weedon, and Caron, Heather and Penny Stuart, I can't help feeling we need a designation other than 'Cadet' to cover the age range. When I hear the term 'Cadet', my mental image is of 8-12 year olds charging around in Opies rather than the real vision of the Hornets, Lasers and Solos of Colin and Co., or the Hurricans and Darts of todays 'Cadet' members. Has anyone a better term than 'Cadet' to describe the ‘up to and including 18-year old' members ? Bar profits for the half-season were £150 and Galley profits (for the whole season?) were £56; how does that compare, I wonder, with today, taking account of inflation ? A big ‘thank you' to ".......the unsuspecting wives of new members who, coming down with their husbands for a quiet day away from household chores, promptly found themselves doing shift work in the galley". Well, I suppose they could have gone sailing ! The "Stansgate Marine project" is mentioned. Having passed the approval stage by the County Planning Authority it has now reached 'Public Enquiry' stage, at which time the Commodore is to appear as a technical witness. Now , the terms -tesms of our lease seem to proclude objections from the club if our landlord is involved. This presents an interesting ‘balancing act' on the part of the club since, through BACSPA "..our views have helped direct BACSPA's opinion in a direction calculated to be helpful to the MSC"; an ‘interesting situation’ as they say. However, it's not clear if our landlord is involved or not. The Laying-Up Supper saw ‘Flag Officer guests' from Stone, Blackwater, Maldon YC and Maldon LSC, Osea, Saltcote and Tollesbury clubs. The AGM elects Terry Hallam (Commodore), Jack Bigden (Vice Commodore) and Nick Tovey (Rear Commodore) whilst names familiar to me are amongst the committee members, such as Robbie Sims, Julian Bigden and the late Jack Reeves. Finally, in 8th place in the Enterprise Series was a certain John Witter; now there's a chap they ought to get on to the committee, no doubt about it. Mike Boreham

Dart 18 KeKKKKKKEKEK RAKE Snippet Corner Bob Fisher's column in Yachts and Yachting (30 August, 1991) threw up two interesting ‘snippets’. The first concerned ‘starting techniques’ but the interesting bit was not so much the ‘techniques’ but the name he mentions. The forename 'Simon' is not all that common, nor is the surname ‘Darney', so when the two appear together, it is likely to be even less common. It appears Bob was sailing (crewing ?) for a Simon Darney in the Hornet world championships in Holland “some years earlier" and I wondered if this was the same Simon Darney who featured so often in the Marconi prize list also “some years earlier" ? The second snippet from Bob's column concerns what might be called ‘starting technicalities’. It is of interest because of the recent club protest raised when a competitor, before the actual start signal, passed the club's Quter Distance mark (G) on the correct side but, because G was some considerable distance on the pre-course side of the start-line, the competitor was able to effectively start ‘outside’ G in the slacker tide, having followed the course instructions as laid down and broken no racing rules. Bob Fisher writes:- "The partial failure of the ground tackle of the inner distance mark........could easily have negated Kolius's starting advantage. As (the inner distance mark) had drifted well behind the line, there were a few smart sailors, Lawrie Smith and Harold Cudmore amongst them, who realised that in the light air they could come up to the mark with a couple of minutes to spare and tack ahead into it to go into the area the race committee has sought to deny the fleet. Perfectly legitimate. It also gave them the opportunity to tack early....... ..out of the adverse current ". Well, it's nice to know some of our home-grown helms are at one with the champions. Our race officers had better watch where they place those start-line ‘distance markers' from now on; you can imagine the whole fleet jostling for room to start ‘outside* the mark, all shouting “what's good enough for Harold is good enough for me" - or words to that effect ! Mike Boreham

FIGURE-OF-EIGHT RACE - 26 AUGUST, 1991 The battle of Northey Causeway - 991 The Battle of Osea Causeway - 1991 If the moment of truth for Maldon's anglo-saxon forebears came on the battle-field of Northey Causeway in the year 991, then the equivalent moment of truth for their successors at the Marconi Sailing Club came at the Osea Causeway in 1991. ‘Twas there that battle not so much commenced but that Battle finished - and scored a famous and well-deserved victory over the warriors of the monsterous Catamaran Tribe ( a truly crue] and untamed race) and their reluctant allies, the Mono Hull people (a rather gentler, but easily led folk). The Battle in question was Richard of Chelmsford who, with the aid of his magic Mirror, joined forces with the whispering wind and coursing tide to lay waste the Cats and Monos (these being the historical names by which the invading ‘ forces were generally known in the Book of Dengie Legend, of which this particular issue is the latest of a long line of documented history of the accursed place). Kk Congratulation to:- RICHARD BATTLE who had no need to use any ‘magic mirror' to win the curtailed Figure-of-Eight race. He relied on patience and light-wind skill to score a well-deserved win in his Mirror dinghy to win the race which was shortened at Osea Causeway. With a westward start and incoming tide, a little bit of wind before the start encouraged some of us to move well onto the pre-course side of the start line, the plan being to sail, with whatever wind was availble at the time, down to the start line, reaching just inside D mark in the strongest part of the helpful tide just as the gun sounded. Alas, such plans went awry when the wind virtually died completely, and we merely drifted slowly with the tide, whilst those nearer the line also drifted with the tide to A mark - but considerably ahead of we who 'got it wrong'. I believe Damian Boreham (Prindle 18.2) was first around A mark, but Richard Battle's Mirror was close behind in second place. The course required Osea to be passed to Port, so the fleet struggled to cross the tide to Osea island. Some of the monohulls made it to Osea shore and crept slowly towards No.l in the slack tide. I, being more hopeful, stayed out in the tide hoping (a) wind would come and (b) the tide would turn any moment. Alas none of things happened and 1, together with others, paddled our way back to the MSC. Of course, as we neared the club, the wind got up, the tide turned and we had the best sail of the day - but no longer in the race. Those made of sterner stuff (or not too worried about packing up their caravans/tents) continued in the race and were rewarded with the same increased wind. Unfortunately, the race was shortened at Osea Causeway, it being feared (not unreasonably) that Northey Causeway would be ‘high and dry'. However, some boats continued the whole course - and just made it across Northey causeway with a bit of pushing and shoving. By chance, Maldon Y.C. also held their Figure-of-Eight on the same day, but shortened their race to ‘round Northey' only. The results:- Posn Helm (and crew) Boat Corrected. cr 15. HOLDIAY RAMBLINGS We took *Rodnigon’ down to Brittanny again this year, or rather, Rodnigorn took us. This time we determined ta get a bit further south than last year when we were frustrated in our attempts to get to L’Abervac’h. Sa off we went via Dover (rally but friendly); Newhaven (what a rip-off); the Hamble; Alderney; Guernsey; the Treguier river to Roscoff - our ultimate point of last year. From Roscoff it was a rice sail in not very nice weather along the racky Brittanny coast and so into L’Abervrac’h. This was as we had imagined the entrance, dramatically rocky but very well marked, although we were not able to use the advertised transits as the visibility was only a mile or so (Thank you, Mr Decca. ) From L’Abervrac’h we pressed on south to the Cheval Du Four. Again, this was well marked although not as dramatic as we had imagined, although we are told that wind versus tide conditions can give problems. Once through the Four we set course far Camaret which is a popular kicking off point for yachtsmen heading to south Brittarny via the Raz de Sein. It can get very crowded here in the holiday season but we were lucky and found a pontoon berth with no problems. Camaret is alsa a fishing port and the town itself has plenty of small shops and restaurants. We then decided to explore the area around Brest and so proceeded eastwards through the Goulet de Brest and south of Brest itself before anchoring for the night in one of the many bays. This area is one of great French naval activities with warships ard shore establishments in all directions. The next day was sperit on an exploration of the River Colne, very pretty with steep wooded banks and a high road bridge, with lots of clearance. the We then returned ta marina at Brest and a cycle round the town. Subsequently we paid another visit to Camaret before turning back north to Rosceoff via the charmel that leads between L’Isle de Batz ard Rascoff. We then motarsailed from Roscoff to Guernsey St Feter Port and then up to Alderney. On this leg we had a clase view of the Casquets, quite a frightening sight even in relatively calm weather. This time Alderney was bath very crawded and rolly in Braye Harbour, we had quite an uncomfortable right at anchor trying ta stay in cur bunks, thank heaven for lee cloths. Setting off on the afternacn tide en raute ta Brighton we had a favourable SW wind and were soon bowling along under spinnaker with eight knots groundspeed showing on the Decca and reached Brighton early the next morning. The entrance to Brighton was quite rough in the Force 5 Southwesterly, so it was nice to get inside the relative calm of the marina. Much better value here than Newhaven, with all kinds of nice facilities, shaps, restaurants nearby. Aryway there we were, 2 hours out of Brighton Marina en route to Ramsgate on the penultimate leg of our return to MSC. We had a rice following wind but the genoa was getting blanked by the main. Sarah was aff watch below asleep (I thought) in her bunk. Time to try the cruising chute, so autopilot on, roll in the genoa ard hoist the chute. At this stage came the realisation that I had underestimated the wind strength and Rodnigon rolled inta a fairly dramatic broach which laid her well over. Strange noises from belaw indicated that all was not well, and having sorted out the broach, a glance through the hatch gave sight of a white, somewhat frightened face peering out of the heads compartment. I told Sarah that in future she should keep the helmsman informed of her movements, but this instruction was rot well received. Still, never mind, at least we were an speaking terms by the time we were dodging the hovercraft which were squirting out of Dover harbour at amazing speeds. As a sort of hardy hint to MSC intrepid travellers, we found out the hard way that anyone intending to cruise in the Channel the Islands area should fit a stripper to propeller shaft. The area seems to attract a lot of flotsam and on three separate occasions we had encounters with bits of net, the first being a twelve foot length of cargo net. Even if you do not have the misfortune to meet any bits of net, the local seaweed is both prolific and tough, and tends ta form a ball around the propeller. This can often be cleared by rurming astern, but does manifest itself by a mystifying loss of power as the weed builds up. The alternative to fitting a stripper is to always carry a mask and flippers, but with the proviso that diving underneath the boat in the Open sea is not recommended. Dave (Beane) & Sarah, Rodnigon Ed’d note: What with "buoy friends’ and ‘strippers’, Dave, are you sure that sailing in Cruisers is a seemly pastime for children to take part in?! Tim and Janet Bigden’s 4 day cruise on ’Gemma’ will appear in next Navigans, space permitting.

o Lie Gordon Gelding - Family Man and Geod Club Member I am sure that many members, particularly those of you who date back to the early days at Stansgate, were deeply shocked to learn of the totally unexpected death of Gorden Golding. It had been only a week previously that we had been reminiscing tagether over the old days and the beauty of the Stansgate location. I first met Gordon in December 1967 when he became Club Coxswain and I became Hosun. Jack Bigden was Commodore, Dennis Byatt Fleetwind Captain, and Terry Hallam Cruiser Captain. Our roles and our sailing Sub Committee work brought us into close ccarntact. Every weekend he was there, either keeping a watchful eye on the proceedings, or at the tiller of Rescue Boat No.1 (still in business as the Cruiser Workboat.) I also remember him organising Barbecues with Jack Bates at the M.A.S.C. It was during this time that a certain young lady, Leonie Carlisle, was racing and winning pennants in the family Heron "Misterbloac", Our sympathy goes cut toa Leonie, her family and friends, in the hope that the fellawship ard memories provided by the Club will pravide comfeart and support in the difficult times ahead. Mirror Fleet AGM, Friday 15th November, Spm, 8 [redacted], Springfield, Chelmsford RIVER BLACKWATER DEVELOPMENT - THE CURRENT SITUATION 1. Speed limits can only be set by the Maldon District Council at 250 metres from the shore. Water ocutside these boundaries have no speed restrictions. 2. Further speed restriction could probably only be achieved by Act of Parliament, or by a River or Harbour Authority. The cost of setting up the latter would be in the region of £500, 000. 00. 3. In general, it could be agreed that so far the vast majority of River users have enjoyed their sports/pastimes withsout serious interruption except for that small minority of unthinking or ill-informed users. 4. All recognised Clubs and Water Sport Activities generally regulate their respective Membership in an exemplary manner. 5. The main problems on the River seem to stem mostly from casual visitors who gain access via Public Launching sites. & Lack of manpower and policing of the River, particularly at weekends, does not provide the degree of safety and control which we all believe necessary on the water. 7. Maldon District Council states that it is powerless to control Public access to the River and has, to date, resisted all requests to control entry at these points, although it has the power to do so. 8. Residents local to these access points have their own problems, especially at Stone, of illegal parking, noise and abuse from the casual visitors as no facilities are available for car and trailer parking close by. 3. Unless we, the River Users, can agree on cur own requirements for leisure and water activities, it seems likely that the Authorities will be satisfied to make na changes. Only consultation on agreed policies for recreation on and around the River is likely to achieve any degree of safety or an improvement in cur environment. NOTE: IF YOU AGREE WITH THE ABOVE PRECIS, WHICH IS BELIEVED TO BE A FAIR REPRESENTATION OF THE CURRENT CONDITIONS CONTROLLING SFORT AND RECREATION ON AND AROUND THE RIVER BLACKWATER, PLEASE LET US CONSIDER THE OPTIONS AVAILABLE TO US TODAY, ACT ON THEM ACCORDINGLY AND NOT WAIT FOR WHAT MAY BE POSSIBLE AT SOME TIME IN THE FUTURE. THESE WOULD INCLUDE: A. SPECIFIC REGULATION AND MANNING OF PUBLIC ACCESS POINTS. B. LOCALLY AGREED ZONING OF SPECIFIC AREAS SET ASIDE FOR SPECIFIC SPORTS AND ACTIVITIES BOTH ON AND OFF THE RIVER, BEARING IN MIND TRADITIONAL PATTERNS OF USE! C. AGREED RULES OF CONDUCT FOR RIVER USERS. D. IMPROVED RELATIONS WITH THE POLICE, MDC AND OTHER AFFECTED GROUPS AT LOCAL AND DISTRICT LEVEL TO WORK OUT WAYS AND MEANS OF ACHIEVING THESE OBJECTIVES TOGETHER. Colin Lambert, Secretary, BACSPA, (Blackwater & Colne Sailing Protection Association) 30th April 1991

6. f Catamarans and Crews... Sad to say that the real (i.e. Summer season) is now firmly drawing to a close. It really seems to have flown by this year. However despite the fact that autumn evenings are drawing in we still have the Autumn Points to go (plus Winter Pursuit for the nuts). A good turn out for races 1 4 2 was welcomed by probably the most chaotic day of the season so far. First of all, we set off full of vigour towards Breezy only to find it half way up the moorings! During this time Steve Glynn did his best to knock out the opposition for the rest of the series by carving a nasty gash into the side of Dave & Anna’s Hurricane. Steve did lend Dave & Anna the 19 for the restart as recompense - and they still managed to win!! In the afternoon, Steve’s boat showing post-nationals strain responded by busting a trapeze rope (Steve's not Toes) and disintegrating the tiller extension. To add to the catalogue, Lucy decided to let her mast drop on No. 1 ~ and she didn’t do a 720....... Then there were the protest meetings, what a day!!! As a point of clarification on this latter item, I ought to point out to everyone the consequences of Rule 74.5 in series racing. Basically it says that if you are disqualified for one of a limited number of things (including taking penalties) then you are not allowed to discard that result from the overall score. You have been warned.......... Having last week spent a few lines describing the perils of rule 74.5 for non-acceptance of a penalty, blow me if the next week we didn’t see another example of it’s application. Autuan 3 & 4 did a auch bettersimpression of June than September but there was very little wind and the doughty Mike Battle (Race Officer) postponed for 15 mins. When we finally left the hard the order of the day was to walk down the shore to the Race Box and wait for the start. Now previously this season, people have been threatened with eternal hell fire etc. but nobody’s done much about it. What, | hear you ask. Walking after the five minute gun. That, dear reader, is when the Racing Rules come in to force, and Rule 55 talks all about illegal propulsion....... other than by the action of wind and water. Quit came the Red Flag, but good old eagle-eyed Mike B had already done his stuff. Anyway, we got under way, against a really fearsome flood tide to beat to Breezy. Caruth and 1 seemed to have learnt sowething in the light airs of the Prindle Nationals and rocketed (!) around to A (via No.1) to see several Fast Cats still endeavouring to cross the line from Maylandsea way. We of course had a little chuckle to ourselves, but he who laughs last etc. About 40 mins after going round A we could only just see it in the distance from our new tactical position off Osea pier..... Thanks to Dave Onyons, Bob Anderson and Derek Holroyd in the Orkney for the tow...... Steve filynn and Tom were the only legal finishers and so won. The afternoon saw the wind pick up to a pleasant 3. The tide had turned and only a few had noticed the Start Marks were now miles over the line..... You've guessed it, several hundred boats were over at the gun, and only a few (naturally your correspondent and crew) exonerated themselves properly. A pleasant sail saw Glynn and Duckmanton Jnr. do the biz (well, one of the Duckmanton family has to do something on the water!) followed by another Prindle 19 sailed by a physically and mentally handicapped helmsman. One slightly sour note occurred when Ethan Chatters had his transom almost chopped off by a Shearwater from Stone. 1 think it very worthwhile to remind Marconi members that the Racing Rules apply when racing, full stop. It is lmmaterial that you are not even in the same club or event or on the same course. | know there is a bit of a feeling that we are not to blame, but for the monent please be absolutely certain that you are whiter than white. Autuan 5 & 6 saw me with a substitute crew. CC was seeing whether any of lan’s expertise would rub off, and I had Steve for the day. Things looked quite promising at 0900 with a nice 4 - 5, but by the time Bob Anderson set us off it was a very unsteady 0 - 1. Several of the wimp portion of the fleet decided that a bit of drizzle was too much for them and didn’t even turn up!! Well, the Prindle 19 wean machines got going and when Bob abandoned were Well ciear of the fleet Of course as soon as the flag went up the wind picked up..... For the afternoon the sun started to break through and we had a gentle 1-2 Westerly. I don’t know what the 19°s had for lunch but as we approached C (on 21CBD,AICBD42 course) there wasn’t a single other Fast Cat in sight. We duly toddled around, having a contretemps with & (and doing a 720) and yet another Stone Shearwater on port tack to finish 6 minutes behind Glynn and Duckmanton and several minutes in front of Tim Wallace (being crewed by a boatless Ethan). Bob definitely got his own back with a 1 hour fifty minute race for Steve and Tor!! For all his fans, the real Fleet Captain (AKA Spot) arrived back from his hols and will again be holding court and telling me what to do as usual! Weekend of 21/22 September was destined to see the Solo/Dart 15 Open. In addition, there was an alternative event up the Mé attended by the less reputable members of the Cat Fleet. Apparently, Big John had, in a moment of weakness, said “Yes” to Caroline - who had not taken it as a joke! Of course, we forgot the essential Race Equipment (Flags N, Answering Pendant and Flag B)* and were regaled with the sight of Nickalls and a top hat! Actually, my theory is that it was the box a normal sized hat came in. Fortunately, John’s ears were firmly glued in place to prevent him being blindfolded peeiea We knew if was a joke as well with the reading being taken from I Corinthians (thou shalt not lay limit marks on the approach side of the start line). However, they both got the words right, and if you want anything from Big J in the future, ask Caroline!!!

7. Obviously, all joking aside I’m sure you'll all join me in wishing them all the best for the future (except on the water!). The last Sunday in September had us all fooled. With gales forecast all around, we turned up to see the Blackwater giving a perfect, undisturbed reflection of the sky. The season's weather has been amazing, with April all but blown out and (it seems) drifters ever since! Paul Metcalfe did the decent thing and kept the course fairly sensible (A1CBG) and off we trolled. I had a slight aberration and failed to avoid Steve Glynn on starboard and seemed to take years to do a 720. It didn’t seem to matter since the wind was so variable in direction that Caruth and I seemed to benefit from the process. All the big boats (Glynn & Duckmanton, Harrison & Bail, Grant Piggott & crew) whistled round 1 closely followed by Ron Event on his Dart 18. Weird things happened to the weather after € with all of us who’d rounded watching an incredibly heavy rain squall creep up astern. Unfortunately for Grant he was at the back...... Fortunately for Chris & I we were (unusually) at the front.... and it eased before it hit us!!! We all eventually got round but hadn’t done enough to shake the blasted Dart on handicap! The afternoon race was almost as bad, but we did manage two laps and Glynn and Duckmanton managed to rediscover their form. Peter Flook and David Ball played a bit of a blinder in the Nacra, and the Dart Heavyweights (Dave Onyons and Ben) showed some of the midgets the way round. All in all an interesting weekend, particularly for Tim Dieu de 8 having borrowed the demo Hurricane 500. What was that word you used to describe it on Saturday? 8. S" FOUR-DAY VOYAGE "GEMMA? We had originally planned a week in France - ALONE. Those of you who know the Bigden tribe will appreciate that the chance for the adults to escape without the various combinations of kids is rare. However it was not to be - one link in the babysitting arrangements fell through at the last minute and we were left with just 4 precious days on our own. As our boat Gemma is a 2ift. Corribee, we don’t go far with the gang on board, so Tim likes to sail to new places and had always had a yearning to try the Haverngore route into the Thames. We are quite the "Maurice Griffiths" fans, and prefer the quiet creeks and unspoilt areas to Marinas etc. Friday Sth June saw us arriving on board with enough supplies for a fortnight —-Tim always complains I take too much. At 07.40 next morning we left with the ebb under blue skies, white clouds scudding across in the stiff breeze - perfect conditions for sailing - except the frosty conditions aboard due to a difference of opinion. That was soon resolved and conditions were so good we arrived at the Wallet Spitway with the tide out of the Crouch still against us (nothing to do with the Captain misjudging, you understand). So we decided to dry out on the edge of Huxey for lunch. Mind you, that was misjudged too and we ate cur lunch bumping up and down, testing the keel plates on the hard sand - not good for the nerves. Just as we motored off, when we could no longer endure the grinding, a friendly seal _ kept circling the boat and popping his head out of the water every so often, he kept us company for a while. We stopped off at Burnham for supplies (more?), namely a chart and mango chutney. Once into the Roach we motored into Yokesfleet Creek, Middleway and Narrow Cuts to take a look at the bridge. A chat on the VHF with the bridge keeper canfirmed the bridge could be opened in the morning 1 hour before High Tide when we plarned to leave (he keeps a listening watch on Ch 16, or call on Ch 72, call sign Shoe Bridge.) Our main concern was the depth. Jack Cootes’ excellent book ‘East Coast Rivers’ recommends the passage only in High Water Springs, but it was approaching Neaps. Gemma only draws 0.8m so we weren’t toc worried as long as the water was calm. Weather conditions affect the depth too, with less water in settled High Fressure. We motored back into The Middleway and enjoyed a superb curry (hence the mango chutney) accompanied by the call of various wild life and a magnificent sunset - Maurice Griffiths was right. The captain recalculated the tidal heights and announced we might not make it in the morning. Next morning dawned - another beautiful day - just the early mist lifting off the marshes in the morning sun and we passed through the bridge at approximately 07.40 with the water like a mirror, tide still flooding. The bridge keeper was more than helpful - you must keep as close as possible to the line of cans on the port side until well over the broomway (the shallowest part). The echo sounder was reading 1.2.... 1.1.... and stopped registering, and we expected to ground any moment. However, with the keeper talking us through the guiding us, the echo sounder started to read again and we were over. Once ofer the broomway we headed for the black beacon, whilst eating a celebratory breakfast. Just before we passed over the edge of the sands, a salutory reminder of how unkind the sands can be - a _ yacht’s mast, complete with shrouds intact, sticking about 3-4ft. out of the water. Can’t have been long ago she came to grief. Our plan was to cross the Thames to the Medway and it was just a matter of bucay hopping - South Shoebury, Sea Reach No.1, Medway, and then parallel with the coast, inshore of the marked shipping lane. A glorious run most of the way, sunbathing in the cockpit. We kept well in to the East Shore in the entrances to the harbour, until a ferry got rather agitated at us as he was trying to leave his berth. As we tacked toa get out of his way, the yacht behind us did the same - he seemed to have been doing our favourite in a new river - following someone whe locked like a local and knew his way in. Into the Swale and Queensborough seemed like the best place ta stop for lunch - but it was hot and crowded and we had to share a mooring with someone’s dinghy just off the causeway so we didn’t go ashore. Set sail again to explore the Swale; on the last bend before Kingsferry Bridge, Tim went to start the outboard and the starter cord pulled out. We had to anchor while he fixed it. After we finally got going under power we then had to wait for the bridge to open, amongst a large crowd of jet skis and motor boats whining up = and down. So far, the lack of scenery combined with this assault on the nerves, had decided us that the river is not one of the best on the East Coast. By the time the bridge lifted at 16.20 there was a queue of boats waiting to pass on both sides, not without some jockeying for position I might add. Once through the bridge the scenery didn’t improve and we decided to motor, although the outboard was playing up -

9. speeding up slightly and then dying on us - fuel starvation diagnosed, but no obvious cause. After a chat with a local from Oare Creek we decided to follow him and either = anchor at Harty Ferry or in Faversham Creek. Following him found us aground - and him as well - sc much for local knowledge again. AS we passed Harty Ferry we could see the Ferry House Inn on the hill, but weren’t happy to anchor under the north shore as the wird was from the N.E. and not recommended with the fierce current on the early ebb, ever though this is the most attractive bit on the Swale. Soa, into Faversham Creek, and after advice from the local Fisherman we tied up against a Cornish Crabber just inside Oare Creek. Ashore is the Shipwright’s Arms - no electricity, gas or running water and an atmosphere all of its own - low ceilings, a curious mix of odd chairs and tables and a simple menu - 3 assorted fillings in french sticks, meat pie or the house ‘speciality’ Garlic bread and salar OR Garlic bread with melted cheese and salad. Sweet (or rather pudding) was Bread and Butter pudding and that was it. Still the beer was good and the locals friendly. We walked along the creek up to Qare and admired the variety of boats on their mud berths, from rotting, neglected hulls to superb, gleaming expensive yachts. Settled down in our bertths after another spectacular sunset, which added to the old world charm of the place, we awoke sometime during the night at an odd angle - sco much for local knowledge - we had dried out half way up the edge of the chanrel. Monday morning was grey and gloomy and the wind freshening, forecast 4/5 with 6 later, but luckily from'the south so we set sail early, already having decided toa cross the Estuary to Brightlingsea, as Havengore would be impossible under these conditions. Once again it was mainly a Buoy hopping exercise, although the variable Visibility meant compass steering some of the time:- coming out of the Swale, head for the Pollard Spit light buoy, Columbine Spit and then 335 to S.W. Oaze. Tim's bit....After about an hour of heading for the S.W. Oaze Janet announced she could see trees on the starboard bow. "Silly ------ ; there aren’t any trees in the middle of the Thames Estuary," I says, hastily checking the chart. However they appeared off and on out of the mist and the Red Sand Tower did look like a line of poplars. By the time we reached the S.W. Oaze the wind had freshened tc a good FS but we managed to take in the jib pole and gybe ontc starboard for the broad reach across the Warp to S.W. Swin and then up the Swin. Janet, true to form** had taken to her bunk at the sight of large grey waves. What a glorious sail, the boat often surfing at 6 knots plus, under fully reefed main and half rolled genoa (by now the wind was a good F6é.) The navigation went well, too, with S.W. Swin, Maplin, Maplin Bank and W. Hook Middle Buoys coming up or cue. This was a good thing as, with the crew prostrate** I couldn’t leave the tiller to do chart work; all I could manage was to grab the chart from the cabin ard raid the goodie box for chocolate and coke. ¥¥Janet adds......In mitigation I rarely get sea sick and never take tablets these days. However my body has a built-in defence mechanism just in case, and I tend to _sleep if conditions are such that queasy feelings might start, sc I missed a chunk of ‘he passage in peaceful dreams. I awoke ta find Tim slightly lost (SORRY - we've both learnt from our yachtmaster course that one is not last - just unsure of one’s position. ) We were due to arrive at the Swin Spitway very close to law water, but the expected buoy had not appeared - instead Tim was confused by a cardinal mark and had turned 90° to port. He is very good at passage planning and following through but he won't mind me saying that my instincts are better in a crisis. So it was instinct (or common sense) that told me that heading towards Bradwell Power Station would land us (literally) on the sand somewhere, and we returned to our original heading and were relieved when the familiar Swin Spitway materialised. #*N.B. I had no intention of heading across Buxey, I had simply wandered off course a little while taking stock of the situation - T.B.)* From there it was home territory, there proved to be plenty of water in the Swin, even though the sea was confused with fairly large waves. We arrived at Brightlingsea about 16.30 having logged 39kn miles over 8 hours - not bad for a Pift. boat. After tidying up we went ashore and persuaded mine host at the Anchor to start cooking early for two extremely hungry sailors. Tuesday dawned even windier and we spent most of the day listening to the gusts howling through the rigging, worrying about alternative means of getting back to the club (we had to return) home Tuesday evening). However the wind started to abate about 15.00 and we set off up the Blackwater, ending up motoring back just after Bradwell. It may not have been ’foreign’ but we thoroughly enjoyed the trip. Janet Bigder

10. "HITS NOT FAIR" The Equal Time Handicap Race Formula - a purely personal view from Mike Boreham The Prologue Handicap racing is never ‘fair'. At best it isareasonable compromise acceptable to the majority; at worse it is a lottery in which some will become convinced they will always be the loser. However, having said that, handicap racing is a necessity if (a) you do not have enough boats of a particular class to form a separate racing fleet and (b) you are sufficiently curious to know 'how well' you can sail against boats of other classes. The trouble is, when you win, it's all due to brilliant sailing - but when you're last, it's due to an incompetent race officer, a ridiculous course and/or an 'unfair' handicap system which is long past its sell-by date and in drastic need of revision. I know how they feels I'm long convinced the 420 (PYN = 115) ought more properly be 151, whilst those Solo flying machines (PYN = 122) are treated too leniently and ought to be racing off 100 - or less. The biggest ‘gripe’ against the ‘traditional’ dinghy handicap sailing is that boats do not all sail in the same conditions of wind and tide. For example, a Cadet dinghy (PYN = 152) ought to take twice as long to sail a set course as a Tornado (PYN = 76). However, in a physically long race of 1-2 hours duration around a ‘normal' course, the tide (and almost certainly the wind) will vary in strength and direction, both in time and space. Thus, if the Cadet dinghy experiences 'favourable' variations of wind and tide when the Tornado is safely finished and on the hard, it clearly gains an advatage not necessarily connected with ability to sail. Conversely ‘unfavourble' variations will place the Cadet in the 'no hope' category, with the Tornado (now nicely put away in the Cat park) left. the winner and the proud helm downing a pint, whilst the poor old (young ?) Cadet skipper is still trying to get around No.2. Again, not necessarily any reflection of ability to sail as such, merely ‘a victim’ of the circumstances on that particular day. Maybe that's why some people prefer to sail on non-tidal waters. Therefore, the ideal might be for all boats to sail in the same conditions of wind and tide for the same length (and period) of time. "Good idea, Mike" I hear you say “How do you arrange it ?" "With great difficulty" is my unhelpful reply, but help might be at hand via the Equal Time Handicap Race Formula. Equal Time Handicap Race Formula C = 5 xM ) xy where C = Corrected Time; E— = Elapsed Time N = PYN A = Actual number of laps sailed 100 = 100 (surprize ?) by the boat in question M = Number of laps sailed by the boat sailing furthest. Essentially, for a given boat (eg. our struggling Cadet dinghy) we work out the average time it has taken to sail one lap (E-+A = seconds/lap) . Then we work how long it would have taken to sail the same number of laps as the fastest boat (ie. (EA) x M seconds). Now we apply the normal handicap number to get the relative performance (ie. corrected time) for each boat. Hey Presto! We have found the worthy winner against whom nobody can complain, grouse or shout "Hits not fair !" If you believe that, you'll believe anything. The snags To start with, to be reasonably fair, all boats ought to sail for more or less the same actual time period (eg. 11 a.m. - 12 a.m.) as well as the same elapsed time (eg 60 minutes) and, in addition, sail in the same general physical area. In this way, all boats ought to experience the same variations of wind and tide in both the space and time domains. That's the snag! Time considerations In my opinion, the race Officer should aim to finish all boats within a time period not more than 20% of the ‘planned duration’ of the race. I.E. for a planned duration of 60 mins, the finishing time-span should be 12 minutes, whilst for a 2-hour race it would be 24 minutes ‘time span' in which to finish all boats. Clearly, this is difficult for the race Officer to judge - and achieve. Space considerations Boats a 100yards apart will often experience quite different conditions of wind and tide, so boats %-mile apart will certainly experience different conditions and be affected quite differently by changes. If the wind dies towards the end of the race, the Cadet dinghy is affected longer than the Tornado. The solution would be to keep the laps short (say F, No.1, A, D - *but that's not fair’says the Tornado) rather than long (eg. B, C, No.1 No.2, D - “that's definately not fair’ says the Cadet dinghy).

ll. How _many laps ? In my opinion, each boat ought to sail at least two laps (another reason for keeping short laps). Consider a race in which, say,a Laser, 420 and Solo are well aheadof the field. They complete one lap and the Race Officer sends them on fora 2nd lap. However, the rest of the field, including 420s, Lasers and Solos, he stops after one lap and then applies the formula as described. Our leading trio are not best pleased; after all, they have sailed twice as far for twice as long - if they're lucky. If the wind drops on the 2nd lap, they'l] finish well down the results list, even though they were clearly the leaders. If the wind increases, they don't necessarily improve their position since they were leading anyway. For this reason I feel all boats ought to sail at least 2 laps, more if possible,in the planned duration of the race. The Epilogue _ If the Equal Time Handicap Race Formula was adopted by the club, I feel that:- (a) short laps should be set rather than long laps (b) a minimum of two laps should be sailed by all boats (c) a 20% 'time span' should be the criteria for the Race Officer to judge when deciding at which point to start finishing boats. (d) the 1992 Easter Egg Series and May Day Bank Holiday Series would be ideal for 'testing' out the system and finding the practical problems of administering it (e) maybe we should forget the whole thing and stick to the 'normal' handicap race system. NAVIGANS PAST 1965 - Arthur Adams writes an epic tale of an epic voyage - what really happened on the Norfolk Broads ? - the Committee tells us 'how it is' and lays it straight on the line; you can ‘Work or Pay' ! January - a statement to the effect that, interms of effort needed to produce it,and the cost of posting it, " ...2..the cost of producing Navigans is becoming uneconomical". With a circulation of 330 (with some 88 posted to Associate Members) there will be a ‘postage levy’ for all members who require Navigans and other circulars to be posted to them. The levy will be 4/- per year. Membership subscriptions are due and they are Ordinary members 10/- (but with wife/husband 15/-); Associate Members 36/- (with wife/husband 41/-), non-MASC Cadets 20/- or 5/- (10-15) and MASC Cadets (10-18) 2/6. A ‘block Racing Fee of 30/-, otherwise 2/6 per race, collected at the end of the season; by the way, “many members" have not yet paid their 1964 race and dinghy park fees ! MBYC held a 5-race Winter series andattracted 50 boats, 9 from Marconi. lan Shaw/Linda Partlett (Enterprise) were 6th whilst David Perry/Eleanor Eldridge capsized in December. That sounds as though they still haven't got it upright yet - what a way to spend Christmas! It appears that, amongst the cadets, "girl. friends and boy friends change" (they do ?) but “in the next generation, congratulations to Ian Rogers and Henrietta Wellings whowere engaged on New Year's Eve". Not capsized I hope; if David and Eleanor get their boat up in time, perhaps they can join in the celebrations. A letter from Brian Tillotson re "the third class". He basically says that a 3rd class should grow spontaneously and not be dictated. He feels ‘the Executive’ should only exercise any jurisdiction over classes sailed by restricting admission of new members whose boat(s) do not conform but existing members won't change boats. February - a successful Burns Night Party was held at Stansgate with haggis provided and cooked by Robbie Sims - he's nay a scoot, surely ? Arthur Adams writes Part I of his 'Mamgu prize-winning’ log recounting buying, collecting and sailing his new yacht in Holland. The Sailing Sec responds to Brian Tillotson's letter " If there is evidence of 5 or more regularly racing in any one class, separate races will be started for them..... The club should not consider adopting the class....until it has proved itself for at least a year. Similarly, if one-design classes are unsupported for a year or more, the club should consider dropping that class...." He goes on to say "....The whole point of having club one-designs is to concentrate interest into those classes..... The committee would be failing in its duty ....if it pressed classes that were similar to the constitutionally adopted classes, consequently the official programme will only show the races for the constituted classes". March - Part II of Arthur Adams' log. Don Budds writes a bit about 'Sea Shanties’. He ends by saying "It is the shanty tunes rather than the words that are interesting. At best the words give glimpses of life On board the old sailing vessels. At worst they are merely obscene doggerel." 1 must admit my recollections of 'sea shanties' from my ‘service days' don't include any interesting tunes; are there any 'clean' sea shanties ? April - A notice appears in Navigans:- "Wanted: Ladies for work as galley slaves. Ability to row not essential - in fact, no earthly use at all". Now does he (I suppose it's 'he') mean 'row' as in ‘row the boat ashore, alleluia" or ‘row' as in having a humdinger of an arguement (as at some Main Committee Meetings I've known !). I won't embarrass the 'he' who (I suspect) penned the ‘Wanted' notice but I understand he does a good turn with the haggis ! Part III of Arthur Adams' log is published. May - a hosepipe ban from lst April - no boat washing. As far as I know we still have a hosepipe ban. Mind you, I reckon with the absense of a hose-pipe on the hard, things are ‘less cluttered up' especially at the end of racing. Perhaps we don't really need a hosepipe if a bucket of water does the trick ? Club ties are now on sale at 10/6. The last time I bought a club tie, I reckoned it was probably from the original stock, at least judgingfrom its width. Jack R@eve proposes organising a series of Torch races. Part IV of Arthur Adams' log is published. June/July - Jack Reeve is the new Editor - and Part V of Arthur Adams' log is published. Yet another engagement; seems like a regular marriage bureau is in operation at Stansgate. It appears a large party of MSC members took off for the Norfolk Broads with 8 hired Blakes (sailing) boats and one private 'Felicity'. Clearly a very good time was had by all and Eleanor Eldrige recounts the tale, admitting to running aground (that's a change from being capsized over Christmas around MBYC). Eleanor writes "The majority of the fleet were happily drinking "; well, what else would you expect from a load of rowdy Marconi sailormen and sailorwomen (actually she goes on to include the word ‘tea’ on the next line, but that’s not now I read it first time}. John Hutchings had his 18th birthday with breakfast provided by Leonie (Carlisle ?), Dave Young and John Witter, followed that evening by celebrations in the local hostelry (but don't try to convince me you were drinking tea again ).

TS John, Dave and Leonie appear to have been the ‘entertainments committee’ for theywrote the verses of "On the Norfolks Broads" to the tune of the Quartermaster's Stores:- "There was Con, Con, with her apron on, etc. There was Jack, Jack, motoring at the back, etc The was Mike, Mike (Sissons) quanting up the dyke, etc. There were boats , boats, 9 Marconi boats, etc ". I assume 'Con' and 'Jack' were Connie and Jack Bigden. A young lady named Sue Palmer (who presumably should have been tucked up in bed and soundly asleep) spent several evenings with her headpoked through the open windows whilst she learned the words to "Oh ! Sir Jasper!". If you're reading this Sue, can you still remember them - and how about an encore at the Laying-Up supper ? Members' boats are listed:- 33 Enterprise, 9 Fleetwinds, 66 Handicap, 26 cruisers, 6 ‘cats' and 6 motor cruisers launches or o/b dinghies. The handicap fleet included an 11' Challenger dinghy belonging to Dennis Byatt; is this the same Challenger we have as a club boat today ? Four club boats are listed, namely Rescue Boat No.1 (16'), Fisherman (14') a Walker (8') and Brazil. August - Under sailing notes there is a complaint about the number of boats without means of identification - a problem not unknown tous these days. The club is to supply (at 2/6) brass plates upon which can be painted the name and number . A whole host of racing results are published covering several pages, and Terry Hallam writes an article entitled "Flags and Burgees". September - a notice to remind everyone that, under the River Authority bye-laws, it is an offence for anyone to walk on either side of the sea-wall, especially the landward side. A special announcement, under the name of Jack Bigden, of a Veteran's race (40 and over) with a course from clubhouse mark to the Jolly Sailor and return (if capable). Although not stated, clearly a ‘stop-over' is intended. This, presumably, was the first 'Jackpot' race - but without the actual 'Jackpot' (trophy). Also, the rules of the first Helmsman of the Year Trophy event (the 'Costain Cup' presented in 1965 by Sir Richard Costain to mark the opening of 'the new pavillion’ at Beehive Lane, Chelmsford, 17 July, 1965). The event was run as a twoeday series consisting of 5 races, approx. l-hour per race and the same course for each race. The event seems to be open to anyone willing to pay the 7/6 entry fee. Winner of the Ladies Cup was (Mrs) D.R.Darney, but I see Leonie Carlisle was2nd and Linda Partlett 3rd. Of course, Leonnie #8 nowLeonie Golding whilst Lindais Linda Chaplin. There were 60 entries for the Marconi (Dinghy?) Challenge Cup with MSC = 22, MBYC = 14, SSC = 12, OSC = 7, MYC = 4 and 3 ‘unknown'. October . a very weighty tome this month, due to the upcoming AGM. Articles entitled "The Club Future" (Commodore), "Policy Statement " (Committee), "The 3rd Racing Class(es)" (Sailing Sec.), "Work or Pay" (Commodore) "Proposals for the AGM" (Committee) and the AGM Notice/Agenda. For the Club Future, Terry Hallam reminds us that the club's 3-year lease at Stansgate runs out at the end of this year. The "Marina Scheme appeal" has been resolved in that the Min. of Housing and Local Government has allowed the appeal and outline planning permission has been granted to Mr.Sparrow (our landlord). Club membership has grown 5-fold in the 3 years ~from about 120 to some 600. Consequently, stress, creaks and groans are issuing from the present administrative ystem. As to the Policy Statement, A.J.Stong (Hon.Sec.) states the terms of lease renewal have been in doubt all year. However, following sanctioningof the Marina proposals, discussions between Terry Hallam and Mr. Sparrow have resulted in the lease being extended under the current terms for one more year. The Committee will, in the year to come, enter negotiations which, they hope, will result ina strong and stable club with a permanent clubhouse and improved facilities. For this reason, the Committee will recommend that Terry Hallam be elected for an additional year, despite the fact that his normal 3-year term of office will have expired. The 3rd Racing Class theme jis taken up by John Witter. After much debate, the Sailing Committee recommend Points Series racing for GP14, Hornet and Snipe classes as well as the existing Enterprise and Fleetwind classes. Torches and Mirrors will also be able to have their own races but will not be encouraged as racing classes. The Handicap Class will continue to have races but Points Series races will be held for any other class able to raise sufficient support. Terry Hallam takes ‘the stand' again on Work or Pay. He outlines the usual problem of ‘lots of work and lots of things to maintain; lots of members but too few helpers’. In fact, he points out that ‘the workers’ are largely the same people, and same number, as when the club moved to Stansgate 3 years earlier. Terry reminds everyone that over the 14-year (?) existence of the club, the subscription has remained at 10/- (full Marconi Members) compared to increases of 2,3 or 4-fold for other clubs. The question is posed; do we remain a ‘do it yourself' club or do we employ full/part-time staff ? Terry points out that managing the club of our size (600 members) "..is a business and requires the application of proper management principles”. I think we've had echoes of that in recent years. Finally the Committee recommends the members to accept the choice of "TO PAY" - now that is a surprize. November/December - the Laying Up Supper switched from Baddow to Waterhouse Lane "where the manageress and chef produced a most excellent meal". Well, do I detect some disatisfaction with the Baddow venue ? Was my ‘jibe' in last month's Navigans Past 1964 a bit nearer the truth than I thought ? However, do I also detect

14. a note of disatisfaction with 'the style' of the Laying Up Supper ? I quote "....within seconds of the band starting.....several couples were dancing". That must be good surely ? Maybe it depends upon how they were dancing, for the reporter goes on to say "What a pity then that so much of the remaining 2% hours, especially the last %-hour, was taken up with the buffet, raffle, Knees up Mother Brown, Hokey Cokey, Conga, etc.." Now I remember fromthe late '70s and early '80s, some (well, most) Laying Up Suppers became somewhat 'boisterous' , particularly one year when 'the antics' of the Mirror crowd drew forth a letter of ‘comment’ in Navigans. However, apart from the ‘Mirror Mob', the real noisey ones were the ‘Hornet Hustlers'; a tendency to ‘over indulegence' might be the way to put it. Nevertheless, the reporter ends by saying "Thank you, the organisers, for a most enjoyable evening". - apart, I suppose, for the last 2% hours ! On the sailing front, a notice asking anyone interested in forming a Hornet Fleet in the club to contact Julian Bigden and/or his crew Mike Turner. Julian Bigden ? Mike Turner ? Hornet Fleet ? Ah! Now that explains all the commotion above. Those two quiet, gentlemanly, ‘family members' we saw at the club in 1991, were not always so - at least, not from the tales I've been told of the ‘good old days' in the ‘60s when the club was a bit younger, and so were they. An extensive prize list shows that Ian Shaw not only won the Cadet Trophy, the Enterprise Points Series, and was lst winner of the Helmsman of the Year Trophy, but also was 2nd in the Pilots Cup and 3rd in the Marconi Challenge Cup. As I've mentioned before, Cadet members throughout the club history have had the temerity to show little respect for our feelings by winning our trophies. No wonder Jack B initiated the over-40s race, and even that is threatened these days with the unofficial 'under 40s' race at the same time. Ah! Well! Maybe we'd better stay in the clubhouse and be wise from the comfort of the bar. Peter Darney actually won the ‘over 40s'race with Brian Tillotson 2nd and Mrs J.Reeve 3rd. All received 1 dozen Export Ale as a prize, so who needs silver trophies, just hand me the opener. At the AGM, Terry Hallamwas (re)elected Commodore, Nick Tovey Vice Commodore and Stan Allerton Rear Commodore/ Hon.Treasurer combined. John Witter was re-elected Sailing Sec. Yet another note stating that an extremely large number of people have still not paid their 1965 racing fees. Finally, a happy end to the year with the announcement of the engagement of John Witter and Eleanor Eldridge. So that's who Eleanor Eldridge is ,but I must admit I had my suspicions. Anyway, it just shows what a Norfolk Broads holiday can do to people. Congratulations Eleanor and John. KkKKKK KK KKK KE KEKKKKKKKKKEK PS to the Navigans Past 1964 (October '91 Navigans) JACK IS VERY DEFINITELY NOT LATE, My apologies to Jack Reeve for describing him as 'the late' in Navigans Past 1964; he rang me from his home in Devon to assure me he was anything but late. I can only plead temporary insanity brought on by the need to meet Maureen's publication ‘latest date’ for the October Navigans. Apologies also to Jack's many friends in the MSC who, not unnaturally, were rather alarmed by the somewhat exaggerated statement. Ah! Well! I can ‘tick off' a few more names of those I know who read 'Navigans Past’. KKKKKKKKKKKK RKKKEKKKKKKKK "BUNG 1T MY WAY" My appeal for ‘archive material’ has produced very satisfactory results, the most satisfying being that I now have the files from the very beginning of the MSC (even though 'the very beginning' is a debatable point). The Inaugural Meeting of the "Sailing Section of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club" was held on 18 April,1952. This, by happy coincidence, means that the club's 40th Anniversary willbe on Saturday, 18th April, 1992, which is the weekend of the 1992 Easter Series. Surely a cause for celebration ? The first club races were held on 12 July, 1952. However, I am mystified by the "honours board" of Commodore's Past and Present in the clubhouse which lists Commodores for 1950 and 1951. Presumably, an ‘unofficial' Sailing Section existed during those two years. If so, does anyone still have the ‘archive material' for those years ? If anyone has any additional archive material of any nature, please let me have it rather than lose if or throw it away. My thanks to Ron Greygoose, Robbie Sims and John Weedon who have provided archive material to date. Mike Boreham

2. S NOTES COMMODORE’ By the time that you receive this edition of Navigans, we will have held this year’s Annual General Meeting. You will have elected the new Committee to manage the affairs of the Club for the next twelve months. It seems that it was only yesterday that I wrote my first Commodore's notes and it is hard to realise that three years have passed since then. Now that the time has come to step down, I would like to reflect on some of the events of the last three years and the reasons why I have enjoyed serving the Club, despite the occasional frustration. I believe that one of the main reasons is “the occasional frustrations". Obviously it is disappointing to the Committee when its ideas are not backed by the Membership, and sometimes I have allowed this to show, but in our Club it is very rare for this to happen. The two instances that come to mind are firstly the problems over the bye law and the start line. Sometimes it is necessary for the Committee to go ‘over the top’ and for the Members to bring it back in line. I believe that this was such a case and that the resulting compromise this year has improved the situation a lot although there is probably more work for next year’s Committee to do. The second was the plans to develop the site. In this case the response was all positive in that, at the Meeting we held in April this year, you clearly indicated how you would like to see us proceed. Again this has given your future Committees a clear way to proceed. I think that these 'frustrations’ demonstrate one of the main reasons that I have enjoyed serving you. It is the fact that when there is a problem, the resulting discussion is made in a positive and constructive manner and not done in a derogatory way. Such situations do demonstrate that we are all able to act together and discuss opposing views to the benefit of the whole Club. Another aspect which has made the job enjoyable is the tremendous support that all of you have given to myself and the various Committees. This has varied from supporting sailing events; supporting by helping at such events; helping at working parties; and helping with all manner of other projects. It is noticeable that in our Club, people approach the Committee and say "I have this idea for the Club and would like to organise it’; too often elsewhere it would be expressed as ’I have this idea, why doesn’t the Committee do.....’ Lastly it comes from the mixture of sailing that we offer and our joint desire to ensure that we continue to offer such a mix. There cannot be many Clubs today who cater for Cruiser and Dinghy sailing from the keen racing to the mucking about. Any Club that can provide for its members events such as East Coast Piers, Regatta, Camping Fortnight, Cruising in Company, Creek Hopping, etc. and satisfy the needs of so many different types of sailing must have a great future. I hope that I hand on to my successor a healthy situation and that we all give him and his Committees the continuing level of support that I have enjoyed. I will close by thanking every one of you for this help and support and wish you all good sailing for the future. Thanks WV.Pe, N.T. Pembleton

1991 HIGHLIGHTS OF A SOLO YEAR 1. Winter Project. Not one but two Portakabins have been cleared out, made weatherproof and fitted out for Race Control. Great fun demolishing the old wooden one with the Cat Fleet Chair Gang - we nearly burnt the cold Revenue Hut to the ground with our bonfire. &. Social Do’s Dirmer at the Cross Keys, Roxwell; Ten Pin Bowling at Southend Pier and the Dinner at Stansgate started the year. The latter was hosted by our Entertainment Manager Tim Sweet and Master "Italian’ Chef Martin Hall. Summer BBQ's, hosted by Ron Greygoose and Geoff Josey gave us some pleasant evenings after Sunday sailing. 3. Team Racing 8 Saloists, 1 ex-Scalo Helmsperson, and 5 guesting Cats made up four teams for a six race series on Saturday 20th July. The event turned cut to be one of the best team racing events I can remember at Stansgate. On the water, judging by Mike Boreham, several interesting penalties, mainly due to superb luffing by Simon Liddington, I’m trying to forget that Larry Botheras’ team won, but it was close. 4. Marconi Open, 21/22 September Our Oper Meeting attracted 11 regular Solo helms and 4 visitors. We also persuaded Tom Ashley, Damian Boreham and Jane Williams to join in with borrowed Solos. To complete our total entry of 19 boats, Graham Richmond brought along the Solo he had just finished building. Strong winds, gusting Force 6 at times, made it difficult for the inexperienced helms but made very interesting sailing for the fleet. Our Race Officer, Steve Keeble, gave us good Clear starts with his no-go box and set excellent challenging courses for the conditions. Unfortunately Graham Richmond bent his new mast on the Saturday sca we don’t know how fast his new boat is yet. The visitors went away happy with first and second prizes: lst Malcolm Gandy - Halfway YC; 3rd Roger Smith - Marconi SC end Alan Husk - Halfway YC; 4th John Salmon - Marconi SC Sth Simon Liddington - Marconi SC 3. Points Series The serious bit is all about Club Racing, so congratulations to our main Points Series Winners: Jahr Salmon - Spring "Meteor Trophy" Johri Rutherford - Summer "Qne Up Cup" Ron Greygoose - Autumn "Captains Trophy" 6. Solent Cruising The Sola Fleet manned half the fleet of three Sigma 36's in this year’s Solent thrash. Good sailing on Saturday and Sunday in severe Gale Force 39 winds , Saturday’s beat up te Yarmouth 1.0.W. was exciting but the surfing run back on Sunday was even better. All who helmed reckoned they had acquired a little extra life experierice. Thanks ta Mike Hellewell for a super weekend - pity about the two sails we tore = and the winch that flew to bits under the strain. 7. Qper Meetings Marconi Soloists were present at the following open meetings: Thorpe Bay; Inland Nationals at Rutland Water; Fishers Green; Ardleigh; King George; Half Way; Bewl Valley; and Hayling Island. Johri Salmon got third place at beth Fishers Green and Ardleigh in light winds. At the Thorpe Bay World Championships with 65 entries, Simor Liddington came 3énd, followed by Roger Smith 39th and John Salmon 41st. Ex Marconi Soloists also did well - Malcolm Gandy coming 6th. Colin Wilsmore getting a £150 cheque for the most impraved helm and Dave Nixon coming well up the fleet at 20th. Malcolm Stuart

Of Catamara ns and Crews... Nothing very auch to report this month, with the winds generally maintaining the drift category, I think we're all getting pretty fed up with it. The procession seems to be carrying on much as before in club racing with Glynn and Duckmanton being boringly repetitive, although a couple of times the Dart 18 fleet has upset the apple cart. The main exception to the drift was (of course) the weekend of the Grafham Cat Open, when Saturday saw the winds averaging 6-7, and Sunday it had moderated to a steady 4-5! Sunday actually seemed very much quieter than Saturday..... It was great to see such good Marconi representation, with Robin & Lisa in the 5.9’s, Grant Piggott in the Tornado’s, Steve and Tom and us in the Fast Handicap, Lee and Jenny sailing a borrowed 4.9, Lucy and Tom in the 16's and last but not least Paul Ellis in the 15’s. I was quite impressed with their ability to cope with a lot (around 2007) boats by setting two sets of concentric courses. I don’t intend to dwell too much on the weekend other than to mention the state of ay crew on Sunday amorning..... and to hald my hand up for the season’s silly capsize! I got the tiller extension stuck in the back of my trapeze harness on a The final weekend of the main part of the season did give us a change. Easterly winds and enough breeze to trapeze (single a.w., double p.a.). We had a low turnout though, only eleven Fast Handicap, and five Slow. I don’t think we need to justify our existence this season!!! Congratulations to Steve Glynn and Tom on their win in the series and to Tom's (joint?) success in the Mugg’s Mug. It made me realise the enormous strain put on Scopes, Mooring Buoys and Pennnants. Yes, I was out trying to rescue a breakaway yacht. We must be mad making large investments in our boats and then leaving them out there to the mercy of the elements! Our problems, it seems to me, have this year come about by breakages on top parts, not the ground chain.
