SEAMANSHIP AWARD The Seamanship Award 15 a new award, donated by our retiring Commodore, Neil Fembleton in November last year, and is ta be granted annually to a Club Member whe has performed a feat of outstanding seamanship. Many stories have been told over the years of the skills shown by some of cur members in times of difficulty and danger wher, afloat, and it was decided that these feats should have some recognition. The 1991 Seamanship Award goes jointly ta two younger members af the Club, Andrew Rabirsorn and Nielson Barnard, both aged 16 at the time in question, and here is the story, supplied by Corrad Barnard, of their achievement. Ori cur Cruise this year tc France we chanced ta meet up with an elderly couple whe had taken their Westerly Tempest on an extended holiday from the Fambridge Yacht Station toa Holland, and then on through to France. The lady was very = sprightly for her age; being the driving force behind their sailing, and in fact conducted all the functions necessary to sail the yacht, save the navigation. The man, a retired doctor, was unable to venture ontca the foredeck due to a physical disability. He had great preblems in getting on and off his boat, and as a result was rarely seen anywhere except in the cockpit. _ We had been in their company off and on during our Cruise and during that time had become aware that he suffered from a number of quite serious complaints, apart from the disability. It was in Boulogne, on preparing to make the crossirig back ta Ramsgate, that he called me cover and asked if they could travel back in convoy with ourselves, and could we keep ar eye out for his wife. He explained that his health had taken a turn for the worse, he could not get off the boat to take the ferry home which he dearly wished tea da, and he had an almost venomous distrust of French doctors and refused tc call one. What he did agree readily to do was to accept extra crew for his yacht. For this purpose beth Andrew Rabinson and my son Nielsen Barnard showed no hesitation in wishing ta help. As a direct result both boys, who are 16 years ald, a took strange boat and sailed it from Boulogne across the English Channel to Ramsgate - a 7 hour trip - helming i hour on, 1 hour of Fs utilising all the instruments, radia, etc. without any assistance, thus allowing the lady toa concentrate her attention or her husband. The bays in fact beat George and myself into Ramsgate by quite a respectable margin. Adventures like these may well happen away from the view of interested Club so Members, we will be relying on the participants themselves their famil companions to let us know their stories. —- Ed. “ j ’ a

10. NAVIGANS PAST 1968 - the road to ‘sailing success’ is paved with.....£1,000-worth of bitumen - hey guys, if you want to pick up a couple of birds, keep your eyes peeled as you pass Mayland Marine ! - here's ‘mud in your eye’, but not for Connie. January - Brian Martin is the new Cadet Skipper. He notes that in 1967 the club had 53 Cadet Members, of which 39 were aged 10-14 and 14 aged 14-17 - but he bemoans the fact that the number of Cadets appearing regularly at Stansgate rarely exceeds a dozen or so. In 1992. we probably have many more 'Cadet Members' than 53 but | doubt we could boast a ‘regular turnout’ of a dozen - despite the very full annual one-week Cadet Training put on over the last ten years or so. It seems a shame, when we have three rather nice Mirror Fleet trophies "just beggin' to be won" each year and the Mirror offers such fine sailing for the parent/child combination. Still, each to his or her own; we're a boating club so nobody has to race - but it does seem a shame. In addition, Brian mentions that only 50 dinghies raced regularly out of a total of 114 registered - "less than half". Now, I'd have thought nearly 50% was a pretty good turn-out over the season; in modern-day figures (1991) that would give us about 70 (monohul]) dinghies out over the racing season. Ah! would that it had been so ! February - the Editor reminds all members of the need to drive slowly on the Stansgate road to reduce the wear-and-tear. Also the need to keep the dinghy park free of rubbish such as bottles, jars and tins. These days you could add crisp packets and bits of plastic. March - an item called "Foc's] Chatter" by Little-Hideout (sounds like a Red Indian - sorry, an Ethnic Original Inhabitant of North America) mentions that one member is busy fitting out their boat in the sitting room. In the past I recall with our Mirrors "fitting them out" by “fitting them in" a spare bedroom. It reminds me of the story of how (former member) Vic Braybrooke came to name his Mirror which he built himself. Some of the work of curing the fibre-glass resin, etc, ‘necessitated’ doing it in his sitting room. Vic's wife, Denise, unwittingly named the boat when she called it (probably more than once) a "Flaming Pest". Eric Payne draws attention to the fact that Osea Island is up for sale. He also mentions that, in the 1920's, the Marconi Company had considered buying Osea for a research station but, instead, erected a hut near the golf course at East Mersea. Clearly 'the powers that be' at that time prefered ‘the putter’ of a golf club rather than ‘the putter' of an outboard engine - or of a loose leech in a fair breeze. What a different tale for the MSC had a 1920s deal been done ! April - a successful Cheese and Wine party is reported, witha talk and film by Mr J C Kemp (owner of the barge 'Thalatta') about life on board the barge 'Memory' - a most appropriate name, I think. Anyway, it was also thanks to Mike Turner, Brian, Leonie, Rosemary and Noreen for the arrangements . On the sailing side, Peter Batey (Sailing Sec) announces the Helmsman of the Year Trophy will be contested by a series of 8 handicap races held throughout the year. May - Pat Black bemoans the fact that he rushed down to Stansgate after work for the Wednesday mid-week race - and nobody else turned up. He offers to ‘co-ordinate’ those who think they'd like to try the mid-week races. Commodore Jack Bigden tells us that the estimated cost of resurfacing the road has risen from £750 to £1,000. He reminds everyone that, apart from the 10/= additional levy on all members (approx. 300) it had been hoped the "regular users" would voluntarily contribute a bit more. Alas, the hoped-for members target of £450 towaras the total needed has only produced £280 - but the target sum has now increased to £700. We are also reminded of the 15. m.p.h speed limit. (NB. I believe MASC were to contribute the remainder of the estimated £1,000). The ladies who run the galley (Eve Whent and friend Chris) have to be 'picked up' from Mayland Marine. To attract a lift fromapassing member, they display their "G" flag (their what ??) on a nearby telegraph pole. The second Helm of the Year race was a tribute to determination. Held in freshening winds and very steep seas, half the twelve competitors retired early, and were followed later by the rest - so it was thought !| The Race Officer packed up shop and went home, but Julian Bigden was stil] out on the course. He had lost a shroud up Goldhanger Creek, sailed ashore to effect makeshift repairs and finished the race just 18 minutes inside the 3-hour time limit. That puts a new slant on the 'time limit' question; one usually assumes it will only be appropriate in near-windless conditions. June an obvious 'tightening-up of rules' is in progress. In future, members will have to ask the OOD to get access to club equipment and property, and also to the Store Shed known as ‘Pete's Palace’ (but which 'Pete' ?) Surely it wasn't our modern-day Pete Clayton (far toeyoung in those days) or Peter Flook (well, we won't mention age) ? Members are reminded that all visitors must be signed in, even if they do not enter the club-house. It is enough that they be onthe club site. Finally, Jack Bigden refutes the 'old chestnut' grumble of Associate Members that they pay a much higher sailing sub than do Ordinary (ie. Marconi) Members. Jack reminds them that whilst 2 guineas of the Associate sailing fees go to the MASC, the Marconi Members pay 9d per week to the MASC Lie, 39/= or £1.95) - presumably in addition to their sailing sub., so it all works out more even than at first sight.

11. July - a dinghy cruise towards Mersey is planned. Our Editor, Eleanor Witter, again gets exasperated by ‘the men members' who continue to fail to circulate 'their' Navigans to their wives (presumably one wife per man ? Eleanor writes "MEN - how do you expect to have Wives who not only endure but actually enjoy sailing or any other Club activities if you don't take Navigans home to keep them informed". In these modern times things are, of course, a little different. In the Boreham abode we have a sort of rugby scrum with no hold barred to get ‘first look'. If I domanage to get-holdof it in pristine condition, I usually dash for the 100, lock myself in and let them beat on the door in 'their' fury. The 3rd Annual Marconi Regatta attracted about the same number of boats as in 1967 (“over 100") but fewer classes, with (as usual) more visitors than club boats. Yet another dinghy cruise by Fred Partlett, this time around to Burnham in a Wayfarer, thence back to Colne and Brightlingsea, then on to Wivenhoe before eventually returning to Stansgate. The trip apparently lasted 7 days, with 6 nights sleeping ‘on board' and only two meals purchased ashore in a cafe. Fred writes “We had no newspapers..... " - but he doesn't say who were the other "we" people ? I must say, however, that I am very impressed by Fred's adventurous spirit - and (presumably) with that same adverturous spirit of other members of his family. The list of club dinghies shows 26 Enterprise, 25 GP14s, 12 Hornets, 4 Fleetwind (the demise of the club's oldest and original fleet ?), 6 catmarans (since then they've bred like rabbits), 12 Mirrors and 37 other assorted dinghies, including Gull 575 (H.A.Taylor) which in recent years, I believe, was given to the club by Mr Taylor and is currently in the tender loving care of the Caruth family. August - true to her word of a previous year, there is no August Navigans from Eleanor due to holidays. PS. Maggie and I were on holiday too; our honeymoon to be exact. September - Mr AD Currah writes to complain of finding a hole in his Mirror and, from the tone of his letter, he clearly believes it must have been "someone" who failed to confess it. However, although sympathetic, Eleanor points out that damage to other dinghies can occur when storms or high winds blow a dinghy over, or a dinghy's own trailer might cause such damage. The problem of boats not being tied down securely has been a problem since the club was founded and I understand that quite recently one of the catamarans went ‘blow-about' and sustained considerable damage but apparently did not damage any other boats - as luck would have it ! A 'write up' by Connie Bigden of her advertures of crewing for husband, Jack, in the over-40s race which seems to have included the (now) traditional 'stop-over' at the Jolly Sailor for re-fueling. Connie, being well aware of the mud at Heybridge, decided to 'stay put' until her helm had pulled the boat well into the sea wall. However, Tom Gaskell asked his crew (and wife) Joan to ‘bring the anchor'. Joan gaily jumped out up to her knees in mud - and Connie joyfully recalls the pleasure of hearing crew tell the helm well] and truly ‘off! in no uncertain terms. Things don't change; in the 1991 race I asked Maggie to jump out - and she did, almost up to her armpits in water and mud. After that, I turned my hearing aid off; after all, how was I to know it was deep and dirty ? It looked quite near the sea wall to me . Jack Bigden proposes a whole week of club “organised activity" (presumably for the 1969 programme) with racing, cruising and picnics. Was this the first thoughts of camping week, to eventually turn into camping fortnight ? October - a request from "the anxious wife of a harried organiser" for people to buy Laying-Up Supper tickets. It seems 'the organisers' had a fixed price in mind when they visited the Heybridge Country Club to discuss arrangements but couldn't resist an “absolutely superb menu which cost just a little more", plus an "extra good band". The result - they need to sell 60 extra tickets to pay for it all. The price of the tickets was an astronomical 32/6. A note tells us that the last (ie. September) Navigans was sent to 354 members (including 84 Associates, etc) at a postage cost of 21/=; this October issue has cost 28/= in postage. Dudley Currah (of letter fame ?) reportsthat 9 Mirror members have decided to form a Mirror Fleet with Murray Todd as Fleet captain. Murray later was a stalwart of the Hornet Fleet. On the sailing side, Ken Beavins won the Mona's Cup. Finally, the GossipColumn states "Robbie Sims was seen driving Joan to church in his Rolls-Royce decorated with wedding ribbon. Is it Robbie and Joan that we should congratulate or Julian and Jill Bigden who were married at Galleywood later the same day ?" So Maurice Greatrex was right when he recalled Robbie and his Rolls-Royce. November - Leonie Carlisle and Gordon Golding announce their engagement. Sadly, Gordon died in August, 1991, but Leonie is happy to share the celebration of her engagement with us some 23 years later. December- the 1968 AGM was attended by more than 100 members - who agree a levy of 10/= Joining Fee for new ordinary Members to help the Road Fund. Nick Tovey is elected a Vice President (a note says " to add young blood to the three ancient marinas (?) of Jack Bigden, Terry hallam and Eric Payne). Membership in 1968 increased by 80 to 599 . With 7 new Associate Members admitted, the waiting list for Associate Membership continues to increase. 1969 will see the new posts of Dinghy park Secr etary i i the post of Social Secretary for 1969 has not yet been filled. A G y and Equipaent Officer - a Mike Boreham

SPOTS GYDE TU THE ROOLS fs my boss said in Navigans last month, I’ve learnt a bit listening to him talking to himself about the Rule Book over the last couple of winters and he’s let me loose at the keyboard of the WP. I’ve also watched you lo ¢ out there in the summer and reckon you need help!!!) The Boss aakes use of a couple of books to help simplify the Rules such as The Rule Book by Eric Twiname (updated by Bryan Willis) and Paul Elystrom’s The Racing Rules. These are very useful later on, but what I would like to do is to outline in a series of “one-liners” the basic skeleton of the Racing Rules. Rule Si Rule infringement If you break the rules vou will be penalized! (See, 1 told you it was simple) Rule 32 Serious Damage Ho matter how auch you have right of way you must avoid a collision Rule 33 Contact between Yachts!) Racing If you collide it’s someone’s fault (NB Rule infringements have no bearing on legal liability in case of accidents) Rule 34 Maintaining Rights if someone's broken a tule you still give them the same treatment for Right of Way Rule 35 Limitations on Altering Course ¥hen someone is giving way to you you can’t just alter course to stop them being able to (there are a couple of exceptions to this, read them yourself) flule 36 Opposite Tacks - Basic Rule The shortest rule in the book, Port keeps clear of Starboard! Rule 37 Same Tack When the two boats are overiapped, windward keeps clear of leeward. When not, boat astern keeps clear of boat ahead. Rule 35 Same Tack - Luffing after the start If you are a Daginner at racing don’t pass close to windward of someone! (see diagram) Rule 39 Same Tack You shall not sail below your “proper course” (defining that can be a can of worms) when another boat 15 within 3 doatlengths Rule 40 Luffing before the start Stay out of the way until you've got used to “mixing if ° on the start line!! Rule 41 Changing Tacks - Tacking & Gybing Tacking and gybing have specific rule book definitions and are not what you or I would consider as tacking or gybing, i.e a tack starts at the moment you are head to wind (before that you are luffing) and ends when the sails are filled on the new tack. A gybe starts “when the boom crosses the centreline” and also finishes when the sails are filled on the new side! li! 41.1 Anyway if you're doing either you have to keep clear of boats on a tack. 41.2 You can’t tack or gybe near another boat if that boat has to start it’s manoeuvre before you've finished yours 41.3 If you are tacking or gybing you have to prove you'd completed it if the other guy protests 41.4 If two boats tack or gybe simultaneously the one on the left keeps clear! Any questions? Watch this space for rounding sarks and obstructions next aonth...... L. Botheras

De He He Ree He He HE He He ICH IKE FEKETE IEE EFFI FEI HISAR IBIS KERR e * * 40 YEARS AGO - 18th Avril, 1952 * * * * The Inaugural Meeting of * * * * The Marconi Sailina Club * * * PKK K KIKI HK IK KIKI KKK KK KAKI KIRKE EKER EEE AERERER ¥ Minutes of the Inaugural Meeting held on 18 April, 1952 The Meeting opened at 6.0 p.m. In view of the interest made evident at the preliminary meeting held on 28th March, 1952, the above meeting was held with the express object of forming a Sailing Section of the M.A.S.C. Some 23 interested persons were present, and the business of forming the Section was proceeded with immediately. Since only a short time had elapsed from the initial thoughts on this subject, and as it is too early to have decided the full scope of the activities of the Section, at an early stage of the meeting it was obvious that a working committee should be formed whose function is would be to plan those activities. This action was agreed by all present. As to the constitution of this committee, it was unanimosly agreed that it should comprise the fol lowing:- Chairman, Hon.Secretary, Hon.Treasurer (and) 6 Committee Members. The meeting duly proceeded to elect these officers and committee members as under:- Chairman: Mr Hallam proposed by Mr Greatrex seconded by Mr Garrett Hon. Treasurer: Mr Nichols ? i ? Hon.Secretary: Mr Gill ? ? Committee Members: Mr Jackson * "Mr Colchester " "Mr Mercer Mr Tate ‘i "Mr Baines i "Mr Nichols Mr Quilter . "Mr Greatrex * "Mr Frost Mr Colchester 4 "Mr Garrett " "Mr Quilter Mr Daines , "Mr Quilter 8 "Mr Greatrex Mr Christensen * "Mr Nichols as "Mr Garrett The Working Committee having been achieved, the meeting went on to discuss certain essential matters which comprised: - Name of Club - By a majority vote it was decided that as a section of the M.A.S.C. it would be known as the "Sailing Section". When operating in its own field the section would be known as the "Marconi Sailing Club". This was also agreed on a majority vote. Object of Club - It was unanimously agreed that the object of the club shall be to promote the sport of boat or ship sailing in every form, embracing social and instructional aspects. There should be facilities for repairs, and design and construction should be encouraged. It is to be hoped that during the winter months lectures shall be arranged covering all fields of the sport, such as seamanship, navigation, and design. Perhaps the most important aim that was expressed was that there should be full co-operation between members so that they can work to their mutual benefit. Subscriptions - It having been generally agreed that all members should automatically pay their membership of the parent club, namely the M.A.S.C., the meeting went on to consider the subscriptions of the sailing section. The result, after some alternatives had been debated and put to the vote, was as follows:- Subscription Amount Proposed Seconded Full Members (with or without their own boat) 10s. Od. Mr Garrett Mr Thomas Associate Members Not more Mr Daines Mr Byatt than 17s.6d Family Group (to include wife and children only) 5s. Od Mr Garrett Mr Christensen The matter of guests was deferred until a further meeting. Next Meeting - It was agreed that the next general meeting of the Section should take place on 15th May, 1952, at 6 p.m. Before then a meeting is to be arranged for the committee. KREKKKKKKKK During the course of the above meeting those present were made aware of a very generous offer by the Commodore of the Burnham Sailing Club, by Mr Christensen. Mr Christensen, on behalf of the Commodore, let it be understood that the Burnham Sailing Club would welcome members of the Marconi Sailing Club at any time, and an offer was made for possibly boats from time to time, and crew vacancies at almost any time. It was generally agreed that this very kind invitation should be accepted with alacrity, and it is intended that a small party should go to Burnham-on-Crouch in the near future to discuss the matter and to personally thank the Commodore. A letter is being sent in the meantime. The meeting closed at 8.15 p.m. Mike Boreham

Well’S DISEASE - notes from RYA Information Leaflet, 1989 Between SO to 60% of rats carry and excrete the organism Leptospira ictera- haemorrhagiae in their urine. Infection with the crganism causes an illness which has been known to result in death of 10% of cases. There has been a recent increase in the incidence of the disease - 133 cases notified in 1988 compared with 68 in 1987 and 32 in 1986. Formerly occurring mainly among sewage or abbatcir workers and miners, recent records show that the majority of fatalities are now related ta water activities. Ir 19859 there have beer 19 deaths of which no fewer than 13 were associated with water users. The nature of leisure water activity means that the average of this at-risk group is fairly young, with most cases occurring in the 13 - 42 age group. ABOUT THE ILLNESS The organism enters the human body through breaks in the skin such as cuts, blisters and abrasions or via the lining of the nose, throat or alimentary tract. The incubation period is 7 - 13 days and the disease starts with a_ fever, muscular aches and pains, lass of appetite and vomiting with prostration. It is vital that the doctor be told of any water-borne activity as the symptoms are easily confused with those of flu and if the patient has a ‘clean’ occupation the possibility of Well’s Disease my be overlooked in the early stages. Subsequent bruising of the skin, sare eyes, nose bleeds and jaundice may eccur. The fever lasts about five days amnd may be followed by significant deterioration. Treatment is usually by Penicillin Antibiotic. (In 1989 the advice was: Laboratory testing of blood will confirm the diagnosis, but this may take undue time in an ordinary hospital. Send samples direct to: The Leptospirosis Reference Unit, Public Health Laboratory, County Hospital, Hereford, HRi 2ER. Tel. 0432-277707, here they will be tested within 24 hours.) RATS AND THE ILLNESS The rat is a creature of the water’s edge. The leptospira organism is passed im urine and, while it does not live Long in dry conditions, it can survive for some time in water. Salt water scon kills off the organism but there is a Significant risk in tidal waters such as the lower parts of the Thames and other rivers. The risk increases upstream and is greatest in canals, ponds or areas caf slowly draining water. There is a Significant risk to users of river banks or reservoir edges. WATER USERS Sailors, boardsailors, canoceists, carsmen, swimmers or Fisherman are at risk in any area with a population of rats. Any skin wound ar blister, cld cr rew, may be infected if immersed in water polluted with the organism. GENERAL CARE: Handrails, steps and walkways should be checked for gaps, nails or rough edges that may Cause minor wounds. All Members should make every effort ta see that food residues are removed = fram Clubhouse, boat and trailer parks or picnic areas. A happy well-nourished rat will produce more rats. Wear shoes te protect the feet from cuts. Dor’?t allow water to collect inside your dinghy, it may be wet but it may not all be water! (The same caution also necessary with pools of water collected on the cutside of boat covers, i.e. don’t let it come inta contact with any wourds. ) Cruiser Owners: if you ever have tc come ashore clutching at the jetty from your tender, you toca are at risk. Waterprocf surgical plasters of an adequate size should be used to cover old skin wounds before going afloat or ta the dinghy park. Such protection will also apply toa club working parties wher members may be clearing old structures or other hazards. Every sailing club should have available to members at all times a supply of clean fresh water tec wash wounds, ard a shower for those wha may have fallen into suspect water.

8. Art - for art's sake. Maggie and I happened to be in Amsterdam for a couple of days in late-1991 and took the opportunity to t visit the Rembrandt Exhibition. Now, I've no doubt it was all ‘great art' but, to be honest, I got a bit bored with room after room of what seemed to be rather drab paintings, and I got far more pleasure from viewing the 'brighter' paintings of some of Rembrandt's 'pupils'. Thus, apart from revealing that I am somewhat lacking in artistic sophistication and could never be the Keeper of the Queen's Pictures (to be absolutely Blunt), it also illustrates the old adage that what is one man's Matisse is another man's Poussin . Once safely back in England and looking forward to the activities and adventures of the forthcoming sailing programme, I wondered if some of the club's amateur artists would like to ‘get together’ at the club during 1992 for one or two days collective painting ? I haven't done any ‘serious’ painting since my school days, but I've recently taken it up again and would like to try some 'Stansgate scenes'. However, to be frank, I find the prospect of sitting in solitary state at Stansgate a bit daunting; I'd rather like the support of fellow club artists and ‘hide in the crowd'. As an extension of this, perhaps 'the club' would allow its artistic members to exhibit their works at the club on one or two of the 'main event' days, such as the New Members Evening (9th May) and East Coast Piers Race (26th July) - just to add an extra dimension to the events. I wouldn't expect more than 'a handful' of fellow club artists to respond to this suugestion and | emphasise jt would only be one or two days in the year for the ‘collective paint-in' . So, if you members with hidden artistic talents would like to get acquainted with like members - and perhaps like the prospect of exhibiting (but without any suggestion of 'competition') - then please phone me. Don't forget - Art for art's sake - we'd leave the competitions to the photographers. Mike Boreham (0277 [redacted]) KReKKKKKKKE KEKKKKKKKK A letter to the Editor "Abandon Marriage - let's all be single" Dear Maureen, Despite the fact that I've written many Navigans articles in the past, I've never before written a letter "tothe Editor’. So what has inspired this particular personal 'first' ? It is simply that I wish to Propose that, as a club, we should abandon marriage! Those who know me well will, I suspect, detect a certain amount of ‘tongue in cheek' in this letter and, indeed, it is not intended to be read too seriously. Nevertheless, I feel that the club's policy on marriage is not entirely logical and maybe it is time to change it. "What policy on marriage ?" asks a bewildered and bemused Executive Committee. "What's he on about now ?" Read on, friend - al] will be revealed. The new MSC Rules adopted at the 1991 AGM include a definition of Family Member as a "Married Couple". Now, what is a "Married Couple ?" In the club's founding year of 1952 most people probably had a quite specific idea of what "married couple" meant and would expect to have a certificate to prove it (curiously, few, if any, have it framed and displayed on the wall - I wonder why ?). However, I suggest a 1952 concept of “married couple" carries little weight in 1992. How would you, the reader, define a married couple ? Would you demand certificated proof of ‘marriage’ or is it sufficient that people live together to be recognised as a de facto married state ? If not, why not ? As a matter of interest, has anmyMSC member every been ‘drummed out' for falsely claiming married status? Has a Family Membership application ever been refused on the grounds "but you are not married" or lack of proof of marriage ? The other curiousity of our membership rules is the inclusion of Married Couple" under Family Membership. What is a 'family' ? Can vou have ‘a family' without children ? If not, how come a (childless) Married Couple can be Family Members ? Why don't we simplify the Membership Rules by allowing each Full Member to nominate (at membership application or renewal date) a 'Permanent Guest' for the year, thus treating the married and unmarried Full Members in exactly the same way (for the same basic membership fee), abandon the meaningless ‘Married Couple' category but continue to rank children of Full Members to be Permanent Guests (but restore the age limit to 18 and under on 1 January of the membership year) - and maybe restore the privilege of Student Membership (for full-time students under 21 at lst January) at a particularly cheap rate so that they can 'legitimately' continue to use the club during the holiday periods, or maybe the previous privilege of including full-time students up to age 21 as 'Permanet Guests' under the single subscription of their parent ? Mike Boreham (married (with certificate), with children - and poor)

Os Of Catamarans and CrewS....see08 Well, folks, despite your attempts to stop these articles by electing me as Rear Commodore, the start of the new season and a few little incidents put me back in the mode of gossip columist. After all, who could not be driven to SOMETHING by the sight of our venerable Commodore getting into the 40th Anniversary swing by dressing in an imitation 50s schoo) uniform at the Fitting Out Party. I mean, I have to report on it due to the fact that so few of you were there.... an Caruth was also brave enough, but can you imagine the sight of lan and Mike playing CONKERS! The weekend had the tin hat put on it by gale force wind on the first Sunday of the season. Yes, I fully admit that I wimped out as well!! Fortunately weekend number 2 came to a good deal more with a nice southerly 3-4 in the morning followed by a slightly more strident 4-5/6. Team Nickalls provided the support services particularly capably, and set some fairly intricate little number to exercise the grey cells. It was extremely fortuitous that neither race lasted much more than an hour for this time in the season. I’m actually sitting here completely cream-crackered with pieces of spaghetti for arms. You see, the gusty conditions involved a fair old degree of mainsheet pumping and no one told me | needed a multi-gym at home in the closed season to keep the muscles going!! Anyway, the racing was pretty good, albeit not brilliantly supported. Lee and Jenny appeared to have eaten something for boat speed, but it also had a nasty wet side-effect!! John Tuckwell and Linda also seem to have been doing the bizz over the closed season, proving to be a real handful for the faster boats on a boat-for-boat basis. The course gave us some really good reaches - definitely Cat sailing “as she is spoke". I was knackered enough after that without the need for the gutsy increase in breeze in the afternoon. More capsizes, Lee and Jenny again, Pete Flook and David, just to name the ones I knew about. Caruth and I had our share of disasters; running aground, getting the jib snap-shackle caught on the diamonds, and finding the knot coming out of the traveller line.... Better checks next week!! Having said that, more mind blowing reaches with one or two tests of the reserve buoyancy in the bows of a Prindle 19! Let's hope that the rest of the season gives us more like this. Spring Points 5 & 6 gave us more of the same with a jolly Force 3 NW. This gave us Fast Cats the chance to try out the route to Number 3. Following Caruth and I giving an example of how to stall on the start line and to make a real pig’s ear of things, we all legged it into the middle distance. Having mucked up, we decided to split tacks with the rest of the fleet and found an ’ansum little lift. Fortunately, nobody else seemed to notice after rounding 3 and left us to our own devices inshore under Osea....in a superb private breeze!! L’equip Nickalls seemed not to have lost any talent over the winter but they had to hold second best to a certain Prindle 19 that modesty prevents me from naming!! Unfortunately, the success was short-lived because my tiller extension JUST touched the flag at Breezy.... Anyway, a super morning’s entertainment for all concerned. Nice to see a steady fleet of 5 Dart 15s showing regular attendance at this stage. Keep it up chaps. The afternoon looked from the shore to have a bit more breeze, possibly Force 4, a quick look aloft for the meteorologists amongst you would have revealed a bunch of nice little cumulus bubbling up (that means wind underneath, folks) and the cause of our enjoyment. Same course (plus an extra lap A-1-C-B) saw an interesting time with Nickalls again doing the bizz from the start. Another tight fight ensued between Lee and Sam Ashley, Steve Glynn ard Stuart Golding, Caruth and I, and, pleasingly, Vince and Andy. Caruth and I had an interesting time when, approaching C, the mainsheet caught on the shroud. I flicked it free and saw the remants of a split ring disappear into the briny!! A quick panic and fumble around, with Chris locating a replacement whilst my thumb remained strategically placed on the pin! Still, it was another superb day, Keep it up all, and let’s see the season go from strength to strength. KKKKKKKKEKEK KEKKKKKKKEK R.I.P. to "The Tree" (a tribute to an old and well-used feature of the MSC landscape) alas, suddenly cut-off and sadly terminated. At the working party on 15 March, Maggie was approached by a very young lad (of about 5) who lamented that "the bridge" had been removed from across the ditch and hoped it would be put back. "The bridge" was near to "the tree", andperhaps the lad was too young to also notice ‘the removal’ of the climbing tree which had stood by the telegraph pole which, itself, formed 'the bridee'. The tree had been used by generations of ‘pre-sailing' children who had climbed up, swung on, sat in - and occasionally fallen out of - its Sranches. When parents 'missed' their children , the first place to look was ‘the tree' and Mother's initial relief that all was safe and well was soon replaced by anxiety at the precarious nature . of their offspring's position. "Be careful up there" was the unhelpful advice; "Stop fussin' and let them play " Father woulc say, silently praying that the silly so-and-so's would not fall and break their necks. A modern climbing frame, carefully constructed and fitted with safety in mind, is a poor substitute for one of nature's own designs; rather like replacing the tea-lady with the high tech drink dispensing machine - that is before the tea-ladies all became tea-persons and the mid-morning tea-break lost a little of its charm and zest. "Thank you tree for all you did and the joy you gave. That you ‘had to qo’ there can be no doubt. You had clearly grown old and weary and seemed ready to fall as you swayed in the wind and rain. You looked far from your prime of life, and your limbs creaked and groaned as you fought to support the youthful loads which, in former years, you had accommodated with ease." Thus it was that "The Tree" was humanely put down, literally cut-off as it approached the winter of its life which had to be terminated in the interests of all concerned. I'm glad I'm not a tree. (A postscript to'Navigans Past 1967; see Navigans, February, 1992) Under the 'November' comment of Navigans Past, 1967, I revealed that on the way home from the Layina Up Supper, Commodore Jack Bigden had been stopped by the police because the boot of his car was open. The (presumably mobile) local gendarmerie must have thought they had ‘scored a hit' because in the back seat of the car sat a highly suspicious-looking character (Tim Bigden) surrounded by what was clearly the contents from the sideboard of the local manor house ie. a large collection of ‘family silver and assorted trephies'. Police suspicions must nave been further aroused when the driver (our Jack) was unable to quote the car's registration number, the car itself being a fast-looking Jaguar typically used by some of our London visitors as a 'get away' car. However, al] turned out well, although the police might have been disappointed to miss out on a ‘promotion opportunity’. It seems that Julian Bigden had won rather a lot of trophies in 1967, but had been unable to collect them in person at the Laying Up Supper, so Tim and Jack had collected them on his behalf (hence the large 'haul' on the back seat). Jack had borrowed Julian's car, hence not knowing the number. As for the ‘suspicious looking' Tim in the back, well, it was rather dark and no doubt he would have looked the epitome of innocence in the warmth of the daylight (as it streamed through the cell window). However, the mystery still remains; how many 'bodies' did Jack lose out of the open boot ? Mike Boreham

Apparently, the cars of Mike Turner, Peter Crick and Julian Bigden all suffered the buffets and trials of our modern technological life-style when they were all "hit by other vehicles" (well, it's always the other vehicle !). February - Fred Partlett (of 'long dinghy cruise' fame) must have felt it much safer by river than by road, for his is the 4th car to suffer from the “buffets.and trials of our modern...etc’. This all goes to show that all superstition is bunkum (touch wood and fingers crossed). March - amongst the winter meeting program was a talk by Fred (minda my car) Partlett on the subject of "Camping with a Wayfarer". I'm sure there must be some of our 1990s membership who maké long distance dinghy cruises; how about an article or two for Navigans ? There seems tbea genuine feeling amongst our current club leadership that dinghy cruising should receive a little more ‘official’ recognition in the sailing programme. However, getting back to the 1969 sailing programme, several new ideas emerge. Each racing class will have a (Sunday) Spring and Main Points Series (ie Enterprise, GP14, Mirror and Handicap) whilst the Hornet fleet will have one Points Series and an Invitation Points Series (Stone S C being those invited). In addition, an all-class Saturday Handicap Series will replace the former “individual spoon races". Stan Campbell (Cadet Skipper) hopes to encourage more cadets to sailing by persuading cruiser owners to take cadets (and parents) on trips, plus dinghy owners to lend boats for the cadet series races. Does Fred Partlett have a ‘long distance’ rival ? Brian Lidstone writes a letter describing his advertures in a Mirror since joining the MSC in 1968. He took part in the club dinghy cruise to Brightlingsea, went holiday sailing with the Mirror ‘all at sea' from Teignmouth to Torquay, and then took a trip from Stansgate to Clacton and back (presumably in the Mirror since it took him about 14 hours for the round trip). April - a note from Commodore, Jack Bigden, advising that the lease for the site will expire in December, 1969, and that the club hope to negotiate anew lease with the new landlord (Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge). May - Stan Cambell hopes to establish a "Cadet Corner" as a regular feature of Navigans. He was pleased with the turn-out for the (1st Cadet) Points race - but apologies for the short course ! For the next race, he hopes Julian Bigden will ‘follow round' to observe and then afterwards point out the errors to the cadets and offer useful tips, etc., so as to improve the quality of sailing. On the 'car denting' front, Dennis Boswell (Herald), Bill Mortimer (1100), Mike Jennings (MGB) and John Witter (in what was described as "an old Austin" - but how old ?) all suffered ‘bangs' or engine trouble. All this goes to show that, if you really try, troubles always come in several thousand. By the way, Cadet Race 1 was won by Colin Smith, with Alan Hoy 2nd and Tim Bigden 3rd (I wonder if elder brother gave him any 'tips' afterwards - and how were they received ?). June - Regatta is reckoned to have been quite successful (only 'quite' ?) with a total of 155 boats entered, which is an increase of about 20 over the previous best. The entry of 40 Marconi boats was about double that of 1968. The 1969 Regatta also saw the hiring of a marquee and band. Stan Campbell says he is disappointed at the (lack of) response to his cadet ‘cruiser trips’ and ‘lend us your dinghy' appeal. July - Eleanor warns there will be no September Navigans, whilst Jack Bigden warns members of the folly of connecting the name of the MSC with any correspondence they might enter into regarding proposed developments at Stansgate (presumably ‘correspondence’ to the local press, etc). The club's public policy was, I believe, governed by terms of our lease which prevented any opposition to development plans of our landlord. Another note from Jack states "For some years now members have been able to enjoy the facilities of Stansgate in comparative ease and privacy. In recent weeks, however, this situation has ceased by the influx of guests and non-members who have had little or no right at allto be at Stansgate". Jack then goes on to

8. j quote an example of a member arriving at the club with his wife and family in one car and later two more cars arriving with his guests. Jack reminds us of the rule limiting guests to not more than two in one day. He also reminds us that a swing gate has been installed at the club entrance and members are expected to close it after use. Finally, he warns that periodic checks of membership will be made and that membership cards will have to be produced. Did I say this was the 1969 Navigans ? It could be almost any year since we arrived at Stansgate and certainly ‘the problems' are no less now than they were then; in fact ‘the problems' may be worse now that more people ‘have wheels - will travel’. The dinghy park boat register reveals 26 Enterprise, 26 GP14s, 13 Hornets, 18 Mirrors and 58 ‘'others' (including about 5 catamarans and one lone 420). August - our Eleanor has presumably received ‘some feedback' for she reminds us that the ‘Editor's Comments' are exactly that. She writes "If anyone objects to what I write about, I do wish they'd send me a stinking letter to print in Navigans". How about a "Fishy Corner" feature in NaviganSwhere members could put in ‘two liners' of comment about the club and the way they perceive it is run - plus the response from those who run it. Maybe the ‘two liners’ could be anonymous if they wished. Eleanor is clearly undaunted by 'feedback' 'cos she goes on to refer to the rule that ‘Cadets shall wear personal bouyancy when sailing at Stansgate' - including rowing and motor-boating. She winds up the Editorial by stating "There must be other byelaws and rules that are not adhered to and my own view is that the committee would be pleased to hear from members who wish to suggest amendments or new rules". I think that what she jis really saying is that if people don't like the rules they should seek to change them - not ignore them. Did I really say 1969 Navigans ? It must!be more recent times ! A ‘general chat' article called SAPWOOD (written by The Gribble) reports Geoff Wardell being in trouble in an Old Gaffer's race (presumably ‘Old Gaffer' refering to boats(?) - Geoff is an ex-Commodore of the MSC) Apparently one of his crew had to be taken off by the Stone SC rescue boat and a replacement crew was provided by a boat aground on a bank - the same bank Geoff had grounded on two years previously. Also, it appears one of our GP14s towed in a motor boat whose outboard motor had fallen off. Finally, it is congratulations to Mick (Mike) Turner and Rosemary on their marriage. I bet they didn't think they'd still be getting congrats some 23 years later - or be regarded as ‘part of history'. Being mentioned in Navigans Past might be a pleasant surprise - but takes us nearer to our pension books. October - not much in Navigans this month. The Editor suggests that dinghies left for the winter at the club should consider taking the mast down to avoid being blown over in high winds and also suggests the boat be tied down. Of course, she should really say ‘the owners should consider..etc' but we know what she means. November - it is reported that several boats have been blown over in the dinghy park - don't say you weren't warned ! Eleanor announces she is thinking of ‘retiring’ from the post of Editor and thanks Avril Stevens for doing all the typing for Navigans. Since Avril was also the Social Secretary, she must have been kept pretty busy on club affairs. Anyway, she can claim some credit, for it is reported that the Laying-Up Supper went off very well. Anthony Wedgewood Benn, MP, had been invited but was unable to attend and wrote a letter of apology. In it he says, "....the presence of the Marconi Club on the Blackwater is very welcome to all who have the interests of the river at heart, and I hope there may be many more years of sailing for you all". "Here ! Here!" say I. "Resign ! Resign" say others. Oh! Well! you can't please everybody. On the sailing side, it seems that every Hornet Class regatta or open meeting on the Blackwater and Colne has been won by a Marconi helm with one exception - and no Marconi boats took part in that event. Amongst the club prize winners were Sue Tillotson (Cadet Series), Eleanor Witter (Ladies Cup), Julian Bigden (Helmsman of the Year) and Jill Bigden (Mugg's Mug). Finally, a note states "The Marconi Company still seems to be losing people at a great rate....". Alas, the same situation exists in 1992 but presumably for a different and much more significant reason. Where, I wonder, does that leave the future of the MASC - and the Sailing Section ? December - Eleanor supports an RYA article encouraging more women to become involved in sailing club activities and writes "Let's have more women joining in the excellent sport of sailing on dry land and in the organisation. If you.........don't like racing in a dinghy.....there are plenty of other ways of..... . feeling part of things". At the 1949 AGM, Jack Rigden (Commodore) reminds us of the lack of securityof tenure of the site. Nevertheless he and Stan Allerton have spent considerable time on preparing plans for development of the club at Stansgate, including a new clubhouse. During 1969, our landlord (Mr Sparrow) had sold his two farms (including the club site) to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. It was proving difficult to discover what plans our new landlords had for the development and use of the site. However, Jack is optomistic that it will all turn out right in the end. Jack thanks Avril Stevens and Eleanor Witter for their work - and also his wife, Connie, for being very tolerant and helpful over the years, especially at times when club work came before the home. The new club officers are Stan Allerton (Commodore), Dave Polley (Vice Commodore), John Witter (Rear Commodore) and Peter Crick (Sailing Secretary). Amongst the Main Committee members is the name of Ron Greygoose. Finally, an article by B Martin (crew) decries the fact that whilst, at club level, helmsmen have at least 13 trophies to fight for, crews have only one (Mugg's Mug). He wants equal rights for crews. Mike Boreham

A View from the Rear of a Catamaran..... Unfortunately, despite the extension of deadlines due to Rank Holidays etc., the onerous life of a Rear Commodore is such that this is being word processed on 10th May'!! Consequently, the memory may not be all that efficient in terms of wot’s gone on since the last issue. As I recall, Spring 7 & 8 was a bit of a problem with a certain Force 9 squall in the pm. All I carn now recall is the operation of landing on Osea, lowering the main and sailing back with a flogging jib and bare mast at a rate af knots! Except, that is, for the earlier inversion that we managed, followed by my imitation of a submarine (you wouldn’t believe how quickly Cats accelerate away from the gybe, and it is ever sc simple to slip off the back....) Ariyway, madesty prevents me saying more. Chris Caruth is selling the film rights and is open to bribery ta recount the whole sordid incident. That lead to the Easter Egg series, and the first dummy run of the new = improved washes whiter results system. My confiderice in my programming ability may be measured by the fact that I lent the boat to a certain Commodore of this parish and spent my weekend looking after the PC. Everyone seemed tao enjoy the use of the "Average Lap" system to calculate the results. It keeps boats of varying handicaps on the water for a similar time. Thanks go to the two Guinea Pig race officers, Ron Greygoose and John Weedon, whe added their considerable expertise in a most positive way. John got very carried away and ever had a General Recall on Monday afternoon! ! Steve Glynn and Tom did the business on the water, including totalling it in front of the Clubhouse, resulting in the award of The Rear Commodore Most Spectacular Incident Memorial Prize. Full results are elsewhere (I’ve forgotten). The intervening weekend between the holidays, Caruth was off yomping around a Welsh sheep, and sco I had Matthew Sharpe as stand-in. Not a good day for the first trip on a Big Boat.... 5-6 from the south. We reached off to Osea and I decided discreticn was the better wossname (Pete Flook calls it judgement) and we turned straight round. The afternoon did not trouble the scorers. May Day weekend dawned as a monohull dream and a cat nightmare.... No wind. Ron Greygoose shawed us all the way to do it until Monday afternoon when the wind got up (finally), but as he could have put his feet up already he had no worries. Jane Williams snuck in by being Race Officer on Sunday and getting a third on Monday morning, but the afternoon gave us more Cat Sailing As She Is Spoke with a cracking reach from No.1 ta Aw... the Micks seem to have benefited from the upgrade to the 19 as they spent most of the afternoon breathing down one’s transoms. Dave Onyons has alsa joined the wise mer, but he spent mast of the weekend trying to untangle a mass of yellow nylen (is it called a reacher because you try to see what level of entanglement you can reach???) Spring 11 and 12 saw another superb weekend with force 3-4 winds... when is the luck going to run out? Grant Piggot and Martin showed us all how to do it with Tim Wallace giving L’equipe Nickalls the run round a.m. and vice versa p.m. I’m still trying to work out what’s changed on the boat over the winter and recever the real meaning of boat speed.... Fortunately though, we did manage to see aff that troublesome Harrisoan (Senior) in the pesky 4.9 that never seems ta be quite far encugh asterr.... Well, good sailing to all, and keep the fingers crossed for Regatta!! Let’s hope the 3-4 keeps up till then. "MAMGU" - Forward and Aft I have aver 3 months or so, during the Winter pericd, attended a series of very interesting talks and field trips an the subject of Thames Barges. These talks were given by Mr Roger Beckett, the owner of Maldon-based "Reminder" and alsa af the still-surviving barge works at Maldem. The talks covered the history of Thames Barges, design considerations, construction, rigoing, sails and how they are sailed. Clubhouse. Towards the end of the series of talks I was browsing through a publication when, hey-presto, the word "Mamgu" appeared on one of the pages. Sa here goes, and I quate - "She was laid down in 1904 at Rochester, being designed and built by Gill & Sams. Although ceanceived as a working barge, she was sald before completicn ta a yachtsman, Mr R. Hill-Dawe, who had a counter stern fitted and accommodation built intc the hull. She was launched as the "Cawana". The dimensions were 37ft. long overall x 22ft. beam, and as a yacht her draught was 473", which contrasted with a loaded draught of 7°6" had she been a working barge. Hecause of this difference in draught, 40 tons of iron ballast was stowed in the bilge, hung from the floors so as nat ta touch the bottom planking. The motors were by the Pierce Arrow Co. of New York and the electrics by the Lancashire Dynamo & Motor Co. The "Cawana" was one of the largest craft of the time (except submarines) to have that form of propulsicm. The installation was removed in 1920 when she was owned by Major C A J Younger. A topsail was not carried and she was deliberately undercanvassed to the cawner’s desires. In 1924 Major Younger presented the "Cawana" to the Portsmouth Sea Scouts for their use aS a training vessel. Hy 1930 the "Cawana" had been sold ta Mr RVE de &. Ed. I've been checking our own copies of Navigans and realised that the Club's Ed. and Bosun have been MSC members for half of the 40 years of the life of the Club. The June 1972 edition of Navigans shows Saturday Ist July as an Open Day at Stansgate to which we went along - I think at the suggestion of former Commodore Stan Allerton who was my boss at the time! Ray was teaching me to drive, and we managed to run out of petrol between Mayland and Steeple and had to walk back to collect some (haven’t done that again, so far.) We arrived at the Club eventually, and Ray enjoyed his first sail in Mirror No. 19799, pale blue hull, owned and helmed at this time by Frank Savill, whose name also appears now on the past Commodores’ Board at the Club. It must have been a nice day because we joined. We bought my boss's 6F14 in October, and when Jenny came along in time for the 1974 sailing season we decided that, somehow, we would all three of us go afloat. In July 1974 a 16ft drop keel boat with a tiny cabin came up for sale at the club ard Jenny started her sailing in a carry cot wedged in beside "Dee Dee's” centre board case inside the cabin. No mooring being available at that time, “Dee Dee" was launched and recovered with the car at the beginning and end of Sunday's sailing, before and after the crowd of racing dinghies occupied the hard. 1974 must have been a nice summer because we turned our thoughts to a cruiser and in May 1975 changed "Dee Dee" for 21’ Ballerina “Coppelia". David began his sailing in 1976 in “Coppelia’s" more spacious accommodation. A few very bad summers made us realise that a fibre-glass boat was essential if we wanted to cut down the many hours Ray spent fitting out a wooden cruiser every spring with the reward of very little sailing because the weather was frequently so bad - you can have some frightening experiences even while safely tied to your mooring - and, no, there was ro fleet of Cats around then! We managed to acquire our Tupperware boat "Tara" late in 1978. In the mid-80s Jermy and David began Mirror sailing as Cadets, and in the last couple of years graduated to crewing in fast Cats. Jenny and David have enjoyed growing up at the Club, long may it continue being the unique place that it is, and I hope many more youngsters will be able to follow the same path. Ed.

They learned that Mr GR Tyler had offered the loan of his 18' sailing boat to the club; three members exnressed their willingness to fit it out. The meeting elected Mr (Eric ?) Cottam as the club's first Sailing Secretary with Mr (Geof* ?) Wardell and Mr (?) Robinson joining him to form a 2-man Sailing Committee. Judging to the 'Burgee Competition' was postponed for a month. The M.A.S.C.(as the parent organisation ultimately responsible for the financial and legal ‘welfare' of the new Section) was naturally involved in the negotiations for the lease for the proposed clubhouse at Heybridge Rasin. The M.A.S.C. insisted on "dotting the i's " and "crossing the t's" and this meant the lease agreement could not be finalised in time for lst June - the proposed 'move in’ date for the Sailing Section. Because the Section could not move in on 1 June, they asked the owners if they would agree to a new 'start' date of lst July, buSthe owners declined, pointing out that they had already made considerable efforts to clear the hut ready for occupation on lst June - so lst June it had to be, and the Section presumably had to eventually fork out the £1 per week for the month of June. Nf course, we know now that it all came right in the end, but the delay must have been frustrating for our pioneer founder-members who wanted to be ‘up and running’ - or rather 'up and sailing’. Howver, nothing daunted, they all agreed to meet again on 12 July at 'the clubhouse at heybridge, assuming the agreement had been completed and signed by then. Just to show their faith was complete, they hoped as many members as possible would arrive at the meeting by water. Mike Borenam

an SUPPORT BOAT STUFF This season, Support Boat Coxswains are having to do a miminum of five duties each. Being one of them myself, I consider this tc be far toc many and we desperately require volunteers to be trained in this activity, both for Jack B and the R. I.E. Naw a word on Radio Communications. Having recently been listening in during a major everit, it became obvious that our radio procedures require a little polishing. The equipment now in use is of an excellent standard, thanks in no small way to the efforts of Frank Bennett. It is however in the way that it is used that improvements could be made. Early in the day and then after lunch, the links between the four stations (Base, Race Box, Jack B and RIB) should be established. Therefore messages should be passed in the following manner: "Race Hox ta Jack B, what is your position, Over." "Jack B, South of Osea, Out." The following points should be noted: 1) It is not necessary to establish the link before passing the message, as seems ta be universal practice currently, e.g. "Race Bax ta Jack B, Over." "Jack B to Race Box, Over." "Race Hox ta Jack B, what is your position, Over." etc. etc. Comparison with the preferred method shows how unnecessarily verbose this one is. 2) The word "aut" at the end of a transmission signifies that the conversation 15 cover. The other party ta the conversation should now shut up. Such transmissions as "Race Hox standing by", as was recently heard mean nothing and can confuse other stations on the ret whe are waiting for an "out" to signify the end of the conversation before transmitting their awn, possibly urgert, message. 3) If you pass a message to another station and do not receive a reply, don’t ust leave it at that. The correct procedure 15 to transmit: "Jack B, nothing heard, Out" This lets him (if he can receive but not transmit) and the ather stations know what is going on and an alternative route for the message can possibly be feund. 4) Official call-signs are: Marconi Base Marconi Race Box Jack B Marceani RIB 5) A telephone link exists between the Clubhouse and the Race Box, ard all messages between these two locations should be passed using this facility and not the radi link. (hh 40 YEARS AGO DURING THE MONTH OF July, 1952 KKK A committee meeting on 3rd July reveals that the Shiowrights Shop at Heybridge Basin is now ‘ours' with only the formality of signing the contract remaining outstanding. The solicitor's bill amounted to the sum of £4, 3s. Od. for their "charges and disbursements". The committee meeting also revealed the plan for the next General Meeting on 12 July at which it was Droposed to judge the Rurgee Competion (hy a show of hands from all present) and then follow up with two races. Race 1 was to be for dinghies, half decked and open sailing boats of any type whilst Race 2 was for sailing cruisers of any description. Handicaps were to be assessed by the Sailing Committee "on inspection of the entering craft" and later adjusted (if necessary) on actual performance in this and future events. N®. Any boat (presumably ‘cruiser') towing a dinghy instead of carrying it on board would be allowed 20 minutes in the hour in addition to her fixed allowance. The course for Race 1 (ie the dinghies) was from the Start Line (between clubhouse and a suitably placed mark) to Hilly Pool Point Buoy (No.9), then to the red can buoy off Herring Point, and back to the starting line which was reckoned to be about 1s miles. The number of laps and direction of start to be decided (just ?) prior to the race. Race 2 (the cruisers) were to sail from the start line to Bradwell Creek main entrace (7 miles), all boats keeping to the main channel "as marked by Corporation Buoys"and leaving Osea Island to port. The ‘finish instructions' for race 2 make interesting reading ; "The first boat to finish will anchor as nearly as possible on a line perpendicular to direction of main channel and level with outermost beacon on spit extending north-east from Pewet Island. All succeeding boats will be timed over the line by the first boat, who should not neglect to time himself. (In the event of a close finish between two or more leading boats, all should anchor. The winner will be determined by a darts contest to be held later). " So ? Who were the winners of these very first club races ......? I quote from the archives:- "On July 12th the Sailing Section of the MASC held its first sailing meeting at the Clubhouse at Heybridge Basin. Many members came by boat over distances from 30 yards to 30 miles. The Chairman, Mr Hallam, in his voyage from the Crouch "took the chair" on the Buxey Shoals before reaching the Blackwater, and so arrived rather late. Mr Christensen brought a starting gun and his assistant Tim Tate managed to prevent casualties. Two races were held. Four dinghies sailed a short race to decide future handicaps (..... .».won) and will be heavily handicapped in future races. Secretary Joe Gill showing great skill in finding calm patches finished third - we expect him to do better when prizes are offered. Four cruising yachts then raced to Bradwell - first boat home was ....., i but as Jim Gould and Ron Hume brought up the rear 18 minutes later, it was decided to allow them a 20 minute handicap. The day ended with the toast to the Marconi Sailing Club being drunk in the bar of "The Green man", " wk So ? I don't know 'who won' but I suspect these ‘inaugural races’ were not taken too seriously and that some ‘judicious adjustment' of the handicaps allowed the ‘right result’ to be achieved. Anyway, we know that Joe Gill was 3rd in the dinghy race and that Jim Gould/Ron Hume 'won' the cruiser race. We also know that Mr Christensen was the club's very first Officer of the Day. kak An Anniversary Race ? How about ‘an all-in' race up to Bradwell in 1993 and each year thereafter to annually celebrate ‘with our founder members' their achievement in getting the whole show on the road - or rather ‘on the river' ? Perhaps we could arrange to ‘pull in' at the Bradwell Sailing and Field Studies Centre and maybe ‘have a toast to the Marconi Sailing Club‘ at The Green Man ? I suggest the nearest Sunday to 12 July could be the chosen date or, maybe better still, a date during the camping fornight allocated to such an event ? Perhaps it was more appropriate that the Saturday Race was in support of the RNLI, who we saw in action without any hesitation later in the day. I?m sure that the sight of Cruiser sails blown asunder and a boiling, wind-whipped Blackwater will stay with all who saw it for some time to come. Perhaps the lesson we should all take is that of being prepared. Who there would now not wear personal buoyancy at all times afloat? Some members still think it beneath their dignity or sense of fashion. Please think again, if not for yourself, for your family and for the peaple who will risk their own safety to save you. The fundamental regime that applies to all craft aflcoat, as emphasized in the Rule Book is the International Regulations for the Prevention of Collisions at Sea, hereafter the IRPCS. The Racing Rules take place as a subset of these LAWS and I remind all sailors, especially in the Cat Fleet, that you have to abide by the IRPCS first and foremost. I always feel more in control when on the wind; the only trouble is the difficulty of keeping a good lookout to leeward, a fact we discavered when a blast on a very loud hooter prompted a peek under the boom which revealed a freighter about half a mile away heading straight up the Colne. We had beer absolutely unaware of its existence until then, in much the same way I suppose, as a hedgehog on the M25 is unaware of the approaching juggernaut. The second memorable moment of this stage of the vcyage was when I wished for three or four arms in order to be able to steer and take a photograph at the same time. Pat was leaning out as far as he could go, hanging on to the sheet with one hand, his other arm waving around above his head like a cowboy on a wild bull. We had just breken through the top of a wave and the whole front half af the boat, together with his body from the knees upwards were suspended above several feet of boiling-white and ard smooth-green emptiness. We were making a lot of leeway and not much progress, with quite a bit of the river on the wrong side of the hull, so once we gat out of the mountains and into the foothills we hove-to for a rest and emptied the boat as best we could. The sky had cleared, there were spells of bright sunshine and the wind, still strong, was gusting even stronger. We were tired and wet but extremely happy toa be back in home waters again and in the shadow of Bradwell Power Station. (Now isn’t that a strange thought - to be happy to be near a nuclear power station ?) We hailed a passing beat and found cut that it was lpm and near high water so we got under way again, this time with a soldier’s wind all the way = up. What a sail that was! From the moment we freed sheets we were off on a plane up the river like an arrow from a bow, the long smooth wake hissing away astern over the flat water. The spray was shooting out horizontally from amidships and sparkling like diamonds in the sunlight against the dark green of the river water, and Pat and I were screaming and laughirg like maniacs all the way. When we stepped ashore at Stansgate at 1.30 somebody casually asked, “Had a good sail?" I didn’t know what to say. Andy Ochecki, °St Moro’, Cruiser Fleet

Yours sincerely, Hazel Payne Radio Communications Following the article on Radio Communications between MSC Base, Race Box and Rescue, Dave Beane would like to add the following information for members who might be interested. Correct procedure is that the station called is always first in the message preamble, and the correct proword is "This is" and not "to". Therefore the correct format would be: "Jack B, This is Marconi Race Box, Request your position, Over." and the reply: "Marconi Race Box, This is Jack B, Position Osea Pier, Over.” followed by: "Jack B, This is Marconi Race Box, Understood, Out." Having done my pedantic bit, I would like to suggest that either or both of Michael Gale’s books on VHF R/T and the appropriate RYA booklet be made available to users of Marconi Club radios. May I also offer to give ai short teach-in on radio procedures should that be considered useful. Dave Beane, Morning Flight, 0268 883531 (Day) GEC-FERRANTI SAILING CLUB, HAVERSHAM, MILTON KEYNES I suppose this sailing club could in a way be considered to be MSC*’s tiny baby sister, or perhaps cousin. It has been in existence for a couple of years with no more than 10 members, but this has lately dramatically increased to a membership of about 20. The club has just moved to Haversham Lake, north of Milton Keynes, where it shares a smart new Clubhouse and site with various other Clubs. At the moment none of the members individually owns a boat, the membership shares a tiny fleet of 3 boats which they hope to expand in due course. One member gives instruction ta those new to sailing who wish to be shown the ropes. My interest stems from the fact that my sister (who once had the privilege, shared by many, of being capsized by my daughter Jenny at Stansgate) has allowed herself to be bulldozed into the post of Hon Secretary, and is also considering starting the club’s Magazine in order to help the members to keep in touch with each other. I hope that perhaps one day in the future a few members of the new Club might be able to come and visit us, and have a sample of tidal salt water sailing which is quite a different experience from inland water sailing. Ed.

A View from the Rear.... Unfortunately, work commitments this month have prevented the usual diatribe and cataloguing of racing, so this is going to be short. (Hurray, they all cry!) In addition I appear to be suffering the odd memory lapse and am unable to recall the detail. It’ll have to mean a return to the Sunday evening correspondent’s session at the WP. The Cat Fleet continues to get more competitive with the arrival of Peter Emmerson and Tornado from Thorpe Bay, and several new Dart 15s. The Marconi faithful are having to look more to their laurels these days, with the Nickalls’ having been beater into an unheard of fourth place. Even in the Prindles, the Micks, Vince and Andy, and Dave Onyons have been giving the Flag Officers (i.e. Glynn ard me) something to think about. I can’t finish without mentioning the Nore Race, and the marvellous turn-out af Marconi members; four Prindle 19s (Glynn, Onyons, Micks and Me), two 18-2s (Caruth and Jones), and the Nacra of Pete Flaok, and Dart of Mike Styles. Steve’s blushes will be saved here, but for most of the race he was miles in front followed by the Micks, Dave O, and us until a famous error and Botheras-charge almost reversed that order. Although results haven’t yet been collected, Caruth C and me were fourth boat to finish, with the four 19s in the first eight, and a semi-submersible Mick (I forgot ta put the bung in) Jones and Peter Flook being close behind. Poor old Ian ripped the clew out of his main about three minutes after a cracking start! The quality of our weekly racing starts to show in that company. Well done all! Approaching we have the arranged-at-short-notice Cat training day on 1lith July and the Piers Race. Reports to follow next month. THE "SAIL-BLAZERS" I found the 'log’ of Messrs Andy and Pat's sail to the Walton Backwaters almost as exhilerating and encouraging as if I myself had done the trip. I say almost because along with the highs one also has to take the lows they described so well; the feeling that things just might not turn out right when all one can see is a grey sky ard an even greyer sea, because that’s the prospect in the direction one must go for that tack! Also, because of the ’urmatural’ laws of chance, things ‘do break down and go wrong, such as Matilda’s wayward shroud and the tangled anchor chain (because it was 2 miles long?) But overall, when they were finally on that wave-riding homeward stretch I bet the outcome had added just a bit more to their affection for Matilda! Their cruise encourages me to repeat what 1 mentioned last year and that is that the Club could promote more of this type of sailing. I know there has been some response - the sail to Weymarks Beach for a mid-day picnic on 3ist August. Perhaps I did not follow this up myself, but it is not practical to produce a detailed programme before the start of a season, nor is it necessary. A better arrangement would be ta allocate a permanent definite space on a notice board inside the Club where one could display an intended cruise giving enough details for interested members. It would not then be required to give notice at least a month in advance for inclusion in Navigans (anyway, for varicus reasons, members might not always read their Navigans in time). Any number of mini-cruises and outings could be posted up throughcut the season. it could result in a flourishing section of the Club, perhaps rivalling the racing fraternity! (There often seems to be a fair number of dinghies sinking in the grass). It could be relevant for the member proposing a cruise to indicate his own dinghy class - imagine the gap opening up between a small dinghy such as a Mirror and a 15 foot Albacore. The uneven matching doesn’t matter on a favourable homeward stretch but could be somewhat daunting if conditions turn rough (when one’s thoughts start to dwell in the wisdom of being a larnd-lubber). There is a fair number of Clubs and places to visit between Maldon and Brightlingsea. Everr & to 3 hours can be pleasantly spent (especially on those warm long days) just sailing across to Goldhanger Club and then returning round Osea Island. The Club ever provides a ’guest’ buoy to secure your dinghy. This gives peace of mind about leaving it to walk along the sea wall to the village. Or you can just sit in the Club and partake of a beverage. The creek is a quiet little haven in contrast toa the hustle and bustle of Mersea (Dabchicks Club) but all places have their particular attractions, and those who fancy themselves with sketch pad and pencil can record their own impressions. **So for ai start let*s sail to Mersea (Dabchick’s Club) as a trial run toa Brightlingsea. The nearest date I could manage and one which is reasonable for tide times 15 25th July.
