Discussion Evening 4th June 1992 Mr Mike Duckmanton opened the meeting by initially reviewing the main points of last year’s meeting and the results. 1. LAST YEAR’S MEETING a) Clubhouse The major topic of last year’s meeting had been the Clubhouse ard in particular the Changing Rooms. As a result of the comments made, both the men’s = and ladies’ Changing Rooms at the Club had been refurbished and the showers replaced during the winter. A comment was made with regard to the duckboards and it was asked if these could not be repaired or replaced with a plastic mat. b) Loackers It was suggested at the meeting last year that putting lockers or racks in the Changirig Rooms may make better use of the space - it was explained that this was considered but it was thought that they would take up too much room and that a better solution would be to encourage people to store their bags on top of the existing racks (and not to leave them on the benches). c) Jack B It was recommended that facility be made to keep Jack B under’ cover during the winter. This was provided by the tractor shed last year and as it was reasonably successful, it will be repeated again this winter. 2. MEMBERSHIP It was reported that the current membership of the Club was approximately 440. Ari apology was also made for the time it took to return all the membership cards this year. A question was asked as to why a level of 500 members had been suggested as being the limit for the Club at last year’s meeting. Mr Duckmanton explained that this was, in the Committee’s opinion, the level that the current resources available at the Club could support. contd....

3. SOCIAL Mr Duckmanton discussed all the social events generally and then asked specifically for comments on the Laying Up Supper. Although there were mixed feelings it appeared to be the opinion of the majority of those present that such an event was worthwhile. There was also much discussion on the price of tickets, and it was explained that the price is currently set to attempt to cover the cost of the event and that toa lawer the price signifricantly would mean that the event would have to be subsidised by the Club. A number of suggestions were made, these included, putting a questionnnaire on the subject in Navigans, taking deposits in advance and improving the distribution of tickets. 4, SITE SECURITY Mr Duckmanton commented upon the security problems that had been experienced at the site during the last year. He explained that all members had been issued with car stickers this year, which would be used to perform membership checks, which it is hoped should increase the general Club security. He also reminded all, of the importance of keeping the main gate shut. S. GENERAL DISCUSSION i) Concern was expressed over the state of the Hard - Mr Botheras explained that this is in the process of being treated. ii) Concern was expressed by one member over the safety of activities at the Club @.g. mooring laying, particularly for new operators. iii) It was pointed out that the Keep Out notice on the stile on the sea wall is the responsibility of the Club. iv) A question was asked as to where the photo of Mamgu was. v) Comments were raised about the future of the Club and the MASC with the decreasing size of the Marconi Company. vi) Membership I would like to offer my apologies for the problems with the sending out of the membership cards this year. We were hampered by a number of problems which included problems at work for some of the key people involved, and failure of the computer system. IF THERE IS ANYONE WHO STILL HAS NOT RECEIVED THEIR MEMBERSHIP CARD THEN FLEASE LET ME KNOW (PREFERABLY BY LETTER). Mr R Beckett, [redacted], Berifleet, Essex, [redacted]. vil) Bar As some of you will have noticed, I’m sure, we were without a Bar for abaut two weeks during the last month, because of a problem renewing our licence. The problem originated when the MASC came to renew our licence and were led to believe that we would have to change the type of licence the Sailing Section had, from a Club Licence to and On Licence (this is related to the change in Licence at the Main MASC Club). The basic implication of this is that under an On Licence, children are nat allowed in the designated Bar area. Ta cut a very long story short, an agreement was evertually reached between the Sailing Section, the MASC and the magistrates to designate a small area in front of the Bar as the Bar area, from which children must be excluded (when the bar is open). This is the reason for the rope and posts. The MASC has now beer persuaded to pursue our original application, which we hope will be sorted in the the next couple of months. In the meantime I would ask you all to accept the current arrangement.

10. NAVIGA PAST 1970 (July - December) - a new meaning to the ‘anti-barging’ rule. - 60 kids run riot - with their parents approval - the rent's going up; ‘the numbers' are going down. July - a report of the Enterprise East Coast Area Championships held at the MSC, with 42 entries of which 12 came from Marconi. Best Marconi overall result was Julian Bigden (2nd) but a special mention was made of Ron Greygoose (26th) and Dennis Byatt (39th) who were taking part in their first season's sailing (presumably lst season in the Enterprise ?). A note about Nick Tovey's "tragic gate start" clearly suggests that 'thereby hangs a tale' - but we're not told it. Marconi member, Simon Darney, achieved 2nd place in the Hornet European Championships held at Hayling Island. August - no Navigans issue 'cos Mary the editor is on holiday. September - Mary reports that items are being stolen from the changing rooms and from dinghies. Julian Bigden came 6th overall in the Enterprise World Championships at Weymouth, Nearer home, an article entitled "Three Mirrors to Maldon" recounts the voyage of Geoff Farnie (and son), Frank Saville (with 7-yers old son, Mark) and Alf Cottam. Geoff 'paints' a picture of the magnificent sight of a barge "tacking up" but says he didn't have the nerve to call "Starboard" - but in our more modern times "I know a man who would" and he's not from the AA! (For the ‘unknowing reader', one of our more Enterprising members failed to notice a barge ‘Coming up fast' from astern - until toolate; this happened a season (or two ?) ago). October - Simon Darney finished 3rd overall in the 1970 Hornet National Championships at Thorpe Bay out of 70 entries. A concluding article of the cruising log "Moonshine in Friesland" reports an unfortunate accident to Donald Wood who fell whilst stepping from 'Moonshine' onto a pontoon. He suffered facial injury and fractured ribs which provided him with an enforced stay in a Dutch hospital and a flight home. The Dutch were very kind and very heipful (as indeed I usually find they are today). But what an unfortunate name for the boat under the circumstances ? ‘Moonshine’ indeed ! November - Mary rates the laying-Up Supper "the best so far" and thanks Avril Stevens (Social Secretary) for arranging it. Clearly Avril had also arranged a separate “Laying UP Party" for the younger members (4 - 12 years old) for a note of thanks appears; "On behalf of all the children who attended the laying-Up Paety7-at the MASC, we would like to thank Auntie Avril very much for suggesting it and making it such a tremendous success. Please may we have another one next year". Apparently, 60 children attended. Stan Allerton (Commodore) gives notice that subscriptions wil] have to be raised, mainly due to the need to pay an increased rent now amounting to £1,000 per year (commencing 1 December, 1970). This will probably mean that the "family-man boat owner" will pay double "the present low rates for facilities similar to those enjoyed in the past." December - Mary asks for "the ingredients of candles" - presumably they were suffering from power-cuts ! At the AGM, it was revealed that club membership was 178 Family, 94 Single Adult, 63 Junior and Cadet, 65 Full Associate Members and 15 Junior and Cadet Associate Members ie. 415 intotal, which was apparently 'down' a little on the previous year. The Sailing Secretary also reported the entries for club racingwere also down due, he believes, to more MSC boats entering open events at other clubs. The Enterprise Fleet achieved 41 Spring Points and 89 Main Points entries, whilst the Hornet Fleet attracted 29 Spring Points and 17 Main Points entries. Alas, the Handicap Fleet failed to produce any entries and the Saturday Pursuit races only 8 entries. Whilst 'Helmsman of the Year ' competition attracted 106 entries, the Cadet Series "was down to 22 entries". However, the ladies saved the day 'cos the Ladies Series was a success with 20 entries, and the Mirror Fleet (in its first year of fleet racing) attracted 17 entries. The AGM itself attracted 95 attendees and they ‘voted in'the Main Committee's recommendation to accept the incresed site rental of £1,000 p.a - and the associated increase in membership subscriptions. A case of ‘Hobson's Choige' I suspect. Stan Allerton was re-elected Commodore, Dave Polley Vice Commodore and John Witter (Rear Commodore). The new Sailing Sec was Ron Greygoose and amongst the names of the new Main Committee was that of Frank Savill. Mike Boreham

JACK B - USER INSTRUCTIONS NOTE: Jack B is to be used by authorised drivers only. EQUIPMENT The following major items of equipment are carried on Jack B: Anchor and warp forepeak Towing lines forepeak Boarding ladder forepeak Mop forepeak Ensign and staff forepeak (when not in use) First Aid kit (including survival biankets) forepeak Radio forepeak Binoculars forepeak Echo sounder cuddy Compass cuddy Spare fuses cuddy (locker, below wheel) Bolt (rigging) cutter cuddy (behind helmsman) Fire extinguisher cuddy (behind helmsman) Boathook (small) cuddy roof Lifebuoy engine cover (forepeak when not in use) Boathook (telescopic) aft bulkhead Fenders tied to rails Bucket aft locker Fuel tank dipstick aft locker Fresh water (for engine) aft locker Engine oil container aft locker 2 x 10 litre diesel cans diesel shed START OF DUTY Ashore: Fill fuel cans with diesel and take out to Jack B. /f Jack B is to be taken off the mooring other than at normally expected times, if possible, first obtain clearance from OOD or other club official. Enter details on white-board inside club-house. Qn board; Open up cuddy and carry out following checks: Radio; Switch on radio on main switch panel and on set. Tune to club working channel (P2). Fuel; Check fuel level and top up as necessery. Keep tank at least half full. Engine must not be run with low fuel level as this may lead to water, dirt and air entering system. Qil; Check engine oil level on dipstick. Top up as required. Water; PRESSURISED SYSTEM - DO NOT CHECK WHEN ENGINE IS HOT. Check fresh water level in header tank. Correct level is about 1 inch below level of filler. Top up from fresh water container - sea water must not be used. Sea water filter; The heat exchanger is cooled by sea water which is drawn through a sea-cock and filter next to the gearbox. Remove top of filter tube, extract and clean filter element and replace. Open sea-cock. Engine cover: Replace engine cover. DO NOT RUN ENGINE WITHOUT COVER IN PLACE - DANGER FROM EXPOSED DRIVE BELTS. Page 1 of 2 Issue 1 10 August 1992

6. Start up procedure: Depress red button on single lever control to disengage gearbox, and open throttle approximately 1/2 way. Start engine. Ensure that warning lights go out and that alternator has cut in (rev counter will register engine speed when alternator is operating - it may be necessary to 'blip' throttle). Return throttle lever to neutral position. Check over stern that water is being pumped from exhaust. DURING USE Jack powerful B is a boat, Drivers should ensure that crew/passengers are ready for sudden acceleration/deceleration. Cuddy is very useful in bad weather but increases windage. Boat will tend to turn and blow downwind when stopped. When running at speed downwind concentration is needed to hold boat on course. Redistributing some crew weight aft may improve trim and control. Extreme care is needed when approaching people in the water, throw a rope where possible. Practice, using a fender, in different wind and tide conditions. DO SPEED NOT IN THE MOORINGS OR NEAR OTHER ANCHORED/MOORED VESSELS. JACK B has a semi-displacement hull which can create a lot of wash. Unexpected waves can cause accidents on board other vessels. Adjustments or repairs are to be made to Jack B only by authorised personnel (hull and equipment - Ray Ball, engine - Geoff Josey). If faults or damage occur return boat to mooring and report as soon as possible. Periodically check that water is being pumped from exhaust. If water flow is restricted stop engine, clean filter. Pump out bilges. Use fairleads on port or starboard quarter when laying or recovering race-marks to prevent rope damage to gunwales. JACK B , ; F nai Bopes propellor/shaft, round The propellor shaft is fitted with a rope-cutter which will sever small ropes. If propellor becomes entangled and rope-cutter does not cut rope do not attempt to free shaft by engaging forward and reverse gears. This has lead in the past to failure of the shaft bearings which are very difficult and expensive to replace. AT END OF DUTY Mooring up: Hook loop of chain over foredeck cleat. Tie restraining cord over bow-roller. Secure chain on cleat with cord and wrap pick-up buoy rope round cleat. Stop engine: Switch off engine and remove key, Close sea-cock. Clean filter. Top-up fuel; Do not leave boat with low fuel as it may be needed in an emergency. DO NOT turn off fuel tap on tank outlet, this is for maintenance purposes only. General: Secure wheel, tidy ropes and forepeak, pull all fenders inboard, turn off switches and replace all covers. Ashore: Refill diesel cans and leave in diesel shed. Record details of duty, problems or damage in Jack B log (on shelf at end of saloon). To ensure prompt attention please report any faults or damage directly to Ray Ball at the Club or on Chelmsford [redacted]. Page2 of2 Issue 1 10 August 1992

As an added incentive, we are tald that the National Fleetwind Championship is to be held at Maldon in 1953. A Laying Up Supper is to be held on 1 November at the Jolly Sailor, Heybridge. I seem toa remember an ice cream wafer cost about 3d (one and a quarter pence in new money) in those days - I know ‘cos I had to sell them from an ice cream tricycle for my Father by way of earning pocket-money. Thus, assuming that the cost of the Laying Up Supper was equivalent to buying 22 ice creams, what would be the cost in modern day terms? Assuming 70Op for ‘an ordinary’ ice cream, I make it that the 5/6d Supper in 1952 is equivalent to around £15.40 in 1992. Do you think we could get a Laying Up Supper at the Jolly Sailor for £15.40 - including the chara return journey’ from Chelmsford? Mike Boreham

OF CATAMARANS AND CREWS The end of two weeks’ holiday affords me one of the rare opportunities to wax lyrical again. For all my fans (well, fan) I must apologise for the sparseness of copy this last couple of months, but work has been extremely hectic. Looking back from this perspective (3rd Sept) we’ve had a pretty good season, with no complaints about the wind force - when was the last time we had a drift?? Compared with 1991 we’ve had an embarrassment of riches. Unfortunately, the other parts of the climate have not really been up to summer standards, and I think we’re all surprised to be in a hose pipe ban! What points of note are there to make since the Piers Race? I haven’t sailed at the Club an awful lot in that time, what with the boat going for some TLC following a gouge placed in the side by Yours Truly’s trapeze hook. However I have to report one of those amazing navigational feats we hear about from time to time, namely the Case of the Commodore and The Jack B. No, Mike, it wasn’t just going to die peacefully; I know you were just being gallant and going to the aid of a Windsurfer, but I always thought that the Jack B was equipped with an echo sounder for a reason!!! You’ve got it folks, he hit the putty on a falling tide west of Osea and had to wait.... and wait.... and wait. The biggest embarrassment was that my crew was with him!! August Bank Holiday weekend saw the entire Club Prindle Fleet disappear into the wilds of Kent (Minnis Bay) for the Nationals. Providing 25% of the fleet was no mean achievement, and some pretty useful performances were recorded all round in some very frustrating wind conditions. Saturday saw your Rear Commodore fly the flag in the first race, posting a respectable third in the 19%s and Dave Allen and Damian getting second in Mick Rich’s 18-2. With the afternoon race starting in very light airs your two doughty flag officers were amazed to be in the group of four boats that crossed the line at the start. Everyone else had a secret tactic of waiting down tide until we’d rounded the first mark! Then the wind went completely and the fleet concertinaed, but your Vice Commodore kept his head and vaguely pointed towards the shore. The wind got up...Boy, did it get up, from zero to Force 4-5 in seconds, but amazingly unsteady in direction. I saw the main chance when Steve got caught aback and capsized to windward, but you don’t get in front of him that easily and they were up and sailing in seconds. Tom and he held that position all through to record their first win in a Nationals race. Caruth and I? Nothing if not consistent, third again as were Dave and Damian with their second. Sunday was blown out, to the point where all masts were taken down. There was a Marconi Helms vs Crews football match on the beach - the difficulty was stopping the goal posts (AKA traffic cones) blowing away - followed by a fun afternoon in Benbom Bros. (Dreamland) in Margate. The things one does for entertainment!! Monday saw two races back to back in a pleasant 4-5, although again direction was anything but stable and there were some big holes in it. Dave and Mike Onyons proved that they were up to the challenge by posting a _ third, closely followed by Steve and Tom and Caruth C and Yours Truly. Dave and Damian Sailed their discard as well as us in that one also posting a fifth. The final race was sailed back to back with the third, and Glynn got a stormer - as did we until the jib block shackle gave up the ghost with a mightly bang. All credit ta my man though, we got it fixed pretty quickly and through some ace downwind Sailing managed to claw our way back to fourth whilst Glynn and Tom were firmly ensconced in second. Then came the Mighty Windshift and all of a sudden with just the last three legs to go I was behind Vince and Andy and the Two Micks were steaming up. Fortunately skill will out and we recovered to our allotted fourth. So as not to miss anyone out, the overall Marconi positions were: 19’ s: 18-2’ s: Steve Glyrnn/Tom Duckmanton —- 2nd Dave and Damian - end Me and him - Sth Ian and Steve Caruth - 8th Dave and Mike 0 - 7th Mick Jones and Andy - 11th Vince and Andy - 8th Mick and Mick - 11ith= Well done to all, and particularly for partying everyone else into a cocked hat on Saturday night. (Anyone who wants more details had better be prepared to pay......) Next we have the Rum Tub and Bung, and the Dart 15/Solo Open, Reports next time. See ya all, Larry Botheras

i 10. THE LADIES SERIES = 1992 Once again, the forma for the Ladies Series seamed to work in that it attracted 7 entries, three winners in the three races and a close finish in the overall result. As with the Cadet Series, the ‘Average Lap' formula wasused and it was planned to hold three races on 8 August (middle weekend of the camping fortnight). In the event, 2 races were held on the 8th (Saturday) and one on the Sunday and it is congratulations to:- LUCY BOREHAM (EUROPE) Cup for 1992, with Debbie Yorston (Dart 15) 2nd and Maggie Boreham (Mirror) 3rd. who won the Ladies With Force 4-5 winds on Saturday morming and a forecast of 'more to cam", the Race Officer Mike Hellewell delayed the 12.00 start for Race 1 until 15.00 in view of the rather 'mixed' range of experience of the competitors and the uncertainty of just how much wind would arrive. The R.O. explained he would operate the Average Lap handicap system and aim to have all boats sail for the same length of time, ideally around 45 mimutes plus/minus a bit. Race1 - Wind: East F4; Course FpXpApDp; Start 15.00; Flood Tide. Maggie Boreham's hopes of repeating her 1991 success met with an immediate "hiccup' when, with 15 seconds to go to the start, she fouled her daughter Lucy in a port/starboard incident and had to perform a 720° penalty - quite literally, not a good start to the series for Maggie. Lucy (Europe) was first to cross the line but the Dart 15s of Debbie Yorston and Pat Stuart quickly went to the front and rounded the Ist mark in the lead, followed by Lucy, Sue Fletcher (420), Maggie (Mirror) Clare Davies (Mirror) and Christine Howard (Mirror). With the wind falling to F2 at the end of the race, Debbie won the race by 12 seconds on average lap time from Lucy, with Maggie 99 seconds further behind Lucy - having managed to capsize on the final beat due to over-enthusiastic roll-tacking by her crew (son Damian). All boats finished within a 10 minute time slot (ie. plus/minus 5 minutes of a median time of 57 minutes). Race2 — Wind: East, top of F2; Course FpXpApDp; Start 16.25; Flood tide. As with race 1, the course provided a good windward leg which, being against the tide, also demanded decisions as to whether it was best to go 'inshore' or ‘offshore’. Those who chose ‘a bit of tide ' offshore in order to obtain freer wind gained, for the wind did not treat kindly those who went inshore for the lesser tide; ‘pinching up' and ‘lack of water' proved troublesame. Maggie (Mirror) was lst over the line, well to windward and inshore; she was followed by Lucy (Europe), Sue (420) and Christine (Mirror) each progressively a little further out in the tide. The two Dart 15s of Debbie and Pat took a rather more ‘laid back' approach to the start and were well off the line. Maggie's apparent good start soon turned to frustration as the 'pinching up' and shallow water resulted in slow boat-speed and eventually she was forced to tack. However, Lucy, Sue and Christine sailed further out and a little freer and made good progress to the first mark which they rounded in that order. Surprizingly, the Dart 15s did not ‘eat up the water’ (or should it be ‘drink up the water’ ?) on the two reaches F - X and X - A in a way that watchers on the shore might have expected. Both Sue (420) and Debbie (Dart 15) seemed to over-compensate for the tide in the approach to A and were well windward of it, leaving a rather surprized Lucy still in the lead as she completed the Ist lap. Witha steady "Top of F2" reported at regular intervals from the patient observer in the clubhouse, the RO sent them on another lap in the expectation of some increase in wind. It was Christine Howard (Mirror) who seemed to find the ‘right touch’ and she sailed her Mirror very well indeed. Sue Fletcher (420) also made the right approach and kept her boating moving purposefully forward. In fact, Christine, Sue and Lucy all seemed to be able to 'sail through' any light wind patches and make good steady progress, but the Dart 15s of Debbie and Pat and the Mirrors of Clare and Maggie seemed to be sailing through 'a sea of treacle’ and couldn't get going in the same way as the others. Eventually, Debbie, Clare and Maggie all retired, but Pat was determined not to be defeated by a wind which seemed to be there - but was difficult to catch. The race was won by Lacy, followed by Sue, Christine and Pat and all finished within a 20 Minute tim slot (ie. plus/minus 10 minutes of a median time of 9 Mimutes Race 3 — Wind: SW F4-5: Course: AsXsDs; Start 14.10; Flood tide. Se NAVIGANS PAST 1971 (January-June) - Eleanor blinds us with science; don't mind the spelin, just make sure the numbers all add up ! - Stan plans whilst Pat ‘patters' and presumably passes al] to port - or should it be port to all ? January - Ex-Editor, Eleanor Witter, provides what she calls "Useless Statistics Metricated and Dinghied". Apparently, 351 copies of the November, 1970,Navigans were distributed, of which 78 went to Associate and Honary (?) Members (I think it was ment to reed 'Honorary' - sory I meant ‘to read Honorary’). On the basis of an average distribution of 350 Navigans per issue, 11 issues per year and a 4-year period of being the ‘ead heditor, Eleanor reveals that:- 94,000 sheet of paper were used, and these would make :- a pile 12.7 m high (the length of 2 Enterprise masts) a road 30.5 km long (to go to Stansgate on 15,000 Navigans) - a load of 465.57 kg (the weight of 5 Enterprise hulls) but the 15,400 staples had a combined weight of only 500g, and Eleanor concludes that won't affect the stability of any boat. On the sailing side of things, the 1970 Spring and Summer Points were considered successful and to be continued. The 1970 Saturday Points Series was disappointing, but will give it another go in 1971 along with Midweek races which are considered 'a must’. Our old friend, Pat Black, is obviously working hard to promote all-year sailing. In "GP Patter" he complains the “Winter Jugs' Series was not well attended, It seems that he and Dave (?) had to be content with a few practice »tarts until joined by Peter Crick to help to give sufficient entries for some serious stuff. Anyway, Pat must have been reasonably pleased with his equipment for he reports that the self bailers proved very efficient. However, I must say that as I read his article, I feel very sorry for Pat and Co.; there they are 'togged up' and ready to 'set sail' in the meanest of weather and no one supports them. Yes, it's a bit much and, even at this distance of time, I really feel that the so-called keen sailors ought to have turned out to sail and.......and..... aaaaaaand..............-.. Hang about, | think I've bin ‘ad. Pat blithly announces that the next Winter Jugs Series will be at The Royal Oak on 21 January starting at 8 p.m. Now I see it all - one thing's for certain, if they didn't get support at the start of the 'series', I bet they needed it at the end. February - a special conference was organised by Essex C C to discuss bye-laws concerning safe navigation on Essex rivers. The police warned that an effort would be made to enforce the 8-knot speed limit. Richard Young (former Commodore of Blackwater (?) S C) spoke on behalf of BACSPA “We are satisfied with the County Council bye-laws, but not with the enforcement of them". Now, just think about it - what did he mean ? Bruce Long asks what has happened to the Stone-Marconi Hornet Points Series Trophy (a minature tiller) 2? Well ? What did happen to it ? Anyone know its 'final' resting place ? March - Avril Stevens (Social Sec) announces the Fitting Out party to be on a "Shipwreck" theme - come dressed as you were when shipwrecked ! Plus a prize for the 3 funniest items 'grabbed' as the ship is abandoned. With tickets at 50p each including vittles**,it must be the bargain event of the year. Now, I wonder what Pat Black ore - assuming he was able to find his way back in the fog after comnleting the whole of the Winter Jug Series. April - Commodore Stan Allerton appeals to people to wear life jackets when sailing. He says "If you can't borrow or buy one - then the Marconi Sailing Club cannot afford YOU as a member", About 30 members attended a talk by Mr Sam Poulton on the build and rig of Thames barges. Mr Poulton was former Commodore of the Maldon Little Ship Club and owner for 29 years of the ‘barge Black Eagle. A note from the Handicap Fleet Captain, Eddy Edwards (surely not ‘Eddy the cagle'?) who asks "Do you feel that something ought to be done to put more life into the Handicap Fleet "? He invites all to attend a meeting at the MASC - presumably to put more life (or something) into the Handicap Fleet. Maybe they ought to join in with the Winter Jugs Series. Julian Bigden writes an article on 'the Rules' whilst Peter Cott Suggests a non-tippy class ought to be adopted, such as the Sandpiper or Devon Yaw. May - The 'Shipwreck' Fitting Out Party went well, with Mabs Byatt winning the '3 funny things' competition - but we're not told what they were ! In an article entitled "The Shadow and the Future", Commodore Stan Allerton recalled that the 1970 AGM had agreed it would paythe new (higher) rent on the basis that they accepted the need for the MSC to exist and flourish, and that they should set upon a course of ‘buy or bust'. He waS now pleased to announce that plans to purchase the site were under way and that permanent planning permission was awaited (for a new clubhouse). ** meaning food/provisions:- ‘victuals’ is how you spell it but 'vittles' is how you say it) Cont. on next page......

The basic conditions of the purchase agreement were:- (1) Tne site comprising some 7 acres was to be purchased freehold by the Marconi Athletic and Social Club for use by the Sailing Club (ie Sailing Section) as a sailing site and for associated recreational activities. (2) A licence was to be granted (to the Sailing Section) by the MASC for an inital period of 5 years at a rent of £1,000 p.a. increasing by 10% per year. At the end of the initial 5-year period, rental for the following years would be negotiated. (3) All other expenses of the Sailing Section were in future to be met from Section funds. Stan warns, however, that getting planning permission for a new clubhouse did not necessarily mean it would be built in the foreseeable future; nevertheless, he adds "but - who knows" ? Hon.Sec., Dennis Byatt, reminds everyone that the MSC was essentially “a Works Club" (of the Marconi Co.), and reminds everyone of the rules for visitors to the club. Editor, Mary Greygoose, has much praise for Pat Black and his "GP Patter" articles in Navigans. To say the least, Pat's 'Patter' was very readable and surprisingly long for Pat, particularly when you recall how brief Pat was when he delivered his annual Hon.Secs Report at the AGMs in later years. In the Helmsman of the year Series, Race 1 is won by Pat Black (GP14) and race 2 by Norman Palmer (GP14) The DDS Count (Dinghies Down at Stansgate) reveal that we have:- 23 GP14; 12 Hornet; 17 Mirror; 34 Enterprise; 36 Handicap. A brief return to Pat Black's "GP Patter" where he reveals that "...Jim James having lost one son to the ranks of the "E" boat fleet has bought forth another from the bag, this one is called Nigel, is smaller than the former but nicely marked and weighs 6% stone soaking wet ; the ideal light weather crew". Presumably, Nigel learned quickly for he won the Cadet trophy in 1973. June - a note from the editor to remind all members that the area beyond the race box was “out of bounds" to all members and was shortly to be ‘fenced off'. Mary asks "Please see that no damage is caused to this fence". Frank Savill won the Mirror Spring Points Series with Julian Bigden winning the Enterprise and Dave Draper winning the GP14. The Regatta was, once again, a success, attracting entries as follows:- 34 Enterprise; 32 GP14; 25 Hornet; 21 Fireball; 19 Mirror; 12 Finn; 6 Flying Dutchman; 8 Mirror 14; 5 Fleetwind; 14 Dinghy handicap and 9 Catamaran Handicap. A note in GP Patter records that Ken Beavins and son Nick sailed round to the Crouch on Regatta Saturday, spent the night there and returned to the club on Sunday morning. Ken is the cadet Skipper. A note from Editor Mary reminds me that we did not always have the use of the present day Cat-field, for she says "Please all you children who have great fun playing in the ditch and climbing the tree (the very same ‘the tree'? in the lane at Stansgate, make sure you keep out of the field and right away from the corn growing. I'm sure you would all be greatly disappointed if you were stopped playing there altogether...". Sadly, a. message records that our former landlord, Mr Pat Sparrow, died at the end of May. It appears we always had a good relationship with Mr Sparrow and his helpfulness no doubt played a signifcant part in establishing the MSC at Stansgate. His funeral was attended by the Commodore and Flag Officers. SOLO FLEET NEWS A Sunday or so ago (20th September) saw another 'Solo Barbecue’. These are usually held after a couple of points races and are most enjoyable. A small whip covers the fuel costs and bring your own food + cans’ produces a very good occasion. If you have missed them so far, do try to find the time next season. How many years has the Solo Fleet held a Team Race? One was held last year, so thinks I, better do it again! Having booked my holiday and this event for the same date meant me missing this feast of rule-book quotes. Thanks tc Roger Smith who generally organised, scored etc. for the Series. Well what happened then? It was held on Saturday Sth September and by all accounts was a successful and enjoyable everit. There was the traditional *discussion’ over certain rules, especially the one about water at a mark and whether tactics were used has been questioned. However the end result was clear, the team with the best score was:- John Salmon, Lucy Boreham, and Peter Collis - well done! The Solo Fleet AGM will be held near the end of October. This is the time to air those views/gripes/grumbles/good ideas that all of you have held back (sc far). I haope to see you there. "Marconi Sailing Club on the River Blackwater in Essex hosted their traditional Solo Open Meeting on 12/13 September as part of the Solo Eastern Area Circuit. The event was held together with the Dart 15 Open and took place in winds of Force 3-5 accompanied on the Sunday by torrential rain. The first race on Saturday was a practice race which was won by Jerry Garner from Halfway YC. The first points race was in a strong ebb tide and was won again by Jerry Garner whe got his new boat going well in the conditions, followed by Dave Nixsomn. Sunday dawned with similar wind conditions but no sunshine and again the tides strongly influenced the racing, the morning race having the beat with the flood tide. The wind over tide conditions produced some hectic dowrwind sailing in the steep chop off the Clubhouse, causing some swimming practice for the less wary. Dave Nixson won this race from Jerry Garner, so it was all down to the last race to decide the series. Raced through some fearsome squalls in bad visibility the race was won by Nixson with Colin Willsmore second, John Salmon from Marconi SC third, followed by Garner. This gave the series ta Dave Nixson, with Jerry Garner second, and John Salmon third. Results lst: 3709, Dave Nixson DRASC énd: 3749, Jerry Garner, Halfway YC Srd: 3604, John Salmon Marconi SC 4th: 3681, Colin Willsmore, Halfway YC" The Sale Fleet extend their thanks to the Cat Fleet and other Club Members who worked ta make this a most enjoyable Open Meeting. Roger Smith

A View From the Rear..... Well, as promised last time, a review of the Rum Tub and Bung (including Out and Hack and Pilot’s Cup) and Dart 15/Solo Open. The RT & B did not have an auspicious beginning when both coxswains DNS, so for the FIRST and ONLY time this season the breach was filled by your Commodore and Rear Commodore. Next time we will cancel the event. Enough of the moans, the wind was a strong W-SW and so the Nass was deemed ta be far enough. As usual the Monos started off followed ten minutes later by the Cats. Mike D and I had our tactics outlined so that the Jack Bwould go on with the Monos and the RIB would follow the Cats. Well, Dickie Davies was bring up the rear of the Cats in his Dart 15 (with Derek Holroyd crewing is one surprised?) and we decided on a change of plan and we legged it towards the front of the fleet. We finally caught the first Monos actually at the Nass..... I forget the exact length of time they’d taken but it was PDQ. As were the Cats, of course. One cor two pecple decided to make a name for themselves, Ethan totalled it just off Thirslet, Graham Richmond and Stuart Golding did the same a little earlier and decided that a toctle back under jib was the best idea, and the Two Micks showed that they hadn’t lost the knack after rounding the Nass. Bouncing around in quite a lot of lump and increasing breeze resulted in a suggestion not to send the Cats around again, and we started the slow march back upwind. Tom Ashley wrecked various halyards aboard Mike Helliwell’s 420 and that was about the sum total of incident. The Cats (particularly Grant Piggott) finished in 50 minutes, a bit short I suppose. Still there’s always next year! The most impressive for me was the Mono wirmer, a Contender from Maldon YC. If anyone else has ever had a ride on one they’11 know what I mean!! The Dart 15/Sale did well, with 36 entries (20 & 16) in total. I tried to lay some fairly decent courses with Committee boat starts (thanks to Jack and Paul Holbrook with "Viridia") and a good mix appears to have been the result. The only real nasty was finishing everyone on Sunday p.m. in a massive rain squall. I took pity an the rest of the Race team (Damian and Pete Flook) and stoad out there in my oGilies.... Mind, it was impressive watching some of those Dart 15 guys "Sprinting" past (i.e. single-handed with trapeze). Finally we got back to Club racing on Sept 20, but I can’t remember much other than the wait on Osea for the wind and subsequent abandonment in the p.m. Oh, yes and for "The Rear Commodore Forgot to Sign Or" in case you’re the one member that didn’t hear Steve Glynn broadcasting it!!! Next week we had very similar although slightly stronger cornditions in the morning and managed to ghost around fairly well. This included the sight of Equip Nickalls finishing well down the tubes, a very rare event these days. By the afternoon the wind had filled in easterly and a respectable double wiring affair it was toc. We had a superb reach from No.1 to A mark which probably sticks in the memory as one of the seasor’s best. There were three gaod ding dong battles, The Nickalls v. the Emmersons, Vice Commodore v. Rear Commodore and The Micks v. the Onyons. Places changed regularly, and a good sail was had by all. Unfortunately The Micks and Yours Truly were deemed to be PMS and so had don All That For Nothing. Yesterday (Oct 5) was blown out so that’s yer lot fer now. Future reports will include Grafham Cat Open and the Mona’s Cup. Larry Botheras RNLT ANNUAL. 14, ONCE MORE TO BRITTANY We had spent a lot of time during the winter in fitting out our new acquisition *Morning Flight’, a Sparkman & Stevens 34. She was originally named Morning Rose and is a sister ship to the Morning Cloud, once raced by Ted Heath in the seventies. Naturally we were very keen to utilise her long range capability and therefore rather optimistically arranged an extension of insurance cover down as far as South Brittany. This did turn out to be rather over-optimistic because the wind stayed stubbornly in the southwest quadrant for practically the whole of our three week holiday. It even refused to change for our return trip, miracles do happen sometimes. Having given the hull undersides a pre-holiday careen we set off on a nice Saturday for a trip across the Thames Estuary via the Black Deep and Fishermans Gat to Ramsgate, quite uneventful but a beat practically all the way. The next day was quite stormy so we made a trip only as far as Dover where we anchored in the outer harbour and watched an air-sea rescue demonstration by a helicopter. We then motored round to the Wellington Dock to lock in for the night and enjoyed a quite effusive welcome from the duty attendant. Nothing whatsoever to do with the tot of scatch which he reluctantly forced down himself, for medicinal purposes only, so he assured us. The next day we set off intending to go to Brighton or Newhaven as ai kicking off point for a Channel crossing but half an hour after our departure the Coastguard broadcast a warning of a force 8 gale soon in the Dover area, so we diverted toa Boulogne because we could get there before the forecast gale appeared. We duly arrived in Boulogne which was quite busy and we managed to get the very last berthing Space available in the Marina. We were a little disappointed because normally the old city is a very nice place to have a meal, but on this occasion most of the restaurants were either closed or full, although we did eventually manage to get a table for our first French meal of the holiday. Some Dutch yotties advised us that a new Marina had opened in Le Treport which is just to the east of Dieppe so we decided to make it our next port of call. As was ta be the norm on this holiday we had the wind on the nose although a fortuitous wind shift about five miles out of Le Treport enabled us to arrive without having to tack. We arrived well after dark but Le Treport is well marked because the white chalk cliffs and a cross above the town are floodlit and carn be seen from seaward for some considerable distance. Having arrived in the drying harbour we had no idea where the entrance to the new Marina was, but soon received directions in very voluble French when we mistakenly attempted to enter the commercial harbour. The Marina entrance lock which is on the south eastern side of the harbour is a fairly vicious one and it is necessary to be firmly tied up before the flow begins. I know this because my arms are now slightly longer than before. The next leg down to Cherbourg was to be a long one of 120 miles requiring an overnight passage. At this stage we started to fall back on proper navigation with DRs and ADF and all that stuff. The last stage of the arrival at Cherbourg is quite crucial because of the very strong tidal flows off Barfleur ard especially we were right on high springs. In the event we had to overshoot Cherbour by a signivicant distance to ensure an arrival upwind and uptide for the final approach. This leg made us really start to appreciate the benefit of the wind vane self steering which we had fitted just prior to the holiday. In the morning the meteo was giving a forecast of SW Force 6 so we had our doubts about the wisdom of negotiating the infamous Alderney race in those conditions. We therefore made our decision to head for Braye harbour in Alderney. A start was made so as to make use of the west-going eddy towards Cap de la Haque and we motor sailed towards Alderney through some fairly rough water. Having placed ourselves in a position from where we could make Braye harbour without getting sucked into the Race, we then decided that conditions were OK to take advantage of the shelter afforded by Alderney to slip down the east side of the island. This proved to be the case and we eventually found ourselves tacking down the Great Russell between Sark and Herm on the way in to St Peter Port in Guernsey. contd....

15. We stayed in Guernsey for a couple of days attending an organ recital in the lacal church and pottering about for a bit of duty free shopping. The recession was obviously being felt by the shops in St Peter Port because almost all were advertising significant price reductions. Come the morning of our planned departure from Guernsey, the wind decided to ease a bit to the northwest. We therefore shaped a course tc take us ta the east of the plateau of Les Roches Douvres with its high lighthouse and thence down to the Island of Brehat at the entrance to the Pointrieux river and inte Lezardrieux. We were very glad of the MF radio beacons on Guernsey, Jersey and the Roches Douvres because the Decca remained fairly unreliable in this area with only intermittent lock on. The timing of entry to the Portrieux river is very critical because of the strong cross tidal flows. On this occasion we managed to get it right and had a nice trip only having to tack past the Isle de Brehat as the wind sagged back into the southwest. The next day we got it all wrong, cur intention to travel further upriver and toa visit Pontrieux was thwarted by missing the lock apening by about ten minutes. Apparently it opens once only at high tide during neaps. Aryway it was quite a nice scenic trip up and down the river with woods on either side. As the tide ard wind conditions were right we decided to carry on downriver and to go further west ta Treguier. The sea conditions were un peu agitee (a bit rough) so we chickened out of the short cut through the rocks of the Fasse de la Gaine and approached through a wider and safer channel. Once in the river proper the wind died right down sa we shook out our reefs and meandered upriver ta the anchorage which is beautifully situated just under a large chateau near to Treguier. Much nicer than the Marina and very peaceful. The following morring we berthed at the Marina to visit Treguier and particularly the supermarket to stock up the foodstore. It being the occasion of my birthday, we found a small poissonerie (fish restaurant) and enjoyed a very nice seafood meal. I think the tip here is to look for the place most patronised by the locals. The peace of the next morning was somewhat shattered by the start of the local = gc- karting grand prix. If anything the commentator made even more noise than the go- karts especially wher he goat really excited which seemed to be about every ten seconds during the course of a race. We got fed up with all this noise after a while and assembled our bikes for a cycling expedition into the French countryside. We did our cultural bit by having a guided tour round an old country house and then took in a funfair in an adjoining town. Here the local drunk managed to fall orn Sarah while we were having a drink outside the local bistro which did not impress her too much soa we gathered our bikes and departed. On the way back we visited the chandlery at Treguier. This is a smashing place, smells and looks just like a chandlery ought to, no twee packets of screws in plastic bags here - just grab a handful and pay at the counter. Back to the nautical scene and with the wind still firmly stuck in the southwest we decided to go east towards St Mala. On the previous day someone had set off for St Quay Portrieux where a new Marina has been established so we decided toa fallow. Soa it was was off back to Brehat with that rare thing known as a beam reach. We sailed via the inside of Brehat this route is prettier and much more interesting than going out to seaward. Arrival at the all tide Marina at at St Quay was very easy and we found that the deal was to pay a sum which seemed a bit over the odds for France for the first night, however the second night was free, naturally therefore, we stayed for two nights. St Quay itself is a nice little town with lots of places to eat out if you so desire. It has a cliff path which continues some miles ta the west = and which gives very good views out over the Charmel. Time now to start our return to dear old Blighty. So an early start for the 70 miles to Alderney, again passing to the east of the Roches Douvres and up the Little Russell between Guernsey and Herm avoiding the temptation to call in at St Peter Port. We ever had the spirmaker up on the trip as the wind fell very light. Despite the lack of wind the overfalls in the Swinge near Alderney were really vicious and caught us by surprise as we still had the spinnaker set. Not for long however as it wrapped itself neatly round the forestay as we started the engine in the panic to maintain steerage way through the overfalls prior to getting our breath back when safely moored in the sanctuary of Braye. contd....

16. We had time for a quick look round the town of St Annes on Alderney before setting off on the tide en route to Boulogne or Dover. With a nice beam wind and a fair tide we fairly whizzed along until the tide turned against us off Barfleur to give us a rather pedestrian four or five hours crossing the Somme Basin. During the night we could hear Solent Coastguard broadcasting force 8 gale warnings but they were for the English side of the Channel and were southwest we decided to carry on, not that we had anywhere much to run for shelter in any case. In the event the wind stayed below a maximum of thirty knots during the night so we continued to make very rapid progress towards Boulogne managing to catch the tidal gate south of Dungeness to give ourselves nearly twelve hours of favourable tide. This being so we decided to carry on to Dover rather than stop in Boulogne. Shortly after so deciding, came a moment of doubt when the wind backed into the west and strengthened to thirty five knots for cur crossing of the shipping lanes to Dover. However, Dover Coastguard kindly approved our request for a non right angled crossing to enable us to make Dover and we beat across with three reefs in the main and a very, very small helping of jib accompanied by very large dollops of genuine English Channel. We were quite pleased to find ourselves off Dover Harbour with the harbour patrol launch waiting to escort us into the western entrance. We logged 175 miles at an average speed of 7 knots on this leg with a lot of help from the tide and even more from the self steering. Our return to the East Coast the next day was notable only for two happenings, firstly a grounding right in the Swin Spitway at dead low water, it must be getting ever shallower! Secondly a still small voice out of the darkness as we crept in to anchor in the Pyefleet. "Welcome back, Norning Flight". It was none other than that intrepid singlehanded sailor John Todds of the good ship Chimo. We are still wondering how he recognised Morning Flight in the dark, John must have been at the carrots or perhaps he has night vision goggles in place of eyes. If you are thinking of venturing on a sailing trip to France, we noticed this year that the French Customs seemed much more active than in previous years. Our papers were checked several times, so it is best to check that all the paperwork is in order prior to your trip so as to avoid any hassle. Dave & Sarah Morning Flight September 1992

GJ WORKING PARTIES 1) Sunday 29th November This is the Working Party when we give the Clubhouse and the site a general clear-up at the end of another sailing season. The lounge curtains are taker home by various volunteers for washing and storing for the winter, and all sorts of cleaning jabs done throughout Lounge, Bar, Corriders, Changing Rooms, and I’ve beer reminded that cur men as well as our ladies would be welcome ta come alara ard help with the cleaning - especially for the Men’s Changing Room. Flease bring gleves ard bowls/buckets with you - ather cleaning materials will be supplied. Outdoors there are various items of Club equipment ta be stored away far the winter. &) Sunday 3rd January - the Winter Working Party is designed tao work off all the Calories we’ve taken in aver the Christmas and New Year. Possible jobs for this working party are: Cat Field Entrances need attention (surface water and problems with cars gourding)/Cruiser Park road pot holes to be filled/Water Pipe ta be laid in Cruiser Park/Tidying Fuel Store & surrcundings/Clearing of items stored behind containers/Gang mower to be dismantled for storage/hedge-trimming. If you can bring along some suitable tocals for the above type of work, it might be useful. A VIEW FROM THE REAR....... My parting shot at this lot (you lucky lot!) and an opportunity to wrap up the 1992 sailing season. The Autumn Points series has been decimated by cancellations due ta the weather, and (I believe) something like only & races have been sailed. It’s been an unfortunate end to quite a good year windwise, I'm sure we’re all glad not ta have had another year af drifters. In the midst of it all has been Helm of the Year, won in a Force 6 by Howard (thank goodness John Nickalls has a weak Stomach) Ragers from the Handicap Fleet, Mana’s Cup (forever tc be remembered as the one when the Sneaks (AKA Nickalls and Metcalfe) went North of Osea) and the Grafham Cat Open attended by Equips Nickalls, Piggott, Onyorns (sub crewed by Mike Fletcher) and Rear Commodore. The weather was unusually seasonable for this event (it mastly blows ald boots) and we only had the Grafham Cold to contend with (chip the ice off the boat stuff!) A certain person who shall be nameless had a ding-dorng with the Race Officer over Prindle 19 handicaps and had the hump most af the weekend (I’m in a better mood now!) but we had a couple of nice days sailing with good twin wiring Conditions. Unfortunately none cof the Marconi cagnescenti seemed ta be able to get topside of the very add wind shifts. The one interesting point was the general negative comments about the unfriendliness of Grafham as a club and the very impersonal feel af the everit. That leads to the last weekend of the Autumn which I had the dubious pleasure of watching from the RIB ably assisted by Tim Wallace. If I thought Grafham was cold.... We were called inte action a couple of times during the day, once prior ta the afterroon race when Tim ’s boat (sailed by by Howard "I’m-a-Gerntlemarn" Rogers ard Faul Wilkinsen) had (according toa Tim) its first inversion - or should I say irnversions..... It ably demonstrated ta me the benefit of the RIB in that situation in that we got in close to pick up the rig with no fear of damage to anyone or any thing. Colin Kidner THE MAMGU_ TROPHY Like myself, most Club Members probably only know the Mamgu Trophy as an ertry in the Club Yearbook. However as Maureen and I have been entrusted by the present holder (Janet Bigden) with returning the trophy to the Club, I have had the pleasure of studying it. It is an attractive and unusual trophy, which consists of a detailed model of the barge-yacht Mamgu in a transparent case. The case sits on a polished wood base, a novel feature of which is a drawer containing details of Mamgu herself and the trophy wirmners, going back to 1963. The trophy was presented tc the Club by the then Commodore, A.M. Adam in 1962. It is presented for the best log submitted for a Cruise (in a dinghy or cruiser) in the preceding season (more precise details are available in the Yearbook). The details of past awards of the trophy and a history of the yacht herself follow; (see also Tony Holbrook’s article on Mamgu’s history in June 92 Navigans.) contd......

NAVIGANS PAST 1971 (July - December) - Fred completes yet another dinghy cruise - but not without some pushing and puffing - and we're a site better off at the end of the year than we were at the beginning. July - An announcement of the death of Joe Gill, a founder-member of the MSC. The notice, written by Eric Payne, says that Joe was Hon.Sec 1950-54 but we know the club wasn't founded until 1952. Eric was, I believe, the person who produced the list of past Commodores whose names are now painted on the Honours Board; it includes Commodores for 1950 and 1951 and I can only think that Eric and friends had an informal ‘Marconi' sailing club/group during those years which, subsequently, provided the impetas to form the official MSC. Alas, we have no information about those years amongst the archives. A note from the Sailing Sec (Ron Greygoose) reports the dismal failure of the 1971 Saturday Points Series to attract entries; I guess it is due for ‘the chop’ in 1972. August - no Navigans due to holidays. September - Avril Stevens (Social Sec) announces plans for the Childrens' Party and for the Laying Up Supper at the Heybridge Country Club - tickets £2.25 each. The Enterprise World Championships at Harwich attracted 214 entries and Marconi boats finished 5th (Roger Hance), 21st (Julian Bigden), 63rd (Mike Taylor), 94th(Arthur Hodges), 95th (Dennis Boswell) and 139th (Ron Greygoose). In the local Loughton SBSC Nimbus (ie Enterprise) Open, Julian came lst and Ron was 3rd out of 36 entries. Bruce Long and John Heslop finished 2nd in the Hornet Nationals at Plymouth. A welcome return to 'Navigans news' for Fred Partlett who has previously featured because of his dinghy cruises. Fred had apparently sold his Wayfarer and built himself a Mirror 16' named "Sobreon" and he hopes that his account of what he calls "a modest weekend cruise" will convince others that the Mirror 16 "can more than hold her own alongside other boats". Originally, Fred planned to set out from Leigh-on-sea and sail out to the Whittaker Beacon and then, depending on wind, tide and weather, either visit Walton-on-Naze or go up the Crouch to Burnham and, in any case, finish up at Stansgate. A very readable account eventually finds them cold, wet and the wrong side of a sand spit, so they jumped out and pulled the boat over it until they could again sail to where they wanted to go, in this case to Burnham, finishing their 'lst leg' of the cruise 11 hours after its start. Next morning they had an eventful sail back to Stansgate. In the end, Fred seems pleased with the boat and satisfied with the adventure. He finishes the account by saying "In retrospect it might appear ludicrous for two dinghy sailors to be pulling their boat across Foulness Sands almost surrounded by water, but soon that privilege will be denied us forever as will the route through Havengore Creek. Make the most of it while you may". I'm not sure to what he was alluding, but could it have been to the plans for an international airport thereabouts around about that time ? Finally, a note about the public footpath through the site which, we are told, runs along the sea wall from Stone and exits from the club along the road. The note asks members not to obstruct the public on the path but hopes that, eventually, fences, styles and signposts will be erected "to help them on their way". I believe at one time the footpath exited through the farm but the route was presumably changed way before MSC came on the scene. October - "THE SITE IS OURS - WHAT ABOUT A CELEBRATION ?" . This happy message is the title to Commodore Stan Allerton's brief notice in Navigans. Yes, the MASC are now owners of the Stansgate site and the Sailing Section are permanent tenants with planning permission. We are told the ‘Deed of Surrender’ was dated 9 September and contracts had been formally exchanged and completion was due on 7 October. Stan says " ...we may occupy our great Sailing Site at Stansgate for as long as we are capable of running The Marconi Sailing Club according to the rules and for the objects laid down". "Ah !", say I, “now that could pose a problem !" On the sailing side, Bruce Long and John Heslop were in the British Team for the Hornet Worlds held in Poland and they finished 10th. The Marconi Challenge Cup (18 September) attracted 39 entries, of which 10 finished, one retired and 28 were non-starters (was it something to do with the weather ?). Marconi's Malcolm MacArthur (Ent.) was lst, with other Marconi results being 3rd, 6th, 7th and 8th whilst John Weedon finished 10th in his Mirror. Of the 39 entries, there were 17 Marconi, 17 Stone, 3 Osea, 1 mMaylandsea and 1 unknown. The Marconi Cruiser Cup attracted 16 entries (8 marconi, 4 Harlow, 2 Blackwater, 1 Maldon and 1 Stone) with best Marconi result being 4th place "Lipara"” (Dr G A Bond). November - the forthcoming working party was to place emphasis on "consolidating our boundaries" with posts and fences supplied by MASC. lan Tate (Mooring Sec) suggests cruiser owners ought to attend the next cruiser meeting as there were proposals and inovations for 1972 which might not be very popular. Now then, I wonder what that was al] about; maybe a future Navigans will reveal all. The Mirror Fleet report a very successful 1971 season with only one Summer Points race not sailed - and that due to bad weather. The end-of-year prize List reveals that Marconi's Hornet Fleet won the Saltcote Team Challenge Cup. Norman Palmer won the Helm of the Year with

9. Pat Black 2nd and Dave Draper 3rd; presumably Pat and Dave were still recovering from their early-year efforts in the Winter Jugs Series !!! December alas, no December Navigans is on file; perhaps they didn't publish one. So ends what must have been one of Marconi Sailing Club's most successful years, culminating in the security of tenure of the Stansgate Site and the confidence which goes with it. What a shame Joe Gill did not live to see 'the ultimate success' of the club which he had helped to start some 20 years before; what, { wonder, will the Navigans archives reveal to someone looking back 20 years in, say, the year 2017 ? "THE HELM OF THE YEAR" FINAL 10. FOG GG iG a dk ak a ki "HOWARD'S WAY" So io GR a a ak kok ak ke dak a a ake ok An exclusive report on the special production at the Marconi Sailing Club, 10 October, 1992 Some quotable quotes:- "A stirring tale of one's man's fight to stay on an even keel" The Billericay Times “A story of comic proportions, at times even approaching farce" The Gt Baddow Guardian "No sex please, it's Marconi" The Commodore (of some club or other If storm, tempest, lightning and thunder are the means whereby the Gods of Old pass . their messages to us mere mortals, then the messages passed via ‘the hot line‘ at Marconi on the morning of 10 October can only be regarded as quite clearly saying "Don't even think of sailing, my friend". With a steady Force 6 (reportedly 7 at times as shown on ‘the dial') accompanied by steep waves and a clear view of cruisers plunging up and down like race horses in the Grand National, the Helm of the Year finalists didn't seem overkeen to get started. Nor, indeed, did the owners of the ‘loaned Mirrors' relish the idea of their precious craft being launched into the Southern Oceans just off Osea Island which, at certain camera angles, looked as daunting as anything seen in the South>rn Hemisphere - sans icebergs. However, given a certain exaggeration of reporting, the owners voiced their opinion that the event should be postponed until a more suitable day (and having also established their own ‘hot line' to the Gods to plead for clemency for their craft) but. nevertheless, allowed their boats to be trolliec to the Hard ready for launching into the aptly named Blackwater. With Jack B ready to go under the captaincy of 'Mad Malcolm' and the RIB having sampled the conditions whilst laying the marks, the 'messages' started to come in from 'the hot line’. The RIB rebelled and refused to start, resisting so effectively that the starting rope parted in such a place that it was not easy to repair in a short time. Score: 15-love to the Gods. Plans to launch the Beaver seemed doomed as efforts to match petrol tank to engine proved futile, Undoubtedly, the shape of the fittings mysteriously changed as expected solutions to 'the problem' met with inevitable failure, Score: 30-love to the Gods. However, the black magic of the Rear Commodore eventually overcame the forces of good, the ‘hot line’ went dead as the Gods of Old clearly capitulated and the match of petrol tank to engine was achieved. All was ready to go, everyone groaned, and the show was ‘on its way'. Game to the Rear Commodore. The G of O did, in fact, make one rather limp gesture in a final attempt to bring proceedings to a halt, for they arranged only four boats for the five finalists. Everyone perkedup a little at this dreadful news but the Rear Commodore, determined to extract maximum vengeance on the G of 0, swept aside this futile gesture of defiance and decreed that one of the finalists would ‘SIT OUT' each race. Game, Set and Match to the Rear Commodore. So, what of the races ? The course was set justoffNo.l at the entrance to Goldhanger Creek and consisted of a (very) small triangle of windward, wing and leeward mark, competitors then passing back through the start line as part of the ‘saucage' of windward and leeward mark; all marks passed to port. Definitely, no room for error at the start or during the race; the helm of the Year Final has little sympathy for competitors who cannot ‘get it right' first time. As the fourMirrors sailed across to the course area, one of them capsized (John Nickalls I believe) - a bad omen, I fear ! Race 1 - Start 12.46. With 30 seconds to go, Ron Greygoose seemed poised for a good start but came in too early to the short start line and had to ‘peel off'. John Nickalls planned it just right and was first over the line. Despite being over the line at the start, Paul Ellis dipped back to the right side and started 2nd with Ethan 3rd and Ron 4th. An incident at the windmark mark between Ron, Paul and Ethan saw both Paul and Ethan retire, leaving John the winner in 10% minutes, with Ron 2nd in 13 mins 43 secs (having sailed to thewing mark in error on the saucage leg). Howard Rogers was the ‘Sit Out' guy. Race 2 - Start 13.13. This time it was Ron who ‘Sat Out' - but it seemed as though they all wanted to ‘sit out' as they were all well off the line at the start. John crossed the line lst with Howard quite close behind. Paul was about 309 secs adrift with Ethan Chatters about 39 secs further behind. Bearing in mind that none of the competitors had any real experience of sailing Mirrors, the choppy conditions (and the difficulty of sailing what must have seemed like 'a bathtub') it was not Surprizing that most experienced difficulties with tacking. It was John who seemed to cope best with tacking and keeping the boat sailing upright and he made the best progress to windward. At the windward mark, John lead by 20 secs over Howard, with Paul and Ethan a similar distance further behind. jas, at the wing mark, John capsized - twice - and was clearly finding it difficult

ll. to literally 'find his feet’ in the restricted room of the small dinghy. This left Howard in the lead at the leeward mark, a lead which was extended when Paul and Ethan engaged in a tactical battle which took them over more of the water than was really necessary. Such was Howards lead that, even though he also capsized on the saucage leg, he still managed to win quite substan ially (despite ‘loosing’ his jib sheet on the final very short beat to the finish). Paul finsihed 2nd and John finished 3rd just a few feet ahead of Ethan, despite having capsized yet again at the leeward mark. Unfortunately for Ethan, he had ‘overshot’ the mark quite considerably and had to sail back to the mark, thus loosing any advantage that John's capsize had given him. The Race officer (Mike Turner) had intended to hold Race 3 and then go in for lunch, with Races 4 and 5 to follow after lunch. However, two things happened; firstly, the gooseneck fitting of one of the boats pulled out and secondly John had to retire owing to a severe attack of sea-sickness. 1 can certainly sympathise with John for I, too, have suffered from sea sickness on the Mirror in rough choppy conditions. A big chap like John, ina small boat like the Mirror, “bobbing up and down" and with your face only inches from the sail (making it difficult to focus/re-focus your eyes easily) is just right to make you feel ‘unsettled'; I know, I've felt it. Thus, we all went in for lunch, Race 3 Start 1501 Force 5-6 (at the clubhouse). Alas, with 30 secs to go, Ron again looked set for a good start but he 'got in a tangle’ on a tack shortly before the gun. Thus Howard was first over the line l0secs ahead of Paul and Ron 3rd about 30 secs behind, John was 'Did Not Compete’ and Ethan ‘Sat Out'. Howard again markedly sailed better to windward, but Ron and Paul had a close race. Howard was the winner in 12 mins 11 secs, some 14 secs ahead of Ron with Paul 5 secs further behind. This win obviously put Howard in a very strong position to win the trophy - and pressure on Ron’ who really needed to win the jast two races to stand a chance. Race 4 Start 15.27. Paul ‘Sat Out' and again John was DNC. Again Howard was lst over the line, followed 5 secs behind by Ron with Ethan 20 secs further behind. Howard again extended his lead on the beats but Ron uickly pulled back the lead on the run/very broad reach. Consequently, the short legs saw Howard's lead vary between 25 secs and 12 secs - one mistake and Ron could have been in front. However, Howard didn't make a mistake and he finished in 12% mins with Ron 15 secs behind in 2nd place and Ethan 40 secs further behind in 3rd place. This win confirmed Howard as Helm of the year - and, indeed, he did it "Howard's Way". Race 5 - During the preliminary ‘sail around’ during the on-water change over of helms and boats, the rudder of one of the boats collapsed. ED’S NOTE The Renewal of Subscriptions Forms and the Discount Paint information makes the January edition of Navigans a very bulky one every year. This has meant holding back one or two contributions that are of general interest. Next month I intend to catch up with Navigans Past, sailing rules quiz (a pity this couldn’t be fitted in the Christmas edition,) a marine ecology article, and a cruise log. A DART 15 NEWS article, 2 or 3 months overdue because the original was lost, can be found on the last page - don’t miss it now it is here! I would like to add my thanks to those of the Commodore to three hard working volunteers who have recently stepped down from their posts. Thanks again go to Leon White who (for the past 8 years I understand) has taken care of the folding, enveloping, addressing & posting of all our editions of Navigans - quite a task each month of the year. Once Navigans was typed and delivered by me for printing, I could leave the rest of the task safely to Leon, a great relief on some occasions! Navigans Distribution is one of the Club tasks that goes on totally unseen (apart from its result) by the membership. (Some other duties are only seen being carried out if you visit the Club in deepest winter!) Warmest thanks also go to Mike Turner and Mike Battle, our Cadet Fleet instructors who have over several years (winter as well as sumuer) taught all they could to any Cadets who came forward to learn about sailing. All their planning and hard work came most vividly to our notice when huge fleets of Cadets took to the water each Cadet Week. We would love to see some more of those Cadets sailing around on other sumer weekends, I would like to mention the wives of our volunteers, who help considerably either by actual involvement, or simply by giving their men the time and space to do their work. From what I’ve heard in the past it is often the much-desired wallpapering and decorating around the home that suffers most! So thank you also to Norma White, Rosemary Turner and Janet Battle. R.Y.A_ NEWS Having been volunteered as MSCs representative to the RYA, I find I have some catching up to do in passing on information received from RYA Eastern Region meetings as far back as June, and whilst some of it is water under the bridge, the contents may still be of interest. Items of local interest were as follows: 1) That the Marina development at Salcott had been turned down by the D.0.£. - I am trying to find out more about this. 2) Maldon Lake - slow progress due to the developer going slow on account of the current slump in house building. Maldon Council are putting some pressure on to get the Lake deepened and have debris removed. They also expressed their thanks to the RYA Eastern Region and the Blackwater SC for advice and support. Maldon Council Planning Review, Blackwater Estuary, BACSPA, RSPB, Wildlife, all being consulted. 3) Wivenhoe Barrage now well under way. Sailing in Holland 1) Dutch yachtsmen are not allowed by their laws to have a hand-held VHF set on board a yacht. These are quite acceptable in the UK providing a valid licence is held on board. The suggestion is, when in Dutch waters, don’t wave your hand-held set about! 2) Yachts that carry pyrotechnics that require a UK Firearms Certificate (Very pistols, some Mini-flares, etc.) should always carry the Certificate on board, as the Dutch Authorities may well demand to have sight of it. 3) There is also the extraordinary situation where the Dutch Authorities require all vessels more than 15 metres long or capable of more than 20 Kmph to carry a Dutch Certificate of Competence, obtained through a written examination in Dutch and taken in Holland! The RYA is continuing its efforts to get RYA qualifications recognised by the Dutch Authorities and has got the full submission from the UK Department of Transport. In the meantime the RYA still advises yachtsmen sailing in the Netherlands to carry the Helmsman’s Overseas Certificate of Competence. Wreck Marking Trinity House has asked the RYA to publicise the fact that their ships may now exhibit a RACON when involved in marking new wrecks. This will be in addition to signals displayed under Rule 27 of the COLREGS (Collision Regulations?) The RACON will have the characteristics: Type Agile Frequency 'X’ and 'S’ Bands; Code: Morse 'D’; Nominal Range 10 Miles. UK__Keep Low Diesel Rate HM Customs & Excise and the UK Goverrment has managed to maintain the present duty on diesel fuel for marine use. Along with Belgium and Greece, the UK has decided not to accept the new EC minimum rate from January 1993, This is good news, since the cost would have increased by £1 a gallon. I will be in touch with representatives of the RYA Eastern Region Council and will be pleased to take up with them any points of interest, be it in relation to Cruising or Dinghy sailing and, of course, the environment. Derek Kirby, [redacted]

4. Do. Re. Mi........ (i.e. the Commodore’s Notes!) Sorry Folks, but the sense of humour (!) doesn’t change with the exalted position!! I hope to keep the general light-hearted tone that you’ve come to know and love me for in "A View From the Rear", but obviously there will be a reasonable degree of gravity from time to time in accordance with "wot’s going on". Initially, we'll be starting off on the latter footing as I outline our initial thoughts as a new Executive and Committee on where we gc from here. Obviously our existence is inextricably linked with that of MASC, and with all the fun and games going on with GEC we are very firmly watching events and putting in place contingency plans to cover all eventualities in that direction. We (the Exec) had an interesting meeting with Norman Cox (Chairman) and Gerry Wignall (Manager) that put things into perspective and removed any of the immediate anxieties we had (particularly with the resignation of Mick Elliott from the MASC Committee). Any good organisation has a "vision" statement (all you BS 5750) people please note!) and although we have not discussed one in detail there is one implicit in both the Exec and Main Committee. I think it can be best summarised as follows: "To improve and develop the resources and facilities at MSC incrementally in order toa enhance the enjoyment of sailing of all members, and, whilst recognising that 1t is a self-help club, to reduce the demands on individuals with respect to their investment in time and energy." There are a number of critical areas that we looked at after the working party, such as the state of repair of the road, the Cruiser Park and the state of the roof and windows of the Clubhouse that are under immediate and urgent consideration. We are also looking seriously at the social calendar, although there has been little response about the Barr Dance. The Laying-Up Supper at Channels was a very erjoyable right and, what is more important did not run up the huge losses of the past. Watch this space for developments in that respect. Their effearts which have gone largely unsung in Camping Fortnight deserve special mention. Thanks for all your efforts!! (PS Ar: volunteers for 1993, please ring Colin Kidner!!) Arid last, but by no means least, Mike Duckmartorn. I know Mike was particularly unhappy at having to step down late in the day but in the past two years that he has served as a Flag Officer, Mike put a lot of thought and energy into consolidating the direction of the Club, and has left an indelible mark on "the way we dco things". I mean, where else did you see a Commodore wearing a tatty flat hat and sailing in pink! ! There’s an awful lot that goes on behind the scenes ard I am pleased to have a very active and energetic Executive to help sort it all out. You very often don’t know the full extent, mainly to avoid undue heartache. The Exec, Main and Sub-Committees pick all of that up and deserve your thanks for making your Sailing Club work in the way that it does. Give them your support and let them know when they de it right as well as when they do it wrong! Sorry for the long diatribe, but I felt it important to set the stall out. Merry Christmas and A Happy New Year to everyone. Larry Botheras, Commodore

6. SIGNING OFF = WITH APOLOGIES. After 9 years as the Results Secretary, I handed over the Results Box to Willie Pitcairn (new Sailing Secretary) who will, presumably, in turn hand it over to Mike Hellewell (new Results Secretary). It would probably have been more logical to give it to Mike in the first place - but I happened to see Willie first, so I ‘dumped it' on him and, anyway, Mike was up to his eyebrows in prizes and trophies. Mike, I understand, plans to 'computerise' the results for 1993, so I guess we will ‘await the results’ with interest. I must admit that I tend to view the magic of ‘computerisation’ with a certain amount of scepticism. Like many another poor soul, my office is adorned with WPC, Database, Windows and Accounts Package, all contained in a grey box which insists on sticking its computerised tongue out at me (ie. the Drive 'A' floppy disc). The Accounts Package presents me with several thousand ledgers, whereas I was more than happy with the 60 provided by the old-fashioned manual system. At the touch of a key, I can see that the computer's Balance Sheet 'balances' and the Profit and Loss Account ‘profits’ ina very convincing way, although I am also certain that the computer's bland statment that our Current Bank Account contains £356,726,532.26 must be incorrect - but, since the computer says it is so, then I guess it must be right and I am wrong. ] must apologise to Martin Newman for forgetting to put his 'Muggs Mug’ win on the ‘major trophy' part of the Prize List, just below the Cadet Trophy listing. Unfortunately, I only had about 3 evenings in which to work out the Autumn Points Series results, compile the Prize List, assemble the Sailing Statistics and list all those who took part in the racing programme during 1992. - and all so that it could get into the December Navigans and be ready for the AGM. Maggie and I have greatly enjoyed ‘the results' task which, like many another support job in the club, has more often than not proved to be a thankless one. Nevertheless, it gave us a great deal of satisfaction and pleasure and that is the most important thing about it; once a club job ceases to give personal enjoy- ment, it's time to let someone else have a go. Computerisation is , without doubt, inevitable, desirable and wonderful, so I wish Mike ‘bon Voyage’ as he sets out on his journey through the software equivalent of the Sargasso Sea.
