MARCONI SAILING CLUB 20. MEMBERSHIP APPLICATION GUIDE 1. All MSC members must be members of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club (MASC) and must have a current MASC membership card and number in order to open or renew their MSC membership. NEW Member applications lacking a valid MASC number must be accompanied by the completed MASC application form. All other applications without a valid MASC number will be returned. All Members must pay the MASC fee directly to the MASC. Every candidate for membership must be proposed and seconded for election by a Full or Famil Member of the Club, both of whom must be personally acquainted with the candidate. ( Rule 1 2. CLASSES OF MEMBERSHIP (Rule 6) Full Being a person who, at the date of election, or renewal, is over the age of eighteen Family Being a married couple, or one or two parents, and all their children who are under eighteen years of age Junior Being a person who, at the date of election, or renewal, is under the age of eighteen 3. Postage fees must be paid where no GEC internal mail facility from Chelmsford is available. 4. Fees include VAT at the applicable rate. 5. All boats incur a Boat Permit Fee (Hard Fee). The First boat of a Member is always deemed to be the boat incurring the highest Boat Permit Fee. Subsequent boats under 10 ft (e.g. tenders) are free. 6. Winter storage fees are payable, in advance, at these rates on boats, trailers and cradles to be kept at Stansgate during the period 31st November to 1st March, following the renewal date. Cruiser Owners must also ensure in advance that space is available for their boats. 7. Renewals and applications should be returned to:- The Membership Secretary, Liz Hill, [redacted] [redacted], Mayland, Essex. [redacted]. Phone. [redacted] The MASC fee, as advised will be invoiced to you separately and is payable directly to the MASC. 8. NEW Members joining the MSC after 1st July shall be entitled to a discount of one half the Subscription fee only. NEW Members joining after lst November shall pay no fees, other than winter storage, until 1st January the following year. 9. Any Members in any category of membership being over the State Retirement Age, shall pay one half the full fees for Full or Family Membership as appropriate (Rule 7). 10. Membership renewal fees are due on Ist January and are payable by 31st. February. Late renewals incur the penalty fee (Rule 8e). fofa DART 15 NEWS (With apologies to all concerned for delay in publishing - first submissian to Navigans appears to have gone missing somewhere in the system —- Ed.) Following the excessive winds on the 30th August, the Dart 15/Solo Open meeting saw ideal weather for sailing, but not if you were Race Officer, particular on Sunday! Saturday saw 11 visiting Dart 15s and one Sting - mast boats coming from Grafham - arid 8 Club Boats competing. Nick Dewhurst arrived minus prizes and decided to go off ta Maldon at about 11.15am leaving the rest of us to put his boat together. The TT regulars maintain that he doesn’t know how to assemble a Dart which is why he keeps pulling these stunts. Those who know Nick will not be surprised to hear that he gat the prizes, made the start, and was first standard boat across the line! Saturday and Sunday saw some close racing between the visitors’ and Club boats, particularly in the last race. Larry set the course to go once round the marks = and then round Osea, leaving it to port before completing the race by going round the marks three more times. Jim Jeffery led Willie Pitcairn, Nick Dewhurst and myself as we started the first of the last three laps. The first three boats stayed in mid charmel, your truly bore off to sail close ta Osea shore. This tactic paid off....madesty forbids that I go on. The final results were: SPRINT STANDARD 1. Mike Cemm Dart 15 1. Nick Dewhurst 6. Tim Dieu de Bellfontaine &. Gerry Reeve Sting 2. Phil Neal 7. Bob Anderson S. Paul Berry Dart 15 3. Jim Jeffery 8. Debbie Yorstan 4. Willie Pitcairn 9. D. Davies 5S. Colin Kidner 10. Nick Pavitt li. Dave Bladon A superb weekend’s Sailing and many thanks to all those Club Members who helped aut, particularly those who volunteered at short notice to drive support beats. A special thank you ta Larry who ran the shaw. The Autumn Points Race 3 took place in light airs. For once yours truly got it tagether from start to finish! By the way, Paul is not invincible! The afternoon race was a drifter. I still don’t know why I bothered. The forecast for Sunday 27 promised a Force 4 to 5 so we got another drifter in the morning. Six Dart 15s started, those who used the bottom of the Blackwater managed to start the race without going via Maldon! Paul won and the rest of us retired for lunch. The afternoon saw a better wind and same close racing early on, and Dave gat a place, he was third! Colin Kidner

Fortunately we've been blessed with the Boreham accuracy over the last few years and so there has been little mention of them in despatches. NAVIGANS PAST 1972 (Jan-May) - Whilst Pete offers us a chance to sail in calm waters and avoid the washing-up, -And Mary gives us some tips on how to stay young, Our Ron prepares to rush to our rescue. January - this month's Navigans is full of facts; deadly dull and not much scope for taking a light-hearted "jaundiced view' of things. However, it is livened up when I read that some 25 members of the Cruiser Section apparently met to discuss "..various more or less controversial ideas on running and maintaining the club" but we're not told what they are. Still, should be good for a ‘jaundiced view' in later months Navigans. February - the ‘doggie members' of the MSC no doubt were delighted with the actions of Joe Stobseth-Brown, who not ae il in his membership renewal form from Australia but also included “a generous donation to FhS tree." ee y ttng of the Club's Planning & Development Sub-Committee apparently agreed its objects would be ",.to plan for development of the Stansgate site..." Well...Yes...that would be a logical conclusion 1 would think ! Plans includeClubhouse, precincts, launching pac itiian’ ‘oorinas and use of the larce field (presumably the current 'Cat' field). Members are invited to send in ideas and comments. A "Statement of Account" to 31 December '71 reveals a Subscription income of 2,380.10, Bar Takings of £964.65 and a successful Social Programme with income of £76.19 covering social expenditure of £25.42. Overall, the club's Reserve Account amounts to £1,669.60. March - a note about the Tree Fund must surely have set even more doggie tails a-wagging; donations received raised the Fund to £18 which, coincidently, is also the number of trees planted along the SE boundary. Pete Foreman is organising a Grand Draw for the Open Day on lst July. Tickets at 5p each and Pete says "The first prize is aimed at the person who must be convinced that sailing is a good thing, the wife, and will almost certainly be a dishwater". ** So, there you are chaps, if you want your wife's approval/permission to sail, buy her a dishwasher to gladden her heart. Well, sounds a good deal to me; what do you say Maggie...Quch. !!! The object of the Grand Draw is to “invest once and for all" in a proper rescue launch. The Cruiser Fleet reports that the main Committee have turned down the arguement for a power outlet in the cruiser storage end of the dinghy park. I'll resist the temptation to say 'How shocking' but I bet some sparks flew around when they heard the news. April - Editor, MaryGreygoose, reports 50 people attended a successful ‘Fitting Out' partv at Stansgate but complains there wasn't quiteenough space to "do the Gay Gordons". If I remember the old wenden clubhouse correctly, I'm surprized there was enough room for a gay group of 6 people, let alone the Gay Gordons and an entourage of 50. Avril Stevens is praised for an excellent buffet and the crowded venue clearly didn't worry Mary for she writes "Most of the jolly crowd were 'young', the rest of us slightly older. It also gave us older ones an opportunity to dance a little closer to our partners, which made us feel young again". Well, it would, wouldn't it ? Ron Greygoose reveals that the recent decision of “the committee" to buy immediately a new rescue boat was apparently “out of order". It seems all equipment and money held or subscribed by an MASC Section belongs to the MASC - and the Reserve funds have been earmarked for site development. It is therefore proposed to seek MASC permission to open a ‘special account’ with the MASC for the sole purpose of buying a new rescue boat. 1s there a new series of articles starting in Navigans ? "An Observer" writes a short note called "Observations" which reveals that frogmen used to examine cruiser moorings examined the wrong ones. Also a cautionary tale of dinghy sailors venturing out in unsuitable “hairy conditions". Pete Foreman tells us the grand Draw on Open Day, lst July, will be called the 21st Anniversary Draw - but we know different, don't we ? Never mind if it's the real 2lst anniversary or not, at least two of the wives will be cock-a-hoop and full of "Yes dear, you go sailing" when ttrey receive lst prize of the dishwasher or 3rd prize of Food Mixer fplus bowl). Mind you, they might fight over the 2nd prize whichis a tape recorder. Still, to be fair, hubby ought to have it to play with (after he's finished sailing) whilst his ever-beloved plays with her dishwasher and makes up enough 'mix' to produce a dozen Upsidedown cakes. Ron Greygoose was clearly very busy for he attended a Cruiser Section meeting to put the case for a new rescue launch with a specification suitable for rescue rather than gwar tog moorings. Oh, what a .surprize ! When I started this Navigans Past series, 1 wanted to show that ‘current day problems' are no more than replays of well-worn arguements and there really is nothing new in 'the problems’ that beset us from time to time. The 'Rescue Boat v Work Boat' arguement has had more replays than ‘The Sound of Music’ on TV and will, no doubt, continue tobe 'sung' in theCommittee Room for as long as Julie Andrews warbles about some Lonely Goatherd clearing his throat ona foreian hillton. Well, at least I suppose he's stil] got a job/ ; ** Maggie asks “Did Pete mean the dishwasher is the lst prize or the dishwasher is ‘the wife' ?. n . As a firm believer in nature having clearly established our roles in life, t'd have thought it could be either. (OUCH !! - only joking)

Complaints about the "blocked dinghy park road" reminds me that both cruiser and dinghies were parked in what is now solely used by cruisers, ie. the ground between the concrete base of the old clubhouse and the pill boxes to theeast of the sea-wall gap. My goodness, it makes you realise just how much the club has ‘developed’ since then. Brian Urry complained that people were driving along the recently improved road at 25 mph instead of 15 mph, and that the rules on speed ought to be applied. Now that is a problem which has been with us since Day 1 at Stansgate and will undoubtedly continue to be with us even after a serious accident occurs.. I've been told of more than one 'near miss' over the years, including one in which they all finished up in the fields and all lucky to be alive. On the sailing side, Nick Tovey reveals that Helm of the Year for 1972 will be sailed as aseriesof 6 qualifyinc races for each fleet (Hornet, Enterprise, GP14, Mirror and Handicap). Qualifiers will be the top two helms (sorry, helmsmen - this in 1972) in each fleet with an extra helms(man) for every 5 entries above the first 5 in the fleet. The final will be raced in one class of boat (yet to be decided) and qualifying helmsmen will have to personally borrow a boat but owners will not be able to sail their own boat. However, owners can crew in their own boat if it is lent to a qualifying helmsman. May - Anote laments the lack of ideas and suggestions for the development of the site "for this ‘coming of age' year" including the "building of a Club house in character with our image". Oh! I see! - you mean short and squat and flat on top; but I hadn't even joined the club then, so how did they know ? Pete Foreman comments on the new Clubhouse and suggests (a)a raised building so that the river is visible over the sea wall (maybe build it on the river side of the wall) (b) better toilet facilites to make permission for camping easier (c) races to finish opposite the clubhouse and (d) a lounge built for summer social events only. Oberver writes another "Obervations" article and reports much annoyance in the GP14 fleet. [t seems that the had their PYN adjusted ‘the wrong way' without their knowledge and felt they were the victims of “a fast one’ (presumably the Enterprise Fleet). Observer reckons better communications are called for "..to ensure the decision to be taken in....a happier atmosphere...".// Observer notes that reactions to Regatta are basically one of three; there are those (a) who don't want to know and stay at home (b) those who participate - but don't help and (c) those who organise the event. He feels that the good people (the organisers) ought to have more support from "the brighter stars in our racing firmament" and from "the stay-at-homes". My own view has always been that those who want (and presumably enjoy) running Regatta - run it; those who want to participate - participate and those who want to stay at home - stay at home. My feeling is that there is no obligation on 'the club' to run Regatta or any other ‘open event' but, if there is a group of people willing to do so, then 'fine' - I'11 help out as and when I am available and it is convenient to do so - but I certainly don't feel obliged to do so. This question of what members ought, or ought not, to do regarding support of Regatta (and other events) is a recurring theme throughout the history of the club and will, no doubt, continue to be so into the future until, one day, someone Proposes the ‘obligation to help' be a condition of membership. On that day ‘the sparks will fly' from more than just the power point that the unsympathetic Main Committee in 1972 wouldn't provide for the cruiser crowd. On that note (letters to the editor please) I'l] end this Navigans Past ‘cos, in June, 1972, it looks like the "Clubhouse controversy’ is about to break upon the heads of the hierarchy and I quess quite a number of people ‘blew a fuse’. 15. NAVIGANS PAST 1972 (June & July) Would that the Commodore the giftie gie us; To see ourselves as others see us. - In what image should we build ; & new clubhouse in our spacious field ? - What shape, what size, how high, how low ? ; How much, who pays ? Oh! wail ! Ah! Wow ! - If Solomon in his wisdom decided ; You can bet the result would be soon derided. - No matter what the "How, Why or When ?" ; It's bound to be beyond our ken (or Jane or Tom - We'll all keep quiet and await results ; too shy to speak or point out faults. - BUT when 'tis done - this monstrosity ; We'll blame it on "The Powers That Be". ++++++ June - Amongst the "baby! announcements is Jonathan David Craig (Bigden), grandson of a, no doubt, delighted Jack and Connie Bigden who subsequently donated the Jonathan David Craig cup for a Mirror Open Meeting. Alas, the Mirror fleet has shrunk in size since then, but Jonathan (David Craig) is now a lot bigger and lives in the OSC with parents Jill and Julian Bigden, and has proved to be a very welcome and engagine visitor to the club in recent years. With his ‘Ordinary Member' hat on, Stan Allerton writes in support of Pete Foreman's "New Clubhouse" comments in the May Navigans, noting that the original (ie 1968) idea was for a single storey building on pillars with storage underneath. He points out that building on the river -side of the sea-wall would not be entertained, not least because of the problems of a shifting foundation !| He also supports finishing races off the club- house, but feels they couldn't start there because of the unfavourable (tidal ?) conditions. With his ‘Commodore's hat' on, Stan also writes a long article on 'Planning and Development' and it is evident “that “rumour and mis-information" has been circulating which Stan attempts to put to rest. Stan’s article is -00 long to cover all his points here, but I am impressed by the straight-forward and succinct manner in which he informs the Members, via Navigans, of the current situation. One interesting ‘snippet’ is that our current day 'Cat' field had only just had the two concrete access bridges built - but we had no planning permission for its use other than as agricultural land. It is worth, however, quoting Stan's closing remarksr- Remember - without prejudice - that whatever we build can only be built with our money and will belong to the Sailing Section of MASC. Remember - without rashness - a decision to raise subscriptions.... to build a £10,000 clubhouse within four years could deny membership to someone else. Remember - with gratification - we must continue to pay our dues .... of £1,000 increasing by £100 per year for the next 4 years to our parent club against the debt of £21,300 incurred for the purchase of the site... Remeber - without flamboyance - the need for a "Club-house in character with our image". Ken Beavins writes a letter stating that one of the club's two fields should be kept as a ‘green space’ for the many club children under sailing age but without special play equipment - only clean grass and open air. He is also keen to retain existing hedges and trees along the roadside of the ‘dinghy park' field - alas the once thick hedge there has long since gone. Ken is not too keen on improved facilties for campers/caravans and is, in fact, against any camping at the club except for the 3-day Regatta. He fears that camping would turn he open, airy and pleasant Stansgate site into a “sort of waterside slum only too common along the Essex rivers and coast". Ken is no longer with us, but I wonder what he would make of both the site and the sights these days ? Would he be relieved that his worst fears were not fulfilled ? - or would he be saddened at what he saw ? ] suspect it would be a bit of both - but you can't stop ‘development and progress', especially if it creeps up on you unnoticed. However, Ken praises Navigans and particularly enjoyed some of the "thought provoking items in recent issues". A letter from J W Pletts reveals that he and his architect son had put forward similar ideas to those postulated by Pete Foreman but, it seems, they had been rejected. Overall, he felt that everything was “already cut and dried" and there wasn't much point in making suggestions. He feels the lines of communications between “the Powers that be" and the ordinary club member leave much to be desired and asks for a special meeting to discuss (a) the current status and future plans for Stansgate and (b) what actions are needed to enable ordinary members to be informed of progress and be able to express their views. Finally, our new ‘old friend’ Observer comments on Regatta which was sailed in strong winds and recounts that “,..the (Marconi) crew of a leading boat in one of the races left his boat and deliberately entered deep water to render urgently needed help to a family of two adults and two very young children whose Mirror has capsized. Sacre ..the following boats in the race, who had ofcourse caught up with the erstwhile leading boat, then deliberately delayed so as to allow it to resume its former position after the rescue operation has been completed." Observer comments that "The incident reflects credit on all concerned, except (it has to be said) on the helmsman who took two small children for a sail in such patently adverse weather conditions".

16. July - An appeal by Pete Foreman (Cruiser Social Secretary) to the dinghy sailors; "If you should hit a cruiser, please tell the owner as soon as possible either through the OOD or directly". Apparently, three cruisers has recently been holed. Now, I wonder where I've heard that message before ? I wonder if the dinghy sailors got ‘all huffy' that their seamanship should be thus questioned ? Even more intriguing, | wonder who made the holes ? Well, the ‘Clubhouse debate' is well under way and battle has been joined. Four letters are published in the July Navigans and maybe there are more to come. In her letter, Jane Long briefly reviews features of ‘local' clubhouses, including the Royal Corinthian where "....ties will be worn after 7.00 p.m.". She is somewhat critical of the new clubhouse of our near neighbours at Maylandsea Bay for she writes "Anyone who has known the club for some years will tell how it has changed from a jolly glowing "who's-going-to-be-Race-Officer ?" club - much the same as ours - into an uninteresting spiritless place. Why ? - they built a new clubhouse". Well, I know what she means. Maggie and I met at the Penzance Tennis Club when it had no clubhouse and everyone gathered together on the grass banks by the tennis courts, everyone was friendly and mixed well. Then they built a nice new clubhouse - and the whole atmosphere changed. Those who formerly freely mixed in a friendly bunch no longer did so, and it was all down to the clubhouse. Mind you, I expect the standard of tennis improved - but I couldn't play anyway. Jane goes on to praise the spirit of the existing club, despite lack of hot water and showers, the presence of the smelly cess pit and the need to shout "Shut the door" as the last person out of the Ladies Changing Room (closet ?) exposed those ladies inside to the keen-eyed view of those on the outside. Jane is not against a new clubhouse as such - she merely fears a change of atmosphere. She writes “What I hope is never said to sailing members is "You can't come in for a drink - you're wet and you'll ruin the floor" After all, it is a sailing club". How close have we come to that position in recent years ? It was only a season or two ac that I argued against confining the wet sailors to the newly created ‘overload bar' in the garage downstairs. Let us hope the 'overtoad bar' doesn't become the ‘wet bar’ by default. Would it be progress if it did ? Dr R T Jones writes to support Ken Beavins view on campers and caravans and fears the club will] become a Caravan Club with sailing facilties. However, Margaret Farnie writes in defence of limited camping/caravaning, perhaps limiting the number of camping units to 3 or 4 and definitely ‘for members only'. Oh dear ! How does that measure up to the 50 or 60 units (including non-members) of recent years ? Is it progress ? However, Tom Gaskell] must take the prize for the most forthright letter of 1 pages in which he doesn't mince his words. He writes "I have read one of the most bigoted and conservative letters which it is possible to write on the subject of preventing people from enjoying themselves after their own fashion without interference with others". I think he means he doesn't agree with some of the viewpoints of another member . Tom then goes on to dispute/disagree with Ken's viewpoints, but supports limited camping and is, surprizingly, against a new clubhouse, although he supports a more economical scheme of "an ablution block somewhere" with a SWIFTPLAN building on top to act as a clubhouse, He finishes up with what I feel are two rather 'deep' sentences :- "It would be interesting to know what our ‘image’ is - to see ourselves as others see us - or should we remain enchanted with our own reflections. The facts are that we are running the club on a shoe string with heavy overheads and exploiting the willing few to run or ruin a valuable asset." I guess the ‘ordinary member' found the whole thing quite confusing - maybe we should have stayed in the Hut on the Wall at Maldon where all was simple, pure and friendly. (Oh yer? If you believe that, you obviously haven't been reading Navigans Past !). Observer laments the fact of queues of cars at Stone and fears they'll all descend on Stansgate. He feels that unless the club enforces the "no vehicular access" notice, then the steady trickle of uninvited gate- crashers will become an unmanageable flow. He proposes a ‘locked gate’ system with keys for club members (keys to be paid for). Finally, Pete Foreman's Grand Draw winners were lst Mr D Byford (presumably the dishwasher - let's hope he is a sailor), 2nd Miss S Keep (Tape Recorder ?), 3rd John Witter (presumably the Mixer - with bowl) and 4th Mrs Perry (prize unknown). I wonder if John made any Upsidedown cakes to go with his Enterprise dinghy (also known to be of the Upsidedown variety - so I am told). Pete tells us that approx. £170 was raised towards the cost of a new rescue launch, which he felt disappointing in view of the prizes offered. Never mind, it was a bold try and Pete is to be congratulated on the attempt - and at least I assume it did, in fact, make a contribution towards the purchase of the new rescue launch. On other matters, the Southern Area Police Regatta was held at the MSC, whilst an Open day on lst June resulted in 12 new members enrolled, which was two more thanthe target of 10. A ‘sample handicap race' was won by Frank Savill in his Mirror, which is described as the club's fastest growing smal] boat class. How times have changed ! There will be no August Navigans, but Editor , Mary Greygoose, asks everyone to “read and inwardly digest al] the letters and comments I have received and have your answers ready for the September issue". It was on this note that Mary ‘wrapped up' the July'72 issue at 1.05 in the morning ! Mike Boreham

17. 40 YEARS AGO - FEBRUARY, 1953. During the month, the MASC intimated the possibility of increasing the £50 grant, for the purchase of a Sailing Section boat, to £75. A Sailing Section newsletter reveals that a few local sailing vessels of 30 tons upwards were available for charter during the summer at a charge of £7 per week, all found (presumably 'per person’ ?), A General Meeting of the Sailing Section revealed that ‘the boat' had been purchased and the meeting agreed "the rules' for its use. Calls for volunteers for ‘foreshore clearance’ apparently produced more raised hands than people present - it was suspected some people raised two hands (presumably in surrender ?). In contrast, a call for bosuns for the new boat brought forth only a ‘part-time’ offer from Mr Adam (did he raise his hand only half-way up ?). Finally, club burgees were on sale at 6/6 each. Commodore's Notes A business trip to Cheshire last week just showed me how simple it is to have one's equilibrium upset beyond measure by a simple everyday event i.e. having one's briefcase nicked!! I'm now absolutely bereft of the 1993 diary and address book, so my apologies if I promised to do something and haven't. I can only suggest that you call to remind me! However, out of every crisis comes a "benefit" - the old Casio Digital diary has been replaced by a Psion 3, and that enables me to write CN's (Commodores Notes) on the train!! Enough excuses, to business! After a great deal of vacillation, it is mow clear that the NRA are going to start work on the sea wall around Easter. Our preliminary meeting on site indicated the high degree of disruption to which we may be subjected, and you may rest assured that we shall be keeping on top of the problem in order to mininise the effect on club activities. Initially, I feel it important to warn you all that this could be a difficult period. The first blockbuster is that we have to empty most of the cruiser park by Easter. Bearing in mind the number of weekends available, that is going to be a fair old task. The only choice we have will be to park them on the car park behind the dinghy park pro tem. If you have a boat in the park, then expect to be contacted with a view to arranging to move. The stalwarts on the Sailing sub have wrought their magic, and we have a few amendments to Sailing Instructions for this season. Of particular note (queries to Colin Kidner or Willie Pitcairn please !! are the removal of average points and the further splitting of the Cat Fleet start into Fast (PY<80) and Medium (PY80-90). The hope is that this will do for the Dart 18's etc what starting separately did for the 15's. It will certainly help the nerves of the Cruiser Fleet between 10.50 and 11.10 on Sunday mornings. Just one point of etiquette, if you are starting after Class X then you should stay clear of the immediate area of the line until after their start. Well, that's yer lot, soon see you afloat, Larry Botheras Many members will be sorry to hear of the death recently of Albert Pearce. Albert joined the Club in the early 1970s, gave a lot of help with building work at the Club over the years and served for several years on the Committee. Many of us will remember him for organising and helping with the cooking at the Annual Outdoor Barbecues we used to hold in the summer, when I seem to remember that the cooking was done in a S-sided canvas shelter, sometimes set up on the hard, and anchored down to girders. Albert moved his Cruiser sailing to Tollesbury about 3 years ago where it was less physically demanding, and became an Honorary Member of MSC. The sympathy of all Albert’s friends in the Club go to his wife Shirley, and to daughter Leslie, and son David at this sad time.

5. THEFTS - ALL MEMBERS, ALL FLEETS. As I am sure has been mentioned elsewhere in this Navigans, several Cruisers were broken into during a seemingly well-organised single operation last month, = and property was stolen. This, as all thefts at the Club, causes great concern to the Officers of the Club, and in order that we carn do as much as possible to help the police, can I ask ALL MEMBERS to da the following: 1) If anyone is infortunate enough to be the victim of theft of any kind, after reporting the incident to the police, please let me know in writing, including any information you may have on time of theft, item/s taken, and name of Folice Station at which theft was reported. 2) If you've seen anyone, or any activity, either on the Club site, or cut on the water (both winter and summer) that causes you to be suspicious, please also let me know. Steve Hill, Hon. Secretary, [redacted] Ed’s_ note: I understand Steve would now like a written report of any thefts (even if considered not worth reporting to Police) for his records. Also a description of a doubtful person/make and registration of a car/ description of a boat showing interest in the Club (some unwelcome visitors may arrive by boat) if you noted it, may be of use even after a theft. If really suspicious call the police, some thieves were apprehended on a busy sailing weekend a couple of years ago by this means thanks to watchful people down at Stone. SEA WALL HEIGHTENING The NRA (National Rivers Authority) recently made their decision to start the long- expected work on the Sea Wall at our Club at around Easter, (Easter Sunday = 11th April). I understand that we will end up with the same sort of Sea Wall as we have now, but higher and wider at the base, encroaching a little more on our space. One advantage we will have is a much better system of gates instead of floodboards to close the gap in the sea wall. As Commodore’s Notes warn us this work is likely to have a very noticeable effect on the comfort of our preparations for sailing and on our activities on land at the Club this summer, so please be prepared to make large allowances for how the Site may have to be organised at its busiest times. Some property (e.g. Cruisers) will have to be moved very soon now (before Easter) and stored in another part of the site until they car. be launched, and I’m sure that some more of our precious space will be temporarily taken up by NRA equipment while the work goes on — probably until late October. The work may also affect the comfort of Camping Fortnight to some extent as well. Lastly, there is the question of safety. I do feel that as our site is likely to be turned into something of a building site, Members will need to exercise more care for their own safety, and I think it will be important that Members impress upon their youngsters the importance of keeping away from any deep holes, heavy machinery and NRA property in general, that will be nearby. I suppose we should be grateful for all the hassle! I’ve read of questions asked about the huge cost of protecting a particular number of acres of now ‘surplus’ agricutural land, and I suppose it could yet be decided to leave the water’s edge in some places to its own devices. An article in Maldon & Burnham Standard about a continuing experiment on this on Northey Island will be on Club Notice Board soon. Ed. GET THAT STITCHED! Apologies to all those who follow the yachting or medical press, who have already read about Frenchman Bertrand de Broc’s achievement in the Southern Ocean. But if you haven’t, and you’ve also wondered how you would cope with a medical emergency when afloat read on...... De Broc suffered a severe facial injury when his boom broke in a storm while competing in the Vendee Globe Challenge non-stop Solo round the world race. The tip of his tongue was almost severed but he proceeded to put three stitches into it while looking into a mirror with a badly swollen eye and taking instgructions from a doctor on-shore via a telex (because conditions were too bad to hear the radio clearly.) Having done that he took some pain killers, rested and made a good recovery. I don’t know if he will win the race, but he certainly deserves a prize for bravery. Lick that! Paul Metcalfe The RYA Seamanship Foundation ’YACHTSMAN OF THE YEAR’ Award mentioned in Bugs Hughes’ thank-you letter published in last Navigans was won by Hampshire Yachtswoman and Nurse Sian Worgan, sailing between Wellington, New Zealand and Fiji. In stormy conditions and after the vessel’s skipper was killed and a crew member injured she managed to treat the injured crew and keep the vessel afloat with the help of another crew member new to sailing for several hours before help was able to arrive. Newspaper article with full details has been put on a Club Notice Board for anyone interested. - Ed.

DINGHY PARK At the peak of the 1992 summer about 160 boats were stored in the park and we still had a few places to spare. This is about the same as 1991. The boats were made up of: Mirror 47 Laser 10 GP14 7 Club 4 Solo 20 420 8 Laser2 7 Others 33 Wayfarer 1] Enterprise 8 Wanderer 5 Of the "Others", no class was represented by more than 4 boats and most were ones or twos. The layout for this year will be similar to last year, but with a few minor changes, again aimed at ensuring that we make the best use of available space. This year the plan is for a total of about 170 boats. The most effective boat parking is to keep the boats of similar size together and facing the same way. The park is a "no-go” area for cars, so if you need to use a vehicle to launch your boat because of its size, please make sure that you occupy a space facing the road at the east side. This year we are giving up some ground for the Sailboard fleet to provide a permanent rigging area adjacent to the tractor shed. This involves some changes to the Solo fleet areas, but overall, makes little impact on the available space for dinghies. Boats can be placed in any empty space in the correct block and starting from the club house end first. Please indicate your boat's position on the chart in the clubhouse. Spaces will be pegged out asa guide however boats should be placed with a maximum gap of 2ft hull to hull. Anchors are required and are members responsibility. If you want to keep your boat on aroad trailer in the dinghy park, don't expect extra space. Road trailers belong in the area beyond the catamaran park and should be marked and immobilised. Finally: No hard fee stickers this season....not needed as OF COURSE YOU WILL HAVE ALREADY IDENTIFIED YOUR EQUIPMENT. I will assume that club fees have not been paid for unidentified boats. NAVIGANS PAST. 10. 1972 (August - December) - As the sweet smells of the farmyard get mixed up with club politics, Stansgate's rural and marine charm comes under the scrutiny of some members. The question is “are they revolting" ? ~ - But the cruiser crowd club together to clobber the clommittee (well, you just try saying it quickly). August - no Navigans published in August because everyone is on holiday. September - a brief note entitled "Enterprise Champion Again" congratulates Roger Hance on his great success at Helensburgh - presumably he won the national championship but it doesn't actually say so. Amongst the cruiser folk, Pete Foreman mentions two cruisers went adrift due to poor tackle and expresses concern that it seems some members are not insured. Observer talks about the Jackpot race as follows:- "The conduct of this race has always been somewhat slapdash seeeeee" 1 guess we've had a ‘problem or two' in recent years as well ! As far as the ‘clubhouse debate' in Navigans is concerned Observer laments "....the sort of emotive language which adds nothing to reasoned debate." but is sympathetic to Jane Long's fears thata new Clubhouse will bring with it a changed atmosphere "....almost overnight by efficient but soul-less development" I guess one person's ‘reasoned debate' is someone else's ‘emotive language’ - and vice versa - and presumably ‘the powers that be' must try to accommodate everyone and be damned forever afterwards. Ah! well ! Pity the hierarchy who will presumably get their reward in some kind of ‘sailor's heaven'; at least the Commodore gets his name on the board, although I'm not sure if it is as a 'reward' - or as a warning to others ! Nicholas Benwell adds a very brief letter, saying he was "....dismayed....that they are going to try to get planning permission for caravans on our site". and he feels such permission would be "....inconceivable..." and "...fears the club's rural and marine charm will be destroyed". Mind you, I'm not sure if our modern day 'farmyard' containers, cruiser mast derrick, gas holder and children's play equipments add to the "rural and marine charm" of Stansgate or not. Atleast the tractor shed and accompanying tractors are in keeping with ‘the farming scene' but perhaps we should replace the tractors with some Shire horses, bring in some free range hens, a cow (milk for the galley) and a couple of goats (get rid of the rubbish). However, on second thoughts,maybe we shouldn't; the last time we tried being 'rural' and imported sheep onto the site, they played leap-frog on the boats, ate the boat covers - and deposited from one end the derivative of what they took in at the other ! Accusations. that we were a ‘stuck up' club might well have been true (literally) had they been made ! I wonder what Stansgate and the river Blackwater were like 1n the 1920s and 1930s? Hard graft, I wouldn't wonder, full of rural charm. October - The Laying-Up Supper is to be at the Chancellor Hall in Chelmsford , and offers a 5-course dinner with wine for £2.50 per ticket. The Cruiser Section news reveals the need to form an action committee to "...plan and cost the erection of scrubbing posts and the second access by the racebox". Did they really plan to bash a great hole in the sea-wal] by the pill-box - and did they erect the present-day scrubbing posts ? I thought those posts had been there from Cro-Magnon times, whenever that was. A Marconi team of Roger Hance, Julian Bigden and Norman Richards won the Enterprise “East Coast Area Team Championship” at Broxbourne S.C. November - the Agenda for the AGM is published and includes the Committee proposal "The committee propose that a clubhouse be erected on the Stansgate Site of similar design and style to the type presented". Also proposed are membership fees for Ordinary (ie Marconi employee) Members of £3 which includes husband/wife and children under 15, Associate members (ditto) at £6, dinghy hard fees £7 and cruisers £10 (drying mooring) and £12 (deep water mooring). Well, I reckon most of that will go through ‘on the nod' apart from a few people who are worried about 'the atmosphere'. They will, no doubt, be reassured that ‘the committee’ are well aware of their concerns and will watch that the nature of the club will not change. In fact, I would imagine that the only piece of really contentious business will be over the Mirror Fleets proposal that a new rescue launch be purchased for the 1973 season. December - Wow ! What happened at the AGM ? The committee proposals were rejected - and one consequence was that the Membership Renewal Forms couldn't be sent out. It seems an Extra Ordinary Meeting is now required to sort things out. Presumably not all the proposals were defeated because Dennis Byatt is the new Commodore. The AGM reveals present membership stands at 266 Ordinary and 84 Associate Members. Observer comments on the AGM as follows:- "Some may tell us that the defeat of the outgoing committee's proposals OnClubhouse and subscriptions at the recent AGM is a sign of a healthy and active democracy in the club. On the other hand it may simply have been the effect of active pre-meeting lobbying among an already fairly tightly-knit and highly articulate group of members with a common interest. Certainly there could be no doubt of the strength of the antipathy with which cruiser people viewed the proposal that their hard fees should in future be greater than those for dinghy sailors. One suspects , however, that they may have felt just a little abashed at the ease with which they succeeded in

11. toppling the Establishment, or (choose your own flavour) rejecting the carefully thought-out work of the committee. weeeeeeeeAS it iS, with proposals for Clubhouse and means to pay for it defeated at the AGM, we have no policy on these matters. However, nature abhors a vacuum, and I do not think it will be long before the new committee comes back to us with an unaltered clubhouse proposal and somewhat modified subscripti proposals." Observer then goes on to thank Stan Allerton (retiring Commodore) for his work and Mary Greygoos (retiring editor). In reply, Mary writes "Thank you, Observer, for your concluding remarks. Your articles have caused quite a 'stir' this year - much stronger words have been used by some." However, Mary issues a mild rebuke to Observer, for she continues "Anonymity however carries with it the responsibility to ensure that your 'Observations' are wise and will strengthen fellowship and club spirit amongst the members. On balance I think you succeeded but next year I hope you will make the Editor's job a little easier". I must be honest and say that, reading Observers remarks at some 20 years removed in time, I haven't found them particularly contentious - but perhaps that is because I have no feel for ‘the mood' of the club in 1972. The fact that 'Observer' felt the need to put his/her ‘observations' on record seems to me to point to a mood of uncertainty and apprehension amongst the members. Although, no doubt, the rejection of all the hard work of the committee was very annoying and disappointing (to the committee), it was probably 'no bad thing’ for’ ‘the membership’ to flex its muscles and show that ‘the powers that be' cannot always expect to get an a easy ride from those whose interest they (the committee) are supposed to serve. So, as 1972 closes for the MSC, Avril Stevens retires from the post of Social Secretary after many years of service (Pete and dT" Foreman take over) and also Mary Greygoose passes on the post of Editor to Dorothy Renshaw . The club said ‘thank you' to Mary in 1972 and has said ‘thank you' many, many times since then for her continued practical support of the club in many way§. It was most appropriate that Mary was the first winner of the Commodore's Trophy and I am sure that we are all delighted that she should now be the club's ‘first lady' as Ron becomes President at the 1992 AGM. Afterthought - when I visited the club in January ('93) I noted that our present hierarchy have clearly taken Stansgate's ‘rural and marine charm' very much to heart, for they have built what appears to be a very nice sheep-pen which, by happy chance, also encloses the gas tanks. All it needs now is a low thatched roof; then the free-range hens can perch on the roof top, the local Brent Geese can be encouraged to 'honk' all over the Commodore's lawn and the sheep left to 'bah' contentedly all night within the safety of their compound. Then, of course,. there would be. the Shire_horses and Daisy the cow-to add. to the-cacophony:.of rural sounds which, together with Daisy's cow-pats and Dobbins droppings, would create a ‘rural and marine’ idyll in which we would all have to tread very carefully indeed and few campers would enjoy an uninterrupted night's sleep. That's the trouble with ‘rural charm's; its full of creepy-crawlies, cow-pats and cockerells "doodle-doing” all night. PS. Maggie has reminded me that it was in 1972 that we paid our first visit to Marconi SC as a guest of Mike and Jennie Hart. We eventually joined as Associate Members and bought Mike's Mirror. Later on we renamed the Mirror ‘Lars Tinn' to reflect our usual finishing position (but someone did once ask me if we hadsScandinavian connections !). A letter to the River Bailiff seeks permission to put down some mooring off the clubhouse, asks if there would be any objection to using the channel markers as racing buoys and enquires if he is the right person to ask about putting a Starting Line Withy on Northey Island. The Sailing Section Report (presumably to the MASC AGM ?) recalls the formation of the club on 18 April, 1952 and the fact of having 50 members by the end of the year. It also refers to the clubhouse as "....an almost ideal club house right onthewaters edge at Heybridge Basin. This building, an old shipwrights shop, is some 60 ft long by 18 ft and is located on the sea wall. It is noteworthy that during the recent calamitous floods ........ although surrounded by water, none entered the building. Any Sunday or Saturday in the winter months found members busy on their craft which practically covered the whole floor space available, and the view of the river from the wide windows made it pleasant for those working within." The Report finishes up by thanking the MASC for its contribution towards the rent of the clubhouse and for the loan to purchase a club boat. Mike Boreham

4. COMMODORE’S NOTES As intimated last month, a hectic time is upon us. By the time you read this, the Cruisers will be out of the Cruiser Park and standing in the Car Park. Hopefully, we will still have had not problems - the first two sessions went well - thanks to the efforts of Pat Black who has masterminded the whole oaperaticmn. As soon as we kriow any more about the details about the contract you will be informed.... The distressing news for all of us is that we have had a number of security incidents since the New Year. Apart from the Club taking advice from the police, I suggest every single person reviews their own security since cone success for ai raider encourages them either to come back or to look for more. The general view is that the less there is ta nick, the less likely we are to have preblems. Obviously there are two major areas where we can all help each other - keeping the gate shut = and ensuring every ladder is locked up. It only takes one person to put everyone else at risk. Don’t feel guilty about challenging strangers on site either. I krow there’s a public footpath, but it is pretty good cover for someone locking over the prospects. As we all know, there is no way to stop the determined thief, but what we can stop is the opportunist. A final point about making your own personal effort is, that whether you get burgled aor not, your insurance premium will suffer. Related to the above is the renewal of the key system. Wher the GEC system was installed it was pretty much the best that could be done at the time, but with keys running at £7 each to buy, being limited to 1000 combinations, and running out of that number row with defective or missing keys, we were at a stage of needing to lock at alternatives. Frank Bennett, being the electronics whizz-kid that he is has irvestigated and built a new system. Cards will be issued - much like a credit card but unmarked - and these will be sent out with Membership packs. The cards are much cheaper (15p) and we shall consider re-issuing every year, and cancelling the old card cade, Initially both systems will run in tandem. This will obviously help improve the security situation, with old keys no longer being an issue. Frank has put a note in with the membership pack, but please ensure that you keep the new = card safe. Social everts have been a bone of contention for a long time, with the limited support from a membership of around 500. The view of both the Executive and myself is that we are no longer prepared to see the effort put in to organisation, all for S0O-60 people. We asked for comments about the desire for a Barn Dance and Roseanna received several calls in support. Surprise, surprise when we find that a number of the *supporters’ were conspicuous by their absence at the event. If it had net been for the sterling efforts of one ar two who brought along parties of friends we would have been embarassed once again. Consequently, there will be no Fitting Out or Midsummer Event organised or financially supported by the Club. If anything is arranged it will have to be on an independent Fleet basis, with permission from the Committee. We are prepared tc continue with the Laying Up Supper, which in 1992 at least "washed its face" and shows signs of some regeneration. This year’s event will be on Friday 1léth November (we get a discount) at the Three Rivers (Cold Norton). We are aiming at a ticket price in the region of £15 (don’t hold me te that too much). That means that since 1991 the price will have been reduced by 40%! I suppose you'll have tc dream up some other excuses now for not going! You might be interested ta know that most of our neighbours on the Blackwater make a healthy profit from their annual dirmners! This whole sorry saga is part of a syndrome that seems to affect the Club throughout its activities, i.e. the few doing the majority of the work for the benefit of the many. You only have to start locking for Committee and Sub-Committee members to see the evidence. Last year, we had only one willing candidate for Handicap Fleet Captain, wher we have aver 100 boats in the park. This year we went through the entire Cat Fleet to find a Captain, and came down to only two or three options, all of whom required a degree of coercion - mind you the Cat Fleet is currently very invelved throughout the Club with the Piers Race (time for fresh faces there - no volunteers?) and the Main Committee, as is the Cruiser Fleet. I am not going tea perpetuate the principal. If you don’t want to get involved, then expect tca see activities scaling down. If you do, then stand up and be counted and help spread the load away from the few. Involvement is relatively light with no more than one or two meetings per month. Help contribute to the future of your Club. Enough of the heavy stuff... by the time you read this, sailing will have kicked off again, ard Sailboat '93 will be done and dusted. Let’s hope 1993 will see a healthy turnout and keer racing. Has anyone seen the revised Rule Bock yet? I hope there's nothing toc difficult to digest! Well at nearly 1000 words I suppose I’d better call a halt - Larry Botheras

After much discussion, the Sailing Sub Committee has decided tc abandon the award of average points to racing members performing duties during the Club Racing events. The following reasons contributed towards this change of policy: 1) No system for average point calculation has yet been proposed which is considered *fair’ tec all competitors. For example, the propesed new system of average pcints was mathematically biased in favour of competitors sailing in fewer races. This meant that the less you competed, the more points you were awarded for carrying cut duties. This was biased toa the extent that the awarding of average points could lead to someone being favoured with a prize in preference to someone else wha had actually competed in more races. =) Net all duties performed at the Club would qualify for average points therefore there was an unfair bias according to event. For example, duties performed during a ‘normal’ series were rewarded with average points whereas the same duties performed during a ’weekend’ series would not qualify. Given this anomaly, sailing ccompetitors would have a vested interest in seeking sailing duties during ’rnormal’ rather = than *special’ sailing everts. Theoretically, it was even possible for certain members whe had duties assigned to them over more than one weekend series ta ’lose out’ in the meting out of average points. 3) All competitors are required to carry cut approximately two duties per year. This should rot affect the outcome af any series as each member will still have the chance of competing in a requisite number af races ever if they choose te arrange te conduct their duties in the same series. By abolishing average points, the incentive to use the system for unfair accreditation of points is removed and calculating places is purely or a *races sailed’ basis. Willy Pitcairn, Sailing Secretary.

7. MARCH CRUISER NEWS - which just missed reaching Ed in time for last Navigans. The first of our 1993 Cruiser Meetings at MASC was on Wednesday 13th January and was well attended. Little did I know when handing out the ‘Marine Watch Information Packs’ that we would suffer the break-ins to so many Cruisers not two weeks later.1 Seo much has been written in Navigans about security, it is difficult to find anything original to say now, so let me repeat some extracts from previcus Navigans§ (taken from an Essex Police Marine Section Newsletter which was also posted at the time oan the Club Notice Board): The winter Lay-up season is the time wher your boat is probably at its most vulnerable. It is accessible by land and easy to climb aboard. Here are a few hints and tips worth some consideration: 1. Remove ALL your valuable property and electronics from you vessel. &. Dor’t leave ladders up alongside, or just lying underneath your boat. If you have ta leave a ladder on the site, chain and lock it up. 3. While your equipment is removed, think about postcoding it all with a suitable marker, e.g. the ultra-violet marking pens only cost a few pence, and we would strongly advise everyone to have one and use it on their property. 4. Have you considered fitting an Alarm System? Whilst we cannot endorse any one Particular model, we carn provide information on a wide range of alarm systems and installers. an Essex Police Boat Registration Scheme operates within an area. We would urge every boat Owner to complete and return one of cur simple forms. The information is used in the event of stop-checks, or if the vessel is found adrift, the owner car be contacted quickly, and possibly minimise further damage. During this Meeting security in general was discussed and there was a unanimous request that an approach be made to the General Committee for the installation of Floodlights. I would like toa thank Tony Holbrock for his talk and film at the January Winter Meeting and also Malcolm Shaft for sharing his Baltic experience with us. RAFT FLEET NEWS A couple of excellent books, suitable for kids from 8 to 80, on the subject of boats. One is the Eyewitness Guide entitled ‘Boat’ going through the development of vessels from Rafts to Liners and Tankers, from rowing and sailing, to engine power. Lots of illustrations and a surprising amount of information for something so easy to read, and it has been produced in association with the National Maritime Museum. There is also a book called ’Ships and Sailing’ - one of the ‘Eyewitness Visual Dictionaries’ and each book in this series goes into detail on the construction of the subject item and ‘naming of parts’ - again with clear illustrations and easy to read. Well worth looking for in the Library, unless you want to splash out and spend 28.99 per book to have them on your shelf at home. After suspecting for a long time that a Windsurfer couldn’t be classed as a Hoat (well, they can’t be if they have a nose and tail instead of a bow and stern and have no port & starboard to speak of, can they?) it seems the Windsurfer is really the latest development of the Raft. Rafts are not watertight structures, but float because of the natural buoyancy of the materials they are made of. You usually sit in a boat, but you sit/stand on a raft. The Windsurfer is the fastest sailing vessel ever made, clocked at over 50 mph, and no doubt that record continues toa be broken by ever faster Windsurfers as time goes by. Ed. At this time of the year Cruiser Park(s) are beginning to blossom spring-like with paint-hued Cruiser owners temporarily taking on the red and blue colours their boats will bear in the new season. The sea fever is becoming rife, claiming more peaple with each fresh morning, and blowing awake the winter weekend’s lie-in. We gc out aon the grey river ta re-anchor cur summer roots in the mud and to saw the surface with the colourful patterns all laid in neat rows, carrot-like, awaiting our craft. However there are those who are already awake to this year’s sailing, contrasting their bright sails against the grey water. It was whilst taking a break from the above pursuits that I watched several starts of our Club’s racing for the day. A bitterly cold day, with a 4, occasionally 65, gusting icily from the South East, which seemed not to daunt these hardy folk, some of whom were no youngsters. And this was not even the first race of the year! The Cat classes and the Solos were virtually the only boats on the river, and the clarity of the helmsmen’s planning, positioning and handling was a pleasure to watch - free of moored craft and other river users. I shall never forget the thrill of rounding a mark in a good wind having approached or the beat, cutting close to the buoy, freeing the sheets and bearing away off the wind, just ahead of an opponent, the wind accelerating the boat to the plane in one powerful flowing movement. There is nothing else like it! So I offer an appreciation to our Cat and Dinghy racers from a Cruiser owner who well remembers the excitement and fervour of racing in a small boat. The skill and commitment of these racers is great to see and gives watching families, and many like myself, a great deal of pleasure. FAST CAT NOTES It has been suggested that in volunteering to write these notes at last year’s Cat Fleet AGM| was simply acting in defence of the Hurricane sub-fleet (and | do not use ‘sub’ as an abbreviation); personally | cannot remember my motives (indeed | all but forgot volunteering at all), but for better or worse | now find myself attempting to follow in the hallowed (if somewhat deep) footsteps of our Commodore. Please bear with me as | attempt to document, in a vaguely accurate way, the successes and (probably more interestingly) the failures of the Fast Cat Fleet members through the season. The season started gently for those who ventured out for Spring Points 1 and 2, with a mild Force 3 greeting the 5 starters in the fleet. It has to be admitted that the Prindles impressed with their strong turnout, whilst the bulk of the Hurricanes were not to be seen on the water; | look forward to this anomaly being corrected in the near future. The first race was won by John and Caroline with a new livery for the 1993 season, taking advantage of Steve’s broken tiller bar (crew-beating never helped anyone); however the Prindle 19s made a strong comeback in the afternoon with both Steve and Tom (Ashley, not Duckmanton, who was stricken by ‘flu) and Larry and Chris vanquishing the lone Hurricane. The second weekend was, well, different. I’m not sure whether to thank the gang for pitying us on our ‘duty weekend’, or to point out that, in general, we should try to emulate the other fleets and finish races. For a variety of reasons (gear failure, exhaustion, confusion, more confusion) the entire fleet elected not to complete the course set by Caroline in either race. Contrary to suggestions | must insist that this was not a Nickalls replacement for the average points system, wherein the course set is sO complicated that none of the entrants can successfully navigate it, thus guaranteeing no penalty to those manning the racebox. Particular condolences must go to Mick Jones, who retired out of consideration for his very cold and tired crew, only to discover that a few more minutes sailing would have brought him a deserved 1st place. No condolences whatsoever are deserved by the heavyweights of the Prindle 19 fleet: both Steve and Larry broke their trapeze lines. Spring Points 5 and 6 brought a return to sanity, and a return of Grant and Martin's winning ways. As became a regular sight last season, they convincingly won both races, with Steve and Tom and John and Caroline second in the two races. Dave Onyons returned from winter grazing to push the other Prindle 19s hard; it looks as if they can look forward to a close season's racing. It was also interesting to see the medium cat fleet start with the fast cats; it’s quite a dilemma, whether to satisfy those who are Sailing, or to encourage those who are not. Either way, I’m sure we all view declining numbers in the medium cat fleet (and, more significantly, the monohull fleet) with considerable concern for the future. As | close I’m looking forward to the Easter series, in hopeful anticipation of some more of the Hurricanes coming out of hibernation and justifying the RYA’s confidence in us. As often seems to be the case, the RYA has made some minor adjustments to the relevant handicaps over the winter, and it will be interesting to see whether the Hurricanes can live up to their new turn of speed. What a pity we don’t all sail the same boat, be it a Hurricane or a Prindle. John Nickalls

BOAT ENGINES AND ASSOCIATED EXPERIENCES The first boat I owned on returning to sailing had an outboard as auxiliary Power ard, whilst quite efficient when used for short duration, it was awkward to say the least wher cone had to refill the engine mounted tank with the slippery petrol mixture. I was looking forward to enjoying the advantages cf an inboard diesel with its alternator power and low consumpticn of a cheap fuel when I got the rext bcaat. The previcus owner of my next boat had described its engine as ’adequate’ and as we left Maylandsea Creek in a flat calm, the accuracy of this description became clear. It was as if the propeller had fallen off! No swirls from beneath the transom, just a barely discernible increase in forward motion that built gradually to a maximum of about four knots! Flat out at four knots, the smoke was black and smelly, therefore tc avoid the smell helping one to get sea-sick, three knots was the effective cruising speed. On the plus side, engine use was generally an easier cperation with fuel being more available and starting more reliable, and a better alternator allowed a full electrical system ta be supplied. On reflection, the tousled pages of the workshop manual bearing the greasy signatures of the previous owner’s attempts ta improve engine effectiveness should have told me that my effearts tc effect any improvements would be in vain. The engine was used a let in the first year and extra prablems really began with my ill-advised attempts toa squeeze mare power by over-fuelling the ald motor. Shortly afterwards we took a trip to Ipswich and following a broad reach up the coast to Harwich with that short sea rolling the boat along at 5 knots, I started the engine ta enter Shotley Marina. The motor always started well, but on this occasion it seemed ta start too well and, kneckirg heavily, it revved as if jammed on full throttle with me frantically working the control lever. I assumed that the throttle had stuck but no amount of pulling, even orn the engine end of the cable, had any effect. My imagination was beginning to run wild, did the diesel devil have it in for me, having overheard my aft-repeated comments about its inadequacy? I was not keen for the engine to aver speed to the point of destruction sc I left it in gear ard we rushed about like a hunted destroyer making full smoke! Through the smake I think I saw 5 knots on the lag, the fastest ever under power! After what seemed several minutes the engine dropped back to idle, but not before I’d breken the stop cable in the attempts ta arrest the revving. The smoke cleared and all seemed normal. Later, a thorough inspection of all aspects of the ergine and its controls showed only one strange thing. The engine cil level had increased by aver an inch on the dipstick. With the boat anchored we went ashore and all was soon forgotten in the haze af the Shetley village pub which was serving a very special whiskey at half price! Time for aur armual summer cruise with engine serviced and running normally = and slightly better, if anything, after breaking its own rev limit. An excellent run ta Ramsgate via the Roach ard Haverngore. The channel through Havengore is as shallow as reported ard, with 4’ draught, quite a close run thing needing careful prior calculation of tidal heights and a lat of echo-scounder pilotage. Ona previous year in a foggy moment I had miscalculated by looking at the tidal height instead of the range for the day wher assessing it to be a spring or a neap tide. This and ather errors resulted in many hours spent high and muddy at the very mouth of the inlet toa the bridge. Whilst sat on the mud there I remember noticing the number of cars that crass the bridge eonta the island, presumably due tc the MOD preserice. I find Foulness Island and its military secrecy somewhat fascinating, and the tales of Deccas having their memories wiped in this vicinity a few years age make it all the more mysterious. I have vague memories of one of the few TSR aircraft being on the island in the sixties oar maybe early seventies. This example of that expensive praject was eventually used as a target to explore the effects af prajectiles on However, or this occasion, through the bridge the timing was correct and we continued on to Ramsgate to find the yacht pontoons full of a variety of craft all having one thing in common, they were as usual larger than us! When we had a 20’ boat I could understand the phenomenon, but it just seems ta carry on! The next day, an excellent close reach across the Channel to Calais, at an average of almost four and a half knots, made the best time for the crossing so far, and we berthed on the south side ef the yacht harbour, a relatively quiet spot, for the night. Many experienced sailors say how easy it all becomes at night, but I’m sure they also had concerns when their experience was limited: We were Sailing along at around three knots with the chute set ard the afternocn sun hazy and warm, ard five miles out of Calais, when a Hovercraft, crossing cur bow a mile away, executed a crash stop by turning around whilst still travelling forward at some thirty knots and, bellowing powerful sounds, headed off back towards Mid-Channel. At about 1700 hrs a whiff of diesel fuel gave the first sign of trouble, and as I pulled the companicrnway steps into the cabin to access the engine I could see diesel fuel spraying about in the area of the filter assembly. The certral bolt fixing was obviously loose, but when I attempted to tighten it, the whole thing fell off, showering the engine in fuel and severing the fuel feed to the engine. When in doubt have another cup of tea, after which I set to examining the sclutions to the problem. The relief was enormous and we motored on kriowing that due to more delay we would see most of the Channel at night. In the event it was a useful and instructive passage back ta Ramsgate, arriving finally at 23.45hrs with eyes seeming full of grit from peering vigilantly through the dark. While she is stil tacking , as defined , she has to keep clear of a yacht on a tack, be it port tack or starboard tack (rule 41.1) In a protest hearing , it would naturally be B's case that she had completed her tack before the collision occured. If she can satisfy the protest committee, then it will be have been A who infringed, as A will have become either clear astern and required to keep clear under rule 37.2, or windward boat required to keep clear under rule 37.1. In this situation, it is B which has to to prove she completed her tack far enough away from A. (Rule 41.) 41.2 TRANSITIONAL. A yacht shall neither tack nor gybe into a position that will give her right of way unless she does so far enough away from a yacht on a tack to enable this yacht to keep clear without having to alter her course until after the the tack or gybe has been completed. 41.3 ONUS. A yacht that tacks or gybes has the onus of satisfying the protest committee that she completed her tack or gybe in acordance with rule 41.2. How far is ' far enough away ' ? This is a matter for the protest committee. If it finds that A started to take avoiding action within a couple of seconds of B having tacked, but cannot avoid collision, then B will probably have tacked too close. The burden of proof is on B. If A alleges that she was forced to start tacking off to avoid a collision, before B had completed her tack, B has to show that A did 'nt have to do this, and that B would hva completed her tack wel before A was obliged to take avoiding action. If, as usually happens, the protest committee is faced with two equally credible but contradictory tales, it will have to beleive A. So the general rule is Tackers Beware ! If B is sure she has tacked in time, she should hail‘ close hauled‘ as soon as she is pointing on tht close hauled course and then count the seconds out loud. If a collision occurs , say, five seconds later, then A should have had enough time to take avoiding action. Experience shows that those who find the need to hail ‘close hauled ' are often nowhere near close-hauled , but are still tacking. A should be hailing ‘you're not tacked ' in the mean time.

If B starts the overlap behind 'mast-abeam’, A retains luffing rights , and is not required to bear away - she can hold her course or even luff, until B gets ' mast-abeam’, at which point A must bear away onto her proper course round the mark on the course for the next mark. The amount of room to be given is defined in rule 42.1 (a) as the space needed by an inside overlapping yacht that is handled in a seamanlike manner in the prevailing condition s to Pass in safety between an outside yacht and a mark. So you are obliged to take account of the wind and wave strength, and safety might require more room at a metal navigation mark than at an inflatable racing mark. You are not obliged , however to, anticipate that the the inside yacht being either a beginner or incompetant will be likely to take more room than she is entitled to.

PITCAIRN J ALLAN Seme of our long-serving Members who remember Cyril Drakeford, will be sorry tc hear of his death which took place recently. Cyril had been a member for many years and as well as being a keen fisherman, he enjoyed sailing (pottering rather than racing) from the Club in a Torch dinghy which he built himself. He also enjoyed attending cur summer camps with his caravan. He contributed much toa the work done at the Club by holding the post of Clubhouse Secretary for several years after the then new Clubhouse came into use. The sympathy of fellow Club Members and sailing friends go to Eva and the family at this sad time.

Colin Kidner OFFICER OF THE DAY DUTY Over the past few months we have experienced an increasing number of problems with OOD’s, primarily for two reasons: 1) The individuals not turning up, and 2) Disagreements over the duties to be performed. This has necessitated a review of both the procedure used to select the OOD and the duties to be performed. With regard to the duties, we believe that because of the way we now select Race Offiers, the role of the OOD has to change, and in particular we feel that it is important that the overall responsibility for the Club is removed from the OOD. In fact, what the Club now needs is someone who can make available to the Members the Club’s full facilities, particularly those which have to be controlled. The objective will be to make the duties more suitable to all adults, and to those with little or no sailing experience. On the question of selection of OOD’s, we would ideally like a core group of people (who could be trained if necessary) and who would then do a number of duties per year. This therefore brings me to the point of all this - IS THERE ANYONE OUT THERE WHO WOULD BE PREPARED TO VOLUNTEER? This would equally suit both non-sailing/newer members and those already active in the Club. If you're interested, then please contact me, I’d be pleased to give you more information if required. Dewhirst Turns Up on Time, and Doesn’t Capsize! or DART 15 OPEN MEETING AT MARCONI SAILING CLUB 17/18 APRIL 1993 Nick Dewhirst proved that he did know how to assemble his boat when he actually arrived at ar open meeting with time to spare, an unusual event. This set the scene for a weekend of serious but friendly racing, epitomised by Big Winds!.The lightest was a top end three, with the fleet unwillingly proving it’s ability when during one race, the wind rose to a seven for a brief period. Only one race was sailed on Saturday, a long distance affair with three races on Sunday to allow another visiting fleet to have an open meeting in one day! Capsizing showed the true innovative nature of the 15 fleet, with for a change, Nick being one of the very few whoa didn’t. Tim Dieu de Bellefontaine roll gybed his boat the long way round and commented afterwards that the manoeuvre was almost quicker than the traditional method, although the mud on the mast tip was an unwelcome extra job. Bob Anderson gybed his boat while he was still in the water rather than attempt it again on the boat, and Dave Berry achieved everlasting fame by reaching past the Clubhouse, using the trampoline as a Sail. Colin Kidner resisted all sensible advice and tried learning to Sprint his craft in the tricky conditions. He was a little demoralised to finish after many of the traditionally rigged competitors, in the only race he finished! One 15 became a_ Land Yacht for a brief period when he of the long name became landlocked by the intricacies of the receding tide. Rather than go round, a quick burst with rudders up proved that ther is future development potential here. Dave Bladon’s boat became tired in the thir— race and rested its rig on one of the marker buoys. Paul Ellis decided he wanted to give his fellow club members a chance to catch up and spent some time closely surveying a Cruiser for a short interlude. As can be seen everyone had a really gocd time and thoroughly enjoyed themselves, with really close racing and much socialising both on and off the water. The three leading local boats all finished all four races within one minute of each other, showing the competitiveness under the benhomie !
