8. BOAT ENGINES AND ASSOCIATED EXPERIENCES - continued from last month The next passage from Ramsgate towards the Swale was largely an engine-driver leg. However in the fickle marmer cf wind and weather a breeze piped up as scon as we had decided to lay to anchor for some food and a kip in the lee of Margate Hook. Later the beat into the dusky sunset over the East Swale was a joy, finally bringing up off Shellness, an excellent anchorage made tenable by the now complete calm and affording views across the estuary with its myriad of flashing lights. Several times since I have used anchorages out in the estuary when windless nights have made it possible and have found new dimensions in sclitude whilst laying to anchor. In the morning the Swale was used to get to Queenborough to meet to meet some friends and ari anchorage in Stangate Creek provided shelter for that night. For the next passage to Walton Backwaters we chose to leave around midday, providing the chance to use cur new-found night sailing confidence. Very light winds in the afternoon made the early use of the engine essential but after some hours a fine following breeze came up and we chased along at 4-5 knots with the chute set. Later the wind built up further and the chute was stowed to make way for jib and pole. The decision to reduce sail and then carry out the operation in time toa avoid the problems borr of late reefing, etc. is a sign of true seamanship, as is the full appreciation of those small signs that help to show the following wind’s true strength. However, on this occasion the wind held steady and as darkness arrived the wind died away to nothing. Having reverted to engine power, the course into the Stour tock us along the rolling swell that had, for some distant reason, increased in level since the wind died. Perhaps the lack of stabilising sails made it seem toa increase, but certainly my little craft rolled along most uncomfortably at her 3 knots, often increasing revs in time with the swell. The strange increase in revs got worse the longer we rolled along and nothing could stop it. The passage had become most unpleasant and wher we were approaching Harwich the engine slowed down alarmingly and it seemed to be straining. I closed the throttle and nursed it, but it stopped after a while. I checked the diesel - plenty. I dipped the oil to find - no ail! Harwich harbour entrance is not the ideal place to drift about especially at might and due ta the number of shore lights it is very difficult to pick out shipping movements. The lights appeared to be straight aut of an RYA training book! I tried adding more oil to the engine and managed to spill some onto the hot exhaust causing billowing smoke to belch from the engine bay hatch - things were not improving! I finally managed to get some cil inte the beast, in fact managing to overfill the sump. The motor complained into life enough to get the boat to a suitable anchorage just inside the mouth of the Orwell where we dropped anchor. We continued up toa Fox?s at Ipswich the next day with many items of cabin upholstery outside trying toa get rid of the smell and dirt of diesel fumes. At Ipswich I drained the gunge that used to be the engine cil, changed the filter and ran the engine on new oil. Once again all seemed well, and placated by lunchtime ale we dozed all afternoon. Once again the ’interest’ of the old diesel continued! Despite the ‘interest’ provided by the engine, I could see in my mind’s eye a new goal. A clean, new engine, installed in a sound-insulated engine bay, with no diesel leaks. With clean new paint all round and no smells or fumes, this area of the boat could actually be a pleasure. At the finish of the season I made the decision ta fit a new engine, the original having done well considering it had functioned for &7 years in the boat. The strange behaviour of the old engine was now virtually proven to be due to excessive piston clearances, combined with my overfuelling of the injection system. This resulted in diesel fuel washing intca the sump via the bore, diluting the oil and then being forced up past the piston as the sump overfilled and increasing the compression ratio. The removal was a dirty but satisfying job, the removal of components triggering a variety of memories from its chequered history, and invelving yet more cily expletives as cold hands slipped and fingers got nipped. I often dream of having the boat laid up indoors, and what a total luxury that would be! The boom was used to hoist the motor out and drop it straight onto the waiting tralier for transport to its new location, and to a much needed overhaul prior ta fitment in a small open fishing boat. contd....

Having decided to spend out or a new engine, the research into types was a_ pleasant exercise involving ringing all the main suppliers of diesel inboards for their literature, then drawing up a comparison table in the marmer of the yachting press. The first consideration was size, not only for basic fit, but also tc gain some space ir the main cabin. With most modern engines being considerably smaller than their Similarly-powered predecessors, it seemed likely that I could achieve this space saving. I looked at Sole, a twin cylinder unit I had had experience of in a friend’s boat and that was very smooth, and with its fresh water cooling, a desirable unit, but even with a good discount being offered it was too expensive. Bukh would not fit due ta its size, and the weight was considerably more than any other 8-10 hp engine, as was its price. It was, however, the only engine manufactured sclely for marine use, and many of its design features shawed it to be the most worthy unit. A Vetus twin was very similar to the Sole - both being marinised industrial engines cof Oriental orogin, but there was some difficulty in supply at the right discount. Valve would fit but was expersive relative to the Yarnmar, and I could not forget the spares price concerns expressed in the yachting press, whether they proved groundless or not! Discount was also not negotiable encugh to make it competitive. The ever- popular Yanmar was small, was lightest and cheapest, and a deal could be done. So the engine, along with new single lever controls, exhaust system components and ancillaries were unpacked and inspected in the comfort of the dining room, another thoroughly pleasant wiriter exercise only slightly marred by the realisation that, in commer with many things boat, the cost of the project overall was rather more than originally thought! The fitting of the new Yanmar involved making a modified engine bed for which I obtained some oak which was machined to form a long wedge shape as the angle of fitment was quite different from the original engine. This was epoxied and screwed to the existing beds and ten inch studs for the mount fixation installed. The motor was now four inches further aft and, combined with it being shorter, the gain in space allawed me ta make the cabin step unit into a useful cupboard. The engine was fitted and roughly lined enough for the prop shaft to enter the drive coupling when slid towards the engine. The final alignment was achieved by sliding the prop’ shaft in and out of the drive flange until little or no resistance was felt. This was repeated while turning the flange to various positions ensuring absolutely correct aligrment. The confined space in the engines compartment made the conventional method of alignment virtually impossible. The old dry exhaust system was scrapped and the Vetus plastic and rubber units installed, saving more space, as the exit was now in the transom with the system running under the cockpit sole, a previously wasted area. This also made much more space in the main rope locker which used to be the home of the silencer. The fitting of a new engine had many obvious benefits in terms of user confidence plus the gain in space in various areas. After some of our recounted experiences, I’m sure you agree! The only mistake was to choose a two-bladed prop - my thoughts being that it could then be aligned with the deadwood toa reduce drag. Th: “faet seldom bothered to line up the marks painted on the coupling, and the prop alsa caused vibration as the tip clearance was not sufficient and turbulence resulted. A three-bladed prop has now cured the problem and increased the speed to a respectable 5.5 knots, so the mouth of the Deben or Alde cannot play games with us any more! Limpet TEAM OF VOLUNTEER OOD? Jan. — March, 1973 — The Ups and Downs of subscription fees; was it a case of "Divisive and Rule" ? — "Full 1.82880 international metres cinque thy father lies; Of his bones are coral made, and thus are designated an SSSI" Fran: A curse on Metrication, Europeanisation and EC Rules and Regs. ANON. January - The new Editor, Dot Renshaw, got off to a nervous start in her first Editorial when she wrote "Well, the New Year is off to a good tart...." Well, we all know what she meant ...... I think ? New Commodore, Dennis Byatt, reveals that an Extraordinary General Meeting gave the 'go ahead' for the new Clubhouse - presumably after the presentation of revised (ie lower ?) membership fees, which were also approved. Voting was "....about 48 in favour to 2 against (1 abstention)". Now the immediate objective is to obtain two or three detailed estimates for the new clubhouse. Our friend, Observer, comes in for same criticism from Pete Foreman, partly for remaining anonymous and partly for his statements which Pete felt eroded the co-operative spirit within the club. Pete queries Observer's comments on the part played by the Cruiser Fleet at the AGM and felt that Observer made it appear ".....the cruisers were guilty of sam malicious plot and that voting on the fees was close". Peter points out the voting against ".....the discriminating fees was 60 — 20, indicative of a united membership since at most 30 of the 60 were cruiser owners". He goes on to thank those dinghy owners who supported the cruiser owners and hoped that never again would such divisive issues be raised. The new Committee has decided to display Minutes of Committee Meetings on a special board at Stansgate, with more important abstracts in Navigans occasionally. Maybe most members will never read them but at least those who are interested could read what was being done at the Main Committee and Sailing Sub-Committee deliberations. Do we still have a 'Mimutes Board' at Stansgate ? February - On the sailing side, it has been decided to have more regular dinghy racing and, henceforth, all fleets would be scheduled to race, including the fleets which supplied the Race Officer. In addition, the Helmsman of the Year qualifying races were to be combined with 6 specific Points Series races, with the best 4 results to count and the lst and 2nd helms overall of each fleet qualifying. These arrangements gave about 12 Spring Points races and about 24 Summer Points races. Sailing Sec., John Weedon, says "The Helmsman of the Year (Costain Cup) should be about the most coveted award in the Club..... ". Yes, I reckon it is. The Commodore reports that estimates have been invited for both a pre-fabricated (but permanent) building and a traditional brick building. Observer finds a defender in Ron Doubleday, who also feels that pre-meeting lobbying by the cruiser fleet played a part in the defeat of the Committee's proposals at the 1972 AGM. Ron points out that it seems the dinghy crowd will now have to pay same 55% more in subscriptions; presumably the 'levelling' of fees was upwards rather than downwards. He felt it was a rather hard increase in the era of "squeeze and freeze" on the wage: front. Just as Pete hoped the "divisive issue" would not again be raised, Ron hopes the subject will be resurrected and says "....may I add a plea for such fair proposals broadly along the lines of those originally mooted but thrown out at the last AGM". Looking back over 20 years, it is interesting to see how the 'two sides' of the debate (arguement ?) developed within the club. I see nothing wrong with 'pre-meeting lobbying’ amongst like-minded people; after all, that's part of the ‘democratic process’. On the other hand, I rather like Observer's anonymity; it's no bad thing for sameone to stir the pot a little to see what comes to the surface. How will our modermday, and newly introduced, "LIMPEI" series develop? Will he/she live up to the name and cling tenaciously to his/her particular metaphorical rock ? Has the name 'LIMPET" been chosen as a disguised warning to watch for ‘explosions’ to shake our sturdy club to its very foundations? Is it merely coincidence that the same name identifies a weapon beloved of war films and 'thrillers' ? To say the least, I await more of 'LIMPEI" with same trepidation - and a tin hat ! March - Dennis Byatt reports the new clubhouse designs are now virtually complete and the first reasonably firm estimate has been received. On the social side, a talk by a Mr (Cdr ? ) Rantzen provided a very entertaining evening. He apparently held very strong views and "the metrication and Europeanisation of the Admiralty Charts came in for same blistering

Well, I guess Arthur should know; a Founder Member, an active Committee Member and a past Commodore. By and large, Arthur's letter seems to be an attempt to 'pour oil on troubled waters’ - which seems an inappropriate metaphor to use in this age of ecologic al disaster s and Green politics. SOLO NEWS Solo Oper Meeting: You may have missed the article Yachts and Yachting published about cur meeting, sco here it is: Solos at Marconi —- Jim in the Hunt Marconi SC held an open meeting for Solos on April 18th which was an Eastern Area qualifier, and attracted an entry of 17 boats. These boats enjoyed close and exhilarating sailing with the wind recorder indicating gusts in excess of Force 6 during the second race. In the first race the lead changed a number of times up the first beat, but Hunt was first round shortly followed by Cook, Barclay and Burrell. By the next mark Garner was in second. The order remained until Garner went swimming at the last gybe mark with Hunt well clear to win, followed by Burrell, Cook and Husk. The second race was a beat against the flow of the tide which had turned, and which made the downwind legs very interesting for those who kept upright. Burrell was first round opening up a huge lead which he held from Hunt and Husk until he went for a swim, letting Hunt through, who went on to win. Burrell held Husk off up the last beat for second and Cook was fourth. The wind dropped off slightly for the last race but was still strong enough to force Burrell out with a broken main sheet block. Garner was first round and pulled away from Cook, hanging onto the lead in spite of a blowout at the gybe mark. Cook suffered the same fate going round the wing mark, allowing Husk, Barclay and Ede through. Garner went for his second swim of the race and eventually it was Husk first, Barclay second and Ede third. Overall results: {st 3883, Jim Hunt, Beaver SC; 2nd 3741, Alan Husk, Halfway YC; 3rd 3757, Allen Burrell, Halfway YC; 4th 3808, Gordon Barclay, Dell Quay SC; Sth 813, Tony Cook, Littleton SC; 6th 2290, Simon Ede, Marconi SC. The Force 6+ wind created difficulties for me, every time the race box door opened my pesition/time sheets blew all over the place. On a more sericus note, the idea af moving the Solo Open to a ’ane day’ date that did not clash with other Solo Open Meetings seemed to have worked with regard to visitor numbers, but may have proved a little too early in the season for some of the Solo Fleet (me included). Plan for next year is still a one day event (Sunday) shared with the Dart 15 class, but with date moved to later on in the season. This has yet to be organised. Sola Fleet membership for 1993 appears almost unchanged at 21 boats, I have a ‘'93 membership list - names, phone numbers etc., if you want one please ask. There are still some unfinished bits of work around the racebox that we should attend to, sc be prepared for a phone call. Dor’ t forget, if you have any good ideas/grumbles re sailing/Solo Fleet talk to me! May — Has Observer gone into hibernation - or fled the country? The Editor (Dot Renshaw) writes " Are you wondering, like me, what has happened to those astute observations that favoured these pages last year ? They could always be relied upon to pramte ‘lively’ conversation amongst the members and I, for one, would welcame them back". § Well, what do you know ? Tt seems the reasons for placing the lounge/bar at the west-end were apparently based upon (a) the wish to discourage 'wet sailors' from using the lounge as a passage way to the changing rooms had they been at the west-end, (b) the view westward towards Osea was considered more attractive than that to the east, (c) the west-located lounge would permit later enlargement and (d) it would be too far for wet sailors to walk if the changing rooms had been at in the west end. ‘The three correspondents disagree with these reasons (they think the east view is preferable to the west view) and plead with like-minded members to let the Committee know their feelings. VOLUNTEER TEAM As mentioned in last Navigans, our system for provision of O. » is not working at all satisfactorily, because of the very frequent occasions when the member whose turn it is simply does not turn up for duty on the appointed day. A team of volunteers who would be prepared to join a rota to carry out the duty of OOD a number of times each year would be a more reliable way solving the problem. The duties, simplified by making them more Clubhouse/Site based, might be less daunting to many of us Members who do not have a great deal of practical experience of boats and/or sailing, but who could still perform this very valuable service to the Club. 1e. 40 Years Ago - June & July, 1953. T would imagine that 'young' John Eastwood will remember what he did on Coronation Day in 1953 - and what he did the day before! A report, presumably for the Marconi "house magazine’, tells a dramatic tale:- "On the Monday before Coronation Day, 2 June, 1953, the Sailing Section were honoured by a visit to their headquarters of their new President, Dr. Eastwood, and his son John. ‘here were to have been races, but the weather beingof a very doubtful nature it was not surprising that only one other boat put in an appearance. Regardless of the adverse weather, the President and his son were initiated in the art of sailing, having sailed up to Maldon in the club boat ‘Avril', skippered by Terry Hallam, Commodore of the section. They returned to the club house just as (??) Fewel in 'Seamew' arrived by sea, and the Hon.Secretary by land. There was no chance of orgamised racing, so it was decided to sail again in Avril, particularly as the President and his son appeared only to have their appetites whetted, and this time the crew was augmented by Mrs Hallam and the Hon.Sec. ‘Avril' followed out ‘Seamew', and the two boats sailed in company for a while. This particular time coincided with a temporary lull in the wind, and it was observed by those less familiar with small boats how steady 'Avril' was. At about the same time the skipper expressed the view that it was time the reef in the mainsail was shaken out - but five seconds later, after a quick glance to windward at a particularly vicious looking cloud, with a long black curving edge to it, he thought again. Just as Avril was halfway across the reach leading up to Maldon, the squall struck. Almost immediately the gentle undulations of the river were converted to row upon row of angry whitecaps, and no longer was progress smoth and leisurely. Only by careful spilling of wind from the minsail was anything like an even keel miintained, and at each gust a violent flogging of the sails took place which sounded like machine gun fire. Young John Eastwood was on the helm just then, with the skipper close at hand, and for one so new to the art he certainly seemed to have mastered some of the tricks, in particular how to manoeuvre so as to catch the foremost crew member, the Hon.Sec. in this case, with bucketfuls of spray. The strength of the wind made it difficult to go onto the other tack, a necessity as Avril was closing the river bank rapidly, but like the good lady she is she never hesitated and came round obediently, and through clouds of spray set off back again. A capsized craft was then spotted, but on approaching closer it was apparent that no assistance was needed - the crew were sitting on the upturned boat eating sandwiches ! The ferocity of the wind soon abated and Avril returned to her harbour as serenely as she left. Our new President seemed duly impressed and we hope to see him often down at our clubhouse.” I notice it doesn't report what young John felt ! Avril's log records that 10/- was duly collected for the trip, but it is not clear who paid ? Commodore’s Notes As you can tell from last month, timing one’s bit for the press can get a little awkward with events occurring post submission. Apologies to Charles Anderson for the lack of recognition of his great contribution in accepting the challenge of Cadet Week. From my perspective the prospect of sleeping in a field for two weeks and then to volunteer to surround yourself with brats is a sacrifice above and beyond... It’s a good job we’re not all cynical, miserable b’s like me!! The NRA saga continues, with a letter from me to try to gee things up a little. Their reply was full of thanks for all our co-operation and an undertaking that the job will be done this year, taking 26 weeks in all (between Steeple and Store), starting ‘late summer’ and the work on our site being completed in the first six weeks, avoiding Camping and Bank Holidays, and aiming at avoiding any inconvenience ta boats laying up.... Watch this space. One subject about to be considered very closely is the "“Wraysbury Lake" scenaric. For those of you who do not know, the Borough Environmental Health Officer issued a Prohibition Notice on Wraysbury Lake Sailing Club under the Health & Safety at Work Act (HASAWA) banning them from carrying out any activities until certain ‘improvements’ had been carried out. These included ensuring someone was availabl to carry out Support duties any time that activities were happening ard (in my opinion) several other equally idiotic and senseless restrictions on a voluntary sports club. Obviously the chief concern of everyone on the MSC Committee is safety, but cur philasaphy has been to draw attention to, or moderate, risks and ensure that everyone understands the periols inherent in in our sport - 2.5 times less dangerous than athletics/30 times less dangerous than horse riding). We are seeking Clarification and guidance from the RYA and any appropriate actions will be taken. It’s been good over the past few weekends to see the sunshine bringing all the fine weather sailors out of the woodwork. As usual the Cat Fleet is looking pretty healthy, but what has happened to the Moros? I can’t understand the point of spending £47 per annum to keep the sun off a patch of grass, which is what the vast majority do. Boats deteriorate more quickly ashore than they do by being sailed. Let’s see a few more of you cut there! Larry Botheras Many members may remember the very rough weather at the Club on the Sunday of the Bank Holiday Weekend last August. Several boats experienced difficulties and th following is an article from the Summer 1993 edition of the RNLI’s journal ’The Lifeboat’ RNLI’?S WEST MERSEA ATLANTIC 21 ON SERVICE ON THE BLACKWATER SOTH AUGUST 1992 Local Knowledge Essential in Arducus Service Multiple Casualties for Atlantic 21 in winds up to Force 10 ‘The wind was SW Force 8 gusting to Force 10 creating very difficult conditions as the wind was against the tide.’ Ar, arduous service by the West Mersea Atlantic 21 lifeboat, carried out in very rough conditions with the crew using their initiative and local knowledge to asist a large number of casualties, has led to helmsman John Frost and crew members Matthew Howard and Javis Wenlock receiving framed letters of thanks from the Institution’s chairman Michael Vernon. At 1155 on Bank Holiday Sunday, 30 August 1992 crew members John Frost, Matthew Howard and Javis Wenlock were near the lifeboat station listening o communication between Thames Coastguard and the Bradwell sector officer. This in dicated that a number of small beats could be overcome by weather conditions near Osea Island in the estuary of the River Blackwater. Contd. «-.

De They telephoned the honorary secretary who authorised the launch of the station’s Atlantic 21 ’Himley Hall’ to go to Osea Island, investigate and give assistance if required. The wind was SW Force 8, gusting Force 10 which was creating very difficult conditions as the wind was against the River Blackwater’s strong tide. The lifeboat was launched with helmsman John Frost in command, accompanied by crew members Matthew Howard and Javis Wenlock. Best speed was made from West Mersea inte the River Blackwater where conditions were found to be very difficult with a very short steep sea, blinding spray and visibility further reduced by dust blowing off fields to the side of the river. The six miles took approximately 15 minutes, and by this time the Bradwell sector officer had asked that they go to Osea Pier on the south side of the island where a 3eft mator baat was reported ta be in difficulty with an elderly man aboard. His son was ashore with their dinghy and it was considered too dangerous for him to venture cut to the boat to collect his father. Helmsman Frost took the lifeboat to the jetty and picked up the son, and then put crew member Wenlock aboard the motor boat, to secure her and transfer the man ta the lifeboat. The casualty vessel was rolling very heavily in the rough conditions and the Atlantic 21 suffered damage to her navigation light. The two people were then taken to the Marconi Sailing Club, nearby on the cpposite side of the river. The lifeboat was then asked by the Coastguard to check numercus other small craft anchored in the area. At 1309 the yacht ’Scloist’ with five people aboard was taker to the safety of a mooring orn the windward side of the river, and her crew also transferred toa safety ashore at Marcori SC. At 1347 they approached the 35ft yacht Ruskina which was anchored rear Osea Pier and had radisced a request for assistance - as all four people aboard were suffering from seasickness and one needed medical treatment. Crew member Howard boarded the yacht and raised her anchor and then helped the skipper to manceuvre to moorings off Stone Point, some two miles to the west. During the passage Howard examined the injured female and advised the Coastguard that an ambulance might be needed. With assistance from the Atlantic 21, the yacht was put on a mooring, but before they could transfer the crew the lifeboat received another call - to a boardsailor a mile west of their position. The injured person volunteered to stay aboard the yacht and the lifeboat went to the boardsailor, advising him to make his way ashore as he was not in need of assistance. While with the boardsailor the lifeboat was asked te attend another yacht west af Osea pier with two elderly people aboard. The yacht had fouled her keel on her anchor warp and crew members Wenlock and Howard boarded her to help. With Wenlock slacking out the warp Howard used the engine to manoeuvre her and clear the fouled warp. This yacht was then taken to a mooring off Marconi, secured and the two peaple taker, ashore by the lifeboat. The lifeboat then returned tc ’Ruskina’ to transfer the four crew, but during the passage the casualty last cansciocusness and was immediately transferred to the ambulance which had remained at Marconi Pier. (sic) A further sweep of the moorings between Osea Fier and Stone Foint discovered five pecple and their dog aboard a yacht who asked to be taken ashore, and they were duly landed at Marconi Pier (sic) at 1430. Having carried cut these evacuations in very difficult conditions the lifeboat crew left Osea to return to West Mersea, but on the way they heard that a motor cruiser had been reported in difficulties in Mersea Quarters, not far from their location. The lifeboat found the motor cruiser very quickly, the skipper having lost control of the vessel in the adverse conditions. She was helped to a mooring at Stone where the four people aboard were taken ashore by the lifeboat. The lifeboat then returned to West Mersea, helping another small boat ta her mooring near West Mersea lifeboat station before taking the crew ashore to the lifebcat station. The lifeboat was rehoused at 1554, her crew exhausted after a four-hour service in severe weather.

FAST CAT NOTES A Clean Start The latest occupancy of the race box by the Nickalls clan may have failed in its prime objective (that of ensuring that none of the competitors finish the races, thus removing the points penalty to those on duty) but it did bring home to us the dramatic improvement in the quality of the starts being made by the fast cats. That the leading craft was not over the line was only due to the thickness of the mete when projected out to the far end of the line; by my estimation the considerable diameter of the pole provides an invisible zone about six feet (or 2m, as they say in cookery books) deep in the region of G mark (when it’s there, Paul). Larry took full advantage of this in starting, and we, with considerable generosity, gave him the benefit of the doubt. In days gone by one could achieve ‘a good start’ merely by having the sharp end of the boat pointing toward, rather than away from, the line when the flag dropped (and one might observe that this is still a valuable maxim in certain fleets). This seems no longer to be the case with the fast cats, and the bulk of the fleet are not far from the line (and going the correct way) at the start. Moaners’ Cup If only we could all keep going the correct way after the start (or rather, if only we could all agree on which way was the correct way). Mona's Cup is becoming the occasion for the annual contention over courses: last year we had the 'wrong way round the island’ dispute, and this year it was ‘when is a course not a course?’. Perhaps it is inevitable as the fleet as a whole becomes more skilled at the basic control of the boats sailed that the differences separating boats will become smaller. Thus the level of competitiveness within the fleet increases, leading in turn to competitors making careful use of the rules to ensure no disadvantage is suffered by failing to take the best legal steps available. Even after a protest committee has found that no infringement has been committed, it is a very fine line between on the one hand perceiving a competitors actions to be an unfair exploitation of loopholes in the rules and on the other hand recognising that whoever sails, legally, the fastest race is the deserved winner. For the enjoyment of all it is essential that this progression toward a greater level of competition is made at the same pace by all those racing, to ensure a common understanding of what is ‘fair and therefore to reduce the personal slant that can sometimes be seen creeping into disputes and protests. Of course this applies equally (if not more so) to knowledge of the rules of Part IV and the use of the right-of-way rules to gain a tactical advantage during a race. Never have | heard so many cries of "water" or "mast abeam" on the Blackwater as in recent weeks (although | cannot vow that all were used correctly!) and personally | believe that a more developed knowledge and use of the rules can only be good for the standard of sailing at the Club. This knowledge must, however, be used at a similar level throughout the fleet to avoid much splintering of fibreglass and so much work for Brian that he can’t find time to come and beat us every week (or perhaps that’s not a bad idea). Those whose knowledge of the rules is greater than most should help to raise the average by advice and example, and those who concentrate purely on boat speed should recognise that the quality of Club sailing has improved to the point where good speed is no longer a guarantor of victory, and that improved tactics can gain many places in a tightly bunched fleet. Men (and women) in a Hurri On a personal note, |’m delighted to see four more Hurricane 5.9s joining the fast cat fleet this year. After Julia and Ashley Machin added the 5.9 to the family fleet ("the Dart is for sale" they tell me "honest") we welcomed Philip Longhurst and Brian Grimshaw with their (lookalike) 5.9 and a mean- looking Hobie. More recently both Brian and Grant Piggott have migrated to 5.9s, and | am delighted to see that the numbers on the water, and the quality of the racing, have shown a dramatic improvement. | only wish | could say that the change of boat had slowed Grant downa little! East Coast Piers Race Those of you with diaries (or wives) will have realised that the Piers Race is drawing ever closer. By the time this goes to press | guess it will be about three weeks away. | hope the new format this year, offering a shorter course for those who feel the trip to Walton is simply too far, will attract some of those who to date have not felt that the event is for them. You can even decide which course to sail after you've set off (although of course those who opt for the shorter course will not be competing against those on the long haul). It's a good event; if you've been put off before, think about giving it a go this year.... and remember, it’s all for charity. The Piers Race was filmed last year for Anglia TV’s 'Sailaway’ series, and the episode is due to be screened in the Anglia region about ten days before this year's race. At the time of writing I’m not sure of the details, but you might like to keep a look out for it in the schedules (and if you see the trailer, look for the jolt as our centreboard hits the top of the cameraman’s head)). John Nickalls

NAVIGANS PAST. 1973 (July-December) - a satisfactory end to a satisfactory year. July - The mid-summer barbeque was a great success, with fireworks as an added attraction (but it is not clear if 'the fireworks’ were planned). Another innovation might have been a ‘Let's throw the Commodore in at the Deep End' competition; at least, I suspect so for I quote Editor, Dot Renshaw "......a pity the Commodore could run faster than Vic Tate and Stan Campbell !" An MSC Open Day attracted 12 new members and which possibly included the crew of a passing cruiser who, upon hearing Jack Bigden's PA announcements, rowed ashore to collect application forms. Som 5 dinghies, 7 cruisers and the new rescue boat took over 50 adults and 40 children for a sail or motor trip in winds reported as gusting up to Force 5. Dot Renshaw reminds everybody of the 15 mph speed limit on the road. The Commodore tells us that plans for the new clubhouse have been completed and 4 builders invited to tender. Alf Cottam writes a letter about the controversy over the planned view from the clubhouse and wonders what's so interesting on the Hard ? He reckons if the weather is fine, everyone will be outside, and if the weather is bad, there will be no one to watch anyway. AILf feels it is time to give thought to mre practical things _ such as ",..who is going to wash up all the extra tea-cups and beer mgs...?", particularly as many people appear to find it too much trouble to return their emplies let alone help wash them up. ‘Finally, he states "....the anonymous writer might mean well but I wish he (she) would stop it." A Mooring List shows 67 cruisers in 1973, August - Dot Renshaw reveals she is to hand over the Editor's job to Brenda Tate (apparently Dot has secured a new job in Paris). A note from former Commodore, Eric Payne, records the death of Cecil Stebbens aged 71. Cecil had been, wntil aged 69, the Water Bailiff and had been a good friend of the club and was particularly helpful during the club's Heybridge days. It was he who towed the barge Mamgu to her mooring off the original 'hut—on—the-wall' clubhouse at Heybridge on 20 April, 1958. In addition, it was he who built several access ramps to the water for the club, ie. for the original clubhouse, later for the dinghy park a little further down river and for Mamgu itself. Cecil was a Trinity House Pilot and it was he who presented the club with The Pilot's Qup for an annual all- in race which still features in our sailing programe. Another note fran Eric Payne tells of the wreck of an old sunken barge which was visible at low water to the west of the Ray Channel just beyond 'the Cut’. He felt it ought to be marked with a withey; can anyone tell On the racing side, Roger Hance won the Enterprise Nationals at Penzance with Julian Bigden 7th. All told, 9 Marconi boats took part in what must have attracted nearly 200 entries at least (we know this 'cos one of the Marconi boats came 198th). Jimmy James (Cadet Skipper) reveals that 4 Cadet Races were not sailed due to bad weather or lack of entries, but race 5 was held "in rather windy condition" and praises Mark Savill for completing part of the course in his father's Mirror. Mark, in later years, won the Helm of the Year Trophy. September — New Editor, Brenda Tate, reveals that she is a lst year novice sailor whose mle family members eat, walk, talk and sleep boats 24 hours of the day; she hopes one day to beat them at their own game. Certainly, ‘the Tates' were very much one of the MSC's 'sailing families’ and very active in many aspects of rumning the club. The Commodore states that final details for the clubhouse are almost completed. He also requests that parents of crab-hunting children please direct them to return concrete blocks to the edges of the hard before the autum gales set in. You can imagine it, can't you; all those little angel—faced cherubs hurling the blocks past the ears of startled dinghy sailors as they (the angel—faced cherubs) hunt the hapless crabs to exstinction. Ain't kids luvly! It is reported that Simon Darney came 3rd in the Hornet European Championships at Firth of Forth with Bruce Long 5th.

8. Alf Cottam entertains us with a tale of a trip to Brightlingsea with Frank Savill in the Mirror ‘Frantic’. Starting off in a Force 6 blowing fram behind and an adverse tide from ahead, they took 23 hours to arrive just off Brightlingsea. Taking a look around Brightlingsea, they arrived back at the (untethered) Mirror just in time to stop it floating off. Leaving at 3.45, they had a long hard slog back towards Stansgate, arriving off Stone in the dark fram where they could see car headlights and much obvious activity at the Marconi Sailing Club. ‘Thinking a search party mustbe under way to find them, they curtailed their voyage at Stone S, interrupting a dinner party in progress and phoned their loved ones with both reassurance and a request for wheeled transport. Alas, it seems nobody had really missed them, for the lights arose fram a barbecue - not fram the launch of a rescue party! October — The MASC has approved the new clubhouse plans and, subject to a suitable agreement between the parent MASC and the offspring MSC, work should begin in January, 1974, with completion by mid-summer. Tickets for the Laying-Up Supper at the Chancellor Hall are £3.60 each. Amongst the 'For Sale’ notices is the Mirror 29015 "Kitwitwee"; the Boreham family bought the boat, eventually renamed it Lars Tinn and it served us very well, teaching Maggie, Damian and Lucy to sail; alas, it gave up on me. In 1993, it remains in the club under the ownership of Joyce Allen. November - Dot Renshaw flew over from Paris to attend the Laying Up Supper which, by all accounts, was a great success. Brenda Tate thanks the Helmsman of the Year for extending his hospitality to all who wouldn't go home to bed. I can well imagine, for HoY winner was Dave Harper who triumphed as the Mirror Fleet representative, whilst his daughter, Deborah, was awarded the Garrett Memorial Trophy. Definitely a good j for the Harpers who were, of course, another of Marconi's ‘sailing families’. December - Commodore Dennis Byatt is able to report a very satisfactory year. ‘The problems of planning the Tew Clubhouse have now been virtually sorted out and he hopes excavations will start in January and completion of building work in July, 1974. The MASC has approved an allocation of £19,000 for the clubhouse (presumably the cost of building it) and, although a new rental agreement between the MASC and MSC will need to be negotiated, Dennis does not forsee any increase in subscriptions for 1974 or, hopefully, for 1975. Purchase of the Mariner rescue boat, erection of a new race-box, work to consolidate and protect the hard against erosion, refurbishment of the approach road and completion of the two bridges (into what is now the cat field) are reported and are indicative of a very busy year. On the sailing side, he reminds us that a successful Regatta attracted 200 entries, whilst the ‘sailing mtch' against Marconi's Rochester colleagues, was a great success. On the more social side, Open Day was also very successful and about 200 people attended the Laying Up Supper. To round off his report, the Commodore thanks Claude Emerson (paid part-time club steward) and Margaret Cottam who organised the galley service. Membership at the end of 1973 was 358 compared to 350 in 1972, and there is a waiting list for Associate Members for 1974 (It was in 1973 that I joined the club as an Associate Member with a Firefly, but we didn't sail very mich until we bought the Mirror). Ray Ball (who was also, I believe, a new member in 1973) wrote an article about a Sailing barge holiday in the barge ‘Marjorie’ from Maldon, the barge having been built in 1902. I wonder if Marjorie still sails. Mike Boreham FRR KK 40 Years Ago - August, 1953. Presumably everyone wason holiday because, although Avril's log shows some evidence of sailing activity, the archive files have nothing for August, 1953, to indicate anything happening on the admin. front. COMMODORE’S NOTES I was fascinated with last month’s Navigans Past to read about the exploits of the Enterprise Fleet at the Nationals at Penzance (in 1973). Y'see I was the Gate Launch Coxswain for the first two days - until we discovered that the boat could not keep track with the Pathfinder (the engine was a 1944 petrol/TVO Canadian Lifeboat version). The rest of the week was spent fishing Ent sailors out of Mourt’s Bay. Just to clarify, the Fleet consisted of 230 entries... quite a sight I can assure you. The following year the Fireballs were there with 200, and I sailed. Being in the middle of that number milling around on the start is quite something. As this is part of the silly season, I don’t intend to write too much, but I cannot let the opportunity pass to thank Charles Anderson for carrying Cadet Week off with great success. I’m sure Charles would not want me to omit all his helpers, in particular Chris Davies and the "senior" Cadets who did a lot of the instructing. Well done one and all and a big thanks from me! The NRA still have no firm idea of start date, but it is almost impossible for hauling out NOT ta be disrupted. We are plarming to get the Lay-Up plan out ASAP, Please don’t assume that you can bung your boat out when you want - organisation is essertial! Piers Race looms, good luck to me (!) and all other competitors and thanks to all our support/mother boat crews before they drag me ashore!!! Larry Botheras CREW WANTED Is there anyone out there who would like to crew in a dinghy on a reasonably regular basis? This will include Club races, plus a few away open meetings each year. Attributes should preferably include agility, love of the water, including occasional swimnming, and desire to win, within the rules. Why not take this opportunity to sail with an experienced mature helm for a season or so. Please contact John Weedon, Tel. Maldon [redacted] FOR SALE Contest 31, "Davolas II". 6 Berth, 31’10-and-a-half inches LOA, 9° 6" Beam, Long Keel, Valve 25hp Diesel, Good Inventory of Instruments and Gear £17,500 Contact John Hooper, [redacted] CAMPING FORTNIGHT with Cadet Week seems to have gone well, and if the weather was not always perfect, it was better thar some past years that I can remember, and at least we had a lovely dry day to pack our tents away. A smaller than usual class of Cadets should mean that those taking part will have learnt a lot about sailing while under the care of the Cadet Week team. The names of the team looking after Cadet Training that I have are: Charles Anderson (Organiser); Chris Davies, Steve Coote, Dave Onyons, Norman Chaplin (Co-Ordinatars); Ethan, Stuart, David, Richard, Nick (instructors/helpers). Many thanks to these and tc any others not listed who helped. The flcor mop used and stored in the Galley was found broken with the head missing - it would be a kindly action if the person concerned donated £5 or so to pay for a replacement; and the lock on one of the cupboard doors appears to have been damaged during Camping Fortnight. NAVIGANS PAST. =e 1974 (January - June) - Marconi's Males no doubt quickly sought Sartorial Sophistication as the cameras began to click, but Eddie was only in it for a lark whilst Frank obviously believed he could go one better by himself. — A change of 'front cover’ format for NAVIGANS; the ‘half—potted plant' logo (see NAVIGANS issue 11, November,1991) has clearly been transplanted and in its place om the front cover is a full- page black and white photograph with other photos printed on the inside front cover. First to grace the Navigans front cover is Julian Bigden, crewed by Diana Byatt, racing an Fnterprise whilst the inside front cover features a ‘Rogues Gallery’ (the Commodore's description, not mine !) with som very youthful— looking club officers on show. John Witter's must surely be an ‘after graduation’ photo and Ron Greygoose's visage takes on an uncharacteristically stern look. |§ John Weedon's tousled hair and cheery smile would not be out of place on Surfers Paradise but the balance is redressed by Commodore Dennis Byatt's steadfast gaze which reassures me that the club is in safe hands. David Harper looks altogether somewhat startled and I suspect the photographer must have ‘dropped in' rather umexpectedly, but Jack Reeve looks as kindly as ever and mich as I remember him in later years. Moving on, we can see that Eric Royle cuts a very dapper figure as Secretary whilst Frank Savill looks every inch the Treasurer. The only ‘familiar’ face I didn't recognise was the bearded and moustachioed Pete Foreman (Social Sec). Ken Beavins won the Mamgu Trophy in 1973 for the log of his single-handed sail in a GP14 to Walton and back, a round trip of about 60 miles in winds Fl - FS and taking 3 days with overnight beach camping. February - A Sydney Harbour 18 footer at the Boat Show fills the front cover and it was, I believe, owned by club member, Bruce Long. My own early memory of the 18 Footers was in Fiji where an 18 Footer regularly started in the races but could never be relied upon to finish. With 5 crew (3 trapezes) and huge sail area, they had formed the habit of taking on several crates of beer as extra ballast. ‘The boat being ‘open-decked' (and the crew being samewhat less than alcohol-free), they inevitably ‘sailed the boat under’ with spinmacker and all sail flying. At least they always won the trophy at the anmal prize-giving for the most capsizes in the season. 4 The Cnriser Mooring List for 1974 reveals 75 cruisers allocated moorings. March — This months 'front cover boys' are John Weedon and son Chris in their Mirror ‘Belly Flop'. The inside front cover has photographs of club trophies and Nick Tovey provides us with a write up of each of them, together with lists of wimners to date (ie. to 1973). Bruce Long's 18 Footer has caused a problem to the club since it is sponsored and thus carries advertising on it contrary to both club and RYA rules. The club committee decided to permit Bruce to sail the boat from the club for one season only and will arrange an HM to decide ‘club policy’ on the mitter but will, no doubt, be guided by any RYA deliberations and decisions. Amongst John Weedon's sailing notes, we are told that;- (a) the Ladies and Cadet Series races will be sailed in combination (and results extracted) so as to ensure at least 3 entries (b) Helmsman of the Year Qualifying races will be held one each month until September and the top two Helms in each fleet would then go forward to the final in October. (c) A few pursuit races would be included in the racing programme. The MSC Accounts to 31 December, 1973, reveal Income of £7,212.5%4 and Expenditure of £5,6007.47, thus no doubt resulting in general rejoicing and happiness that all is well with the club. April - more photos of club trophies and Nick Tovey again gives a brief history of each, together with lists of winners up to 1973. Editor, Brenda Tate, reports the sailing season had started with a bit of a bang in that:- (a) the Sydney Harbour 18 had capsized and split her tramson

6. (b) a brand new cruiser had ripped off her skeg on the Hard before even entering the water (c) a smell crew member had to be rescued from the strong tide and (d) none of the club rescue boat engines would start . Brenda reveals there was "...much wailing and gmashing of teeth. However, the sun has been shining and there's no VAT on the wind, yet !". | Brenda also offers a pair of husband Vic's old seaboot socks The Commodore reports increasing complaints about dogs rumming loose (no doubt ‘going about their business'); also of speeding cars within the club site. Bill Buchanan writes a fairly light-hearted letter to the Editor on behalf of "the potterers” in the club. Whilst full of admiration for the MSC's daring young men on their flying trapezes,etc., he reminds readers that pottering can be fun and is as much a part of the MC as racing. May - the cover picture shows Bruce Long's impression of the new clubhouse (was Bruce the architect?) whilst the inside cover shows photographs of the original site at Easter, 1959, camplet e with the Nissen hut used as a cow shed and which was sufficiently flimsy to be pulled down with a tow rope and Morris 1000. Other photos show the wooden hut erected by members in about 1963. ‘The base of the old wooden clubhouse (and presumably also of the cows’ very own Nissen hut ‘hame-fromhame') is,of course, the Richard Dixon wrote an interesting article about a training cruise in the schooner "Malcolm Miller"; it appears he was a somewhat ‘older trainee’ than the average of 16 - 21. June - som 235 entries fron 43 clubs took part in Regatta. ‘The Marconi entries mstered 38 (ie. 8 Enterprise, 16 Mirrors, 2 GP14, 6 Hornets and 6 Handicap). Fortunately, the garages of the new clubhouse (presumably still being built) were able to be used as changing rooms. Best Marconi results were Norman Palmer (GP14) 14 out of 46, Roger Hance (Enterprise) 2nd out of 40, John Weedon (Mirror) 3rd out of 42 and Ray Hampson (Hornet) 6th out of 19. A debate has obviously been going on within the club about the adoption of a new dinghy class and four ‘cases' are put forward in support of a particular class. [Eddie Fdwards.supports the Lark, Arthur Hodges supports the single-handed Laser, Peter Campion the Bonito whilst Frank Savill makes the case for the Solo. To help the debate, a photo of each of these four boats was printed on the inside cover. Presumably the honeyed words of Frank won the day, for our Solo Fleet, although not 'big' in racing mmbers as such, has always provided very keen, competitive and active participation in club affairs and events. Mike Boreham sppeioisicicck 40 Years Ago - September, 1953. Committee Member, Maurice Greatrex, undertook to organise the erection of partitions within the Clubhouse and an Entertainments Committee was also formed. Apparently the booking of meeting roans was 7/6 per night at the Lion and Lamb and 10/6 at the Golden Fleece. It was reported there was a growing interest for the adoption of the Fleetwind dinghy with, hopefully, peta yea a Lia The kits cost £45 and completed A letter to Mr M J Rantzen (Manager, Patents Dept., Marconi) thanked him for the loan of two books on navigation (You might recall that Mr Rantzen featured in the Navigans Past article in the June, 1993, issue of Navigans in which he had harsh words to say about the adoption of the metric chart). Maldon Borough Council were prepared to licence the club to use the old May and Baker slipway near the clubhouse for the payment of £1 per anmm. Mike Boreham

oe COMMODORE’S NOTES The Bank Holiday weekerd has had about the only good weather for the summer and saw the doubty (doughty? - Ed!) Prindle/Nacra Fleet decamp to Lake Bala for their National Regatta. We again had a brilliant showing and, but for a nasty accident ta Steve Glynn that prevented him and Tom Duckmariton sailing in two races, may well have wrested the 19 championship from the Bala local wizard. Despite that he came second, followed by the well-known "Dark Horse" combination of Vince Talfourd(!) and Damien Horeham in third, and tne Onyons brothers in fourth. Steve Caruth and yours truly had what is best described as a mixed event, with lightning speed in the light § stuff and emulating a backward sailing Mirror in the heavy! Still, an excellent showing, particularly when you add Olly Harris and Judy Garham in their Nacra 5.2 (Lilo-Lill) doing the bizz in the Nacra event. The sailing was only marginally less important than the social events, with the Monday night Bunk House Barbecue giving everyone the opportunity to take incriminating photoes of a high ranking flag officer of the club in his cups (see, chaps, if I admit to it, blackmail won’t work!!), closely followed in, degree of inebriation by a certain Mick Richardson - who nobody has ever seen get really drunk before. I can’t remember...... My personal thanks go ta Peter Richardsern’s wife Barbara for stuffing copious quantities of water down my throat prior to being escorted ta my pit! The reckoning was it beat the best of camping fortrights by a distance. It was a glorious weekend in a glorious setting. The way that a club of 43 members rallied round to cater for a similar number of competitors was very impressive. Also needing report this time is the ECFR which was a great success. My congratulations must go to the ECPR committee who produced an event this time that surpassed all those previcusly. The atmosphere at the prize-giving for me told the whole story. The majority of people stayed and were vociferous in their support for all the factions. From a sailor’s viewpoint the event was absolutely perfect. The Inshore Series balanced well against the Main Event. The attendance of around 15 Dutch competitors also shows what a first rate event we run. Most of the comments compare it very favourably with "Ronde om Texel" (Round Texel) which attracts annually nearly 1000 Cats but is shorter. The successful running of this sart af event is one of the best pieces of publicity for the Club and has been responsible for the recruitment of a number of new members aver the years. Particular mention must go tao the Glynn youngsters and their friends who over a couple of days offered to open the gate for you in exchange for ccin of the realm. The result was around £40 contributed to the ECPR funds. A nice bit of work from the Brat Pack!!!! That’s yer lot, see you next month. Federation of Eastern Counties Sports & Recreation: Concern was expressed on the increasing activities of the ‘Environmental & Conservation Lobby’ and its possible interference with existing and potential waterborne recreational activities. The Chairman had been sympathetic to our concern; he heaped that common sense would prevail and that it would be possible for harmonious relations to be developed with such bodies. Crouch Yachting Federation: It was reported that part of the river had been affected by a sewage problem, it seemed that a particular gate had been opened at an unsuitable time; steps were being taken to regularise the problem. Harwich Area Sailing Association: The importance of RYA’s active involvement in local matters was stressed, commenting on the conflicting pressures of commerce and jobs in sensitive areas. It was reported that Walton & Frinton YC were concerned about spoil dumping in the Dovercourt area, which could perhaps cause silting of the entrance to the Backwaters. FAST CAT NOTES There can only be one subject for this issue’s notes, and that is the coming of age of the East Coast Piers Race. It is easy to say "thank you to all those who helped in...." but it is also easy to overlook the magnitude of what we as a club have achieved over the last 6 years. From Robin Smith's suggestion in 1987 the Race has grown into the best known event in the UK multihull calendar, and it is now taking on a European angle as our Dutch colleagues recognise that life does not end at Texel. The profile of Marconi S.C. has been dramatically raised and it is now seen nationwide as a focus of catamaran sailing; we can attribute a large part of the rise in Cat Fleet membership to the success of the Piers Race. The team of organisers who have made the event so successful must indeed be thanked, and heartily congratulated, but | hope that all who have the club's interests at heart will consider whether there is anything they can do to take a little of the burden (and the credit!) next year. In my opinion Steve Glynn and his team made this year's Race the best yet; the land-side organisation seemed to go off without a hitch, the number of competitors was up on last year, a new (optional) shorter course was introduced to appeal to those who sail the smaller catamarans and (in my mind most importantly) the race management itself was fluent and most professional. The Race has now reacheda stability which allows those involved to step back from the day-to-day panics (a little!) and to consider possible strategic improvements (for example the new shorter course), as well as changes in emphasis; should the Race develop more overtly as a charity event, or should it take on a harder competitive image? To ensure the healthy growth of the event, ideas, and assistance, would be welcome from all. LIES, DAMN LIES AND HANDICAPS Having taught myself how to crunch numbers in analysing the Easter Series | thought it might be interesting to repeat the exercise with the Piers Race results. Plotting the corrected time for all competitors (who chose to sail the full course) against the handicaps of the craft gave the points on the graph shown; the line superimposed on the points represents a linear regression based on the points, or more straightforwardly is the straight line which most closely follows the location of the points on the graph. As was clear from the Easter Series the faster cats, in general, have done better (although the large number of entries in that magnificent class the Hurricane 5.9 tends to hide the effect from the naked eye). This may be considered surprising, | 42000 especially as | believe everyone encountered a lull for a time as the faster boats were around Colne Point which, as the wind filled in again before the finish, should have helped the slower boats. | TT a guess it’s just yet another reason for moving up to a Hurricane. DON’T GIVE UP... 38000 F The Piers Race is, by any appropriate measure, a long race. With the winner taking over five hours and the last finisher coming in nearly two hours | 36000 later one might expect the racing to be, well, laid back, at least after the confusion of the start has abated. The reality is quite different, and many 34000 competitors talk of prolonged duels lasting for many miles. Of the margins separating the 85 finishers on corrected time no less than 40 were under one minute, and 9 under 10 seconds. Peter | 32000 and Barbara Emmerson (the first MSC team overall) are to be congratulated on beating no less than Rob White by a mere 3 seconds; a gentleman 30000 named Bleekveld judged his race to perfection (assuming his ambitions to be somewhat moderate) in beating our own Flying Colours by 1 second. Suddenly we found ourselves in the middle of a Windsurfer race, with high performance men and women (and the boards went well, tac) passing us on every side and, seemingly, from every direction. "Look out, skipper!" "Dor’t worry, we have right of way as they are all either overtaking, on port, or windward boat!" "But doa they know that?" With only a one burner cooker, dinner was coffee and cold Cornish pasty! But the night was young, the sun still shone and life was idyllic. By 9pm we were past Selsey Bill and headed towards Brighton. With the dusk came the desire to wear safety harnesses, but the wind had dropped to a steady force = ard the Number One Crew (Dave and Brian, the skipper) stood down, whilst the Number Two Crew

19. (Keith and me) tock command. We took bearings on various lights and shore = staticns tc check that we were on the lay line, but a lack of compass lights made exact riavigation difficult as we reed to shine a torch on the compass and this ther destroyed our night vision. We did actually try the spinnaker for a while, but the concertraticn needed ta fly it properly in the dark was too much. Brian had disappeared below te sleep, but Dave decided that he preferred tc sleep on deck, so he lay on the floor of the cockpit (more like a mouse pit really) and fell instantly inta a deep sleep. By the time the crews changed watches (fam) we ceauld Clearly see the light from Beachy Head, although the mist had come dawn and the tide was preventing any major progress. By Sam we had made it as far as Eastbourne = and cur next target was the Royal Sovereign Light Tower, which we duly passed at about Bam on Sunday morning. According tae the tide tables, the tide was generally giving us some degree of assistance, but at times we seemed ta be making little progress. We were generally clase inshore ard may have been suffering from same degree af back eddyirig. At this point we began to have scme navigational difficulties! The mist was still about so it was not easy to get a good accurate fix on any object other than the Sovereign Light and although we were on cur lay line, we could not clearly establish how far we were from the Royal Sovereign. For some time we thought that we were aff Rye, but were confused because we couldn’t see the power station at Dungeness. At this point we gave up trying to plot cur pesition and settled for breakfast of Hread and Marmalade, with Tea. As the sun came up to clear the mist, we could see the power station still on the horizon, although at first we mistock it for the channel tunnel workings at Folkestone. In fact we were actually off Hastings, but as the tide turned (?) in our favour we rapidly came up on Dungeness Point passing the point about SO metres fram the shore. Most of the morning we had been flying the spirnaker, but suddenly the wind arrived and with a force 5 dead astern and a following sea, it became toc difficult to manage and we returned to a gcose-winged gernca. New at this paint you have tec use your imagination about the boat. It is 27 feet leng, but the first five feet is taken up by the pointed bit and fittings and then a large bow well for the crew to stand in whilst "doing things". There are two quarter berths below the cockpit floor, but na mattresses (toa much weight) and the tap three feet caf each berth was being used as a storage area for bags and the chart table. The bit between the bow and the cockpit consisted of the forward 6 feet containing spare sails, anchor, water containers, cupboards containing the food, the cocker and the sanitary system (a large plastic bucket!) Behind this area were the ends of the quarter berths separated by a small companicrnway (four feet) which was the cnly place you could stand upright (previded you kept your head in the open hatchway!) The cockpit flocor was about eight inches above water level, whilst the side decks were about 12 inches higher. Needless tc say, cooking ard washing, etc., were extremely difficult and accordingly we lived on Pot Noodles and sandwiches. By 4pm we were off Dover, hands clasped in prayer that we wouldn’t get run down by the Haver Craft or Ferries which seem ta charge about at 20 krnots+. We were aiming at the South Goodwin Light Ship, but had passed it before we saw it. It was rot a problem as we were only about a mile from the coast so navigation was fairly easy. Suddenly disaster....nc wind. The tide continued ta sweep us towards Ramsgate but we were ricw travelling at about 1 knot. "Out with the engine!" said the skipper, ard a small 4HP Mariner was clamped ta the transom bracket. Off we go! However, nobody had ever run the engine for more than 10 minutes before, so we had no idea af haw long it would run on a tank of fuel, and we only had 3.5 gallons on board. Worst case was that we would push on until we had one gallon left and then anchar until the wind returned. Up past Ramsgate with the bigger yachts creaming past us on their inboards, past the North Fereland and out into the estuary. Navigation is not easy when you have na alternate points for bearing taking. We were looking for a small buoy about 3 miles almost due North from the North Foreland, but we were probably less than a mile fram it wher we saw it. We had originally planned to take a fairly straight route across the estuary, but the difficulty of finding the bucys made us change cur mind ard head towards ane of the better lighted channels, although this may mean a closer

For those of you whe have never sailed at night in a small yacht, there is very little depth perspective when looking at light buoys. Although they flash ta set patterns, the patterns are repeated and picking out the correct Buoy can be quite difficult. If you aim for the wrong one, you run aground! We reached the Edinburgh Charmel and became confused as to which Buoy we should aim at, having passed the channel entrance almost without seeing the appropriate buoys. On our way through we managed to touch bottom, but by putting all our weight on one side ard boosting the motor, we were quickly off and heading in the right direction again. At this point the gremlins struck. The navigation lights went cut and despite studious joggling by Keith, we only managed ta get the bow lights working. At this point we were in the process of creassing the Black Deep, which is a main shipping channel ard wherever a large vessel seemed ta be headed towards us, we shome all of the toarches ante the sails, at which paint they all altered course to avoid us. Naw accerding ta the chart, the choice was ta go up the Black Deep until we were off Clacton or to cut acress the Sunk Sands into the Sunk Channel. A difficult process as at low water the whole area dries out. About half way up the sand sthere is a tower, which locks a bit like a miniature Eiffel Tower, and by which is ai narrow channel which we thought we might scrape through. Now this tower is unlit ard we could only see it by silhcuetting it against the lights of Clacton and Jaywick. After much bumping on the bottom, much screaming and shouting af "Over there! Turn left!" (note the nautical terms) "Watch out!" we finally made it inte the Sunk Charmel and frem there across ta the Swirway. The motor had been on for 7 hours and had been refilled twice, sca we had done about 3 hours to a tank full, about 3.5 litres. Not bad for a little motor! But row the wird came up and Dave was fighting the helm against the tide, waves and wind. We sailed under main alone and the boat leaped forward like a shark chasing a kill. We headed for the Swirway. It was now midnight, the stars were hidden and the navigation buoys blended in with the coastal lights. We are not sure we took the correct channel, but at tam Monday we were in the mouth of the Colne having crossed the spit totally blind. We quickly identified the Nass Beacon and headed towards it, missing the Hench Head by about 20 feet, as the tide tried tc sweep us back out ta sea. Hy 3 am we had reached the Nass, despite having to tack several times and fight the last of the tide rushing out of the Blackwater. We had planned to go straight in te Mersea Roads, but it was dark, we were net sure of the charmel ard we were tired, sc we moored up te the buays by the Nass and started to tidy up the boat whilst waiting for daylight. Once we had everything stowed and packed for taking ashore, we sat and relaxed, whilst Dave did his normal I-can-sleep-arnywhere trick and crashed cut! We decided ta staw some of the gear ta be taken ashore on deck, and, despite having two very large ard heavy bags thrown ante him, Dave coantirued te sleep peacefully. With the arrival of daylight we motored irntca West Mersea and because the tide was rising were able ta tie up ta the pontoon to unload, before putting the boat on its mooring. Not a bad trip! Total time 34 hours, total distance about 160 nautical miles, average speed 4.7 knots. Dave ard I have talked on several occasions about doing the trip again. We have concluded that we would only agree if the boat was at least 60 feet lorg, had two or, preferably three hulls, full satellite navigation, decent berths (not that he would use them) and heat shewers! Our relations with our nearest neighbouring Sailing Club are good and I’m sure will continue sco, but I decided it might be interesting, to same members at least, if I published the exchange cf views between me in my personal capacity, and Janet Alderman as Secretary of Stone Sailirig Club. Letter toa Stone: "I am writing to complain of a state of affairs that causes me nervausness oar some af the occasions wher I am sailing past Stone Sailing Club i.e. when there 1S a race taking place. Sometimes a long line of racing boats are stretched across the river, often with little space betweer them for another sailing vessel to get through without causing one of the racing boats to deviate his course to allow him through safely. This they are sometimes very reluctant to do, and occasionally unpleasant remarks are addressed ta the occupants of other boats whe wish to pass along the river. This letter was prompted by an incident on 8th August when a Stone sailing cadet indicated brusquely that we in our small cruiser should not get in his way while he 1S racing. AS our courses, in opposite directions, were close but not converging, and he did not have to alter course ta avoid us, this was totally unnecessary. Does the racing fraternity at Stone expect all other passing river traffic tao put on their handbrakes and wait for the whole fleet to pass by? Racing boats on what is a marine public highway must expect to follow the regulations which allow other traffic ta use the river alsa, and must expect caccasionally that individually they may have tc alter course toa accommodate that other traffic - racing does not absolve them from that responsibility........." Reply from Stone Sailing Club: " ....... I regret that you found it necessary to write to the Club and have to say that yours is the only complaint of this nature that we have received. I am aware that, particularly wher there are light winds, cur boats car appear ta be stretched acress the river when going from ane mark ta another but can assure yau that all cur members are fully aware of the port and starboard rules which affect all boatS using the river. Many cruiser cawners, perhaps having raced dinghies at some stage themselves, appreciate that the boats are racing and we often find will take avoiding action even if they do have ’right of way’........."
