6. FASTNET ?93 -— A Racing Tale from a Cruising Man This is the story of an out-and-out cruising man suddenly finding himself part of the frenetic racing scene. Most MSC members will be familiar with Natasha IV, a Westerly Fulmar on Mooring BS. Many will remeber Natasha III, a Contessa 28, and Natasha It, and Galion 22 which returned to the Club owned by Ray Hillman. Few perhaps will remember Natasha I, a 20 foot Vivacity, but over the years Jackie and 1, plus or minus Nicola and Mark, have cruised extensively along the North Sea and Channel coasts, aided by such non-racing items such as jib furling and spinnaker socks. Imagine our surprise ther in the Autumn of last year, wher: my company, GPT, asked me if I would like te take part in the Fastnet race this year on a yacht sponsored by BT and their Industrial Suppliers. I was therefore presented with a challenge, and of course, a marvellojus opportunity, but I recognised that I would need te change my relaxed cruising attitude to one of being part of a hard working, dedicated racing team. The team turned out to be seven from BT, and one each from Ericsson, Northern Telecom, GPT, Sun, Amdahl, Tandem and Hewlett Packard, plus the yacht owner’ s representative and Stuart Quarrie our tactician and coach. Stuart writes in Yachting World and Yachts and Yachting, and has taken part in all the Fastnet races since the fateful one ir 1979, when he was on one of the yachts that foundered. That year is uppermost in people’s minds, but before and since then the safety record has been good, though it is recognised as a tough off-shore race, and one of the world’ classics. So we had a team of 16, and the BT members where chosen by a selection within the BT Off-shore Sailing Club. Many of the team had taker part in previous Fastnet Campaigns, but this was a first for GPT. The yacht chosen was a 57 foot Swan called "Noonmark V", but named "Teamwork" for the racing. We had to become a hardened racing team, which for the cruising members was a change iri mind set, and meant learning many new skills. This started last autumn with the team split betweer two Sigma 38 yachts for a weekend, practising sail changing techniques and tuning the yachts for maximum performance. We also "practised" some involuntary broaches wher putting up the spinnaker in the heavy wind of that weekend, losing total control of the yacht on a number of occasions. On the Sunday it was gusting 45 knots, so we practised staying on the yacht! For winter study we were giver some video tapes produced by Stuart, and in the spring had two training weekends or Teamwork. This really brought home the magnitude of the forces at play or a large yacht, and the sheer weight of the sails. It took at least three people to lift the largest sails, and we had four sizes of genoa and three spinnakers to contend with. On the second weekend we went off-shore, and got used ta living a dual-watch system, which is like having two crews which change place ever three hours at night, and four hours in daylight. Since 1979, the Royal Ocean Racing Club (RORC) has insisted that in order to take part in the Fastnet, at least half of the crew must have undertaken three off-shore races that year. During the run-up, Teamwork took part in the Cerventes Trophy race to OQuistreham, the Morgan Cup channel race and the Cowes-St Malo race. In the first we did particularly well, coming 3rd in class, and 4th overall out of 95 starters. Ir the Morgar Cup we came Sth in class and 9th overall out of 93, but could only manage 43rd in class in the St Malo race where conditions favoured the lighter boats, and 194 yachts took part. During the races we ran a system where the bowman and Stuart were always or call, and seven of us were in each watch. The bowman needed to be a masochist, who actually enjoyed retrieving halyards from the top of the 70 foot mast, and who felt it was quite natural to climb up the spinnaker pole downhaul, 15 foot up and 20 foot out over the water, in order to put up a new spinnaker ard peel off the old. For a cruising man, the frequent changing of sails takes some getting used to, and at night at 30° on the foredeck in rough conditions it is physically very demanding. The tasks of putting up a new Genoa, two of you hauling on the halyard and one tailing on the winch, followed by dropping the old sail and bagging it by flaking intc a long racing bag, takes at least half an hour. The peeling of sails in this way means that the boat is always driving under full sail, but of course the wind contd. «ss

7. might change in half ar hour! With spinnakers it was also necessary to stop the sail before bagging, which entailed gathering the sail together from the head and = each clew, and tying with wool stops at 6 foot intervals. This prevents the sail filling prematurely when hoisting, which can be disastrous wher it wraps around the forestay ard is impossible to get down. On an out-and-out racing boat with a well practised team, everyone would probably have a specific job ta do, but we tended to split between the younger ones on the foredeck, handling halyards and sail changing, ard the colder ones steering, trimming and tailing, with bursts on the coffee-grinder winches. However, everyone helped wherever necessary, apart from bowman activity, which in addition toa requiring a certair agility, is alsa frequently under water. Sleep in 3 hour slots does not come naturally. To start with half an hour is last getting waterproof clathing off, and more particularly on, and the general noise level of sail trimming and changing sounds very loud below deck. In the end one becomes so tired that sleep for short periods becomes very deep, to be rudely = broken by your wake-up call from tne watch above. My toes still feel the effect of skidding the full width of the boat on one foot while attempting to pull oan waterproof trousers. Sacks are lethal on wooden floors. I have tc confess that for all the hardships the yacht was extremely luxurious, and having a deepfreeze, we had really excellent pre-prepared food. We had a strict rota for the cook’s job, and for me it was not easy juggling with three red hot trays of shepherds pie in rough conditions, but very rewarding for a hungry crew. With all cur training we now felt ready for the Fastnet; 605 miles from Cowes to the South Western tip of Ireland, going either side of the Scilly Isles, round the Fastnet rock to part, and back ta Flymouth outside the Scillies. The course instructions were simple enough. Just before the race the bottom of the yacht was cleaned and polished by the crew, and then on 7th August we joined the other 240 yachts off Cowes. These included 23 Admiral’s Cup yachts from 8 nations, and 13 Whitbread yachts working up for the Round-the-World race starting in September. With Press boats and helicopters as well, the atmosphere was electric, and the start was something I will never forget. The various classes were started at 10 minute intervals, but even so the congestion was incredible. The start line had a bias that favoured the Cowes end, and everyone was there, sailing at 9 or so knots with nowhere to go. A collision occurred in front of us causing quite bad damage to two boats, and then the gun fired at 2.40pm ard we were off ta a good start. Five minutes later the Italian yacht "Nocorette" that caused the earlier crash was totally out of control, heading straight at us. We ran along the deck to escape the impact, but somehow they recovered control and missed us by inches. They were, of course, disqualified. Adrenalin continued to flow as we short-tacked cut of the Solent, through thge Needles Channel, and then we settled down to the long beat down charmel, the wind generally Westerly. The forecast suggested heavier weather coming, which would favour a Swarr compared to the light-weight flyers, where crews need tc sit aut on the side deck for their weight, ever sleeping there! By Portland Bill the fleet had spread right cut, and we were only see about 10 yachts for the rest of the race. By the evening of the second day we had rounded Land’s End, and were well into the Irish Sea wher we heard a Mayday call from a Japanese Admiral’s Cup boat, which had lest a crew member overboard. It was 11 o’clock at night, Force 5 with a moderate sea rurming, and we were the nearest boat - about 4 and a half miles away. We were Just about to abandon the race and start the search, when he was recovered by his own yacht having beer in the sea for about 20 minutes. He was very lucky. He had a Torch but dropped it when struggling in the water to get his neavy clothing off. Or Teamwork we all double-checked the security of our harnesses. £4 hours later we were rounding the Fastnet rock, 5 miles off the coast of Ireland, having sailed around 400 miles with the Force 4 to 5 wind right on the nose. At night it looked very menacing, with sheer rock walls and a lighthouse perched on the top. The RORC staff on the rock told us that we were 49th round, and we celebrated with a specially made cake with a picture of the rock on top. contd...

8. The wind had backed as expected, and was increasing, giving us an exhilarating spinnaker run back ta the Scillies, and on to Plymouth. The yacht was automatically giving its position back to BT every 6 hours and this was then faxed on a map tc each Company, keeping everyone informed. With gusts up to Force 7 we absolutely flew, and the effort and concentration needed tc steer was such that we changed helmsman every 30 minutes. Running down the wave fronts, we reached 14 knots on several occasions and great care was needed not toa lese control and broach. 8 o'clock in the morning, after 4 nights at sea, we crossed the finish line under St Annes Battery in Plymouth. 46 yachts were in front of us, but those included 36 Round-the-World and Admiral’s Cup racers. We were 14th in Class 1 out of 70 and entered the marina with our built-in hi-fi blaring out "Simply the Best - better than all the rest: from Tina Turner. Our wives were there to greet us and champagne flowed. It was an emotional moment. Of the 240 yachts that started, 21% failed to complete the race, some with mast or boom failures. We had relatively few problems. The most severe was a 12 foot tear in the No.1 Genoa, solely caused by letting the sail back or to the spreaders wher tacking. On a large yacht racing sails are much more fragile than one might imagine. This was repaired by hand-sewing and taping over the next 24 hours, but probably cost us the Swan Cup, as there was only one hour between us and the winner. The or other breakage was a halyard snapshackle that fractured under strain at the top vu: the mast. Our bowman saw toe it! The fastest yacht, a Whitbread, was 27 hours ahead of us in real time, and the last yacht to complete the race was 88 hours behind us, almost double our time. Sc what are the memories? Great comradeship, hard physical work, living life in 3 hour slots, lack of sleep, cooking dinner for 16 while heeling at 30 degrees, dolphins playing round the bow, and the thrill of a fast spinnaker run. But above all, a sense of achievement, and grateful thanks to my Company for giving me the opportunity. Brian Bowsher, 26th September 1993

A Statement with reference to the Cadet Series(made at the 1992 AGM) May I/we draw the attention of our fellow members to what I/we believe to be an undesirable development within the club - namely, the adoption of discriminatory rules aimed to benefit one section of the membership at the expense of another. I/we understand that the Sailing Sub-Committee proposes to adopt a policy whereby certain boats are to be banned fran competing in the Cadet Series. I/we believe it is widely accepted that the Cadet Cup was donated by Eric Payne many years ago for open competition by Cadet Members (ie those aged 18 and under). As far as I/we am/are aware, competition for the Cadet Cup has always been open to any Cadet Member sailing any craft with a discernible * Portsmouth Yardstick Number. It seems the Sailing Sub-Committee now proposes to ban from competition any Cadet Member wishing to sail in any catamaran whatsoever, and to ban any Cadet Member who wishes to sail in a monohull with a Yardstick of less than 114. I/we do not believe such a ban would be in compliance with the spirit and wish of the original donor of the Cadet Cup, nor do I/we believe such a ban would be in compliance with the aim of the MSC to provide "boating for all'. A list of the past winners of the Cadet Series was recently published in Navigans. The list contains the names of many Cadet Members who have inevitably been successful in other MSC competitions - not merely the Cadet Series. Fach past winner of the Cadet Series can be justifiably proud of having won the trophy fairly in open competion, both within the niles of sailing and within the spirit of the competition itself. To now propose to ban certain boats because some members perceive that they represent 'unfair' competition implies that some previous winners have won not on merit but because they were unduly favoured by the type of craft they sailed and thereby the competition was 'unfair'; this mist be the logic of the new proposal since it now intends to ban the same type of boats fram future competitions. Whilst I/we appreciate that the Sailing Sub-Committee is motivated by good intensions 'to encourage the younger, inexperienced Cadet Members’, I/we believe the new policy to be fundamentaly flawed in its logic and its implementation to be grossly unfair to a group of Cadet Members who, by example, have contributed much to the well-being of the club. I/we suggest that the Cadet Series competition for the Payne Cup be left as a competition open to all Cadet Members to sail in whatever boat they choose, provided it is in compliance with the original ‘intension of the donor. I/we suggest that additional Cadet Members trophies be obtained for specific award, eg. Cadet Members aged 14 and under sailing in measured dinghies (excluding catamarans) of PYN 114 and above. I/we further suggest that a special 'mini-series' be held during the Cadet Training week solely for those Cadet Members taking part in the Training Week, possibly restricting the competition to Mirror dinghies. Thereby, one hopes that the parents of the young Cadet Members will be persuaded to bring the young competitors each week to the club to take part in dinghy racing, in particular the Mirror Spring, Summer and Autumn Series for which 3 rather attractiv cups await e to be won in 1993, The source and financing of the additional Cadet trophies is, of course, a matter for the Sailing Sub-Com and mittee Main Committee to entertain, but perhaps one (financial) source might be fram those MSC Members who feel there is a need for additional incentives to persuade the younger Cadet to sail To this end, I/we would be willing to consider donating a trophy for competion by girl Cadet Members aged 14 and under, the actual detail of the campe to be titio decided by me/us. n However, I/we would look towards other MSC Members who wish to encourage Cadet Member sailing at Stansgate to similarly donate trophies.

COMMODORE’S REPORT 1993 has beer an interesting year in many respects. The outward appeararice 1s that not much has happened, but much has occurred that has helped to clarify the Club’s Situation for the future. Going into the year, our relationship with MASC and the calculation of the "Contribution" were items of great concern, particularly with the avowed intent of GEC to ensure that the majority of members were GEC emplayees. This situation was exacerbated by the pace of redundancy within the Company. Fortunately, our dogged determination to resist the imposition of a draconian rise in contribution was successful, and has brought into sharp focus the relationship between MASC ard its Sections, so much so that a sub-committee has beer set up to investigate the way forward for the organisation as a whole. FPerscenally, I have high hopes for the outcome af this group. The degree to which we are able to carry out improvements toa our facilities is totally linked with the foregoing. We are unable to make capital expenditure without the (praper) agreement of the MASC Committee, or to take action tao raise money for specific projects. Consequently, our financial plan is based on a break-even target, with minor repairs or renewals only allowed for. Major development will have ta await clarification of our position. However, we have managed to improve facilities in a number of ways. Firstly, cur hot water capacity was extended over last winter, and nobody need now fear the dreaded cold shower. Even at the ECPR it was still bearable at the end of the queue. My thanks go cut tc Steve Glynn and Frank Bermnett for their activities in that respect. Secondly the access control system has been renewed with something that has already proved much more successful. Frank Bennett designed and built the system for a tiny fraction of the cost of commercially available alternatives. Currently, plans are in hand for the essential repair of the ground floor windows of the Clubhouse, installing security lighting in the Cruiser Park, and for the repair of the Workboat. Much of my personal objective this year has revolved around making the tasks undertaken by individuals in the daily rurming of the Club less onerous. We now have a laptop PC that is used by Frank Bennett for Accounts, and doubles as our major event-results machine. We shall be further investigating the systems used for Membership records and Navigans production ta try to relieve the loads on those pecple. Another item of note has been the poor response of OODs this year. Very few plecple have turned up to do their allocated duty, which only crops up once every four or five years. Consequently, several parts of Club facilities have been unavailable at times of high demand —- particuarly the Bar. The repurcussions of this are more widespread than may be apparent, since decreased bar cpening equates with lower sales and thus lower profits. This will only result in one outcome, a further increase for all in subscriptions. The Executive and Main Committees have spent a great deal of time discussing possible alternatives, with no great success. I cannot let the opportunity pass without mention of the NRA. The work in raising the Sea Wall is important to all of us, but the problems of dealing with ai large bureaucratic organisation are plain to all of us. Unfortunately, we have very little recourse other than to play on their sympathy toa gain other spin-off benefits from the contract, but I do record my thanks for the forbearance for all the members of the Cruiser Fleet who have been inconvenienced over two winters. However, work is now under way, and will be complete by the start of next year. Fram the New Year access to the Hard will be limited, to allow construction of the new entrance. I reserve my final remarks for my colleagues on the Executive and the Main Committee. The support and initiative of these people makes my job much easier and enables the Club to operate smoothly. At the moment I am privileged to have the immediate team of Steve Glynn, Colin Kidner, Steve Hill and Frank Bennett to work with and they are all characterised by the ability to intercept problems and get on with things without a word fram me. The members of the Main Committee have given their time and contributed toa much healthy debate over the year as well as picking up individual jobs as required. I place on record my thanks to them all. Larry Botheras

Mona - SCANDINAVIAN CRUISE 1993 Skipper: Malcolm Shaft. Crew: Helen, Laura, Simon; Jenny tao join im Norway. Day One - Saturday 24th July 1993. Having arrived at Heybridge Basin and loaded up the last of our bags late the previcus evening, we had a very early start extricating Mona from her inside berth, and with Colin the Lockeeper’s invaluable expertise, locked out of the basin at 04.30. Wind. as forecast, was a favourable SW, sc sails went up off Osea. Mona gathered speed and swept purposefully past Stansgate and down the Blackwater. The rest af my watch was spent tinkering with the self steering and the Autohelm which had been returned from repair just in time for the trip, and I was more than a little miffed to discover that it would only turn us round in circles. We were therefore committed ta hand-steering all the way. We ran with the ebb dawn the Wallet, ard shaped a course between the Shipwash and the Inner Gabbard. The wird increased and cur rolling dead run became increasingly uncomfortable, particularly for the Geoff-watch crew (now including me!) It was therefore with some relief that having cleared the Gabbard we were able to bring the wind ontc the aft quarter, giving a much pleasanter motion. During the evening the wind died away, sca the engine was started, and course was altered back to the original one which would take us round all the shipping lanes. Day Two - In the small hours the wind freshened and we were soon sailing well again. Dawn broke tc reveal what was ta prove a much surmier day than expected. During the evening we were called up by an initially unseen Survey Vessel asking us toa change course ta avoid his mile-long trailing cables! The steady SW 4-5 increased as the evening progressed, and by midnight it was 6 gusting 7 with Mona bowling along at 7-8 knots. Day Three - Mona now heading a steady 035° which was to remain virtually unchanged for the rest of the trip out. Laura stayed on the tiller for hours on end and got sa used to steering 035" that she later found great difficulty in steering anything else. Morning found us negotiating the oil- and gas-rigs of the German SHight. Another sunny, lively and speedy day’s sailing, with the crew all settled well, including the skipper whe much te his embarrassment had suffered the indignity of bouts of sea sickness for the first 24 hours of the trip. Evening breught an hour of torrential rain effectively blocking out all visibility, but preducing in its wake the most superb rainbows. The rain alsa took the wind, meaning resorting ta the engine, but giving us a gentle night. Day Four - A calm bright dawn with the prospect of landfall. When Simeon row suggested using the Spinoa I was more than happy to go along with it. Ina steadily rising wind it gave us a supert run into Kristiansand. The landfall itself was probably the mast spectacular I have seen. The Norwegian coast is arn impressive Sight, and we not only sailed ta it, but were totally swallowed up by it as we sailed into the Fiard. We came alongside the pontoon at Kristiansand mid-afternoon, 84.5 hours after locking cut at Heybridge, having run the engine for something less than 15 hours, and averaged a shade under 6 knots for the trip. In spite of it being fairly lively overall, we probably arrived marginally less tired than wher we _ had left Erigland! Days Five & Six —- were spent relaxing in Kristiansand and the surrounding area, waiting for Jenny to arrive with Simon’s family. Helen and I sought aut the charts necessary far fully exploring the next part of the coast, which according toa the Cruising Association Handbook was well worth a visit. Prices in general, as expected, were high, the ultimate and rather extreme example being showers at over €2 a time! Day Sever, - Spent a rather lumpy night on board, a wind shift having resulted in a strong scend coming into the bay. Day very grey and overcast, but we decided that we would start our coastal exploration attempting to find a rather complicated route that would take us inside many of the outlying racks and islands. The route involved heading out of the fiord, then heading back in a little further along the coast. It was all rather nerve-wracking in the misty conditions, especially when surrounded by rocks just feet away and the echo sounder deciding to go on the blink. I have to admit that after a couple of hours of rock-hopping, having become totally confused, and finding ourselves with access to the open sea, we opted out and completed toa passage to Lilysand on the outside, arriving at this lovely little port through an impressive gash in the cliffs. The sun by this time had come out and we tied up ta a convenient pontcon and had a pleasant evening stroll on the hills above the _ town. Returned to the boat for a delicious meal of fresh salmon.

6 Day Eight - Bright, sunny day. Lazy morning around the port. Lively carnival atmosphere. After lunch decided to retrace our steps along the Blirndieie, the much- vaunted inshore passage. Proved to be much more straightforward from this end! Absclutely spectacular. With great trepidation, became truly Scandinavian and tied up bows-on to a rocky island with stern anchor cut and close enough to jump ashare. Getting poetical I decided that if there was a paradise on earth, it couldn’t be far away. The rest of the crew just decided that I’d gone a bit locpier than usual. Explored the island - tremendous views from the top. Laura swam, keeping a careful eye an the enormous jellyfish that seem to thrive there. Day Nine - Woke up ta discover we were still afloat - just. Matored back up the Blirndleie tawards Lilysand, then aut to sea and a lovely geroa run along the coast towards Arendal, the last ten miles taking us once more inside recky islands, many af them with little cottages built into the rocky crags. Sailing right into the fiord we came up to Arendal just as the International Fowerboating Championships were (thankfully) coming to an end. We were in time to see a chap with a garland round his neck. We tied up at the guesthaven and had an enjoyable walk round the town. Day Ter —- Busy morning spring Cleaning. Got talking to a local who had seer Mona from his office window and had recognised her as an Ebbtide 33. He had sailed in Company with ome across the Atlantic a few years ago and had wanted ta buy a 46. Having gained considerable credibility in my eyes, his advice that there were some beautiful spots to tie up at just around the corner was taken sericusly. Having filled up with water we left, stopping across the fierd for our first refuelling since leaving England, only needing Se litres to fill the tanks up. Then we made our way along the fiord ta find one of these idyllic spots. We found some beautiful scenery, but nowhere to stop. Finally in some desparation we tried unsuccessfully toa get clase enough toa rocks to tie up. Eventually we found a spot completely suproaunded by rocks, shallow enough to anchor in. Day Eleven - It had rained all night, still very damp and miserable in the marning. We were approached by a speedboat, and I was convinced that we were geirg to be told that we shouldn’t be anchored there. It turned cut he wanted tc sell us bread and pastries. Making such good progress that we made landfall sooner than intended, and arrived at the Hatteberget Light irs Sweder, just before dawn. A quick sleep, then out to explore the island. A fascinating place, and it turns cut we've arrived in the middle of the 420 World Championships. Good walk and climb up the rocks. Day Thirteen - Bought local charts at the Supermarket, the chandlers only sold designer sailing wear. Prepared ourselves for more rock-hopping, taking inside ¢5 mile passage far Gothenburg. Started off heading for what seemed like ai narraw fissure in the rocks. Gentle passage up the fiord, passing under a huge suspension bridge. We almost ran aground keeping well over to starboard toa avaid a ferry that I assumed was manceuvering to pass under the bridge, only to discover that he was in fact berthing on the starboard side, which Helen had been telling me all

A fascinating discussion ensued that cavered = such topics as Maggie Thatcher, the Falklands, Freddie Mercury, the European Community, Fishing restrictions, etc. It also turned cut that the fishing boat that had = surk had been hit by a Russian ship. The fisherman krew the crew well; there had been twa of them, brathers. One had been picked up by the ship, the other had drowned. The fisherman commented that at least the ship had stepped, he was sure that wouldn’t have happened just a few years ago. Day Sixteen - Little wind, sc we decided to have a lay day on the island. We hired bikes ard managed to explore quite a lot cf it. It was very flat, particularly after the type of scenery we had got used to over the past few days, but ideal for cycling. Heavily wooded with chalets hidden deep in the woods. Good cycle tracks and one of the straightest roads we had ever seer. Day Severiteer. - Made an early start at 95.30 and headed south for Anholt. The wind scorn picked up from the South West. Sailing well, but realised we wouldri’t be able to held course for Anholt without tacking. Several hours cf bashing away hard on the wind began to take their toll of us, so we bore away for Falkenburg back on the Swedish coast where we arrived in the early evening. We sailed threugh the narrcaw entrance, lavely when you haven’t got tide rips across the ertrance to worry about, and we tied up at a friendly yacht club just before a forecast blow arrived. It was a wild, wet night, but we felt very snug in our bunks. Day Eighteer, - A brighter fresher morning and we managed to get through to the Scuthampton Weather Centre, who predicted a South of West Force 4 or S&S all day, followed by an increase overnight that would be a full gale by the morning which would then take a while to die down. We decided that we should be able to just held a course for Molle, a place we had visited the previous year at the entrance to the Sound, and we left at midday. Wind was more SWly than predicted, fairly lumpy sea, and we couldn’t hald course, so decided to motorsail in an attempt ta reach Molle, with its unlit entrance before dark. We began to have concerns as to what we would do if we didn’t get there in time, as it didn’t look as if it was going ta be the

8. sort of night for jilling about in the increasingly restricted waters we were getting to. In the event we made it with about an hour ta spare, surfing threugh the entrance with breaking water all around us. We fournd a space just big enough alongside the quay in the tiny harbour. Manceuvred as close as I could, which wasn’t very close at all, but Laura made a heroic leap and secured us. A heavy scerd was coming intc the harbour, and the wind soon got up. We ended up secured with at least three bow lines and several springs for a very windy night. Day Nineteen - Still extremely windy with lecal forecasts promising gales for the next 24 hours at least, with the possibility of a short lull. The lull only came in the evening, too late for us to go anywhere, sc had a day in the very pleasant port. We bought smoked fish from the quayside, and the skipper made history by deaing his awn washing. Walked cut tawards the headland, and visited a tiny but extremely well stocked maritime museum. The curator was an interesting chap wha, a few years age, had sailed a 7 metre Maxi singlehanded to the West Indies and back. Hrought the log up to date in the evening. Weather still guiet with the promised resumption of the gale yet ta materialise. Day Twenty - Very windy, sco we went for a walk, looking out over a very windy Sound. A slight lull in the afternoon, so we decided tao brave the waves rolling into the entrance ard made the short trip across the entrance ta the Sound to the lovely little fishing port of Gillejie in Dermark. We managed to tie up next tao a trawler in a very creawded harbour. Day Twenty One - We spent the morning shopping, intending to move on at midday, but continued strong Westerlies would have made the intended progress due west uncomfortable toa say the least!. Sc we settled down fer another enforced lay day, giving the crew a rest, particularly Helen who was just recovering from the effects cf her bug. Day Twenty Two - Made an early start in flat calm and very sunny conditions. Attempted tc sail with the spinoa, but everitually had to admit defeat and researt to the engine. We rounded the long peninsula of Sjaellands Odde and across ta the the lovely little island of Sejero. We tied up to the harbour wall and ate cut at vfery reasonably priced harbour cafe. Day Twenty Three - Made another early start toa try tc make up for the limited progress of the previous week. Good sail inte the Breat Belt, ther headed by falling wind, so we motored inta increasingly misty conditions. The surrounding islands soar disappeared completely. We decided to head for the almost deserted island of Mushalm, and had just located the island and were heading cautiously in, when Laura discovered that our water tanks were unexpectedly empty, having been filled only twa days earlier. We decided ta ga somewhere with facilities, and crept into the tiny fishing harbour of Reerso with very little shewing on the echo sounder. We tied up in ar empty berth by the diesel pump and started filling up with water only ta find that water was pouring from the calorifier under the cockpit. Emptied the two level cockpit locker and climbed in and under to inspect the calorifier ard discovered that one af the water pipes had worked loose and come off. At least we knew where the water had gone! Started tc tighten up the pipes wher the Harbour Mistress arrived. Asked if there was a chance of getting diesel and she said there was. Went back under the cockpit. Just then a large German yacht arrived and tried to squeeze inte the small space behind us, necessitating us moving Mona forwards. I was still trying to fix the calorifier when attendant arrived to give us diesel. Filled up with diesel and then went back to work. It now decided to rain. Eventually the calorifier was sorted cut and the contents of the locker returned to their rightful Place. Collapsed down below to very welcome supper. Day Twenty Four - Yet another early start in ever worse visibility, and motored south for unseen bridge-building operation. Contacted Information Service on VHF toa discover there was a special small ship channel taking you through the bridge building works ret shown on our chart! Helpful chap gave us the position of the first buoy and we got through without seeing anything of the bridge building operation whatsoever, apart from very indistinct misty shapes. We heaved a collective sight of relief only to discover a huge ferry hurtling out of the mist towards us and spent a very anxious couple of hours until we were safely clear of the ferry and shipping lanes. What was particularly frustrating was that we had passed through some reputedly very attractive scenery without seeing any of it! We located the island of Largeland, and the wind got up and gave us a very pleasant and therapeutic sail down the coast towards the little port of Snodsberg, the only port

9. on the east side of the island. We arrived a year to the day and almost the hour that we had last beer there. We discovered that water was once again pouring out of the calorifier and further probing under the cockpit resulted in me being scaked with extremely hot water and revealed that the water was coming from the safety valve indicating that there was a fault with the thermostat. Feeling less than enamoured with hot water systems, I decided that I would have to isolate the system before we left in the morning. Day Twenty Five - Got up early to do necessary adjustments to hot water system, then the tricky manoeuvre to extricate Mona from the tiny harbour. Laura was confined ta her bunk for a second day, being seemingly second victim of the mystery virus. Fresh Westerly giving a superb fast sail down the remaining Langeland coast, and across ta Kiel, tying up once again at the British Kiel Yacht Club for sumptious hot baths for the female members of the crew and a cold shower for the male! Day Twenty Six - Motored round the corner and locked into the Kiel Canal for an undemanding day motoring through the fifty mile length of the canal, enjoying rare sunshine. We arrived at a lovely little, incredibly cheap (less than £4), marina just inside the lock gates. We spent the evening trying tc solve the twin’ problems of haw best to leave the tricky waters of the Elbe and how to get Laura home, who was leaving us early to get her A level results and sort out a University place. Eventually having talked to a friendly Dutchman tied up alongside, we decided to lock out at first light ta take the extremely strong tide the 16 miles or sa down ta Cuxhaven where we would try and sort Laura’s travelling arrangments out. Day Twenty Seven - A quick trip to Cuxhaven, entering sideways with four knots of tide sluicing across the entrance, and tying up by half past nine. Into Cuxhaven to find a very helpful travel agent. As the next ferry to take Laura from Hamburg to Harwich wasn’t until next day, and the weather forecast indicated that the best time for Mona to leave the Elbe was that afternoon, arrangements were made, with some difficulty, for Laura’s overnight accommodation at Cuxhaven. So with some trepidation we left Laura on the pontoon and filled up with diesel from the fuelling barge (that had closed but kindly reopened long enough to give us fuel and incur the wrath of a following German a powerboat who understandably expected the same treatment). We were just in time to capitalise on the fast flowing ebb and covered the 25 miles to the Elbe Light Vessel in some 3 and a half hours. Our first night passage as a three-man crew was comparatively pleasant, most of it being taken up with steady motorsailing. The morning however was one cf those dawns that somehcw never quite manage to happen, bringing with it the forecast, but somewhat premature, cold front. Last year’s experience of a Force 9 gusting 10 off the German Friesland Island of Borkum had resulted in distinct feelings of unease when approaching this area for the second time. Now these fears were being partly realised with rising head winds, confused angry seas and little visibility. Although conditions were nothing like last year, there followed several hours of extreme discomfort until we finally tied up in Borkum some 120 miles and 22 hours afer leaving Cuxhavan. Day Twenty Nine - Weather dictated a lay day in Borkum enlivened by the discovery of excellert, reasonably priced German food in the restaurant, and a phore call toa England revealed that Laura had arrived home safely and had gained her University place. Day Thirty - A very early start at 0400 to discover that the lights at the rather tricky entrance to the Yacht Harbour had been switched off. Somehow we managed to feel our way out and followed the long channel out through the shallows. Still lumpy seas and dawn brought with it drizzle which stayed with us in varying entensities all day as we motorsailed along the Friesland Islands. Then in the afternoon as we approached the narrow gat between Tershelling and Vlieland, a NE 6 that had been promised for the next day but decided to arrive 24 hours early, sprung up behind us and made the entry in wind-over-tide conditions agains a fast flowing ebb decidedly interesting. At one point we were surfing completely enveloped in spray. We tied up in the picturesque island of Vlieland after a somewhat exhilarating end to an 86 mile day’s passage. Day Thirty One - By unanimous decision we agreed to have a lay day pleasantly spent wandering round the little town and along the beach. Jenny spent most of the afterncon doing her washing.

10 Day Thirty Two - A pleasant trip, after a lively exit from Vlieland, through the Waddenzee toa Der Helder. Very pleasant accommodating Yacht Club in the middle of this very active military base. Good forecast with, unbelievably, North Westerlies going Northerly - unheard of for the trip home. Day Thirty Three - An early start intended, but just casting off lines wher the engine stops, and an expert is required. The yacht club aobligingly cemtact the local engineer who turns up promptly at 0915 to diagnose that one of the valve springs is broken because of some emulsifying of the engine cil. A Spare needs to be sent fram Dortrecht ard worn’t arrive before Friday morning at the earliest which is all rather frustrating particularly having ta watch these rare Northerlies blow aimlessly away. Still, spirits improve as the day wears on, and even more so that night when the rain starts, so we lie in bunks feeling slightly relieved we’re not out in the North Sea after all. Alsa feeling that if the engine had to fail, it did soa before we'd finished urntying the lines. Day Thirty Four - Enforced day of leisure spert on a pleasant wander around Den Helder, with a lunch of bread and roast chicken. Day Thirty Five - After an anxious wait the engineer arrived with the spring, and with much muttering and sucking of breath, combined with thoughtful puffing on roll- ups, the spring was duly fitted and the engine reassembled. All ready to geo at mid afternoon, winds blowy but still favourable. We cast off about 1530 and had a speedy departure with Northerly 6 and fair tide. Heavy seas but tremendous progress of at least 98 knots, and great to be moving again. Jenny once again proved herself extremely competent at transferring accurate positions onto the chart from the GFS in difficult conditions. A long night at the tiller, but it was very rewarding in terms of progress. Dawn saw us clear of the shipping lanes and an easing of the winds down to a light North Easterly. By late morning we can see Sizewell, and from there a slow but pleasant run in brilliant sunshine to Harwich, motoring the last part. We decided to make our first visit to Shotley Marina ard almost regretted the decision after jilling about in the entrance and touching bottom for the first time in the whole trip. Eventually got in and enjoyed a gocd meal at the club. Day Thirty Six - Little wind, but we managed to start sailing just outside Harwich Harbour. The tide turned against us off Frinton, but we managed tc keep on sailing. Gradually gained ground and in the end managed superb sail right back to the Club. Day Thirty Seven - Slight panic when the engine wouldn’t start, then it responded just ain time for us to lock in at Heybridge Basin some 1,581 nautical miles after locking out just over five weeks before, having visited some twenty ports, enjoyed some superb sailing and spent a week each in Norway, Sweder and Denmark. Arrived back in the middle of Bank Holiday Monday mayhem, 30th August. IN SEARCH OF THE VIKINGS Mona’S 1993 SCANDINAVIAN CRUISE, JULY 24TH - AUGUST SOTH 1993 Malcolm Shaft

"Get out the *Y@E&$*E@!! way - I'm racing" 11. (an ordinary sailor's guide for sailing on the Blackwater)_ Ref. Maureen's comments in the November '93 Navigans, I don't think she is being over—sensitive about good manners between sailors on the river - but I do think she might be a little naive to think it will be any different in an age of 'the professional foul', 'gamesmanship' and 'the will to win at any cost' -— assuming it was really any different in the 'old days’ anyway. Over the years I have experienced, as a dinghy-racing helm, similar incidents of blatant ‘ignore'(Once)' of 'the rules', some of which might be due to genuine ignorance but most due to 'gamesmanship' sometimes accompanied by varying degrees of verbal abuse. To be fair to Stone S.C., with the number of Open Meeting, National Championships, etc., 'the abusers’ of language and/or rules need not necessarily be members of the Stone SC - merely visitors for the event. Fran a dinghy—racing viewpoint, the remedy would be to raise a protest for each incident but, apart from the difficulty of finding witnesses, it is unlikely that regular protests would be popular with our own Marconi hierarchy, let alone be viewed with much sympathy by Stone, and anyway, who wants to hang around in the evening whilst a joint Protest Committee is formed ? On the other side of the coin, I fancy there must be quite a few cruiser owners (and Stone dinghy-racing members) who have as great a jaundiced view of Marconi sailors behaviour as we might have of that of our neighbours. Not too long ago whilst on an air journey, I struck up a conversation with a very nice fellow traveller who turned out to be a keen dinghy-racing member of Stone. He was clearly unimpressed when I mentioned I belonged to Marconi (but envied us our 8 acres) and appeared genuinely surprized that we had a racing programme; he firmly thought weconsisted of 'potterers' and cruisers whose moorings had encroached upon Stone's traditional sailing waters. He was, however, very much aware of our catamaran fleet, particularly in the vicinity of Breezy and, I imagine,had much the same opinion of Marconi's ability to follow the rules as we have of Stone's. What is disappointing is the apparent 'knee—jerk' reaction of the Stone SC hierarchy in taking the stance of ‘not our members'; it is unrealistic to believe that the members never break, or ignore, the rules or that they never display bad manners or use abusive language to others who ‘get in their way’. I would hope that our own hierarchy, should they receive a similar complaint, would treat it with both courtesy and sympathy and assure the correspondent that, whilst only due to a very small minority, the Marconi Glub strongly disapproves of such behaviour and would always do its best to discourage it. Over the years I have often voiced my view that the Marconi SC should not seek to ‘develope’ along the same path as the Stone SC but should remain essentially a ‘casual sailors' club in which a minority (albeit, a significant minority) choose to arrange a racing programme for their own amusement and pleasure. ‘The danger I foresee as the club ceases to be the Marconi Works Club sailing section and becomes a 'regular' sailing club is that-it will be taken alor- the path of promoting an ever—increasing number of Open Meetings and National Championsitips on the basis of ‘improving' the quality of sailing and ‘earning revenue' to avoid the necessity of increasing the membership fees 'too mich’. With two such clubs in near proximity to each other on the Blackwater, I fancy it will be relative hell for the cruiserman as he tries to thread his and her way through the melee of racing dinghies trying to reach the next mark by the shortest possible route. In fact, we'd became just like any other club on any other crowded waterway. In times past (mid-1960s) there was probably rather more 'mingling' of the Stone SC and Marconi both amongst the sailors on the water and the Officers of each club. Since those days the two clubs have developed along different paths with (hopefully) quite different aims. However, perhaps it is time for our hierarchy and that of Stone to meet a little mre informally a little more often and, by virtue of personal contact, perhaps cane to appreciate each others problems (and aims in sailine-life) a little better. At one time, there was a degree of intermingling of the cadet fleets (members, not Cadet boats); that could be revived to some extent, perhaps by inviting the Stone SC to hold their cadet week at the same time as our own and at our site ? Qk , so there might well be good reasons for not doing so, but unless actual contact between the two neighbouring clubs is improved, the relationships on the water can only deteriorate. Or maybe there is no probelm? Maybe we (or at least some) are being too sensitive ? I think not. Mike Boreham

NAVIGANS PAST 12. 1974 (July - September) - the sad death of Terry Hallam, twice Commodore of the Marconi Sailing Club. July - Editor (Brenda Tate) reports that Open Day (22 June) was a great success with the Tate's Island 23' cruiser "Snowgoose" (amongst others) doing 'trips round the bay'. It being Mid-Summers Day, the Tate's apparently celebrated with cold christmas pudding and custard with additional 'Cordon Noir' provided by the Bonfire Chefs. A combined cruiser/dinghy fleet trip to Brightlingsea saw 3 dinghies make the voyage, ie. an Enterprise, a GP14 (Dave Polley) and our old friend Fred Partlett in his Mirror 16. NB. Whilst looking through the list of dinghies, I noticed Colin Harper had an Optimist at the club. Did he really race in the Optimist at Marconi ? Dennis Byatt (Commodore) reveals plans for the formal opening of the clubhouse witha "Filling Out Party’ in March, 1975. He also reminds everyone that if boatowners hit another boat (particularly the moored cruisers) then they should report the fact to the owner - or at least to Vic Tate (Moorings Sec). In addition, Dennis tells us that Minutes of Committee Meetings are put up in the clubhouse in order to keep members informed of the business of the club. What a good idea ! Sadly, the club's first 'official' Commodore, Terry Hallam, died suddenly on 1 July, 1974, at the relatively young age of 54. This series of Navigans Past has revealed to me many of the tensions, arguments and ‘battles behind the scenes' which went with the growth of the club and undoubtedly Terry Hallam was often in the thick of it. In his obituary to Terry, former Commodore Stan Allerton writes:- "Many spendid and sometimes infuriating episodes form the backcloth of my memories of Terry but at the front of stage stands the man so many of us admired and will continue to remember with much pleasure and a little sadness". Terry Hallam was, of course, Commodore on two separate occasions, both of which could justifiably be regarded as the two most crucial stages in the club's history. These were the founding of the club itself at Heybridge and the tremendously ambitious decision to move to the virgin Stansgate site. I understand that initially Terry was not in favour of the move but, once committed, worked hard to ensure its success. As Stan Allerton says of Terry “His experience and success will never be equalled in the club, for he led during the days of ‘do it yourself' when each member contributed to its work and growth, when unity and friendship were taken for granted". In 1993, the club is still essentially a 'do it yourself' club but the membership is a lot bigger and no longer has the cohesiveness of being almost entirely 'Marconi' and, of course, there is a greater diversity of sailing interests within the club. One wonders what Terry would make of it all now ? Finally, the Editor quotes John Witter (Vice Commodore) at the last Main Committee Meeting as saying "The question of an extra window in the Ladies Changing Room will also be looked into" (presumably via the existing window?). August - it was Marconi's turn to run the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships at Stone ('our turn' apparently came around approx. every 13 years which was undoubtedly "unlucky for some'). The B&CDC class winners then competed for a "Cock of the River" trophy which was held at Marconi and was won by a Stone S.C. Unicorn single-handed catamaran. Another (underlined) reminder that all collisions should be reported. I suspect that "behind the scenes' someone was getting somewhat annoyed with the cavalier manner in which some people managed to 'bang' into other people boats - and then literally and colloquially 'push off' and say nowt. Now, where have I heard that one before ???

13. September - Brenda reports that Force 10 winds were recorded at Stansgate with _"Stansgate narrowSs...... just a boiling cauldron of foam." The Commodore reports that no significantly new information is available on the possible new Marina Project at Ramsey Wick for which outline planning permission had been granted way back in the early or mid-1960s - and to which, I believe, the MSC could not raise any objections by virtue of clauses in the purchase agreement for the Stansgate site. Amongst the sailing results are:- Marconi CHallenge Cup lst F Apthorpe Osea SC (420) 2nd S Kenworthy Stone SC (Mirror) 3rd Vic Braybrooke Marconi SC (Mirror) Mirrors also featured well in the mid-week races (straight handicap) where, in 11 races, they supplied three lsts, seven 2nds and six 3rds. John Weedon reveals that, with two 420s already racing, several people have shown interest in forming the nucleus of a new racing class in the club, ie. the 420. Finally, poor John Witter will soon be afraid to say anything at any meeting, for our ever-watchfull Editor quotes “John Witter had had a complaint about the beer. He eays he is going to try some and bring it up at the next Committee Meeting." It can't true - can it ????? Mike Boreham SEARO EK 40 Years Ago - October—December, 1953. For those of you who may have read my enquiry published in last October's issue of Practical Boat Owner regarding the removal and whereabouts of the Wie guns emplaced on the Tongue Sand Tower, the following may be of interest to you. Although a reply has not been published by PBO I did in fact receive several interesting responses, the most informative being the one below. Should you wish to see the articles referred to in this response, please contact me - Malcolm Yeoman, [redacted]. "A/A GUN, THAMES ESTUARY FORTS. I read with interest your letter in Practical Boat Owner concerning the above. Both the two guns which were on the Tounge Towers, and the two which were on the Knock John Towers were removed last year. Of the four guns, three are now in Orkney at the Scapa Flow Visitor Centre, and the remaining one is at Coldharbour, Gravesend, in the care of the Kent Defence Research Group. By way of explanation as to how this came about: I am a native of Herne Bay but have lived in Orkney for the past fifteen years. Part of my job with the local authority contd....

3. was to create a visitor centre/museum on the site of the old naval base at Lyness, Scapa Flow. I had been looking for heavy A/A Guns for the museum and recalled that there used to be some on the forts. I made enquiries with the Air Vice Marshall’s Office in Pitreavie whe arranged for a helicopter to go from Manston to check if they were still there. The next step involved me going to Manston where the Air Vice Marshall kindly placed a Sea-king and crew at my disposal. I was taken out tc the Tounge and Kriock Johri Towers to look at the guns. I then made arrangements with the Ministry of Defence to release the guns to Orkney Islands Council. The Biggest hurdle was yet to come. I obtained the assistance of REME at Colchester but had to wait (because of the Gulf War) for the use of a Chinook helicopter from 7 Squadron. The project finally came together last June when I flew ta London and sperit a very interesting day with the RAF at Manston. A Sea-king took a party, including myself, out to the forts. Technicians from the REME and Joint Air Transport Command cut the guns free and they were airlifted to Manston by a Chinook from 7 Squadron RAF Odiham. I hope this answers your questions. Please find enclosed complimentary guide bocks and copies of photographs taken at the time of the recovery. Yours faithfully, R.D. Hughes, Special Projects Manager. " BROUGHT UNDER TOW BY KELLY’S EYE - an account of the incident which brought about the taking into tow the vessel Varuna II by Kelly’s Eye during the summer of 1992, for which Pete Sayer was awarded MSCs Seamanship Trophy. Or, August Bth 1992 Margaret and I, sailing Varuna II in company with Pete Sayer on Kelly’s Eye, set aut from MSC to commence a two-week holiday bound for Zeeland via Belgium. Our outward ports and places of call were Bradwell, Nieuwpoort, Ostend, Breskens, Middelberg, Veere and finally Zierikzee, arriving on Friday @2ist August. After a two-day stay at Zierikzee we commenced our return passage which included stops at the Delta Marina, Middelberg and Vlissingen. All the passages sca far had been without incidents. We departed Vlissingen on Wednesday 26th August at 1430 hrs. In the ship’s log we recorded that at 1600 hrs we had a large reef in the main, no headsail, and under engine. The sea was very lumpy and arrival at Blankenberge could not come = soar enough. At 1700 hrs disaster struck when the engine started tc lose power and we could smell diesel fumes. Thoughts of limping along and sorting out the problem at Blankenberge were shortly ruled out when the engine finally stopped. Our position was about half a mile east of Zeebrugge harbour mole where at this particular time numerous vessels were frequently entering and leaving the harbour’ entrance. We considered a number of options to overcome the problem, these being: a) To take long tacks out to seaward, but with little favourable tide remaining, and the prospect of entering the marina under sail, this option did not appeal tec us. b) Anchering in shallower water was ruled cut because it would be on a lee shore. c) To turn about and go back to Breskens, be it with a more favourable wind was an option we did not want to take since our destination, Blankenberge, was just 5 miles away. We decided to radio Pete on Kelly’s Eye whe by row was about to cross the buoyed channel to Zeebrugge harbour. Having discussed our options with him, he offered to assist us by taking Varuna II in tow so the engine problem ccauld be investigated and possibly repaired. The job Pete had of getting Varuna II under tow was no mean task. He was single- handed and we were close to a busy harbour entrance where a strong tide was running. He had to organise locating a suiteble tow line (I had not got one of sufficient length on board) and then control his vessel at close quarters to enable a tow line to be thrown to us. All these tasks were carried out calmly and expertly with an excellent throw of the line which was secured to Varuna II. CONntGs-6

4. Under tow, with the large swell persisting, our vessels’ positicns relative ta each other were, to say the least, quite nerve-racking at times. However, with some skilful steering by Pete and Margaret, we avoided collision. The outcome of it all was that the engine problem was due to a leak on the injector fuel feed pipe, and fortunately we had a spare pipe on board. The repair was carried out and within 20 minutes of coming under tow the engine was running again. Fete ther released the tow line which was recovered on tc Varuna II and we were theri able to continue our passage safely, arriving at Blankenberge at 1915 hrs. Thank you, Fete! Malcalm Yeoman. Good inventory. £10,950. Contact Tim Lowe, [redacted] HANDICAPS Many Dinghy and Catamaran races are handicapped using the publisned Foartsmouth Yardstick Numbers. These numbers are purported to be an average performance figure obtained from club returns. Presumably this means that the average boat in a class, Sailed by the average crew in average weather conditions will be equally handicapped compared to any other boat sailed in the same circumstances. Let us consider that last variable - weather Conditions, this being wind strength and tidal flow. At low wind speeds the relative performance will depend upon waterline length and the hull’s wetted area. but as the wind picks up, then all-up weight = and underwater shape will determine the point when the boat starts ta plane. A boat on the plane has a substantial speed advantage over one travelling at displacement speed. Eventually as the wind speed increases further then the average sailor will lese control. As the threshold at which both the above occur is at different wind strengths with each class of boat, then the average potential handicap cannot be a constant factor across the wind range. Wher, it comes to tide, however, it is possible to give an illustration of a_ typical Situation, simplified for convenience. A race consisting of a circuit rounding two marks one mile apart with a one mile an hour tide flowing along the line of the course. Yacht °’S’ with a handicap of 150 sails at @mph. Yacht °F’ with a handicap of 75 should therefore sail at 4mph under average conditions. Yacht ’S’ will travel at 2 + 1 mph over the ground with the tide, and at 2 - 1 = mph against the tide. 1 1 This gives a lap time of = + 1 + 2 2 2535 Ars. Yacht ’F* will travel at 4 + 1 mph with the tide, and 4 - 1 mph against the tide. i 1 Giving a lap time of 4+1 + 4-1 = QO.53 hrs. In still water however, yacht °S’ would have taken exactly twice the time of Yacht ‘FF’ to finish level on handicap. In the example above Yacht 'S’ exceeded this time by 25%! Why do we use the present handicap system, ther? I suspect it is because there is nothing else that could be easily applied which is better. There may be a set of circumstances that allows your class of boat to be favoured at some time, especially if it is a fast handicap class in tidal conditions (i.e. Stansgate). J.F. WEEDON

NAVIGANS PAST 7. 1974 (October - December) - unwanted visitors, unwanted marinas, unwanted gas holders, and nobody wants to be Hon.Treasurer. — And who'd want poor Dawn ?~ She's built like a hay-stack and smells like a muck-cart, but I'm sure somebodymust love her. October - the clubhouse is obviously in ‘unofficial’ use since it is reported that the Helmsman of the Year was sailed in fairly disagreeable conditions but ".....many enjoyed the splendid view from the window of the new clubhouse." Dennis Byatt reveals he will be unable to take on a 3rd year as Commodore but tells us that John Witter is willing to take over for at least one year. Dennis also advises there are several vacancies on the Committee. Standing for Vice Commodore is Ron Greygoose with Vic Tate (Rear Commodore), John Weedon (Sailing Sec), Eric Royle (Hon.Sec) and David Harper (Clubhouse Sec) - but the post of Hon. Treasurer remains vacant ! A sad note records the tragic death of Heather White. November - the ‘cover plate' is entitled "Hello Sailor" and apparently shows two Viking invaders patiently sitting upon what looks suspiciously like an ‘outside loo' (or maybe "Viking Thrones') - but turns out to be the local groins. The 'Vikings' also turn out to be Siegfried (Stan) Campbell and Viking (Vic) Tate. Roger Hance appears to have won the Enterprise Nimbus Trophy with Julian Bigden 5th and Mike Taylor 8th out of 34 qualifying helmsmen. The Cruiser Section meeting held at The Generals Arms apparently had a lively discussion on whether the £1 per evening room—hire fee should come from club funds ! They concluded that all those attending should contribute 10p each towards the cost of room- hire and any money left over should go towards buying equipment, etc. Ah! Well ! Last of the big spenders I guess. A note reminds members to leave their over-—wintering dinghies with mast down and cover secured. A Resolution for the AGM reads:- "Members shall not display gross forms of advertising on or about boats registered with the club, except where such advertising is specifically allowed within class rules and at the Sailing Committee's discretion". It was proposed by Bruce Long and seconded by John Weedon. December - the new Commodore, John Witter, tells us that the new clubhouse was actually "handed—over' to the MASC on 27 November, 1974. As new Commodore, he promises to try and continue the policy of keeping members as much informed on club affairs as possible. John reveals a problem of security at Stansgate with at least 5 rubber dinghies stolen during the season and which were thought to have ‘left by road', plus some unwanted mid-week use of the the site by 'visitors' on picnics, whilst others looked for whatever they could find. Then, of course, there were the Essex residents who insisted on their perceived ‘right’ to "..... play in our garden." The Main Committee's thoughts are therefore turning towards the provision of a magnetic lock/key system for both site and clubhouse. John warns, however, that it will be expensive and only justified if members act responsibly and always close/lock both clubhouse and site gate after them. He points out that about 200 official keys for the old club are still in circulation and he sees the new magnetic key system as "....a radical departure from our previous rather lax methods of giving access....." At the AGM, the retiring Commodore (Dennis Byatt) hopes members will express their views freely, because the Committee is very anxious to take note of members' interests. He reminds us that at the last AGM he had the disappointment of advising that formal

&. planning permission for the clubhouse had not yet been received. Now he could report the clubhouse complete and formally handed over. He also noted the fantastic rise in building costs over the last two years and is releaved that the decision to build the new clubhouse had not been delayed so that they were starting afresh now. Dennis notes that the Calor gas cylinder has received (adverse) comment and agrees it is an eyesore but hopes to camouflage it in due course with fencing and shrubs (but not too successfully as it turned out and our modern-day sheep-pen still awaits its thatched roof !). On the sailing side, Regatta attracted 250 boats whilst the 1974 Blackwater & Colne Dinghy Championships were ‘inherited with a deficit' and handed over to Dadchicks SC (for 1975) with a credit balance. A major item of concern is the proposals for a new marina at Ramsey Wick, particularly regarding sea access and its influence on (club) moorings. Dennis reminds us that as part of the purchase agreement for the Stansgate site, the club agreed not to object to planning permission for the marina. Amongst the 'thank you's' are Frank Savill (Treasurer), Pete Foreman (Social Sec), Brenda Tate (Editor), Margaret Cottam (Galley) and Claude Emerson (paid part-time clubhouse steward). Eric Royle (Hon.Sec) reports membership numbers as follows (1973 numbers in brackets) :- Orinary Members 244 (241) Associate Members 103 (90) Family Members 30 (27) Total Members 377 (358) The Cruiser Section news reported on a talk by Gordon Swift (owner and skipper of the stackie barge "Dawn") as follows:- "Gordon brought along a photograph of Dawn coverted to a sailing hay-stack and described the trip to London; the need to dig a trench through the stack in order to lower the mast; the return journey loaded with manure; and back to London again with flour. No wonder our bread no longer has character." I guess he could be right ! Mike Boreham sok RII 40 Years Ago — January, 19%. A Committee Meeting reports progress on a ‘loan scheme’ from the MASC to individual members of the sailing section (presumably ‘Marconi members’ only) to help them purchase Fleetwind dinghies, presumably in kit form. A sub-committee (Messrs Wardell, Nicholls and Greatrex) was formed to draw up a Set of Rules for submission to the AGM of the Sailing Section in February. I think there mist have been a ‘group insurance scheme' for the Sailing Section, for a letter fram Eric Payne to the insurers was copied to the Sailing Section. Eric's letter reports that his yacht Electra IT (formerly Rainbow) had been driven over on its side whilst laid up at Hedgecock's Yard at Maldon. Although there was no visisble damage to the superstructure or in the cabin, he suspected possible damage to the hull since the heel appeared to have broken off. He hoped it would be floated onto the hard at the next Spring Tide for closer inspection. Eric had written of the club's copy of the letter "...... it may be the first claim since the scheme was inauguratred." Mike Boreham

MARCONI SAILING CLUB Page’4 MEMBERSHIP APPLICATION GUIDE (24.) All MSC members must be members of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club (MASC) and must have a current MASC Membership card and number in order to open or renew their MSC membership. New member applications lacking a valid MASC number must be accompanied by the completed MASC application form. All other applications without a valid MASC number will be returned. All members must pay the MASC fee directly to the MASC. Every candidate for membership must be proposed and seconded for election by a Full or Family member of the Club, both of whom must be personally acquainted with the candidate (Rule 11). Classes of Membership (Rule 6) 2.1. Full Being a person who at the date of election or renewal is over the age of eighteen 2.2. Family Being a married couple or one or two parents and all their children who are under eighteen years of age. 2.3. Junior Being a person who at the date of election or renewal is under the age of eighteen Vat Fees include VAT at the applicable rate. Boat Permit Fee All craft incur a Boat permit Fee. The first boat of a member is always deemed to be the craft incurring the highest Fee. Subsequent craft under 10ft (tenders) are free of charge Winter Storage Storage fees are payable in advance at these rates on boats, trailers and cradles to be kept at Stansgate during all or part of the period 30 November to Ist March following the renewal date. Cruiser owners must ensure in advance that space is available for their boats. Applications Renewals and applications should be returned to :- Liz Hill, The Membership Secretary, The Hawthorns, [redacted], Mayland Essex [redacted] Phone 0621 [redacted] The MASC fee, as advised will be invoiced to you separately and is payable directly to MASC New Members New members joining after Ist July shall be entitled to a discount of one half the Subscription Fee only. After Ist November no fees other than Winter Storage shall be payable until Ist January following. Retirement Any Member in any category of membership over the state retirement age shall pay one half the full fees for Full or Family Membership as appropriate (Rule 7) Late Renewal Renewal fees are due on Ist January and are payable by the last day in February. Renewals received after this date incur the Penalty Fee (Rule 8e). Persons wishing to resign their membership at renewal must indicate so on the form and return it together with all MSC keys and property to the Membership Secretary

A Different View from the Rear............. I am sure that those of you who experienced the Laying Up Supper will agree with me that it was an excellent evening. The food, entertainment and company were first class and I am sure there will be a rush for tickets for next year’s event once the word gets around. Many thanks to all those who helped to make the evening a great success and especially to Steve and Debbie Glynn. The fruits of the year's sailing were presented to a large number of people on Sunday 14 th November by our President's wife, Mary Greygoose. I was pleased to see a number of different people receiving prizes for the first time. A complete list appears elsewhere in this issue. Those of you who could not be at the prize giving will have to get in touch with me and arrange to collect your trophies. My congratulations to all prize winners in 1993. Willie Pitcairn has decided to step down as sailing secretary due to pressure of work. I am sure you will all join me in thanking Willie for all his hard work in making this year's sailing programme work extremely efficiently. Tom Duckmanton takes over, he has a hard act to follow! The work for next year’s events has already started and the sailing programme has been drawn up and agreed by the sailing sub committee. The main changes are as follows: First race coincides with BST. Mid week series starts mid May. Pilots Cup replaces Rum Tub and Bung. Handicap team race against Osea Sailing Club. The Codes of practice for the activities of different sections of the club will be reviewed in the coming months to ensure that our activities are as safe as possible. Sailing instructions for racing are also being reviewed and modifications will be made. Rostas for Race Officer and Support boat crews are also being drawn up. If you know that you will not be joining the club next year and you took part in this year's race programme, it would be very helpful if you would phone and let me know. Is there any one out here who would like to become a race officer? Perhaps you have given up sailing and have some time on your hands on a Sunday! It would be a great help if you could lend your support to this aspect of the club's activities. Give me a ring if you can help. I have heard that some people may be reluctant to start racing because they find the thought of being rostered for race officer or support boat driver duties too off putting! If you start racing then you will only graduate to these exalted positions after you receive adequate training. If you don't race but would like to become involved in either of these activities then please contact me as soon as possible. In the recent stormy weather a number of boats were not adequtely secured because they were blown about. Please check your ground anchors and the rope used to tie the boat to it's ground anchor. Why not spend a few pounds ona length of high quality rope to secure several thousand pounds worth of boat securely! There are still a large number of boats and trailers in the cat park which are not clearly identified with the owners name and telephone number. It makes the job of the fleet captain a lot easier if boats can be easily identified. Vacant pitches should also be identified otherwise they are likely to be reallocated next year. Colin Kidner.

e. COMMODORE’S NOTES Hope you all had an excellent festive season, and I am in the fortunate position of having a little more time to pen (or should I say word-process) some deathless prose. Firstly, I should like to welcome all the newcomers to the Main Committee. We didn’t get the right number of nominations for the AGM, but a number of volunteers have come forward to be co-opted. Thanks to Tom Duckmanton, Peter Flook, Derek Kirby and lan Carruth. The wettest year for a decade has put the NRA into (literally) the thick and slimy. Hopefully they should recover time and enable us to launch at the beginning of the season. We are most definitely on their case. We have had a_ large number of instances of the Clubhouse being left open. Ir discussion, we have decided to remove the hold-back bolt from the door and to fit a Closer to it. The upshot of this will be that the Clubhouse doors will be permanently closed outside the normal season or special events (Moorings, Working Parties etc.) Let’s see if this works!!!! Keep on taking the tablets, Larry Botheras CRUISER COMMENTS 42 Members, representing 25 Cruisers, attended the Cruiser AGM on 15th December. The Meeting opened with a review of events held in 1993 which included: a) Fitting Out Supper at Stansgate held on Saturday 24th April 1993. b) Assistance to the East Coast Piers Race in aid of the Seamanship Foundation. c) Club Cruise to Walton Backwaters & supper at Walton & Frinton Yacht Club. d) Cruiser End-of-Season Supper at Stansgate on Saturday 25th September. e) A good attendance at the MSC Laying Up Supper held at Three Rivers Golf Club. Launching & Hauling Out: As there is a limit to the number of Cruisers that can be dealt with in one day, it was agreed as a trial that a ’Notice of Intent’ Board be placed in the foyer for the Cruiser Owner to notify date of intention to launch/haul out his Cruiser. This will enable each Tractor Driver to know in advance how mary Cruisers will want to haul out on his particular day - and a phone call to the Tractor Driver in addition to a booking on the Board will ensure that one particular day is not over-booked. The Board would also be useful for booking the Scrubbing Post. Please contact Derek Kirby for more information. Trailers: Attention was drawn to the poor condition of some trailers and Members were urged to ensure these are properly maintained, especially after immersion in the water at launching or recovery. A broken-down trailer can seriously jeopardise the completion of the whole day’s operation not only of the boat concerned, but of all the others being handled on the same day. Security: The question of security was again stressed. Remove as much gear as possible from the boat; ensure ladders are locked up; Clubhouse and Gate are locked. Always assume you are the last person to leave the site. Sea Wall; NRA are now working on the Clubhouse area, and access through the sea wall will be closed end December to approximately end February. (Ed’s note: Delay to this timetable is likely due to wet conditions which has brought work to a halt for a time). Election of Cruiser Fleet Captain: There were no nominations for this, so yours truly agreed to carry on - no one seemed to object to this. Paint Orders; Malcolm Shaft has again agreed to take this on, for which we thank him. Details will have been published in last month’s edition of Navigans. Club Sweatshirts & T Shirts: Murray and Ann Bates are taking orders for Club wear and brought along samples to the meeting for members to see. Ordering was brisk, sea get your orders in. (Ed’s note: They were very nice sweatshirts and more details later, hopefully). Chain & Shackles: Dave Thomas will be taking orders for Chain and Shackles again, watch out for details in Navigans. The use of anodes on moorings has proved successful, details of availability will be given later. contd. .c«

Over £6,000 was raised by the event for the Lifeboat Service .
