THE LIFEBOAT FLEET In 1986 the RNLI- announced a 7-year plan to complete the modernisation of the Lifeboat Fleet, with a fast Lifeboat at all 210 Lifeboat Stations. On 30th November 1993 the last of the ‘traditional’ displacement lifeboats was replaced at Aldeburgh, thereby fulfilling the RNLI plan. However, Lifeboat replacement is a continucus process as some of the older fast Lifeboats are nearing the end of their lives and new classes of boats are being introduced. Ray Ball

Handicap Fleet Many of you, no doubt, have decided that this is the year you will find more time te sail your dinghy. Furthermore, you have resolved to come down and join in the Sunday races and extend the fun you get from sailing. If you’ve not raced before then read on for arn easy lessor. One fellow sailor has said he might have entered the races if he’d known what he had to do and what the flags meant. Well I’ve beer racing for twc seasons and have managed without knowing too much about all the detaiis. I?ll try te give a basic summary. First, the races on Sunday usually start with the Fast Cats at 11.00am and ©&.00pm. In the hour before, you should find the course and start-time for each race written up on the blackboard outside the portakabin in the Cat Field. The course will tell you which marks to go around and whether to leave them to port or starboard. Having decided to sail, go inside the portakabin and sign on for the race, i.e. find the form for the Handicap Fleet and enter the name of your helm and, if you have one, of your crew, then your class of boat, sail number and finally, if you know it, the handicap number for your boat. Be or the water and on the right side of the starting line in time for your start. The order of sailing is; a) Fast Cats, b) Medium Cats, c) Slow Cats, d) Handicaps and Mirrors, and finally d) Solos. The starts should all occur at 5S minute intervals. A gun (hooter), if you can hear it, should be fired at each start and for the Fast Cats there will also be a 10-minute and S-minute warning before their start time. There are also flags at the Race Box, if you can see them, which go up and down. Watch out for the ‘3’ flag (this is not square, not triangular, but tapered and coloured red at the wide end, blue at the narrow end, and white in the middle) because this goes up 10 minutes before your start and goes down at the start. The Handicap fleet and the Solos start inside the D buoy, whereas the Cats start outside it, so you have the best chance of hearing the gun and seeing the flags. If you are not sure of the racing rules, which none of us are, then you’d do best to keep a little clear of the other boats at the start to begin with, although there aren’t usually that many other starters to worry about anyway. If you sail the right course and stay upright then you stand a good chance of winning. As you cross the finishing line the gun will be fired; this might be dont a lap or two early if the race is taking too long. Note the start line is the continuation of the line from the line from the triangle on the race box to the ‘mete’ (a pole in the water), whereas the finishing line is from the triangle on the race box to the D buoy; the difference between the two lines is not a lot. Finally, don’t forget that when you’ve finished you must sign off in the portakabin; this is done on another form for the Handicap Fleet where you enter whatever it asks for - similar to the signing on forn. It’s all very simple, isn’t it? For more details look at your copy of the MSC Sailing Instructions. Oh, one other thing - it helps if you’ve got a watch but, even if you haven’t, you can always ask your fellow sailors on the water how long it is to your start. Handicap Fleet party. NAVIGANS PAST 6. 1975 (January - June) - Marconi's Mirror—batchelors go sail-about round the Isle of Wight with many a tale of daring-do and a pint or two (or three or four). ‘Nuff said !!! - Maureen and Ray have a mighty row in the middle of the night. We know 'cos it was reported in Navigans. January - on the front cover is a photograph of the new clubhouse, whilst inside are four photos showing the progress of the building of the clubhouse during 1974. Of particular interest are the photos showing the old clubhouse, whilst one shows both old and new clubhouse together. It appears from the Editorial that same "uninvited gifts” from the German airforce during World War I have been lurking in the muddy depths around Northey, Osea and Thirslet Spit. As the Editor says "The Mud Race seems to take on a new meaning." Perhaps that is why, in some of the years since 1974 "the traditional mud race' adopted a marked reluctance to go anywhere near the mud. More on the clubhouse fram the new Commodore, John Witter. He thanks the MASC for the investment, the Committee of the MASC for accepting the proposal to build, Ron Rider and colleagues of the (Marconi) Building & Facilities Group, Mike Taylor and team for the actual construction - and the members of the MSC who gave many hours to basic planning and final design. Further notes fron John on the public right-of-way through the site - and a note that The Daily Telegraph (6 December, 1974) had featured an article entitled "Wedgies wailing wall stops riverside stroll." Now that brings back same memories !!! Alf Cottam suggested that Mamgu's ship's wheel be mounted on the wall "...in the passage directly opposite to the main entrance doors, with suitably enscribed plaque." Is the wheel still in the clubhouse? I expect it is but we're so used to it ‘being there’ that we don't notice it or appreciate A note records the death of Fred Taylor, the Maldon sailmaker, whose sail loft had consequently been taken over by McG JH Dennis. ‘The note (by Eric Payne) records that Fred never used a measure but judged a fathom of line by the span of his arm(s) and was "...only a little bit out even when long lengths were involved." February - The Main Committee decided that a club log-book should be kept all year around. It was also decided that the memorial to Terry Hallam should take the form of a light on the new clubhouse and which would serve as a navigation aid to all river users. I believe it is shown on charts as ‘THe Hallam Light’. On the social side, Sam Poulton of Maldon gave a talk on spritsail barges and on the characters who sailed them, both past and present. § Sam, it seems, had bought a spritsail barge for £50 (presumably "years ago') but high maintenance costs caused him to have it broken up even though the current price of such a barge was nearer £6,000. A second speaker, John Jowers, spoke about the Fisherman of the Essex coast. Drifters used ‘shoot nets’ up to a mile in length and were known to drift up the Blackwater with the tide when fishing. A pair of Drifters working together could cause the ‘amateur sailor' some considerable problems if he came upon them and "...got caught between them........and the chances of loosing mast, boat and finishing up on a slab at Billingsgate wasn't right out of the question it seams. Rick Anstey (Cadet Skipper) hopes to initiate a busy cadet programme for 1975 with tuition, training, practice and competition in the Points Series races. He also wants the cadets to take part in the Race Box duties and rescue boat duties. March — An account by Bruce Long of his participation (as part of the British Team) in the 18' Scdiff World Championships (ie. the Sydney Harbour 18' Footers). The Cruiser Mooring List records 73 cruisers allocated mooring for 1975. April - Brenda Tate's Editorial states "That old saying that a man who goes sailing for pleasure will go to hell for a pastime can certainly be applied to some club members who braved the elements and were sailing in a snowstorm on Easter Sunday."

7. Amongst the 'gossip' items are the announcements of the birth of Victoria Lucy Bigden (Gill and Julian Bigden) and (wait for it) the birth of Stuart Golding weighing in at 7 lbs. 11 ozs. with masses of black May - It seems that the club's Sailing Instruction No.5 (obliga an anchor for dinghies) carrying of tory has been subject to much debate - but the mule was retained on the grounds of safety. Rick Anstey's first Cadet meeting at MASC appeared to have got off to a good start. last year's las, Regatta gave same cause for concern. In his plans for the 1975 Regatta, Ron Greygoose warns "Last year same of our visitors 'camped' in the farm building and cigarette ends, matches, etc., were found in the barn. We must stop this happening again." We get the first installment of a literary classic describing the "Mirrormen Bachelor Thrash" around the Isle of Wight. Participants were Rick Anstey, Bill Baker, Roy Battye, Vic Braybrook, Dave Harper, Vic Tate and Keith Taylor. The arrangements had apparently been made in the dying embers (ie. the wee small hours of the next morning) of the Laying Up Supper. 0h! I see; it was one of those ‘good ideas’ that, in retrospect (and the clear cold light of the morning) no-one could think of a way of ‘getting out of it’ ! The ‘planning meeting’ in January pondered much over why on earth they were going, what could they conceivably do when they got there - and what colour of bow ties would be needed ? ‘The car journey down to the I.o.W. sounds suspiciously like a pub crawl whilst advertures on the hired cruiser included a ‘near miss' (reputedly 5' 3") with the Yammouth/I.o.W. Ferry, and demands in the local 'topless bar' for milk, thus leaving nothing too much to the imagination that the ‘quiet sailing weekend' definitely took a turn for the worse (or the better, depending upon whether you were there or not). Ah! We don't have a Mirror Class like that any mre - which is probably just as ! well June - the old, old problem re-appears; Editor, Brenda Tate, reports a hole in the bows of 'Snowgoose' just above the water line. It is believed it was probably caused during Regatta but nobody reported it. Not surprisingly, she again reminds everyone of the need to report collisions to the OOD (or, failing that, in the club Log Book) and that an effort should be made to contact the owner. John Witter (Commodore) reveals the official opening of the new clubhouse was performed by the club President, Sir Eric Eastwood, with the occasion marked by the presence of the Commodores of other Blackwater clubs, representatives of the Marconi Company, the MASC, neighbours of the club and other guests. Ron Rider and Mike Taylor each received a commemorative plaque. [Eric Payne (Vice President and former Commodore) completed the formalities by recalling some of the many amusing incidents from the club's early history. Regatta was very successful with just over 200 entries, of which 41 were from Marconi. Pat Black (GP14) was 14th out of 35; C King (Int. Moth) 14th from 16; John Weedon (Mirror) 2nd from 32; Mike Williams (Hornet) 1st from 8; Roger Hance (Enterprise) lst from 40; Mike Taylor (Fast Handicap) lst fram 14 and P Drury (Slow Handicap) 1st from 12. A note about an anchor lost (and found, but only temporarily) from a cruiser mentions it was put into "Pete's Palace". Pete's Palace was, I understand, a very large (possible several large) ex-Marconi packing case(s) which Pete (Lawson ?) had converted very ably and neatly into club storage sheds and which stood behind the old wooden clubhouse. The note doesn't say whether the anchor was ever found. In the club's Points Series, it seems the Mirror Fleet was the busiest with 12 races sailed at an average of 10.9 entries per race and a total entry in the Series of 19 helms. Same words of praise and appreciation for Ray and Maureen Ball who were staying aboard the cruiser "Coppelia'. I quote "They were awoken at 4 a.m. on a wild night to find that Mike Sisson's "Duet" had broken her mooring and was trying to make friends with the end of the groyne. As Coppelia was not afloat (she was to be launched next morning) they dressed, got in their dinghy and amidst rain and thunder rowed out towing Duet and put her back on her mooring. A very comendable effort." Mike Boreham

BOAT SIGHTS AND SOUNDS At right the natural silence experienced at a sheltered creek anchorage feels like the mud and marsh are helping the night tc suppress the light and sound of day. The clarity of the might sky encourages me to seek the end of that vast heavenly spectrum. Looking up at the constellations and catching the odd meteorite trail that burns earthward towards the end of its lonely journey, the mind struggles tc grasp the infinite spread above. Ofter we stargaze while at a dark, silent anchorage arid enjoy the feeling of the mind stretching to accept the vastness caf this contemplation. Wher. one first takes over a yacht, there is a whole range of new sounds that the skipper should become familiar with as they talk of the craft’s health and fouridation. The quest to locate and silence all unnecessary sounds from the craft 1 have owned is a vocation that lasts forever, as conditions and time extract their price from her structures. Sometimes they provide you with arn early warning of chafe and fray, of locsening arid seizure, and at others, they toy with your dozy senses whilst the yacht gently moves and tugs at her anchor. The noises of wind tell of the need to reef, the change in sound of the craft's passage through the water tell of speed maintained or increased. This array of sounds awaits the attentions of a good skipper who, via his excellent human sensory array and his awareness ard perception, will achieve oneness with the sea arid his craft. DINGHY PARK With Easter upon us it is time to think of opening the dinghy park for the new season. The layout for this year will be identical to last year when at the peak of the summer 166 boats were stored in the park. These were made up of: Mirror 32 Solo 17 Wayfarer 11 Enterprise 9 420 8 GP14 7 Laser2 6 Laser 6 Topper 4 Wanderer 4 Club 4 Others 60 Of the "Others", no class was represented by more than 5 boats and most were ones or twos. This year the plan is for a total of about 170 boats. The most effective boat parking is to keep boats of the same or similar classes placed together and facing the same way. As last there will be dedicated blocks in the park for the following: Solo(20), Mirrors (45), 420/GP14/Enterprise/Wanderer (28), Large h/c >15ft (22 Laser/Topper(15), Laser 2/Hornet/Fireball(18), other h/c(16), Club (4). The park is a no go area for cars so if you need to use a vehicle to launch your boat because of its size, please make sure that you occupy a space facing the road at the east side. Otherwise, please, no cars in the park. The park will be available for occupation after the pre-season working party in March. Boats can be placed in any empty space in the correct block, but it is logical and efficient that spaces are taken from the club house end first. Spaces will be pegged out as a guide however boats should be placed with a maximum gap of 2ft hull to hull. If you want to site your boat on a road trailer in the dinghy park, don't expect extra space. Road trailers belong in the area beyond the cat.park and should be marked. Anchors are in short supply. If you took some home last year please bring them back. Check list Dinghies can go in any vacant plot according to size/fleet area. Ground anchors are a must. See the dinghy code of practice. Mark your equipment boat/cover/trolley/trailer. No road trailers in the park. Put the hard fee stickcrs where they can be seen. Indicate your boat's position on the chart in the clubhouse. Ring me if you have any problems. My biggest frustration is the (presumed non) member who is apparently too shy to identify with his/her boat in the dinghy park. I can only conclude that the owner has something to hide, like non payment of hard fees, so please please make my life a little easier and MARK YOUR BOAT WITH YOUR NAME Dave Fletcher, Dinghy Park Secretary [redacted]

NAVIGANS PAST ii. 1975 (July - December) - did the MSC receive a (royal) visit froma prince or princess of whales -. 99 July - Marconi's Mirror Fleet again features well, this time at the Blackwater & Colne Dinghy Championships where John Weedon (1st), Ray Hampson (2nd) and Roy Battye (3rd) filled the first three places out of 15 entries in the Mirror Class. Of the 15 entries, 9 were fram Marconi. A total of 25 Cadet Members turned up for Rick Anstey's Cadet Training on Saturday, 14 June, and there were 7 entries in the 2nd Cadet Race on 13 July and which was won by Stephen Perkins. August - the height of the holiday season saw 7 of the Cruiser Fleet go exploring the Fast Coast whilst another 7 'went foreign’ to Holland. The Editor notes that John Weedon has bought a 420 (named Blackbird) and thus the club now has five 420 dinghies and several Mirror Fleet members are thinking of changing to the 420. The Commodore's Notes record the visit of a whale (yes — a WHALE) to the Blackwater. It is assumed he (or she) wanted to have a close look at our nice new clubhouse - but it was reported that no application for membership was received from the visitor. Also reported is the news that past-Commodore Stan Allerton has been elected Chairman of BACSPA (Blackwater & Colne Sailing Protection Association) whilst Frank Saville has been elected Secretary/Treasurer. September - the Commodore's Notes record the ‘retirement’ at the end of the season of Margaret Cottam after many years of rumning the galley. John Witter thanks Margaret for her many years of service and support to the club - and the hunt is on for a replacement. Mid-week sailing results records 11 races, of which five were won by Mirrors, two by 420s, two by Solos and one each by a 505 and a Graduate. Winner of the Ladies Race was ‘Spike’ Burston, with Kim Braybrook 2nd and Pat Stuart 3rd. The Cadet Series was campleted with 7 races held and an average of 9.6 entries per race. A total of 23 different Cadet Member helms took part and 18 Cadets were listed amongst the crew list. The Series result was lst Robert Tate, 2nd Chris Weedon, 3rd Stephen Perkins, 4th Robert Weedon and 5th Colin Harper. October - John Witter's Commodore's Notes reveal that "....we have now reached agreement with the MASC on long term financial arrangements which will give the MSC a licence to manage the Stansgate site for a period of 6 years from January, 1976, at an annual contribution to the MASC of £2,000 plus annual rates". Membership Subscription proposals for 1976 are:- Ordinary Members (ie Marconi employees) £5.00 Associate Members £ 8.50 Cadet Members (16-17 if not covered by above) £ 1.00 Hard Fees: Ist Boat £10.00 2nd Boat £ 3.00 Tony Drury (Handicap Fleet Captain) provided a write-up of the Graduate National Championships held at Saundersfoot. Pity the poor Race Officer in the 2nd race; apparently successive wind changes caused some 100+ boats to cross the finish Line within a period of just a few minutes and the R.O "lost count' and abandoned the race. I bet they're still moaning to this day in the bars of the Graduate Fleets around the country. A report by Mike Turner of the Saturday Practice Race for the Hornet Hallam Trophy (presumably to be held on Sunday) reveals the usual problems of campetitors ‘assuming’ the usual Marconi start line - hence failing to use the designed 'long-line' start. las, a similar happening in the 1993 Run, Tub and Bung gave rise to one of our visitors expressing his views of Marconi somewhat forcefully. The gentleman's sailing ability was exceptional and much to be commended; alas, his ‘apres-race' volubility possibly less so, although I can well understand his annoyance and disappointment. a a us that tickets for the Laying Up Supper are £3.75 each with a special rate for Cadets a sous

—" November - a nice cover photo of Julian Bigden sailing a Laser with a very diminutive son Jonathan peering over the gunwale (no doubt wondering why that funny person with the camera was shouting rude things at his Dad). John Weedon makes an offer that surely no music—lover can refuse. On offer is the old piano which used to be in the old clubhouse. It is free to anyone willing to take it away. Where, I wonder, did it cam fran and where was its 'final' resting place ? Presumably, the modern day equivalent would be a kareoke machine. The 1975 AGM elected Sir Eric Eastwood (President), John Witter (Commodore), Ron Greygoose (Vice Commodore), Vic Tate (Rear Commodore), Eric Royle (Hon.Sec), Ted Barnes (Hon.Treas.), John Weedon (Sailing Sec), Dave Harper (Clubhouse Sec) and Roy Battye (Social Sec.). Nick Tovey was re-elected as a Vice President. :- December - the Report of the AGM shows the 1975 membeship as follows (1974 figures in brackets) Ordinary Members 289 (244) Associate Members 101 (103) Family Members 44 (30) 434 (377) with a note saying there were 39 Cadets. The Accounts for the year show a surplus of £91 (Income £ 11,135; Expenditure £ 11,044). On the Incame side, the sale of the old wooden clubhouse and boat shed brought in £ 393 but on the Expenditure side the Fitting Out of the new clubhouse cost £ 2,897. Overall, the value of the Sailing Section's Reserve Account with the MASC was £ 1,507. The Commodore reports much improved site security because of the use of magnetic locks but expresses disappointment at the state in which the clubhouse is left after Members use it. Mike Boreham IRI A EK 40 Years Ago - February & March, 1954. February - a notice in the files advertises Fast Coast Cruises between the Medway and Orfordness for 1955 under the auspices of the Maldon Youth Hostel. Cost per person for a 7-day cruise for 9 people was £ 6.00 each with food extra at £2.10s.0d - £3.0s.0d per person. March — 2] members attended the 1954 AGM of the MASC Sailing Section. Eric Payne felt the name should not be the ‘Sailing Section’ but it was explained that the 'the club' was one of many groups belonging to the parent MASC -—- hence it remained a Section of the MASC. Eric also queried the cost of insurance for the club boat,Avril, but he was assured it would be less in 1954 and the years after because 1953 had to cover the journey from Hullbridge to its moorings in the Blackwater. Eric Cottam said that as they were starting a Fleetwind Class, they would need a Race Officer "...someone not interested in racing...but willing to fire the gun..... ‘ The Club President, Dr Eastwood, offered to be Race Officer if and when he was available, but the offer seems not to have been taken up since it was proposed "...each skipper (and crew) take it in turns to act as Race Officer or Officer of the Day..." It was also proposed to mm races only on Saturdays. It was revealed that 8 Fleetwind kits were being purchased via the MASC whilst 2 others were being purchased ready built. The MASC 'scheme' provided a loan for half the cost, repaid over two years without interest. Membership of the club had now reached 60 and the club was now "..officially recognised as one of the Blackwater Clubs". A suggestion to look for another site (since the present site was rather inaccessible) was not taken up, it being pointed out that sites were difficult to find, particularly since building on the sea wall was not now permitted and, anyway, the present club was within easy reach of The Jolly Sailor. The AGM elected Terry Hallam (Commodore), Geoff Wardell (Vice Commodore), E C Talboys (Sec.) G W Nichols (Treasurer) and Eric Cottam (Sailing Sec); surprizingly, they seem to have dropped the post of Rear Commodore. At a Committee Meeting later in March, it was decided the club should join the RYA. Mike Boreham

It seems Alf Cottam's crew got left behind and kept sinking - but Alf hadn't noticed! Caron was obviously somewhat wary of what lived beneath the waves for she caments "...the mud bed felt horrid. It was like walking on crab's backs."" Anyway, it seems she and Dad had a good race (presumably in the Mirror) against Roy Rattye and just pipped Roy to the post. Philip Cherry (aged 5) recounted his adventure when he crewed in a dinghy and fell in head first but his life jacket kept him afloat until helped out of the water. A lesson and experience he no doubt remembers to this day. Colin Harper wrote of a trip in a Trident cruiser to Brightlingsea, whilst "An Anonymous Young Lady" wrote a poem entitled "No Stormy Weather". I'm not sure if Ian Campbell was a Cadet or not, but he presented a 43-page cruiser log entitled "Marconi's Invasion of the Continent". Sara Anstey was also a Marconi Cadet and wrote an article entitled "Mumbles Gnmbles"” to recount the horrors of the 1975 Mirror Nationals at Mumbles, Swansea, which was attended by Roy Rattye, John Weedon, Stan Oaker and (of course) Rick Anstey. Sara writes "...All it did was rain and poured, the highest wind was gale Force 7, but it was just about as high as that every day, there were about 50 capsizes nearly every day and about half of them were towed in". ‘Thus, Sara sets the scene and she continues "...Before the start it was chaos and confusion, boats were bumping into each other and capsizing. There was one 9 mile race every day and I think that was a bit much for me and just about enough for my Dad." Sara then describes the inevitably worsening scenario of disaster following disaster both on land as well as on water. Perhaps with some chagrin, Sara notes "The Mums and my sisters were alright, most of the time sitting in the clubhouse..... "I think this was definitely a wistful cry from the heart of "It's not fair" fram Sara but she's obviously made of tough stuff because, having given vent to the realities of the 'experience', she diplamtically ends by saying "Despite all the bad weather we all enjoyed it thanks to the Mmbles Sailing Club who made us very welcome" and, indeed, I'm sure they all enjoyed it (once it was over). Wherever you are now, Sara, and whatever you are doing, I'm sure you'l] recall Mmbles Gnmbles with Se Se Se ee GS ee er winter). Other Cadets who wrote articles were Rachel Cherry (aged 7), Chris Weedon, Richard Battye, Penny Stuart (aged 8), Robert Weedon (aged 11) - and Carol and Tim Foreman (with same nagging from Mum). This issue of Navigans is finished off by a cartoon from Heather Stuart and a drawing by Laura Anstey (aged 5) which is (hopefully) reproduced at the end of this Navigans Past. The January issue of Navigans certainly was a ‘bumper issue' with 14 pages plus front and back cover. February - Editor, Brenda Tate, says she knows the sailing season cannot be too far away as (son) Robert's Moth is lying alongside her in the lounge. Many a forgiving club Wife and Mm will know the feeling; we once had two Mirrors in our spare bedroom over winter. You notice I said "once"!

3. COMMODORE’S NOTES There are two incidents that I believe require my comment before the season gets much further under way. On Good Friday a Club official was harangued and brewbeaten by a group of worried Windsurfers ta release the RIB, or failing that Jack B, to enable them to goa in search of one of their colleagues whe had drifted off and couldn’t be located. There had been a streng wind all day and they may have nad cause to be worried but this must not happen tc a Club Official again. I would like to inform the Members concerned that Good Friday was not a "Club Day". There was no OOD/Support Roster for that day. Therefore it falls intca the same category as any other weekday, and the Code of Practice operates. This states that the second course af action, once the Baddow Star is not operational, is ta call the Coastguard. Secondly, the Easter Marday events that led to the comments in the Daily Telegraph and the Daily Mail on Tuesday. I don’t know just how much people really know the work of the RNLI op Coastguard, but I have a sneaking suspicion that there is an attitude that says "if there’s a support boat out there I’1l be OK, and if not the RNLI will be there". I don’t krow how many of you will recall the name Union Star, but that was a coaster that suffered engine failure in Mount’s Bay on 19 December 1981 in mega winds. They did not accept a tow from a salvage tug (to save money) and went oan the rocks. The Penlee lifeboat Sclomon Browne was launched and never came back. I had two school mates on that boat. It might seem a bit heavy to make these sorts of comments, out my earlier remarks are aimed at showing that with that attitude you are not just risking yourself, but other people as well. There is far tac much bravade afloat these days. It’s not clever or macho to go aut irs weather you can’t handle, and if we weren’t estuary-based there would be much more frequent problems. Dern’t be fooled by the excellent seamen who can handle their boats in extreme conditions; that comes with years and years of experience. And keep irs mind the prospect cf something happening further out ta sea - the sight of land disappearing as you Swim with with a capsized unrightable boat is rot one ta be recommended (and I’ve experienced it). The watchword then, whatever your activity, 15 aim to be entirely self-sufficient and sail within your limitations. Ve FAST CAT NOTES "30 rescued as winds capsize racing fleet"; "...the clubs should not have put these people at risk."; "Some of the boats ... from the ... Marconi Sailing Club, were blown up to three miles along the river." (Daily Telegraph, 5th April 1994.) On one thing most of us can agree: incidents attracting such publicity help neither our club nor our sport. Writing these notes in the aftermath of the carnage | am equally sure that we have every reason to be thankful that Easter 1994 did not see serious injury (or worse) on our sailing waters. What could we have done to avoid the incident? The start of the morning race was delayed to allow an earlier storm to pass by; perhaps unfortunately, it slipped away to the north and we were given no indication of the fury that might lurk within. Personally | was aware of the existence of the threat of strong winds, and | believe that most of those sailing recognised the probability that the glorious conditions pertaining at the start were unlikely to outlast the race. It is an oft-quoted truism that those entering a race do so at their own risk, and that the decision by the club (or more accurately those of its members who happen to be on duty on the day) to run a race in no way absolves competitors of the responsibilty to decide for themselves whether or not to take to the water. Fair enough, but would Larry have liked (finding himself perhaps in the position of Stone’s Commodore Harry Elias) to have explained to a press inquisition that it was not the responsibility of the club to ensure the safety of its racing members? | suspect that would have appeared as lame when printed in the Telegraph as Harry's “It was just a Force Two when we set out." | believe we have to take great care to protect our members, our club and our sport both from the threatening elements of wind and water and from the shadow of those who might wish to add further bureaucracy to our sport, possibly demanding formal qualifications (for competitors as well as support boat drivers), or impractical levels of support cover. Most of us will remember the Health and Safety official who last year succeeded in closing Wraysbury Lake Sailing Club for safety-related reasons. Should the race have been run? | believe so; if we were not to venture afloat when inclement conditions threaten then we would lose a large part of the season as well as fail to develop our sailing skills in stronger winds. It does not seem to me that we should consult the Coastguard as to the advisability of racing; to do so would place the coastguard in a difficult position, from which he could only escape by making an extremely conservative recommendation, one against which the club would be foolish to go. Given that, how could we have acted to limit the subsequent damage? | did not notice a forecast (including the strong wind warning) posted in the Clubhouse; neither did | notice an empty forecast board, and | do not know whether it is the formal responsibility of any of the 'duty members’ to post the forecast. | suggest that having a specific board (clearly identified) for a current weather forecast, and assigning a clear responsibility to post a forecast on each morning on which club sailing will be held, would allow those intending to race to better assess the risks to which they are exposing themselves, and as a consequence help the Club’s position. On this occasion was the rescue cover adequate? Certainly we only had one vessel immediately available (the RIB), although the Jack B abandoned mooring-laying to join the clear up operations after the squall hit. The area of the course had been deliberately restricted with this in mind; it became clear however that restrictions obeyed by boats racing were not necessarily recognised by the same vessels when they were cartwheeling before a Force 9/10. It seems to me that although the provision of further support boats would have reduced the time to attend each of the craft following the impact of the squall, it is not obvious that there was an unacceptable shortage of cover. | believe we all accept the impossibility of guaranteeing instant attention from a support boat, and that this is one of the risks (for some, possibly the attractions) of our sport. Could the rescue (sorry, the politically correct epithet ‘support’ doesn’t seem to fit) operation have been better carried out or managed? | believe we owe a great debt to those members who played a part, either on the water or the land, and from my perspective | would like to thank especially Mick Richardson, whose driving of the RIB was both skillful and reassuring. Some of the radio traffic seemed temporarily to reveal an element of confusion as to the whereabouts of some of our competitors, although whether on the part of our members or those of Stone was not clear. Without a detailed post-mortem, in this case perhaps only by chance metaphorical, it might be difficult to identify areas where improvements could be made. In the event, the more serious consequences were avoided (or avoided us). Several large insurance claims will now no doubt be submitted, another fact which should concern all those who each year face increasing premiums; | wish those involved good luck. Easter Monday's storm has cast a shadow over the new season at the club, after a sparkling first weekend with some excellent racing in fine conditions. | hope and trust that the Fast Cat Fleet, having licked its wounds, will soon return to the water, older, hopefully wiser, but undeterred. Tip of the month, from Caroline at the height of the storm: “Now don't get too competitive, John...". Seemed fair at the time.

THRASH Those whe joined in the 1990 and 1991 events with Britannia Sailing, Southampton will know what to expect from the weekend and you have prebably been dining out on the stories ever since. This year we plan to get out of the Solent and, weather permitting, sail round the I.0.W. This means an early start Saturday, and the challenge is to beat Britannia’s somewhat corservative timings: ITINERARY FRIDAY 4 NOVEMBER 1994 1800 hrs Arrive at Shamrock Quay, collect Oilskins if required. 1900 hrs Safety Briefing. £000 hrs Evening meal at Waterfront Cafe Bar. SATURDAY 5S NOVEMBER 0700 hrs Breakfast on board yacht. 0730 hrs Depart Shamreck Quay. 1130 hrs Round Bembridge Ledge by 1300 hrs Lunch on board. 1730 hrs Round Needles Lt Ho Bay. 1900 hrs ETA Yarmouth (Isle of Wight). 2000 hrs Meal ashore SUNDAY & NOVEMBER 0700 hrs Breakfast on board. 0800 hrs Skipper briefing. 0930 hrs Depart Yarmouth (latest). 1600 hrs Arrive Shamrock Quay. 1700 hrs Depart. If you would like to join in let me kriow and I will either put you in touch with a boat organiser, or you may end up organising a boat yourself - main job is to get the 30% deposits in soon. CRUISER COMMENTS That was Easter, that was! What a weekend. Those on the A and C row Mooring Parties found the weather made a tedious task harder than usual. Good Friday was a complete blaw-cut, however we were at least able to move all available moorings an toa the Hard for next day’s laying. Saturday was better, whereby Ac-AS and also Ce-C8 were laid, and the remainder of C row Moorings were moved onto the Hard. Or, Sunday, which turned out tc be the best day of the weekend by far, the C team went at it hammer and tongs, completing two days’ work in one. A splendid effort, and congratulations to all concerned. On Easter Monday the A team were on parade again to lay the remaining A row Moorings. Having just laid the next four moorings and loaded up the barge with another two moorings, the mother-and-father of all squalls hit the estuary, causing the abandorment of any further work, so I guess the A team will be on parade again next weekend to lay the remaining 5 moorings. I wish the B team better fortune. 10. Handicap Fleet and its Handicapping So what is the Handicap Fleet? It is the name given to those monchulls in the Club which race against each other under a handicapping system. In fact, the varicus catamaran fleets race under the same system. Only the Solos, being a one class fleet, have no need for handicapping. The handicapping scheme used for racing is Called the Portsmouth Yardstick Scheme. Each class of boat has a handicapping number, the Portsmouth Number (PN), associated with it. This is used very Simply tc scale the race time of a boat so that each boat has in theory an equal opportunity to win a race when the adjusted race times are used. The adjusted time is calculated by the formula: (adjusted time) = (actual time) x 100 / PN Usually you just leave it to the race box to de this calculation. You can see why they measure times in seconds! Here are some PNs: B7 305 116 Wayfarer 99 Osprey 117 Laser Radial 103 Hornet 118 Eriterprise 105 Fireball ) B Wanderer 109 Laser II 119 GP 14 110 Kestrel Let Eurape 111 Cherub ize Sale 114 Laser 136 Topper 115 420 144 Mirror (single handed) 146 Mirror Notice that if I, in my Laser II (PN = 109), finish in a time of 109 minutes, and the GF 14 (PN = 119) finishes in 119 minutes, then we tie because our times beth adjust to 100 minutes. Thus, finishing in 109 minutes, I beat him if I finish ahead by more than 119 -109 = 10 minutes. This PN difference is a good guide for catamarans because they often finish their races in a number of minutes roughly equal toa their PN number. For monohulls, sailing a shorter course, they usually finish in some lesser time and sao would have to proportionately scale the margin given by the difference in PN rnumbers. For example, if I finish in 75 minutes, I would need tc beat the GP by 10x75/109 = 6.88 minutes. Note, if we divided by 100 instead of cur PN number, we would get 7.5 minutes; incorrect, of course, but probably a good enough approximation for deciding if I beat her or not. Hence for monohulls, whose FPNs are fairly close ta 100, we have: the margin between us and the other boat that would cause us to tie is approximately given by our time divided by 100 and then multiplied by our PN difference. We could probably do this caiculation in cur head! I’m afraid I’ve got bad news for the slower boats. In our tidal waters the handicapping system will favour the faster boats. This is because the slower boat suffers more than the faster boat sailing against the tide - the slower boat may not ever manage tc beat the tide! She will then gain sailing with the tide, but unfortunately it will not be enough to compensate. John Weeden did arn article on this subject in the January 1994 issue of Navigans. Have you seen Malcolm Stuart’s notice about the planned yacht race around the Isle of Wight? Laura and I did a similar weekend with the Club a few years ago which was great fun and we certainly intend to have a go at this. We want to get a boat or two marmed by Handicap Fleet sailors and show the other Fleets what for! Let me or Malcolm know if you are interested. A late item of news: Sam Ashley has acquired a Laser Jaguar - I think that is a Laser with some fancy paint work - and is likely ta be racing it when he’s not crewing for Graham Richmond in the Hornet. Ever. later news: Young Mark Bulkeley was caught in the Easter Monday disaster where the race was suddenly hit by a storm. It was his first outing this year and he was racing in his Laser Radial for the first time. He dry capsized the boat and weathered the worst of the storm, hailstones and all, then sailed it to shore. He was the only monohull to venture out at the MSC, but he survived with great presence of mind. Well done, Mark. Dor Gill, Handicap Fleet captain, 0245 [redacted].

Oh, for the joys of a lovely Mackintosh and a fancy printer... | can'tresist taking the opportunity of typing this on a borrowed outfit, and if | don't finish it before the deadline for its return there will need to be a change of printing style part way through for which | apologise if ithappens. - Ed. T antic Crui David Cole owns the Arthur Robb designed wooden 55' ketch ‘Anatina' and very kindly asked me to join for a cruise across the Atlantic to Venezuela in November 1993. The boat was lying at Villamoura Marina in South Portugal in the capable hands of ‘Johnnie’ (who had spent the last three months applying approximately 16 coats of varnish to the masts and almost every piece of teak in sight) and Dick (who had been over every possible item needing maintenance) and we arrived there by air on 20th November. Three fairly frantic days of storing ship and preparing everything ensued, and then we departed on a sunny evening into the empty wastes of the Atlantic. There were five of us on board, David, myself, Philippa Anderson, David's younger son Adrian, and Adrian's friend from Harvard Business College - Pip Woods (26) an Anglo-American who had never been sailing before. As we drew away from the mainland coast the wind and waves increased. We set watches of three hours each, and we were rather dismayed to find that a full rig of oilskins was needed. Water was occasionally finding its way on board, and even into the cockpit, and it was essential to be clipped on with safety harness at all times. The only saving grace was that it was not particularly cold, and the wind was fair on our South Westerly course. We went to Porto Santo (Portuguese), a small island a few miles from Madeira which we decided would be preferable for us to visit as it is not beset by tourists. There is a small artificial harbour which protects from most of the swell where we anchored at dawn on the fourth day amongst about twenty ocean voyagers - mostly French. The sun was lovely, the solid ground between our feet. We ordered a bottle of Madeira at the harbourside and drank it rather quickly. The island is volcanic. Columbus lived here for a bit as he fell in love with the daughter of the first governor. We went to see a sma/l museum in his house. We hired bikes and went round the island which is about the same size as the Isle of Wight, quite poor, but simple and agreeable. Enough rain to have some green vegetation and some palm trees. After four days we left. Again we were somewhat dismayed to find the weather very boisterous as the yacht drew away from the island in late afternoon and it was necessary to get back into the routine of night watches and sharing cooking duties, not very onerous as several people felt sea-sick. The worst aspect of the cooking was that the motion was very violent in 20' seas with a cross-sea running and the boat corkscrewing along on a fast reach. Every single item one used - the coffee grains, the milk, the cooking oil, the cups - everything needed to be wedged all the time or else it would fall to the cabin sole and join the general ice rink there beneath our bare feet. It was necessary to keep one's foot on a floor cloth or one would start to slide to the far side of the cabin down the polished teak. After four days and nights the fantastic clouds on the horizon at dawn resolved themselves into the volcanic peaks of Gran Canaria. It was breathtakingly beautiful, and not just because it lay there in the midst of the vast ocean but because it made one realise a bit what those first voyagers must have felt as they came across them for the first time beyond the empty sea-horizons which since the dawn of history had been the only known boundaries of Europe. As we approached the island the wind and waves died down and eventually the ship was becalmed and everyone bathed. For the rest of that day we skirted the vast volcanic cliffs and mountains of the uninhabited West Coast where there is no coastal plain and no sign of human habitation. In late afternoon we came to the small marina at Puerto Mogan (Spanish). Although it was only built in 1977 it is extremely well designed and agreeable with masses of well tended flowers and small dwellings and shops in an excellent town plan from which cars are largely excluded. Here we spent about four days swapping crew members, getting some electronic instruments put right, doing some mechanical maintenance, trying to mend the decaying genoa by hand, buying all the stores for the big hop, topping up water tanks and bottled water. The best thing was the wonderful quality of the fruit and vegetables grown locally, best | have ever seen anywhere. By contrast the local chandler was worse than hopeless, anda ridiculous, self-important, (Swedish) so-called 'maintenance engineer’ actually succeeded in delaying us from getting essential last-minute jobs done. Luckily we managed to find a wonderful English ex-regular soldier in his own small cruising boat who came on board and dealt with everything most competently.

14. Philippa Anderson left us to catch a plane for England, and Davia's elder son Martin arrived with his friend Nicholas Morse. Soon it was time for us to leave and once again there was a moving moment as the yacht drew away from the quay and a tiny waving figure on the shore grew smaller and smaller astern. (That was Philippa Anderson! She'd missed her plane.) The passage to the Islas do Cabo Verdes took eight days, and once again there were big waves and strong winds. The genoa | had stitched began to come unstitched along a further section of the foot due to the strain imposed each time it collapsed and re-set itself with a loud crack like a whip. Luckily the wind was fair still and we were not obliged to beat to windward, but the rolling motion was as tiring as ever and should we lose anyone overboard in those rough conditions there would be no chance whatsoever of beating back, relocating him, or being able to manoeuvre anywhere near to reach down, secure and pick up the body. We navigated with a new Magellan GPS instrument whose only failing was that it seemed to eat dry-cell batteries rather fast and there was some doubt about whether we had enough replacement batteries on board. Occasionally we took sun-sights by sextant and worked them out with a small Japanese computer, taking about ten minutes to do the calculations, but mostly it was far too rough to even take sights as the horizon would be obscured by heaving waves. We started a watchkeeping routine. Each day one person would be excused watchkeeping and would cook all the meals, wash everything up, sweep the cabin floors and wipe everything in the heads with disinfectant. | may say this was a counsel of perfection which we did not always manage to fulfil, especially as all these tasks are very difficult when the weather is not good and the motion of the boat in the waves is violent. It is all one can do to keep one's balance below-decks and hold on to prevent oneself from falling, let alone clean as well, or perform a tremendous juggling act in the galley getting all the ingredients together from the various stowages for cooking and all the crockery and cutlery together from their various stowages for serving each of the three meals for six required each day. Meanwhile, the other four would keep deck watches, usually alone, three hours on and nine hours off. | did not much enjoy the night watches as the weather was not good, large waves, strong wind, overcast sky and quite frequent line squalls. However watchkeeping was not too onerous while the Autohelm did all the steering. Sometimes the waves and wind would become too much for the Autohelm and the watchkeeper would have to start steering by hand, andsometimes there would be a line-squall coupled with a shift of wind which would require hand steering to prevent a gibe. After eight days of strong weather we reached Puerto Grande Islas San Vicente in the Cabo Verdes Arquipelago where we anchored next to the battered-looking old town of Mindelo, all very exhausted and glad to be in a relatively sheltered open anchorage, though the rolling continued all night and day. The pilot books all warned about the Cape Verdes, saying the natives were so poor they would board yachts and steal anything not secured - dinghies, outboards or anything else you care to mention. This was reprehensible as it has prevented, at any rate English people, from calling here. Only twenty British yachts visited last year. There were some Australian and Scandinavian and French voyagers there, and one Italian with a broken mast. No British. In our experience the natives were courteous and, as far we we could see, as honest as one can possibly expect. The are poorer than we can imagine, coming as we do from a prosperous country, and if one leaves things lying about unattended like expensive dinghies with expensive things in them, as far as | can see it ought to be understood that it is the fault of the rich for leaving things around and not the fault of the poor for taking them. Things representing untold wealth to the locals left about carelessly by visitors may be assimilated. That's all one can say on the subject. The inhabitants of the Cape Verde Islands are descendants of African slaves mixed with Portuguese, many very good-looking and athletic, and some with really beautiful faces. Some can understand French, but the local dialect is a kind of Portuguese which unfortunately few Europeans can understand. We stayed four days and managed to get the genoa sewn up after a fashion by a tailor (‘Charley' who could sort of half-understand French) with a Singer hand-wound sewing machine and using our sail-bag to cut up to make patches, and the last of our reel of sail-twine as he had none of his own. Little piccaninies would surround the dinghy at each landing and beg for your hat, your watch, your shoes - even your rubbish, but we soon got used to them, and in the end grew quite fond of them. They were press-ganged into carrying hundreds of bottles of mineral water for us. There was no water available on the islands for replenishing the yacht's tanks. It had not rained there for three years. All the Island's water has to be made in a de-salination plant from the sea, and the plant itself keeps breaking down. All electricity comes from winamills, many of which are no longer revolving in the perpetual wind. After four days we departed for the Atlantic crossing. Once more we sailed out into a huge sea and a strong wind -not the gentle Tradewind we had hoped for. Before the end of the first day we came up with six tiny open boats in a little group hand lining. They looked so lonely and vulnerable out there tossing up

15. and down in the immense waves, sometimes lost to view and sometimes flung up as on a peak. At the same time we were joined by a wonderful school of lively porpoises who zoomed in and out round the bows as we thundered along at about eight or nine knots with huge carpets of foam spreading out each side of us to mark our passage through the seas. No ships appeared on our horizon during this part of our voyage. Once we sawa lonely little flock of white egrets going roughly North-west. What on earth were they heading for? Were they lost? At about the half-way mark a beautiful tropic-bird with long plume-like tail feather trailing astern came and flew quietly round us as if asking us to drop a little of our rubbish overboard for it to inspect. Twice | saw plastic bottles floating miles from anywhere, horrid evidence of untidy and careless civilisation. Flying fish took off at our precipitate approach and sped away, but sometimes they landed by mistake on our deck and got fried and eaten. Something enormous took my huge flashing metal lure, wire trace and shark book and broke my 5 Ibs breaking-strain mono-filament line and swam off with it, unfortunately. It was usually too rough to trail a line over the stern and the waves made it inadvisable because there was no means of preventing it from getting tangled in the log-line on the opposite side of the taffrail. We saw storm-petrels and boobies and oncea pair of sinister killer-whales powered past us looking like nuclear submarines hell-bent on a distant prey - luckily not us. We could not celebrate Christmas Day as the weather was too rough. The Christmas presents | had brought were stowed for convenience in the foc's'| and as that compartment was separated from the after part of the vessel by a water-tight bulkhead and no one was able to leave the cockpit with any safety | was not able to get the presents until 28th December, so it all fell a bit flat. The only thing worth mentioning about Christmas Day was that the Autohelm failed. This was a great blow. Up to then we had managed to keep watches (three hours each) singly, but now it became necessary to steer all the time and we decided to keep watches in pairs because we found it too tiring to steer in the heavy seas for more than half an hour at a time. Unfortunately Nicholas Morse was not experienced at steering a sailing boat, and at about seven in the morning in the dark during a particularly severe line-squall he sensed that something was wrong as he felt the force go out of the mainsail. He knew he should take immediate drastic action to prevent a gibe, but he turned the wheel the wrong way and the boat, which was travelling at more than eight knots, took a wild sheer to port and heeled over too far to starboard. The heavy wooden boom carried away the wire fore- guy and the metal rail to which the four-part downhaul tackle was secured pulled the whole of the lower half of the boom off, splintering the wood like a strike of lightning and letting the top half of the boom and the mainsail smash over to starboard. He then lost his head and turned the wheel hard the opposite way, gibing the broken splinters of the boom back again and causing the yacht to heel over even further to port, burying the side-deck which picked up a quantity of water. Unfortunately someone had decided the cabin was too stuffy during the night and had unscrewed and opened all the scuttles which consequently spouted all this into the cabin. Here it began sloshing about on the cabin sole which was so beautifully fashioned that it was unable to get away into the bilges beneath, contributing considerably to a distinct lowering of morale. Luckily daylight was breaking. We continued to run before the strong wind and David went forward and managed to pull the mainsail down the track and secure it and the two splintered parts of our boom. We ran on under the genoa, but that was slowly disintegrating before our eyes. During the day we lowered the genoa, set the yankee which was smaller, and also set the small boomed stays’! on the other side to balance it and make steering a bit easier. And so we carried on, and on the twelfth day it was 'Land Ho!" and lovely Barbados hove up over the horizon to leeward. Never had green trees and and yellow beaches and white surf looked more beautiful. We had a lovely stay in Barbados and |! surprised myself by falling for the Bajans. They are so happy on their island! It made me realise how sad it is that they are really not happy in London, and to some extent it's our fault, though of course it's much easier to be happy in a land of sun and plenty than it is in a land of fog and dearth. Adrian, Martin, Pip and Nicholas Morse left by plane. We managed to get the boom and the Avohelm mended and the genoa sewn up. Unfortunately we left the Zodiac inflatable in the sun on the hot beach one day and while we were away having lunch in the local Hilton Hotel it astonished the drinkers round the bar at Val Knowles's Boatyard Restaurant by exploding with a loud report. It proved impossible to mend, but Val Knowles managed to find a rather beaten-up Hutchinson dinghy which David was able to acquire secondhand from a Bajan and that had to serve as our tender from then on, unfortunately just a bit leaky in wind and water. Hilary Cole arrived by plane. Michael Richie arrived too, owner of the wooden sloop ‘Secret’ which had been built for him at Aldeburgh and 'Sani' Fogel from Maine, owner of a very handsome Hinckley 35 sloop.

16. After Barbados, a boisterous overnight passage took us past lovely Saint Vincent to Admiralty Bay, Bequia. We hada lovely time at Bequia which is wonderfully green, mountainous and fertile. A few years before, ‘Sani' had built a house on the other side of the island and she took us to Friendship Bay in an old Chevrolet pick-up truck so she could show it to us, and we could all bathe in the surf off the white beach. She very kindly gave us a wonderful lunch in a very jolly open-sided palm-thatched restaurant beside the sea where we Sat in the shade drinking rum punches and pina coladas, kept cool by the trade wind blowing through the spray from the surf. Next day we had a glorious sail past the active volcano at Kick 'em Jenny to the ‘Treasure Island‘ anchorage at romantic Tobago Cays, sheltered from the spume of the thundering Atlantic swells only by the shallows of the coral reef. That was followed by a short sail in dull grey weather between reefs and palm-fringed islands to Union Island. The Union Island Yacht Club Hotel seemed rather sinister because it was fronted by a small sea- water lagoon containing about a dozen large brown nurse sharks. On the terrace here we were joined for lunch by some friends from England, the Powers, and Mary Barton (widow of Humphrey of “Vertue XXX V" fame) came and sat next to me. The anchorage at Union Island was uncomfortable and full of swell and we all felt rather sad because ‘Sani’ left us here and departed by plane from the small airfield for Maine. We weighed anchor and left for Canouan Island. Here we anchored off the ferry pier. It was not well sheltered and the swell was continuous. We landed with difficulty. There are not many trees on Canouan. It was very hot. We walked a short way to the only place we could find where we might be able to get /Junch. It was a sad littte modern ‘Bed and Breakfast' establishment run by a little old bird who told us she had been a nurse in Scunthorpe for twenty years before coming back to her home island with her husband and spending their savings on setting up their small establishment. She gave us what she called ‘English cooking’ but unfortunately it didn't flatter us much. Lateron we all began to feel a bit ill and we came to the conclusion we were all suffering from heat-stroke spending too much time not in the shade during the heat of the day when we were not quite acclimatised to the tropical heat. We left next day without regret and set sail for unbelievably beautiful but poor, romantic Carriacou Island. This was the one | liked almost best of all the places we visited. We had supper ashore in a fairly dot-and- carry-one establishment run by a large jolly local called ‘Bubbles’. Next day he took us for a tour round the island in his old mini-bus. For lunch we stopped at the Cassada Bay Hotel. Quite the most beautiful place | had ever seen in the whole world | thought, and now | cannot wait to try to visit it again. Next - the Spice Island! Grenada. Prickly Bay. Everything you could possibly want grows wild here in profusion - bananas, coconuts, oranges, lemons, limes, avocadoes, mangoes, guavas, grapefruit, nutmeg, mace, peppers, cocoa, coffee, not to mention flowers and trees of the most exotic colours, ferns, orchids - it's paradise! No wonder the horrible Americans invaded it and tried to wrest it from the British under the Presidency of perfidious Reagan! All were sad to leave there. An overnight dash took us to the remote Testigos Islands which really are small and poor, about the same size as Eigg, Rum and Muck, ! should think, but stony and sparsely vegetated and swept by unceasing wind. Final hop was to Islas Margarita, Venezuela proper. Here once again there was no shelter other than the open roadstead at Pampatar, and nowhere to land except through surf on the open beach where the dinghy would almost invariably get upset, and everyone soaked either when landing or leaving. Luckily, as the water was warm, this usually only led to a good deal of laughter and was not at all worrying. In fact, in a funny way everybody began to enjoy it. Trying to get away from Venezuela was a nightmare, involving having things stolen, losing my luggage on internal flights, being frisked by very unpleasant Veneauelan ‘soldiers’, drunken agents, desperately dangerous driving in huge clapped-out American cars - a taxi, but | only found out too late that the ‘driver’ had stolen it just before | got in! He would insist on going at ninety miles an hour (to imitate ‘Alain Prost ha! ha! ha!). Being overcharged for an air ticket, being charged 1000 Bolivars by a porter, being refused twice at weighing-in by officials after | had bought my tickets (were they hoping for bribes?) and finally being refused exit until | paid a rotten tax just to get out (having already paid yet another tax at the Venezuelan Embassy in Grenada just to get in!) Due to the fact that a sheaf of Bolivars had blown away across the tarmac on the wind when| tried to extract my boarding card from my pocket, | found | had not quite enough Bolivars to pay the exit tax. It was then a question of racing across the International Airport building to try to find a money-changer (how do you do that in Spanish?) and racing back again in time to catch the plane. Miss that and it would have meant spending two nights in the airport building waiting for the next one, and perhaps even forfeiting my fare. Not surprising | was relieved finally to catch it at the last possible minute - it was late leaving, needless to say. Don't go to Venezuela unless you're good at Spanish! Owen Laurence-Jones

From the reports I have been getting, a great time time was had by all. Having armnounced at the Supper the opening of the downstairs bar on the following Friday might, a few of us decided to have a dummy run. This toa turned cub ta be most successful. Incidentally we have beer considering a name for the Bar and it appears it may become "The Dell", named after a road sign that has mysteriously appeared on the premises. (PLEASE ALSO SEE *CALLED TO THE BAR’, NEXT PAGE, Ed.) Friday the 29th April saw the opening of "The Dell" attended by approximately 20 Cruiser Members. Our thanks ta Joan Smith for providing the snacks and Bob Godbold for marming the Bar. Anyone willing to run the bar on subsequent Fridays, please coritact Bob. With sco few yachts in the water, plus 'B’ Mooring party being ar parade on Sunday, the turnout was disappointing. Having dealt with the Social & Sailing everts, may I please draw your attention ta matters related ta launching, trailer storage and maintenance which briefly are as follows: 1) Do rot launch with trailer towing bar fixed to trailer. It’s alright when launching but the bar fouls the slipway when retrieving the trailer. This can result in not being able to detach the wire strop, and the trailer remaining in the water too long (possibly submerged) causing a hazard to ather craft. 2) Having launched, please don’t ignore your trailer until you next need it for hauling cut. Make sure the wheels are greased and everything is in working order, ta avoid problems later on. iJ Empty trailers of Cruisers from the Car Park are tc be stored down the far end of the CAT FIELD until preper spaces can be allocated once the NRA vacate the site. The importance of TRAILERS BEING MARKED WITH THE BOAT’S NAME carmot be cverstressed. The need to make sure you clear up your space once you vacate the Car Park has already been stressed in last month’s Navigans. 4) Should anyone in the Cruiser Park currently blocked in by boats on the one side and the NRA on the other need to move another Member’s trailer, PLEASE MAKE SURE THEY RETURN IT TO ITS ORIGINAL POSITION afterwards. Weather permitting, the NRA should be in a position to return part of the Cruiser Park to us at the end of May. Until then please help each other, or contact me should you have any problems. Handicap Fleet News Receritly, I have had reason ta believe that there are dinghy sailors at large in the MSC whe get a great deal of pleasure from their sailing without racing. 1 must admit I’ve missed out on this more relaxed form of sailing and their letters published in Navigans make it sound very enticing. I look forward to joining forces with them sometime, but ... I am not attaching any outboard motor to my Laser II ! I also have reason tao believe that some of this non-racing fraternity would very much like to have the use of winches to help them pull their boats up the hard. Well, the geod news is that there is a winch you can use. This information comes ta me from the upper echelons of the MSC and, further, it was suggested I wrote a few words here on usirig 1t. Now for the bad news! I thought I had better get some first hand experience of using this winch by pulling up my boat. I pulled the winch cable (half inch diameter?) ta my boat off the end of the hard. Halfway down, I thought it would be easier to pull the boat up to meet the cable! Then I operated the winch. Every turn of the handle, around a two foot diameter circle, brought the boat up about one inch. Same considerable time later, the boat was up, I was exhausted, and everyone else had gore home. My sailing gloves were ruined, worn out and covered in dirt ard grease. Further, a lot of people who saw me doing all this think I must be a bit simple. They’re right! I have row asked Roger Nex to do some research on winches suitable for dinghies. If anyone has useful information on this subject, then contact him on [redacted]. If you ever find the winch is the only option open to you, then here is some advice on how to use the wretched thing. First, the winch that 1s suitable for dinghies (ha, ha!) is the small one that is nearest the entrance to the hard. The winch is covered by a box, as are each of the other three winches alongside it. Roll the box back cut of the way. Release the ratchet, which is held down by gravity so just flip it back. You will most likely have to free the ratchet first by winding up the cable slightly. Disengage any cogs from the large fixed cog that turns the cable axle. Do this by first lifting a greasy bar, that crosses the top of the winch, to allow the cags to move. Remove the handle if attached. Now pull the cable down to your boat. On the way, it will probably necessary to route it through a pulley attached to a ring embedded in the hard about 30 feet in front of the winch. You will find the pulley with a chain by the winch. Carry these (only about one cwt) to the ring and chain the pulley ta it. Having attached the cable to your trolley, walk all the way back to the winch. Engage gear. There are two gears. The cone you want you get by lifting the greasy bar and sliding the handle axle, which carries a small cog, so this cog engages the large fixed cog. Flip the ratchet over to its operating position. Attach the handle and wind, and wind, ad nauseam. There are some instructions on the side af the winch that you probably ought to read. Let it be known that I represent all the Handicap Fleet, racers and norn-racers alike. Finally, on behalf of the monohull Fleets, I would like to give a big thank you toa the Cat sailors and others who put so much work and time into running the Regatta. Their best efforts were frustrated by a lack cf winds, but we appreciate very much what was done and a good time was had by all. The lst episode of the log of the "Barbara Starr" makes amusing reading, for obviously the lady-author was yet another of the long-suffering wives who loyally set out to ‘enjoy’ her husband's main passion in life - cruising. ‘The lady-author is not identified in this episode, but her opening sentences undoubtedly set the scene with some accuracy: " Friday, 15.8.74. 21.00 hrs: Finds us in the dinghy motoring to the "Barbara Starr", clad in all our wet weather gear. I even have my umbrella up. ‘The rain is pouring down as though punishing us for the sins of our forefathers." The start of the voyage next day does not seem to bring any greater joy; "Being a nervous inexperienced sailor I'm getting the wind up. "Where's my life jacket ?". Bench Head coming up..........The boat is rolling, so is my tummy, but Cliff is enjoying it. It's all right for him, he can swim." Things are obviously going fram bad to wo.......... well,I leave it to your imagination as our author continues "Apples and oranges rolling around the cabin floor. Bad housekeeping...... even the dinghy is trying to jump aboard. I'm scared to death. Going to retire to my bourdoir with a fit of the vapours for a while." It was reported that same £2,400 was taken over the bar, reception and galley during Regatta and a special "thank you" was extended to Ron and Mary Greygoose for their organisation of the marquee (beer tent ?) over the whole weekend. It seems that the "Camping and Cadet Week" followed the Regatta weekend with organised activities and tuition for the Cadets each day. The report on the Cadet week revealed 23 Cadets taking their Elementary Day Boat Certificate, of whom 15 passed. The practical tests were taken in Force 5 winds, heavy seas and cold weather. Of the successful 15 cadets, 4 were young ladies. Finally, Brenda Tate reports a "Batchelor thrash" for the cnuiser-crowd off the coast of France; whether this was the Mirrormen's 'thrash' to the Solent which had somehow taken a wrong turning is not clear - but I suspect it was a separate group of 'thrashers' doing their bit to achieve immortality in Navigans. Mike Boreham we eisiekicick 40 Yeara Ago —-_ May, June and July, 1954 May - The hulk of an old mine—sweeper had shifted and was obstructing the beach in front of the clubhouse in Heybridge Basin. The Water Bailiff suggested the club ask Maldon District Council to move it —- but the Council replied they'd already asked the owner to move it and would, if necessary, try to enforce its removal. Eventually a letter from the Council intimates that a sufficiently high tide to move the hulk would not occur until late August/early September (1954), but the owner had been advised he should remove heavy timbers beforehar so as to make it easier to move the (lightened) hulk when the time came. In the meantime, the club had also written to Maldon Distruct Council about the use of a nearby earthen wharf. Again, the Council were not able to help directly but were helpful (to a certain extent) by advising that ownership was "....rather vague."" The wharf was, in fact, owned by May & Butcher (from whom the club rented its clubhouse) but it seems that (i) the Catchment Board were responsible for the sea wall, (ii) the River Authority were responsible for the foreshore. However, the ‘demarcation lines' and appropriate proportions of who was responsible for what was, so it seams '...rather vague’. However, M & B had no objection to the club using the wharf provided they were willing to vacate it if, and when, M & B wanted it for ship-breaking work, The suggestion was made to hold a rally during July; was this effectively the fore-runner of Regatta ? Similarly, the circulation of a News Sheet to all members might well be regarded as a somewhat remote precursor of Navigans. Mike Boreham

COMMODORE’S NOTES Life has still been just as hectic, I’m afraid, so there is going to be a certain lack of deathless prose yet again. However, there are a couple of things that I would like to mention. One is that the end for the NRA works looks ta be definitely in Sight! Obviously there will be a grea deal of tidying up and putting right (particularly the road) to be done, but you may rest assured the team are on their case. Secondly, I have a little bit of a gripe. I am very happy for anyone to come up with Suggestions for ways of improving the Club and its facilities. However, there are correct channels to go through to do so, in that the items should be taken up through your Fleet Captain in the first case, and that indivudual will go through the Sailing Sub or (if appropriate) to the Clubhouse team for them to consider. Recent correspondence in Navigans concerning winches is a case in point. The Main Committee has considered this item, with all its ramifications. Articles in Navigans do nothing to help athe discussions. Most things have come up for consideration at some stage ard the experience of the Committee is very broad-based and long-standing. Consequently, we make decisions based on a full appreciation of ALL the facts. If we keep on getting contentious comments, then Navigans will have to be edited in the formal sense of the word. As most of you will know, I’ve sold the Prindle!! A nice final sail on Grd July, and it passed peacefully into the hands of Mike Styles. I hope you get the enjoyment out of it that I have, Mike. I’m hoping to join the ranks of the Bedstead Flyers (i.e. Sail a Hobie 17, wings and all). Watch out for the poor old chap whilst he’s learning to sail it!. As always, Larry and Colin did a superb job in running the event. A ’Thank You’ toa them and the other Club Members who did duties.
