A DIFFERENT VIEW FROM THE REAR These notes should have beer written last month but I plead pressure of work and hape you will understand why they are late! The good news! Some cof you may be aware that the Club took space at the East Coast Boat Show this year. the objectives were to maintain a high profile for the club and to recruit new members. This year membership is down slightly and to avoid the possibility of raising subscriptions in the future it was decided ta ‘speculate toa accumulate’. by al accounts the show was a spectacular success and our stand created a lot of attention with the potential of a number of new members. I must thank all of the following for their support and hard work:- Ron Greygoose: Providing a video highlighting the activities of the club. Clive & Jack Rusbridge: Providing transport for displays and video equipment to and from Burnham as well as manning the stand on Friday! Steve Hill for organising the display boards. John Weedon for providing a wide variety of photographs highlighting all of the club’s activities. Bob & Elsie Anderson, Peter & Jean Flook, Ron and Mary Greygoose, Mike Smith, Murry Bates, Mike Helewell and Hilary Ashley, Tom and Debbie Duckmanton, Steve and Liz Hill and Anthony Smith: for manning the stand during the show. Regatta and the Dart 15 and Solo open meeting have all happened very successfully thanks to the help and support of a large number of people. My grateful thanks to you all. The positions of A and C marks have been the subject of discussion and transects have been agreed so that they should be laid in their usual positions next year. It is possible that they may be moved during camping fortnight! It seems that the more senior members of certain fleets are finding it rather taxing making their way up Goldhanger Creek ta find C mark! Now the bad news! Some of us are not aware of the IRPCAS! (International Regulations for Preventing Collisions At Sea). It is no good standing on your rights if that action leads to a collision and worse still serious damage and or injury! By all means hail but be prepared to alter course if the other party has not seen/heard yau or worse still does not understand the problem. If possible try and contact the person after the incident and explain why he/she was in the wrong and what they should have done.( Try and be as diplomatic as possible!) If this is not possible contact a club official with a view ta involving other organisations. Good sailing and see you on the water. Colin Kidner.

6. Handicap Fleet News - Jackpot and Mona's Cup Another Sunday of glorious racing. What’s more, we had a half decent turnout of eight boats on the start line. In the second race, Claire Davies managed to rig her Laser and we were nine! Laura and I put in a creditable performance at long last. Home for a barbecue, a bottle of wine, and life seems worth living again. Please keep it up! It was so nice to have enough boats out that everyone was competing with someone. Welcome back to Howard Yourig in his Fireball. His last year was a sabbatical racing cruisers. He’s got a new crew, through Navigans, Mark Johnson. Good luck to you both. I should also mention Peter Woodhouse, new this year, in his green Laser. He began the season gcing for my number of capsizes record, but is now staying upright = and looking for race honours. Graham Richmond in his Hornet is losing his crew Sam Ashley with trapeze-knees, but he hopes to get a replacement in quick-sticks. Jack Rusbridge at last had his GP 14 out today, although I hardly recognised it; he’s painted and varnished and it looks a real treat. Mind you only three layers of varnish, whereas Laura’s dad used to do six layers every year with rubbing down between each layer! And Claire rigging a Laser? Yes, she’s now got a Laser Radial and is getting to grips with it. I’m sure she’1l soon be giving us, and particularly Mark Bulkeley with his Radial, a bit of stiff competition. Oh, I'd quite forgotten why I’m writing this article. Yes, it’s to tell you about some races and why you must sail them. Two races, the Jackpot (Sunday 24 July) = and Mona’s Cup (Sunday 18 September) both go to Maldon and back. Those of you who da not want to sail in circles and triangles, these races are for you. They are also ideal for the slower handicap boats because you arrive at Maldon at high tide and therefore you do not battle against the tide going there or coming back. The tide is unfair toa you in normal Club races, but here it is definitely in your favour. All boats take part in these races and you can still join in the Jackpot even if the helm is not over 40 years of age, although if you aren’t you won’t win the trophy. Basically, these races take you down between the channel markers until you get ta No 10 = buoy that you go around leaving it to starboard and then come back again. Your ‘Sailing Instructions for Club Racing’ details the course, but it makes it look complicated which it is not. Is there a No. 5S buoy? It’s shown opposite No. 6 on the back of the Year Book, but my chart of the river shows this buoy to be Na. 7. By the way, the ever numbers are the red port laterals and, guess what, the odds are the green starboard laterals. Oh, I nearly forgot to mention that the Jackpot is in two legs since we stop for lunch at the Osea SC. This means we arrive like a Normandy landing on their little sandy beach, much to the amazement of the sunbathers, where we pull the boats out of the water. And why is it Mona’s Cup? The Year Book says it is in memory of the landlady of the Jolly Sailor at Heybridge Basin. I think the race once used to goa ta the Jolly Sailor where the competitors stopped for lunch. One boat that should enter these races is Toby Hampden-Acton’s Drabscombe Dabber. This boat fascinates me. It has, apart from the jib and mainsail, a little sail on a mast (the mizzen?) at the stern of the boat. He told me it had a loose-footed mainsail and I said mine was loose-footed as well. But then he told me it didn’t have a boom, and I thought he was pulling my leg. Apparently, this was commen on the old working boats where the mainsail could be dragged over the cargo when they tacked or gybed. One problem, if he races, as the boat hasn’t got a Portsmouth Number! Alas, he intends to sell it; he has problems getting it in and out of the water and doesn’t want to use the winch. Jackpot and Mona’s Cup, don’t forget! Don Gill, Handicap Fleet Captain, 0245 [redacted]. The elderly Pisces belonging to the junior branch of the Ball family is looking goad with a fresh coat of paint in a new colour on its deck. The first launch will = show whether they’ve managed to cure its penchant for taking water intca the hull cavity. When it came to naming the boat, all my suggestions of fishy names (what’s wrong with *Captain Haddock’......?) were rejected and the resident history student came up with the name of Wulfmaer. An appropriate name for a boat on cur part of the Blackwater being that af an Anglo Saxon warrior who died in the Battle of Maldon on 10th August 991, valiantly helping to make life for the Vikings at least a little inconvenient. Ed.

A Different View From the Rear..... If you are one of those people who think that sport is Only for the younger members of society, let me tell you otherwise! On Saturday 9th July I drove the Jack B for the Sea Vets meeting. These folk are Windsurfers who race every twa weeks at venues centred around Reading. They divide themselves into three categories, Seniors who are 38+; Vets 50+; and Super Vets 60+. There were 7 Seniors, 10 Vets and 3 Super Vets competing. Clive and John Rusbridge organised and ran the event, which consisted of four races round a triangular course off Osea Island. The start was delayed due to lack of wind but things improved and a Force & to 3 breeze eventually arrived. Those folk who are used to tidal conditions had few problems but one or two pecaple were caught out trying to get round A-mark and landed up amongst the Cruisers. The prize wirmners were as follows: Ist Overall lst Senior John Smith end Overall ist Veteran Peter Selway end Senior Tan Edgeway end Veteran Terry Adcock ist Lady Joyce Haywood ist Super Vet Dennis Haywood The efforts of Race Officers, Support Crews ard Galley Staff were alse recognised with gifts of wine or flowers. Jean Flook kindly presented the prizes. On the 24th July it was the Jackpot, the event in the Club calendar for those of us over 40! As last year, we stopped off at Osea Sailing Club for lunch, and again excellent refreshments were provided. I offered to take Hugh Davies for a ride as Dick was taking Pamela with him. I was kept entertained on the way up, principally with a count-down to lunch and food and on the way back Hugh appeared to have little faith in my helming as he was convinced that we were going to be the last Dart 15 home! Oh ye of little faith! We were in fact first Dart 15 home and third in the Jackpot! If Hugh doesn’t put on too much weight before next year’s race I may well take him again. Willie Pitcairn ard I are off to the Dart 15 Nationals at Sandersfoot next week. Watch this space! See you on the water. Colin Kidner. JACK B — SUMMER REFIT. FAST CAT NOTES 9. Maybe thick fog will be the next variety of weather to be thrown at Piers Race entrants, or possibly snow... with the ridiculous wind against tide conditions this year’s race brought, many competitors will be hoping for an improvement next year. However for those that were lucky enough to avoid both gear failure and collisions with either the emerging spits or other boats, the Force 6 easterly with the rapidly ebbing tide led to a challenging race that few will forget quickly. It has been fabled that spinnakers lift the bows of catamarans... | remain to be convinced. The fleet of 103 started with the expectation of sailing the full course, but it quickly became apparent that although the conditions were quite sailable for the leaders there might well prove to be problems in ensuring the safety of all competitors. The severe and very short chop making conditions difficult for the mother boats on their stations across the mouth of the Colne conspired with the high number of early casualties to convince our Commodore (whose company on the water was sorely missed this year by the few Dart 18 sailors present) to shorten course at the Bradwell gate. Although the significance of the various signals to be made by the Race Committee had been very clearly explained at what | thought was an excellent briefing, it was not until a number of the leading boats had reached the gate that a lemming-like urge to brave the waves and turn back downwind gripped the fleet. Paul (Metcalfe, who, being not pregnant, had kindly agreed to crew with me) and |, observing with some concern as we approached the windward mark the extreme spinnaker-induced bend in the mast of one of the leaders, decided not to fly the kite, a decision which lasted only until we remembered the aforementioned fable... clearly the spinnaker was going to make the ride home much more relaxing. Perhaps relaxing was not the right word, but it certainly proved to be a memorable experience, although at the time we felt that we had failed to make up the handicap penalty of 2% that our sail plan cost us. Probably our performance was not helped by the need, with our sadly limited sail handling ability developed in many hours of practice, to start the spinnaker-dropping process half a mile before the leeward mark. Again, in spite of Larry and Charles’s excellent briefing, the leaders showed some hesitation in returning up the course for the signalled second lap, but apart from the minority who, perhaps wisely, decided that one ordeal was sufficient for what might otherwise have been an unremarkably pleasant Sunday, the fleet thrashed its way back up to Bradwell and enjoyed another sleigh-ride to the finish line. The full results are printed elsewhere within these covers; my congratulations go to all who finished either one or two laps of the course, and my commiserations to those who were unlucky enough to suffer damage. My particular interest in the race was the handicap system to be used; for the first time in a significant UK event we used the ’French’ system adopted by the IYRU Multihull Committee, which gives time correction factors based upon measurement of the vessels only, and not upon past performance (unlike the PY system traditionally used in the UK). To ask which system is ’fairer’ is, | believe, to miss the point. Different classes will always have sailors with different levels of skill, will perform better in different conditions, and will prefer different courses; it will never be possible, to the precision needed to distinguish the two systems, to measure the accuracy of the performance predictions they offer. However | believe the IYRU system can dispense with the argument that under the PY system, for example, "the Prindle handicap is falsely increased by the low standard of its sailors" (palpably true though that may be) and, in addition, can readily allow handicaps to be calculated for a variety of boat configurations, thus allowing the IYRU system to be perceived as fairer and more equitable. Conversely the I[YRU system, like the IOR before it, could lead to designs being evolved to take specific advantage of its peculiarities, leading perhaps to less manageable or less seaworthy catamarans. Also, the Portsmouth Number of a class can vary from year to year, whilst its |YRU TCF will not; whether this is an advantage or not | am not sure. Inspection of the results shows what | feel is a healthy mix of classes at the top of the fleet, although the two Hobie Miracles were convincing in their victory. On balance | feel that the [YRU system is the way forward, being widely used on the continent, and the majority of those competing this year seemed to welcome its use. Further analysis of the figures must await a later edition of Navigans. As always at this time, thanks must go to the band of organisers who again managed to make the event a thoroughly enjoyable, well-run and professional affair. Although | will not attempt to mention them all, | must especially thank Steve and Debbie Glynn for all that they have contributed over several years of Piers Races. The race has become a major event in an international calendar - this year 16 competitors crossed the channel to enter - and the organisation has evolved to match it. As always, the RYA Seamanship Foundation stands to gain from the event, and through it the Piers Race has become, over the years, the single largest supporter of Sailing for the Disabled. Next year Steve and several others are stepping down from the ECPR committee, and Mike Duckmanton (or Duckman, as he is known to his many television fans) is taking over as chairman; please, if you feel you can offer a little of your time in any part of the race organisation, give Mike or Steve a call. John Nickalls

li. FAST CAT NOTES More statistics As promised, or threatened, | have passed the Piers Race results through the trusty PC in an effort to establish how valid the handicapping system may have been. The resulting graph is reproduced here, although | would hesitate to suggest that it reveals much. A lone Dart 15 is visible off to the 11500 right, and the somewhat tardy | arrival of a certain Prindle 18-2 is sitet | recorded at the top of the graph. It are | is clear that the bulk of the 7 = entrants had handicaps around 2 10000 | ". 100, and the imaginative reader 2 | “ might agree with my optimistic Ss 1 . opinion that the distribution of 52. | 7) és points shows no obvious trend,as 8 | " ' . one reads across the graph, either 8500 1» upward or downward, i.e. there is | s no obvious bias in the handicaps wt 7 aie resulting in all the slower boats — , doing particularly badly or . 90 95 100 105 110 115 120 125 130 135 140 particularly well on corrected time. HANDICAP Certainly | heard no complaints about the handicap system with which we experimented this year, and | hope that we will continue to use it for the Piers Race in the future. Our results will be fed back to the [YRU and the RYA, and | anticipate we will see further events using the system in coming seasons. How hard to compete? Some months ago | mused over how strictly we should apply the rules when we are racing, and suggested that we have to be careful that the competitiveness of our sailing and the extent to which we seek to exploit the rules for tactical advantage, whilst adding a valuable extra dimension to our sailing, should not vary so much across the fleet as to lead to ill-feeling or even damage. Over the August Bank Holiday weekend | clearly misjudged the mood of the fleet sailing at the time and | apologise to Brian and Roy for the violent luff | made when they started to overtake our boat to windward on an offwind leg; although | hailed loudly, the luff was Clearly felt to be unnecessary (although no contact was made between us). Judging from the comments made in the bar afterwards, however, perhaps | ought to explain why | did what | did, and why| felt justified. Rule 39.2 reads "After starting..., a yacht clear ahead or a leeward yacht may luff as she pleases unless the windward yacht has been mast abeam at any time during the overlap". Rule 35 reads "... the right of way yacht shall not alter course... except... when luffing as permitted by rule 39.2.". All text books on the subject cover this area in some depth, and will show that a leeward yacht may luff as abruptly as the helmsman wishes and without warning (until the mast abeam position, or an obstruction, is reached); certainly no hail is required. | am not suggesting that we should go onto the water with the intention of hitting each other, but the point of these rules is to allow the leeward yacht a defence against a boat overtaking to windward and blianketing it; the result is that, to pass successfully and in safety, the overtaking yacht must position itself a considerable distance to windward. To quote Mary Pera, "If W is so rash as to put herself in a position where L can hit her, she has only herself to blame." In previous races at the Club, applying these rules (without hailing in some cases) has been accepted without comment (and I'm sure many have heard me assault them with a cry of mast abeam as| try desperately to overtake). | know there are others who will use these rules; | suggest that the only safe way to overtake to windward (certainly if one leaves the sheltered confines of club racing) is to keep a safe distance away and a good lookout under the sail, hailing mast abeam when the leeward yacht's mast is abeam the helmsman in his normal position (but see Rule 39, and others, as well as the definition of mast abeam for details), at which point the overtaken yacht must bear off to a proper course. It is worth noting that luffing applies also on windward legs; if on a light wind day you are drifting close-hauled and some fiend catches a puff and starts to overhaul you close to windward you may luff and touch him. If you succeed, he faces a 360° penalty (although you may only luff as far as close-hauled, that being your proper course, unless you have remained ahead of mast abeam). Again, the moral is keep your distance when overtaking to windward. There are plenty of people competing both within and outside the Club who will use the freedom the rules very deliberately and specifically give. John Nickalls

13. 7MORNING FLIGHT’ —- 1994 CRUISE Hi Everyore. We are just about to set sail for Spain so it seems a good time to let you know how we are getting on so far. We left Suffolk Yacht Harbour on the 7th June for what should have been a gentle shakedown cruise across the Thames Estuary, but turned into something more challenging. We hastily put in a reef, dug cut the seasick pills ard got into a more seamanlike mode! We called in at Ramsgate for a well-earned rest and then went on to Brighton pausing only ta wait for the tide in Dover. The Weather was really grotty, cold, wet and grey. Sarah’s dad came down tea Brighton for a couple of days for a final briefing (and to bring further essential Supplies, namely, 48 bags of crisps for Dave and 1550 teabags for Sarah!) We left Brighton with the wind abaft the beam for the first time all trip, and headed to Dartmouth. All was going beautifully until we switched the engine on to motar into the river and our brand new engine disappeared in clouds of smoke and steam!! It would have helped if the engine-overheating light had worked. We got towed into Dartmouth by a Hurley 22, anchored up the river and set about fixing it. We were anchored up the river above Dartmouth, it was brilliantly hot, quiet (except when the tripper boats went by giving an amplified commentary) and very pretty. Unfortunately we then discovered that the engine problem was recurring and the boatman kindly put us in touch with a local marine engineer. Even more unfortunately he needed the beat out of the water to work on it, and the yard where he was based was owned by the dreaded MDL. Before we had time to take out a second mortgage, however, we discovered that they had a special offer on - lift out, up to 2 weeks on the hard and lift in for £60 all-in - so it ended up cheaper than if we had stayed anchored in the Dart. Although it was a bit frustrating, particularly being out of the water, the weather continued ta be glorious and we took the chance to get a lot of jobs done as well as cycling and walking and going to the pub to commiserate with other people who were Similarly stuck in the boatyard. It 1S Surprising how long it takes to da the simplest jobs when it’s hat, the telephones aren’t ringing, and you have as much time as you want. I found it could take me all morning just to cycle up to the village shop for fresh milk ard bread! Dave managed ta fix the heads (which had not been working since we set off), installed a refrigeration unit in the cold box and a fan. I made the canvas cover for our bimini tap (a sort of fixed umbrella which covers the cockpit area at head height for keeping the worst of the sun off us when we get to tropical climes) and various other sewing jobs. We also made shelves and more storage for the forecabin, and I sorted out all the stores, made copicus lists, and goat the forecabin into a reasonably habitable condition. Those of you who came to Suffolk Yacht Harbour to see us off will remember that we had to keep the door toa the forecabin firmly shut to prevent all the stuff piled up in there escaping, but now there’s room for Derek to get in his bunk when he = arrives to sail with us across the Atlantic! We alse spent a lot of time fixing the varicus small but irritating deck leaks we have. Not entirely successful and I suppose that eventually we shall have toa take off the toerail and reseal it, but we are trying to put off the evil day, as it’s rather a big job on our boat. The last evening we were in the Dart we came across Brian and Jacky on Natasha IV from MSC. Small world!! They have retired too and are spending the summer cruising the West Coast. We were sorry to leave Devon because we liked the places and also the people whe seemed very friendly and helpful but decided we must press on and spent the next week or so cruising the Cornish rivers. We found Salcombe somewhat yuppified but loved the Yealm River and also enjoyed Foawey ard the Helford River. Both banks of the Yealm are forested and owned by the Woodland and National Trusts so that you can walk in them. We have found that a lot of the coastline and river banks are privately owned, which makes it jolly difficult ta get ashore legally sometimes (theugh Dave doesn’t worry unduly about that!) let alone walk. We bought a brand new outboard in Fowey, Dave having only just been restrained from chucking our old one into the sea when, as well as either not starting or stopping for no apparent reason, it started giving him electrical shocks. I was safe - it wouldn’t do anything for me at all. Our new one is a Mercury 2.5 and I have no trouble starting it and it runs fine. No doubt it won’t last but it’s pretty luxurious at the moment - I haven’t had ta row anywhere for days. Contd. ....

14. We spent a couple of days in Falmouth getting some last-minute chandler y, restocking food and booze and doing the laundry. That all becomes quite a chore when you have tc lug everything ashore, onto bicycles , uphill ta the laundere tte and back. — The weight, particul arly of the booze, 1s enough to make you teetotal !! We fourd the chores day far more exhausting than sailing in cur current rather laid-bac k style. We then sailed on to the Scillies, highly recommended tc us and living up to tide it. The islands are a series of jagged rocks - some inhabited and some not. As the goes out the landscape changes dramatica lly as more sharptoot hed rocks appear, giving an almost lunar appearance - I could sit and watch for hours! The islands have a lot of visitors but have managed ta avoid becoming touristy mainly because the attractions are the scenery, flowers, birds, and fishing. Surprisingly most of the yachts here are French, and their anchoring techniques have led to a slight cocling ain the "“entente cordiale", Dave having started off by calling me intolerant and ended up swearing (under his breath of course, preserving his stiff upper lip) as we re- anchored yet again. We met up with an old colleague of his, Gordon Bilsborough from Nimrod days, whe is now assistant harbour master in St Mary’s here. Not only that, but it turned out that he and Jane used to live in St Albans and their solicitors were --- Woolley and Westorn!! Dave has row got his SSB rig set up after a few experiments with different aerial arrangements and is chatting away happily to the world (mostly Europe, although contact with the UK is patchy. We usually catch the Maritime Mobile net either ir the morning or evening and have joined it. Our callsign is GOTAG if anyone wants to call us. We have listened out for Stan in the Med on Tuesday mornings but haven't yet heard him - we shall keep trying. Sarah’s dad has been provided with a receiver sco he should be able to hear us transmitting sometimes. We won't really start transmitting much until we get down to Spain. It’s certainly a way of making friends. Last night we were sitting in the main cabin when there was a knocking on the hull and a couple from the next boat appeared. It transpired that they were keen radio hams, had heard us transmitting from the Scillies and had been keeping a bit of a lookout for us. They have certainly taken to the cruising life. They first went to the Med in a 31 ft boat with their 3 small girls and stayed for 9 months. wher: the money ran cut they came back, saved, bought a bigger boat and set off again - for three and a half years before having to return. Later they managed another couple of years and have been in the UK for the last 3 years getting ready to go again! They always took the girls and taught themselves using correspondence classes - one of the girls took her O Levels in the British Embassy in Turkey! Just shows what carn be dore if you set your mind to it - also shows how you can be bitten by this way of life! Their current boat is called "Dreamer". Sc far most of the yachties we have met have been on holiday, but at Falmouth we found a truly international meeting of boats, many of whom seemed to be long- distance. Ir, particular we met a very pleasant Dutch couple who are setting cut to cruise Spain, and then South America. The bloke spent 2 years sailing 20,000 miles in the West Indies a couple of years ago, so he was very interesting and gave us some new ideas - particularly as he felt Venezuela knocked spots off anywhere in West Indies - but currently we still plan to sail north from St Lucia via various WI islands to the OSC. Dave and I are both fine - not arguing more than usual, and in fact pretty relaxed. It’s a healthy sort of life, although you do get aches and pains in the most peculiar places and both of us had quite a lot of backache while our bodies adjusted toa sleeping on 1" thick mattresses. I am also covered with bruises, but that’s nothing unusual ! Both of us have nice brown arms, legs and faces, but the prevailing cool breeze means we are usually wearing shirts and shorts - we have had less baking hot weather than those of you in the South and East and the last two weeks have been very overcast and quite chilly. We went sea fishing the other night and I actually wore a thick jumper as well as a lined cilskin jacket and still felt chilly when the sun went down. It has just turned warm again though, thank gcoodress. The fishing expedition was interesting - certainly although we went along to learn how to fish to supplement our food stores, it principally reminded me that we can’t rely on catching anything wher ever the "experts" are having trouble. The launch was about 50 ft long and the keen anglers congregated at the front. When we eventually found some fish they were launching themselves onto the experts’ hooks with gay abandon, but none on Contd...»

15. curs! Eventually the boat owner decided to show all us tyros how it was done, and he couldn’t catch anything either!! We reckoned that as the boat slipped backwards on the tide, the fish whe were caught at the front were warning the others!!! It was jolly goad fun though, and we did at least learn the theory (and giving credit where due, Dave actually caught = pollock simultaneously). We have also managed to get in a bit of culture (no, I haven’t managed tc get Dave into a museum yet, but I’m working on it). We went ta a film show about the history and wildlife of the Scillies one evening and also went across to the Island of Tresco for a Jazz and Classical music concert in the tropical gardens there. It was actually in the part of the gardens called Valhalla which has lots of wooden painted figureheads salvaged from wrecked ships of the 17th and 18th centuries. Considering what had happened to them they were a curiously cheerful locking bunch! Well, that’s about all the news for now. We are sitting here in the Scillies waiting for a nice North or Westerly wind te give us a civilised reach/run down to Spain and will send another report from there. We do think about you all sometimes and if anybody would like to write we’d love to hear from you. The best way is toa send the letters (stamped for Europe until October) to Sue Carr, [redacted] St Albans, Herts, and she will forward them on to us. Most of the time we will be Poste Restante, but when we can, we will give a Marina or Cafe address, as it’s more reliable, but we can’t do that until we get to the places and suss them out befare ringing Sue! Regards, ard fair sailing from Sarah, Dave and ’Morning Flight’. St Mary’s, Isles of Scilly, Friday 2é@nd July 1994.

BETTY BEAVINS Betty Beavins passed away peacefully in Monday 24th October 1994 after a short illness. the Marconi Sailing Club was her second home and after sailing a Blandford twelve-footer with my father at Heybridge we as a family followed the Club to Stansgate. Dinghy racing became local cruising for Mum and Dad in their Pandora. When Dad passed away 16 years ago, Mum continued to come to the Club and seemed a permanent presence at the top of the Hard, sitting with her sister Connie and their friends, and ever ready to chat to anyone and everyone. Everytime we returned to my mooring, Jan and | would look for Mum. She always watched us come and go, and if we got any manoeuvresa little wrong, we would discuss the reasons later! She was always interested in everything and everyone. | will always look for her when | return to the Club with warm memories of a wam person and remember her wonderful understanding of life's patterns and how, when the shock and grief is past, she would want all of us to celebrate the quality of her life. Thank you all for your expressions of sympathy. Nik, Clare and Sarah Beavins. Batty Beavins - ...... The Funeral Service, which took place on 1st November was a celebration of her lively and cheerful approach fo life. She was involved in many charitable and supportive activities, as well as being a longtime member of the Marconi Sailing Club. Some of our older members will remember her husband, Ken, who died in February 1979. He was a keen GP14 sailor, and Committee Member, and wrote the ‘Observer’ column in Navigans. Together they did much to create the family atmosphere of the Club as we know it today. A measure of the regard with which they were held was the presence at the Service of some of our longest serving and past members, including Stan Allerton, David Polley and Fred Partlett together with their wives; Elsie and Leonie; and other members of more recent times. Mary and | will remember her most for her indomitable spirit and her infectious laugh as she took her weekly swim from the Hard. The Club has made a donation on behalf of the general membership, but if inidviduals would like to make a personal contribution, the family request was that any donations could be made to the "Macmillan Nurses Fund" and sent c/o the Co-Operative Funeral Service, 13-15 Market Hill, Maldon. COMMODORE'S REPORT Last year | commented on the fact that there appeared to have been no major material enhancements to our facility. | think that you will all agree with me that this year, the comment is totally the opposite. We can all see the benefit that the laying of the tracks around the site will give us through the year, with the lack of churning up of grass. Obviously we had a “one off" chance to carry out this work when the NRA finally completed their activities, and some forthright negotiations took place with the MASC in order to expedite almost £20,000 of unplanned capital expenditure. | am indebted to the contribution made in this respect by Pat Black and Neil Pembleton. The whole project was managed by Pat, and from an idea at a Committee Meeting in early September to project completion in mid October, is an excellent achievement. Unfortunately this may well impinge upon our capital expenditure for the rest of this financial year (ending March 1995) but | am sure that you will agree that the results are worth it. In addition this year has seen the replacement of the downstairs windows with uPVC units and the further refurbishment of the downstairs bar (at no cost to the Club). Thanks are due to Steve Glynn and Mike Smith respectively. Moving on to our relationship with MASC. This took a significant turn for the better when Peter Woodhouse replaced Norman Cox as Chairman. | was suddenly able to talk on a more business-like basis and to get my voice heard in a different way. We have just concluded an honest and open agreement with MASC that covers our contribution until 1999. My other colleagues will comment on the events of the year, but | feel that there are two areas on which | must comment specifically. Firstly the Laying Up Supper. In 1992 this was an event that was dying, but die to the efforts of Steve and Debbie Glynn in 1993 the event has become once again a "proper Club occasion. This year as well looks like being another enormous success. If we only get together socially as a Club on one occasion per year, then this has to be the occasion. The mix of attendees from the various fleets is excellent and shows that our true strength as a Club lies in our "diversity with a common purpose”. Secondly, | should like to comment on the ECPR. This event is the major flag-waving event for the Club, and has made us the largest continuing contributor to the Seamanship Foundation. It is now an international event, and has placed us in the forefront of small multihull Clubs. | am not taking for granted the huge amount of support and effort given by everyone to the ECPR committee, and would like to publicly thank every member of the Club for the support that they give. Having undertaken this position for two years, | am about to enter my final year as Commodore. My personal mission is to continue to make life easier for all the volunteers who contribute to the Club by their efforts. In this respect we already see the installation of a powered winch on the Mooring Barge, and a new Membership PC (with hopefully a new system soon to follow). | promised last year that the investment in continuing to ease the load of individuals would continue, and within the constraints of the issues of capital, this will remain. However, no matter how much kit we buy, the jobs are ultimately done by people. At the moment the difficulty comes in planning possible successors for particular positions. Next year we will be faced by the end of Colin Kidner's term of office as well as my own. To ensure true continuity it is vital that possible successors are identified early in order to immerse them to some extent in the activities of the Committee. This is not a "Committee stitch-up" but a genuine desire on the part of every one of us to see the Club Management having some form of stability. Projects and policy take time to develop, and a Parliamentary swing from right to left and back every few years is a waste of resources. | am very happy to talk to anyone on a strictly confidential basis about any ambitions they may have in this respect. There is one particular subject that | have left until the end, and that is my personal thanks to all my colleagues on the Executive and Main Committees. Each one of them has contributed in a positive and thoughtful way to debate throughout the past year. Some of them have carried out an enormous amount of work on our behalf, and | have no hesitation here in singling out Frank Bennett. It is the end of one era, though, with Steve Glynn coming to the end of his term of office. During the three years of his tenure, the practical advances within his portfolio are legion. Not only has he carried out many of the activities himself, but his pragmatic input at the planning stages has been invaluable. | place on record my gratitude for his efforts. Obviously | have singled out a couple of colleagues for special thanks, but it would be iniquitous were | not to thank them all for their continuing support and efforts over the year. Thank You. Larry Botheras

NAVIGANS PAST He ee i i i 2 oe 2k 2 This chapter of Navigans Past is dedicated to the memory of Betty Beavins whose recent death leaves not only many sad friends and relations, but also severs yet another link with what many might regard as the heyday of the ‘old-style’ Marconi Sailing Club. Maggie and I cannot claim to have known Betty for many years. Indeed, we have only really got to know Betty and her sister, Connie Bigden, since the publication of Navigans Past and then only in the sense that we always took pleasure in passing a few minutes chatting with Betty and Connie on most Sundays at the club during the season. Betty always seemed to be full of fun and the enjoyment of life; she was always a joy to talk to and pass the time of day. Such was her sense of fun and humour that I am sure she would have been delighted, and in agreement with, the mis-typing in the October Navigans which described her as 'Batty' Beavins; Betty would have liked that. Betty will be missed. Maggie and I will always think of the area on the hard by the winch box-covers as ‘Betty's place’ and remember her with great pleasure. 2 oe oe oe i oi 2 2 1976 (July - December) - Marconi's Mirrormen made their presence felt in more ways than 'won'. - In the meantime, we think it was Eileen who again exposes the ups and downs of taking to the high seas. July - a rather thin Navigans issue with not much exciting content to comment upon some 18 years later. Rick Anstey (Cadet Captain) reveals that the Cadet Series is ‘wide open' with 3 different winners in the 3 races held so far. August - no Navigans due to the holiday period. September - Brenda Tate records the entry of two new members to the club, quite literally ‘just born to it'; they are Colin Cherry (introduced by Wendy and Tony Cherry) and Nicholas David Turner (nominated by Rosemary and Mike Turner). Marconi Cadet Member, Malcolm Hutchins, won the Sea Cadet Mirror Sailing Trophy for his Division and then went on to win the Sea Cadet Midland District Trophy. Mersea Week saw much success for other Marconi Mirror sailors. Marconi's Mirrors were not only Ist, 2nd and 3rd in the Dabchicks Points Series but also in the Round Mersey Race (Mirror Fleet), Dabchicks Regatta, Mersea Town Regatta and the West Mersea Regatta in which Frank Savill also took Ist in the Solo class and John Weedon (presumably in the 420) came Ist in the Handicap Fleet. Still with the active Mirrormen, Marconi held a Mirror Open in September which attracted 27 entries and in which Ray Hampson took 3rd overall. Outside the sailing activity, a more somber view of the club is revealed as John Weedon (Commodore)warns of the cost of repairs to the road and other expenses about to be encountered:- Road Repairs £ 250 Hard Repairs £ 400 Workboat Engine (replacement) £ 450 Current engine repairs £ 100 This is to be Editor Brenda Tate's last Navigans issue and we can still say "Well done and thanks, Brenda" to a member of a ‘club sailing family’ who were always at the centre of sailing and social activity during their time with the club. The new Editor is to be Shirley Wood.

October - Shirley admits to not being a very active member to date and thus she seems to have ‘jumped in with both feet and into the deep end’ all at the same time. Again, Marconi's Mirrors feature in the sailing results. In the club's Mona's Cup race to Heybridge and back, the first 3 places were filled by Mirrors with Ray and Katie Hampson (1st), Roy and Richard Battye (2nd) and Dave and Colin Harper (3rd) out of a total entry of 25 boats. Helmsman of the Year was sailed in Mirrors and was won by Rob Swale (crewed by Colin Harper) with Chris Weedon 2nd (crewed by Deborah Harper) and Ray Hampson 3rd (crewed by Julian Hampson). Summer Points Series Results were:- Hornets: John Tillotson 11 races, av. entry 4.3 9 helms Enterprise: Rob Swale 14 races, av. entry 5.7 14 helms Mirror: Ray Hampson 14 races, av. entry 12.9 28 helms Handicap: John Weedon 14 races, av. entry 7.9 26 helms November - John Weedon notes the declining numbers attending the Laying Up Supper and warns that either the price will rise or the club will have to absorb the deficit (all sounds familiar, doesn't it; ‘problems’ are obviously cyclic in nature). The venue had, in recent times, been the MASC in order to accommodate the numbers, but a smaller venue might have to be considered in the future. If I remember correctly, Maggie and I went to this Laying Up Supper with Mike and Jennie Hart. As I also remember it, the 'Mirror Crowd’ were (shall we say) rather noisy and perhaps a little (or a lot) ‘into their cups’. This ‘noisy lot’ (plus dissatisfaction with 'the Group’ hired to provide the music) gave rise to a letter of complaint to Navigans. I must admit that, although we were ‘Mirror people’, we were rather glad we were on the opposite side of the room to both the Group (Mirror) and the Group (Music) for, despite their 'best' endeavours, neither Group were too melodious with their rendering, although both were full of enthusiasm for their performances. However, our errant Mirrormen couldn't have been so bad after all and must have worked hard to rehabilitate themselves, for several of their number went on to become Flag Officers, including two Commodores at least. A ‘cruiser letter', on what was described as "...a devastating trip...", aptly illustrated the very worst feelings (literally) of small boating on big seas. The author attempts to remain anonymous, but the very amusing style of writing (and the fact that ‘the other half’ is named as Cliff) makes me suspect that Eileen Clarke had once again put pen to paper and so metaphorically placed a barnacle where she would much rather have placed a bomb - under someone's favourite antifouled bottom !! Thanks Eileen, just keep taking the sea-sick pills. The Mamgu Trophy cruiser-log winning entry was from Vic and Brenda Tate, with son Robert (then 16) who was ‘Acting Skipper’ and daughter Mary (then 6 + a bit) who was ‘Flag Officer’. The log was of a trip to Holland in a borrowed boat called "Ace of Diamonds". December - no December Navigans on file. Either they didn't publish one or 'tis lost from the Editor's archive (or I missed it out when photocopying Maureen's archive set; perhaps our Editor could tell me ?). Ed’s note: Yes, copy to come! . Mike Boreham 3 ee ke ke Y Ago - (A : ber, 1954 A letter from the Local Valuation/Rating Office states that the Yacht Store & Workshop (ie. the MSC clubhouse) had a gross value of £ 20 and ratable value of £ 12. The club had obviously written to the Maldon Borough Council with regard to the possibility of a permanent mooring for a barge. In reply, the Council invited an application but warn that permission would probably be refused in the vicinity of the present clubhouse at Heybridge, but might be agreed for a mooring opposite on Northey Island. On the strength of this, the idea of a barge HQ was abandoned and a sub-committee formed to (a) review the potential of the current clubhouse and (b) seek possible premises/sites for a clubhouse between

Heybridge and the Blackwater Sailing Club. Presumably, as part of this task, a letter reveals that the owners of the present clubhouse were not willing to sell clubhouse and adjoining cottage at this time. Alas, the owner of the minesweeper hulk failed to float it in August and is being pressed by the Council to lighten it even more so as to float it off in September. It was, indeed, finally removed from the foreshore in September. In addition, rumours suggest the Essex River Board plan to heighten the sea wall at the clubhouse and this obviously causes some concern to the club. It was decided that the President's Cup would be contested by a series of races on 16/17 October, 1954. A Newsletter (26 October) reveals the Laying Up Supper planned for 19 November at the MASC. Unfortunately, the Maldon Little Ship Club had to decline an invitation to send two representatives to the Supper since they were holding their Annual Ball on the same night. The AGM in November saw Geoff Wardell elected Commodore and Eric Cottam as Vice Commodore/Sailing Sec. A proposal to add the post of Rear Commodore was passed on the basis that since Commodore and Vice Commodore planned to race their Fleetwind dinghies most weekends, 'someone’ had to stay ashore to 'mind the shop’. It was thought a non-Fleetwind (therefore presumably non-racing) member serving as Rear Commodore would fill this need. Thus it was that Maurice Greatrex was elected Rear Commodore. The planned purchase of a 'club flattie/dinghy' for use as a tender to the club boat Avril was also ear-marked as a possible rescue boat if provided with outboard motor ! The Heybridge Basin Yacht Stores offered to pay the costs of material to renovate the slipway if the MSC provided the labour free-of-charge. It was decided that the new committee would meet on the Ist Tuesday of each month in the MASC TV Room. Presumably it was 'tough' for any MASC member who happened to want to watch TV that night ! Mike Boreham 2 2 3 2 2 2 2 ok One over the Eight is Intoxication but Three under the Eight is Confusion The recent death of Mona Clark marks yet another link with the club's origins which has slipped quietly away. Mona was landlord of The Jolly Sailor at Heybridge and no doubt enjoyed a good relationship with the MSC crowd for she donated the Mona's Cup for what was then a long distance down-river race, and is now one of our two up-river long distances races. No doubt some of our predecessors in the MSC managed to achieve ‘one over the eight’ whilst cementing our good relations with the locals at The Jolly Sailor. 1 had hoped to quote some of the ‘write up’ about Mona from the local Maldon paper but unfortunately I cannot lay my hands on it - and Maureen's deadline is today ! I would imagine the original concept of the down-river race was that it would be open to dinghies and cruisers. Thus, not only would it have been more convenient to specify that all channel markers should be observed, but also a ‘fairer playing field’ (if that's the right expression in this case) in that dinghies couldn't take a short-cut across the shallow parts whilst cruisers had to stay in the middle. Like other of our long distance races, the Mona's Cup now seems to be a ‘dinghy only’ race along with the Jackpot. It is still customary to specify “all channel markers to be observed" to this day. Unfortunately, one of the starboard (ie. green) markers is missing and has been for many years; do you know which one? _In addition, it is not uncommon for some of the competitors to accidentally miss out marks. This is not surprising for few of us sail regularly to Heybridge and the dinghies do not need to develop the habit of observing the marks as would the cruiser sailors. When I looked after the Sailing Results it was not uncommon for someone to phone me during the week after to complain that such-and-such persons did not sail the course because they missed out a mark (usually Number 7 or Number 8) and what was I going to do about it. "Nota lot”, I'd say, "you should have protested.”

8. So what's this about "Three under the Eight" ? Well, in all good faith and working on the best advice and information available to him, our 1994 race officer specified Number 5 (starboard up and Port down). Unfortunately, Number 5 hasn't been in place for years and years (I think) and he should have specified No.7. | cannot say I was particularly aware No.5 wasn't there; nor, presumably, did anyone else. Thus, not only did some boats sail ‘inside’ No.7 (not a mark on the course) but nobody could possibly have passed No.5 correctly - it didn't exist but no-one seemed to notice! I guess that, like myself, most competitors "observed all channel markers". I wonder if it would be fairer to merely specify channel markers Nos. 3, 8 and 10 for the up-river (and back) races? I'm sure we don't want to see Mona's Cup and Jackpot reduced to protests over alleged course violations; at the same time we all want to compete on a metaphorically level playing field whilst sailing through rather more real stormy waters to Heybridge and back. So where does this leave me’? Technically speaking, I suppose the 1994 Jackpot could be deemed ‘null and void' and I didn't win the 1994 Jackpot after all - shame really. To All Marine Watches: At the end of the season, just a reminder for you to remove as much property from your boats as you can. Marine crime is still commonplace (as many of you know) and it is up to all of us to do our bit to combat the criminals that prey upon us. Property marking kits are in circulation at many clubs....if you haven't seen them, ask. If your club hasn't seen a kit yet please contact us and ask to loan one. We will put you on the list and get it to you as soon as one is free. Please take a look at the attached stolen property list. Unfortunately it contains only a fraction of the property stolen in Essex this year and is only a drop in the ocean of crime that has occurred throughout the country as a whole. If you recognise any of the items mentioned, and know were they currently can be found, please tell us and w will do our best to get it to its rightful owner. We would like to remind all of those with dinghies that these need to be clearly and permanently marked. So many of them look alike that it is almost impossible for anyone other than the owners themselves to identify them. Paint names can be washed off. Screwed on plates can be unscrewed. Details need to be literally carved into a fixed feature if we stand any hope of getting them returned if lost or stolen. If you are doubtful about any purchase you are about to make we will be only too happy to check it against the stolen lists for you. It could help us in cutting down on crime and satisfy you that the sale is genuine. We at the Marine Police would like to take this opportunity to wish you all a happy and crime-free 1995. On Sunday 11 December a party of 23, made up of fleet members and spouses, attended a most enjoyable evening at the Raga Indian Restaurant (Billericay) as an end of season celebration. This was ably organised by Colin Kidner. | think | can speak for all the attendees when | say, thank you Colin! | was not privy to all of the conversations during the evening, but | feel certain not all of them revolved around sailing. | know its hard to believe but maybe there is a life outside of sailing! The speeches were refreshingly short, during which, Colin made the presentation, on behalf of the D15 ASSOCIATION, of the O.T.T. trophy to Tom Scott. In reply, Tom referred to some of the comments made in the Yachting press: Tom also reiterated some of the criteria associated with the awarding of the trophy: in particular and | quote:- "An irrepressible enthusiasm for sailing". This invoked a thunderous round of applause from those present. May this enthusiasm reign eternal. On a more general note I’m pleased to report that the fleet is growing in numbers: I'm also led to believe that at least a further two club members are looking to buy 15’s. It looks like becoming the largest single class in the club. (Hope you’re reading this Peter: private joke). All of the D15 helms old and new, have threatened to take part in club racing during the ‘95 season. There is already a lot of talk about getting boats ready for Easter. This has got to be good news. If there is anyone out there who is not yet totally convinced that a D15 is for them (I can’t imagine why) and would like a trial sail | will be most happy to oblige. Wishing you all good and successful sailing in 1995! Some highlights from the solo boat in this years Southampton based cruiser weekend. The general plan was to meet at Shamrock Quay on the River Itchen near Southampton at 18.00hrs on Friday evening. After a night on board the Sigma 38 cruiser we would sail around the Isle of Wight clockwise reaching Yarmouth late on Saturday evening. Sunday would be the final leg with racing along the Solent and Southampton water reaching home base at 16.00hrs on Sunday. The Friday night on board gave us a chance to meet our skipper Andy and generally get used to the conditions etc on board. Bunks [berths?] were selected and alarm clocks set for 06.00hrs for a 07.30 departure [groan] was required by the plan. After a good meal and a few drinks at the local it was lights out for the magnificent seven. Bunks were interesting, I "had" to tread on Malcom Stuart's head to get out of mine. Saturday was a 2-3W with drizzle but we were the first of the three Marconi cruisers out into the river Itchen. The tide tables dictated our future for if we did not make Bembridge Ledge [Eastern up of IoW to you] by 11.30hrs we would miss the tides and possibly fail. Motoring along we soon discovered the engine gave only 1/2 max speed, the three Ford engine experts [?] were sent below and after much discussion/adjusuments our speed was further reduced. The other two boats were way in front by now. A near dead run down Spithead allowed the foredeck crew a good lesson in spinnaker drill as we passed huge Napolionic forts and the impressive IloW cliffs. The lead boat was a hazy image in the distance. Bembridge Ledge passed before schedule, we had a chance of getting around! Past Sandown, Shanklin and Venmor now on a reach we seemed to make good time. The power and complexity of the tide was evidenced by many dramatic changes in sea state, from calm water into very turbulent water all within a few feet! Passing St Catherine's Head the southern most tip of the loW at about 14.00hrs we began to beat down towards the Needles. The cooker only worked on one ring and the "Yarmouth arrival time " sweep [£1.00 a go] we ran had times ranging from 19.30 to 22.30hrs. Our dinner this day was hot coffee, sandwiches made by me [tuna + mayonnaise or tinned ham inc. the wobbly jelly bits] and nice bright sunshine. By Compton Bay we had caught and passed the second boat and although viewed at a distance we were sure of being level with the first. The Needles were a hazy vision about two miles away when darkness fell, the lighthouse now guiding our course. Night sailing must be tried, a constant watch was kept on the lights of the other two boats as well as the gigantic Stena Sealink ferry that passed us. As we rounded the Needles they were silhouetted by the beam from the lighthouse - quite spectacular. During this period skipper was quite active, looking at the pretty variety of red and green lights that marked our intended course through the narrow gap twixt loW and Hurst Castle. Another 30 minutes and our wheezy engine took us into Yarmouth harbour at 19.45. To mark our arrival the locals had light a huge bonfire and were giving a firework display, only later did others discover how exceptionally friendly the IoW'ers were. Skipper expressed slight concern as we watched the pretues and ignored the bits of string and other tubs. After a detailed review of all parking slots we moored about 20 boats out from the harbour wall. Great place Yarmouth, good food and beer, nice atmosphere. Sunday departure was scheduled for 09.00hrs which allowed an easy breakfast/start. Sunday was an odd sort of day, the weather was great, force 3-4SW and bright sunshine. However the skipper surfaced in a rather competitive mood and on this boat were six helms plus him, not quite in the mould of an experienced cruiser racing team. I picked an easy job, the mainsheet, this allowed me to hear skipper's detailed and continuous opinion of us, especially the foredeck crew! After a few doubtful spinny hoists + a tulip it was alleged that skipper had a discussion about motivation with John S! Race one was between channel mark, Yarmouth to the mouth of the Hamble. Lunch was great: a pub, a chance to read news in the Sunday rags + a pint. Skipper seemed relaxed but that compettive spirit came up in him again for race two and the foredeck crew were once again getting it a bit wrong. Geoff J and I on helm and mainsheet proved to be the best team. Once under the Itchen toll bridge [aim for the middle!! he kept saying, we thought there was plenty of room] the faithless motor coughed into action and our tremendous circumnavigation of the loW was complete. It was a great weekend, good sailing, good company and our target achieved. Tim Sweet PS will this get me the Mamgu trophy?

9. Come in No.5; your time is up ! My thanks to Malcolm Stuart for a note in response to my "One over the Eight” article in the January, 1995, Navigans issue. At least 1 now know that one member of the club reads Navigans Past as well as myself (several times) and the dutiful members of my family (after I've dropped several hints like "Is there anything interesting in Navigans this month?"). Malcolm says:- "_...the traditional course for Up River All-in races is not "all channel markers" but just Nos. 3, 8 and 10 to avoid dinghies cutting the corners. The recent use of "all channel markers" by race officers is, 1 think, misplaced. Limiting the constraints to the main turn point channel markers gives the element of fair competition between craft of different displacement whilst maximising the element of skill involved in finding the best route”. I haven't found any positive clues to what the ‘traditional’ courses are for Mona's Cup and Jackpot, or whether they are ‘all-in’ or restricted races. However, I reckon I agree with Malcolm in what he says about Nos.3, 8 and 10 - and if I hadn't been a bit overkeen on the ‘Delete’ button on the Word Processor, this point might well have been more obvious in my article. Unfortunately, I managed to delete a ‘linking paragraph’ between the bottom of page 7 and the top of page 8, which should have read:- "Besides Mona's Cup, the other major Up River long distance race is the Jackpot which was, I believe, initiated as the ‘over 40s' race in about 1966 or 1967 but I cannot find any specific reference to the ‘terms' of the race as such in the archives. Thus, it is not clear to me if the Jackpot was meant to be ‘all-in’ or not, but it does seem in practice to have always been a ‘dinghy’ race (as distinct from the Mona's Cup ‘all-in’ race) and, consequently, there would be no need to specify ‘all channel markers’ for the Jackpot course." Without the above paragraph, my article in the January Navigans doesn't quite ‘flow’ too well. However, this month's Navigans Past article might give some clue to ‘the traditional course’ of Mona's Cup in the item written by Eric Payne in January, 1977. By the way, you dinghy sailors, how many of you know where Southey Spit buoy is (without looking it up on the chart first)? Naturally, I assume all the cruiser folk know where it is with no problem !! Mike Boreham 38 Kk PS. As I write this, I have just been given a possible explanation of why 'No.5' channel marker doesn't appear on the charts or, indeed, physically in the river. The explanation is as follows:- If it is true that channel markers traditionally are numbered going up-river with odd numbers (green) on the starboard-hand and even numbers (red) on the port-hand, then the natural progression of 1(st.), 2 (pt), 3 (st) and 4 (pt) follows quite logically. There appears to be a need for two port channel markers (Nos. 4 & 6) to be quite close together but no need for a starboard marker ‘between’ them; _ this starboard marker would have been No.5 if it had been needed. However, there is a need for a starboard marker up-river of No.6 and this, logically would be No.7 (green) since it is up-river of No.6. Thus No.5 has probably never existed because it was not needed up-river of No.4 or down-river of No.6. Follow it so far ? It's all quite simple really. Ah! Well! It all sounds very convincing but why didn't I think of that ? Does anyone out there have another explanation ?

10. NAVIGANS PAST 1977 (January) - Laying Up Supper; cheap and cheerful or great and grand but can it be both ? - Cruising ? Is it a form of sleeping sickness ? January - Editor, Shirley Wood, points out that she is Ron Wood's daughter and not his wife; "Please don't marry me off yet !!" she pleads. A new social sub-committee has been formed. This seems to be a brand new committee formed to take responsibility for organising social events. Roy Battye (Social Secretary) says support for social events in 1976 was disappointing with “only” 170 turning up for the Christmas Dance and 150 for the Laying-Up Supper, which he felt rather poor for a club boasting around 400 members. Judging by numbers in some years, I'd have said that was a pretty good turn-out ! The 1977 Laying Up Supper will be at the Lion and Lamb (Chelmsford ?) instead of the MASC (venue for last 2 years) "...taking account of the general feeling of the membership...”. Another letter re. '1976 Laying Up Supper’ and the ‘antics’ of the Mirror crowd from B M Sosin:- "From the formation of the club, the Laying Up Supper has been the ‘formal occasion of the YOO A....51. A letter by Clare Urry...... gives a clear answer to the reasons for the difficulties, and I am sure her views are shared by many members. ....it is necessary to decide what sort of occasion it should be...... many members like myself are not prepared to pay some £4 per ticket for an indifferent formal dinner/come disco party...... (they are) prepared to pay a reasonable price for a quality evening, formal supper...... a cheap Laying Up Supper could be a success; the occasion cannot be both". I must say that Maggie and I thoroughly enjoyed the 1994 Laying Up Supper. I know some thought the speeches went on a little too long and maybe, in retrospect, they did and we didn't have too much time left for the disco dancing. Nevertheless, as the speeches came to an end, I was very surprised at how late it was, so obviously the speeches didn't bore me. I particularly enjoyed Ashley Machin's speech and, as I listened to Derek Kirby's speech and Charlie Anderson's supporting commentary together with those of the Commodore, I had a great feeling of ‘oneness and pulling together’ in the club which has not always been present in past years. At the end, both Maggie and I felt it was one of the most enjoyable Laying Up Suppers we had attended in our 21 years membership of the MSC. We obviously enjoyed some good company at our table. Still on the social side, a meeting in January is to be on the Racing Rules (with Roger Hence leading the meeting) and a discussion about "..the choice of dinghies....and....the issue of a new class within the club." On the same subject, Tony Diment writes to extol the virtues of the 420. In last months's Navigans Past, | queried if a December, 1976, Navigans had been issued; it is clear from Tony's letter that it had, indeed, been published and our current-day Editor, Maureen Ball, confirms it. Extracts from Brenda Tate's log of the trip of Ace of Diamonds to Holland in 1976 as follows:- "Vic asleep below, so was Robert, at the helm." "....all went smoothly apart from Robert and Mary being seasick but this they did with the minimum of fuss and mess." I awoke about midnight and grabbed the washing up bowl quick. Once it was over I felt almost human again, but I had to perform one-handed gymnastics to get myself plus the bowl out into the cockpit avoiding Robert who was fast asleep on the floor cuddling the genoa." "I was standing by the pulpit on deck with a bow line ready. Vic shouted to Robert to throw the gear lever into reverse but, horror or horrors, the cones did not disengage and Ace stayed ahead. She hit the pontoon with an almighty wallop, her bow rearing up out of the water and then sliding down again."

il. "We took the children on the pony bus to see the sights and then retreated back to our peaceful holiday haven. We spend a very pleasant evening, Vic and Robert in a local bar with a gentleman from a Maldon boat Wigwam, 1 on Natasha with Brain and Jackie and their neighbours, a couple on Barbaree I] out of Bradwell. It's a small world." Now I know what cruising is all about !!! Eric Payne writes an article about Mona's Cup which is worth repeating here:- "I wonder how many of our present members know the origin of Mona's Cup ? In the early fifties, when our headquarters were situated at Heybridge Basin, we made frequent visits to the Jolly Sailor whose proprietress was Miss Mona Clarke, who inherited it from her parents. As she was a very friendly soul, and took a special interest in our sailing activities, she kindly presented us with a fine challenge cup to be awarded to the winner of an annual all-in race, and this is still included in Our programme. On one occasion, Mona actually came aboard Mamgu and fired the gun starting this race. In later years, this has tended to be supported by dinghies from our present premises at Stansgate but in future, more cruisers should be encouraged to participate and it is suggested that Mona should be invited to be present for the occasion. On one occasion when this race was sailed from Stansgate the first mark of the course was up river, and the Southey Spit Buoy had to be rounded but as the tide was falling some cruisers found there was insufficient water to make it. Mona now has retired but still lives at Heybridge and The Jolly Sailor is now run by Eric Priestley, incidentally an ex-Marconi man. Incidentally, our first Laying Up Supper was held at The Jolly Sailor in October, 1957; we hired the large inner room and ate our sausages and mince pies standing up, and went through to the bar for our drinks; there was no music to drown our exchanges of events during the past sailing season, and it was a thoroughly enjoyable evening. Amongst our guests was Douglas Thompson, Commodore of the Blackwater Sailing Club and Sam Poulton from The Maldon Little Ship Club. The price of the tickets was 4/- (20p in 1994), or 6/6 (32.5p) including the price of the coach which brought us. Our first formal Laying Up Supper was held at the New Street canteen, which we were pleased to call The Palm Court, on Friday, November 1, 1958; most of the Commodores of the clubs on the Blackwater were present as was Bill Hillman, Commodore of the B.B.C. Ariel Club, whose premises are on the Thames at Teddington. The price of the tickets was 9/- (45p in 1994-money) including the band, but not the drinks. We used to race against the Ariel Club at Teddington and, in return, they came to Heybridge the following year, but eventually it was dropped largely because of the distance and absence of boats available. However, a trophy consisting of our respective burgees mounted on a plinth still exists, but as the Ariel S.C. were the last to win it, they are retaining it." Alas, Eric Payne is no longer with us. I met him a few times in the early '80s when I first joined the Main Committee for a year or two and exchanged pleasantries with him. In retrospect, I would very much liked to have got him to talk about the early years of the club, in particular the days of the 'Hut on the Wall' and Mamgu years at Heybridge; at that time, of course, I had little or no idea of the history of the club. 1 am sure there can be few who had such an intimate knowledge of the club of those days and, like most organisations, it is the bits that were not recorded in the Minutes, etc. that are the most interesting or revealing. Iam sure Eric would have been able to shake some dust off some ‘old bones’. Mike Boreham

12. 40 Y Ago - Jan & Feb 1955 The Sailing Programme shows the following planned for 1955:- 6 x Fleetwind Series Races 4x Handicap Races Handicap Race to Bradwell Rally to Osea Team Race against MBYC (at Maylandsea Bay S.C. using their boats) Team Race against MBYC (at Heybridge using MSC Fleetwind dinghies) ye Team Races against Maldon Little Ship Club plus Maldon Regatta and Heybridge Regatta and a variety of events which | suspect are Blackwater cruiser events, ie. Brown Cup, Page Cup, Freeman Cup, Krohn Cup, Smith Cup and Dyer Cup. as well as the Blackwater & Colne Dinghy Championships, Burnham Week, the Fleetwind Championships at Portsmouth and the East Coast Fleetwind Championship at the Blackwater Sailing Club. It seems the MSC had been asked to organise the East Coast Fleetwind Championships for 6/7August but, of course, the club did not have the necessary facilities. However, the BSC had kindly offered their clubhouse and their starting and launching facilities as it seems they were ‘racing away’ that weekend. The MSC Committee therefore decided to go ahead on that basis, hoping the local farmer would allow use of his field for car and boat parking. The Organising Committee was Messrs (Eric) Cottam, C Clarke and ? Wells. The President's Cup had no formal rules governing its award, but it was decided to award it to the winner of the Fleetwind Series on the basis of best 4 results out of 6 races. Obviously, entrance money was charged for each race in those days because it was thought that winners of individual races could receive ‘spoons’ or other small prize paid from the money. (/ seem to remember winning the occasional spoon in the late '70s). It was decided to print a Rule Book for issue to new members and also to publish an annual fixture list. A student, Colin Barbrook, applied for Associate Membership because he was building a Fleetwind as part of his course at Shoreditch College. Alas, the club couldn't accept him since he had no existing member to propose him; however, Mr G W Harrington obviously had no such trouble as he was accepted as an Associate Member. Rights over the use of the slipway were presumably uncertain since the Ministry of Transport now had to be consulted. Pre-event notices of future MSC meetings included talks by Mr Francis Jones AINA on ‘Modern Yacht Design’ and Mr Maurice Griffiths MINA on 'The Design of Small Cruisers for the East Coast’. Having just read Maurice Griffiths' book 'Swatchways and Little Ships’, I feel sure both these talks would have been well worth attending. ll. 1995 MSC PAINT ORDER In these times of ever increasing accountability even the humble club paint order is no longer immune. To comply with regulations laid down and prescribed by the Office for Club Reallocation of Antifouling and Paint (OFFCRAP), I am obliged to publish a report on the quality of this year’s orders. Fortunately this year a general appraisal will suffice, but I am reliably informed that next year League tables will be mandatory, so be warned, next year you could find yourself under the table. As far as this year’s orders are concerned this was the situation:- General Presentation was of a very mixed standard. There were several examples of clearly presented orders whilst some members had clearly given little if any thought to layout. items appearing more than once on the same order and other items being squeezed in with seemingly gay abandon. There are still members who seem to expect me to know without being told, the colour Antifouling they intend putting on their boats. My propensity for burrowing round the undersides of boats might lead some members to assume that I can be expected to remember the colour they used last season, but surely does not imply an ability to anticipate their future intentions. Spelling continues to be a problem. Danboline causes much confusion, both to you and us. We were prepared to accept Danbolin and even Danblin. Polwax also appeared as polywax which conjures up images of some kind of beauty treatment for parrots or even worse some concoction made from parrots. We will be keeping a careful watch on the behaviour of one particular member during the coming season to see whether the two and a half litres of Antifooling that he ordered has the desired effect. Arithmetic. There was a much appreciated iraprovement in overall standards attained in this department. It was however distressing to see the same silly mistakes cropping up as they have done year after year. | would remind certain members that 33% is not a third ! I would point out that Size and Quantity are two entirely different concepts. There is perhaps some justification for putting 750ml under quantity instead of size, but little I would have thought for putting 2 (as in two cans of Antifouling) under size. On a positive note, all cheques were correctly completed, and in all cases matched the amount listed on the order. This in itself was a great improvement on previous years. Having said that, not all the totals on the order forms were correct, some members attempting to procure additional discounts and one or two generously donating what I can only assume to be gratuities or even bribes to the examiners. User Friendly Rating. Many members scored well in this department, and endeared themselves to the examiners by concentrating on larger simpler items that are the easiest to transfer to the Master Order. I don’t like singling out particular individuals for criticism, but one member scored particularily badly in this department by putting in no less than three separate orders and another who had already scored badly in many of the above areas, compounded everything as far as the examiners were concerned by ordering two dust wipes. Once again I have cause to be concerned about what can only be seen as one member’s unhealthily obsessive desire for three tins of Swedish Wood Oil. There was I’m pleased to report an overall improvement as far as the concept of time is concerned.. The majority of members had their orders in before the closing date in spite of the deliberately misleading ploy on the part of the examiners to print the closing date on the order form as !£th January 1995. Extra points were awarded to those members who spotted this. There were of course the inevitable latecomers, and if the experience of previous years is anything to go by, I will be approached at least once in late February to be asked if I am doing the paint again this year. Anyway now we've just got the annual process to go through of uniting member’s with their paint orders, but that’s another story. Thanks for your co-operation and please excuse my self indulgence! Malcoln Shaft

le. NAVIGANS PAST A tribute to Tom Ashley, aged 20 years, who tragically died in a car accident, 13 January, 1995. The gathering together of so many of his family, relatives and friends for a celebration of his life was a fine tribute to Tom Ashley. The time for mourning came when we first heard the news and in the days after when we reflected, in isolation, upon the event. When she heard of what had happened, Maggie wept; when I telephoned my daughter and son to tell them what had befallen their friend, | wept; as they heard the news, many others must also have wept. However, when we gathered together on 24 January to take our farewell of Tom, it was an event specifically to remember and savour the good times of his life - but it was hard not to weep, and many did so. Tom was one of the group of youngsters who have come to their maturity at the sailing club over the last few years, enjoying their life and each others company as they pursued their sport in keen competition but always in friendly rivalry. As each started to go their separate ways, either to a job or to higher education, they nevertheless ‘kept in touch' and came together during the holiday periods, sharing their companionship and experiences and always maintaining their friendship. Sometimes ‘the group’ would spend the evening at our house, staying overnight with boots and bodies seemingly everywhere, but always well behaved and always welcome. In this way we have formed an attachment to these friends of our own offspring. Alongside this has developed our own interest in their personal hopes, plans and achievements. Sometimes we have been allowed to hear the tales of some, but I'm sure not all, of the things they'd been up to in the recent past. Thus it was that we came to knowa little of Tom and came to like him a lot for his sense of humour, his pleasant disposition, his 'laid-back' manner. At the same time, we knew he had a serious side to him and that he had plans and a determination to fulfil them. He had many qualities which were both admirable and likeable and which were, I am sure, clearly recognised and appreciated by those who knew and loved him. _His talent for sailing was apparent to all and he easily deserves to be ranked amongst the very best of the sailors at the MSC within recent years. Tom was a fine young man. It was because we knew him to be a fine young man that we all felt such a personal anguish at his death. Not only do we extend our sympathy to Hilary, Sam, Ben and Joe, but also our love and support for a family who are very much part of the MSC way of life. 2 2 0 oe 2 2k 28 ee ek ke This chapter of Navigans Past is dedicated to the memory of Tom Ashley 1977 (February) - As we wonder what the cruiserman really ‘asked Daddy', Linda manages to put her foot in it at Maldon.
