START OF SEASON CAUTIONARY REMINDERS ADDERS In April Navigans it is traditional to caution members (who should remind any children they bring to the Club) that at this time of year there is the possibility of coming across the occasional adder lying in the sun, often concealed in long grass. The sea wall work has reduced the amount of long grass we have for the time being, but it’s worth being careful where you tread, and if you do come across one, please do not disturb it. It’s a part of our wild life population which is harmless if left alone. THE RIVER IS COLD for many months into the Sailing Season, even on apparently warm sunny days. Though Support Boats are out during all Club Races, it may happen that for some reason that you can’t be picked up quickly after a capsize. It is important that you take measures before you leave the shore that would delay the onset of hypothermia. Navigans has offered the following advice over the years: Wear adequate clothing i.e. wet suit/dry suit etc. forPo Make sure your boat and its gear are sound. Ensure personal buoyancy and the boat’s buoyancy are both adequate. If you are inexperienced either with sailing or with our sailing area, please ask advice from the OOD, Fleet Captain, or other experienced helms. —y If you start to feel cold and tired, return to shore straightaway, rather than wait till you are too cold to think rationally. IN ROUGH WEATHER: If Club Racing goes ahead in windy conditions this does not necessarily imply that it is safe to go afloat. Some very experienced helms and crews may be well able to cope with that day’s prevailing conditions, having spent years building up their skills by going cut in gradually more testing weather, but less experienced sailors could have a difficult and uncomfortable time. So please remember that even though Support Boats are there for Club Races, you should aim to be entirely self-sufficient, sail within your limitations, and remember on all occasions that the decision to go float, whether ta race or to potter, 1s always made on your own responsibility. Ed. As we have given prizes for Cats and Monohulls in such races in recent years, this should not cause friction with the half-boat sailors. 3. The Dart 15 Cats will not use the IYRU system in their Club Points races. 4, The Sailing Sub Committee will revisit these decisions at the end of the Season. So what about the Medium Cats? Well, the Sailing Sub Committee has yet to make = any decisions dur to an initial shortage of information and due to widely differing views amongst the Medium Cat sailors. 40 Years Ago - March and April, 1955 The Blackwater Sailing Club confirmed their offer of the use of their club facilities for the Fleetwind East Coast Championships which was being organised by the MSC. Maldon Little Ship Club agreed that the MSC was eligible to enter "the open trophy races". It was planned to form an inter-club programme between the MLSC, Maldon Yacht Club, Blackwater SC, Maylandsea Bay Yacht Club and the MSC. The MBYC also invited members of the MSC to attend the opening of their new club premises during Easter, 1955, and also avail themselves of its facilities during the season; presumably this was really aimed mainly at the cruising members. It seems three (team ?) races were arranged against Maldon Little Ship Club, consisting of 3 boats a side and with an entrance fee of 1/- per boat. The MLSC was to donate a cup for the series of races. At the (main) Committee Meeting, Mr C Clarke raised some questions about the rules for the award of the President's Cup but was told this was the province of the Racing Committee. However, at a later Committee Meeting, it is recorded that the rules for the President's Cup were:- 6 races; all to count 2/6 entry fee for each race (payable at the end of the season) lst prize - a replica of the cup 2nd prize - a plaque. (Was this the C.(ie. Cliff) Clarke who has featured in Navigans Past by virtue of the amusing articles written by his wife Eileen in past issues of Navigans ?). It was decided to conduct a survey to decide the best places for racing marks. Some 22 members attended a talk by Mr Francis Jones AINA on "Modern Yacht Design". However, it was decided that the room at the Marconi Apprentice Training Centre which was usually used for meetings was now too small. It was decided to hold the next meeting “at a local inn", which turned out to be the King William IV in New Street, Chelmsford. The talk was to be by Maurice Griffiths. 14. NAVI PAST 1977 (March - May) _ - the class struggle continues. - presumably, whatever it was that Vic cooked up, it didn't go down too well with some people ! March - a nice action photograph on the front cover shows Mike Turner with a grim smile on his face as he hangs on the end of a Hornet trapeze amidst much spray and rough water. He looks very wet indeed - and is clearly enjoying a hard sail; even his helm is smiling. Commodore John Witter reveals that the sale of Stansgate farms to a dutchman who has purely agricultural interests in the land seems to indicate that the projected marina development on Ramsey marshes will probably not go ahead. He also tells us that a threat to establish a rubbish tip at Stansgate had also diminished; it appears that the Maldon Council had changed its mind and now intended to enlarge the existing tip at Maldon. John also reminds everyone that the "which club class ?" debate was a discussion which had arisen on previous occasions during the club's development - but this time there was a particular difference. At this time the club already had four established classes (Enterprise, Mirror, Hornet and Handicap) with possibly a Sth class if the GP14 was included. Previous discussions had been conducted when only two classes existed (ie. Enterprise and Handicap) discounting the ‘original club class', the Fleetwind. John makes the very good point that the MSC is basically a family club, and it was not the custom to make membership conditional upon ownership of a particular class of dinghy. Nor was it the custom to stipulate that members must race a certain number of times each year. Thus the Committee itself could not dictate which classes were to be adopted by the club. The Committee could only recognise ‘trends’ and steer people towards a particular class which might be adopted if there was sufficient support. He feels there is a need to either re-establish the GP14 or to establish a class such as the 420, as well as look into the perceived demand for single-handed sailing. He states "In the final analysis, however, the choice of classes must be arrived at by examining the track record of those offered. This means that a common and proved desire for a particular class must be demonstrated so, if we really need a new class or two, some effective lobbying will be necessary to establish a class that meets the specification required by the majority seeking a change." Contributions to this Navigans issue from Cadet Members of the club included this one from Sarah Lingwood (aged 10):- "It was at 1975's regatta we were sailing up to the start, in Hotpot, anyway Dad got in a bit of a tiss and said "Ready about. Hey ho and over we go." _1 quickly got uncleated the jib sheet and stepped over the other side, to my surprise Dad didn't do the same. The dinghy rockeda little then it turned over on its side. I thought I might have to swim for it. I was too scared to help Dad and as the water was only (to my surprise) knee deep, 1 waded ashore. Dad was yelling "Come and help me", but I was half way up the beach - but of course I didn't belong to Cadets then !" I think that comes under the category of ‘voting with your feet’ !!! Russ Fuller (Cruiser Fleet Captain) records the death of Reg Patten who built some 67 Sea King boats at Leigh High Street, including that owned by Russ which was called Kalinka. Russ recalled that his request to Reg for a recommendation of the type of bilge pump he should have fitted was met by Reg's firm response that he would not need one. More cruiser log notes from Brenda Tate's Ace of Diamonds trip to Holland:- - "Vic cooked lunch; we had salad !" - "Everyone went to the Yacht Club except me; they sneaked away while I was putting Mary to bed." - "The Bowsher's came in during the day and we all congregated on Ace for the evening. I can't

15. remember if that was the night I cooked a bean and sausage supper for everyone or not." - "Mary and I began to have attacks of queasy tum again, so Vic gave us something to do. I went on the helm and Mary became Flag Officer, taking down the Dutch and hoisting the Belgium colours and the yellow duster." April - Russ Fuller proposes some mini-cruises for combined cruiser/dinghy groups, perhaps to Bradwell Beach for example. On the racing side, 7 races are planned for the Handicap Series, the handicap fleet being split into fast (120 and below) and slow (above 120), with cruisers invited into certain of the fast handicap races when water depth permitted navigation around the "normal club courses". Ken Beavins writes a letter touching on the ‘which club class ?' debate. He reveals his rationale when he sold his Blandford 12' many years previously and sought its replacement by a suitable recognised racing class on the Blackwater. He eventually settled on the GP14 Lady Clive as the compromise between cruising with the family, racing, occasional single-handed sailing and cost. However, he clearly no longer owned Lady Clive for he ends by saying "Her purchase was one of the (few) right decisions I have made. | still miss her." May - A plan for the Mirror Fleet dinghy parking shows some 57 mirrors accommodated (including the Boreham family's Kitwitwee (later named Lars Tinn) safely tucked away in a corner furthest away from the hard entrance! We obviously didn't race in those days, or at least not very often. Brenda Tate provided the final episode of the log of the Ace of Diamonds cruise to Holland :- - "After a peaceful sail down, arrived off the Ostende pier heads. We followed a Dutch yacht in but were surprised when, on reaching the dog leg of the pier, he suddenly swung the helm and came out at full chat. So did we when we saw the Townsend Ferry coming straight for us." - "In 14 days we travelled 300 miles. The passage from Lavington Breishens was 105 miles, Ostende to Brightlingsea 90 miles." Another log (author not named) records the delivery voyage of a new 48' motor-sailor Victoria from Maldon to Flushing (Holland) on Ist September, 1976, and which was a ‘voyage not without incident’ - meaning it was full of incident. Soon after getting underway, it was revealed that (a) the log was not working and (b) the compass was too small and located too far from the wheel for it to be readable. The rest of this saga continues in the June ,1977, issue of Navigans. ty COMMODORE’S NOTES Well. the last week has seen the lot. from snow and ice through to almost Summer weather, and the latter tempted a number of folks including The Old Chap out on Sunday in a gently rising 3-4-5. A couple of laps without the main jammer and a winter of sedentary activity took its toll, and 1 was shattered at lunch. The wind got up more. the chop got up too and a few sensible people took a decision based on discretion - only to watch first Micks Warr & Richardson nosedive and completely invert (5 mins 20 secs from launch) closely to be followed Ian Caruth & Mick Jones (7mins 5 secs). Unfortunately, lan’s mast leaks....but he only discovered that on Sunday. Still. plenty of hands turned to to recover aforementioned beast in a very competent and professional way. Enough of the stories, the “Commode’ has words of warning for some of you. Just because the Stansgate section of the M1 is now open, it doesn’t mean that 70mph is sensible. In two weekends I’ve had two instances of meeting another car, whose efforts to stop resulted in showers of gravel being thrown up. If you want to drive like Michael Schumacher - not on the access road, please. We shall think up retribution because, frankly, it is totally unnecessary behaviour and will lead to an accident. BE SENSIBLE!! Well, time as always these days is short, so I'll see most of you afloat sometime. A Different View from the Rear....... By the time you read this Easter will have been and gone, and many of you will have been out and sailed! If you are a Catamaran Sailor then you will be aware that the Sailing Sub have agreed to use the ISCHRS handicapping scheme for Catamarans. The essence of the scheme is that it uses measurements in order to handicap small catamarans rather than using the performance figures to apply handicaps. The stated purpose of the regulations is to enable trampoline multihulls of various types to race together on a comparative basis, and to protect the inerests of the owners in keeping development under control without hindering further research. One effect of using this handicapping system will be to extract separate results for monohulls and catamarans in all-in races. Please let us know your views on this matter; its progress will be closely monitored. There are a number of anomalies which are being attended to by John Nickalls and Robin Smith. Please read John’s article elsewhere in this issue. On behalf of the Sailing Sub Committee I would like to thank John for all the work which he has done in bringing this scheme to fruition. Towards the end of last season the Johnson Outboard Engine was not working very well. It has now been repaired by Mick Richardson for a fraction of the cost quoted by a (professional?) firm of Marine Engineers. Thank you, Mick! The Sailing Sub Committee has recommended that the use of this engine should be restricted to authorised Jack B and RIB drivers only. These members will be asked to undergo a short training course on the Do’s and Don'ts of this engine and its use. (Ed's note: see notice on Page 2 to Orkney Helms). The reason for this change is to attempt to reduce the repair costs resulting from misuse and to ensure that the reliability of the engine improves. This is not to say that in an emergency a competent Club Member should not use the engine - rather that this should be the exception! FAST CAT NOTES IYRU Handicap System. Handicap racing is a dead loss. If we want to know whether we can sail better than the next man we'd better make sure we're sailing the same boat, or we're simply measuring how badly the handicapper got it wrong... or are we? Handicapping of small boats has, in the UK, traditionally relied upon the Portsmouth Yardstick scheme managed by the RYA, in which handicap race results are returned to the RYA annually for analysis. The results of the analysis are used to amend the ratings given to the boats in the scheme (which, according to the apparent soundness’ of the data held can be Primary or Secondary Yardsticks, or Recorded Numbers). This scheme has always been seen to be flawed: changes in the ratings between seasons demonstrate that either the old rating or the new one was wrong, and there is often no real reason to suspect it was the former; only a very limited number of multihulls have Primary Yardsticks, and indeed many craft are not rated in the scheme at all; the perception that better crews gravitate toward particular classes leads to the perception that the ratings of those classes are unfairly penalised. These problems led to the adoption for last years Piers Race of the ‘French’ system, one based purely upon measurement and not upon race results. At a practical level the system allows the handicapper to accommodate very easily deviations from standard configurations, as well as in principle overcoming the complaints about the PY system. Given the success of the scheme at the ECPR, the high level of acceptance that it seemed to achieve and the more general move toward the ‘French’ system (since adopted by the lYRU for promulgation as a handicapping system for small catamarans) the Catamaran Fleet AGM supported the new scheme (now luxuriating in the title ‘International Small Catamaran Handicap Rating System’, or ISCHRS) for Fast Cat racing, chose to retain the current level rating system for the Dart 15s and referred the Medium Cat choice to the Sailing Sub-committee. Since then the Sailing Sub-Committee has detailed the system (see the notices displayed in the Reception area at the Club); the key points are as below: The ISCHRS applies for the Fast and Medium Cat races, and for all-in catamaran races. No trophies will be awarded for mixed monohull / catamaran races (i.e. there will be separate trophies for monos and multis). Once you have entered a series in a particular boat or a particular configuration of boat (e.g. with / without a spinnaker) changing the boat or configuration will result in a new entry to the series. Note that this applies to all catamarans, including Dart 15s. Dart 15s will continue to use their PN ratings for Dart 15 races, but will adopt the ISCHRS ratings for all-in cat races. A measurement-based system has the deceptive advantage of being beyond dispute (save perhaps for the very principle upon which it is based); surely there can be no disagreement over the figures plugged into the equation which produces the rating? Although the IYRU has accepted the scheme we are still seeing some teething problems, some of which are real and some the result of unintentional misinformation. The figures upon which the ratings are based were submitted by the various manufacturers and published by the French Sailing Federation (FFV); these figures are currently being confirmed by the IYRU and will then be formally published. As with all things voluntary this is taking rather longer than expected, but as the people involved are those who produced the figures for the French scheme there is no reason to expect any change to the list displayed at the Club. There are however a number of flies in this ointment! 1 Until a genuinely official list is published it will always be possible for a person to measure his own boat, find it heavier (or shorter!) than the list specifies and complain that his rating is punitive. | believe that such problems can only be avoided by quoting certified measurements from the manufacturer and avoiding the measuring of individual boats for which such measurements exist. 2 Questions have been raised about the accuracy of some of the measurements in the (unofficially) published list. A particular, and rather high profile, vendor of probably the most popular catamaran has published sail area figures for his 15’ craft which do not agree with those on the ISCHRS table, and when questioned apparently supported the company figures. Further investigation with the sailmakers revealed that actually the ISCHRS figures were correct (and the brochure figures were not) but the ISCHRS figures incorrectly omitted the area of the rotating mast, causing an error in the rating. (As a result the ratings for the Dart 15 will have been amended by the time this goes to press; | have removed them from the table shown below.) The other Dart figures are correct, and although we have no reason to suspect them, it is possible that similar problems will exist elsewhere. 3 Boats not in the list but which are raced at the Club must be measured and rated. This should be done by reference to the class rules wherever possible for the reason given in 1 (above), but typically several of the required parameters are not quoted. Clearly the measurement of waterline length is not an easy task, but even some of the simpler parameters would appear to pose problems: the ISCHRS and the Texel tables quote different overall lengths for the Dart 15! The class which poses the greatest problems at the Club in this respect is the Hurricane 4.9, and we have tapped every source of information we can find. Unfortunately the class rules do not agree with the report from the sailmakers, and the "well-known" length of 16ft 4%in does not agree with the figure measured at

Texel. As a result we have been forced to compromise by choosing values which, within the RATING typically small range of uncertainty, seem fair. Larry Botheras Cruiser Comments This year's sailing season is fast approaching but before turning my mind to coming events | would like to reflect on the success encountered by storing moorings on pallets. This has cut out a lot of manhandling (this is politically correct since we have not yet. as far as | kKnow*. had ladies on the mooring parties.) It 1s so much easier to collect moorings from around the Cruiser Park using the tractor fitted with fork lift. There are two small points worth mentioning which are: 1) Please make sure the wide side of the pallet is facing forward. thus ensuring the forks will fit under the whole pallet. 2) Make sure the pallet is not too far under the bow of vour boat. otherwise access is restricted by the roof of the tractor fouling the stem. or maybe stern. of vour craft Looking forward to launching now. there is a launching list on the Club Notice Board. Please use it to avoid congestion and also make sure you book/advise the tractor driver in advance giving as much notice as you can. Once launched please ensure vour trailer is returned to the current year's Winter Storage position and secured - especially ladders as your boat may be afloat but other people's may not be. Lastly don't just forget vour trailer until vou want it at the end of the season. Please make sure it is properly maintained. Still on the subject of launching. CRUISING DOWN THE PAN? ~~ The morning was beautiful. coming out of Plymouth harbour in our new yacht. a slight mist wisping over a smooth sea. the boat glistening with the morning dew, rigging taut. ready to enjoy the breezes that would surely come later. Leaving the idyllic scene I went below to enjov contemplation and early ablutions. Somewhat later - Oh no. not again. the pump on the marine loo seems to be jammed. Now when you have been experienced in marine toilets and their problems as much as I have. you get to realise that the next hour may see the blasted thing in bits as you try to effect a repair to the often dubiously fragile components within. A history of several boats behind me. and with every one a problem loo. Many years ago. the first. a 22 footer giving the worst moment of all. Moored for the night to the quay just below Haven Bridge in Great Yarmouth and on route to Norwich next day. I turned over and noticed the time as 0305 hrs and as | sleepily tried to stretch away that small boat stiffness. my hand flopped out of my berth and onto the cabin sole. My hand found a carton of margarine as it floated past. Floated Past!!! As the realisation hit me that my hand and a large proportion of my arm was underwater a reflex occurred that must have blocked the memory that | had little headroom in that small cabin. and attempting to get out of my sleeping bag the thump of my head on the coach roof. followed closely by a large emission of blue language immediately woke my normally slothful companion! Chaos ensued as two people scrabbled blindly to get out of a cabin that resembled a floating larder and get into the cockpit to get to the bilge pump. bucket. sponge and anything else that would remove water from the boat. Outside we could see that the boat was low enough in the water to result in some of the mooring lines becoming tight! Having removed most of the water we now looked for the leak and found that the toilet bowl had cracked where it was bolted to its plastic base unit and. as the sea cock had been left open this was the cause of the morning's early action. The location of the toilet also made 1 difficult to have the approved system of an anti-siphon loop. (Which of course is only a true anti-siphon loop if it features a vented loop at its highest point). From then on it became a rule that never would the large toilet exit sea cock be left open. On the next boat the loo kept me busy with the end of the piston often falling off until | replaced the circlips with a split pin. In the end I fitted a complete new unit. having learnt a lot about the insides of this unpleasant but essential piece of equipment. As I already had found out. many pump cylinder plungers have circlips to retain the piston assembly and this can be a source of trouble. the best systems being those with nuts to the top and bottom of the plungers. On the cheaper heads. the small lever often featured on the top of the plunger to provide the flush function is made of a highly dubious soft alloy material and soon gives trouble. Some people advocate the use of vegetable oil to keep the plunger working smoothly but I have found that this oil will eventually attach itself to the walls of the pump cylinder and cause more problems. The only oil to use seems to be Baby Oil. and a very small quantity only to get over an immediate friction problem that indicates the need for a strip down. Also the juddering operation of the plunger can be down to little more than the top water seal being dry. An application of Vaseline to the exposed portion of the plunger rod can often cure this. It seems that there is no substitute for some units other than an annual clean out and its re-assembly. lubricating the moving parts with Vaseline. Back in Plymouth I realised that I had forgotten to open the exit sea cock with the excitement of the new boat. etc. Having done so. the pump handle still seemed jammed. Out with the tool kit and to bits with the thing! Diagnosis - an inverted Aortic Joker Valve - Nasty! This can occur if the sea cock is left shut. As the exit pipe becomes pressurised and then. as the plunger is raised for another stroke. the valve. intended to stop liquid returning to the toilet. is blown inside out. Sometimes the valve will return to its natural state and sometimes not. depending on the age of the valve. On my return to Essex I rang Cleghorn Waring. the suppliers of the Par toilet unit and they were familiar with Aortic Valve Inversion! An overhaul kit contained the valve. and all is now well. Given my personal experiences over the last 10 years. the Par is the best of the cheap units of its type with all spares readily available, but the £650-odd that a Baby Blake costs is probably justified as one still sees these units around in their original state after many years. and I have met owners who have never touched them in that period! Limpet M.S.S.E. Rel. (Marine Sanitary Systems Engineer - Reluctant)!

Commodore’s Notes This is a deliberately late contribution from me (apologies Maureen) having decided to wait for the outcome of the mid-year meeting on Tuesday 6 June. I need not have bothered really. as you are all obviously delighted with the way the Club is running. There were four non-Committee members there. Despite that. the discussion was good and covered the thorny subjects of OOD‘s and membership recruitment to name but two. I did wonder why we bothered though. On to the lighter side... the bedstead took a trip up to South Shields for the Hobie Nationals over Bank Holiday and your Esteemed correspondent was eighth... out of eight (17°s). It's summat to do with being older and wiser when the wind blew I think. together with busting bits most days (batten through sail. trapeze gear. etc.). I did have one great start and moment of stardom when I lead by loads to the weather mark. only to have Metro Radio helicopter fly over me... Now where have | heard that one before? The Club was pleasant. the location lousy and the water cold. Alex has strong views on the area that are unprintable. It looks as if they re trying to make Clacton from a demolished industrial site. Oh. well. Regatta was badly attended this year and will not be taking place in 1996 as a consequence. It will probably resurrect in years to come. but it needs to be driven by competitors not the race committee. Thanks to Colin for his efforts. and apologies for dumping him in it by going to the Nationals. This year is the first year I qualify for Jackpot so SuperCrew and I are looking forward to Five-Ohing it at the weekend. See you at Mill Beach. Larry Botheras

CLUBS AND CLASSES - ‘YACHTS AND YACHTING’ REPORT. MARCONI SAILING CLUB REGATTA The Regatta opened on Saturday 27th May with the RNLI Pennant Race. As it’s name suggests the entrance donations competitors choose to make go to the RNLI. The event was sailed in a strong southerly wind. The gusty conditions caught out several boats on the downwind leg where concentration and discretion paid off. After five laps of the triangular course Nigel Skudder and Keith Hills sailing a Laser 2 finished first. The first BIRC boat across the line was the Laser 2 sailed by Gavin and Jason Mills. Sunday saw the start of the Regatta with a strong south westerly together with bright.warm sunshine. There were sufficient boats to give the Kestrels. Solos and Gulls their own class starts. The remaining boats were divided into Fast and Medium Handicap. The helms of the faster boats were asked to sail a large triangle sausage triangle course whilst the slower boats sailed a similar course inside the larger course. Conditions in the morning were such that some of the Fast Handicap boats and Gulls decided not to race. The remainder found the wind conditions a good test of their skills. The afternoon race was run over a similar course but with the wind casing and blowing more from the south west. Monday dawned with a Force + from the south west which increased during the morning before casing during the afternoon. The courses were adjusted to give competitors longer and faster reaches. The Fast Handicap event was won in convincing fashion by Michael Taylor and Jonathan Willey. Medium Handicap saw Stuart Curtiss and Shaun Seear coming home first. The Solo class was a close affair between Ron Greygoose and John Salmon. Ron taking the honours by a whisker after taking into account the discards. Malcolm Gandy and Graham Richmond won the Kestrel class with Gordon and George Williams winning the Gull class convincingly. Overall Results; RNLI Pennant Race Ist. NAVIGANS PAST 1977 (June) - as we plunge ‘hell for Leather’ into Osea's wild waters, a salty outsider gives us a ‘narrows viewpoint’ of the Marconi Sailing Club. June - obviously, the 1977 Regatta was a ‘blustery event’ both of weather and organisation. Editor, Shirley Wood, says "...it seems that the question of its future, if it has one, must be asked and looked into’. Commodore John Witter possibly makes the understatement of the year when he says "...this time the elements were less favourably inclined towards us with most of the period challenging sailing during the races we were able to hold". Tom Gaskel judges the Regatta to have been a success despite the weather but writes "At what cost though to the few members who actually did the hard work - before, during and after. Their numbers get less every year and each year we have an ever increasing plague of people". Tom goes on to point out that the bank holiday was meant to be a holiday for everyone, that the commercial profit arises from the fact that the regatta helpers (e.g. behind the bar) receive no wages for their work and that the number of helpers seems to get fewer as the event gets bigger. Tom continues "Our resources are inadequate - 3 ladies loos and 2 gents for nearly 1,000 people. The drainage is inadequate and the memory lingers on - the big ditch will be foul for the rest of the season". However, Tom is not ‘negative’ about regatta as such; he continues "To be constructive - there is no need to abandon a spring jamboree, Mardi Gras, festival regatta, Stansgate Week or W.H.Y. (what have you) but let's make it a closed event. Members and guests by invitation". Ray Battye (Social Secretary) says "The weather could have been kinder for the regatta and the succeeding cadets week". As a by-the-by, it is amusing to quote from John Leather's book "The Salty Shore" in which he recounts his experience of sailing through the Stansgate 'narrows' at what we can assume was the time of the regatta:- "One day during the summer of 1977 a friend and I were beating his small cruiser through the narrows at half flood, against a strong westerly wind, rising to gale force. Suddenly, scores of sailing dinghies were launched off from a sailing club at Stansgate and within five minutes the whole narrows and the river south of Osea was covered with capsized boats, drifting to leeward, their crews clinging to them, rescue boats thrashing about in inadequate numbers and manoeuvring under the bow of sailing cruisers finding as much as they could do to keep clear of the melee. "Looks like the battle of Trafalgar," muttered my companion grimly as he put the helm down and we plunged about to avoid a capsized dinghy with her helmsman sitting on the upturned bottom, clutching the erect centreboard blowing him to leeward like a sail. Such are the modern perils of the narrows, which have been known to shake up ten tonners in a gale." Oh! Dear! What is that quotation? "Would that God the giftie gie us to see ourselves as others see us" (or at least something like that). Many thanks to Malcolm Stuart who reminded me of the John Leather item. The book 'The Salty Shore’ is all about the river Blackwater and well worth having on your bookshelf. Amongst the cruiser fleet news is that of Russ Fuller who reports "My thanks go out to John Witter and others who helped out on the Friday before the Regatta when one of our friendly Thames barge owners did his best to move Kalinka's mooring with the boat still attached. It would seem the barge lost some tar in the process but without John's prompt attention the result could have been far less happy". The adventures (or misadventures) involved in the delivery voyage of the Victoria are continued from the previous month and are illustrated by the following quotes:- - “So far che weather had been warm and the sea slight, but a remark was made that whereas the wind had been steady it was now tending to gust to what one would call 5 plus". - "I will make no guess as to the strength of the wind for the next six or seven hours, but the sequence of events should give some idea of the weather conditions prevailing". It is probably worth quoting most of the remaining article:-

10, - "To begin with, it was the noise of the wind and rain that made conversation difficult, shouting being the order of the day. Steering by compass was now very difficult indeed and we needed to get sail off. We had the following sails on - mainsail fully up with no reefs in, genoa (heavy) fully up but we could do something about that as it had furling gear worked through a drum anda series of lines from the cockpit. A jib with reefing gear was bent on and secured up forward ready to hoist to replace the genoa. It was decided to furl the genoa and hoist the jib which should have been quite simple at that point in time, but it was stuck and just wouldn't move. By now we were sailing on our ear and John went forward to try to release the furling gear without success. Later, whilst John and I were trying to release the furling gear from the side of the cockpit, there was a most almighty crash and the boat heaved over the other way. In the dark and confusion nobody knew immediately what had happened except that 'yours truly’ was shot across the cockpit and unable to move. We had gybed. A torch brought from below shone on to me to show that when we gybed I was trapped by the mainsheets, which by some freak of fate had entangled themselves in the snaphook attached to my harness at the chest end of my lifeline. Two and a half parts of the sheets had entangled and it took four or five minutes to free them (the half had been cut into by the hook and a knife needed to free it). 1 was scared stiff that we would gybe again and I would repeat the performance perhaps with fatal results. I could feel no serious damage, which was a miracle considering I had been flung violently across the cockpit completely without control, in the dark and with no warning. When I was extracted from the mainsheets, we had the genoa aback and needed to gybe again to get on course. The quickest way was the most dangerous and put the mast under very severe strain in that we wanted to put the stern through the wind under engine to save going through a 360 degree or thereabouts under the prevailing conditions. This manoeuvre was executed successfully...... ; - "Attempts were still being made to furl the genoa when with no warning whosoever there was a terrific crack and a shudder and the genoa tack came adrift, the sheets became detached and the genoa shot up the forestay to within twenty feet of the masthead. We had an uncontrollable thirty feet or so of jumbled up sail flying out almost horizontally from the masthead and exerting goodness knows what strains at the point not designed for such. It was urgent now that the main should be reduced to lessen the risk of losing the mast, but we soon realised that it would have to come right down as the reefing gear was incomplete and therefore no reefing was possible. This was executed with some difficulty, which I will explain later, for at this time a searchlight shone on us from two or three hundred yards astern, and a loud hailer blared out something which due to wind, rain and general conditions could not be deciphered. I did however wave and after three or four minutes the ship veered off and continued on its way. In retrospect 1 consider this is what happened. Our 'masthead genoa’ was in fact an indication of distress according to International Maritime Law, in that it constituted something conspicuous flying from the highest point of the ship. Some very alert lookout had seen it and true to tradition had closed us to see if we were in need of help. When close enough to see that a sail had carried away and that the man at the helm waved ‘casually’ they assumed that we were capable of looking after ourselves and departed". - "By now the sea was such that to look over ones shoulder could cause fear, for all that could be seen was the white curling tops of the next line of waves. Poor Jimmy had to look, for his Dad was at the wheel and looking ahead and he was looking for lights and timing them with a stop watch, for which he deserved a medal”. hate but let's get back to why we had trouble getting the mainsail down. Our lee rails were under the water at times and we had to get it up on the wind and with the genoa gone, she didn't want to do it under sail alone. This meant starting the engine, which was, as I said, a heavy vehicle road one which had a shallow sump, and therefore heavily healed there would be no oil in the sump to circulate. This risk had to be taken so the engine was started and the oil pressure monitored. We did get into the wind, the boat did come upright (and the sump) so we could get the main down and the engine running. How John and I did it I'll never know". - "What to do next ? The situation was as follows:- the genoa was thrashing halfway up the mast, but still acting as a steadying sail. The main was down, but the engine was running, so we could ‘relax’, review the situation calmly and decide our next move". - "There was a unanimous decision to re-establish our position, which isn't surprising since for a couple of hours we had been at the mercy of wind and sea. It must be pointed out that we knew we had plenty of sea room to leeward so at no time had we been in danger of running ashore".

- "It might be worth noting here that conditions were such that all crew members had life jackets or buoyancy aids on (life jackets being blown up) and all were secured by some means or other to the boat. This was mainly because of the darkness and the atmosphere which noise, movement, spray, torrential rain and general uncertainty created. At times there was considerable confusion but at no time was there panic”. - "Back to positioning ourselves. We knew that we were somewhere in the vicinity of the North and West Hinder so the helmsman (myself) steered as straight a course as possible, Jimmy had the stopwatch and the navigator was at his chart table below. Most lights, even if different colours, normally flash 'X* number of times in so many seconds. Jimmy's job was to look for lights, start the watch on the first flash of the next sequence, let it go through its sequence and stop the watch on the first flash of the next sequence. He then handed the watch down the hatch and said '4 reds every “that"' or '3 whites every "that"’ - the "that" being the time (of successive sequences). 1 added "fine on the port bow" or "on the starboard beam" whichever was appropriate". - "Within twenty minutes we had a light and two light vessels looms to look at, but the waves were big enough and we were small enough to blank out whole sequences for quite long periods. We did however know that the two light vessels should have been the North West Hinder which were about twenty miles off the Belgium coast, and about 8 to 10 miles from us. They were roughly where they should be but too distant to confirm without doubt. It was decided to close to what must be the West Hinder which we did, and within an hour could clearly count the light sequence. In fact we closed to within three or four hundred yards to get a good point of departure for the next buoy”. - "It was almost light by now and we were over the Hinder Shoals with the seas very big and confused which made steering even with a huge wheel quite difficult. They were by far the worst seas any of us had seen from a small boat, except maybe Bill, but he was below". - “We were very weary, very tired and those that had spent the night on deck, very wet (in spite of all the weather gear) and cold". - "It should be remembered that all this time the genoa was flogging at the masthead, for even with lifelines it would have been too dangerous to work right up forward in an effort to get it down, even if we could see how whilst it was dark". - "At about 8 o'clock, after passing Middlekirk and Ostende Bank West Buoys, we could see the coast quite clearly, visually and on radar, from Neuport in (the) south to Blankenburg in the north, with Ostende a welcome sight in between". - "Perhaps readers have wondered why we couldn't pick up the lightships on the radar. The reason was as follows:- on very small ships with the aerial say 25ft above sea level, spray, sea clutter and heavy rain all help to interfere with transmission and reception so much that the equipment ceases to function efficiently. The fact that the buildings ashore were much higher, more stable and had a greater reflective area did enable us to see the coast when we were fifteen miles off and yet not see the two lightships at three or four miles distant". - "The seas were more pronounced in direction as we got clear of the Hinder and it was decided to try and get the genoa down as we would have fouled everything had we tried to run up into the harbour". This adventure story is continued in the next Navigans Past. From the NATIONAL COASTWATCH INSTITUTION The Reinstatement of Coastal Watch Stations At Padstow and Cadgwith seven Fisherman lost their lives when their vessels foundered within sight of the shore. At Lands End four school children lost their lives when they were washed off the rocks into the sea. Another four died in the Lyme Bay canoe tragedy. All of these tragedies. and many others in various parts of the UK, might have been averted had an experienced eye been watching and the Coastguard watch service maintained instead of being cut for purely financial reasons. With the support of the fishing industry, commercial shipping and boating. yachtsmen, powerboat owners and public opinion, the Sea Safety Group (UK) has launched Operation Coastwatch. To do this we are setting up a Charitable Trust under the name of ‘National Coastwatch Institution’, A phased plan has been developed in order to reinstate 29 selected Watch Houses around the United Kingdom coastline in the immediate future, with another 14 to follow at a later date. All will be complete with full standard Watch House equipment but with the addition of both Radar. VHF and 121.5MHz Direction Finding equipment. Phase One covers the reinstatement of four Watch Houses in the South West, it is envisaged that these will be at Swanage. Cape Cornwall. Gwennap Head and the Lizard (Bass Point). Phase two covers the coasts of East Anglia and two stations on the South Coast. with phase three covering the wild and dangerous coasts of West and North Scotland including the Minch. All Watch Houses will be manned 24 hours a day for 365 days a year. by fully trained volunteer personnel drawn initially from the large corps of ex-Auxiliary Coastguards. We will be employing a full-time training staff to both carry out initial training and to ensure standards are maintained. The principal role of these stations will be to: * re-establish a visual watch in all coastal areas around the UK. * co-operate with search and rescue organisations. * assist the Coastguard when requested. * keep the Meteorological Office regularly updated on local conditions at each site. * provide a telephone service on local weather and sea conditions to anyone who requires it. * by means of Radar. assist with vessel tracking for the MAREP (Merchant Ship Reporting Scheme). * assist the Customs and Excise when required. * assist in the reporting of the MEPA (UK) “OSREP’ pollution watch. Funding will come principally from industrial. corporate and similar sponsorship. Stations will be named and call-signed under long term sponsors’ names. It is estimated (1994 figures) that it costs only an average of £25.000 per year to man and maintain a Coastwatch Station. What price if one life is saved? Further support will be sought to cover off-station training for personnel and for some local Watch Houses from public donation and national fund-raising. For the 29 Watch Houses planned under the seven phases we need an income of one million pounds per year. This is not only attainable but essential for the safety of our inshore waters to be enhanced to cover all craft not fitted with radio or those that suffer rapid and catastrophic disaster which gives no time for a distress message to be sent out as has happened all too often in the past. with the resultant loss of life. Footnote The Chairman of the NCI has given us the following up-dated details of developments. Base Point Watch House on the Lizard was opened on 18 December 1994. The immediate programme is to open (or re-open) Watch Houses at Peverill Point. Swanage, Cape Cornwall and Gwennap Head: Hurst Point and Shoreham: Great Yarmouth. Gorleston and two others in East Anglia. Contributions and other offers of help can be sent via the Chairman at: [redacted]. Brea. Nr. Camborne, Cornwall, TR14 [redacted]

Our most long-term supporters of the Marconi Sailing Club will be sorry to hear of the death recently of Maurice Greatrex. an early member of the Sailing Club. and who was at one time one of the 5 Committee members who were sufficient to run the Club in those early days. Maurice visited the Club on the day of it’s 40th Anniversary celebration in June 1992. and has has always kept in touch with the Club’s activities through Navigans. Our sympathy goes to Maurice's family at this time. Commodore’s Notes Well. we've finally had a few days of summer and doesn't it make a difference? Lots of things on the horizon. like the close of nominations for next year’s committee - Commodore and Rear Commodore included! Any volunteers? We are also very close to a major change for the Club in the appointment of a Club Steward. This is in recognition of the difficulty in filling the OOD duty, and the fact that this duty has become less of a “safety role” over the past few years and more of a bar role. However the costs are not insignificant. so when we come for a subs increase in November, remember that it’s the lack of volunteers and poor attendance that make this step necessary. ECPR approaches rapidly. and this is now our major Club showpiece - Regatta has fallen by the wayside and following a loss in 1995 will not run in 1996, L* Equipe Botheras will (weather permitting) be sailing Mick Richardson's Prindle 18-2. just to show some of these guys that I can still sail an old man’s boat! Mind you. I'm not sure that the Cat Fleet will appreciate the fact that I am chartering a Westerly Merlin on the Fal after ECPR- I told you all a long time ago I'm a sailor of many parts! It will be great to get back to a decent stretch of water after all these years as an East Coast Ditch Hopper! Hopefully, there'll be chapter and verse of the experience in months to come! Well. that’s about all for now. Larry Botheras ISLE OF WIGHT IN PASSING David (Ball) took the opportunity to keep up his sailing instructor's skills by accepting an invitation to spend 2 weeks instructing at a sailing school on the Isle of Wight. So it was home from Bristol on the Saturday and off to the Isle of Wight by train on the Sunday. The short crossing on the ferry from Southampton to Cowes had its interest for him - seeing a former MSC Cruiser (the catmaran ‘Roving Red Admiral’) flying a German flag: and a car ferry trying to get out of the way of a sailing race that insisted on starting no matter what the passing traffic consisted of! I wonder what would happen if a yacht race got in the way of the car ferry out of Harwich? No doubt David will learn a lot from sailing in completely different waters, and will have a lot to talk about when he gets back. Ed. CRUISER FLEET NEWS Margaret and Malcolm Yeoman have asked me include in Navigans their grateful thanks to all those Members who helped them on Sunday 2nd July to bring ashore their cruiser Suruca with its defunct engine to allow for repairs to be carried out. It was a stressful but successful operation where many hands made light work. Thanks also go to all those Cat and Dinghy Sailors on a very crowded Hard for their forbearance. With the time available for the task limited by the imminent high tide. the clash of activity could not be avoided. Ed. CRUISER COMMENTS Six Cruisers. SURUCA, GREEN PANTHER, ANGEL II. SEA BRUME. SILVER PEARL. & HAPPY MEDIUM, plus two guests from T.E.Y.C. namely, REBECCA & MRS MALATROP (that’s the name of the boat. not the guests) made the trip to St Katharine’s Yacht Harbour. Originally it was planned to leave on Saturday 17th June. but the weather was not conducive. so we stayed put. However, the day was not spoilt since we made up for it with a pleasant get-together in The Dell Bar. Sunday was a much better day, so at 06.30 we slipped our moorings for what was supposed to be a passage to Thurrock Yacht Club for a stop-over before making the final leg up to St Katharine’s. As it turned out we made such good progress, albeit motoring. that we were able to continue up to St Katharine’s arriving at 18.10. just ten minutes before hight water London Bridge. All. that is. except for Sea Brume who would have none of this motoring nonsense, so they stopped over at Thurrock Yacht Club, joining us the following evening. We spent three nights there. everhone doing their own thing, meeting up on each other's boats for refreshments! - followed by a get-together supper Tuesday evening in the Yacht Harbour’s Clubhouse. We all locked out the following morning at 09.00 for the trip down to the River Medway were we did a bit of a bomb burst - Green Panther, Angel II and Sea Brume electing to lock into Gillingham Marina: Happy Medium. Suruca, Mrs Malatrop and Rebecca dropping anchor at the far end of Stangate Creek: while Silver Pearl elected to take up a mooring at Queenborough. since they wanted to be away early the following day for the return trip to MSC. We all eventually met up again at Queenborough on the Friday ready for the next stage which should have been a cruise to Harty Ferry. However. the weather had other ideas with N - NE 4/5 winds occasionally 6 forecast, with overcast skies and much the same forecast for Sunday, and we elected to return direct to MSC. It was there we said ‘auvoir to our visitors whose company was mutually appreciated. then left at 10.30 for a bumpy passage back home. The bright spot was the superb weather we had enjoyed from the first Sunday through until and including the following Friday. Next on the Calendar, though possibly it will be history by the time you read this, is a ‘Duty Free Caper’. i.e. leaving the Moorings at 07.00 on Monday 17th July for a sail to Harty Ferry were we stop overnight before leaving there at 06.30 the following morning. sailing along the Kent coast to Ramsgate arriving about 14.00 Tuesday afternoon: have two “Lay Days’ in Ramsgate. one of which (probably the first day) will entail a day trip to Ostend on the SALLY LINE ferry. The return passage may be either back via Harty Ferry or direct to home waters. this will be decided at the time. In case you are wondering whey we are not leaving until Monday, the reason is MSC is hosting a MACWESTER MEET with a Bar B Q etc. at The Dell Bar on the Saturday afternoon to which MSC Cruiser Members are welcome. but please bring your own victuals for the Bar BQ. Any Members who are away - the use of their moorings for Saturday evening (15th July) would be appreciated. The next major Club Cruise will be on 26th - 28th August which is the now annual trip to Titchmarsh Marina. with supper in the Walton & Frinton Y.C. on Sunday evening. Please watch the Cruiser Notice Board in the Clubhouse for this plus any other Cruiser Events announcements. Derek Kirby - Cruiser Fleet Captain RESCUE: Just space here to mention that Tony and Pat Holbrook of “Two Jays’ checked on a yacht off Bradwell which didn't seem to to be sailing in a normal manner. They found its skipper, a lone sailor. in the water where he had been some time and who was in a bad way. With the help of another passing sailor the casualty was lifted into the dinghy and cared for until the West Mersea came to take him ashore.

6 Handicap Fleet News —— Dinghy Cruise and Picnic - SATURDAY 5TH AUGUST. At our Fleet AGM we decided to fix a date for a dinghy cruise for all to join in. Racing types are invited as well as Cruising types! Sorry to give such late notice of our agreed date which is Saturday 5 August. This is in the middle of Camping Fortnight so we ought to get a good turn out. Low tide is about 1330 and I suggest that we are ready on the hard at 1100 to set off. There will be no safety boat so we look after cach other - Laura cynically says it’s only us in our Laser 2 that needs it. Derek Hymas has kindly said he will organise what we will do on the day. He’s in a Mirror. We will try to stop somewhere and have a picnic. The Club's Regatta has been and gone. Can I once again thank everyone who helped to organise this event for dinghies. Unfortunately, this is likely to be the last one, since it is felt to be too much hard work for what we as a Club get out of it. It is hard work and a big thank you to all those who have contributed over the years. The Regatta results were given in last month's Navigans but might I draw attention to how well our Fleet did: Mike Taylor and John Willy Ist in Fast Handicap: Malcolm Gandy and Graham Richmond Ist in Kestrel class; Mark Bulkeley 3rd in Medium Handicap: and also. from the Solo Fleet. Ron Greygoose and John Salmon Ist and 2nd respectively in the Solo class. Note the name Malcolm Gandy above. He used to sail a Solo and by all accounts was very good. He got very good results at the Solo Nationals, Inlands, and other events such as the Eastern Area Championships which he won four times. He gave up for three years but has now got himself a Kestrel that he sails in our Fleet races. he wins each time he sails but. of course, the conditions haven‘t been right for us! I’m trying to get hints from him on how to sail my machine. He's sailing with the experienced Graham Richmond as crew at the moment. so at least we won't be beaten by Graham's Hornet. They entered a Kestrel open event down the river recently but only came 2nd with a win and two 2nds! The Boothby Cup was a disappointment. Despite all my efforts to field a team of three. come the day we only had two boats: Malcolm and Mark Bulkeley in the Kestrel and Peter Woodhouse with his Laser. As individuals they were also competing in the Maylandsea Bay Challenge Cup where Malcolm and Mark came 3rd, I think. Many of you will have noted our Commodore and his wife, Larry and Alex, racing with us in their 505. What a way to teach your wife to sail! Alex has been introduced to the mysteries of the spinnaker already and simultancously to the art of capsizing. Why is it that they ended up on the RIB while the RIB helm and crew and myself. from the Jack B, were in the water righting their boat? I suppose it’s something to do with rank. We are very pleased to have them sailing with us and long may it continue. It's so long ago that I nearly forgot. The Fleet party given by John Weedon and his wife Mavis went very well. It’s a pity none of the non-racers came, but it was nice to meet some of the racers’ spouses we've not met before. Thank you John and Mavis for a very enjoyable evening. Don’t forget the Cruise and Picnic. Racers, get racing - you've been very uncommitted this year so far. Good sailing all. Don Gill Gull Sailing Dinghy Available for ‘Adoption’ The Club owns a Gull Sailing Dinghy which it would be ‘nice to see-being- sailed in return for being cared for and maintained by any Member who has a need of such a boat. My elderly information source tells me it is a wooden dinghy, 11°3” loa, 4°6" beam, 60 sq ft sail area (I assume a main and a jib), with a PY of 116 - Club's experts might know if this last still applies now. I'm told this Gull is fully equipped and ready to sail. Whenever I express my wish for a nice big cruiser (more work off the water and more terror on it!)
