NAVIGANS PAST 1977 (July) - where there's a (Regatta) will, then there's a (Regatta) way - and where's there's a wind, then there's a wave (with 'stormy weather' in the offing in both cases). The 1977 Regatta - Club Commodore, John Witter, summarizes the results of a committee meeting which 'went over’ the views and comments arising from the organisation of the 1977 Regatta, and which were:- (a) Sailing: well covered with good distribution of help. Minor problems with spotting due to inclement weather. Rescue facilities stretched but coped. (b) Galley: good preparation and supply of food, etc. Some people spent more time in the Galley than ideally we would like, but this was often at individuals own insistence. (c) Bar: good service given by Brewers. Generous support behind the bar during peak periods but in general too much for one person outside the peak periods. Some spells of duty, particularly during Saturday evening party, became stretched and more advance commitment required to spread load. (d) Clubhouse Facilities: This was the area in which we were most stretched to meet the demand. There are, however, problems with providing extra facilities but these are under consideration. Despite the shortcomings, many people return each year knowing what to expect. The Committee apparently reached no conclusions as to the future of Regatta, since the views received had been more on the ‘organisational aspects' and expressed mainly by people who were not particularly pessimistic about Regatta. The views of the sailors, along the lines of "what do they want from Regatta ?", are also required. John states "The question of Regatta is clearly an emotional one and unless some of those who enjoy it and want it (to) continue say so, the view will be one sided and it will surely die." John continues "It should also be borne in mind that the problem of getting voluntary help to do things at the Club is not unique to the Regatta but is present throughout the year and is an older problem to which we have to find a solution if the Club Officers and Committee are not to become disillusioned. " John goes on to outline his personal perspective of Regatta which was:- (i) to provide good competitive sailing and an opportunity for our members to sail against members of other clubs on our home waters. He points out that 1/6th (presumably approx. 35-40) of the 225 entries were members of the MSC and were represented in 9 fleets. (ii) to offer an opportunity to sail from our unique and much admired facilities to members of mainly local clubs on the river and in Essex and thereby reciprocate the facilities available to our members at other clubs. (iii) to limit the disruption of Club life to a minimum of weekends in the year and to avoid opening the Club to all on too many weekends in the year. This was in deference to the wishes of the members who are not competitive sailors and who like to enjoy the privacy the Club can offer for the majority of the year. (iv) making a profit from Regatta was not the main objective, although naturally a successful one does make a substantial profit...... Ditti cess he would not spend the time supporting the event if profit was the prime motive. (v) did not support Tom Gaskell's suggestion of a ‘closed jamboree’ rather than an open sailing event since it would be against the interest or tradition of the MSC and would be a recipe for disaster for the competitive sailing interest of the club. The idea of cruiser members racing with the dinghies within an essentially ‘closed’ event was an ideal of the early Regattas which had died very quickly. (vi) Holding several (single class) open meetings during the year in place of the (multi-class) Regatta would still require a great deal of organisation and commitment and it would be difficult to interleave club racing with open events without rescue launch support from other clubs. John reports that analysis of the entries showed that the help for the Regatta organisation came mainly from the (club member) entries themselves and their families with additional support from the fleets on a rota basis and goes on to say:- "The question of size and how to limit it and still offer open sailing is one to which there appears to be no easy solution but 12 years ago (ie. 1965) we were equally worried about size when we had 80 boats and since then we have held Regattas with more entries than this year's without the benefits of our present

clubhouse...... The main differences I think now really arise from our ability to accommodate more people under canvas than previously and not from the sailing organisation". John rounds off his extensive ‘Commodores Notes' by saying:- "I do not expect my personal views to be supported unanimously by the members or the Committee, but the Club consists of a lot of minority interests making up the whole and one of the jobs of the Committee is to try and cater for all these interests over a period of time and a balance has to be struck.......... In conclusion I would say I have no regrets about the many hours spent on the Regattas since they first started and my reward is knowing our members and visitors are enjoying good sailing." Note from Mike: I believe I am right in saying that John and Eleanor Witter helped (in a big way) in running over 20 successive Regattas and, despite being keen racing sailors in (between them) the Enterprise,Solo and Mirror classes, never (or at least rarely) managed to actually sail in the Regatta themselves. They are, of course, not alone in this and in similar fashion the Greygooses and the Weedons have always been well to the fore to help with Regatta over an equally long period of time and others, no doubt, are also worthy of mention. | However, one of the most remarkable of records must be that of Robbie and Joan Sims and family who carried out the role of Race Officer/Race Box team for 24 successive years and only missed out on the 25th anniversary event by virtue of Robbie being Commodore and having to perform other duties. Even then Robbie, Joan and family again completed additional 'tours of duty' as Regatta Race Officer before their move 'up country’ brought their record run to an end. John Weedon (Sailing Secretary) says "As far as future years are concerned | will be willing to assist in any way and I am sure that others will do also - provided we have the support of the Club". Roger Smith writes in to say "...as a fairly new member...... whilst I appreciate that the lions share of the organisation of such an event must fall on a few experienced people I wonder if the Club makes best use of its resources...... I was prepared to help....but have not been contacted........ I hope we continue to stage a Regatta." A view from a cruiser member (Freddie Harrison) highlights the very real problems arising from the presence of a large number of people at the club during Regatta. Not all of them were entirely honest and upright (at least, not in the context of competitive sailing when otherwise sober honest citizens seem to think ‘anything goes' and everything is excusable in the quest to compete and win). Apart from the annoyances of pilfering of boat items, etc., Freddie writes "Like many others I removed my cruiser from Stansgate the week before the Regatta to give the racing enthusiasts more room at the start line....... I returned to Stansgate to find crowds of strangers, a drunk at the bottom of the ditch and, to crown it all, my poor old banger with its paint work deeply scored fore and aft plus a flat tyre...... next to me was a shiny ‘R' registration which might have got the same treatment if it had not been for the vigilance of two Marconi members." Freddie goes on to basically support Tom Gaskell's viewpoint of a closed 'Club Regatta’ with open meetings during the year to attract the visiting experts. No debate about Regatta would be complete without a contribution from Malcolm Stuart who has, by word and deed over the years , always been an enthusiast for 'the open Regatta’ no matter what the perceived problems. Malcolm puts forward similar arguments to those of John Witter in favour of Regatta. Malcolm writes "As regards the work entailed one would expect to find, as in all things, a pendulum effect whereby the trend shifts from lots of willing helpers one year to fewer the next. No amount of prior organisation will completely eliminate this...... (I) hope that we can continue with an event that requires no further justification than that it attracts World Champion Helmsmen to our Club." _ He then presents us (in line with his irrepressible sense of fun and humour) with a ‘formula’ for working out some statistic or other which appears to have a great deal to do with the concept of the passing of water (as distinct from that of passing over water):- = Cl. Ha) 5 + PLL. where C.L. = Crossed Legs and P.L. = Portable Loos in caravans and with tents. Perhaps it has something to do with the number of people likely to be jumping up and down in anguish - or something!

The maiden voyage of Victoria - The July, 1977, Navigans contains the concluding episode of the adventures and misadventures of the delivery trip of the Victoria to Holland (or was it Belgium?). Those who have not read the previous two episodes of this story from 1977 Navigans will need to read 'Navigans Past’ in the April and July, 1995, issues of the present-day Navigans. We take up the tale with the Victoria's genoa flying wildly out of control from the mast like a giant streamer, and life for the crew being generally uncomfortable:- "The skipper went right up into the bows....and after inspection he called for a knife.....the necessary rope was cut, the sail dropped low enough to be got at and was eventually stowed. This is an over simplification for the job took almost an hour under impossible conditions........ This then was our first bit of luck in a night of setbacks....... With our large (pennant) down, which had acted in some ways as a steadying sail, we began to roll violently. Frightening noises below subsequently proved themselves to be tool boxes and provisions. A thorough inspection below showed that we had made water, but nothing serious.....It was confirmed later that the water had spilled out several time (from the toilet) when we were healed or were tossed about.” "...we decided to put the mizzen up as a steadying sail. | One had to experience the change to appreciate the difference a very small sail can make.." "After an hour or so we had come inside the shoals off Ostende and we were comparatively sheltered. All hands came on deck and, with great relief 1 am sure, watched as ‘yours truly’ (because he had been on the helm most of the time) was given the great privilege of taking Victoria through Ostende breakwater to make her first landfall. That was one of the most satisfying moments of my life. Within an hour we were tied up and asleep." "Inspection showed the following:- (1) The Genoa was only slightly torn and damage marginal to one seam and the eyelet where the sheets were attached. (2) There were two deck leaks, one caused by the strain put on the handrail protecting the steering console and one round the forehatch. (3) A starboard side stanchion was bent as was the guardrail running from it. Its base screws had also gone and the angle plate strengthening damaged. It was where the end of my lifeline was attached when I was flung across the cockpit!!!" Other than the above, no damage was found.” "In retrospect it is very difficult to know how some of the problems could have been avoided as it is easy in hindsight to hold a post mortem....... Again in retrospect I feel that no maiden voyage should have had such bad luck. However, it proved the boat for the owner and proved the crew to themselves." "The following advise could be given as guidance should somebody wish to make a similar passage:- (1) Do a short night sail prior to the crossing to see that the compass is adequate. (2) At the same time familiarise the crew with working on deck in the dark for sail changing and other necessary activities. (3) Have an alternative destination well planned should the original not prove feasible. (4) If there is a chance of sea sickness, take all precautions for avoidance well in advance. (5) Remember that cold fronts invariably mean foul weather, so don't be afraid of them but be ready for a change of plans and some very uncomfortable sailing. (6) If it is ever intended to cook or even boil water on the passage, a fiddle rail and gimbals on the cooker are most essential even if only for safety. (7) Make sure that some of the crew has enough experience to take care of the boat under any conditions that might be experienced on passage. "I think apart from the compass, which was essential, and the cooker, which wasn't, Victoria's crew fulfilled all such requirements and a successful passage was made even if the original destination had to be changed. Would I do it again tomorrow? Of course I would." Note from Mike: as far as I can see, the three episodes recounting Victoria's delivery (and maiden?) voyage were written by ‘Anonymous’ for I can see no attribution of an author given with the articles Mike Boreham 2 9 2 2 ae 2k oe 2 2 a

10. TRITON OF OSEA,, Port de Plaisance, Rochefort France To Doreen & Derek Kirby Rochefort. Wednesday 6th April. As you see I’m having a practice with the PC. I'm probably one of the few people who take longer to type a letter than write in longhand. but at least this way you can decipher it! The weather here improved about midday, and the sun came out for the afternoon. We spent quite a while poring over the charts and almanacs trying to make sense of the firing range problem, and are now much clearer about the areas involved and need to get more information about their firing times. We don't seem to be able to pick up Arcachon Radio clear enough here to make head or tail of the broadcast. perhaps we will try the automatic message on the phone. Ray made a valiant effort today and had a look at the grill! Upon dismantling it he discovered it did not have a control screw as he had expected - however with a little adjustment of the angle of the dangle and a good fiddle he put it back together again. At least the cooker got a thorough cleaning and | think it has improved a bit. Monday 10th April. Phoned the repondeur and got a very short message ‘Aucune zone engager’ (No areas engaged). however the next day I tried again and got a great long fast spiel far too fast for me to understand. I went to get my recorder but Daniel saw me and insisted on phoning himself (he has a phone on board). He listenened to the message. writing it down. then explained it to me - and then phoned again so that I could hear it again and (hopefully) understand the message. The gist of the message was of course times, days and positions (Lats and Longs). It started off with ‘Du centre d’essai’ which referred to the centre of the test area. I'll try a few more times and see if I can get the hang of it. The weather seems to have settled into a pattern. It's often chilly first thing. then warms up through the morning. then is really hot in the afternoon. Long may it continue! We've been keeping busy plodding through our list of jobs. Ray's installed the new VHF. which involved some tricky wire threading almost standing on our heads trying to get it under the floor and up through the battery box! The SSB is also installed (quite differently than planned, but it looks fine). haven't had time to use it much yet. On Saturday 8th we went to a Classical Concert here in Rochefort at the Coupe d'Or Theatre, which we are told is built as a miniature copy of the Paris Opera House. It certainly is miniature! There are only ten rows in the stalls. and only three rows in the circle! You felt there were almost as many people in the orchestra as in the audience. However it was really beautiful. very ornate with a domed ceiling with painted cupids, gilded pillars and great draperies. It certainly made a change from our pontoon! Tuesday 25th April. We are nearing the end of our stay here and intend to leave some time through the coming weekend. The weather has been quite changeable for the past week and we have had some rain on the majority of days. We are amazed by the speed with which it alters, within minutes it can go from cold and damp to glorious sunshine (and the reverse). Our list of jobs has been worked upon steadily and most of the important things are sorted out. although there are a few things we hope to get in La Rochelle. The English chap from the boat behind us. the Moody Eclipse. went to La Rochelle by car and asked about a lift-out at the place we had been given a quote in November when we were here before. It is now obvious that we had been given the winter rate. which was almost half what it is now! Also they were getting very booked up. so once again, Daniel to the rescue, he phoned and sorted out the current prices, and booked us a lifi-out for 15.30 on Tuesday 2nd May. We are considering leaving a few days before then and having a good sail to test everything. and then staying on one of the islands for a couple of nights before we go to La Rochelle. However unless the weather improves we'll stay here. There was a Force 8 forecast for Biscay yesterday and it is certainly blowing at the moment. Afier all the research with the firing range we have decided to make life simpler by going directly to Santander (at least that is the plan at the moment!) It is about 200 miles to Santander from La Rochelle. so depending on our speed. somewhere between 5 to 6 knots. it will take 33 to 40 hours. We have planned to be out of the water for a week in order to allow for any wet days when we can’t antifoul. but after that we will be looking for a settled period of weather to cross the Bay. Monday Ist May. Well the weather has certainly improved. the last few days have been hot and sunny, real shorts weather, but we are still here in Rochefort. dt is the May Bank Holiday and the favourite mooring spots are apparently very crowded, so we have decided to go straight to La Rochelle tomorrow. We have managed to sort out the wetherfax programme and can now get daily charts and analyses, all we need to do now is understand them! We have heard on the grapevine that Dave and Joan (Thomas) left about two weeks ago and hope to arrive at St Helena this weekend. they are averaging about 120 n. miles per day. Santander, Sunday 14th May. Well here we are in Santander. After being lifted out at La Rochelle on the 2nd May. the weather turned really warm and we sweltered for a week on the shore. antifouling and generally getting the boat ready to leave. There was virtually no wind and the temperature was well into the high 80s. We were reading the weather forecasts each day and the chap in the Capitainerie suggested we visited the Meteo Office which is actually in La Rochelle. They were extremely helpful and showed us the predictions for the coming week. These showed a deterioration from Thursday 11th with gale force winds by the Friday and Saturday. As it turned out they were pretty accurate. which is why we are still here in Santander. We decided to start off on the Tuesday morning about 6 am. and went out to St Denis on Ile dOleron. a bit further north than Port Douhet where we drove

11. to with you. We picked up a buoy on Monday afternoon intending to get a good rest in order to leave about 6 o clock on Tuesday morning. However the current whips around the corner there and it was really uncomfortable. We were obviously not going to get much sleep. so about lam we let got the buoy and set off. We are sailing in company with Brian and Joan Lee who own the Moody Eclipse which was on the same pontoon as us in Rochefort. Although the wind was OK strength-wise it was almost behind us. which made rather a loppy motion. and impossible to set the sails. so we motorsailed the whole journey. It was reasonably uneventful. except Brian picked up a fishing net around his rudder miles off shore and in 100 metres of water. He went to great lengths to try and free it, hanging off the back of the boat at one time. Also we tried to tow him around to see if it would drop away. but to no avail and after an hour and a half he cut himself free. In spite of this delay we arrived at Santander at 8.30: 198 nm. in 31.5 hours. At one time during the crossing I heard an enormous bang. and looking at the chart. realised we were very close to the firing range. I noted in the log that I had heard this explosion: mentioning it later. I was informed that it was. in fact. Concorde flying over! Everyone was very friendly and welcoming at Santander. although when we arrived it was quite early and there was no one at all who spoke any English. There was great hilarity as we did our best with the phrase book. then the Capitanio arrived (a lady) who spoke French so we got by all right. It was a good marina with free hot showers and electricity. but a long way from the town and no public transport. One of the marina workers insisted on giving us a lift to town and we were having a good mooch round when the heavens opened and we got pretty wet. We are just getting used to the hours kept here by the shops etc. It seems even later than France. with nothing much opening in the afternoon until 4pm and the restaurant here doesn’t open in the evening till 9pm. Gijon, Wednesday 17th May. After a few storm bound days in Santander we heard a forecast for a SW force 4. so we set off at 6am on Monday bound for Ribadesella about 60 miles away. By midday we were in enormous seas with wind gusting up to 34 knots. We discussed about 6 different options. none of them ideal, and luckily about 4+ pm the wind eased and an hour later we came to the little entrance between the mountains and popped into Ribadesella. There is no marina. just a quay along the main road. We moored to the best bit which had a notice saying ‘Reserved For Fishing Boats’. just to sort ourselves, but a chap whizzed up in a car and said (in English) “Good evening. this is good. OK here 2 metres OK”. He gave us some leaflets on the locality and disappeared. never to be seen again. We were there two days and there was no charge. nor formalities. We have seen the Aduana (Customs) in Santander and here in Gijon. They copy down information from passports etc. but are not too sure what they are reading. We now have our address as 7 Southview. Hockley. as this was an address in our passports under “Emergency Contact’. also when they asked where we had started from. I said Rochefort. and they wrote down Oxford! The forecast for Biscay this morning was SW v NW 5 to 6 rising to 7 occasional 8 (on Radio 4). however the local one was 2 to 3 and we had a lovely summer sail today, 29 miles here to Gijon. The scenery on the trip was really stunning. The Cantabrian Mountain Range runs parallel to the coast here, and they drop right down to the water in places. with steep rock faces. and sometimes come down in tree-covered slopes or fields. The highest mountains are snow covered and the whole picture is quite breathtaking at times. In the clefts of the rocks you can see small sandy beaches and the occasional little village. hidden from view except at just the right angle from the sea. We feel we should have taken longer to cover this area as we are sure we are missing a lot. Perhaps we'll come back again some time. Here in the Marina at Gijon we are on the International pontoon with a British Cat. a small Swedish boat on the way to the Canaries. and a few French yachts. all travelling south as we are. The facilities here are excellent: showers. water and electricity all included in the price of £7.25 per night for us. Brian's 33 footer is £4.50 so we can't complain about the costs so far. Also everyone. harbour officials, the Authorities and the public in general have been very welcoming and helpful. We were a bit anxious due to the trouble with the Spanish Fisherman. as we are right in that area at the moment, but haven't had any problems at all, touch wood. Well. that’s brought you up to date with our travels. we are making our way along the north coast and around Cap Finisterre to be in Bayona by 8th June to meet up with the Rally Portugal mob. and will later be in Lagos on 20th June. We are picking up the English end of the UK net on the SSB and have heard them speak to Joan, though we can’t hear her reply. They left St Helena almost a week ago and are on their way to Ascension Island. Hope you are well and enjoying life. please send our best wishes to Barbara and Don and anyone else at Marconi. I'll try and write again later, if not, you'll get an occasional postcard! Hazel & Ray Becket

Commodore’s Notes Well. the season has rocketed away. and it only seems five minutes since I wrote the August/ September Spiel. I thought the above cartoon would make most of you smile. It brought to mind one or two incidents on the charter we did in Falmouth. but I'm saving those for the Laying-Up Supper speech. except for the foray into Land Yachting! We were moored close to the Cat Clinic in Mylor. and they ran taster evenings. A quick 30 minute drive to Perranporth Airfield with a nice gentle evening breeze and we were introduced to the Learner version - a proper landyacht with a wind surfer rig size variable to cope with the size of the pilot - yes | had a 6 metre rig to everyone else's 5.0. It was absolutely brilliant fun. very much like cat sailing only more so. and I was gob smacked to be invited to try the “proper” Class 5 job - narrow tyres and all. Speeds were exceptional. the latter had an 8 to | mainsheet - Harken Blocks and all. Tacking and gybing was an acquired art with the main requiring to be eased to get the battens to pop and then hauled in rapidly. taking care not to stall the rig. Could this be a diversion for the winter? 1995 season is rapidly drawing to a close as is my term as Commode. Fortunately. one or two people have come forward to fill the gaps that will arise. It certainly doesn’t seem like three years since | started this lark. Things have moved on nicely. with technology easing individuals' burdens (articles in this Navigans have been scanned and processed through Optical Character Recognition). As you will now know. the attempt at recruiting a Steward had limited success. with Bill Barker leaving because of the finances and tax. Whilst here it seemed to run well and is certainly going to be pursued again. Anyone with ideas for candidates please talk to Steve Hill or myself. Only one more article to go! CRUISER COMMENTS What has now become our annual sail to the Walton Backwaters. staying at Titchmarsh Marina with an evening meal on the Sunday at the Walton and Frinton Yacht Club. was another success. Fifteen Club Boats attended together with three guest boats, making 18 in all. Weather conditions on the Friday were not too promising. making the get-together in the Dell Bar a short one with most people wanting to get aboard at low water before it got rough. The Saturday morning, however. could not have been more different with blue skies and a light NW wind taking us gently up to Walton where we all arrived. or nearly all. by late afternoon, In the evening the crew of Green Panther. i.e. Mike. Joan and Neil ran up the gin pennant and played host to the Fleet with two types of ‘punch’. Sangria & Pimms together with cocktail snacks. thus providing a pleasant end to the day even if it did start to drizzle towards the end of the evening. Sunday morning was spent with a visit to Thames Coastguard Station at Walton-on-Naze where Senior Watch Officer Tim Smith and his fellow Officers made us most welcome. in fact. we spent a good two hours there. (Whilst at the Station members were given a booklet entitled “Safety on the Sea’ the back page of which was a perforated section to be filled in by boat owners as part of the Coastguard “Yacht and Boat Safety Scheme’. If you would like to let me have these I will return them en-bloc to the Coastguard.)

3. Just as well the visit was arranged for the morning. for all hell broke loose during the afternoon and the Coastguard resources were at full stretch with yachts running for safe anchorages. In fact. Titchmarsh Marina had to turn boats away as they were fully booked. The evening was spent at the Walton & Frinton Yacht Club where we were provided with an excellent main meal. sweet and coffee at a very modest cost. The forecast for Bank Holiday Monday was not good so those who were able to spend another day at the Marina returning home on the Tuesday. when, in fact, the Wallet was quite busy with many ‘stop over boats’ making their homeward passage. The crews of Green Panther and Capricorn had to be back for work on Tuesday. so they arranged to leave their boats at the Marina until the following weekend. However. Suruca. with her stalwart crew of Malcolm and Margaret Yeoman. assisted by Roy and Margaret Bellord made the homeward passage on Monday to find the worst part was getting ashore in the dinghy. A brief view of MARS as seen in its environment of green,red and white light. Despite the introductory title, this is not an exploration of the Red Planet. This article is very much Earth- bound, or should I say ‘sea-bound'. In this case, MARS is a non-government confidential and voluntary reporting scheme for seafarers to highlight ‘incidents’ which they have experienced and which might otherwise go unrecorded and/or not receive widespread circulation amongst those who would find them of interest and benefit. Sometimes the reports include two (or more) very different viewpoints of the same incident at sea, in confined waters or simply alongside in harbour. I find the reports very interesting to read even though I am not a seafarer. Thus the following appeared in the publication Seaways, June, 1995, (The Journal of The Nautical Institute) and is taken from the MARS (ie. Marine Accident Reporting Scheme) Report No. 95024 and is reprinted with the permission of Capt. Robin Beedel, FNI, Compiler of the MARS. ee a 2 2 eee Not that t "A recent nation-wide ITV feature programme showed the work of Gosport and Fareham Inshore Rescue Service. In the programme, one of their rescue craft, a high speed, semi-inflatable took a dis-masted Catamaran in tow. In the process, the young lady crew member made the tow rope fast to the rescue craft's towing bollards with, if my memory serves correctly, what seemed to be a superfluous number of ‘figure of eight’ turns, but more with a final locking turn. dangerously, For obvious reasons, a tug must always be able to free itself quickly from its tow and where a quick release hook does not provide this facility, then the simple Towing Hitch, which can be quickly and simply thrown off, should be used to make the tow fast to the tug. I am sure that if sea-going members of the G & FIRS were to contact a traditional tug boat or an RNLI lifeboat, someone there would demonstrate the correct hitch.” IR KK I quote from another MARS report in the same issue of Seaways. An illuminating Experience This report was submitted by ‘someone’ on a large container ship travelling at 20 knots on a dark but clear night somewhere between Sydney and Auckland. "We were keeping a vigilant watch............. suddenly presented with a single green light....... it was obvious ...it had just been switched on. No discernible radar echo.....1 estimated the vessel was 4 miles ahead. We deduced Sees a yacht.......running with the wind and therefore crossing ahead of us. | As the bearing remained steady, I was just about to alter course when the green light changed to white (and deduced the yacht was coming about and would show red any second). After two - three minutes (no change)...decided white light must be stern light.....and (yacht) was turning about. Just then an anxious voice came on Channel 16 VHF "this is yacht ******* calling vessel in front of me, do you see me....... I have put my deck light on so that you can see me" (having switched off the combined lantern). The ‘big ship’ reporter deduced green would still be showing (if not switched off) and made a considerable course alteration accordingly and ".....(the yacht) altered his course to pass safely round our stern. I courteously but firmly chastised his action............. twenty minutes later I heard a further confrontation on the VHF between the same yacht and another vessel”. oe eo eo Most of the MARS Reports are written from the point of view of the ‘big boats’ and concerned with the professional side of the international maritime activities. However, it might be interesting if some of our cruiser members were to write an account of their encounters/experiences (from the point of view of a ‘little boat’ and the leisure side of things) and send it to MARS. Their views might not be right as seen from the bridge, but they could be illuminating! Mike Boreham

Marconi Members go for gold Whilst the MSC's core activities are centred on the club racing programme, not all members confine their activities to our particular patch of water. It's worth noting some sailing achievements outside the club. The Anderson's adventures - Philippa and Charlie Anderson's family of four youngsters followed up the Marconi Cadet/Camping Fortnight by ‘going for it' on the river Crouch. Jo-Jo (Josephine, 10 years and 3.5 st.) was invited to crew in the Cadet dinghy of family friend, Dominica Lindsey, at the Royal Burnham Cadet Week. They finished 4th out of 30 in the 7-race series and also won the long distance race. Prior to that, they had some good club racing results on the Crouch. Philippa reports the two girls "did a lot of chatting" as they sailed; obviously the formula is successful. Now the two girls are planning winter training (sailing - not chatting). Good luck. Charlotte (8 years and weight unknown) sailed an Optimist at the Royal Corinthian Otter Week and also took part in an informal round-Osea race (organised by the owners of Osea Island), sailing her Optimist from the Marconi club hard all around Osea and then insisting on practising capsize drill in a force 6. Good on yer, Charlotte. Not to be left out of things, the two young men of the family, Thomas (14) and Rupert (12), also sailed at the Royal Burnham Cadet Week, with Thomas helming a Scow and Rupert helming a Cadet. Unfortunately, schoolwork curtailed much of Thomas's sailing activities but Rupert continued on to the Otter week in which he was invited to helm a Scow for its 7 year old owner, Cloe Warren. They met with great success, not only winning the points series, but also making a clean sweep of the long distance race, the crew's race and the single- handed race. What a smashing way to spend the school holidays. The older generation - a rather older generation (ie. those at or just finishing University) also got into the sailing act on the river Crouch during Burnham Week. Jenny Ball, Lucy Boreham and Stuart Golding crewed on a Contessa 32 and helped bring it into 3rd place in its class, scoring two 2nds, four 3rds, a 4th and a Retired, despite not being too familiar with the boats’ bits and pieces (although they had no trouble with sail trimming). It is understood they have an invitation to go back next year; let's hope they can make it. An even older generation - Malcolm Gandy finished 4th in the Kestrel nationals at Weymouth. Earlier this year, Malcolm said he was back into sailing to "sail just for fun" - he's obviously having a great time even if he's not taking it too seriously ! On top of the world in the far North West - former MSC member Damian Boreham earned himself a gold medal when his team won the first 'YRU World Dinghy Team Racing Championships held at West Kirby in late August. Damian and his 5 team mates from the Spinnaker Club (Ringwood) had earlier this year won the UK Selection Trials and thus represented the UK as the UK 'A' Team in the World Championships together with a UK 'B' team from West Kirby which included Russell Peters, recent winner of the televised Ultra Series. Amongst the competitors were national dinghy champions and others in the top level of their national sailing scene. Mike and Maggie Boreham went up to watch the last 4 days of the week-long event and found themselves witnessing some of the most riveting and exciting close quarter, dynamic and fast sailing action you would wish to see - and it was all very spectator friendly with viewing stands at the side of the marine lake right alongside the West Kirby clubhouse. The UK 'A' team finished top of the initial Round Robin elimination series, losing only one race (to UK 'B’). Thereafter the UK 'A' team won all their remaining races, beating UK 'B' in the Quarter Finals, OSC 'B' in the Semi-finals and Ireland 'A' in the Finals after a tense and exciting series of races not without their near disasters and nail biting endings. Eleven teams took part in the event; two from each of the UK, OSC and Ireland and * one each from Australia, Canada, Czech Republic, South Africa and Japan. Teams from France and Poland, although initially expected, did not compete. The event was sailed in 24 specially built Firefly dinghies. Don't forget, if you are sailing away from the club, let the Navigans' Editor (Maureen Ball) know all about it; after all, there's more to a sailing club than just club sailing. * Netherlands also had a team taking part.

Handicap Fleet News Well, we had our cruise and picnic and everyone thoroughly enjoyed it. We had perfect weather and an ideal breeze. Derek Hymas had been busy behind the scenes organising and had plotted a trip down to the beach just beyond Bradwell power station. He even offered us the optional extra of a visit to the power station which we decided would be trying to do too much and also we thought our wet suits weren't quite right for the occasion. Low tide was earlier than we would have liked and the wind was against us going out. so we decided that Derek in his Mirror and Jack and Diane Rushbridge in their Mirror (I didn’t even know they had one) should set off as soon as possible. Laura and I set off later in pursuit. Even later, Mike and Maggie Boreham set off in their Wanderer after making sure they had everything, which included three passengers. Well that was the total task force! I had hoped to see some of our cruising fraternity, since this event was really intended for them, but I'm coming to the opinion that cruising types may be of a more solitary nature than the racers to whom the social side is very important. At our beach. | was not keen on taking our tender Two (at last. I think I've found a suitable name for our dinghy!) onto the rock embedded mud but fortunately there was a yacht aground waiting for the tide and with owner's permission | moored onto her. The two Mirrors were happy to be lifted onto dry land. The Wanderer eventually arrived and of course Mike had brought two anchors for her. After a convivial hour for lunch we returned although Derek and us first went across the water to sail around Tollesbury creek. A pity that Laura and I had to leave early that day because we could have spent all afternoon spinnaker reaching across the river (Laura did relent when she realised how quickly we were getting back. so we did a few to appease me). I’m afraid we ve made Derek most envious of our Two and I think he is going to rig himself a trapeze on his boat. Thank you. Derek. for organising a most enjoyable and memorable day. The August Bank holiday was a big disappointment with racing cancelled Sunday afternoon and all day Monday because it was too windy. At least we did get some racing in on Sunday morning when we set out in something like 4. The 4+ soon changed into 5 and there were many excursions into 6 before most of us retired. Larry and Alex retired actually a bit before the race start and were quite pleased they did. Clare Davies bravely took out her Mirror and eventually decided to come in before her luck ran out. Paul Bulkely just got fed up with capsizing his Laser. Laura and | gave up after our second capsize (Laura disappeared, when our boat turned turtle, much to my horror. then suddenly appeared behind me saying “You know you can breath when you re under there”!), Even Malcolm and Graham capsized in their Kestrel. which was reassuring. Laura was very apprehensive when we started this race and I thought she was spilling too much wind: to encourage her, I suggested she sheeted in a bit more, just to be told in no uncertain terms she was scared stiff and not enjoying it one bit. Larry tells me this is how we get the nautical expression ‘sheet scared’! Thank you. Howard Rogers. for setting such an exciting course - I didn’t know it was possible to have as many gybe marks as that! Howard informs me that Paul did actually finish even if he didn’t realise it and that. of the three Solos racing with us. one retired on the first beat. another on the second and Ron Greygoose finished. Howard said he had an even better courses lined up for the afternoon although he had only two cat sailors and Malcolm Smith (Solo) signing on for them! I acquired an_ extra ‘Laser’ buoyancy aid that Sunday. Some kind soul found it lying around. assumed it was ours and popped it under our boat cover. Note: Laura and I have our names clearly marked on ours. The jacket is now in the Club's lost property (i.e. boiler) room. Anyone looking for a crew? A Stuart McIntyre is looking for such a job (cruiser, cat or dinghy). He can be contacted at home (22 [redacted], Chelmsford) on [redacted]. Summer series results are up on the notice board. I’ve not got details, but I think Mike and Maggie won. Well done. Well done, too. to Malcolm Gandy and Graham Richmond who came fourth in a field of 17 in the Kestrel national. Not bad for their limited experience of this boat. John Weedon came seventh. Both tell me they should have done better! Stuart Golding was crewing for someone, but they didn’t have anything to shout about. I understand that Damian Boreham has just won a world championship! No details. but I think dad is reporting separately on this. I also understand that lan Caruth has just won a flying gazcbo championship at the Prindle nationals. Have details, but I trust it will be reported in the Cat news - if not, I could tell the story next month! How quickly the season goes. I look forward to seeing more of you sailing in the couple of racing months left. Don Gill

FAST CAT NOTES Maybe it’s a sign of advancing senility, but the years tend rather to blur together for me. Luckily for my own state of health, a few key dates can still be called upon at will (like 21st September 1991) but otherwise “the year I joined MSC’ or ‘the year we got the Hurricane’ are something of a mystery to me. to be unearthed only by recourse to the archives (or, more likely, Caroline). Maybe this is a protective mechanism evolved to allow me quietly to forget the advancing years. but, if so. it reckoned without the Piers Race. Am | alone in perceiving that the time interval between adjacent Piers Races is a small part of that between any other two apparently annual events? No sooner had the embers of last year’s event cooled than ‘the committee’ had reconvened and this year’s was fast approaching. And what a race it was... a very good turnout, fine weather and, as is coming to be expected, great organisation. My thanks of course. and those of the Fast Cat Fleet, go to all those who helped in either a major or a minor capacity. Marconi SC has established a reputation and set an example for others to follow in events of this sort: in so doing it. and its members have become the largest single supporter of Sailing for the Disabled through the RYA Seamanship Foundation. ] understand that a number of ‘tweaks’ will be made to the event next year. with particular attention being given to the form of the Briefing and Sailing Instructions, entry criteria for the ‘reduced’ course and how we can ensure that the best use can be made by the competitors of excellent sailing conditions. I am sure we can look forward to an even more enjoyable weekend in 1996. The results of this year’s race are printed elsewhere in this issue of Navigans (Ed's note: Next issue, see Page 20!): my congratulations go to all those who completed either of the courses. In particular I must congratulate Paul Metcalfe.

11. whose performance was not merely ‘good’ or even ‘excellent’. for it was “here comes glorious Daddy” that his arrival back at the Club was heralded by James. Now there's a level of performance to which we can all aspire. I understand that the Glorious Paul Metcalfe has offered to run a series of seminars over the winter entitled “Glory and How to Attain It’; whether he will address sailing techniques or those of the indoctrination of infants has not been revealed. Blossoming Reachers (or Blooming Reachers?) I must admit to being delighted that Steve and Tom have seen the light and decided to trv a reacher. Caroline and | have found that it has revealed a whole new aspect of sailing catamarans, and downwind has been elevated from a sometimes tedious, sometimes frightening experience. to one which is always challenging. often exhausting and thoroughly enjoyable. I’m sure that Steve and Tom. and any others who follow the same path. will not regret the decision. After last year’s Piers Race I reported that we'd seen no sign of the kite ‘lifting the bow’. contrary to claims from aficionados. However at the time of writing we've just returned from a windy August Bank Holiday Series. which saw us (for the first time in more than a year) going downwind without the reacher: I'd forgotten just how unpleasant it could be. We'd used the kite on the first lap and had a very fast but reasonably controlled descent across the river. going low but with the apparent wind well forward. On the second lap discretion (or rather a misplaced view of what would be discreet) took over and we crossed the river in a series of pitching nose-dives and surges of acceleration (at what was a considerably lower speed). I must now eat my words: | infinitely prefer the more controllable way the boat sails with the kite up (although the need to maintain clear water to leeward for the emergency bear-away. combined with the negligible visibility in that direction remains something of a problem). And I am sure Caroline will find her newly-lengthened arms very useful. John Nickalls Wandering Around The Western Approaches In A Month Of North Easterlies Afier the traumas of the '94 season when following a comprehensive winter refit Mona had got just as far as Dover before the engine decided to give up the ghost. our aim for the '95 season was fairly straightforward. Simply to get away. get some decent sailing in and hopefully see a few interesting places on the way . Not having previously explored the English coast beyond Poole or the French coast beyond St. Malo we settled on the general idea of exploring the West Country and Brittany. The plan was to get down to a line somewhere between Cherbourg and Poole as quickly as possible. and then take it from there depending on wind and weather. By the start of our trip the prevailing South Westerlies hadn't been much in evidence for several weeks so we were anticipating their likely return before too long giving us a slog westwards and hopefully an easier run home. The saga of last summer's enforced stopover in Dover had lasted until we had finally got away at Easter this year. The whole sorry tale could only have been called 'Depression Over Dover' including as it did a collision whilst under tow and a near sinking following removal of the engine. Not surprisingly perhaps Helen had developed a phobia about going anywhere near Dover but it was something that couldn't easily be avoided. if we were going to get down to the West Country. With both our daughters on college vacations and in need of holiday work we weren't entirely sure of the composition of our crew until just before we left. In the event Laura came with us and we left Jenny behind with some fairly tentative arrangements for her to catch up with us a couple of weeks later. We locked out of Heybridge Basin at half past ten on Sunday 23rd July with the intention of starting with a gentle sail to Harwich allowing us to skirt round the top of the Estuary the next day. As it happened we had such a good sail down the Wallet that we decided to keep going and ended up after a lively sail. in a falling wind and foul tide desperately trying to continue sailing to Ramsgate in the small hours. Finally resorting to the engine we made harbour and securing to the Refuelling barge snatched some sleep before it opened in the morning and we were able to fill our tank. After a walk round Ramsgate we felt somewhat revived and decided that in spite of Helen's misgivings it would be sensible to make the most of the afternoon tide to potter down to Dover which we duly did. anchoring in the outer harbour. contd....

12. So it was that early the next morning we prepared to leave for Brighton just as we had done a year before. Fortunately this time the engine roared into life and a ghost was hopefully laid to rest. We were blessed with an Easterly three that soon built up into a healthy four or five and ensured rapid progress down the coast. With the genoa boomed out we goose winged in blazing sunshine towards Beachy Head. The only drawback to a perfect scenario was the limited visibility. At this point I suggested that it was a shame to waste this favourable wind. So we decided to keep on going and give Brighton a miss. As the afternoon wore on the wind increased and the seas built up to give us an ever more exhilarating roller coaster of a ride. Once or twice Helen expressed some concern that we had too much sail up but | felt that we had things under control. As we approached Selsev Bill. well offshore. warnings came on the air of Force Sevens. We were getting apparent wind speeds in the upper twenties and the seas were building up appreciably. | began to consider how we could get some sail down with the genoa poled out and the mainsail on its preventer. Then a particularly violent wave rolled us into a gybe. The preventer parted like a bit of rotten cotton and the mainshcet snatched across the cockpit catching Helen's shoulder and jarring her neck quite badly. With Laura on the tiller | managed to get the main down with the wind behind us and set about de poling the genoa which we eventually accomplished by rolling the genoa up bit by bit until we managed to take the pressure off the pole. We then carried on sailing under staysail alone still making good speed. while Helen aimed some deserved and extremely meaningful looks in my direction. and tried to relax her neck. With the wind registering a constant force seven and very lumpy seas it wasn't the pleasantest of night sails but it was extremely satisfying plotting our progress south of the Isle of Wight and into Poole Bay arriving off the entrance to Poole Harbour at dawn. The wind dropped and we motored into the harbour and picked up a buoy. We'd just tidied up when a thunderstorm that had been threatening for some time finally hit. | have to admit that it was extremely pleasant lying on our bunk under the forehatch watching as lightening flashed and torrential rain hammered down on us. After a rest in Poole where we met up with my parents. we sailed with them the next day to Weymouth only to discover that we had picked the last firing day of the summer in the range off Lulworth. Our enforced detour six miles out to sea combined with the still poor visibility ensured that we saw little of the Dorset coast. Having left my parents in Weymouth the next morning we tackled the delights of rounding Portland Bill in a stiff South Westerly (one of the few we were to have all summer) without catching more of a glimpse of it in the extremely murky conditions. Once round however the sun came out. visibility improved and we settled on a fairly reasonable slant across Lyme Bay. It was a thoroughly relaxing afternoon with the wind vane doing the steering and Mona making a steady six knots. There were no ships and little else to worry about. | kept scouring the chart for hidden dangers waiting to ensnare us. which I was convinced must be there somewhere. but couldn't find any. Helen decided that this particular chart was a thoroughly bad buy as there was virtually nothing on it. Having laid the other side of the coast off Exmouth just as it was getting dark. the wind dropped to nothing and we motored along to Torbay feeling our way right into Torquay courtesy largely of Decca and then into the Marina. tying up just after midnight. Just before we left Torquay the next day. Dave Steward arrived in Swiftsure on his way back from Dartmouth having left the club the day before us. We pottered around to the Dart on what was to prove to be the first of several hot windless days. not so good for sailing but almost ideal for exploring the rocky shoreline and rivers of Devon and Cornwall. Once through the impressively narrow entrance of the Dart we were carried rapidly on the flood past Dartmouth and up to Dittisham. a peaceful and really lovely spot where we picked up one of several visitor's buoys. Nearly all the West Country rivers we visited were equipped with a healthy supply of these. Now very much in pottering mode we carried on round the coast in brilliant sunshine but limited visibility to the breathtaking Yealm and on past Plymouth to Fowey. taking advantage of the settled conditions to anchor in a bay near Polperro for lunch and a swim. and venture close under the craggy cliffs. Both Helen and I thought that we knew the West Country well but we were amazed at how different it all was when approached from the sea. As we motored in flat seas towards Falmouth I began to contemplate the possibility of taking advantage of the settled conditions and pushing on further than we had originally intended and perhaps get to the Scillies. In the meantime. suffering from the heat and the continued drone of the engine. we switched it off as we rounded the Dodman and swam from the boat. This gave us the rare experience of swimming in fifty metres of water and swimming round an apparently motionless boat whilst the Decca continued to register our speed over the ground as somewhere approaching two knots. The Fal Estuary had been one of the places we particularity wanted to visit and we weren't disappointed. We arrived in the middle of an evening race which made things interesting. We spotted Red Admiral and picked up a visitor's buoy off the Royal Cornwall Yacht Club.

13. From Falmouth we made our way with just a littke more wind but still poor visibility round a suspiciously quiet Lizard into Mount's Bay. We considered anchoring off one of the harbours for the night but in the end made for Newlyn where we rafted up against a fishing boat in for repairs. The pilot books aren't very keen on Newlyn but from our experience and observations it was a pleasant interesting stop and far preferable to neighbouring Penzance. We were woken just after midnight by one of the most spectacular thunderstorms we have ever witnessed. It seemed to remain almost dead overhead and accompanied by torrential rain continued unabated until about eight in the morning. Somewhere along the line we decided that it would be prudent to delay our departure from Newlyn. It turned out that the whole of Newlyn had been deprived of electricity and at least one fishing boat had had a direct hit and had lost all its electrics. Tragically the Seaman's Mission were unable to provide the hot showers and cooked breakfast that had been highly recommended to us. We later walked into Penzance where we once again basked in brilliant sunshine. The next morning we were up bright and early and with a North Easterly three to four occasionally five given for Plymouth on the six o'clock forecast we cast off and headed out of the harbour eagerly anticipating a fair wind and fine sail to the Scillies. Even as we left the harbour it was obvious that the BBC hadn't got it quite right. We were confronted by a blustery wind and short heavy seas that even with Mona's weight. we were having problems powering through. A sizeable fishing boat that had left the harbour ahead of us turned back. Watching his re-entry through the narrow harbour entrance quickly dissuaded us from trying the same. We were committed. Once we had fought our way off the immediate lee shore we set about getting some sail up. With some difficulty we had the main up double reefed and the staysail set. Hard on the wind to bash our way out of the bay. the motion was now far more comfortable. Then amendments to earlier forecasts started coming over the radio. Talk was now of Easterly sevens that we were already experiencing. continuing and possibly increasing for the next two or three days. Although once out of the bay the Easterly would have given us an easy run to the Scillies. the Pilot Books make so much of the lack of good shelter in The Scillies and that in a good blow you should make for the mainland as quickly as possible. it seemed rather foolhardy to consider running there in a near gale. Also we now only had a couple of days before Jenny was free to meet us and so our stay in the Scillies would have been an extremely brief one. All these considerations were debated as we made our way as best we could across the bay. The only reasonable alternative was to make for Falmouth which we did thereby committing ourselves to a long slog hard on the wind around The Lizard. Under her snug rig Mona handled the conditions extremely well. steering herself most of the time without need for any assistance from the wind vane. and making between five and six knots into extremely heavy seas. As we closed the Lizard the tide turned against us and our tacks became less and less favourable. On each tack the Lizard would loom out of the mist as if to haunt us. As evening drew on the wind dropped and we were able to motor sail into St. Mawes anchoring in a sheltered spot just off the quay. We had arrived back in the Fal in the middle of Falmouth Classics and the next day we explored the Estuary with the added excitement and interest of admiring and avoiding legions of Falmouth Working Boats. The wind died as the day went on but apparently thunderstorms centred over The Scillies continued. so we weren't too upset by our decision not to go there after all. We followed the Fal right up to Malpas and just about managed to avoid running aground in pushing up far enough to reach the yard at Malpas where Mona had been built. We were staggered by just how beautiful the whole Estuary but particularity the upper reaches are. We then went to Falmouth Marina where we tied up between two Saga's also designed like Mona by Alan Pape and we were immediately told that the manager of the yard had an Ebbtide 33. We also did our bit of celebrity spotting seeing Libby Purves and Paul Heiney on their new boat. We also saw their old boat Kate O'Malley which was now sporting a German flag. The next day Jenny arrived and we set off to explore more of the Fal Estuary picking up a visitor's buoy at Malpas and enjoying a superb walk through the thick forests. From the Fal we made the short trip to the Helford River which lived up to its reputation as a magical spot. Relaxing at anchor and drifting about in the dinghy. we considered our options. If we were going to get to Brittany we needed to go soon. Our problem now was once again too little as opposed to too much wind. Also we were all in an extremely relaxed state and it took a bit of an effort to consider a longish passage. In the event we left in the morning and were blessed with clear skies and a fresh Easterly. Once clear of the river we got a slant which took us Clear of The Lizard and which we were able to hold all day, making good progress. We hardly saw a ship and our only scare was a sudden burst of three very loud reports followed by a dull roaring when there was nothing at all in sight. and which we eventually decided must have been Concord. The wind died as night came on but we managed to keep on sailing until about one in the morning when we resorted to the engine. As we homed in on L'Aber-Wrac'h, the last place on the Brittany Coast before Ushant. the dawn which seemed to be contd...

14. extremely late in arriving brought with it a drastic reduction in visibility. With the aid of Decca we located the off lying buoy but were concerned about proceeding as all the information we had on board emphasised the importance of picking up the right leading marks and of the folly of entering in fog. Eventually I called up the Harbourmaster who was extremely helpful and gave me the confidence to proceed. We only really saw the place once we were safely in but once the visibility had cleared a bit we could see what a spectacular place it was. After exploring the rocky shore and pressing further inland we decided we had to spend another day there. In the morning we were pleased we had decided to stay. because visibility was if anything worse. Then out of the murk Natasha I V came into the harbour. Brian later demonstrated how useful his Yeoman Plotter linked to GPS was in such conditions. They were in the middle of an extremely comprehensive tour of Brittany and having wintered in Dartmouth last winter were intending to winter further down the coast prior to entering the Canal du Midi next season. We then spent most of the day exploring upriver in the dinghy. Leaving L'Aber-Wrac'h as we had found it. unseen, the mist closed in even more severely and we had a worrying couple of hours when we could barely see a few yards. until things improved somewhat. We were also contending with spring tides which were certainly making their presence felt. As the day went on the wind increased from the west and we had a lively run. with the Decca giving us eight or nine knots over the ground. We rounded Ile De Batz in fine style close enough to see the rocky shoreline in graphic detail. We then crossed the bay to the newish Marina at Trebeurden which has been created by building a sill in the opening of a rocky cove. The entrance is dramatic and the whole area is enchanting. We spent a fascinating day exploring the immediate coastline. From Trebeurden we had another lively and stimulating sail in better visibility passing inside Les Sept Iles and entering Riviere de Treguier after some confusion with the marks at the entrance. We made our way up the narrow and beautiful river arriving at the old town of Treguier a short while before low water. It was fortunate that it was no sooner, because arriving and departing at the marina. at anything other than slack water. is extremely difficult. The steep walk into the town proved to be well worth the effort. The remarkable cathedral with its hollowed out spire and the market square are particularly noteworthy. After dropping down the river again and spending the night at anchor just inside the entrance we delayed our start long enough for the morning mist to clear slightly and then set off in a total calm for Guernsey. The long motor was enlivened by a period of balloon spotting. We managed to retrieve one minus its label and then one intact before agreeing to ignore the rest. We stayed overnight in St. Peter Port before braving the Alderney races where we recorded ten knots over the ground under sail before struggling into Cherbourg having gone too far inshore too soon and fallen foul of the inshore eddy. We were very impressed with the revamped marina at Cherbourg which seems to be capable of coping with a seemingly never ending stream of visiting yachts. From Cherbourg we rounded the Pointe De Barfleur and went into St Vaast de la Hougue a tidal fishing port that by building a single water gate has managed to create a sizeable marina whilst remaining a lovely little spot. We had a swim in incredibly warm water and caused all sorts of mayhem in a restaurant when I decided to be adventurous in my eating habits. An early start saw us hard on the wind and just holding a course for Le Havre which we reached in the early evening after a satisfying sail. The next day we decided on a shortish afternoon hop round the corner to Fecamp. As we left the harbour and came out of the immediate shelter of the headland the North Easterly was quite stiff and still motor sailing Mona set off with a vengeance. As we left the harbour Laura got stung by a wasp. The sting later turned out to be quite nasty. In the confusion while that was being dealt with we became aware that a woman sitting on a sailboard was trying to attract our attention, waving her arms frantically. We circled round and made our way over to her and Helen went on the foredeck to try and communicate. This wasn't easy but it became clear that she wanted to get off. She had obviously come out of the shelter of the land and been unable to get back in. Now she had had enough. and had apparently given up. We still had our sails up and were drifting away so we circled round to get the sails down. She seemed to think that we were leaving and put her head in her hands. We got the sails down and closed in again. By this time I was aware that she had drifted into the main shipping channel and a ferry was heading straight for us. As we closed in she got off the board and made to swim towards us. We told her to get back on the board which she did. We then threw her a line which she eventually secured to the board. We then pulled the board in and helped her onto Mona. Once she was safely on board we set off to get out of the ferry's way and made our way back into harbour with the board in tow. We eventually managed to call up the harbour authorities and tell them what was going on. and a contd...

15. launch came over to see if the woman was all right. As we passed the beach she seemed to make a recovery and asked us to drop her on her board near the beach. We felt happier taking her into the Marina. We wanted her to rest but as soon as we had got the board on the pontoons she went off. When she came back later in the day to collect her board she indicated that she had gone into shock after going ashore. Later that day Jenny decided that it might be a good time to get the ferry home. so she left on the night ferry and we set off for Dieppe. We were once again plagued by poor visibility and little wind. what little there was being North Easterly. A long motor was temporarily disrupted by a large sack round the prop. which necessitated a tmp over the side to clear it. Fortunately no damage appeared to have been done and we made our way into the surprisingly pleasant port of Dieppe. The ferries have now moved to a new outer harbour and the inner harbour is being developed as a marina right in the centre of things. After a much needed lay day when I almost scuppered things by draining the fuel filter on the engine and breaking off the tap on the filter (fortunately I was able to get a replacement with the help of marina staff). we continued our tour of ferry ports and headed for Boulogne. a place with more interest than its initial facade suggests. In spite of a very early start that day to optimise the tides. Helen insisted on a walk up to the old walled city which was in fact well worth the effort in spite of my protestations at the time. We were now fast approaching the Bank Holiday Weekend which was our intended deadline for getting back. Things were looking rather more unsettled but the words South Westerly. which we thought had vanished from the English language were beginning to reappear in bulletins. Leaving on the tide with a West South West Six we raced down to Cap Gris Nez. We held a right angled course across the lanes and tore across some pretty lumpy seas. By the time we'd cleared the lanes the tide had swept us nicely up to the Goodwins which we rounded and enjoyed a brisk sail to Ramsgate in what had now become a North Westerly seven. In Ramsgate we took advantage of the newly installed marina facilities. the days of rafting up now seemingly over. With an unsettled forecast we crossed the estuary in mixed weather. A strong North Westerly died away and became a weak South Westerly giving us a gentle run down the Swin, getting back to a North Westerly Seven as we sailed up The Blackwater. which seems to be pretty well par for the course. The next day Bank Holiday Sunday was even livelier as we locked into Heybridge Basin and we had our first full gale warnings of the entire trip. five weeks to the day after leaving. Malcolm Shaft.
