16. NAVIGANS PAST 1977 (August-December) - links with the past gradually fade as Dugdale-Bradley reminisces but links with the past are sadly broken with the death of Queenie Hallam. August - a front cover picture of a low-tide scene from the 1977 Regatta describes it as "cold and windy”. Shirley Wood (Editor) reports the annual barbecue (presumably the habit of calling it a BBQ had not yet become implanted in our mind) a great success with the inevitable ‘midnight swim'. Shirley says "I refused to participate this year, but I was still forced to tolerate the moans and groans from a cold, complaining brother who did!" Shirley also reports changes to the boating scene with Mirrors being changed for 420s and Hornets whilst Enterprises were being changed for 505s. Malcolm Stuart advertises for sale "Tutor Class 8 foot GRP dinghy ..... Good safer sail trainer for youngster under the right conditions". Does he mean it's a bit tippy? September - the front cover shows Ron Greygoose behind the bar at Regatta. Amongst the sailing results for the 1977 season are the Marconi Dinghy Challenge Cup (29 entries) with the winner from Stone S.C., the Pilots Cup (3 entries) won by Colin Leveridge (Debutante), some 10 mid-week races of which 5 were won by Mirrors, the Jackpot (14 entries) won by Pat Black (420) (with Mirrors 2nd and 3rd), the Mona's Cup (24 entries) won by Chris and Robert Weedon in their Mirror and a Jubilee Race (41 entries) won by Chris Weedon/Katie Hampson (Mirror) with Dave and Colin Harper (420) 2nd and Malcolm and Stephanie Gandy (Mirror) in 3rd spot. Peter Clayton (Hornet Fleet Captain) reports on the visit of 6 Marconi boats to the Hornet European Championships held at Cramond Boat Club (near Edinburgh). He says "Socially the week was very good which perhaps reflects our poor showing in the results. Mike (Taylor) and John (Tillotson) did best with a 22nd overall" - however, Mike and John did get a best place of 11th. Reports of the club's Mirror Open records 31 entries (10 from Marconi) with 22 boats crewed entirely by juniors (under 18 years old). Windy conditions with force 4/5. Marconi was well represented in the Ist race by Simon and Jane Kenworthy (2nd) and Malcolm and Caron Stuart (3rd). The 2nd race (after two general recalls) gave the Marconi team of Chris and Robert Weedon a 3rd place. and they improved still further by winning the 3rd race. Maylandsea Bay Y C helms took Ist and 2nd places overall but Chris and Robert Weedon finished 3rd . October - hoping to inspire a few new faces to volunteer for committees, etc., Commodore John Witter supplies an organisation chart of the club's management and committee structure. Cadet Skipper, Rick Anstey, reports success for Peter Elwell, Linda Savill and Rachel Cherry in attaining their Elementary Tests, with Heather Stuart and Sara Anstey passing their Intermediate Tests, thus making 7 cadets receiving the Elementary, and 10 cadets achieving the Intermediate, RYA Certificates. November - John Witter mentions the laying-Up Supper at which John Dugdale-Bradley reminisced about Stansgate in the 1950s. I suspect that Mr Dugdale-Bradley was one of Marconi Sailing Club's ‘characters’ although I'm not sure if he was actually a member. The Mirror Fleet AGM (7 attended) elected Deborah Harper as Fleet Captain in succession to Stan Oaker who had joined the Solo fleet. The 1977 Prize Winners List includes:- Ray Hampson (Helmsman of the Year),10 qualifiers, two races Eleanor Witter (Ladies Cup), 6 races, 9 different helms with average of 3.7 per race. Chris Weedon (Cadet Trophy), 6 races, 21 different helms with average of 8.9 per race. Katie Hampson (Mug's Mug),

17. December - Ron Greygoose writes his first 'Commodore's Column’ having been elected Commodore at the 1977 AGM. Joyce and Jack Reeve announce they have given up their Mirror but will still be continuing their land- based activities; I remember them often digging the weeds up, etc. in the beds alongside the clubhouse. New-elected Social Sec., Dave Lawson, reports on the children's Christmas party (50 children attended) and also announces a winter meeting at which Donald Forbes a nationally acknowledged expert on rigging and sail setting (a subject upon which he had lectured to the British Olympic Sailing Team) and Roger Hance (nationally well known MSC Enterprise sailor) would presumably talk about setting up rigs and sails. Retiring Commodore, John Witter, refers to the Ist Regatta (1965) which had been put on by the MSC at the request of other local clubs because, at that time, the bank holiday was fixed by the moon and not by the Government, resulting in the other clubs rarely having any water to sail in for that particular bank holiday for most years. John had been both Sailing Secretary and Regatta Secretary for the 1st Regatta event. John also reports that 1977 had seen an increased demand for cruiser moorings. John Weedon's Sailing Report acknowledges the donation in 1977 of the Jubilee Cup "by the Commodore" (presumably John Witter) and notes MSC successes in the Blackwater & Colne Dinghy Championships for John Tillotson and Mike Turner (Hornet Class winners and 2nd in the Cock of the River final) and the Saltcote Open Cadet Cup “won again" by MSC through the efforts of Colin Harper and Robert Weedon). MSC Membership numbers are quoted as follows:- 1977 1976 Ordinary Members (ie. MSC employees) 260 282 Associates (ie. non-Marconi) 101 98 Family (members by virtue of having a close relative employed by Marconi) B.A 40 Totals 41 420 Honorary Members at end 1977 17 Changes to the committee meeting arrangements during 1977 had been aimed at giving the sub-committees more responsibility for longer periods. Thus the Main Committee had met every second month and the Executive Committee in the alternative months thus created. The conclusion of the arrangement had been that, although the sub-committees welcomed more autonomy, the less frequent Main Committee meeting schedule has not been successful due to "the reduced forum for communications between the sub-committees and their respective functions. Some committee members also felt that it was not as easy to become involved with the overall club activities." The (retiring main) committee therefore did not recommend continuation of the arrangement although sub-committees should retain the same level of autonomy. The Membership Renewal Guide for 1978 shows:- Ordinary/Family Member £5.40 £ 16.20 (1 boat) (no MASC fee) £ 19.44 (2 boats) Associate £17.74 £ 28.54 (1 boat) (inc. MASC and postal fees) £ 31.78 (2 boats) Cruiser Fees Ordinary/Family £20.52 (4.5 - 7.5 metres) Associate £32.86 ee . ring Ordinary/Family £24.84 (7.5 - 12.0 metres) Associates £37.18 Cee th ary Finally, yet another link with the past was broken with a report of the death of Queenie Hallam who died on 9 December, 1977. Queenie's husband, Terry Hallam, had twice been Commodore of the Marconi Sailing Club at very significant times of the club's development. Mike Boreham

18. 40 Y Ago: May- 195. A number of subjects were reported and expanded upon at Committee Meetings over the period:- The Fitting Out Supper - was held in the early part of the year and made a profit on the coach of one shilling (5 pence in today's money) whilst the profit on the raffle was twenty-six shillings (£1.30 at today's currency). The club boat Avril - Since Mr C (Cliff ?) Clarke had done a great amount of work on the re-fit of the club boat Avril it was agreed that he should "...have the privilege of a bosun's mate." Lucky Mr Clarke! Presumably, all at the club's expense. A letter of complaint from a member who had booked Avril but found out quite accidentally that it had subsequently been booked to some other person. The complainant writes "Apparently, but for a fortuitous telephone call by Mr Nichols, I should have been completely unaware that my booking had not been accepted and would have travelled to Heybridge and been involved in a dispute as to the right to take the dinghy. I cannot but feel that I have been treated with gross lack of courtesy and consideration". The Committee agreed to send a letter of apology and that, in future, all bookings would be made via Mr Clarke. Club Steward and Clubhouse - The question of a Club Steward was raised, mainly by Mr Nichols. He suggested that a member be made Club Steward to be responsible for the condition of the workshop and it was agreed that (a) a broom be bought, (b) fixture cards printed and (c) a first-aid kit be kept in the club-house. 1 wonder if our ‘volunteer’ Club Steward was ceremoniously presented with the broom (silver handled ?) at the AGM when, presumably, he/she would take office ? At a subsequent meeting,Mr Nichols again felt there should be a Club Steward to organise the Clubhouse and keep account of the boats stored in the workshop. Mr Clarke suggested a circular about boat storage be sent to all members but the Committee decided to find some other means "....in view of the small response to the last circular". So what's new? Who reads the 1995 Navigans? Perhaps only you and! - and I can’t remember what was written anyway? By the end of the 1955 season, the store/clubhouse was now full of boats and it was felt either the club had to expand the premises or find a new site. A long discussion took place but nothing definite was proposed. However, a suggestion from a Mr Rose that the club might like to use (ie. purchase ?) his Motor Torpedo Boat (MTB) Whimbret for use as a floating clubhouse was not accepted. A letter from Eastern Electricity Board rejected an application from the MSC because it was signed in pencil. Gay events - An invitation from the organisers of Chelmsford Carnival to take part in the ‘Illuminated Boats’ class was declined! However, the Sailing Section (ie. MSC) decided it would have two Fleetwinds on display at the MASC Gala Day in July, namely Mr Pavitt's Diablo and Mr Wardell's Lion (with Dr Eastwood's red sails). Sailing matters Presumably, some doubt had arisen as to the insurance position when a dinghy was helmed by a person other than the owner (presumably when the club borrowed the boat for a team event against another club). Commodore Geoff Wardell reported that it seemed that, with other clubs, the damage to the boat was paid for by the owner (presumably on his/her insurance). A letter from the club's insurers confirmed the owners insurance would cover damage whilst being sailed by another person but that some club's took out insurance at the rate of ten shillings per boat per meeting in order to protect the owners No Claim Bonus. However, since the premium was greater than the No Claim Bonus amounts to be lost, the Committee agreed to pay the No Claims Bonus in the event of a claim. The club won a team race against Maylandsea Bay Yacht Club by 20.25 points against 19 points. Presumably there was some feeling of ‘favouritism’ with team selection/participation for Mr (Terry) Hallam complained the race had not been fully publicised. Commodore Geoff Wardell replied it was on the fixture list as distributed to all members and anyone interested could have attended. A clue as to 'the problem’ might be revealed when Maurice Greatrex suggested that in future team races the leading helmsmen of the Fleetwind races should represent the club. However, the race itself seemed to have been very enjoyable since a letter from the MBYC says "....] think the racing was the best we have ever had" - and they were the losers!. The East Coast Fleetwind Championship, 1955, - was organised by the MSC, using the Blackwater SC clubhouse (except for the Sun Lounge which was being reserved for Blackwater SC members only). Entry fees were (a)

19, Practice Race 2/6 (ie. 12.5 p in today's money) and 5/- for the 3-race series (plus 1/6 per boat for the services of a steward). Strong winds accompanied the event and in one race there were 9 capsizes out of 18 starters. The event was won by Mr.Wiffen with MrJ Hammett third (both of Maldon Little Ship Club). The 2nd place was obviously ‘an outsider’ for he isn't named but came from the Tudor Sailing Club. A note says that the saluting cannon are "...now in the possession of the Club and are satisfactory." Presumably these are the (two) cannon the club uses today? How ‘green’ are the seat of my pants? - A letter from Maldon Council confirms a ban on painting of boats on the sea-shore between Decoy Point and the Canal Lock at Heybridge Basin (as well as the Marine Parade east of the Marine Lake). for the area below high water on ordinary tides (effectively meaning the whole beach area). The ban was imposed after complaints of damage to clothing resulting from oil and paint left after boats had been repaired or painted. Clearly no namby-pamby ‘green’ issues here; only materialistic (quite literally) issues were at stake. However, it seems the Blackwater Sailing Club intended to organise a meeting to register a joint protest. Subsequently it turned out that the ban applied only between May and September and it was felt that ".,.no useful purpose would be served by a further protest....... ". This was clearly before 'green' politics. Raising high hopes on the seawall - plans by the Catchment Board to raise the height of the seawall resulted in a meeting with the Area Engineer and a request for drop-boards in the seawall opposite the main doors of the clubhouse. It was noted "A number of concrete slabs were observed on the sea wall and the club has applied to buy some to put in the slipway". The club's request for drop boards was agreed provided the club undertook the responsibility of ensuring the boards were in position and padlocked no later than Ist October each year and remained so until at least the following 31st March. The club also hoped to have rings fitted into the sea wall and perhaps bolts to hold channelling to provide a runway up the seawall for (dinghy) launching trolleys A'pleasurin’ thru' t' win'r - The Laying Up Supper was to be held in late October, 1955, at "The Jolly Sailor", with arrangements for a pianist and the provision of a coach (presumably from, and return to, Chelmsford). The date was subsequently changed to early November "...the Friday after pay-day". Alas, no bar extension was possible because the application had been submitted too late. Invitations for two were sent to the Maldon Yacht Club and the Maylandsea Bay Yacht Club. In addition Mr C Stebbings (Water Bailiff?) was to be invited. The programme of winter meetings would be held in a room at the Lion and Lamb, Chelmsford. Mike Boreham 2 2 2 ae ae 9 ok oe 9 ak Breeze II - and very pretty too. As Maggie and I leaned casually against our Wanderer on the hard, patiently awaiting the start of the afternoon race during mid-July, we cast our eyes with a great deal of admiration, and some envy, at the pretty tan-sailed, gaff rigged, clinker built dinghy with its smart yellow painted hull and varnished deck and interior fittings. I'm sure we've seen it a few times before and admired it for the very pretty craft that it is. We didn't recognise the insignia or, indeed, the helm and crew as they prepared to launch their little craft on what was, by any standard, a marvellous day to be cruising about in the Blackwater. We watched them launch and plucked up courage to ask them what class of boat they were lucky enough to sail. "It's a Tideway'", they said, "It's 35 years old". It certainly looked to be a credit to those who were responsible for its condition (presumably those who were sailing it) and it gave us great pleasure to watch the duo sail their little craft off through the cruiser lines. The scene was, | thought, almost idealic with the whole appearance of Breeze I/ (for that was its name) very much a part of my image of 'the traditional Blackwater’ as a 'waterman's river’ rather than the hurry-scurry of our modern-day motorised and plastics era of convenience boating. Imagine, therefore, our pleasure when we read in Yachts & Yachting that Breeze IJ had finished 3rd in the Tideway Championships (the 28th Challenge Trophy meeting) in June, 1995, at the Dabchicks Sailing Club. The description of the racing with "...the run down to Packing Shed Island...... The beat back up the Ray channel...." was evocative of the romance of the Blackwater as portrayed in books. It brought into my imagination the beautiful sight of these lovely little dinghies racing each other in close company, rather like a group of graceful water fowl going about their business in their natural habitat. I don't know if those named in the report (Nick and Sue Hillman) are the same as those we've seen sailing it at Stansgate, but we must congratulate you on the fine appearance of your boat - and on your fine performance in the Championship. Mike Boreham

Commodore's Notes Boo Hoo. only 4+ more weeks of the sailing season left! And Alex and I have only had chance to sail the New Toy (AKA the Tornado) ONCE! Since we've had it. Saturdays have been lovely. as have Mondays but Sundays!! Force 5 as a minimum ts not the sort of weather to check out an unfamiliar boat. even a big pussy cat like the Tornado. Not only is it that length of season left. but the old term of office closes in quickly. Doesn't three vears fly by when you re enjoying yourself? I shall be pleased to have a break. It’s been an interesting time with plenty of action and change. As a relative newcomer to the club as well (only 1990!) it’s been interesting to see the changes take place. No longer do we seem to have the groups thinking it’s “their” club. and damn the rest. we seem to have a group of people leading the various fleets who realise that the strength of the club is its diversity. Obviously “democracy” is not everyone's cup of tea. and one or two people over the last couple of years have crossed swords with the committee (and myself). but we carry on! | keep on grumbling about the lack of volunteers. and we are going to be in greater need since. after five years of sterling service at the butty bar. Jean Flook is calling it a day. Thanks for all the egg sandwiches and choccy cake Jean! Last year another volunteer tried to pass the mantle on. Ray Ball thought he'd had enough of anti-fouling the Jack B. No replacements came forward and luckily Ray said he'd carry on. Any body fancy doing either job? See Colin Kidner! This does indicate though the problems we have. If you don't volunteer for jobs the club will eventually fall apart. We have a hard core of people who do loads of work. and a majority who do nothing. Let's spread the load a bit more. Well. that's it for now. See you at the Laying Up Supper - my speech is going to be a good one! If you're sailing and see a pair of white bows charging towards you. run!! Larry Botheras A Different View from the Rear...... What a summer! I hope everyone has had a great time over the last few months encouraged and helped by the heat. There are a number of people who have worked very hard and perhaps the heat didn’t make their tasks easier. On behalf of the Sailing Sub Committee I would like to thank a number of people whose dedication and hard work benefit many club members as well as others outside the club. Firstly. Charles Anderson for organising. and Chris Davies and all those who helped run. this year's Cadet Week. | know from talking to some of those who took part what a wonderful time they had as well as learning an immense amount about sailing. Cadet Weck is an important investment for the future of the Club. Lastly Ray Ball and his band of helpers who renovated Jack B during Camping Fortnight. Ray has done this job for many years now and the Club. that’s you and me. owes him an enormous thank you. The Jack B is an expensive Club asset. Without the hard work which Ray does. it would be worth a great deal less. | would like to ask if someone else would take this job on to allow Ray time to enjoy his holidays without having to work so hard! Cadet Week 1995 It may seem a little late in the day to be reviewing Cadet Week. The truth is that it has taken until now to regain sufficient strength to be able to put fingers to keyboard. What a wonderful way to start the summer holidays! We have already heard in these pages of the inspiration brought to Cadet Week by The Remarkable Family Anderson. but what of the rest? Did Hugh Davies survive to the end of the holiday? Did Dee May get sent to yet another Cadet Week? Did Nadine Debney eventually speak to her mother in French? Did Mitch Glynn finally find a solid area on the Mirror for his Dad to fix to? Did the King twins at last come across one adult who could tell them apart? The weather was so kind to us: Charlie and I weren't sure that we could really cope with so much real live sailing in one week. All our preparation (who am I trying to kid?) had gone into research for the twenty or thirty pencil-and-paper exercises that we usually need during extended hurricanes. We completed capsize drill in double quick time. worried more about sunburn than wind-chill and had to put up with the odd complaint of “Surely we're not sailing again?’ As usual we were presented with a collection of boats in varying states of “fettle’ - Malcolm Stuart's confidential inspection reports are available for a modest sum - but the better weather ensured that we did not break as much gear as in previous years. The noticeable effect of the better weather was the blossoming of both enthusiasm and skills in cadets who in previous years Just occasionally appeared to be with us under duress (perish the thought!) It was interesting to observe. over just a couple of days. a growing realisation that there might just be something in this sailing thing after all. Once again we had wonderful support from proud parents. cordial cat sailors. fine first aiders and itenerant instructors. Yes. that motley band of students reassembled to form the highly disciplined. articulate and beautifully-groomed Instructor Force that distinguishes Marconi Cadet Week from the rest. They did a superb job. the kids enjoyed their company and they even admit themselves that they enjoyed it - at times! SOLO NEWS Open Meeting. The traditional Solo Open was held at the Club on 10th September 1995. The event was attended by 11 visitors and 11 Members of the home Club. making the largest Solo Fleet at the Club for some years. The morning race was postponed for an hour due to lack of wind. The race started in a light and shifty SW breeze. The order at the first mark was. Gordon Barclay (Chichester SC). followed by Mark Holland (Stewartby Water SC) and Steve Ede (ex MSC now Ardleigh SC). By the start of the fourth and final leg Holland held the lead. followed by Barclay and Ede. Holland held on to win the race. but Barclay was passed by Ede on the way to the line. During the lunch break the wind shifted from the south to the east and picked up to a force 2-3. For the second race the wind strength proved ideal for Alan Burrell (Ardleigh). he was first to the opening windward mark. followed by Holland and Jerry Garner (Halfway YC). On the third leg Ede moved through the fleet to third spot. then on to second place during the second beat and passed Burrell on the second run to lead at the last mark. However on the final beat to the line. Burrell pegged him back to take line honours with Barclay coming in third. The rain came in for the third race. killing off the wind. Disappointingly. the race had to be shortened to a single lap with Holland. having pulled away from the Fleet on the run. easily winning from Ede. with Burrell finishing third. NEWS - Notes from Maldon Branch Newsletter The Lifeboat at Burnham on Crouch is to be upgraded with an Atlantic 75 rigid inflatable to be stationed there next year. operating from its base in the Marina. The increasing number of craft navigating the Crouch and frequent shoal movements mean that the present ‘D° Class inflatable is being used in conditions beyond its design capability. The *D’ Class will continue to be used for incidents in shallow water and up-river. operating from its existing base behind the Royal Corinthian. NAVIGANS PAST 1978 (January - June) - Snakes alive ! If a small boy had been a cat with a magnetic personality, would he had lost most of his nine lives around the Medusa Buoy? - Red flares (in the sunset?) over Goldhanger offer something far from tranquil in Osea's narrows. January - The Handicap Fleet notes written by Fleet Captain Pat Black reveal that he retired as Fleet Captain only to find himself elected 420 Fleet Captain, even though the 420 had not yet been granted Fleet status. Another group seeking self-rule was the Solo crowd who elected Frank Savill as their Fleet Captain, again before they had actually been granted Fleet status by the MSC. Perhaps they know something we don't? 420 Fleet notes are, not surprisingly, written by Pat Black who explains the 420 fleet had its genesis during 1976 and now boast some 10 boats in the club. John Weedon donated the Blackbird Trophy for the 420 fleet. Pat also predicts the downfall of the Osea SC in the forthcoming season's 420 team racing against that club. Pat also announces that his favourite series, the Jugs Series, will start at 20.30 hours on 3 February, 1978, in the Dog and Gun at Great Leighs. February - Ron Greygoose (Commodore) notes the "night of the big storm" resulted in the river breaking over the sea wall and flooding the dinghy park and garages to several inches and completely surrounding the clubhouse with floodwater. However no significant damage was done to the building although the sea wall itself was badly eroded in two places and part of the clubs new breakwater (ie. the planks in the seawall gap ?) were washed away. | also suspect our Commodore has joined the 420 fleet and I can't help but wonder if an anonymous ‘ditty’ entitled Four and Twenty Thoughts might have been penned by Mary Greygoose ? Four and Twenty Thoughts "As ‘the boss’ is hovering on the brink of joining Pat's Birds in the drink, I prepare myself for another season of watching (plus nokkies), with very good reason. He'll be braving the storm in an unknown boat, I'll pray to heaven he'll keep afloat There'll be our ‘little breeze’ on the trapeze, raring to do with two good knees. What a lot they'll have to learn - to set the Spinnaker, while fingers burn. Anyway, good luck to them and everyone who sets off from Stansgate to have some fun. A Faithful Onlooker Russ Fuller writes a cautionary tale about what befell a work colleague of his as follows:- "Having gone out for the day with a friend who keeps his boat in Walton Backwaters, a day's fishing was completed somewhere near the Medusa Buoy off Walton. The boat carried a compass and torch but not alotmore. The return passage, under outboard power, was commenced in conditions of slight mist. The owner knew the vicinity pretty well. Pye End buoy came up through the mist, then No.2 Buoy appeared, steering mainly by compass due to the mist. At this point buoys are closely spaced - everything should be fine. Compass bearing OK - where is the next buoy ? Time passes - open sea - more time passes - drop anchor. Kept warm in small cabin - 2 adults - 2 young boys. A shore rescue service noticed parked trailer and starts searching. Through mist my friend identifies Medusa buoy flashing. Darkness fell - good torch carried, several passing ships signalled - not seen. Eventually boat passed close - flash SOS. - its the lifeboat - rescue. Marvellous attention from the lifeboat crew, eventually everyone home safe and well. Several days later small boy seen playing with magnets. Yes, they were in his pocket that day! Do some tests, boy moves across cabin - compass swings about 120 degrees. Have your children got any magnets?" Ray and Maureen Ball wrote an article describing an RNLI rescue at Stansgate during May, 1977, where two (chartered) yachts ran aground in rough weather on Goldhanger Spit at the eastern end of Osea. We sail this area

so often that it is hard to believe it offers any real dangers but, as Ray and Maureen point out, “it was eerie, and perhaps a little sobering, to see red flares coming from Goldhanger Spit which is the site of such innocent pursuits as our Mud Race". It seems the two yachts had run aground in weather of north-east winds force 6, gusting 8, a strong ebb tide, short, heavy waves up to 6 feet. The crews were taken off by the West Mersea Atlantic 21 ILB and landed at Stansgate. After the rescue. the ILB went upriver to warn other yachts to remain westward of Osea and not attempt the passage through ‘the narrows’. The incident was reported in THE LIFEBOAT magazine. Rick Anstey (Cadet Skipper) reports more successes with Intermediate and Elementary Day Boat Certificates and announces that "in keeping with tradition....Cadet Camping Week (will be) immediately after Regatta." with some navigation tuition on cruisers around Bench Head. March - Steve Evans (Enterprise Fleet Captain) bemoans the fact that many Enterprises lie in the dinghy park and never seem to shed their cover (so what's new ?) and Russ Fuller (Cruiser Fleet Captain) reminds everyone of the need to be aware of the Code of Practice for use of Tractor and Winches. April - The Commodores's Notes records the club's thanks to Mike Taylor and Mr J A Cottam Snr for providing their services and ‘concrete moving’ equipment entirely free of charge; presumably this arose from the requirements of the work party, Unfortunately, what was intended to be a ‘thank you’ to the Ladies of the club for their help ("Thank you one and all, especially the ladies") went slightly awry as it came out as "especially the lasies". Hornet Fleet news records Mike Turner and John Tillotson finishing "a very creditable 7th overall out of 28 entries in very difficult conditions” in the Burnham Easter Egg event. May - The front cover picture shows Commodore, Ron Greygoose, sailing a Mirror (single handed) in the Helmsman of the Year Final. Alas, the Young Peoples party planned for the Friday night before Regatta was called off due to lack of 'pre- booking’ support and it will be replaced by an informal party. A diagram of the cruiser moorings shows some 76 moorings allocated (included the two club rescue boats). June - Commodore's Notes records the undoubted success for the 1978 Regatta, with the remark that "for the first time in living memory, the ‘domestic’ facilities survived the weekend..."._ A special thank you to Cyril Drakesford (Clubhouse Secretary). It seems Cyril had just decided to take a well earned ‘sit down’ on the sea wall when it started to rain! Alas it seems the water pipe to the Portaloo had developed a leak and started to spray a jet of water right onto the spot where Cyril had chosen to rest his weary bones. A total of 233 boats entered the Regatta (with 37 from Marconi, 32 from Maylandsea Bay YC and 24 from King George SC) with over 40 clubs represented. The Enterprise Class was the biggest with 43 entries. Unfortunately, it seems someone had 'borrowed' Dave Lawson's cruiser tender and let it go ‘drift about’, Amongst Regatta results were Chris Weedon (2nd) and Colin Harper (3rd) in the 420 class and Mike Taylor (505) 3rd in the Fast Handicap Class. Otherwise, Marconi members didn't feature in the 1978 prize list. Ken Beavins was invited to write an occasional article by the Commodore. He writes "...it would be all too easy to infuriate members by perpetually lecturing them about conduct (litter, dogs, kids and shut the gate). Have you noticed how the quality of...bar staff varies from week to week" (Ken's point being that it was good when Jack and Joyce Reeve did it but not so good when he (Ken) did it). He goes on to mention some of the other tasks which have to be done at the MSC and says "I do wonder though how much longer we should go on without having some more formal arrangement which spreads this work more widely amongst the membership". A note of dissent in the Mirror Fleet with an anonymous note lamenting the lack of Mirror Fleet news in Navigans. To be honest, I wouldn't have noticed for, truth to tell, we rarely bothered to read Navigans in 1978 even though we had been members of Marconi SC for some 5 years by that time. That was probably because we didn't sail very often and raced even less! Mike Boreham

Commodore’s Report The last year has seen further consolidation of the Club's position, with littke material change since 1994, However. as the investment in 1994 was so great. this is perhaps no great surprise. In continuing efforts to improve the facilities available at the Club. and to overcome the OOD problem. we decided to recruit a Steward to run the Bar and Clubhouse on Saturdays and Sundays. I think that the consensus is that the experiment was a great success, despite the short term duration due to the individual's financial circumstances. With the term coming to a close in August. the Committee decided that it was not appropriate to recruit a replacement at that stage. but to hold off until the start of 1996. Moving on to our relationship with MASC. This has been fairly much “on hold” for most of the year. due to Peter Woodhouse leaving the company and having to step down from his post as Chairman. In addition. recent changes with the departure of Gerry Wignall. new MASC trustees. and a review of the relationship with other sections bode well for us for the future. As far as 1995 events go Regatta was undoubtedly a failure. with only some 60 competitors. The Committee has taken the view that this event will go “on IceTM until demand turns round and we can again mun a viable event. On the other hand ECPR was again a major success. The Club has been mentioned extremely favourably in correspondence in the Yachting press which has covered the ability of clubs to organise successful multihull events. Other clubs have been criticised (notably Stokes Bay and Rutland) whilst we have been held up (along with Texel) as an example. This is obviously excellent PR. and probably has greater value than any advertising that we could do. Last year I made a plea for “successors” to come forward and outlined the reasons why we needed fresh volunteers to bolster all the committees, With very few exceptions this has been a complete failure. As a group the membership MUST realise that the future of your enjoyment of these facilities is dependent upon their successful management. It is no excuse to say that you only use the Club “a bit” and can’t contribute. That attitude will eventually lead to the gradual and then speedy decline of the organisation. I believe that every single one of us realises what a precious sailing site we have. and that none of us would wish to lose it. My warning may appear alarmist. but the average attitude of individuals will lead to this situation. Please search your conscience and if you can for goodness sake volunteer. At the end of my term as Commodore, I must place on record my thanks to all the Executive and Committee members that | have had the pleasure to work with over the last few years. The standard of discussion and sometimes lively debate at meetings has resulted in several good ideas and decisions coming forward. The Committee is no longer a real talking shop. but very much an action oriented decision making body. As last year I have no reservation in thanking a few individuals. Firstly. Jean Flook has decided to hang up her apron after a number of years of providing an excellent service from the Galley. I should like everyone to show their appreciation in the traditional way, Secondly, Colin Kidner. who is now passing into retirement as Rear Commodore: his organisational abilities have been of huge assistance. I hope he enjoys the “rest camp” of the Commodore's role! Finally. again. Frank Bennett. Frank has again carried out a huge amount of work unseen by the vast majority; from tractor maintenance through the club radios and electrics to the sewage plant. as well as counting the beans. It has been a great privilege to work with someone so committed to the future of the Club. and someone whom we should all look to with gratitude. As you see. I do not escape entirely scot free. some people think that after making this mess I should still be involved as a Vice President - just as I thought I could put my feet up for a while. You never know, Alex and I might get some more sailing in! It has though been a great pleasure and privilege to hold the position. and to sce the way in which the various interest groups have become united over the last few years. I wish Colin and his new team all the best. and thank all of you for your support over the last three years. Larry Botheras

3. | CLOSE THE FLOODGATES | It is extremely important that we keep the Floodgates closed during the winter months. This is not a matter of choice - it is a requirement placed on us in return for the convenience of having a gap in the sea wall. 1. We don’t, as a Club, want the infamy that would follow if we were responsible for allowing the sea into the surrounding farmland in the event of an unexpected extreme high tide - and there is always a greater risk of these in the winter months. 2. We don’t, as individual sailors, want to find ourselves humping all our tenders, dinghies, cats, the RIB and our cruisers over the top of the sea wall if the NRA decides to close the gap permanently because we cannot be trusted with our responsibility for our own property and that of our neighbours. PLEASE CLOSE THE FLOODGATES EACH TIME YOU OPEN THEM. DO NOT LEAVE THEM OPEN FOR SOMEONE WHO MAY OR MAY NOT COME AFTER YOU. ALL MEMBERS WHO FIND THEMSELVES ONE OF THE LAST FEW ON SITE LATE IN THE DAY, PLEASE JUST CHECK GATES ARE SHUT BEFORE YOU LEAVE - AND CLOSE THEM IF NECESSARY. IF INDOUBT - CLOSE THEM ANYWAY. Cruiser Comments A reminder that the year is coming to an end is inevitably signalled by the Sailing Club’s Laying Up Supper which was held at the Three Rivers on Friday 10th November. Once again the Cruiser Fleet was well represented and I am sure a good time was had by all. The Winter Lay-up is almost complete with just a few dichards still afloat, well. that was the situation when drafting these Comments. Generally speaking. we have found the standard of trailers has improved this year although there were one or two still requiring a little TLC. These trailers don’t come cheap and suffer a ducking in the briny twice a year, so a little maintenance is worth while and surely your boat deserves it. By the time you read this most. if not all. of rows A. B and C Moorings will have been brought ashore. Where possible these have been put onto pallets. If yours has not, please try to find a pallet ready for next year’s Lay-up. We are trying to get some more delivered. so keep a lookout. Members whose boats are not laid up in the Cruiser Park will find their moorings on pallets along the sea wall in the Cruiser Park. Lastly, two dates for your diary: Wednesday 29th November 7.30 pm is the Cruiser AGM being held in the Conference Lounge at MASC. and on Sunday 10th December the Mast Derrick comes down for the winter. It only remains for me to wish you all a Very Merry Christmas. also a Happy New Year with good sailing in 1996. Derek Kirby. Cruiser Fleet Captain

NAVIGANS PAST This is the last of my series of Navigans Past. The first of the series was published in the Navigans of January, 1991, and was inspired by the turmoil arising from ‘the problems' of 1990. It set me wondering if the club had passed through similar phases of divided and entrenched views. I'm rather relieved to discover it had, indeed, had its problems. The purchase of the floating clubhouse barge Mamgu, the move to Stansgate, the purchase of the site, the design and building of the clubhouse were all major turning points in the club's history during which harsh words were uttered and sailing friendships strained. Navigans, of course, only presents the public face of the debates and the rather more interesting ‘hidden agendas’ and real ‘goings-on’ rarely had even a faint glimpse of the light of day. In other words, what really went on behind the scenes? Alas, we will probably never know. Although I have attempted to collect together as much club archive material as possible, much of the more interesting items remain within the minds of those who took part in the events of the past. Sadly, many of those concerned are no longer with us and by the nature of things these sources will get less and less as time progresses. Eventually we will finish up with a bland formal record of the Marconi Sailing Club which masks the real drama of what went on behind the scenes and we will have lost all the scandal and gossip for ever - what a pity! A total of 40 episodes of Navigans Past have been published since January, 1991. I hope you have enjoyed reading them as much as I have enjoyed writing them. 96 ee a ee 1978 (July - December) - birds of a feather flock together but wise old birds are clearly hard to beat. July Shirley-Ann Wood (Editor) takes a philosophical line as she writes "Come rain or shine, the show must go on". It seems that no sooner had the charcoal chefs started to cook at the annual barbecue and the music had started to play than the rain it did fall...and fall...and fall...until everyone was too wet to notice any more. Shirley says "The midnight dip was well supported...(all completely mad)". J must admit I had to re-read this comment just to make sure I hadn't read what at first glance I thought I'd read. Mirror Fleet Captain, Deborah Harper, responds to the previous month's appeal for Mirror news with not only congratulating Vic and Kim Braybrook on winning the Spring Points, but also Malcolm Gandy on managing to break not only his own centre board but also Deborah's centre board all on the same day. Deborah was still at school and at an important point in her exams so it was rather difficult for her to give a large amount of time to fleet captaincy duties. A note from coxswain Norman Kerridge reminds all (rescue) duty drivers and crew that they should be available one hour before the races (together with the Race Officer) but also on the water at least 30 minute before the start. On a rather more light hearted note, Norman also reports on some of the 'birds' he has spotted on the Blackwater from the comfort of the rescue boat. They are, of course, club members and some of you ‘old hands’ might raise a wry smile or two as you perhaps recognise a few of them - perhaps even yourself? Norman's list of "feathered friends" are:- The Great Bearded Bates - One of the Hornet family. Has great difficulty in flying back to the clubhouse without injury. Usually flies up the opposite end of the river to the rescue boat. Has a mutual attraction to fishing lines and hooks. (Murray Bates) The King Moth Eater - A wild untamed young bird. Spends more time in the water than it does in the air. Probably won't live to a great age. (Not sure who this is; anyone like to tell us?) The Orange Savill - A solo bird with an unusual habit of standing up in the water. The female of the species spends all her time collecting food for all the other birds of the river. Frank Savill and Jill Savill (who ran the galley in those days)

The Curly Headed Windypeg - This jovial bird is easily recognised - usually amongst a flock of female birds of another variety. It’s speed across the river is mirrored in the deep red plumage of its female offspring. The latter looks after the older members of the flock - usually from the rear. (Now who is , these particular 'bird' family?) The Blackwater Grey Goose - A difficult one to spot as it's a quiet type but through intelligent use of its enterprise (sorry) has become the King Bird of the river . (In later years it was renamed the President Bird, sometimes also as the Helmeted President Bird; its faithful companion can often be seen anxiously watching from the bank for its safe return, hopefully with a trophy or two to offer as a peace offering). Sailing Secretary Bird - Not often seen on the river as it prefers to spend most of its time with its mate in the clubhouse. Has a distinctive call of "It's a Rojer - It's a Rojer". (Mike Vaughan ?) The Black and Blue Bird - The colourful female of the species is often seen wrestling with a flying spinnaker and heard cheerfully chirping under trying conditions. The adult male stays well away but the male chick is a leading member of the fledglings whilst the young female sits gracefully around. (another ‘bird’ family which someone might recognise - and expose ?) What birds can you spot in 1995 - and what are their chief characteristics ? No prizes for the best ‘spotters’ but maybe Maureen would allow you to remain anonymous ?) Dennis Byatt is struggling as Cruiser Racing Captain as he writes "No one could accuse the cruiser members.....0f being racing fanatics. A cruise across the North Sea to Holland or Calais - yes, but a thrash around the sticks - not really." He then goes on to try to whip up some enthusiasm for the Barnacle Points series. One simple race to Herring Point (Please don't say "Where's that"!) and back was supported by only two boats; Dennis in Bill Buchanon's E Boat hotly pursued by Ken Beavins. Ken writes a short piece about his holiday cruising ".....long tacks all the way home from the Wallet Spitway.....with a stead force 4 in the late evening and small hours, topped off by a successful night mooring pick-up will take a lot of forgetting”. A letter of thanks from Sir Robert Telford (Managing Director of GEC-Marconi Electronics Ltd) , upon being congratulated by Vice-President Eric Payne on the award of the knighthood. A log of the summer cruise of Ace of diamonds describes some pleasant scenes of drift net fishing, rigging the accompanying Mirror dinghy and socialising on neighbouring yachts. It all sounded rather restful; even the mention of having ”..... finished some varnishing....." has, at least for me, a suggestion of an unhurried cruising holiday in peaceful surroundings on the east coast. August - the cover picture features the steam tug Brent making her way up to Maldon with Chris Cooper and Mirror on the hard in the foreground. The format for Helmsman of the Year is changed for 1978. This year one boat from each class will qualify, with each qualifier's own boat being used on a round-robin basis with only the helm changing boats. The death of Byron Bridges (boat name /dle Vice) was reported; clearly a man of quiet humour and sadly missed. The Sailing Sub-Committee agreed (after requests from members) to grant average points to those performing the duties of O.0.D., Race Officer and Assistant Race Officer and Rescue Boat Crew, with a maximum of two such ‘average points’ races per series. Norman Kerridge (coxswain) reports the new mast on the rescue boat broke after only some 200 yards of its first trip. He also reports that the radio is the worst on the river and seems to suggest some irony in that this should be the case for the Marconi S.C. ! However, the club's ‘radio reputation’ on the river must be reasonably good since we were invited to man the Bridge Radio and co-ordinate the rescue services for the Blackwater & Colne Championships. September - in an earlier 1978 Navigans, Ken Bezvins revealed that Commodore, Ron Greygoose, had invited him to write an occasional series of articles for Navigans. Ken's latest contribution again highlights the eternal problem of a club such as the MSC which tries to cater for all tastes in boating. Ken writes "Last weekend the

tides were right for bottom scrubbing. I was all for beaching near the club but wiser counsels prevailed. Betty's advice was good for although we were a long way down towards Stone the starting guns, public address commentary and other noise overspill from the open meetings in progress at our Club were clearly audible to an obtrusive degree. Anyone who has spent nights afloat on the Blackwater knows that it is often anything but quiet even in the small hours, and we all know how much din is created by speed boats, but I wondered last weekend whether it was necessary or desirable for us as a responsible club to contribute so readily to the general noise." I might add that Ken had been, in the past, a keen dinghy racer and now supported the club's cruiser racing program so he was not ‘anti-racing' but he was, I think, very keen to preserve the tranquil image of the river in general, and of Stansgate in particular, as a quiet sailing backwater. Cruiser Captain, Russ Fuller, points out that, whilst in the older design of cruisers it was normal to pick up mooring under sail, the modern design of cruisers made them rather less steady or, put another way, they are now "so skittish" as to make it wiser to pick up moorings under motor power. October - Commodore's Notes announces that the club's current (and founding) President, Sir Eric Eastwood, is at last to be allowed to retire after some 25 years in office (having intimated for a number of years that he felt it was time to do so) and MrJ A Pateman (Managing Director, Marconi Avionics, Rochester ?) was to be invited to become the new President. Sir Eric had served since the foundation of the club in 1952 and must have been a very useful ‘contact’ in the early years in getting things done. Sir Eric and Lady Eastwood, and presumably Mr Pateman, were invited to the 1978 Laying-Up Supper (tickets £6 adults; £5 Cadet Members). Rick Anstey reveals that Helmsman of the Year was won by a Cadet, Chris Weedon. I'm not sure if Chris was the first cadet to win HoY ? Deborah Harper won the Ladies Cup which was another triumph for the Cadet members. On a person note, I was interested to see that Mike Bees (Brightlingsea SC) won the Marconi Mirror Open (24 entries of which 11 were MSC) in his boat Bumble. Mike Taylor was the highest placed Marconi entry (3rd) with Malcolm Gandy (5th) and Malcolm Stuart (6th). Those were the days when the Mirror Fleet reigned supreme - or at least were a force to be reckoned with in the MSC. This might have been the year that Mike Bees finished 3rd in the Mirror Nationals with Bumble and| still see his name reported by Yachts & Yachting in rather faster competitive sailing circuits. Later on, we bought Bumble (from a subsequent owner) as our second Mirror and still have it in our garage. The cruiser racing fleet's Barnacle Points series was won by Colin Leverage's Bluster, with Ken Beavins 2nd (Spiridion) and Dennis Byatt 3rd (Roanoke) out of 12 entries. November - the front cover shows a crowded seawall at the top of the hard on what must have been a very hot day during the 1978 Regatta. The 'White Hut' looked spick and span in those days and even had a full compliment of 3 chimney pots. Now, in 1995, it's nice to see it restored to good order. Let us hope it continues to remain a landmark on the Blackwater. Does anyone know the true full history of the 'White Hut’ (not just myth, legend or supposition). A slightly exasperated note from Dave Lawson (Social Sec) who points out that those who think the Christmas Dance tickets are expensive (£1.20 each) should bear in mind that a professional dance band (how nice, not a disco) costs in the region of £135 which together with hall charges, electrician, doorman, etc. results in ticket prices based upon a no-profit budget. The final episode of the log of the summer cruise of Ace of Diamonds records the end of a perfect holiday. The writer concludes "..... we all felt our holiday cruise had been a pleasure, we hadn't covered a great distance but we had met some nice people, which is probably what a Cruise is all about.”

10. The AGM in November reported membership numbers as follows:- 1978 1977 Ordinary 270 260 Associate 97 101 Family S57 el 424 418 Honorary Members 16 At the AGM, Ron Greygoose (Commodore) reminds all members that it is a self-help club. He remarks that some 300 races had been conducted (excluding Regatta) but warns he detects that some of the enjoyment might have gone for the diminishing band of stalwarts who continued to offer their services rather than see standards of the club fall. Amongst other items of interest, Ron reported that Maldon District Council had requested payment of a licence fee for the siting of the concrete hard and scrubbing post on the foreshore. Other clubs had received similar requests and a combined negotiation team through BACSPA had resulted in a more acceptable licence agreement. As for camping at Stansgate, legal objections to camping had been overcome but he warns the club must be very circumspect in how camping on the site is to be regulated. He pays tribute to Jim and Corrine Coy for organising and laying down the foundation for good camping behaviour. Some problems with our neighbours had occurred due to complaints of trespassing on neighbouring property during busy camping weekends. The Retiring President, Sir Eric Eastwood, was presented with a small parting gift and also with Honorary Life Membership of the MSC. David Urry won the Garrett Memorial Trophy and I finish up this series of Navigans Past by quoting the poem written by "a budding young sailor" who was aboard Eric Payne's boat Hullabaloo when he won The Blackwater Cup. The poem was actually given to Eric Payne on his 80th birthday; Eric was, of course, both a founding member and very prominent member of the Marconi Sailing Club:- Happy Birthday racing Mr Payne Sailing up and down again. Hullabaloo, that nice boat, Winning some of the races afloat. Captain Payne at the helm of course, Trying, trying do his crew, With all their might to sail the course, Triumphantly over the winning line." To those old enough to remember ‘the good old days' (whenever you think they were), I hope you have enjoyed being reminded of them and that they bring back fond memories of races won, arguments lost, friendships sustained and enmities forgiven and forgotten. To those relative newcomers to the MSC, I hope the series has served to convince you that the Sailing Section of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club has always been a club of individual high achievement, best endeavours, hard work, great fun but, most of all, a grand place to sail whatever the boating interests and aspirations of a widely diverse membership. Let's keep it that way. Mike Boreham

Connie Bigden Many members will be sorry to hear of the death recently of Connie. Connie Bigden nee Chapman and sister Betty Beavins were always very close. Connie's husband Jack and Betty's husband Ken were both outgoing characters with a passionate love of sailing. This passion is shared today by their children and grandchildren. Both Jack and Ken held office in the Club and contributed enormously to its development at Stansgate and to its family atmosphere. Connie and Betty gave Jack and Ken their loyal and steadfast support and were always seen to be happily chatting on the Hard and watching over their progenies. Tragically, both Jack and Ken died prematurely. Connie was extremely proud when the new Club Support Boat ‘Jack B’ was named after husband Jack. Mary has known the family since Betty used to take her to school. Jack invited me to become Club Bosun in 1964 and persuaded us to try camping in France: and sons Julian and Tim got me started in the Enterprise Fleet. An era has passed but the family names of Bigden and Beavins will live on in the annals of the MSC for generations to come. Ron Greygoose. CRUISER COMMENTS The Cruiser Fleet AGM was held at MASC on Wednesday 29th November at which 35 members attended, representing 26 boats. The Meeting opened at 194Shrs and a resume of events is as follows: 1. Apologies: Colin Kidner (Commodore), Mike Turner, Fred Hawthorne, Brian Court, Ron Phillips. 2. Review of 1995 Sailing Season: Three Cruising-in-Company events were organised: 27-29 May - Shakedown Cruise to Burnham at which 11 boats attended, staying at Burnham Yacht Harbour, with an evening meal at Crouch Yacht Club. 17-25 June - St Katharine’s Dock at which 6 Club boats + 2 guests attending making a total fleet of 8. Three days were spent at St Katharine’s Dock with members doing their own thing, i.e. sightseeing, etc.. with us all meeting up up for supper on the Tuesday evening before locking out for a trip into the River Medway before returning to the Blackwater at the weekend. 26th-28th August - Walton Backwaters which was attended by 19 boats. Once again we enjoyed the hospitality of the Walton & Frinton Yacht Club for an evening meal on the Sunday. Of the above events, 3 boats attended all three events, whilst 6 boats attended 2 of them. 3. Nominations & Election of Fleet Captain & Vice Captain No nominations were received for either of these positions, so yours truly. ably assisted by Malcolm Yeoman agreed to continue for a further year. 4. Sailing Proposals for 1996: A copy of the letter sent to the Commodore by Ray Hampson resigning as Cruiser Racing Representative was read out. This post will now be held by Mike Turner who, whilst not at the meeting for business reasons. had contacted Derek Kirby to confirm this and requested that the question of Cruiser Races be mentioned. This was done and whilst most Members were not too keen on serious BJRC-type races, there was interest in a more light-hearted approach to ‘port to port’ races, say, three a year for which some form of trophy/trophies may be awarded. Derek Gardiner said he had already spoken on the subject to Mike Turner and has agreed to speak to him again on the response of the Members present. With regard to ‘Cruising in Company Events’ it was generally felt the shakedown cruise to Burnham with an evening meal in the Crouch Yacht Club be arranged for the Spring Bank Holiday, 27th May. With regard to the Late Summer Holiday, 28th August. it was felt a change of venue would be popular, therefore arrangements are trying to be made for a visit to Woolverstone Marina on the River Orwell with an evening meal in the Royal Harwich Yacht Club. Watch this space for details of both events plus any others that may be organised. Members were reminded that notices regarding Cruiser events are now displayed on ‘dayglo’ signs on the Cruiser Notice Boards both in the Clubhouse and the Dell Bar. 5. Letter to the Editor Cruiser Section Query. Could the Club hierarchy inform us if any considerations have ever been given to a well-known problem peculiar to the Cruising Members, albeit not of their making? I refer to racing events through our expensively rented moorings where never a year goes by without some superficial damage appearing between visits. Of course these events are rarely witnessed or reported, so proof is not easy, except when they are witnessed! However, trying to relax on a nice day on the moorings during racing events (as was once the norm) soon puts the picture in perspective! The general conclusion seems to be that supersonic Cats, i.e. twice the beam, three times the speed, with corresponding reduction in reaction times, represent the main threats to our expensive pride and joys! Now I am the first to admit the Blackwater river and our Club location is an ideal site for this rapidly growing fleet and I enjoy their races and assist in the mid-week racing rescue services on some occasions when I think extra hands may be necessary. However, with all that water opposite, as well as up and down the river, to allow or to want to race through our narrow strip of moorings is illogical and shows nothing but contempt for the risks imposed on other people’s property! Perhaps the state of affairs is down to us, only a load of wimps would do nothing except whinge about it amongst ourselves! My 1995 experience when ACCORD (now sold) was bashed, witnessed and reported was interesting! To summarise: Not so much as a “sorry, mate” telephone call from the attacker’s owner and when I later tried to obtain the insurance data of the offender from the relevant Club Official, it was refused for reasons you wouldn’t believe! Any comment from the management? Ronald V. Phillips

Connie Bigden Just a quick note on behalf of Julian, myself and our families to thank all those members of The Marconi Sailing Club who came to our Mum’s funeral, or who contributed to the donation made to the RNLI. Also thanks to Ron Greygoose for his tribute in the January Navigans - the sentiments expressed by Ron reminded me of times when both Mum and Dad derived huge amounts of pleasure from seeing and participating in the development of the Club. I know that their wish would be for the Club to continue in providing ordinary people the opportunity to experience and enjoy the extraordinary pleasures of sailing. Tim Bigden. COMMODORES NOTES. Greetings and may 1996 bring us all whatever we desire! As a Dart 15 sailor I would like at least Force + winds, sunshine and no rain on every Sunday during the coming season. It would also help if my work load meant that I didn’t have to work at the weekend so that I could sail more often. Once one starts with wish lists one can. of course, get carried away to the point when one forgets about other folks and what they would like, which more often than not is rather a different list! Can I remind members of a few fundamentals: |) All craft have the right to use the full width of the river for navigation. li) The MDC 8 knot speed limit down all the shore line applies to all boats at all times. ili) The start line for the Catamaran Fleet was moved outside the mooring area. iV) There is no legal requirement for any boat to be insured. Whilst the Club requires all Members’ boats to be insured and requests details to confirm that the rule is observed. there is no legal requirement for parties to exchange insurance details in a marine accident. It would be a breach of confidence for the MSC Registrar to pass details of one Member's insurer to another. V) All Club Members benefit from each other. Perhaps you will allow me to make the following wish: Can we all resolve to be considerate towards each other, both on and off the water. If any member feels that they have a grievance may I suggest that if it cannot be resolved informally in the first instance. then submit the problem to the Main Committee rather than air the problem in Navigans. One could of course put oneself forward as a Committee Member (or even Commodore)! A volunteer is worth ten pressed men they say! Best wishes to you all for 1996. Colin Kidner. P.S. 1 am looking further into the kind of problem that lead to Ron Phillips” letter in January Navigans. The Cat Sailor concerned also had some problems getting hold of the information he required immediately after the mishap because it had been removed from the Notice Board at the Club. It is hoped to look at better ways of ensuring that in any future similar situation the required information will be more easily available. Watch this space.

Contact: Vince Talfourd, [redacted] — Flat Out Fisherman Last year, whilst in Calais and relaxing after an exciting crossing, I was rocked into reflection over the behaviour of the fishing boat and its occupants. It seems that fisherfolk, bastions of the time-honoured marine community, weatherbeaten, windswept. sou wester'd seers of all things nautical. sons of salts. all own or operate powered craft that have common features. Firstly. as I am constantly reminded at ports and rivers all around. these craft cannot travel at a speed that produces little or no wash. whatever length they may be! In the Basin de | Ouest the French pecheurs seem to love shaking their visitors up as much as possible with excessive wash at all times of day and night. Eastbourne Marina recently provided us with an English example of full throttle fisherman’s disease with regular wash-induced rock and roll sessions and. as I watched the phenomenon from the safey of land. a good half of the basin was suffering this annoyance with some boats nearly touching spreaders. I sent a letter to the Marina management suggesting a speed limit and perhaps a word with offenders at the lock - No reply was received, Has their lot become so bad as to make them join the ranks of the unpopular water user? Are they so used to the roll and pitch of their boats’ decks that they don't realise the havoc their washes cause’? Are they always late for something? Can‘t be for the fish because. by all accounts, there arent many left to be caught! Limpet

CRUISER COMMENTS Sailing Events: Well, here we are again at the beginning of a new year with all the anticipation that it brings. First. may I wish everyone a healthy and happy New Year. coupled of course with enjoyable sailing. Arrangements are in hand for two Flotilla (sailing in company) Events to be held on the Spring Bank Holiday and Late Summer Bank Holiday weekends. Watch Navigans and the Club Notice Board for details nearer the time. In addition to these it is hoped to organise other get-togethers. some probably on an ad hoc basis. These are more likely to be picked up from the Notice Boards in the Clubhouse and the Dell Bar. since we may not have time to get them in Navigans. Winter Meetings: It is possible that by the time you read this we may well have had Ray & Hazel’s talk on “Cruising on the Mediterranean’ for which I would like to thank them. Our next meeting will be on Wednesday 21st February when Brian & Jackie Bouwsher will relate their experiences whilst sailing from Dartmouth the the Channel Islands. and on to Rochefort on the west coast of France just north of the Gironde. and Bordeaux where they laid NATASHA IV up for the winter which. incidentally. is where Ray & Hazel started their journey into the Med. Not bad continuity. ech? The last of this year’s Winter Meetings will be held on Wednesday 20th March. and I am delighted that Nigel Harmer our River Bailiff will be coming along to give us an insight to his duties. problems and how we can help each other in protecting our environment. He also hopes to bring along a member of the Policy Planning Department to enlighten us about the Estuary Management Plan and perhaps the River Warden to explain about his role along the waterfront. I believe the March Meeting to be of interest to all Club Members, and therefore extend the invitation accordingly. Lastly. two points of interest from the RYA Eastern Regional Committee Meeting: a) The Walton Backwaters High Hill buoy in Hamford Channel now has a light. characteristics: Fl R 10sec. position 51° 54°03N. 01°16°07E. This buoy and others in the immediate vicinity are maintained by the Walton & Frinton YC at their own expense and to the considerable benefit of all yachtsmen who use the waters. b) CEVNI RULES. Any vessel navigating on French Inland Waters must carry a copy of the Rules. A booklet containing an extract in English. French and German is now available from the RYA. Entitled “Vagnon Carte de Plaisance”. it costs £7.50 plus £1 posgtage. That's all the news for now. I guess I will have to start setting to on “Happy Medium’ now that Christmas and New Year's holidays are out of the way, albeit I have not yet got round to doing the jobs around the house that I promised Doreen I'd do during the winter whilst the boat was laid up! Hey Ho! Derek Kirby. COMMODORES NOTES. Going on from last month's homily. the Code of Practice for Dinghy Owners has been amended. Any member helming a boat which collides with another must contact the third party with all necessary details. There is a membership list in the bar where telephone numbers can be found. In case of any difficulties then the Club Secretary should be contacted to obtain telephone numbers. I have also asked that the Sailing Sub Committee should discuss the problem of High Speed Sailing through the moorings to seek a solution(s) to this problem. It seems that there are folk who use the club site who cannot be bothered to get out of their cars and close the gate after they have entered. If you leave the gate open then the ‘light fingered brigade’ have a golden opportunity to enter the site and leave with boats and or trailers. I shall not be nice to anyone I see leaving the gate open! You have been warned. The membership level is causing concerns. We need more members. Larry has kindly volunteered to produce suitable advertising material that we intend to place in appropriate journals. The theme of this material will expound the virtues of the various club activities and site. Some observations have been made about the Club Logo. If you feel that we should or should not change it. perhaps you would let me or fleet captains have your views. Those of you who look forward to eating at the club on a Sunday will be pleased to hear that we have a professional caterer Starting a service which will coincide with the new sailing season. I believe we can look forward to breakfasts. snacks. lunches and dinners. all at very reasonable prices. See you on the water soon. Colin Kidner. BARN DANCE 1996 Saturday 2nd March 8pm. Wanted: Trapeze Harness to suit 12-14 Year Old Please Contact Charles Anderson, [redacted] REPLY TO LIMPET Regarding Limpet's remarks in February 1996 Navigans (Ed's note: Regarding fast moving Fishing Boats in Marinas) | think many people would find it strange that, having chosen to go afloat. he dislikes his boat moving around. For a fisherman, as for everybody else. time is money, and no doubt the Fisherman were there long before somebody decided to place a marina next to the fairway. A while ago, on leaving Dunkirk harbour under power in Sharazad (now Winkler), two of us were on top preparing the sails. A considerate French fisherman, throttle well open according to custom, hooted us and pointed helpfully at his rapidly approaching wash, giving us time to hang on and avoid an unwelcome dip in that rather smelly harbour. I should conclude by saying that when driving the Jack B I always try not to shake up the old folk in the Cruiser Moorings! Alan Boswell CRUISER DAMAGE- Reply to Ron Phillips’ letter in January Navigans. Asa novice Race Officer, and an often erratic Dart Sailor, I have a lot of sympathy for Ron, who is concerned about Cruiser damage from racing boats and Cats in particular. However I think that. with goodwill, sense can prevail. I find that as RO the easy option of sending the starters to “B’ Mark is usually prevented by the prevailing wind, and I’m obliged to set a course starting up-river. I understand that all Cats will still be starting outside ‘D* mark in 1996. Most of us hope that we can send them on a long beat up to ‘No.2° but I'd love to put a dog-leg in to keep them clear of Cruisers. However if a mark to achieve this is put near the pillbox on Osea, then the beating boats can cause chaos crossing the boats coming downriver. Laying temporary marks just outside the moorings is a problem due to drifting. but could be tried.

5. Having achieved a start. via No.2 etc.. I'd be tempted to use the space over towards Goldhanger more. (depth allowing) and would ask that “X° mark is moved downriver to add variations. However even if most of the course is set off the Moorings. those of us with little (proper) Cats will always want to keep out of the tide if it’s against us, and we do tack in and out of the Cruisers. especially at the finish. Committee Boat starts away from the site are not feasible week in, week out, and setting courses a long way from the Club does reduce the safety factor, especially when one Rescue Boat has to stand down. It has also been pointed out to me that we would improve our performance in Open Meetings if we had much shorter ‘legs’ as they do at Grafham, but this does mean the Race has to be near to the Race Box. (If my own legs get any shorter I won't be able to launch the Dart at all.) I have to confess to putting a hole in a Tender last year. but telling the owner my name and address on the next lap was no problem, and he kindly repaired the damage to his boat and my pride. His generous and reassuring salutations confirmed my view that we have an excellent spirit at MSC, and I’m sure I’m not the only one looking forward to next season - not only for the sailing but all the camaraderie that goes with it. Best Wishes for 1996 Dick Davies CRUISER COMMENTS We had a splendid attendance at last month's meeting, and my thanks go not only to Hazel and Ray for their presentation but also to those of you who attended. It is your support that makes arranging these meetings worth while not only to me to those people who have given up their time to put together topics of interest. By the time you read this Brian & Jackie Bowsher will have delivered their talk (Ed’s Note: on 21st Feb.) on sailing from Dartmouth to Rochefort. France. via the Channel Islands in Natasha IV. for which I thank them. This leaves the last of our Winter Meetings to be held on Wednesday 20th March to be given by our River Bailiff and his colleagues. Topics are likely to include the Bailiff s duties. the River Warden’s duties. and the Estuary Management Plan. The subjects being covered should be of interest to all MSC members and I look forward to a packed house. PREPARATION OF MOORINGS. It is amazing how quickly the time goes by especially once Christmas and New Year's Eve are out of the way. Naturally our attention turns to refurbishing our boats ready for launch day, but may I remind you before this happens that there is the small matter of Moorings. These also need a little TLC and it is not always a good idea to leave it to the last minute. Don Holdsworth has just taken delivery of chain and shackles. He also has a stock of both chain and boat anodes. These are limited but he can order them for you if you contact him. His rates are very competitive. (See below.) Whilst on the subject of Moorings. may I remind those of you who have Drying Moorings to make sure they are OK since they do not get the same independent scrutiny as rows A. B & C. Booking your holidays this year? How about tacking four days on to each of the Spring and Late Summer Bank Holidays to make the most of the Burnham Shakedown Cruise, plus the proposed visit to Neptune Marina, Ipswich Dock, which could be followed by a trip up the River Deben to Woodbridge. Think about it. We will be holding our Cruiser Fitting Out Supper on Satuday 20th April at the MSC Clubhouse, numbers are limited to 50. Watch out for the booking form in the next edition of Navigans. VAT ON MOORINGS AND STORAGE The RYA acting on behalf of Swansea Bay Yacht Club has succeeded in a trial case against HM Customs & Excise with regard to the payment of VAT on members’ Mooring and Storage fees. This anomally has existed since the general removal on sports activities in 1994. Until we have official confirmation from our local VAT office, the Club must continue to pay VAT on these items, but I confidently expect to be able to discontinue the charge within a month or so, and then to submit a claim for back payment as was done with the other Subs components in 1994. It should be realised that some of the gain will be offset by our inability to reclaim input VAT on associated expenditure. but there is certain to be a net advantage. Assuming a satisfactory result from the claim I anticipate refunds to individual members for the whole of their VAT for the period from when the tax was removed from the other Subs. components, plus a useful contribution to Club funds from the earlier period back to 1990. This will bring uniformity to the treatment of the VAT refund for all subscription components. Esther presents our awards River | rescue A WRITTLE couple who saved the life of a lone sailor, Tony and Pat Holbrook, were selected as the Weekly News man and Woman of the year. In June last year the couple were sail- ing on the River Blackwater when they heard faint cries for help. Realis- ing the man was barely conscious, Mr Holbrook tied a rope areund his chest to keep him from going under and with the help of another pass- ing sailor, managed to haul the man into a dinghy while Pat called the coastguard. Tony described Thursday's ceremony as “wonderful.” He added: “It is something we will remember always.” Reproduced from the Chelmsford Weekly News of 8th February 1996 by kind permission of Essex County Newspapers. Tony and Pat were amongst “Nineteen Essex Heroes’ who were presented with their awards by Esther Rantzen in the Essex County Newspapers New Year Honours 1995 Awards. SAILING CLUB LOGO I've been asked to invite Members to put their artistic thinking caps on and come up with any fresh ideas for an improved Club Logo. I'm brazenly going to abuse my position as Editor by saying that I've always been rather fond of what Malcolm Stuart sometime s humorously refers to as our ‘Dying Duck’ and personally have no wish to see it replaced by something else. You can see our tough old bird in his usual place on the front page ofthis Navigans if you need to refresh your memory about an excellent idea that has served us well from our earliest days. Perhaps our archivist. Mike Boreham. might be able to tell us when the seagull logo first came into being? Having said all that. if any Members have any new ideas please do. as soon as possible, send them to Ed. who will faithfully pass them on to the Committee for consideration. I'd like also to hear from members who would like the bird to be left as it is. or perhaps just prettied up or modernised a bit? Ed's going to nail her colours to the mast - Save Our Seagull! Ed.

ADDERS: In April Navigans it is traditional to caution members (who should remind any children they bring to the Club) that at this time of year there is the possibility of coming across the occasional adder lying in the sun, often concealed in long grass. It's worth being careful where you tread, and if you do come across one, please do not disturb it. It's a part of our wild life which is harmless if left alone. THE SCRUBBING POST is not a safe place for children to play on at any time. Members please ensure that any children you bring to the Club keep off the Scrubbing Post. THE RIVER IS COLD for many months into the Sailing Season, even on apparently warm sunny days. Though Support Boats are out during all Club Races, it may happen that for some reason you can’t be picked up quickly after a capsize. It is important that you take measures before you leave the shore that would delay the onset of hypothermia. The following advice has been offered in Navigans in past years: Wear adequate clothing, i.e. Wet Suit/Dry Suit etc. and Personal Buoyancy. pnSeBDet Make sure your boat and its gear are sound. Ensure Personal Buoyancy and the Boat’s Buoyancy are both adequate. If you are inexperienced, either in sailing or in our sailing area. please ask advice from other experienced helms. : 5. If vou find yourself beginning to feel cold and tired, return to shore straightaway, rather than wait until you are too cold to think rationally. IN ROUGH WEATHER: If Club Racing goes ahead in windy conditions this does not necessarily imply that it is safe to go afloat. Some very experienced helms and crews may be well able to cope with that day's prevailing conditions, having built up their skills over the years by going out in gradually more testing weather, but less experienced sailors could have a difficult and and uncomfortable time. So please remember that even though Support Boats are there for Club Races, you should aim to be entirely self-sufficient, sail within your limitations, and please remember on all occasions that your decision to go afloat, whether to race or to potter, is always made on your own responsibility.
