USEFUL FORESHORE We have all got used to the Club’s Hard being used to receive casualties as its vantage point and access both from the sea and the shore makes it invaluable to the Emergency Services. Already this year the Coastguard has co-ordinated several shouts from the Club. The first was on 20th January when three gents were lost in their 15° dinghy. convinced they were behind Osea. Having set fire to some rags soaked in oil on a biscuit tin lid to attract attention (not to be recommended) it became clear from the reports that they could not be near Osea at all. As the West Mersea Lifeboat proceeded up river it was immediately despatched to Northey as this seemed the most likely location. Indeed. they were found and, being cold. were brought back to the Club where they were warmed in the Coastguard Landrover while we recovered their dinghy. The second job was on Sunday 25th February when, just after 0230, my pager went off. I am often feeling these days more like Victor Meldrew and. as I rolled out of bed. I heard myself saying ‘I don’t believe it’. The call through to Thames Coastguard briefed me to join Dick Townshend (Sector Officer) at, again, the Club. A pregnant Mum on Osea was contracting every three minutes and with the causeway closed by the tide for several more hours the extrication would have to be by sea or air. By the time I had stumbled into my trousers and as many warm clothes as I could lay my hands on in the dark. I ended up following the Landrover and Dick to Stansgate. The decision had been made to use West Mersea Lifeboat again as the on’scene time had been calculated to be quicker. and as the sea-state was calm. the crossing would not be too bad. As we opened the Club's tide gates. the Mersea LB and crew went past upriver on their way to the Captain's House steps on Osea. This was shortly followed by the arrival of the ambulance at the Club and we made ready to receive the patient. The casualty arrived on the Hard considerably relieved to see the ambulance and waiting Paramedic. Between contractions she was chair-lifted ashore and into the warmth and horizontal comfort of the ambulance. As it turned out it was someone I know. and she was soon delivered of a 9Ib 20z boy. Ned. Exactly 30 minutes had elapsed between the initial call and the arrival of the Lifeboat at MSC: my congratulations to Amanda and Ben as well as to the crew from Mersea LB for a brilliant response time. My thanks to the Club for maintaining such an excellent facility, but you probably don’t need to be reminded of that. 5. The Tideway Challenge Trophy - Hosted at the Club 25th-27th Mav Readers may remember that. some months ago. Mike Boreham did a very complimentary piece about my Tideway Dinghy entitled “Breeze II - And Very Pretty Too’. I was able to thank him when he visited Sailboat *96 and the Tideway Owners Association Stand at Alexandra Palace. Some 18 months ago I was inveigled into becoming Chairman of the Association and so. naturally. it was “Breeze II” that was chosen by the rest of the Committee to represent the older boats in the Class. In the event it Was a most enjoyable. if tiring. weekend. The Tideway seemed to be well received at the show. perhaps this was because it was the only ‘traditionally built’ boat there amongst the high-tech racing machines that seem to predominate these days. For those of you who sail these hi-tack (sorry) tech fashion accessories. I will give a brief description of our class. The Tideway was originally built by L.H. Walker & Co of Leigh-on-Sea. It is a 12° clinker built hull of Mahogany planks on Canadian Rock Elm timbers. It has a galvanised steel centreplate and . ready to sail. weighs in at about 300 Ibs. A stable and safe boat! The sail plan is gunter sloop with about 81 sq ft of sail - 90 with the genoa instead of the standard jib! We often do well at Handicap Racing. helped by the huge P.Y. of 152! Some 500 such wooden boats were built by Walkers. Tepco Boats of Leigh-on-Sea are the current builders and have built one wooden Tideway which was snapped up by an American to be sailed at Rhode Island. New York. and over 50 GRP Tideways which are now accepted by the Association and race with us with no apparent advantage or disadvantage. There is an almost fanatical following for the Class as a cruising dinghy and training boat. They also seem to last well, with the oldest boat known to the Association still sailing having been built in 1954. My own was built in 1960. On 28 previous occasions the Class has met up to race for The Tideway Challenge Trophy. This year Marconi Sailing Club has kindly agreed to be the hosts for the 29th Challenge on Saturday 25th - Monday 27th May. Racing will only take place on the 26th and 27th, with free sailing on Saturday 25th. Some of the members of the Association would like to extend an Invitation to anyone who would like to try a sail in a traditional Wooden or GRP Tideway on the Saturday of that Bank Holiday weekend. So if you are about and fancy a very relaxing sail in a boat that turns heads because of something other than the speed at which it goes past, COME ON DOWN. MORNING FLIGHT’S ‘1994 CRUISE’ - Further Progress - Fourth Newsletter. Just to bring you up to date with Morning Flight's travels on the other side of the pond. Sarah had to go back to work after her one year sabbatical was up so she flew back from St Martin in June 1995 and I set out northwards for Bermuda so as to be well clear of the Caribbean in the hurricane season (a wise move in the light of later events as it turned out to be a very bad year for hurricanes in respect of both frequency and intensity). Bermuda was very tidy and organised after the vagaries of the Caribbean Islands. Martin my crew member. described it as looking like a very large golf course. The itinerant yachts in the harbour seemed to be almost equally divided between those returning to Europe via the Azores and those going as far as Maine for the summer. We spent ten days relaxing and sightseeing in Bermuda before continuing north across the Gulf Stream to Newport. Rhode Island. This trip was fairly uneventful except for being threatened by the tail of Hurricane Alison, albeit by then degraded to a tropical storm. However, by the time it caught up we were safely tucked up in Newport Harbour. contd....

he Morning Flight then pointed her bow north again and eventually arrived in Penobscot Bay. Maine. by way of the Cape Cod canal. We did get sight of one whale north of Cape Cod. Martin had to fly back to UK from Maine. so since then I have been single- handed except for two occasions when Sarah has flown out to join Morning Flight for holidays. I spent most of the summer in Maine which is a very friendly and pretty place with a very active sailing community, There was also a number of British boats in the area with whom I stayed in contact with via the magic of SSB. With the onset of autumn and after spending six weeks in the UK, with Morning Flight tucked up in Rockland Boatyard. it was time to head south back through the Cape Cod canal and thence via Mystic Seaport and down Long Island Sound into East River and Hudson River to moor virtually in the heart of New York and what an experience it was to sail right alongside the famous skyline. From New York I sailed down to Cape May and through the Cape May Canal and up the Delaware River as far as Chesapeake and Delaware Canal. This is the entry to Chesapeake Bay which I spent some time exploring before entering the Intra Coastal Waterway in Norfolk Virginia. The 1.C.W. is a wonderful facility extending all the way down to the Florida Keys. but it is both narrow and shallow for much of its length. so it is quite wearing to navigate. especially so for a single-hander. and Morning Flight touched the putty on several occasions and towed other yachts off on others. There are also lots of bridges. especially so in the south. For this reason Morning Flight’s progress down the US east coast consisted of some trips using the I.C.W. punctuated by longer legs in the open sea where one could relax a bit and gain some distance on route to Miami. One highlight of this part of the voyage was a visit to the Kennedy Space Centre at Cape Canaveral with a guided tour of the centre which included a visit to the launch pad. Sarah came out to Miami and we spent Christmas 1995 there while waiting for a suitable weather window to cross the Gulf Stream to the Bahamas. This we eventually achieved and arrived in Bimini to check in before crossing the Great Bahama Bank to Nassau for Sarah to fly back to the cold of the UK. The water in the Bahamas is beautiful. but also very shallow over the banks with lots of coral heads. Navigation is therefore mostly by eyeball and only in good light. The tidal range is a maximum of three feet so it was quite normal to anchor in nine or ten feet of water (Morning Flight drawing 1.8m). After spending time in the Bahamas and in particular in the Exuma Islands I headed south via Turks and Caicos and thence to the Dominican Republic. a very poor, but also very green and lush country with extremely friendly people. I had been learning some Spanish en route and this turned out to be extremely useful in the Dominican Republic and in Puerto Rico. Puerto Rico lies across the famous Mona Passage from the Dominican Republic. However despite its reputation I had a good sail across to Mayaguez in 15-20 knots of NE wind. The direction of the trades in this part of the Caribbean means that travelling east invariably involves a windward passage. Afier travelling in short hops along the South Coast of Puerto Rico, mainly at night or early morning to take advantage of the offshore night wind and calmer seas. I arrived at my present location in St Thomas in the Virgin Islands. The immediate plan is to sail via the British Virgin Islands to St Martin and then to be in Antigua for Classics Weck in April where both Sarah and I are booked in as crew on the S & S (Sparkman & Stephens) Classic Yacht ‘Stormy Weather’ for the Classic Series races. (Ed's note: She won the 1935 Transatlantic and Fastnet Races according to Oxford Companion to Ships and the Sea.) Then John Todds will come out to Antigua and will sail with me via Bermuda to the Azores before he flies back to UK in order to bring Chimo to the *96 Classics event in Brittany. Hope you enjoy this potted account of Morning Flights travels since we last sent you a letter. (Apologies for the handwritten script but my printer has succumbed to the sea air.) Please give or print Best Regards to my many friends at MSC and tell them that the kami-kaze Seagull (somewhat patched) is still alive and well at the port cross trees. Regards. Dave Beane, Morning Flight (St Thomas. CRUISER COMMENTS The Cruiser Fitting Out Supper held last month at the MSC Clubhouse was well attended and our thanks go to Mark Fletcher and his Ladies for a most enjoyable meal as well as excellent service. It cannot be easy providing a three course meal for sixty people in the confines of the Clubhouse. | only hope they did not fiind it too daunting. and hope they will be able to provide similar facilities on future occasions. Fitting Out and Launching is well under way even though the weather at times could be better with less north/easterly winds and a little higher temperature. Nevertheless we look forward to the first of this year’s events which is the Shakedown Cruise to Burnham with a race included for those interested. This takes place on Bank Holiday Weekend 25-26-27 May - see Club notice board for details. With so much activity going on around the Cruiser Park at present. may I remind Members to be sure they do not leave their cars in a position that may cause obstruction to those Cruiser being moved for launching or to the Mast Derrick. Whilst on the the subject of the Cruiser Park, would members please make sure the water taps are turned off after use. Would those who have been allocated a different mooring from last year please make sure your dinghy is moved to its correct location. I am sure it goes without saying. but would members. once launched, please ensure their Winter Storage space is left in a tidy state. With regard to launching. it seems some members having launched have gone off sailing. leaving the poor old tractor driver to retrieve and store their trolley for them. instead of picking up a convenient mooring. coming ashore quickly to stow the trailer before going off for a sail. Once your boat has been launched your trolley must be removed from the slipway. especially on Sundays. when dinghy/cat racing is in progress. That's all for now, have a good season's sailing. don’t forget the Dell Bar is normally open on Friday evenings for a general get- together to start the weekend: also keep a lookout on the Club's Notice Board for Social events float. COMMODORE’S NOTES Perhaps a word in the ears of those who go racing on a Sunday and their relationship with Support Boat Crews: Please remember that Support Boat Crews have a duty to save ‘life’ before ‘property’. I am sure that none of us would want to put them under pressure to ‘save my boat/help me save my boat’ (especially in conditions where they might be soon needed to help occupants of other boats in difficulty). The mind plays odd tricks on us when we are tired. wet and cold. and it’s very easy to lose sight of reality when it’s blowing a hoolie: there's a four foot chop: the Support boat is on a Ice shore and all one can visualise is one’s pride and joy (the boat) being lost. The boat can always be retrieved later. Please don’t put lives at risk by insisting that Support Boat Crews rescue your boat and not you - they know better! Colin Kidner WEDNESDAY EVENING PURSUIT RACES Why not take a break half way through the week with an informal and friendly challenge! The format is an upside-down handicap race with the slowest classes starting first and the fastest last. The aim is to sail the furthest around the course by the predetermined finish time. Starting from the Hard. the slowest class goes at 7pm and. with sufficient boats. the Dinghies and Catamarans can be separated into two events. This allows the faster Catamarans having too long a wait before their ‘off, Interesting courses guaranteed. but the wind is not always under our control. The normal Finish Time is 8.15, or 8.20 for Catamarans if racing separately. When circumstances warrant. the bar will be open after racing. See you there - John Weedon CRUISER COMMENTS Well. yours truly is afloat at last. just in ume for our shakedown cruise to the River Crouch. stopping over at the Burnham Yacht Harbour. | must say their rates are very reasonable: £8 for Happy Medium (9 Meter) per night. also the facilities are superb. greatly extended from last year. Mike Turner and Derek Gardiner organised a race round to the Crouch for the intrepid sailors. Whilst others (me included) sailed whilst it suited but put the iron topsail on when it did not. Full marks to Mona and Fantasea Who stuck it out to the bitter end. though | believe Fantasea succumbed in the end. | must admit to being confused at one stage Whilst inward bound near the River Roach. | saw Ron Phillips in his new vacht ‘Cheveron’ outward bound. then realised he had a berth at Burnham Yacht Harbour and was sailing out to mect us. We had a total of sixteen Cruisers sailing round from MSC and were joined by the crews of ‘Cheveron’ and “Telemon W’ the latter having come round by road for Sunday's evening meal at the Crouch Yacht Club. making a total of 45 members. A most enjoyable ume was had with Mike Turner handing out the trophics to those who raced. with the overall winner being “Moonflect’ (Robin Lovett and Dick Hooker). It was also nice to see “Silver Pearl” joining the fleet. having sailed down from the River Orwell having had a refit at Fox’s Marina. On more mundane matters may I draw your attention to those reminders listed on Page 5 of last month's Navigans: Park carefully in the Curiser Park/Turn off Water//Move Tender to New Storage Position if appropriate/Return ashore to store your trolley immediately after Cruiser is Launched/Winter Storage Space kept tidy. Please remember to offer your support for this year's East Coast Piers Race duc to be held on Sunday 28th July - it is for a very good cause. The next major cruise will be that to Ipswich Dock (Neptune Marina) on 24/25/26th August. which for those able to take the Whole week off could include a sail up the River Deben and visit to Woodbridge. but more about that later on. Don't forget to make a note of iin your diary. In the mean time. watch out for forthcoming events on the Club Notice Board and in the Dell Bar. Don't forget ‘Friday Night is Dell Bar Night’. Derek Kirby. Cruiser Fleet Captain

CRUISER COMMENTS Having just returned from a three week cruise to Holland I was reminded by Maureen that this will be the last Navigans for a couple of months. so | thought I had better get cracking with this report. Firstly may I say Doreen and I enjoyed our cruise even though the weather could have been better at times. It was a pity we did not have time to acquaint the crews of *Suruca’ and ‘Kelly's Eye’ with some of the information gleaned whilst in Holland, likewise to ‘West Marie’ who we met en route to Ostend whilst we were going in the opposite direction to Dunkirk. However in each instance we conveyed what we could over the VHF radio. Briefly. for anyone intending to cruise the Delta, especially the Veerse Meer and Grevelingen Meer. there is now a charge for staying overnight at any of the picnic areas or islands. The charge of 7'/; Guilders (about £3) is not unreasonable for the facilities provided. the problem is how to pay. It seems you are required to purchase an electronic card. rather like a telephone charge card (and which. incidentally, can be used to make telephone calls), Thus armed you locate one of these machines to purchase your ticket. It seems most of these machines are near car parks since they can be used for car parking as well. I must also add the tickets purchased for the Veerse Meer will not do for the Grevelingen Meer, these have to be bought at locations in the Grevelingen Meer. We were fortunate in arriving carly in the season when things are quieter, I feel it is going to be mayhem during the height of the season, since many yachtsmen. including other nationals seem unaware of the situation. It is difficult for contd...

6. me to cover it clearly in Navigans. but if anyone is going to Holland and wants some information in more detail. please contact me. or failing that. enquire on arrival at somewhere like Middelburg. RNLI - Local News The Burnham Lifeboat Station is being allocated an Atlantic 75 inflatable Lifeboat scheduled to arrive on the Crouch just before Burnham Weck (the last week in August). It will be housed in a floating boat house in the Marina, and the existing Class D Boat will be retained in its Boathouse behind the Royal Corinthian. The suitably modified Severn Class Lifeboat (a new Class that has had a few teething troubles) will be on its station at Harwich in the autumn and in the meantime the Waveney continues in use there. Two recent editions of °999° on BBC TV showed Walton Lifeboat becoming entangled with the mast of a yacht breaking up on the Gunfleet Sands - what a baptism for the new Cox'n - and another Service at Palace Pier Brighton. Having many years ago played wave-dodging in that last area I could well understand how it occurred. The state of the Atlantic 21 and the fact that three medals were awarded for the rescue gives an idea of how horrific the conditions must have been. (A risky operation for all concerned when two girls were plucked to safety from the supports of the pier in rough seas - this was after the Lifeboat’s bow and port sponson had been punctured and deflated). You will not need reminding that the entire cost of running the RNLI is met by voluntary contributions - not by the government. Amongst many ways of contributing to funds is buying from the RNLI catalogue. To help the Maldon Branch, within whose area you sail. can you add to your Order Form our Branch Reference 61 42 54. It will not cost you anything but it will help us. If you are not already a member of the RNLI then please consider joining and supporting what is sometimes described as the ultimate insurance policy. Commodore’s Notes I am sure that some of you will be aware of the incident which occurred off the Club foreshore during the East Coast Piers Race when the helm of a yacht suffered a severe heart attack. the crew were extrememly distressed and needed help. Fortunately the River Warden, Christopher Reynolds-Hole was passing the yacht and was able to go aboard and make a call for help to the Club (the crew of the yacht being unable to use the radio or distress flares). I have spoken to the River Warden who was very complimentary about the assistance which various Members of the Club gave. I have also received a letter of thanks from Dick Townshend (reproduced below - Ed.) The following people deserve special mention for their work during the incident: Debbie Glynn. Linda Chapman, Dave Saunders and Charles Anderson. I also have to thank the Committee of the East Coast Piers Race and everyone who helped to ensure that event passed off successfully. The details of sponsorship have yet to be finalised, so watch this space. I believe that a record number of Cadets participated in a very successful Cadet Week. A big Thank you to Charles Anderson. Chris Davies and their team of helpers. Camping Fortnight has been discussed at the last Main Committee Meeting and I would be grateful for any views members may have as to how this event can be improved for all Club Members (not just those who spend two weeks’ holiday camping!) Finally, regret not being able to spend more time at the Club sailing. I have an enormous work load courtesy of Sir Ron Dearing! Colin Kidner. ASSISTANCE TO THE RESCUE SERVICES Once again the Members of Marconi Sailing Club have provided the most valuable assistance to the emergency services and in particular to the boating fraternity. The distressing incident today involving Mr Tarling once again highlights the exceptional lengths to which your members and their friends will go - in their wish to help others. All too frequently. we request your members to help us with the most unpleasant of tasks in our efforts to minimise the risk to life of those who use the River Blackwater. Today was no exception andI offer the most sincere and profuse thanks to your Club and all those personally involved. Yours sincerely, Richard Townshend, Sector Manager. HM COASTGUARD. YOUR CLUB NEEDS MORE RACE OFFICERS AND ASSISTANT RACE OFFICERS Like all voluntary organisations, this Club needs the active co-operation and help of all its Members. Without the Race Officers and their Assistants no racing would be possible. and racing is the reason most of the dinghy and catamaran owners joined the Club. The number of qualified Race Officers has dwindled to such an extent that many are doing 3 or 4 duties this season. I think that is too much. A similar problem exists with Assistant Race Officers, we desperately need more people to help out. In an attempt to address the problem I have produced a revised list for the last part of the season. I know those concerned will say it is short notice and the day nominated will not suit for lots of perfectly good reasons. However, if you have a problem. please swap with someone else. Leaving me a message saying you can't do a duty on a particular day does not help me or the Club. and Iam NOT going to spend hours on the phone trying to find a substitute - that is your job. The situation would be helped if those sailors who know they have not done a duty, or enough duties, could contact me and VOLUNTEER. Many of you, I know are on the Support Boat Roster and will not wish to do another duty. However, no racing can take place at all without a manned race box. On a personal note | feel that having 5 people manning 2 rescue boats every Sunday is excessive. The responsibility for safety lies, in my view, entirely with the helmsman of the dinghy or catamaran. Rescue Boats should only be required in extreme situations and then only for saving life and limb. Salvaging boats is a bonus, not a necessity. By taking so many members for rescue duties, the pool available for the Race Box is dramatically reduced. Surely in winds below 15 knots we only need | boat with | or 2 crew. If the wind does pick up I am sure we could find volunteers on the day who did not want to go out, but would be happy to help in a Support Boat. Finally, perhaps some of the Cruiser Fleet might want to help out at the beginning or end of the season, or if the wind is too strong or too light to sail. This all sounds like the usual grumble from a Committee Member but I, like all of you, joined the Club to sail. After allowing for work and domestic commitments it is frustrating to find that you have duties on perhaps 20% of your available sailing days. Remember, there are only 41 race days in a season. So please contact me, either at the Club, Dart 15 Sail No. 1704, or by plone 04 G1621-826953. Rob Davies, Sailing Secretary. LAYING UP SUPPER: Friday 8th November 1996. 7.30 for 8pm till lam. CRUISER COMMENTS In spite of the dubious weather forecast. 18 Cruisers made the trip from MSC to Neptune Marina, Ipswich, on the Saturday of the Bank Holiday Weekend. making a formidable flotilla on entry to the Marina. In fact other visitors calling up the Harbour Master on VHF requesting entry were requested to wait until the Marconi fleet had entered, such was the effect our collective arrival made. We even had a reception committee waiting to take our lines by way of Peter Clayton (‘Peace’) and John Todd (*“Chimo’) waiting to take our lines. Monday was a lay day with a tour of Tolly-Cobbold and lunch organised, followed by a guided tour of the historic Dockyard for which we were joined by the crews of “Silver Pearl’ and ‘Two Jays’ who came round by road. Sadly. some of the fleet had to return home on the Monday: however it was great that 11 of the Cruisers were able to join us for the rest of the week for a trip up the River Deben to the Tidemill Yacht Harbour at Woodbridge. It was while there that we had the mother and father of thunderstorms and gale force winds which kept us holed up there until the Friday, but if you have to be weather bound, I cannot think of a nicer place to be.** The only problem was, it put paid to the Bar B Q planned to be held at ‘The Rocks’ just above Ramsholt on the Thursday. However. we made up for it with a good meal and get-together in “The Bull’ at Woodbridge. Most of the fleet stopped off at Brighlingsea on the way back on Saturday: we on the other hand had a family engagement on the Saturday and had to hot foot it back to MSC. the rest of the fleet arriving on Sunday in glorious sunshine. It was great to see so many boats and members attending and clearly, from the feedback received, everyone enjoyed themselves. Whilst on the sailing mode, I am arranging an end of season (for me at least since I intend to lay up ‘Happy Medium*® on Monday 30th September) Cruise to Brightlingsea, including dinner in the Colne Yacht Club on Saturday 28th September. High water is about 14.00 so I expect we will leave the moorings about mid-day. Exact details yet to be confirmed with the Harbour Master with regard to berths. Also the water taxi will be running so you need not take dinghies. The only point I would make is that should the weather prevent members from sailing to Brightlingsea, they make arrangements to go round by road for the evening meal. The chart for Cruiser Winter Storage 1996/7 will be displayed on the Cruiser Notice Board by the end of September, together with the “Hauling Out List’. Please make sure when hauling out you have made arrangements with the Tractor Driver in advance. Please don’t just turn up and expect it to happen. As far as space allocation is concerned may I picase make it clear that spaces wiii only be a!located to those who have paid for Winter Storage. OPERATING THE FLOODGATES We were approached one evening recently at the Club by a Cruiser Member who had arrived to go onto the water and found himself, in the dark, faced unexpectedly with the Floodgates closed (as they now must be until Ist May next year). After Ray described the method of opening the gates, the member suggested in a discussion with me that (a) all Members ought to be shown how to use the Floodgates and (b) full information on them should be published in the club circular. Though it is obvious how the gates work by looking at them (in daylight), I agreed it might be useful to put a few pointers in Navigans - a couple of which genuinely might not be all that obvious. 1. For those of us without the strength of an ox, the Floodgates are much easier to operate than the old Floodboards. 2. If you are faced with closed Floodgates in the dark and haven’t had much practice using them, you will need a torch or your car headlights to see what you're doing. A practice run in daylight is even better and/or ask for a demo from a seasoned Cruiser member before the need arises. >) The Floodgates are never locked by the Sailing Club and no key is required to open them. +. Looking at the closed Floodgates from the landward side: (a) The gate on the left is held in the closed position by a large square bolt which drops into a square slot in the ground and the bolt is raised and lowered by the winding handle on top of the left hand gate. When closing, this gate must be closed first. Clockwise turn of the handle raises the bolt to open the gate Anticlockwise turn of the handle lowers the bolt to secure the gate in the closed position. There is a hinged metal plate which can be dropped across the slot in the ground when the gate is open to keep it Clear of stones, litter etc. (b) The gate on the right is held in the closed positon by a lever which engages with the closed and bolted left-hand gate. 5. To take a tender through the gap, opening the right hand gate only should be sufficient and will save time. 6. Always close the gates after use at the times of year when they should be closed - this information is painted on the gates. The Club has a duty to keep the Floodgates closed during the winter (1st September 96 to Ist May 97) in order to keep any exceptionally high tides out of the site and the surroundi ng countryside. The mention of Floodboards on Page 5 of the Yearbook refers to the Floodgates. 7. It requires a dit of physical strength when closing the gates, to pull each gate firmly to its closed position as you lower the left-hand gate bolt or the right-hand gate lever. Most could manage it single-handed but a helper makes it easier, 8. If there is a strong onshore breeze blowing, make sure you open the gates right back against the wall. I was suprised to see that they can be blown shut - on anything passing through the gap. I'm afraid it wasn't much use on that particular evening informing an unprepared Navigans Editor that she should know - then and there in dark - how to open the gates. She'd Jorgotten what she'd practised at least a year earlier. She also claims to belong to the last generation we are likely to see of helpless females and she still looks to the men in her householdfor most technical matters. However, she’s since had another practice, for the purpose of these instructions, and could probably do it now!

THE BLACKWATER PROJECT After 3 years of consultation and preparation the Blackwater Estuary Management Plan was officially launched in July of this year, A full copy of the Plan. for members to read. is available in the Clubhouse lounge at Stansgate. It is also available to view in local libraries and in the Maldon and Colchester Planning Departments. It is well produced and covers a wide range of topics and interests related to the sustainable use of the Estuary and its surroundings.. The interests of the Sailing fraternity have been channelled. in the main. through the Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection Association. BACSPA of which the Marconi Sailing Club is a longstanding member. BACSPA also has representatives on the Eastern Region Committce of the RYA. The primary concern of BACSPA is the conservation and protection ofthe Rivers in the interest of sailing and other watersports. As a result of the extensive consultation and involvement of local interest groups such as BACSPA the Plan has achieved widespread support. The Plan is expected to evolve with ume and be modified to mect new and changing requirements. It is recognised that the project will be judged on the speed and effectiveness of the implementation process. An Implementation Forum is to be held annually to formally assess progress and make new proposals. The main thrust. however. will be the continued use and involvement of local interest/topic groups to actively implement and progress particular aspects. The first Implementation Forum was held on 24th September 1996 where both BACSPA and Marconi SC were represented. The Blackwater Project team also issues a free quarterly newsletter entitled “The Blackwater Matters’. The object of this publication is to keep everyone up to date with what's happening on and around the Blackwater Estuary. Copies ofthis are also available at Stansgate. Perhaps one of our members could contribute an article”? If anyone would like to Know more about the Estuary Plan. or have any suggestions to make. please don’t hesitate in coming forward, Ron Grevgoose. ai Commodore’s Report The last year has seen further consolidation of the Club’s position, with little material change since 1994. However, as the investment in 1994 was so great, this is perhaps no great surprise. In continuing efforts to improve the facilities available at the club, and overcome the OOD problem, we decided to recruit a Steward to run the Bar and Clubhouse on Saturdays and Sundays. I think that the consensus is that the experiment was a great success, despite the short term duration due to the individual’s financial circumstances. With the term coming to a close in August, the Committee decided that it was not appropriate to recruit a replacement at that stage, but to hold off until the start of 1996. Moving on to our relationship with MASC. This has been fairly much “on hold” for most of the year, due to Peter Woodhouse leaving the company and having to step down from his post as Chairman. In addition, recent changes with the departure of Gerry Wignall, new MASC trustees, and a review of the relationship with other sections bode well for us for the future. As far as 1995 events go Regatta was undoubtedly a failure, with only some 60 competitors. The Committee has taken the view that this event will go “on Ice” until demand turns round and we can again run a viable event. On the other hand ECPR was again a major success. The club has been mentioned extremely favourably in correspondence in the Yachting press which has covered the ability of clubs to organise successful multihull events. Other clubs have been criticised (notably Stokes Bay and Rutland) whilst we have been held up (along with Texel) as an example. This is obviously excellent PR, and probably has greater value than any advertising that we could do. Last year I made a plea for “successors” to come forward and outlined the reasons why we needed fresh volunteers to bolster all the committees. With very few exceptions this has been a complete failure. As a group the membership MUST realise that the future of your enjoyment of these facilities is dependent upon their successful management. It is no excuse to say that you only use the Club “a bit” and can’t contribute. That attitude will eventually lead to the gradual and then speedy decline of the organisation. I believe that every single one of us realises what a precious sailing site we have, and that none of us would wish to lose it. My warning may appear alarmist, but the average attitude of individuals will lead to this situation. Please search your conscience and if you can for goodness sake volunteer. At the end of my term as Commodore, I must place on record my thanks to all the Executive and Committee members that I have had the pleasure to work with over the last few years. The standard of discussion and sometimes lively debate at meetings has resulted in several good ideas and decisions coming forward. The Committee is no longer a real talking shop, but very much an action oriented decision making body. As last year I have no reservation in thanking a few individuals. Firstly, Jean Flook has decided to hang up her apron after a number of years of providing an excellent service from the Galley. I should like everyone to show their appreciation in the traditional way. Secondly, Colin Kidner, who is now passing into retirement as Rear Commodore; his organisational abilities have been of huge assistance. I hope he enjoys the “rest camp” of the Commodore’s role! Finally, again, Frank Bennett. Frank has again carried out a huge amount of work unseen by the vast majority; from tractor maintenance through the club radios and electrics to the sewage plant, as well as counting the beans, it has been a great privilege to work with someone so committed to the future of the Club, and someone whom we should all look to with gratitude. As you see, I do not escape entirely scot free, some people think that after making this mess I should still be involved as a Vice President - just as I thought I could put my feet up for a while. You never know, Alex

12. and I might get some more sailing in! It has though been a great pleasure and privilege to hold the position, and to see the way in which the various interest groups have become united over the last few years. I wish Colin and his new team all the best, and thank all of you for your support over the last three years. COMMODORE’S REPORT 1996 Colin Kidner 1996 has not been a good year for me and sailing. I have not been able to spare the time to get down to the club at weekends. Those of you who read my notes in Navigans will know that I have been a victim of the continuing change in the education ficld. I sincerely hope that 1997 should see an end to the results of change. which will mean I have to work less and can play more at weekends. I should like to deal with the negative side of the Club first. The access road to the Club is a cause for concern. The repairs to the damage which the NRA traffic caused are not satisfactory. Privatization has its down side. The NRA is now called the Environmental Agency and seems to be playing “hard to get’ over the road repairs. I suspect that the grip which is being put on public spending by the government has something to do with the reluctance of the Environmental Agency to agree to do something about the poor reinstatement work done by the NRA. to the access road. I have to thank Larry for taking on the task of dealing with the Environmental Agency and trying to get some redress. So far he has no success. What we need is a high profile barrister to help fight our claim. The second half of camping fortnight seems to be a cause for concern. Some Club Members are of the opinion that there is a lack of control and order which results in club facilities being abused. Others are of the opinion that this is a time for relaxation and enjoyment and do not do not feel that there is a problem. The arguments will be considered in the next few months. so any ideas which members may have will be gratefully received by the main committee to allow full and frank discussions to take place in order to resolve any difficulties. Now the good news. [ wish to put on the record my sincere thanks to all Club Members and particularly Executive and Committee members who have worked to ensure that the Club ‘works’ for us all. I have no hesitation in mentioning the work done by Frank Bennett in spite of a very serious accident earlier in the year. Fortunately Frank is now well on the way to a full recovery. Ironically this accident led to Frank looking at our Club Insurance and to his horror he found that Club Members were not covered for ‘waterside activities’ I am pleased to say that this oversight has now been remedied. Management of the MASC and its finances seem to be under much tighter control. I feel confident that the future of MASC remains assured. Mr Brocklesby and Mr Marsh visited the Club during Camping fortnight and saw the results of the hard work done by MSC members. They were impressed. The membership has gone over the 400 mark this year. which means that the Club finances will remain healthy. It is intended to run the series of advertisements in Yachts and Yachting again and to signpost the Club whilst this campaign is running. This tactic resulted in members joining the club. I hope you all agree that new Galley service provided by Mark Fletcher has been a great success. I am confident that this service will continue next season together with an improved bar service. The latter will depend on agreeing mutually acceptable terms and conditions with Mark. I have to pay tribute to Charles Anderson and Chris Davis and their team of helpers for their efforts in running a very successful Cadet Week. I believe some 40 young people took part. learnt a great deal and had a great time. Congratulations Charles and Chris and many thanks. It is through these activities that the enjoyment of sailing is allowed to develop in the minds of young people. Enthusiastic youngsters will be the life blood of the sport and this Club in the years to come. I am sure that you will all join me in wishing Jo Jo Anderson and her helm. Dominica, every success in the Cadet World Championships in Bombay during December. I look forward to seeing many club members at the Curry Evening on the 29 November at 7.30pm at MSC. I understand that both girls will be at the curry evening and I urge you to attend so that you can meet them and wish them the very best of luck. ECPR was again a successful event. and allows the Club to work as a team in running a high profile sailing race as well as raising money for RYA Sailability. Thank you Mike and your team, who organised and ran the event. I would like to pay special thanks to the Cruiser Fleet for their support in providing the mother boats between here and Walton on the Naze. Without your support the event could not take place. Next year will be the tenth anniversary of the ECPR and we are looking forward to a bumper entry from the continent if all goes well. It is hoped that the Prindle and Nacra European Championship will occur just before or just after the Piers race so that continental sailors can attend ECPR and Championships and only have to make one trip across the Channel. Keith Starky works very hard every month sending out Navigans to us all. He has had to relinquish this task for reasons connected with his work. Thank you Keith you have done a great job. This means we are looking for a Club Member to take on this task. See me or put your name on a post card. My hope for the future is that all members of the Club can work together so that the interests of all Club Members can be advanced in 1997 and beyond. Remember. sailing has been around for a long time. In 7000 BC., Greek seafarers sailed to the Aegean island of Milos, 75 miles from the mainland. to obtain obsidian. Let's hope that Marconi Sailing Club will be around long into the future.

RNLI SPONSORED ROWING RACE This annual fun event is taking place on Boxing Day. Thursday 26th December 1996. Start time 12.30 hrs from MLSC Clubhouse. Hythe Quay. Maldon. Race is over a distance of 5km. Entry fee for boats taking part is £1, and the real funds are raised when those taking part get sponsorship from family. friends and work colleagues. etc. Over £6.000 was raised by the event last year. The Classes are: Men’s Singles or Men’s Pairs in either Yacht Tenders or Non-Yacht Tenders: Men’s Multiple. Ladies Singles or Ladies Pairs in either Yacht Tenders or Non-Yacht Tenders: Ladies Multiple. Mixed Pairs in either Yacht Tenders or Non-Yacht Tenders: Multiple Mixed. Anyone mad enough to row a Rubber Dinghy. Under Fifteen. Prizes include: Fastest Men’s/Ladies Boat: Best Fancy Dress: Panther Award for Highest Sponsorship Money Raised: Cadet Class Trophy for Under Fifteens Sponsorship Forms and Entry Forms required by those taking part are available from Michael McCarthy. [redacted] For the less active among us it is an enjoyable event for the many spectators who come along to watch - you just need to dress up warm. Lifeboat collecting boxes are there for anyone who wishes to make a contribution to the Lifeboat Service. Hot Refreshments available and 2 pubs very close by. CRUISER COMMENTS It's amazing to think this is being written for the December issue of Navigans. Where has the time gone? CRUISER COMMENTS It is possible that by the time you read this the Christmas Festivities will be a pleasant memory and we are now either into or approaching the New Year, so first of all a Very Happy New Year to you all. The Cruiser Annual General Meeting was held at MASC on Thursday 21st November and was attended by 47 members representing 33 craft, with apologies received from Mike Egerton. Pete Sayer. Mark Whitely, Roy Bellord and Mike Turner. Cruises in 1996. The meeting commenced with a review of the 1996 Sailing Season starting with the Fleet Cruise to Burnham (16 boats): Neptune Marina. Ipswich (18 boats with 11 boats staying on for a cruise up the River Deben to Woodbridge.) The final event was to have been a Cruise to Brightlingsea, however, the weather intervened resulting in the crews of 10 boats making the trip to the Colne Yacht Club by road whilst 2 boats “Juliet Whiskey’ and Avocet’ did make the passage. Twenty Five Members that evening sat down to a fish and chip supper plus a jug or two. Cruiser Racing. The introduction of Races or Chases on the back of Club Cruises is proving popular and credit to Mike Turner & Derek Gardiner for bringing in this new dimension to our sailing events. Prizes were awarded for the following: Freshers Chase: Ist Moonfleet 2nd Timari Two 3rd Gintrap Mid Summer Chase: Ist Timari Two 2nd Petronella 3rd Gintrap Fancy Dress Chase: Ist Moonfleet 2nd Ocean Slipper 3rd Reflections Green Man Chase: Abandoned due to weather conditions but consolation prizes awarded to the four entrants. Overall Winner: Barnacle Trophy awarded to Moonfleet. ECPR. Once again the Cruiser Fleet gave their support to the East Coast Piers Race for which a special vote of thanks was given by our Commodore at the Club AGM and was recorded on last month's Navigans. Winter Storage. With the Winter Laying Up now complete, attention was drawn to the limited space available for what seems to be a growing need. This will have to be addressed to the Main Committee. The need of Cruiser Members to observe the security code was stressed as was the case of maintaining trailers, plus the need to fix towing eyes on both ends of the trailer if not already fitted. Paint. Chain & Shackles. Malcolm Shaft will be ordering Paint, and Don Holdsworth will be ordering Chain, Shackles, and Anodes so please get your orders in early. Fleet Captain & Vice Fleet Captain. Yours truly and Malcolm Yeoman respectively were re-elected to these posts, with Mike Turner and Derek Gardiner again looking after the Cruiser Racing Events. Cruises in 1997. Tentative arrangements are in hand for Mayday Weekend (4th-6th May) to Brightlingsea; Spring Bank Holiday (24th-26th May) to Burnham: August Bank Holiday (23rd-25th August) to River Orwell, either Shotley or Wolverstone Marina and for those who can take the rest of the week off another trip up to Woodbridge. Letter of Thanks: | am writing to Navigans to express my sincere thanks to some Club Members for their recent help. | have been working in various locations abroad for the last few years. and though I have kept up my club Membership. | have had very little quality sailing time on the Blackwater. This year I managed to get my Silhouette launched. and sailed a little. but unfortunately. bad weather prevented me from recovering her before I had to leave the country. I made all the long-distance arrangements to recover on the last weekend in October. and flew home especially. Murphy's Law operated. as might be expected. and after a tiring and frustrating day. she had moved from F11 to C4 and had lost the outboard prop! Just before my outward flight. I phoned Peter Clayton to ask him to try to arrange for her to be towed back to my own mooring, more in hope than in...whatever. To cut the saga short. when I later got in touch with Peter. he. together with an unknown band of heroes. had actually recovered the boat. Special thanks to Ian (?) who went into the water. I believe. To say that I was relieved and grateful would be an understatement. as I had no idea how I was going to arrange matters at a distance and was getting pretty worried about the situation. Please express my appreciation through the pages of the newsletter. Bryan Simpson, Co. Tipperary, Republic of Ireland. Date to be confirmed. Over the weekend of 16th-17th November, eight members of the SOLO fleet spent the weekend on the Solent. This has become an annual event. but this year was in “Ist Class Eights”, rather than the usual Sigma 36s. The Ist Class Eights are used for match racing and the boats were ex. RYA. We soon found that there was a little more to match racing than we realised. including differences in the rules. The wind on Saturday was O to force 2 so it was relatively easy to become familiar with the boats. They handle like a large dinghy. Sunday was a different story with wind up to force 5. We switched to racing round the cans (old habits die hard) but had to lengthen the legs as we did not have time to hoist and lower the spinnakers. Much room for improvement here! Thanks to Roger Smith who made all the arrangements for a very enjoyable weekend. Geoff Josey, SOLO Fleet Captain

John Salmon. Sailing Secretary CRUISER COMMENTS Firstly, may I wish you all a Very Happy New Year coupled with good sailing during 1997. I for one will be glad to see the back of this snow and cold weather. roll on summer. There was nothing better to focus the mind on either sailing or the weather than to be at Dave & Joan Thomas's presentation held at MASC when they shared with us the experiences of buying a new Catamaran Cruiser in South Africa. commissioning it. then sailing it from South Africa to the Mediterranean. Talk about the spirit of adventure! Wow! It was fascinating. many thanks. Ed's Note: The film covered briefly the completion of the new Catamaran ‘Dajo’; her delivery by road from boatvard to the water and the trip from Cape Town, via St Helena, the Ascension Is, the celebration of crossing the Equator for the first time, and the approach to Cape Verde Is. Here the film ended but ‘Dajo’s’ trip continued via the Azores to her destination of (ribraltar. It was watched with great interest by a sizeable audience of Cruiser Fleet \fembers, some (a verv few - well, two) of whom think that getting asfar as the Bench Head feels like a trip into dangerous, foreign waters! Most of you will know we have for the past few years been trying to improve the quality of our Winter Storage Trailers. especially since the increase in demand for Winter Storage made the mobility of trailers more essential. I must say the standard of maintenance by Members has increased greatly and is much appreciated by all concerned. However. a census of trailers this winter shows there are 34 (including the Club's Jack B. Workboat and Mooring Barge Trailers) which require towing eyes on both ends and there are a further 6 Trailers requiring an eye at one end. We are currently engaged in obtaining a quotation for having this work done as a one-off exercise. As soon as the information is to hand. Members affected will be contacted with a view to having this work carried out. Naturally this does not apply to those craft using road trailers. Should anyone have any queries regarding this or wish to take advantage of the situation to rectify steering problems etc. please contact me. With regard to Flotilla sailing this year, the proposals outlined in the January Navigans are pretty well completed - full details will be made known at the last of our Winter Meetings on 20th March. and of course through Navigans. Don’t forget if planning your summer holiday. why not add four days onto the August Bank Holiday and join us up in the River Deben. Our next Winter Meeting is due on Thursday 20th February when our speaker will be Frank Turner who has done a study and written two books on the World War Two Maunsel Forts in the Thames Estuary. Most of us have sailed close to these and it is impossible to do so without wondering about the How. When and Why. so come along. | am sure you will find it most interesting. Derek Kirby. 6. RYA EASTERN REGION CLUB FORUM This year’s forum was held at the Gosling Sports Park. Welwyn Garden City on Ist February. and Sailing Secretary John Salmon and mysclf attended the day's proceedings which lasted from 10.30 to 16.45, The event was well supported, largely due to the interest in the content and implication to Clubs ofthe introduction of the new Racing Rules of Sailing (RRS) 1997-2000 issued by the International Sailing Federation (ISAF) and which become effective on Ist April. The morning session was taken up by a series of presentations on the role of the Sports Council. Legal Matters. and Club Development. In the afternoon there were sessions on the Dinghy Handicap System. the New Racing Rules (1997-2000) and a Joint Session by Eastern Region Co-Ordinators for Coaching. Race Training. Windsurfing and Race Management. The Sports Council's Role: This talk was given by Rosie Mayglothling. Senior Development Officer of the ‘English’ Sports Council, On Ist January “97 the “GB° Sports Council was divided into two parts - ‘UK’ and ‘English’. A more corporate approach would be applied across the country in order to remove inconsistencies between the former Regions. She stressed that very large sums of money were now being put into Sport for both Capital and Revenue projects. and that the driving force was the achievement of success at the national and world levels. i.e. More Medals! A number of sports had been awarded ‘priority’ status and sailing was amongst them. Regional and local coaches would be funded to help identify and develop talent from an early age. Also Sports Services teams would be set up for Priority Sports. Each Region and the Club needs to analyse and plan for the identification. training and development of the talent within its ranks. The aim is to take the sport forward at Club level. The organisation is in place and money is available. The RYA Youth Training Scheme has been achieving good results. e.g. Olympics and World Youth Championships, but further development is possible. Legal Matters: This talk was given by Edmund Wheelan. Manager of the RYA Legal and General Services Dept. He first outlined the work of the Department in monitoring and searching for any legislation which could unfavourably affect sailing. Legislators range from the UN. EU & UK Government. through to the local Council or Harbour Master. He stressed the point previously made that more money than ever before was available to Sailing Clubs - “Every Honorary Club Secretary should become a ‘Serial Begging Letter’ Writer.” He advertised publication G13/95 - ‘Round the Red Tape’ and advised Clubs to fight for a reduction in Rating Valuation and to apply for Discretionary Rate Relief. Councils claim back from the Government 75% of any relief given. He spoke also of concerns expressed by Race Officers and other Club Officers over their liability in case of accidents during a race. Participants are still responsible for their own actions. They accept the risks, However anyone found ‘negligent’ may be liable for claims for damages. Clubs should ensure that all members are insured against such claims. He recommended the Policies offered by Fenchurch as being the best (but not the cheapest) available. Club Development: Keith Ellison, RYA Development Officer. defined Club development as “getting new members and keeping them’ and it required forward planning. He believed that the best way to attract new members was by means of Open Days (n.b. we have one scheduled for Sunday 25th May). He then made the following suggestions a) Promote event widely - invite local sports writers to the Club before the event to optimise publicity in local publications. b) Go to Local Authority Sailing Centres and Schools to invite anyone who has attended a course. but as vet has no Club application. c) Smarten up Club and ensure everything works. d) Meet at gate - take names and addresses. Welcome them. c) Take for a sail in suitable boat. Reef if windy - must not frighten them. at all costs. f) Talk to them and ask. *Would you like to join?” g) Keep in touch - invite to a Social event. h) Have clear policy on training. e.g. before or after joining. i) Try to attract small groups from Schools and Youth or Company Organisations. Jj) Talk to new members. keep up the welcome or they will drift away. k) Invite the new members and those who did not join to a Social event. On the last question of how to introduce new members and novices to Club Racing. he suggested No Racing Days when a treasure hunt could be organised (around the racing marks?) He spoke scathingly concerning expericnced racers who shout abuse at novices. In his opinion they should be told to go and sail elsewhere. As volunteers were harder to find. he advocated that Clubs should franchise out as many non-sailing based activities as possible or cmploy staff where this is practical.

Suitable Club boats should be available for beginners to use (or possibly hire). Some Clubs buy new ones and sell them off after a few seasons hopefully to new members. “New” would mean brand new or one of the unused boats littering the dinghy park. He concluded by stressing the need to plan ahead. and offered to visit Clubs in the area if there was sufficient interest to make the journey from Lancashire worth while. Lunch was taken with old friends Derek Baker and Stan Attans of Stone Sailing Club. Dinghy Handicap System: John Anstey, Chairman of the Portsmouth Yardstick Advisory Panel. gave a very lively discourse on the methodology and the limitations of the system. He strongly advocated that Clubs adopt local handicap which reflect the conditions pertaining on their own stretch of water. and take account of the relative skills of the participants. Scepticism abounded! New Racing Rules (1997-2000): This was the talk everyone was waiting for. Trevor Lewis is a ‘Class Act’. He is Vice Chairman of the RYA Racing Rules Committee. He bears an uncanny resemblance to our own ex-Commodore John Witter. has an encyclopaedic knowledge of the old and new rules which he can deliver with considerable wit and at a breathtaking speed. He began by showing the assembly a copy of the new mules book. which is now being distributed. one free copy per Club. Additional ones are available £5.50 per copy. You will be glad to hear that this new ‘simplified’ version of the rules contains more pages than the old one. Trevor has published an article giving his interpretation of the rule changes and used it as the basis for his talk. He has given permission for this to be published in this issue of Navigans PAGES 9-11. Everyone who participates in racing and race management should read his article in association with a copy of the new nules. In next month's issue of Navigans I will report on the remainder of the proceedings. and offer a few personal comments. Please make a note in your diaries for Wednesday 9th April, 7.30pm at the MASC. when it is planned to hold a New Rules and Race Management Appreciation evening. Make sure you bring this Navigans and your new ISAF Rule Book with you. Ron Greygoose ETIQUETTE FOR MEN - YACHTING Contributed to Navigans by Club \fember Af Silvey, Varuna Il. First published in 1901, the article applies to a style of Yachting not likely to be familiar to many MISC sailors, and belongs to a different age and from ours. It states rules of etiquette that I'd love to see us trving to practise in our hectic modern sailing and racing, has much that is good sense, and much that can only be amusing to the modern Club sailor... I can't resist publishing it all, as space permits, in a couple of Navigans editions. Dress As far as mere appearance is concerned the blue serge yachting suit is infinitely more becoming to a man than any other he may wear on board, or for the matter of that, ashore either. The others are a blue or black flannel pin-strip or xarey flannels. With these you may wear a yachting cap, which may be covered with white linen as a protection to the head: or a cloth cap, but the latter does not go well with a serge suit. Take an oilskin suit for rough weather. Two of the greatest essentials in any man’s outfit when asked on board a yacht are a cordial desire to be amiable under all conditions, and to be possessed of fit and proper foot covering. Your boots and shoes should be of brown or white leather with indiarubber soles it possible, red rubber (not black, which has a nasty habit of staining), or with leather soles, sewed. If the sole has any nails in it they should be brass, on no account iron or steel, as these rust when decks are wet and the rust comes off on the deck. Some owners are excessively faddy about their decks, so it possible have no nails at all. Lite on Board The great guiding rule is that on a yacht every one - host and guests - has an interest in the spotless appearance of everything. The cabin room 1s, at best, of course tar less than the room allowed to a guest in a house. The lite 1s luxury qualitied by a campaigner’s care to fold everything away, do everything in the least possible space, and submit to certain exigencies of the sea. CON (disse.

Of course if you choose to lie in your berth and take your chance of dressing in a lop of a sea, and snatching a biscuit for breakfast, vou may do so. But you cannot get up when you please, and then expect breakfast laid as formally as it would be ashore. Usually your host talks to his skipper over-night and arranges what to do and when to start if such and such a wind happens to be blowing. Then, if he is considerate, he comes and puts all the possibilities before you. In the morning vou are awakened and hear that such and such a wind is blowing, and in consequence the orogramme will be so and so. The essence of good manners on board a yacht is to accommodate yourself at short Y 7 notice to hese the conditions, accept the suddenly dictated routine, and give as little trouble as possible. HANDICAP FLEET NEWS There are two themes to this article: first. to encourage the Handicap Fleet to race. and second. to solicit help with race duties. Before tackling these themes can I. on behalf of the Fleet. congratulate Malcolm Gandy and Graham Richmond on winning the 1996 Kestrel Nationals. Racing: Last year the turnout in the Fleet races was pretty dismal and | guess | now have to encourage people to race. | did this exercise in Navigans some years ago which resulted in Navigans being livened up by letters from you explaining why some of you chose not to race, and exhorting the alternative pleasures of sailing. Nevertheless. there might have been other results since in one race that year there were 10 boats competing against each other. | will put my argument to you again and hope for new miracles. And why not race? OK. so some of you like pottering around exploring creeks and things. or perhaps vou don’t have the competitive urge (Yes. I suppose I was being provocative!) But consider some of the advantages of racing. First you can go out in all weathers and have the comfort of knowing that the race box is keeping an eye on you and there are two safely boats out there if you do get into trouble. It’s exciting sailing in conditions you might otherwise have avoided. It's fun trying to get the best out of your boat. playing with spinnakers and experimenting with the trim of your boat. It’s fun trying to find the best course. allowing for wind and tide. It’s fun being out on the water with other boats and you can learn a lot about sailing when you discuss the race afterwards. So why not join in the racing and make friends with your fellow sailors” Handicap Fleet Duties: Now to my second theme. Some of you have received a Ictter from me on this matter already. The letter was aimed at both racers and non-racers. but new members will not have seen it and others might care to read what | said. So. again with my cut and pasting skills. I finish off this article with what that letter said: I have been asked by our Sailing Committee Secretary to ask if you or your crew are willing to help with race duties during the vear. The possible roles are: Race Officer Jack B Helm RIB Helm Race Officer Assistant Jack B Crew RIB Crew Normally these duties are done by those who would otherwise be racing. Whether or not you race. are you willing to help in any of these roles? Doing these duties is usually very interesting and pleasurable but. unfortunately. the racers would rather be racing! The Jack B and RIB helms need to have had appropriate training which is available from time to time. so let us know if you are interested. The Jack B and RIB crews are required to go into the water. if needed. to help sailors in distress. but this is not normally necessary. The Race Officer needs to know what to do and training should be available in the near future - if you are interested.....! The Sailing Sub-Committee is hoping to form a “Race Management Team’ that will be collectively responsible for running the Race Box. This Team would between them do the Race Box duties. The Race Box needs to be manned by two or three people. The Team would almost certainly be non-racers. They need not even be sailors! A Navigans article (December *96) Suggested a possible Team of 9. Perhaps the non-sailing partners of racers might be interested? Full training will be given. If you or anyone are interested or willing to do any of these above duties. please would you contact myself or one of the following: Clive Shenton Rear Commodore [redacted] John Salmon Sailing Sub-Committee Secretary [redacted] Wishing you a good season's sailing. START OF SEASON SAFETY REMINDERS: ADDERS: In April it is timely to caution members (who should remind any children they bring to the Club) that at this time of year they might sometimes come across an adder lying in the sun. often concealed in long grass. Please be careful where you walk and try not to disturb the animal which is harmless if left alone. THE SCRUBBING POST is not a safe place for children to play on at any time. Members please ensure that any children you bring to the Club keep off the Scrubbing Post. THE RIVER IS COLD for many months into the Sailing Season. even on apparently warm sunny days. Though Support Boats are out during all Club Races. it may happen that for some reason vou can’t be picked up quickly after a capsize. It is important that you take measures before you leave the shore that would delay the onset of hypothermia. The following advice has been offered in Navigans in past vears: : 1. Wear adequate clothing. i.c. Wet Suit/Dry Suit etc. and Buoyancy Aid. _ 2. Make sure your boat and its gear are sound. 3. Ensure Personal Buoyancy and the Boat’s Buoyancy are both adequate. ‘4. If you are inexperienced, either in sailing or in our sailing area. please ask advice from other experienced helms. ‘sa If you find yourself beginning to feel cold and tired while sailing. return to shore straightaway. rather than wait until vou are too cold to think rationally. Annee nee nese eae eee ea eee ennn nesses sansnnnneeseeseeneeeeeesee ed IN ROUGH WEATHER: If Club Racing goes ahead in windy conditions this does not necessarily imply that it is safe to go afloat. Some very experienced helms and crews may be well able to cope with that day's conditions but less experienced sailors could have a difficult and uncomfortable time. So please remember that even though Support Boats are there for Club Races. you should aim to be entirely self-sufficient. sail within your limitations. and remember on all occasions that your decision to go afloat. whether to race or to potter. is always made on your own responsibility, Ed. New radio regulation starting in February 1999 will propose the removal of CH16 as the general calling channel and restrict its use to distress only. For “the foreseeable future’ HM Coastguard will continue to monitor the channel. so non-GMDSS-equipped vessels can still make initial distress calls on CH 16 without having to use digital CH70. This still leaves unanswered the problem of a calling frequency for general use after February 1999. In December 1997 the UK will propose to the World Radio Conference that CH16 remains a calling frequency but there is considerable opposition to this from many countries.

GMDSS MPT 1279. The new standard for VHF radios with Digital Selective Calling (DSC) devices for vessels installing GMDS has received approval. Ron Greygoose ETIQUETTE FOR MEN - YACHTING - 1901 continued from last Navigans. Dinner Dress On some big yachts (mostly steam yachts) the men dress for dinner when at anchor in harbour. But a sounder rule is a dark blue suit for dinner at sea or at anchor. In small yachts - anything under a hundred tons - you would not dream of putting on a dress suit. In fact is better not to under any circumstances. but you must of course be guided by the rules of your host. Of course it often happens at sea that no proper dinner can be served at all. and even if it be managed the state of the weather will prevent any change of dress. The Helm Do not interfere with the skipper. Do not. even if you fancy yourself. offer to take the helm unless the wind be steady. and from the skipper’s manner you are pretty sure he will not mind. Bear a hand if vou see that you can be of service. but ask first. But. unless the yacht is being worked by a “Corinthian” crew (/.c. an amateur crew), the supposition is that the paid hands will be equal to their work. Tact Life on board a yacht is by necessity - the whole menage being packed into so small a space - one that calls for tact. Do not blunder all over the ship in the early hours when folks are dressing. You will be awakened perhaps at 6.30 by the men scrubbing the decks overhead - early to bed and early to rise on board. - if you wish a cold bath go up. not too late after they have done scrubbing. and take a tub cither by a swim overboard or by Stripping and asking one of the crew to douche you with a bucket. There is no bath so delicious. ~ The crew may have begun already to polish the brasswork. so take your stand at a place where the splashing will not interfere with them. and sce also that vou are not near any open skylight through which the water can make its way into cabins below. The bath over. remember to wrap up sufficiently before descending to your own cabin to dress. for there is only one stairway in the ship. that is to say only one which you and your host and fellow guests can use. Therefore it is advisable to tumble out for this little treat as early as possible. and before the ladies have left their cabins . Ladies’ cabins usually have a bath sunk in the floor. so have some men’s cabins. and sometimes you may have access to a real bathroom on board. In these cases of course the above does not apply. The Crew Remember that the crew like their privacy. and respect it. Let your walk forward be bounded by the mainmast in a cutter or yvawl. or a little beyond. and by the foremast in a schooner yacht. Don’t stare down the forecastle hatchway. or thrust yourself into the bows of a ship where the crew are gathered and talking by themselves. Remember that they have far less space than you. A Common Dilemma If you feel sca-sick. and can remember such a detail. take up your position to leeward. The ship of course heels that way. and (what is most important) the wind there blows off the ship. This advice is obvious enough. but in nine cases out of ten the sea-sick tyro tries to climb up on the side of the ship facing the wind. as a shecp makes for the exposed hedge. This is not a pleasant subject. but the advice is necessary and many an owner as Well as guest will be thankful for it if it is followed. Be careful at sca not to lean your elbows on the table when dining. Yacht tables are swung so that they keep Ievel no matter how the yacht rolls. If vou lean on the table this adaptability is disturbed. and the glass and crockery may be upset. Do not be fussy or nervous. even in difficultics. Nothing in the world is so little likely to come to grief as a well-found vacht. Ensigns and Burgees (in 1901) A yacht should fly the burgee of the club its owner belongs to at its main-top mast head. Yaw! yachts and steam yachts at sea fly the ensign when the owner is on board. Cutter vachts and schooner vachts do not ordinarily fly the ensign at sca. but hoist it on an ensign-staff astern when in harbour and when the owner is on board. When a yacht is in harbour and waiting for the owner to come on board she flies the burgee as usual. but the ensign is hoisted as the owner steps on board. Only yachts belonging to the Royal Yacht Squadron and above a certain tonnage are allowed to fly the White Ensign of His Majesty's Navy.

2, Members of certain royal yacht clubs (e.g. the Royal Thames Yacht Club. the Royal London Yacht Club. and the Royal Western Yacht Club) are allowed to fly the Blue Ensign. Other clubs fly the Red Ensign. But even some royal clubs choose to fly this. with or without their distinguishing badge in the “fly” (e.g. the Royal Victoria Yacht Club. the Royal Yorkshire Yacht Club), Flags must be hoisted at 8am and hauled down at sunset. It is good form. if you belong to several clubs and enter the harbour of one you belong to. to hoist that club’s flag. even though it be not the flag of the club you are most proud to belong to. and to wear that flag during your stay in port. Flag officers of a club do not carry a burgee but a swallow-tail flag. The commodore’s is plain. the vice-commodore’s has one ball. the rear-commodore’s two balls. If vou belong to a club and pass a yacht which. by its swallow-tail. tells you that it belongs to a flag-officer of that club. it is good form to dip your own burgee three times. whereupon he will acknowledge the salute by dipping in return. In steering a boat up alongside a yacht do not go straight for the steps or ladder. but take the boat up with a sweeping curve. much as a coachman drives up to a front door when he has plenty of room. The Essence of Good Manners Apart from these fidgety little points. with which a guest on board will have nothing to do. the essence of good manners on shipboard is. first. good comradeship and a willingness to accommodate yourself to a life liable to be directed by the weather: and second. unselfish resolve to take up as little room as possible. make as little fuss. and give others as much privacy as you can manage. 10, Historical Titbit Most of us are clued up enough to know the most common mainsail rig these days is known as ‘Bermudan’. Our high flyers may Even be aware that this same system is alternatively known as “Marconi Rig’ in some parts of the world. What is probably not universally known is how or why. The following explanation is not only logical but was lifted from an old encyclopaedia. so must be close to the facts! Apparently the earliest Marconi radio aerials (very high) were held upright with a system of wires called (you've guessed it) “shrouds” and the assembly was called Marconi Rigging! It was later applied to the support system of the higher aspect triangular mainsails being developed for 20th century sailing craft (particularly racers) and hence the name. Now for the homework question: (Editor will do the marking) Given that a spritsail is held up with a sprit. a gaffsail is held up with a gaff. and a lugsail is not held up with a lug. how did the more common name “bermudan’ which we all use replace the name ‘Marconi’ in the sailing boat context? Commodores Notes. Yes folks I am still around but still very busy at work. We have a new boss who is beginning to use his new broom and since I still have a mortgage to pay off I am unable to afford the luxury of stopping work. In effect this means not a lot of sailing during 1997, yet again! However I am still working to further the interests of Club Members behind the scenes. The Main Committee has approved a request from the East Coast Piers Race Committee to support the Cirdan Trust in 1997. This is a locally based sailing charity which gives disadvantaged youngsters the opportunity to experience the joys of sailing. They operate out of Maldon with three boats, Queen Galadriel, Xylonite and Duet. You will see more of Xylonite at the Piers Race since she will be the committee boat for the start as well as offering trips for spectators down river during the Piers Race. You will be aware that there were one or two problems arising from Camping Fortnight in 1996. Main Committee has agreed that there should be a designated site for those members who leave their cars on site when they are away on cruises. This is shown on this sketch map and is the eastern end of the Cat field. It should be roped off and signed before long. Cruiser owners, please note. The problems arising during the second half of camping fortnight have been discussed by the Main Committee and the following proposal was agreed unanimously. All members who attend camping fortnight will be asked to accept a Code of Conduct when booking. Essentially this will mean that members agree to behave with due consideration for everyone who uses the Club. Prior to Camping Fortnight, the Main Committee should have the name(s) of the person(s) who agree to act as key holders and supervise the site and bar to ensure they are being used in an acceptable manner. It is likely that the terms of the Bar License will change in the near future so that a designated member of the club becomes the Licensee. In any case unless suitable people agree to supervise the site and the bar during camping fortnight the bar will not open.
