6. Marconi Sailing Club Open Day - 25th May 1997 - 10am - 4pm This will be an opportunity for all comers to try out the sailing we have on offer at Stansgate. There will be a reception at the gate to welcome arrivals; talks given; visitors will be shown round the site by Club Officers; sailing trips organised with the loan of essential sailing gear wherever possible. The usual Galley will be in operation, with free teas, coffees and soft drinks on offer. On the last page of Navigans is a poster giving full details, and if any Members are able to place one on a Noticeboard, perhaps at their place of work, it would be helpful to spread the word as widely as possible. Please see below for John Salmon’s request for Helms and their Boats to participate, and for the loan of any spare buoyancy aids and clothing for visitors who may not be equipped for going afloat. I hope the weather will be kind to us allowing the sailing of a variety of craft to be sampled. Ed. BOATS FOR OPEN DAY At the Club Open Day on 25th May we would like to offer visitors the opportunity to sail on the Blackwater under the guidance of competent helms/boatowners. If you are prepared to make yourself and your boat available for this purpose please let me know as soon as possible. Wayfarers, Wanderers, or fairly stable dayboats are clearly very suitable for the purpose. but, depending on the weather, other types of boat may also be suitable so don’t be shy. Some Catamarans would also be desirable. This is an opportunity to instil into others some of the joy of sailing at our Club and possibly to increase our membership so your help will be worthwhile and most appreciated. I would also like to hear from anyone who could lend sailing clothing and buoyancy aids for use of visitors on this occasion. [redacted] LEARNING TO SAIL & ACQUIRING MORE ADVANCED SKILLS When you belong to a sailing club such as ours you can learn all about sailing with time and practice and the support and advice of fellow members. If you would like a course on sailing, either basic or more advanced, you can do so on our own river at Bradwell Waterside. Bradwell Environmental & Outdoor Education Centre (calling it ‘Bradwell Sailing Centre’ saves time) is run by Essex County Council Community Education. One-day. weekend and mid-week courses are available. (I believe the minimum age for residential courses is usually 13, but worth checking this with the centre.) Adults as well as young people are catered for, and can take part in the courses either to gain certificates or just to participate in sailing - learning as they go without the feeling of pressure - under the care of experts. Some of the courses available in 1996 were: RYA Shorebased: Dayskipper. Yachtmaster. RYA Practical: Competent Crew. Dayskipper. Coastal Skipper RYA Dinghy Levels 1.2.3.5 Instructor RYA Inland Waterways Helmsmans Course RYA VHF Course RYA ICC Certificate of Competence RYA Powerboat Levels 1.2. Safety Boat - 2 day course. Advanced & Instructor Courses. RYA Small Craft First Aid RYA Diesel Engine Course - useful for Cruiser owners. Canoeing and Windsurfing also available. The centre's Sigma 33 cruising yacht “Brigantes’ is used for RYA Practical Courses and also Taster Courses - weekend or day sailing within the sheltered Blackwater Estuary for the beginner in sailing. or further afield for the more experienced. Boat comes with a professional skipper and takes a maximum of 5 additional people. Full details of courses and prices available from Bradwell Environmental & Outdoor Education Centre. Bradwell Waterside. Southminster. Essex. CMO 7QY. Tel. 01621-776256 or Fax 01621-776378. The centre can be found by following the road from the Club to Bradwell Waterside (passing the Bradwell Marina entrance) and you ll find it on your left. behind Bradwell Quay Yacht Club. shortly before the road rises over the sea wall. Jenny and David (Ball). and other Cadets of their generation. have learned many of their skills at Bradwell. and they have done some teaching there. both expericnces they have enjoyed. Just as important, Mum and Dad found the costs of courses quite reasonable. Ed.

Historical Titbit I was most interested in Ron Phillips” historical titbit. My records seem to imply that since the turn of the century yachtsmen on both sides of the Atlantic had been experimenting with a new rig that would eventually replace the traditional gaff rigged topsail and mainsail, which had a heavy spar. clumsy mast rings and bulky mast attachments, with a single triangular sail that rose straight to the top of the mast. The British called this new arrangement a Bermuda rig because a similar one had been in use on that island for two centuries. In America it was called the Marconi rig because of the many shrouds needed to stay the new mast made it resemble a transmitting tower used by Marconi the Italian inventor of Wireless Telegraphy. A large jib overlapping the mainsail was later added to the new rig, and since it was first used in a regatta off Genoa in 1927 it became known as a genoa. It eventually got the nickname Jenny. The new rig found its finest application in the J” class boats with a 75 - 87 foot water line, of which it seems only 10 boats were ever constructed. and by 1940, economic conditions and I suppose the war made them obsolescent. Derek Kirby. CRUISER COMMENTS The last of this year’s winter meetings was held at MASC on Thursday 20th March during which this year’s Flotilla Cruising events were discussed. together with the proposals for this year’s Cruiser Chase Events. There is one minor change to the Burnham Shakedown Cruise due to be held on weekend 24/25/26 May. in that arrangements have been made for us to attend an informal Dinner Dance at the Royal Burnham Yacht Club at a cost of about £9 per head as opposed to a meal in the Crouch Yacht Club who were offering a choice of meals at £15.50. £17.00, and £18.00 per head. Again I must stress the Dinner Dance at the Royal Burnham is informal and that casual dress is acceptable - no need to wear jackets and ties. I would also mention that members of Hoo Yacht Club will also be there having sailed round from the River Medway, so there is a chance to meet some kindred spirits. We will by now have had our Fitting Out supper at MSC, therefore in anticipation may I thank Mark Fletcher and his helpers for a most enjoyable evening. We are indeed lucky to have his services. The Cruiser Launching List is now up on the board at MSC. I wish you all a successful and trouble free launch coupled, of course, with an excellent sailing season. Whilst on the subject of launching. may I remind you to be considerate when leaving your car in the Cruiser Park whilst launching is in progress. Remember, boats and trailers are on the move and there is nothing more frustrating and dangerous than trying to manoeuvre round parked cars. If you are afloat and going out to your boat. leave your car in the Car Park, please. Derek Kirby. Cruiser Fleet Captain. (Ed’s Note re Cruiser Car Parking in the run up to Camping Fortnight: This year we hope to avoid the annual problem where a Camper arrives at his allocated spot at the Club to find a car parked, quite legitimately, on it. It is proposed to set aside an area where Cruiser cars may be placed at this time, clear of the usual camping plots. Please see Commodore’s Notes on Page 5, with sketch map of the site showing the usual camping areas and the proposed ‘long term’ car park area for these two weeks. Camping starts on Saturday 2nd August this year and it would be helpful if all parked cars that are going to still be there that morning were placed in the special area.)

Commodore's notes. Open Day may well have happened by the time you read these words and I would to thank a number of people on members’ behalf. The members who are on the Sailing Sub Committee will have done a great deal in organising and running the event. thank you all. Whilst it is invidious to single out individuals I feel it is only right and proper to mention Margaret Yeoman who took on the job of co-ordinating the publicity for the event. At the last Main committee meeting Margaret detailed what she had done, who she had contacted, where posters had been displayed, the list went on and on! If nobody turns up then it certainly will not be for lack of publicity. On behalf of the club, a big thank you Margaret. As I mentioned last month, unless there are members who are prepared to take on the role of “Supervisor of the Day’ the bar(s) will not open for the sale of drink. The Main Committee have stated that they must see a list of names of people who are prepared to supervise the site on a day to day basis prior to camping fortnight starting. The named person(s) will be a ‘key holder’ for the day(s) he or she is prepared to do. The named person will be on site and hold the ‘key’ for access to the key box in the bar and be responsible for the orderly running of the bar(s) for the day. This named person will have the nght to close the bar when he or she needs or wishes to. This means that he or she does not have to stay up to all hours to keep the bar open for one or two folk! He or she will not be entitled to hand over that responsibility to a third party. I hope that this procedure will lead to a satisfactory time for all club members. If you are going to be at camping fortnight and would like to be a Supervisor of the Day please contact Pat Black or myself. The Main Committee accepted the following code of practice for Camping Fortnight. See you on the water. Colin Kidner. CAMPING FORTNIGHT CODE OF PRACTICE. Introduction. If club members and their families who are camping behave with consideration and courtesy towards all club members then the problems which occur should be minimal. Remember the Club belongs to all club members and is run for everyone's enjoyment. 1. Do you know who is the Supervisor of the Day? Z. Keep your pitch clean and tidy. 3. When you exercise your dog please “poop scoop’ after your dog and dispose the poop where others are not likely to step in the mess. 6. Dart 15 News Dart 15 Open Meeting - 19th & 20th April 1997 - at Marconi Sailing Club. Extract from Yachts and Yachting. May 1997: Perfect Dart 15 weather hit Marconi SC on April 19th-20th with a steady strong wind sorting out the good sailors from the brilliant ones. Twenty-seven boats turned up at this popular venue from clubs from North, South, East and West. Young and older, ladies and gentlemen, all pitted their skills and wits to compete on equal terms on a variety of testing courses. — The competitors in the first race proved too keen and a general recall encouraged a concentration of the mind. However, once off there was an exciting fetch to A mark - some competitors enjoyed it so much that they went sightseeing to Stone andfound themselves rather off course. With a building wind there were a number of thrills and spills, with some particularly exciting downwind legs with big waves - a shock for some of our reservoir enthusiasts. At the front were Bob Carter, and local men Peter Tovey and Willie Pitcairn. The wind and waves got even bigger and a number of retirements occurred but the afternoon race was close and exciting with some very experienced sailors surprising themselves with capsizes and quick recoveries. Nick Dewhirst proved too fast to catch, closely followed by Andy Jeffries and Barrie Hoggardfrom Beaver. The eagerly awaited long distance course took competitors around Osea and Northey Islands. This proved a tactically testing course with shifting winds and long reaches and beats. Stamina was high on the list of requirements and muscle man Paul Frost was closely followed by Tim Dieu de Bellefontaine, with three seconds separating them on the line. Hoggard came third. All to play for in the fourth race. With tide pushing over a start line there was much excitement on another recall - a short race followed, with an arrow shaped course and the first ten positions changing hands with surprising regularity on the last beat. Carter kept his head and took line honours followed by Peter Tovey and Kevin Kirby (MSC). Overall Results: Ist: Bob Carter (Grafham Water SC), 2nd: Peter Tovey (Marconi SC) 3rd: Nick Dewhirst (Whitstable YC), 4th: Willie Pitcairn (MSC), Sth: Paul Frost (Grafham Water SC). Many Thanks to Hillary Dieu de Bellefontaine for the write-up. Roger and Kathleen Smith did an excellent job as Race Officer and Assistant Race Officer, shortly followed by Bob Anderson as a good marksman with the cannons. We were also very grateful to Harlow Sub Aqua Club for providing rescue cover for Sunday racing, including the long distance race. Lastly thanks to my wife Heather, and my children Rebecca and James for manning the race reception all weekend. Peter Tovey, Dart 15 Fleet Captain PS: Thanks to Colin Kidner (Commodore) for stepping in at the last minute to be OOD on Sunday and giving out the prizes. 8. CRUISER COMMENTS = Covering this and next edition of Navigans which is why it is so long! Firstly, may I say thank you to those members who responded to the request to have eye bolts fitted to their trailers, and to Murray Bates for organising the exercise. There are one or two members who have undertaken to fit towing eyes themselves - this must be done before launching, and I would mention that the large shackle used previously is no longer available. Due to the May Bank Holiday it is possible that delivery of your Navigans may be delayed, therefore what I am about to say regarding the 24th-26th May Shakedown Cruise to Burnham may be a bit late. However, details were discussed at the last Cruiser Meeting and referred to in previous editions of Navigans. Unfortunately, Doreen and I are off to St Katherines with our three grandsons that weekend so we will not be with you, other than sailing with you as far as the Spitway. But no need to worry, Malcolm and Margaret Yeoman will be looking after you so any queries to them please. In the meantime a notice has been placed on the Club Notice Board requesting details of those requiring a berth at Burnham Yacht Harbour, also numbers wishing to attend the informal Dinner Dance at the Royal Burnham Yacht Club - cost £9.50 per head. Members of both Hoo Ness and Medway Yacht Clubs will also be there so it should be a great night. I am only sorry Doreen and I will miss it. Have a nice time! Any vacant moorings for visitors on weekend 14th/15th June? On the social side we have two busy weekends in June. On the weekend 14th/15th June we are hosting members of the Polynesian Catamaran Association of whom our own Dave Barker is the sailing secretary. At the same time members from Walton will be joining us in the course of their 24 hour endurance sail in aid of the RNLI and Walton Lifeboat. They expect to bring between 10-15 cruisers which, together with their road party, could account for 60 people. Quite a party! It is intended to hold a Bar B Q at the Club to which both groups and MSC Cruiser members are invited (bring your own food for the Bar B Q). Naturally the Dell Bar will be open. Since it is unlikely we will have sufficient moorings available for all visiting yachts, most will probably anchor off Osea Island and we hope to organise a trot boat to ferry back and forth those who do not have dinghies . Ifany Club Members are planning to be away during this period, it would be greatly appreciated if they could make their moorings available by letting me know. Don’t worry if you have to leave your dinghy on the mooring, it will be looked after. Just to make it more interesting, I notice the Blackwater Barge and Smack Race is scheduled for 14th June. On the following weekend, 21st/22nd June, the Cruiser Fleet plan to hold a ‘Summer Solstice’ get together at the Club on Saturday 21st. commencing 18.30hrs. There is some interesting entertainment being arranged. plus a Bar B Q for which there will be a nominal charge of £5 per head and of course the Dell Bar will be open. I would mention that whilst this is being run by members of the Cruiser Fleet, all MSC Members are invited. With regard to the catering, it would help if those wishing to attend could let any one of the following know, we do not want to under cater. nor do we want to go over the top - thanks. Murray Bates. Then it is hoped to construct a permanent Bar B Q on the concrete base left by the old shed. Work is also in hand to construct a sectional garage next to the mast cabin adjacent to the Cruiser Park in which will be stored the cruiser paraphernalia normally stored in garage number 5 which will then be vacated by the Cruiser Fleet. In the past the positions of No.1 buoy has varied slightly on each occasion that it hasbeen removed and replaced. ‘i Last year it was upriver from our startline and dried out at low water, making entry into Goldhanger Creeks a ‘hit and miss” affair. This season, No.1 is positioned several hundred metres further down river. This location is so different from previous experience that I queried the position with Nigel Harmer the River Bailiff. A somewhat exasperated Nigel assured me that it had been placed in the correct position as shown on Admiralty Chart 3741 (1995) and that he had recently checked the position. In order to be more sure of our facts Peter Clayton and Tony Ferguson volunteered to measure the position of No.1 buoy using both GPS and shore bearings. Surprise. surprise! Guess what? No. 1 buoy is positioned exactly as shown on the chart. Full marks. Nigel (but you said that last year). No.1 buoy is located at 51° 43°.43N..0° 48°.12E. Commodores Notes. If you were at the Club during the ‘Open Day’ you would have been impressed by the incredible atmosphere. Some fifty one ‘sets’ of visitors came through the gate during the day. Whilst some were there for a day out and a ride on a boat, most of the visitors appeared to be genuinely interested in joining the club. Without exception they commented on the friendly and informative welcome they received. They were all impressed with the site and the facilities of the club. Six new members signed up on the day and I feel confident that we can expect about another ten applications during the coming weeks. It was a team effort which resulted in such a successful day. My special thanks go to Sue Shenton who gave Clive a ‘pink pass’ on their wedding anniversary! A big thank you to every one who helped out in one way or another. See you on the water. Colin. CRUISER INTEREST Oil Pressure Alarm The Engine Display Panel for our boatis at our feet!! If the oil pressure warning light were to come on, thereis no way that we would see it in the seconds, that I am told, it would take the engine to seize! The Volvo Alarm Panel costs the earth. My solutionis to connect a Sounder directly across the oil warning light. A suitable one can be obtained from Tandy’s for about £7. (Piezo Electric Siren 49-489.) Don’t use the cheaper buzzers, they're not man enough. When switching on the engine electrics, the alarm sounds until the engine is started and the oil pressure is up. When shutting down the engine. as the oil pressure drops, it reminds you to switch the electrics off! Therefore, as with all proper alarms, it is self checking. Things That Stick Up....Antennae If you are a high tech Marconi person, go and put the kettle on!! This is not for you. As a Radio Amateur I am well aware that antennas are a mystic art, even more so to sailors who just want to sail. Fortunately, we are able to purchase ready made marine antennas ready to “stick up”. But, there’s more to it than that! Fitting. 1. Fit as high as possible. The range for a VHF antenna atop of, say, a 10 metre mast, in open sea should be about 27 miles. At 2 metres it’s about 9 miles! (Refer to Dipping Distances). 2. No tight bends or kinks in the cable. The piece of “wire” attached to the aerial when purchased is a co-axial transmission line and as such depends on the relationship of the centre conductor to the concentric copper braid and must not be bent on too tight a radius and must not be kinked. Depending on the quality of the cable, a 1” radius is getting too small. Any distortion will look like a short circuit to the RF signals. 3. Always use good quality connectors at the base of the mast. A pair of “N” connectors is recommended....they are not cheap but are the only “watertight” ones. fit a plastic boot and smear with silicone grease. Don’t cut the cable very short....push some of it back into the mast....if you need to remake the cable later you will probably have to cut off at least 4° due to corrosion. Don’t leave a large loopin free space....crews are notoriously clumsy! If you haven’t fitted connectors before find someone who has (a Marconi fitter or Radio Amateur?) Testing. Receivewise at the Club you should be able to hear clearly Port of London Control and Thames traffic on Ch.12. Most traffic around high tide. This doesn’t prove the antenna and cable. The only proper way to test is by using a VSWR Bridge. This samples the forward power and the reflected power and gives the result as a ratio. Ideally this should be close to 1.1:1 but anything less than 2:1 is acceptable. Measuring DC resistance proves very little since a 10m piece of cable shorted at the far end could measure a fraction of an ohm...not readable on an analogue meter. Notes: a) Sets are designed to give max power, 25 watts, with the alternator running at 13.8 volts. expect only 20 Watts from a fully charged battery without the alternator. b) Current on transmit could bein region of 5-6 amps so ensure 12volt supply leads are stout and all connections really good preferably straight back to the battery terminals without joins, but with an in-line fuse. If connections are not good there will be loss of power: sparking can ignite any Calor or battery gases! Other Antennas. GPS and Decca antennas use similar cable which should be treated as above. However they are usually “active” antennas....they have an amplifier inside them. These are powered by “phantomingTM a DC voltage up the cable so great care must be taken to avoid any short circuits. Story. Having the right test equipment I always check out my installation before launching each year. Testing a friend’s rig I found that virtually no RF was getting beyond the deck connector. On removal of the plastic boot from the connector I was confronted with a cable resembling a curly cord complete with a kink. I cut off the offending 4” of cable and refitted the plug. Measured results were really good and were confirmed by a radio check with the coastguard. I rest my case! Eric Lawley. “Pegasus”

The Main Committee has stated that they must see a list of names of people who are prepared to supervise the site on a day to day basis prior to camping fortnight starting. The named person(s) will be a ‘key holder’ for the day(s) he or she is prepared to do. This named person will have the right to close the bar when he or she needs or wishes to. This means that he or she does not have to stay up to all hours to keep the bar open for one or two folk! He or she will not be entitled to hand over that responsibility to a third party. Camping Application Form is in this Navigans. Remember to send s.a.e. with your form and payment to Hilary Ashley, Marconi Summer Camp, [redacted], Mayland, Chelmsford [redacted]. Camping fortnight is the time when the Club’s available space and facilities are being used to the full. If everyone on site follows the guidelines below it will enhance the enjoyment of all and reduce the workload on those volunteers who take it on themselves to try and keep everything running smoothly. Like you, they are on holiday and have also paid their camping fees. All these points have arisen over many years of camping experience at the Club. Code of Practice 1. Do you know who is the Supervisor of the Day? Please help when asked to volunteer for camping duties. Keep your own pitch clean and tidy and please help by keeping the site and Clubhouse tidy at all umes. Please put your refuse IN the skip, not BY it. (If the skip is full then take your refuse home where possible.) uw TVs. radios, and CD players should be played at a volume which will not disturb other campers. Please check with your neighbours that your volume setting is acceptable. 4, Ensure your laughter/talking is not causing a disturbance to your neighbours. ws Dogs should be kept on a lead at all times on the club site. When you exercise your dog please ‘poop scoop’ after your dog and dispose the poop where others are not likely to step in the mess. 6. Children must keep off the Scrubbing Post at all times (it’s not a safe play area), and must not climb on or interfere with property belonging to the Club or its Members. Parents should keep an eye at all times on the behaviour and safety of their own and guest children. Frequent checks should be made - they should not be left unsupervised for hours onend. Are they annoying other people by playing too near their caravan/tent? hs If you see people/children using members’ or Club property inappropriately please tell them to stop. If you feel you may be intimidated by the person(s), inform the Supervisor of the Day. 8. If you or any of your party break or damage property belonging to the club or a club member, it should be reported to the Supervisor of the Day. 9. Please leave the wash basins. WCs, changing rooms in a condition as you would want to find them. 10. Please leave Galley Clean and Tidy whenever you use it and never unplug fridge or other appliances that should be left on. Freezer/s might be available for campers’ use - provided they still work and we have the space to set them up. I don’t know if Mark’s Galley Service will operate again this year. Notices will go up when the time comes, and washing up facilities in the Galley will be available at times when the Galley Service is closed.

Camping Application Form is in this Navigans. Remember to send s.a.e. with your form and payment to Hilary Ashley, Marconi Summer Camp, [redacted], Mayland, Chelmsford [redacted]. Camping fortnight is the time when the Club’s available space and facilities are being used to the full. If everyone on site follows the guidelines below it will enhance the enjoyment of all and reduce the workload on those volunteers who take it on themselves to try and keep everything running smoothly. Like you, they are on holiday and have also paid their camping fees. All these points have arisen over many years of camping experience at the Club, Code of Practice: 1. Do you know who is the Supervisor of the Day? Please help when asked to volunteer for camping duties. Keep your own pitch clean and tidy and please help by keeping the site and Clubhouse tidy at all times. Please put your refuse IN the skip, not BY it. (If the skip is full then take your réfuse home where possible.) 3; TVs, radios, and CD players should be played at a volume which will not disturb other campers. Please check with your neighbours that your volume setting is acceptable. 4. Ensure your laughter/talking is not causing a disturbance to your neighbours. oh Dogs should be kept on a lead at all times on the club site. When you exercise your dog please ‘poop scoop’ after your dog and dispose the poop where others are not likely to step in the mess. 6. Children must keep off the Scrubbing Post at all times (it’s not a safe play area), and must not climb on or interfere with property belonging to the Club or its Members. Parents should keep an eye at all times on the behaviour and safety of their own and guest children. Frequent checks should be made - they should not be left unsupervised for hours onend. Are they annoying other people by playing too near their caravan/tent? 7: If you see people/children using members’ or Club property inappropriately please tell them to stop. If you feel you may be intimidated by the person(s), inform the Supervisor of the Day. 8. If you or any of your party break or damage property belonging to the club or a club member, it should be reported to the Supervisor of the Day. 9, Please leave the wash basins, WCs, changing rooms in a condition as you would want to find them. 10. Please leave Galley Clean and Tidy whenever you use it and never unplug fridge or other appliances that should be left on. Freezer/s might be available for campers’ use - provided they still work and we have the space to set them up. I don’t know if Mark’s Galley Service will operate again this year. Notices will go up when the time comes, and washing up facilities in the Galley will be available at times when the Galley Service is closed. On no actount should any wood be removed from the Cruiser Park. Even if it appears to be scrap- it isn’t!

CRUISER COMMENTS Having missed the July edition of Navigans due to being on holiday (although I noticed the Ed. ghosted a couple of comments from my June ramblings) the Ed’s got me on the run again looking for copy to cover August, September and early October! The year’s gone and IJ have hardly got my feet wet, apart from rain that is. Where to start? Oh, well, here goes. First may I say thank you to Malcolm and Margaret Yeoman for taking over the shakedown Cruise to Burnham. I was most impressed, listening to the VHF whilst on passage to St Katherine’s with the way Malcolm had got all the berths organised. I am sorry the function at the Royal Burnham was a bit noisy, no doubt the pros and cons of this venue for next year will be discussed at the end of year review at the Cruiser AGM. The fact that 19 boats attended says much for the choice of Burnham Yacht Harbour as a shakedown venue. . On weekend 14/15 June we hosted boats from the Polynesian Catamaran Association together with 6 Cruisers from Walton who were taking part in a 24 hour endurance event in aid of the RNLI. Eight boats were in fact on passage, however one had to return with engine trouble, causing another to return with it as escort. Both groups, together with some of our own members had a great get-together and Bar B Q at the Dell Bar. My thanks to all the helpers and those members who made their moorings available. Enough to say the Walton event was such a success a repeat next year is well on the cards. It may even become an annual event. Since we often enjoy the facilities of other Clubs it is nice to be able to reciprocate. Whilst I realise you may be reading this rather later than invisaged, I would like to draw your attention to the following chart amendments, just in case you have missed them. These were published in Macmillan 2nd Supplement to April 1997: Swin Spitway: 51 40 44N 01 04 81E Woodbridge Haven Buoy: 51 58 15N 01 23 90E Again just in case you are interested. BBC Essex transmit inshore broadcasts Mon-Fri at 0740 & 0840: Sat at 0657, 0757, 0857, 1205 & 1305. Sun 0657, 0757 & 0857. Our next Flotilla Cruise will be to Shotley Marina on August Bank Holiday weekend 23-25 August. Arrangments have been made with the Marina where it is anticipated most of us will arrive during the early afternoon. On Sunday evening a meal has been arranged in the ‘Shipwreck’* in fact I believe we are taking over the upper lounge and bar which has excellent views of the river. The meal will be: Starter: Melon Port Balls or Smoked Peppered Mackerel. Main Course: Carvery with choice of meats, potatoes fresh vegetables. Vegetarian meal available if required. Sweet: Choice of Blackcherry & Kirsch Gateaux with cream or Home made Fruit Crumble with Custard. Coffee and Mints. Cost £12 per head. A list will be placed on the Club Nitice Board nearer the date. Will those wishing to attend please indicate in spaces provided so Marina bookings and meals can be notified. P.S. SHOTLEY VISITORS: Please see Lock Guidance Notes in this Navigans; also please fill in the Shotley Marina Visitor form and send to Derek as soon as possible. For those able to take the rest of that week off, another trip to the River Deben and Woodbridge has been arranged. I have already made provision with the Tide Mill Yacht Harbour and, again, would those wishing to come along please signify on the list when it is on the noticeboard. The proposal at present is that we lock out of Shotley on Monday, stopping over at Ramsholt in the Deben on Monday night. Then up to Woodbridge on Tuesday, who knows, we may even get our Bar B Q in on the return trip at Prettyman’s Point before leaving the River Deben. Winter Laving Up. Since Ed’s asked for copy up to early October I suppose. reluctantly, I must turn my mind to this year’s winter lay-up. I notice at the time of writing there are some pallets stacked by the sea wall. Those of you who need pallets for your moorings had better lay claim to one before the campers use them for firewood. I will shortly be making up the Winter Storage Layout Plan, so please be advised spaces will only be allocated to those who have paid 1997/8 Winter Storage Fees. Space is at a premium and it is possible some reorganisation/reallocation of existing spaces may be necessary. Lastly, please do not ignore your trailer until lay-up time. A little maintenance now could save a lot of trouble later. Derek Kirby, Cruiser Fleet Captain *Ed’s Note: Very nice meals at the ‘Shipwreck’ at Shotley, but I wish the establishment had some other name! MIDSUMMER BARBECUE - CRUISER FLEET June 21st 1$97. This day dawned, or rather the situation at 0900 was, as any other day in June, windy and showery. Only extremely brave souls risked the violent gusts and put to sea, so there was Mona battling down the river under, it has to be said, rather reduced rig. On shore, activity centred around the tractor shed where strange things were happening. As the afternoon wore on the showers increased in intensity and one, witnessed from safety within the “Jolly Sailor” in Maldon almost washed the moored barges away! The reason for the activity at the Club was made clear that evening as, coming ashore in a lull from the weather, a delighful smell wafted across the water towards us from the tractor shed. No, it was not tractor au vin but the most mouth watering display of barbequed chicken, succulent sausages and a delicious assortment of salads. The evening was rounded off with a rowdy sing song led by Bob off Seachrain, ably assisted by birthday boy Dick Papworth (we won’t report his age). On behalf of everybody present I would like to thank Murray and Anne Bates and their band of helpers for the splendid food; Neil and Boo for managing to tend the bar; and Bob and Dick for the singing (not to mention Tambourine Lady Margaret Yeoman). SHOTLEY MARINA - Booking Form for Trip is on Page 8 * ’ m4 ' LOCK TRAFFIC CONTROL The lock is manned 24 hours a day enabling access to and from the marina at all states of the tide (although those vesscls who draw over 2 metres should always check first. in case of extreme low tides). TRALIGHT FFI CONTROL C Lock movements are generally controlled by Traffic Lights and boats are requcsted not to enter the lock against a Red Traffic Light unless specifically advised to do so by the duty lockmaster. BERTH ALLOCATION Berth allocation is normally conducted in the lock and a map showing the allocated berth is issued with other relevant Marina information. V.H.F COMMUNICATIONS Shotley marina operates on Channel 80 for general Marina Traffic Control. Channel 37 is also monitored for those vessels not fitted with Channel 80. Vessels are advised to monitor those channels whilst approaching the marina. locking through and whilst underway within the marina basin. This allows for instant communication between the tower and yourselves if and when required. MARINA APPROACHES The Lock is approached by passing through the Marker Posts positioned in the river Stour and procecding along the dredged channel to the Lock entrance using the Inogon Leading light as guidance. The marker posts are positioned 2.5 cables North West of the Ganges Buoy and are marked as follows: Port Hand - Yellow and Black post with an East Cardinal Topmark - Quick flash White cvery 5 seconds Starboard Hand = - Green post with Starboard Hand Topmark - Group flash (4) Green every 15 seconds. The Marker Posts are approximately 50 fect apart. INOGON LEADING LIGHT The Inogon Leading Light is situated on the starboard side of the Lock Entrance. When a vessel is on the correct line of approach in the Entrance Channel a vertical Black line is scen in the centre of an orange screen. Any deviation from the correct bearing will cause the black vertical line to change to arrows. Follow the arrows to come back to the correct line of approach.

10. LOCKING IN When approaching the Marker Posts it will be apparent whether or not the Lock is busy. A). If there is little or no other traffic and a green traffic light is being displayed then proceed to the Lock. if a red light is being displayed call the Lockmaster on the V.H.F. B). If a number of boats are waiting at the posts, join them and stem the tide to await your turn. Owners of particularly large or difficult boats to manoeuvre should call the Lockmaster on the V.H.F. on arrival. Specific instructions will be given as to when to enter the channel. Other vesscls should monitor the V.H.F.. however. it is generally not necessary to call unless specific information is required. On entering the lock be prepared to moor either side and move to the front of the lock. or as near to the next boat's stern as safety allows. Boats should be secured fore and aft by lines to the cleats on the floating fenders. LOCKING OUT A). If there is little or no-other trafficand a green traffic light is being displayed. procecd to the lock. Ifa red light is being displayed call the duty Lockmaster on the V.H.F. B). If the lock is busy then proceed to the waiting pontoon to await your turn. Owners of particularly large or difficult boats to manoeuvre, should call the Lockmaster on the V.HF. advising him of the boats size before leaving the berth. Specific instructions will be given as to when to Icave the berth. On entcring the Lock be prepared to moor either side and move to the front of the Lock . or as near to the next boat's stcrn as safety allows. Boats should be secured fore and aft by lincs to the cleats on the floating fenders. On proceeding from the Lock towards the Marker Posts at the end of the dredged channcl. the helmsperson should look behind him/her at the Inogon Leading light to ensure that the boat is kecping to the channcl. FREEFLOW Freeflow occurs at the time leading up to high water, and varies in length from a few minutes to one hour or more. In gencral. Spring tides have longer freeflow periods than Neap tides. However. the predicted time of Frecflow is dependent upon Lock movements during the previous 12 hours and are therefore difficult to accuratcly predict. Care should be taken when going through the Lock as there can be a considcrable current flowing in from the Harbour. It is necessary for some visiting boats to slow down or stop when entering to cnable the Lockmaster to allocate a berth. - ~< cs DEEP DRAUGHT YACHTS At low water springs owners with a draught in excess of 1.8 metres should contact the Lockimaster to check that there is sufficient water over the sill for them to safely enter the Lock. \marina\proceed\lockaids, wps

Commodore’s Notes. Life at work is still suffering form the Dearing Syndrome. Those in education will know what I’m talking about. To add to my problems we have another OFSTED inspection in November so there will be plenty of ‘bull’ going on between now and then! Whilst I didn’t sail in the Piers Race, I did have the pleasure of a ‘behind the scenes’ view of the event from the deck of Xylonite. Mike Duckmanton has decided to call it a day as chairman after three years in the job. Many thanks, Mike, for all your efforts and the team who support you. I also spent time talking to Libby Purves and Paul Hiney, the former came down to present prizes, as well as Nick Back from the Cirdan Trust. The event was a great success from my perspective and I know that the Cirdan Trust Committee are delighted with the support of Marconi Sailing Club. The money which will go to the Trust will be used to provide bursaries for deserving people and we will receive reports from these folk in future. If previous examples are anything to Zo by I am sure you will be happy with the change from Sailability. Watch this space. I understand Cadet week was a great success this year with over 70 young people participating. Thank you Charles, Chris and your team of helpers for all your efforts in making the week so worthwhile and such fun for those young people who participated. I have had only one report of poor behaviour during Camping Fortnight. The young man in question felt that going in anc out of windows instead of doors was acceptable and when challenged by a club member gave some ‘verbal abuse’ in return. I am sure you will agree with me that we can do without this sort of thing. The reliability of the galley service continues to exercise the Main Committee and we are trying to resolve the problem. I’m writing these notes at the Club watching the Solo Fleet competing in their Open Meeting. There are some 20 visitors and 7 club boats participating on a warm , sunny and breezy afternoon. There is nothing to beat * messing about on the river’, not that the Solo Fleet are, if you see what I mean. I may see you on the water. Colin. FLOODGATES - Reminder We are required to keep the Floodgates closed between Ist September and Ist May over winter each year (these dates have been permanently marked on the gates). This is to prevent the possibility of the higher tides more likely to occur at this time from flooding through the sea wall gap which has been left for our convenience. It is the responsibility of each and every Member to check at the end of the day before leaving the site that the Floodgates are properly closed. The Floodgates are not locked so no key is necessary to open or close them. On windy days make sure you open them up right back to the wall - they could be blown shut on your car as you drive through. Viewing the gate from the landward side, the left hand gate is bolted into a slot in the ground and is closed first. Turning the top handle anticlockwise lowers the bolt into the ground to close the gate. The right hand gate has a lever to secure it closed against the left hand one - this is where a little bit of muscle is required. Reversing these actions allows you to open the gate. Opening the right hand gate only gives enough room for a tender to pass through, but both gates need to be open to make enough room for a car. : at a Ed. EAST COAST PIERS RACE AND CADET WEEK. ~~ 7 I understand that Cadet Week was a successful and enjoyable event with a record attendance, and the East Coast Piers Race went very well. Hopefully I will have a report of all the news of interest from the two events in next Navigans. JACK B Jack B has kad its summer refit and I would like to thank all those who contributed their time and effort. In particular I would like to thank Murray Bates for cleaning the boat with his high pressure cleaner, Jenny and her team of varnish scrapers and sanders, Maureen for a lot of varnishing and polishing, and Geoff Josey for servicing the engine and repairing the sea water pump. The excellent weather and good teamwork ensured that Jack B was only out of the water for a few days. Belated thanks are also due for major work done on Jack B during last autumn/winter: Thanks to Geoff, as always. for maintaining the engine and to Mick Richardson for repairing some stripped threads in the engine bell housing. Peter Clayton and Murray Bates replaced the ageing propeller shaft seal with a new greasable unit. Stripping out parts which have been together for 10 years in a marine environment is a time consuming exercise, but the result was worth it. The rudder shaft seal and bearings required renewal in the winter. This turned out to be a fairly major undertaking and special thanks are due to Peter and Murray for carrying out the work and arranging for the manufacture of replacement items. The Club is indebted to all those people who carry out work in the background which is essential Pto the smooth running of Club equipment and dependent activities: _- Ray Ball. APPEAL TO DOG OWNERS This is a salutary tale of a nasty illness which has spoiled my summer, as I picked up the food poisoning bacteria ‘Campylobacter’ in the later part of June. I quote from the Information Booklet sent to me by the Local Health Authority when my doctor had to advise them that I had this illness. “Campylobacter Enteritis is not only associated with raw meat and poultry but infects pets. Around 50% of dogs excrete the bacteria in their faeces and as a result the animals’ coats become infected, and the infection passes to humans who stroke their pets.” I do not know howI became infected as I have known about this risk since a neighbour’s small son was blinded by the illness 30 years ago and I never handle animals without washing my hands afterwards. We have no pets at home. However, I do know that I ate “al fresco’ at the Club at the time that I must have contracted the disease, so the Club grounds have to be a possible source. I do, therefore, appeal to dog owners to follow the Club guidelines and keep their pets leashed so that they are aware of their movements, and please poop-scoop after them. It is not good enough to let them defecate on the shingle and hope the tide will wash it away. So, come on. Dog Lovers. we all know that theyre cuddly with heart-melting eyes, and it’s not their fault that they push their noses into some unsavoury places. Surely it’s worth a little extra care to make sure that your pet is not respnosible for someone being sick for a couple of months or, even worse, a child being disabled for life. Barbara Holdsworth

NEW MEMBERS. A warm welcome to the new Members who joined us in the summer - Peter Vines, Dart 15; Jeremy Richardson, Hornet; Eric Ferguson, Steven Gibson, Paul Pestell. BURNHAM WEEK People talk about “Burnham Week” but what really is it all about? If you have not “done the week” then really you don’t know what it is. I can tell you it is a wonderful combination of many aspects of life. It combines qualities such as skill, judgement, patience, nerve, brute strength, gentleness, co-ordination, co-operation, endless resources of energy, tact and diplomacy and, most important of all, to be able to consume vast quantities of alcoholic beverages until the early hours of the morning and recover by 0700in the morning. Burnham Week consists of eight days of racing, so this has to be repeated without the loss of concentration or energy reserves for this period cf time. If you reach the end of Burnham Week and you feel refreshed and fit, then I cesta that you ve not worked at it hard enough and can’t possibly have enjoyed it! _- Over two hundred boats of 30 differing classes with 5 minutes between start times took part this year.. All on the Crouch between Whittaker No.6 and Cliff Reach. You certainly need to know your Port from Starboard particularly when in the confined waters of the Roach on Low Water Springs. The Sailing is the No.1 for Burnham Week with many evening activities being organised by all the Clubs in the evening, where analysis of the day’s performance, celebrations and commiserations can result in an even poorer performance the following day. “Timari Two’ and “Helm’s Angel’, both cruisers from MSC, took part this season, unfortunately in the same class. Start lines were rather crowded as our Class 7 had up to 20 boats competing and on most days there were spinnaker runs out of the river to the ‘battleground’; the ‘battleground being the chosen area of the river for the day where we chased each other round courses of sausages and triangles with gay abandon until we ran for ‘home’, This occurred all week because West or South West winds meant beating in conditions so varied - from 2 or 3 knots to 35 knots of wind. One day we estimated 200 plus tacks trying to keep in the shallow water on the northerly bank. The biceps are now bulging well, but unfortunately after this day’s exercise the skin on the fingers had been worn away revealing several red looking divots that are just starting to heal over. You also have to be brave and bold anda little daft. On launching our ‘small’ kite in 30 knots of wind, the boat speed rose from 4 to 8.5 knots in about 0.5 seconds, but a weak fitting broke and let the pole pull upward, spinnaker now wildly out of control. A glance sideways revealed one of our opponents struggling as his spinnaker caused a violent broach and he lay flat on the water, motionless, for a few seconds. This was a 3'/> ton 28ft. cruiser, not some flimsy dinghy. We survived the week's racing however, having had to watch the fleet on Monday sail past us as we sat motionless, stuck on the mud by trying to tack in too shallow water! Alert III offered assistance but we hid with embarrassment, declining a tow! *Timari Two’ did not disgrace herself however. finishing third overall, having gained two ‘firsts’ and a trophy as well, Many thanks to our crew and especially Mike and Graham from ‘Seabrume’ who so kindly helped us survive the week. ‘Helm’s Angel’, crewed by a group of wild Scotsmen did very well with two ‘firsts’ and two ‘seconds’ and were duly awarded runner up cup. As I said earlier, Burnham Week is not all plain sailing. Evening activities diverse as Quiz Evenings. Mad Cow Disco, Guinness Night, Street Parties, Pimms Parties and, best of all, RBYC Fancy Dress “what you were wearing when the ship went down” were fantastic. I’m glad I’m back at work now this week. I nodded off today and woke up with a jolt as I dreamed of Burnham Week 1998. If you've never ‘done Burnham Week’ then make sure in 1998 that you “do it”! Derek Gardner

View from the Rear As we near the end of another season (didn't it go quickly?) I make a rare foray into print to thank a few hard working members and to ask for volunteers. You may not know that the Rear Commodore's job involves three committee meetings every month plus some others for Open Day Organisation and ECPR liaison. In addition to this commitment I had to take on the role of Safety Boat Co-ordinator and it is for this job that I seek a volunteer so I can "See more of the Family" next year. So what does it entail? The Safety Boat Co-ordinator's job is to schedule the crews for the Jack B and Rib. using the list of drivers and crews that I have. The Schedules are then published in Navigans. The next part of the job is maintaining and updating the schedules as inevitably people swap their duties with others on the list. You do not have to arrange the exchanges, only update the schedule. The Sailing Secretary then informs the Race Officer for the Day of the names of the crews and it is the RO's job to check their availability. The job does not necessarily involve attending Sailing Sub-Committee Meetings although it would be nice to see you if possible. If you would like to help me and the Club please phone me on [redacted] andI will give you more information. Now to the thanks. Firstly, thanks to all the drivers and crews of the Rescue Boats who turned out and did their duties without causing me further loss of hair. I appreciate your efforts. Next my thanks to the unsung heroes who keep the Rescue boats serviced and fuelled. Graham Jones on the Rib, Ray Ball on the Jack B and Dave Bladon who keeps the Rib fuel bunkers topped up. Thirdly. thanks to all the members of the Sailing Sub Committee for their regular attendance and contributions. The meetings were often long as we tried to make your sailing more enjoyable and better organised. Lastly I must single out one Sail-sub member for special thanks. Your Sailing Secretary, John Salmon has worked tirelessly and efficiently at his job. He has always sought to drive us onwards and upwards, never being afraid to criticise our current practices to provoke ideas and enthusiasm for improvement, and then working hard to implement the solutions. Many Thanks John. On a purely personal note I did little sailing last year, but what I did do was most enjoyable. I thought the Piers Race was the best one yet. and the welcome extended to the Tornados, Prindles and Nacras at Yaverland was memorable. Unfortunately, apart from a glorious second on the first day my performance was better forgotten. My aim is to get more sailing done next season. as | am still too young to take up golf. regardless of what my wife says. Have a good winter. and I look forward to seeing you all next season. Clive Shenton, Rear Commodore New Members: A warm welcome to the new members who have joined us recently. John Easton, Westerly Pageant, ‘Sea Gem’: Vincent Sullivan . Mirror; and J.R. Holliday. Solo Matters Our Solo Open Meeting took place on Sunday 7th September and was very successful. attracting 28 entries of which 17 were visitors. The weather was kind with a light but steady sailing breeze which held up well for the whole day. Marconi boats were just out of the prizes with John Salmon and Roger Smith in 7th and 8th positions respectively. Many thanks to all Club Members who helped in any way with the arrangements and a special thank you to the ladies who helped with the Galley at short notice. The Solo Training Day with James Hunt scheduled for Saturday 6th September. the day of the funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales, was cancelled. Hopefully another date can be arranged for a Training Day during next year’s sailing season. I have made arrangements for the Solo AGM to be held at the MASC, Beehive Lane. on Thursday 6th November, starting at 2000 hrs. Please let me know if you have any items you wish to be added to the agenda. Geoff Josey, Solo Fleet Captain, [redacted].

Helm of the Year 1997 - Tim Wallace After a few days of gale force winds, Saturday 11th October dawned bright and sunny with light winds. It was not to last - by mid morning it was raining and continued on and off all day. The weather did not dampen the competitive edge of the 5 helms: Howard Rogers. Handicap; Geoff Josey. Solo; Tim Wallace, Fast Cat: Mick Jones, Medium Cat: Brian Spencer, Dart 15. Five races were held in Toppers. Brian Spencer winning the first two. Race 3 was abendoned when the wind died to nothing. and Tim Wallace won Race 4. The outcome of the series was all down to the last race which Tim Wallace won and. with two second places. he is the Club’s Helm Of the Year 1997. Congratulations. Tim. Our thanks to the rescue drivers and crews who carried out their duties in the cold and rain and to Clive Shenton for arranging. collecting and returning the Toppers. and for helping in the Race Box. The highlight of this year’s cruising activities must have been the August Bank Holiday flotilla cruise to Shotley Marina and River Deben. Over the whole week a total of 30 Club Cruisers took part. 24 visiting Shotley Marina - some of which had to return home on the Monday - but these were replaced by others who joined us up to Woodbridge in the River Deben, resulting in 22 Cruisers being present. Seven boats got off to a flyer on the Friday, stopping overnight at Brightlingsea. the remainder Starting from various other points to ease the early morning start. However. with a following wind and a strong ebb tide the passage to Shotley did not take long. It took us just 2'/, hours from Brightlingsea, in fact, we all arrived a little too early for the Marina to have cleared the pontoon allocated to us. On arrival we found we were allocated the whole of F & G pontoons, thus keeping us all together, which was great. The rest of Sunday was spent settling in and on Sunday evening 60 members sat down to an excellent three-course meal in the marinas ‘Shipwreck Bar’. Monday saw the departure of those who were returning home, with the rest of us locking out at various times to make the short trip to the River Deben. Our single handed members decided to lock out early to take part in a foul weather exercise, being caught in the mother and father of rain storms. but this soon cleared with the rest of the day turning out to be bright and sunny. The majority of the fleet had an overnight stop at Ramsholt, making the 9 mile trip up to the Woodbridge Tidemill Yacht Harbour the following day. Here again the Harbour Master did all he could to keep the fleet together. his task not helped by some visiting yachtsmen not leaving when expected. Nevertheless he did an excellent job. It’s

S. not easy to handle 22 boats in such a confined space, we did our best to help by staggering our arrivals, each boat arriving at five minute intervals. On Tuesday night the crews of the single handed fleet, namely Rasputin, Icarus, Aldebaran, Sundowner, Capricorn II, Winkler and Juno hosted the rest of the flotilla to a second evening ashore at the Yacht Harbour producing, amongst other things, some potent punch which did wonders for the vocal cords during the resultant singalong to the musical accompaniment of Bob Baker and John Walker on their guitars. As with last year, the weather prevented us holding the proposed Bar B Q down river at ‘Prettymans Point’, the strong winds making it difficult to anchor in such numbers. From this point on the fleet started to do a sort of bomb burst. each choosing their time to exit the River Deben and their venue to wait until their return home. All in all it was a most successful and enjoyable get together. Laying-Up Security. Most if not all of you will have laid up your boats by the time you read this, so may I please draw your attention to security. Please remove anything of value if it is at all possible, especially electronics, clocks, barometers, anchors, etc., etc, Also make sure your ladders are kept locked to your trailers. Remember your ladder can be used for boarding other members boats as well as your own. Moorings/Pallets. Moorings will also be in the process of being lifted (see dates and times above) . If you are laying up at the Club please ensure you have a pallet in front of your boat (not too far under the bow or stern). Those not laying up at the Club will find their moorings stored along the sea wall adjacent to the Cruiser Park. Hazardous Waste Disposal. When wintering their boats prior to laying up for the winter, would members please note that the Club has no provision for the disposal of hazardous waste such as used engine oil and batteries. These materials must be taken off site by members and disposed of in such places as Council Refuse Sites etc. Please do not place these in the Club skip. nor beside it. Avoid parking cars in the Cruiser Park. If you must do so, ensure you are nearby to move your car if required, that roadways and other people's trailers are not blocked in. and that you leave plenty of space for manoeuvring of tractors, boats and trailers. Cruiser Fleet Working Party at Stansgate on Sunday 14th December from 10am. Tasks will include the following: 1) Sorting out the dinghy racks. removing any dinghies incorrectly stored. 2) Ensuring all dinghies are identified with boat name. 3) Making sure all trailers are similarly marked. 4) Sorting out and possibly vacating Garage No. 5 to the garage in the Cruiser Park. 5) Servicing the winches. 6) Servicing strops and removing for winter storage. 7) Take down mast derrick. (This was not done last year due to members wishing to use it after the proposed take-down date. Please make sure you are done by 14th December) 8) Generally clearing up the Cruiser Park. There are many jobs to do and. as they say, “Many hands make light work’. Please do not leave it to the willing few - a good turnout would be appreciated and with all hands to the pump we should be through by 3pm or sooner if possible. Ed. 1997 Cadet Week Charles Anderson For Chris and me it seems hard to believe that another Cadet Week slipped by with so many apparently enjoying it. We started the week with 74 cadets and lost a couple on the way due, fortunately, to other commitments and not to an accident. This number was split roughly into two fleets of senior and junior sailors. Lucy Boreham and Sam Ashley put the senior fleet through their paces while the junior instructors were Olly Waller, Claire Davies, Peter Clayton. Jenny Ball, Mark Bulkeley, Grant Strong, Ian Chaplin, Thomas and Rupert Anderson: each junior tutor had a small groups of about 4 or 5 pupils to instruct. The week started with the traditional capsize drill in the teeth of a 5 gusting 6 from the east: a wind which was to stay with us for four of the five days. For the juniors the week then continued with a variety of shore-side activities which included points of sail, knots. parts of the boat and sailing theory all mixed with sailing and relay races afloat. Sadly the strong winds did not allow much helming for the juniors and some of the smaller sailors found even the jib work tough going. The seniors started the week with some assessment trials from which the fleet was subdivided to allow the more advanced sailors to get on with racing while the others were reminded of some fundamentals. The races were keenly fought with only 34 points between first and third places out of four qualifying races. The fleets came together for the Long Distance Race which is normally to the Thirslet buoy and back. However the one day when the wind vanished meant a change to an up-river race followed by a round Osea race. Sadly the former was abandoned and an extremely enjoyable picnic lunch and swimming on the East End of the island saw the wind make with the tide. This allowed the second half of the long distance event to take place and at both junior and senior levels it was greatly enjoyed. We had the good fortune of the Bradwell Outdoor Centre issuing RYA level and stage certificates. I am pleased to confirm that they signed 24 adult stage levels and 5 junior stages. well done to you all. They did mention that the address section in the back of each book must be filled in so please make sure you have done this. Although the club is not itself a recognised training centre, this exception to an RYA rule was made possible by the fact that we boast two RYA instructors on the team in Lucy and Olly. Our thanks go to John Perrott and Malcolm Yarwood at the Centre for their support and for the six Toppers they lent us. These were extensively used by the cadets and one or two adults. I think it fair to say that everybody enjoyed the sailing helped largely by the weather and even more by all those who helped us each day. Although individual thanks were announced at the end of the week Chris and I would like to once again express our gratitude to everyone who helped, from the tutors to the rescue crews. Thank you all once again and we look forward to seeing you all out on the water before next year’s cadet week. contd....

19. COMMODORE’S REPORT 1996 1996 has not been a good year for me and sailing. I have not been able to spare the time to get down to the club at weekends. Those of you who read my notes in Navigans will know that I have been a victim of the continuing change in the education field. I sincerely hope that 1997 should see an end to the results of change which will mean I have to work less and can play more at weekends. I should like to deal with the negative side of the club first. The access road to the club is a cause for concern. The repairs to the damage which the NRA traffic caused are not satisfactory. Privatization has its down side. The NRA is now called the Environmental Agency and seems to be playing ‘hard to get’ over the road repairs. I suspect that the grip which is being put on public spending by the government has something to do with the reluctance of the Environmental Agency to agree to do something about the poor reinstatement work done by the NRA. to the access road. I have to thank Larry for taking on the task of dealing with the Environmental Agency and trying to get some redress. So far he has no success. What we need is a high profile barrister to help fight our claim. The second half of camping fortnight seems to be a cause for concern. Some club members are of the opinion that there is a lack of control and order which results in club facilities being abused. Others are of the opinion that this is a time for relaxation and enjoyment and do not do not feel that there is a problem. The arguments will be considered in the next few months, so any ideas which members may have will be gratefully received by the main committee to allow full and frank discussions to take place in order to resolve any difficulties. Now the good news. I wish to put on the record my sincere thanks to all club members and particularly Executive and Committee members who have worked to ensure that the club ‘works’ for us all. I have no hesitation in mentioning the work done by Frank Bennett in spite of a very serious accident earlier in the year. Fortunately Frank is now well on the way to a full recovery. Ironically this accident led to Frank looking at our Club Insurance and to his horror he found that club members were not covered for ‘waterside activities’ I am pleased to say that this oversight has now been remedied. Management of the MASC and its finances seem to be under much tighter control. I feel confident that the future of MASC remains assured. Mr. Brocklesby and Mr. Marsh visited the club during Camping fortnight and saw the results of the hard work done by MSC members. They were impressed. The membership has gone over the 400 mark this year, which means that the club finances will remain healthy. It is intended to run the series of advertisements in Yachts and Yachting again and to sign post the club whilst this campaign is running. This tactic resulted in members joining the club. I hope you all agree that new galley service provided by Mark Fletcher has been a great success. I am confident that this service will continue next season together with an improved bar service. The latter will depend on agreeing mutually acceptable terms and conditions with Mark. I have to pay tribute to Charles Anderson and Chris Davies and their team of helpers for their efforts in running a very successful cadet week. I believe some 40 young people took part, learnt a great deal and had a great time. Congratulations Charles and Chris and many thanks. It is through these activities that the enjoyment of sailing is allowed to develop in the minds of young people. Enthusiastic youngsters will be the life blood of the sport and this club in the years to come. [ am sure that you will all join me in wishing Jo Jo Anderson and her helm, Dominica, every success in the cadet world championships in Bombay during December. I look forward to seeing many club members at the

20. |} curry evening on the 29 November at 7.30pm at MSC. I understand that both girls will be at the curry evening and I urge you to attend so that you can meet them and wish them the very best of luck. ECPR was again a successful event, which allows the club to work as a team in running a high profile sailing race as well as raising money for RYA Sailability. Thank you Mike and your team, who organised and ran the event. I would like to pay special thanks to the cruiser fleet for their support in providing the mother boats between here and Walton on the Naze. Without your support the event could not take place. Next year will be the tenth anniversary of the ECPR and we are looking forward to a bumper entry from the continent if all goes well. It is hoped that the Prindle and Nacra European Championship will occur just before or just after the Piers race so that continental sailors can attend ECPR and Championships and only have to make one trip across the channel. Keith Starky works very hard every month sending out Navigans to us all. He has had to relinquish this task for reasons connected with his work. Thank you Keith you have done a great job. This means we are looking for a club member to take on this task. See me or put your name on a post card. My hope for the future is that all members of the club can work together so that the interests of all club members can be advanced in 1997 and beyond. Remember sailing has been around for a long time. In 7000 BC., Greek seafarers sailed to the Aegean island of Milos, 75 miles from the mainland, to obtain obsidian. Let’s hope that Marconi Sailing Club will be around in the future Colin Kidner. Sailing Secretary’s Report This season was badly hit by weather with four races abandoned and only 124 individual competitors took part, 7% less than last year. Of a total 38 events the Solo fleet had the best representation sailing 36, followed by the Fast Cats with 35, Dart 15 with 32, medium Cats with 28 and the Handicap Fleet showed up 17 times. Both the Solo and Dart 15 fleets had bigger fleets than last year. In terms of size the fast Cat fleet had the biggest with 22 competitors, next biggest was the Dart 15 with 21, Solo’s had 17, Medium Cats were 13 strong and again the Handicap bringing up the rear with 8. The Club was well represented at a national level and boasts two National Champions. Dave Onyons won the Prindle National Championships and Malcom Gandy is this year’s Kestrel National Champion. We held two successful open meetings, the Dart 15’s and the Solo’s with tumouts of about 30 boats in both cases. I need to address the more routine matter of race duties. This year it has been a struggle to keep the race box properly manned and we need more volunteers to come forward and help. To help get 1997 more organised that 1996 was, I have prepared a preliminary race programme with names pencilled in for duty already. Copies of that programme are available here and, if you want to choose your duty date rather than have it thrust on you, now is the time to talk to John Salmon who is taking over this post next year. Rob Davies

MOORING SHACKLES Following on from Derek's comments re mooring shackles in Cruiser Comments. I would endorse Derek’s comments that moorings should be thoroughly checked during the winter. However the fitting of new shackles, whilst the responsible thing to do, should not induce a sense of complacency. I have found over the past few seasons that shackles near the surface have suffered badly despite being renewed at the beginning of the season and using an anode. Last year, when my mooring was recovered, | found that it was only the wiring that was stopping the pin falling out. This year I changed the shackle under the buoy halfway through the season to make sure. There is a school of thought that says monel seizing wire increases the erosion of the shackles. The scientists amongst us may care to comment on this. On the other hand I have found that plastic cable ties tend to harden and break off, leaving the boat totally at the mercy of the shackle pin thread. A bit of a Catch 22 all this! Perhaps it would be worth sharing a few shackle pin horror stories in Navigans with a view to identifying a ‘best practice’ for ensuring the safety of our boats. My method is to thoroughly grease shackles with petroleum jelly and secure them with two independent wraps of seizing wire. Any other ideas/comments to Navigans. please. Incidentally | understand that the ‘lost’ race marks were also fitted with new shackles at the beginning of the season which, perhaps, underlines my points above. Ray Ball

Notes from Triton of Osea, Ionian Islands, Greece Ray and Hazel left England in March 1997, and travelled overland via Calais, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, and Switzerland to Brindisi in Italy from where they took a ferry to Greece to join their boat: It was great to be back on board and we set about tackling the jobs we had scheduled for the season. Cleaning, painting, varnishing. gluing - all the usual chores plus a bit of plumbing, mechanics and electrics etc. As we had the car this year we managed to get out and about the surrounding area a bit and, as everywhere in Greece seems to be steeped in history, mythology and ruins, there is plenty to see. We had the boat relaunched on 13th May and sailed into the Gulf of Amvrakia, a local nature reserve which has dolphins, otters, jackals, pelicans and other rare sea birds. We were in company with Jack and Jackie Manning who are on their fourth season here, so are local experts on the area. That first balmy evening we sat in our cockpits in the setting sun having a leisurely drink and watching the local Fisherman setting their nets while standing up in their small boats, and Jack said “This is one of those evenings you will always remember.” How right he was! By the middle of the night the wind had turned. we had swung onto a lee shore and we had one fishing net around our anchor chain and another round our propeller and rudder. Not a comfortable position to be in. However, it could have been worse and after some hours of diving and cutting, Ray and Jack finally freed us. The high spot of the disaster was that in the nets they cut off were a dozen Tiger prawns, so at least we got a tasty lunch. Over the next few weeks we had the Manning Cook’s Tour of their favourite anchorages. Roy and Margaret Bellord were with us briefly at the start of the season but soon set off for the French canals as they were making their way back to the UK. We had also been listening out on the HF radio for Joan and Dave in Dajo, following their progress through the Balearics, Sardinia and Sicily, and they finally arrived on 17th June for another Marconi reunion. They arrived about 1.30am into the bay at Sivota on the Island of Levkas. It was not easy in the dark so we talked them in on the VHF and then Ray and Jack went out to meet them in the dinghy (they were in company with another yacht) and they each took on a pilot for the last part of the journey and anchoring. Great celebrations and rather a late night for us all. It was very good fun to sail together after all this time and we had great pleasure in accompanying them to the spots we had now made our favourites. We had one evening at a taverna run with a rod of iron by a matriarchal figure nicknamed Olive Oil by the Brits due to her likeness to Popeye's girlfriend. This lady, of a certain age, will treat the customers to the amazing sight of her dancing with a table on her head - usually searing her apron! One of her sons leads the traditional Greek dancing in which everyone is encouraged to join and, inevitably, ends up with at least one yottie falling over. Needless to say a good time was had by all. July and August tend to get more crowded here with both the Greeks and Italians having their annual holidays and we decided to take the opportunity to visit a less popular area and explore the Gulfs of Patras and Corinth. By now we were all ‘doing our own thing’ and not sailing in company, and we had a quiet leisurely cruise calling in at new harbours and finding peaceful little bays on our trip south. The weather had been particularly kind to us this year and we have had some good sailing winds. Through the gulf of Corinth the strength of the wind is always enhanced and we surfed into Trizonia in 35 knots of wind. gusting up to 43 knots (force 8. gusting 9). There were. luckily, plenty of willing hands to help and we were soon safely alongside a quay in the abandoned marina (started about 5 years ago but the project shelved due to lack of money). Trizonia is a delightful little island, no vehicles and everything delivered by the ferry which is about 25° long and carries people, animals and all goods. We had arrived a week early in order to sail further east to visit the ancient site of Delfi before returning to Trizonia in time for Ray's special birthday party get-together with other boats, but as the strong winds persisted we did our sightseeing by taxi and stayed snugly in harbour. In the area surrounding the Ionian Islands where we are usually based, which is known as the Inland Sea, the Greeks have got used to the many foreign visitors, but in the gulf area they do not see so many and are not used to speaking English. Those who can, really enjoy the opportunity to speak to you. In the town of Messolongi we were befriended by a couple of locals. Christos showed us his pride and joy, a vintage Harley Davidson motorbike which he and his son are rebuilding and Spiros who owns a local restaurant and became a great friend over the times we went there. He took us up into the mountains for the day and showed us his local village. It seems a tough lifestyle, keeping goats or growing tobacco, and life is still very basic. We had a typical Greek lunch including fried pumpkin which we had never tasted before. It was a wonderful day and quite an eye-opener on how other people live.

6. fh Since returning to the Inland Sea we have continued our gentle cruising style. The weather has not been as stormy or as windy as this time last year and it has been possible to visit some of the areas which are very beautiful but only tenable in calm conditions. The general holiday season is now drawing to an end and even the most popular anchorages are no longer crowded with is wonderful. We have really enjoyed this year and it has been so different as we have done no passage making. The novelty of returning to towns and anchorages that we have visited before has been very relaxing. We have made many new friends and have met up with many people that we met before in previous seasons and are now even recognised by the local shopkeepers and taverna owners. The Greek Ionian Islands are an ideal cruising ground. Beautiful scenery, friendly locals, cheap tavernas (average two course meal with wine, approx £6). and lots of free. safe, anchorages. You can be charged on the town quays, although it is a bit hit and miss, and so far this year we have only paid out 480 drachmas (£1.10), which was for two nights tied to a quay. Hazel and Ray Beckett, September 1997
